title: 1,000 Hawaiian Words You Will Never Forget
subtitle: 500 verbs and 500 nouns, each with a ridiculous memory story
author: Olin Kealoha Lagon
notes: No official frequency ranking of Hawaiian words exists. The lists are built from everyday words beginners hear and use most. Verbs 1 to 100 are the core action words. Numbers are for order, not an exact frequency rank.
Hawaiian treats describing words (to be big, to be red) as verbs, so many of those are in the verb list.
Sound hooks are memory tricks, not perfect pronunciation. Check words against wehewehe.org and native speakers.

Version 1.1 (2026-09-24): every word was audited against Pukui-Elbert (1986) and Māmaka Kaiao on Wehewehe Wikiwiki (wehe.hilo.hawaii.edu), with an independent second check. Spellings, meanings, stress marks, bonus facts and the stories tied to any corrected word were fixed. A native speaker review is still the gold standard.

pronunciation_guide.okina: The ʻokina (ʻ) is a quick catch in the throat, like the break in uh-oh.
pronunciation_guide.kahako: The kahakō (ā ē ī ō ū) means hold that vowel a little longer.
pronunciation_guide.w: W often sounds like a soft V after i and e, and sometimes after a.
pronunciation_guide.every_vowel: Every vowel is said. Nothing is silent.
pronunciation_guide.hoo_prefix: Hoʻo in front of a word means to make it happen. Lohe is hear, hoʻolohe is listen.

schema.id: v001 to v500 for verbs, n001 to n500 for nouns
schema.hawaiian: the word with ʻokina and kahakō
schema.search_key: the word without ʻokina or kahakō, lowercase, for search
schema.pronunciation: English-style syllables, CAPS on the stressed syllable
schema.sound_hook: the English sound-alike used in the story
schema.story_paragraphs: the memory story, one string per paragraph
schema.say_it: an action to do while saying the word
schema.bonus: extra fact or phrase, or null
schema.backup: optional second memory trick, usually null
schema.picture: 3 to 8 word summary of the scene for review cards

words.say_it: Point at the door and yell "Heh-leh!" like you are launching that rooster.
words.bonus: Hele mai is come here. Hele aku is go away.
words.picture: Tūtū yelling "Hey, Leh!" at a racing rooster
story_paragraphs: There is a horse race at Kapiʻolani Park, and one of the racers is a rooster named Leh. He will not move. The gate opens and he just stands there pecking at a malasada.

Then Tūtū stands up in the bleachers, cups her hands and screams "HEY, LEH!" and the rooster takes off like a rocket. Feathers everywhere. The second she stops yelling, he stops dead. So she yells the whole race. "HEY, LEH! HEY, LEH!" He passes every horse and wins by a mile. Tūtū loses her voice for a week.

words.english: to return, to go back home
words.say_it: "Ho," tiny freeze, "ee." Throw your arm out on the ho and flinch on the ee.
words.bonus: Hoʻi hou means come back again.
words.picture: Slippah boomerang, "Ho... EE!"
story_paragraphs: You throw a rubbah slippah like a boomerang down the beach. As it flies away it yells "HO!" At the very end it freezes in the air for half a second (that is the ʻokina), then it squeals "EEE!" and flies straight back and smacks you in the face.
No matter how far you throw that slippah, it always comes home. Ho... ʻi.

words.english: to run, to sail, to ride
words.say_it: Knock on your chest like it is hollow and say "ho-lo" with each knock.
words.bonus: Holoholo means to go out cruising for fun. That bunny is always holoholo.
words.picture: Hollow chocolate bunny running the marathon
story_paragraphs: A giant hollow chocolate bunny is running the Honolulu Marathon. Because it is hollow, every step echoes inside its body. "HOLLOW. HOLLOW. HOLLOW." At mile 10 it jumps on a surfboard and sails across the Ala Wai. At mile 20 it steals a moped and rides the rest of the way, still echoing.
Run, sail, ride. The hollow bunny does all three.

words.say_it: Hop in place and say "leh-leh" on each hop.
words.picture: Giant flea with a ʻukulele
story_paragraphs: A flea the size of a chihuahua is playing a tiny ʻukulele. Every time it strums, it jumps so high it flies over Diamond Head. Strum, "le-le," launch. Strum, "le-le," launch. Pilots have to swerve around it.

The name ʻukulele is built from ʻuku, flea, and lele, jump, so it literally reads "jumping flea." Why the instrument got that name is not settled. One popular explanation is fingers hopping across the strings like fleas.

words.say_it: Stand up straight, chest out, and let out one long "koooo."
words.picture: Pigeon at attention, "Koooo"
story_paragraphs: A pigeon on top of a bus stop refuses to sit. It stands at full attention like a palace guard, chest out, going "KOOOOOOO" for hours. People throw bread. It will not bend. A kid tries to push it over. It just keeps standing and cooing.
That long coo is the kahakō. Hold it.

words.english: to sit, to stay, to live
words.say_it: Point at a chair. "No. Ho."
words.bonus: Noho is also the word for chair.
words.picture: "No, Ho!" Santa moves in
story_paragraphs: Santa shows up at your house in July. He wants to keep moving. You point at a chair and say, like a strict parent, "NO. HO." He sits. You say it again. He stays. By Christmas he has moved in, gets his own mail and hogs the remote.
Sit, stay, live. Santa did all three because you said "No, Ho."

words.say_it: "Pee," freeze, "ee." Lift your knee on each one like you are climbing.
words.bonus: Piʻi is also used for anything rising, like water or prices.
words.picture: Kid who needs to pee on Koko Head stairs
story_paragraphs: A little kid is climbing the Koko Head stairs and he really, really needs to pee. The only bathroom is at the very top. Every step up he whimpers "PEE." At every landing he freezes, crosses his legs (the ʻokina), and squeaks "EE!" Then keeps climbing. Pee... ee. Pee... ee. All 1,048 steps.

words.say_it: Wave an invisible hat. "Ee-ho!"
words.picture: Paniolo riding the elevator down, "Ee-ho!"
story_paragraphs: A paniolo rides an elevator down from the 40th floor like it is a bucking horse. The whole way down he waves his hat and yells "EEEE-HO!" The doors open in the lobby and he rides the elevator right out into the street.
The kid from piʻi is going up. The paniolo is going down.

words.say_it: Flop onto the couch while you say it.
words.picture: Coconut tree fall onto a bull, "Oo-leh!"
story_paragraphs: A guy climbs a coconut tree, loses his grip and falls in super slow motion. "HAAAAAA" as he lets go (that long ā). Then he hiccups in midair (the ʻokina). Then he lands flat on the back of a bull, and the whole crowd yells "OO-LEH!" like a bullfight.
Haaa. Hiccup. Oo-leh.

words.say_it: Do a freestyle stroke with your arm and say "ow" each time.
words.bonus: Say it twice and you get ʻauʻau, to bathe. That one is coming up soon.
words.picture: Jellyfish stings, "Ow!"
story_paragraphs: You jump in the ocean and every single stroke, a tiny jellyfish stings you. "ʻOW! ʻOW! ʻOW!" But you are stubborn, so you swim all the way to Molokaʻi, yelling ow the whole way.
The little catch at the front is your throat closing for a split second before each ow.

words.say_it: Point at your own eye and say "eye" while pretending to shovel food in.
words.bonus: ʻAi is also the word for food, especially poi.
words.picture: Eyeball at the buffet
story_paragraphs: A giant eyeball with little legs walks into an all-you-can-eat buffet. It has no mouth, so it eats straight through its pupil. Spaghetti hanging out of the eye. Kalua pig disappearing into the eye. It blinks and a whole pan of mac salad is gone. The manager just watches, horrified.

words.say_it: Tip back an invisible cup. "Ee-noo!"
words.bonus: Inu wai means drink water.
words.picture: Camel at the juice bar, "Ee! New!"
story_paragraphs: A camel walks into a juice bar. The bartender slides over a brand new flavor. The camel takes one sip, its eyes go wide and it screams "EE! NEW!" Then it drinks the whole blender. Then the ice machine. Then the fish tank. Every time it tastes something, "EE! NEW!"

words.say_it: In a sleepy cow voice. "Mo-eh." Twice. Feel dumb. That is the point.
words.bonus: Moe also means to lie down, which is what the cow did. Hiamoe is to sleep or fall asleep, the moment its knees gave out. A dream you have while sleeping is moeʻuhane, whatever that cow is dreaming about on the road.
words.backup: Picture a whole family asleep on one big mat after a long party. Every single snore comes out the same. "Moe... moe... moe..."
words.picture: Giant cow too tired to finish its moo
story_paragraphs: It is 3 in the morning and you are driving home on a dark two lane road. You come around a bend and there is a cow standing in the middle of the road. This thing is the size of a two story house. It has been awake for four straight days. Its eyes are bloodshot and it is swaying side to side like a palm tree in a windstorm.
You honk. The cow slowly lifts its giant head to moo at you. "MOOOO..." but it is so tired it cannot finish. Halfway through, its eyelids drop and the moo just dies into a long, sleepy "...eh."
"Mo... eh."

Its knees buckle, it tips over in slow motion and BOOM, the whole road bounces. Now it is snoring, and every snore sounds the same. "Moe... moe... moe..." You cannot get around it, so you climb onto its big warm belly and go to sleep too, rising and falling with every "moe."

words.say_it: Throw your arms open like an opera singer. "Ahhh-lahhh!"
words.bonus: Ala is also the word for road or path. Hoʻāla means to wake someone else up.
words.picture: Opera singer alarm clock
story_paragraphs: Your alarm clock is an opera singer who lives in your closet. At 5 a.m. the door bursts open and she belts "AAAAH-LAAAAA!" so loud your eyes pop open and the windows crack. She even wakes up the sleeping cow from moe, which stands up very confused in the middle of the road.

words.say_it: Big gasp in on "hah," slow breath out on "noo."
words.picture: Diver's first gasp of brand new air
story_paragraphs: A scuba diver runs out of air 60 feet down. He kicks like crazy, rockets to the surface, bursts out of the water and takes the biggest gasp of his life. "HAAAA!" Then he tastes that first breath and it is so fresh it is like brand "NEW" air.
Haaa. New.

words.say_it: Pinch your own finger and yelp "Ah-kee!"
words.bonus: Nahu is the general word for a real bite, like a dog bite. ʻAki is the quick nip that lets go.
words.picture: Crab on your car key, "Ah! Key!"
story_paragraphs: You drop your car key on the reef and a crab grabs it. You reach down. The crab nips your finger, a quick little snap, and lets go. You yell "AH! KEY!"
You reach again. Nip, let go. "AH! KEY!" Reach. Nip, let go. "AH! KEY!" It never holds on. It just snaps and backs off, like a tiny boxer with pinchers.

A crowd gathers on the reef. Every time your hand goes down, they all yell "AH! KEY!" with you. After forty tiny nips the crab gets bored and drops the key. Your fingers look like they were tickled by a stapler, but you drive home a hero.

words.say_it: Say "mo-mo-nee" and do a big exaggerated gulp at the end.
words.bonus: You will also see the shorter form moni.
words.picture: Piggy bank yelling "Mo money!"
story_paragraphs: Your piggy bank comes alive. It opens its mouth and yells "MO MONEY!" then swallows every coin on the table. Then your wallet. Then your credit cards. Then your car keys (the crab gives them up). It gets so round it rolls down the street, still yelling "MO MONEY!" and gulping everything in its path.

words.say_it: Karate chop the air. "Koo-HAH!"
words.picture: Karate llama, "Koo-HAH!"
story_paragraphs: There is a llama at the petting zoo that knows karate. Every time it spits, it throws a karate chop and yells "KOO-HAH!" and a loogie flies 40 feet across the parking lot. Kids line up to watch. Parents are furious. The llama bows after every shot.

words.say_it: Dip your toe in invisible hot water. "Ow-ow!"
words.bonus: Lumi ʻauʻau is the bathroom, the ow-ow room.
words.picture: Hot bath, "Ow-ow!"
story_paragraphs: Remember swimming with the jellyfish, ʻau, one ow? Now you get home and jump in a bath that is way too hot. "OW-OW!" Two ows. One ow is swimming in the ocean. Two ows is sitting in a hot tub that is cooking you like a lobster.

words.english: to rest, to take a break
words.say_it: Lean back with your hands behind your head. "Ho-ʻo-MAH-hah."
words.bonus: That is the hoʻo trick. Hoʻomaha is also used for a vacation.
words.picture: "Whoa, Ma!" "Ha!" in the hammock
story_paragraphs: Ma has worked 30 years without a day off. She finally gets to the beach, drops into a hammock and pulls her hat over her face. The whole family runs up and yells "WHOA, MA!" She does not move. She just laughs "HA!" and goes right back to resting.
Whoa, Ma. Ha.

words.say_it: Pull back like you just saw something gross. "Eek-eh!"
words.bonus: ʻIke is also the word for knowledge.
words.picture: Germ-vision glasses, "Eek, eh!"
story_paragraphs: You put on a pair of magic glasses and suddenly you can see everything. Every germ on your phone. Every crumb in your keyboard. The tiny bugs living in your pillow, waving at you. You scream "EEK! EH!" and now you know way more than you ever wanted to.
Seeing and knowing are the same word. Once you see it, you know it.

words.say_it: Make binoculars with your hands. "Naah-naah."
words.bonus: Nānā mai! means look here!
words.picture: Nana with binoculars
story_paragraphs: Your Nana sits by the front window with binoculars the size of a car engine. She watches the whole street all day. Who parked crooked. Who came home late. Who is dating who. When you try to sneak in at midnight, a spotlight clicks on and a voice sings "Naaaah naaaah, I seeeee you."
Nana is always nānā. Hold both vowels long like she is stretching out her stare.

words.say_it: Whisper it low. "Lo... heh."
words.bonus: Lohe can also mean to obey, like when you hear and actually do it.
words.picture: Giant ear hears a low "hey"
story_paragraphs: There is a giant ear living under your house. It hears everything. You go to the far corner of the yard and whisper really low, "hey." The ground rumbles and a deep voice from under the house says "I HEARD THAT."
Low. Hey. The ear hears even a low hey.

words.say_it: Cup your hand behind your ear. "Ho-ʻo-lo-heh."
words.picture: Giant ear leaning in, "Whoa!"
story_paragraphs: Same giant ear under the house. But now it is trying hard. It cups a huge hand around itself and leans in. When it finally catches your whisper, it goes "WHOA... low, hey!"
Lohe is hear. Hoʻo makes it happen on purpose. Hearing on purpose is listening.

words.english: to kiss, to sniff, to smell
words.say_it: Lean your nose toward something and say "ho-nee."
words.bonus: The honi is the traditional greeting where two people touch noses and share breath. That is exactly what the bear did.
words.picture: Bear sniffing honey
story_paragraphs: A big brown bear walks up to a jar of honey, presses its nose right against the glass and takes a long sniff. Then it gives the jar a big kiss. Then it walks over to you, presses its nose to your nose, breathes in and whispers "honey."

words.say_it: Poke the table and drag out "Paaah."
words.bonus: Pā is also a fence, a yard or a dish. In Hawaiian, even the wind can pā you.
words.picture: Pa touching wet paint
story_paragraphs: There is a fresh WET PAINT sign on the wall. Your Pa cannot stand it. He has to touch it. "Paaaaa, don't!" But he does. Then he touches the car. Then the dog. Then the ceiling. Everything in the house has Pa's handprint on it.

words.say_it: Grab your head like it hurts. "Man-ah-ow."
words.bonus: Manaʻo is also an opinion or idea. He aha kou manaʻo? means what do you think?
words.picture: Caveman, "Man, ah, ow!"
story_paragraphs: A caveman is trying to think for the very first time in human history. He squeezes his head with both hands, his face turns red, steam comes out of his ears and he groans "MAN... AH... OW!" Thinking hurts.

words.say_it: Snap your fingers on the end. "Ho-ʻo-mah-NAH-oh!"
words.picture: Ghost jolts the caveman's memory
story_paragraphs: Same caveman. He lost his club. He thinks so hard it hurts, "man, ah, ow," and then a ghost floats through the wall and yells "WHOA!" The shock knocks the memory loose. "WHOA... MAN... AH... OW! It's under the rock!"
Think plus hoʻo. Making the thought come back is remembering.

words.say_it: Wave off an invisible bowl. "Poi? Nah."
words.picture: "Poi? Nah." on repeat
story_paragraphs: You are at a lūʻau. Aunty offers you poi. You say "Poi? Nah." Five seconds later you forget you said that. She offers again. "Poi? Nah." You forget again. This goes on for three hours. "Poi? Nah." "Poi? Nah." By the end of the night Aunty is crying and you still have no idea what happened.

words.say_it: Slap your forehead. "Ho-ʻo-mao-PO-po!"
words.bonus: Maopopo on its own means clear or understood. Maopopo iaʻu means I understand.
words.picture: "Whoa, my, oh, Popo!"
story_paragraphs: Your Popo is teaching you how to use the TV remote for the 40th time. Blank stare. She shows you again. Blank stare. Then on the 41st try, a light bulb goes on over your head and you shout "WHOA... MY... OH... POPO!" You finally get it.

words.say_it: Wave like you are meeting a crowd. "Oh-LEH-lo."
words.bonus: ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi is the Hawaiian language.
words.picture: Parrot keynote, "Oh, hello"
story_paragraphs: There is a parrot that only knows two words. "OH, HELLO." It says it to everyone. The mailman. The dog. The refrigerator. Somehow it gets booked as the keynote speaker at a giant conference. It walks out on stage, the lights hit, 5,000 people lean in, and it says "OHHH, HELLO." Standing ovation.
Oh-hello, pushed together, is ʻōlelo. Stretch the first O.

words.say_it: Lean in like you have gossip. "Hah-ee."
words.bonus: Haʻi ʻōlelo is a speech.
words.picture: Gossip aunty at Longs
story_paragraphs: There is an aunty at Longs who cannot keep a secret. She walks up to you and says "Hah... ee!" like "Hi!" but with a little catch, and before you can say anything back she tells you everything. Who got married. Who got divorced. What your cousin did at graduation. You only came in for toothpaste.
Every story starts with that "Hah-ee."

words.say_it: Tap your knee. "Knee-now?" Hold the "nee" a little long for the kahakō.
words.bonus: Nīnau is also the word for a question.
words.picture: Toddler on your knee, "Knee now?"
story_paragraphs: A toddler is hanging onto your knee like a koala. Every two seconds she tugs and asks a question. "Why is the sky blue? Can we go now? KNEE NOW? KNEE NOW?" She will not let go of your knee until you answer, and she wants the answer now.

words.say_it: Smack the table like a buzzer. "Pah-neh!"
words.picture: Frying pan buzzer game show
story_paragraphs: You are on a game show where the only way to answer is to smack a frying pan with a spoon. BONG! "PAN, EH!" Every contestant is slamming pans. The host asks the capital of Hawaiʻi. BONG! "PAN, EH! Honolulu!" The studio is so loud people in the audience are wearing earmuffs.

words.say_it: Hands around your mouth. "Kaah-HEH-ah!"
words.picture: "Car! Hey! Ah!"
story_paragraphs: You call your car like a dog. You stand in the driveway, whistle and yell "CAR! HEY! AH!" Your car starts itself, its headlights blink like happy eyes, and it rolls over and nuzzles your leg. The neighbors film the whole thing.

words.say_it: Pat the seat next to you. "Kah-mah-ʻee-lee-oh."
words.picture: "Come, my Leo" lion at the coffee shop
story_paragraphs: There is a lion named Leo sitting alone at a coffee shop. You pat the chair next to you and say "Come, my Leo." He sits down and the two of you talk story for six hours. He tells you about his ex. You tell him about work. The barista keeps refilling the lion's latte.
Come-my-Leo, said fast, is kamaʻilio.

words.say_it: Pirate voice, fist in the air. "ʻAe!"
words.picture: Pirates voting "Aye!"
story_paragraphs: A pirate ship is voting on everything. "Should we eat lunch?" "ʻAE!" "Should we paint the ship pink?" "ʻAE!" "Should we give the parrot from ʻōlelo a raise?" "ʻAE!" They agree to every single thing, and by sunset the ship is pink and the parrot is the captain.

words.english: to refuse, to deny, to say no
words.say_it: Shake your head hard. "Hoh-OH-leh."
words.bonus: ʻOle means not, without or zero. Hōʻole is the hoʻo trick again, making something a "no."
words.picture: Haunted golf hole spits the ball out
story_paragraphs: There is a haunted golf hole at the course. Every time someone putts, the ball rolls right up to the hole, and the hole spits it back out and shouts "HO! ʻOLE!" It refuses every ball. Pros cry. Nobody has ever scored on it.

words.say_it: Hold up your pinky and hiccup. "Ho-ʻo-HEE-kee."
words.picture: Hiccuping gecko pinky promise
story_paragraphs: A gecko on your kitchen wall makes you a pinky promise. It swears it will eat every cockroach in the house. But every time it makes a promise, it hiccups. "WHOA... HEE-KEE!" It raises its tiny pinky, hiccups again, and then eats a cockroach the size of a slipper to prove it.

words.say_it: Hold your fingers an inch apart. "Ho-ʻo-puny-PUNY."
words.bonus: Punipuni on its own means fake or a lie.
words.picture: Puny fish, "marlin"
story_paragraphs: A guy comes back from fishing and says he caught a 400 pound marlin. Then he opens his cooler. It is a fish the size of a french fry. Everybody on the pier looks in and says "WHOA... PUNY PUNY." He keeps insisting it is a marlin. Nobody believes him ever again.

words.say_it: Deep whale voice. "Ah-LOW-hah."
words.picture: Whale's "a low ha"
story_paragraphs: You already know this one, but here is a picture anyway. A humpback whale pulls up next to your kayak and sings one deep, low note that shakes your whole body. "A... LOW... HAAAA." Then it gently bumps your kayak with its nose like a hug. You feel loved by a 40 ton animal.
A low ha. Aloha.

words.say_it: Stomp your feet on each beat. "Mah-keh-MAH-keh!"
words.bonus: Makemake au i ka poi means I want poi.
words.picture: Toddler screaming for a mocha
story_paragraphs: Warning. This is not the English word "make." Every vowel gets said.

A toddler is in a coffee shop throwing a tantrum on the floor because she wants a mocha. She is kicking and screaming "MAH-KEH-MAH-KEH! MAH-KEH-MAH-KEH!" which sounds a lot like "mocha mocha." The barista gives up and makes her one. She wants another.

words.say_it: Flap your arms. "Ah-kah-AH-kah!"
words.picture: Crow cackling at people who trip
story_paragraphs: There is a crow on the power line that laughs at everybody. Someone trips on the sidewalk. "AH-KA AH-KA!" Someone drops their plate lunch. "AH-KA AH-KA!" Someone walks into a glass door. The crow laughs so hard it falls off the wire, and now the whole street laughs back at it.

words.say_it: Siren voice, long on the end. "Oo-ehhhh."
words.picture: Baby siren on the ambulance
story_paragraphs: An ambulance comes screaming down the street, but when it stops, there is no siren. It is a giant baby strapped to the roof, crying. "OOO-EHHHHHH! OOO-EHHHHHH!" Cars pull over. Dogs howl along. The baby will not stop until somebody gives it a pacifier the size of a surfboard.

words.say_it: Big closed-mouth grin, then whisper "mee-no-AH-kah."
words.picture: Crow in the library, "Me? No ʻaka"
story_paragraphs: That laughing crow from ʻakaʻaka? Now it is stuck in a library. It sees a man trip over a book cart and it wants to laugh so bad, but the librarian is glaring. So it just smiles, a huge silent beak grin. It thinks "Me? No ʻaka." Me, no laugh. Just a smile.

words.say_it: Scrunch your face and cross your arms. "Hoo-HOOOO."
words.picture: Furious owl
story_paragraphs: An owl is furious. Somebody took its branch. Its feathers puff up to twice its size, steam shoots out of its ears and it screams "HOO-HOOOOOO!" The second hoo is extra long because it is extra mad.

words.say_it: Big smile, arms wide. "How-OH-lee!"
words.bonus: Hauʻoli lā hānau means happy birthday.
words.picture: "How, Ollie?!" helicopter tail
story_paragraphs: Your dog Ollie is so happy to see you that his tail wags hard enough to lift him off the ground like a helicopter. He floats around the living room knocking over lamps. You just stand there and ask "HOW, OLLIE?!"

words.say_it: Shaky voice, hands up. "Mah-KAH... oo."
words.picture: "Ma! Cow!"
story_paragraphs: Remember the giant sleepy cow from moe? A little kid is walking past, and the cow suddenly wakes up and stands. Two stories tall. The kid runs screaming to his mom, "MA! COW! MA! COW!" He hides behind her, shaking.
Ma, cow. Makaʻu. The little catch before the last "oo" is the kid gulping.

words.say_it: Shift your weight side to side. "Ho-po-HO-po."
words.picture: Pacing grasshopper
story_paragraphs: A grasshopper is pacing in the kitchen. Hop to the left. Hop to the right. Did it leave the stove on? Did it lock the door? Is the lizard from hoʻohiki coming? "Hopper, hopper, hopper, hopper." It cannot stop hopping back and forth, worrying.

words.say_it: Cover your face and giggle. "Hee-lah-HEE-lah."
words.bonus: You will hear this one a lot in local English. "No be hilahila."
words.picture: Ripped pants, "hee-la hee-la"
story_paragraphs: A huge tough-looking football player bends over to tie his shoe and his pants rip right down the back in front of the whole stadium. His face turns bright red. He covers his face with his helmet and giggles "hee-la, hee-la" while tiptoeing off the field.

words.english: to do, to make, to work
words.say_it: Pretend to hammer. "Hah-nah, hah-nah."
words.bonus: Hana hou means do it again, the encore shout at a concert. Careful, Hāna the town on Maui has a long ā. The verb is short.
words.picture: Hannah the eight-armed robot
story_paragraphs: Hannah is a robot with eight arms who cannot stop working. She builds a house before breakfast. She fixes your car during lunch. At night she is still going, knitting a sweater for the sleepy cow. Her boss begs her to stop. "Hannah, please!" She just keeps making things.

words.say_it: Pretend to carry something heavy and hot. "LAH-veh!"
words.picture: Tourist carrying lava
story_paragraphs: A tourist at the volcano scoops up a bucket of glowing hot lava and carries it back to his hotel room. "LAVA! I'm taking LAVA!" He carries it through the lobby, into the elevator and onto his bed. The bed catches fire. The hotel catches fire. He is still carrying it.
Lava sounds like lawe. And yes, you should never take lava rocks home.

words.say_it: Hold out your hand like you are offering something. "Haah-AH-vee."
words.picture: Harvey gives away his pants
story_paragraphs: There is a guy named Harvey who gives away everything. His car. His house. His couch. His shoes. His pants. He stands on the corner in his boxers handing out his last sandwich. Every time he hands something over, he laughs "HAAAH" and then hiccups before the "vee."
Haaah, hiccup, vee. Harvey.

words.say_it: Point like you are sending the dog. "Kee-ee!"
words.bonus: Kiʻi is also the word for a picture or statue.
words.picture: Dog fetching keys, "Key-ee!"
story_paragraphs: You send your dog to fetch your keys. It sprints off, comes back 3 seconds later, drops them in your hand and squeals "KEY-EE!" Then it goes and fetches everyone else's keys too. By noon the whole neighborhood is locked out and your dog is sitting on a mountain of keys.

words.say_it: Snatch the air. "Ho-poo!"
words.picture: Octopus basketball, "Ho-poo!"
story_paragraphs: An octopus is playing basketball. Every shot anybody takes, one of its eight arms shoots out and catches the ball. It yells "HOOP!" every time it grabs one, but it cannot say the P cleanly so it comes out "HO-POO!" Nobody on the other team scores all season.

words.say_it: Flick your wrist like you are tossing something. "Kee-OH-lah!"
words.picture: Crayons out the car window
story_paragraphs: A kid in the back seat on a road trip gets mad and starts tossing crayons out the window, one after another. "Kee-OH-lah! Kee-OH-lah!" It rhymes with Crayola. By the time the car reaches the North Shore, there is a rainbow trail of crayons all the way back to town.

words.say_it: Pull an invisible rope with both hands. "Hoo-kee!"
words.bonus: Huki and pahu (next) are the pull and push pair.
words.picture: Fish pulls the fisherman, "Hook-ee!"
story_paragraphs: A fisherman hooks a fish, but the fish is stronger. The fish pulls him off the pier, across the bay, and out to sea on water skis made of slippers. The whole way the fish is yelling "HOOK-EE! HOOK-EE!" and pulling harder.

words.say_it: Push your palms forward. "Pah-hoo!"
words.bonus: Pahu is also the word for a drum or a box. That is why Pa is pushing a drum.
words.picture: Pa pushing a giant drum, "Pa, who?"
story_paragraphs: Your Pa is pushing a giant drum up a hill. It is taller than a truck. He is sweating and grunting. The neighbors come out and ask "PA, WHO? Who told you to do this?" He cannot answer. He just keeps pushing. The drum rolls back and flattens him. He gets up and pushes again.

words.say_it: Lift your arms overhead. "Haaah-PIE!"
words.bonus: Hāpai also means pregnant, carrying a baby.
words.picture: Waiter lifting a giant pie
story_paragraphs: A waiter comes out of the kitchen lifting a pie the size of a trampoline over his head. His arms are shaking. He groans "HAAAAH..." and then shouts "PIE!" as he lifts it the last inch. Then he carries it across the restaurant without dropping a crumb.

words.say_it: Scissor your fingers. "Oh-kee. Oh-kee."
words.bonus: ʻOkiʻoki means to cut into pieces.
words.picture: "Okie" barber
story_paragraphs: A barber with scissors the size of hedge clippers says "OKIE" every time he snips. "Okie." Snip. "Okie." Snip. You only wanted a trim. He keeps saying okie. Now you are bald and so are both of your eyebrows. "Okie dokie," he says, and hands you a mirror.

words.say_it: Pull an invisible tray out of the oven. "Koo-keh!"
words.picture: Chef who only makes cookies
story_paragraphs: This one came into Hawaiian from English, so it is a gift. Picture a chef who can only cook cookies. You order a steak, you get a cookie shaped like a steak. You order soup, you get a bowl of melted cookie. He shouts "KOO-KEH!" every time he pulls a tray out of the oven.

words.say_it: Scrub the air in circles. "Ho-LO-ee!"
words.bonus: Holoi pā means wash the dishes. Pā is dish.
words.picture: Hollow bunny in the spin cycle
story_paragraphs: The hollow chocolate bunny from holo finished its marathon and it is filthy. It climbs into the washing machine. The spin cycle kicks on and the bunny screams "HOLLOW-EEEEE!" as it whips around. The machine shakes so hard it walks across the laundry room and out the front door.
Holo plus a scream. Holoi.

words.say_it: Pat the dirt down. "Kah-noo."
words.bonus: Kanu also means to bury.
words.picture: Canoe tree
story_paragraphs: A farmer digs a hole in the loʻi and plants a whole canoe like it is a seed. Waters it. Next morning, a giant canoe tree has shot up, and there are baby canoes hanging off every branch like mangoes. People come with ladders to pick them.
Canoe sounds like kanu.

words.english: to gather, to harvest, to pick up
words.say_it: Scoop with both arms and giggle. "Oh-hee!"
words.picture: Mango rain, "Oh, hee hee!"
story_paragraphs: You are under a mango tree and a storm shakes it. Mangoes start raining down on your head. Bonk. Bonk. Bonk. Instead of running, you start gathering them in your shirt, giggling like a kid. "OH, HEE HEE HEE!" Your shirt is so full you can barely walk.

words.say_it: Shovel motion. "Eh-lee!"
words.picture: Ellie the elephant digging
story_paragraphs: Ellie the elephant is at Waikīkī digging with her trunk. She digs so deep she hits water, then lava, then comes out the other side of the world in a rice field. A farmer looks down the hole and yells "EH, ELLIE!"

words.say_it: Pound your fist on your palm. "Koo-ee!"
words.bonus: Kuʻi also means to punch. Kuʻi ʻai is pounding poi.
words.picture: Kung fu poi pounder
story_paragraphs: A kung fu master is pounding kalo on a board with a stone poi pounder. Every strike he yells "KOO... EE!" with a sharp catch in the middle, like a karate move. The poi comes out so smooth that people line up around the block.

words.english: to take care of, to protect
words.say_it: Pet the air gently. "Maah-LAH-mah."
words.bonus: Mālama ʻāina means care for the land.
words.picture: "Ma, llama!"
story_paragraphs: Your mom adopts a llama and treats it better than any of her kids. It gets the good bedroom. She tucks it in. She brushes its hair. She makes it musubi. You walk in and she yells "SHHH! Maaaa... LLAMA is sleeping!"
Ma, llama. Mālama.

words.say_it: Hammer with each syllable. "Koo-KOO-loo."
words.picture: Cuckoo building a 30 story loo
story_paragraphs: A cuckoo bird pops out of a clock, puts on a hard hat and starts building a bathroom (a "loo") in your backyard. It is 30 stories tall. Every time it hammers a nail it sings "CUCKOO-LOO!" The city tries to stop it. It keeps building.

words.say_it: Twist an invisible lid, then laugh. "Veh-heh!"
words.bonus: Wehe and pani (next) are the open and close pair.
words.picture: Laughing pickle jar
story_paragraphs: There is a pickle jar that nobody can open. The strongest guy in town tries. Nothing. Then a tiny grandma walks up and twists it open with one finger. The jar lid laughs at everyone who failed. "VEH-HEH-HEH-HEH!"

words.say_it: Slam an invisible door. "Pah-nee!"
words.bonus: Pani also means to replace or substitute.
words.picture: Fridge door on Pa's knee
story_paragraphs: Pa is sneaking a midnight snack. He hears footsteps and slams the fridge door shut, right on his own knee. "PA! KNEE!" he screams. He hops around the kitchen holding it. Every time he closes a door for the rest of his life, he checks his knee first.

words.say_it: Drop an invisible starting flag. "Ho-ʻo-MAH-kah!"
words.picture: "Whoa, Ma, car!" drag race
story_paragraphs: It is the start of a drag race. In lane one is a souped up truck. In lane two is your Ma, 78 years old, in a shopping cart with a jet engine strapped to the back. The flag drops. The engine roars and the whole crowd screams "WHOA, MA, CAR!" as she blasts off the line.
Whoa, Ma, car. Hoʻomaka.

words.say_it: Punch the air. "Pau!"
words.bonus: Pau hana means done with work. You probably already know that one.
words.picture: Comic book "POW!"
story_paragraphs: Every time you finish anything, a giant comic book bubble explodes over your head. "POW!" Last dish washed. POW! Last email sent. POW! Last bite of poi. POW! By the end of the day your house is covered in comic book explosions.

words.say_it: Tap your wrist like you are checking a watch. "Kah-lee."
words.bonus: Kali iki means wait a little.
words.picture: Collie at the Kalihi bus stop
story_paragraphs: A collie dog is sitting at a bus stop in Kalihi. It has been waiting there for 17 years. Its fur is gray. It has a little beard now. People bring it food. Buses come and go. It will not get on. It is waiting for something, and it will keep waiting. Collie. Kali.

words.english: to try, to taste, to test
words.say_it: Fan your mouth. "Ho, AAH, oh."
words.picture: Ghost pepper, "Whoa, aah, ow!"
story_paragraphs: You try a ghost pepper on a dare. First you say "WHOA" because it looks tiny. Then you bite. Your face melts. "AAAAH!" Then the burn hits your throat. "OW!" Whoa. Aah. Ow. You try it again anyway because you are stubborn.
The catches in this word are you choking on the heat.

words.english: to be able, can; to arrive
words.say_it: Flex your arm. "Hee-kee nō!"
words.bonus: Hiki nō means can do, no problem. Hiki also means to arrive, like the mouse getting upstairs.
words.picture: Mouse moving the piano, "Hiki nō!"
story_paragraphs: A tiny mouse shows up at your house to move your piano. You laugh. The mouse cracks its knuckles, says "HIKI NŌ," and carries the whole piano up three flights of stairs on its back. It arrives upstairs, sets it down and plays a song.
Can do, and it arrived.

words.english: to come out, to exit; to graduate
words.say_it: Pop your head up like a gopher. "Poo-kah!"
words.bonus: Puka is also a hole, like a puka shell. Coming out of a hole is puka. Graduating is also puka.
words.picture: Gophers in graduation caps
story_paragraphs: A field is full of holes. Out of every hole pops a gopher wearing a graduation cap. "POO-KAH!" Pop. "POO-KAH!" Pop. They throw their caps in the air and dive back in. It is the world's weirdest graduation ceremony.

words.english: to enter; to put on clothes
words.say_it: Step through a doorway. "Ko-mo."
words.bonus: E komo mai means welcome, come on in.
words.picture: "Come, oh!" door with costumes
story_paragraphs: There is a door at a party with a sign on it. Every time someone walks in, the door yells "COME, OH!" and a robot arm shoves a ridiculous outfit onto them. A banana suit. A tutu. A hat shaped like a spam musubi. You cannot enter unless you put something on.
Enter and wear. Same word.

words.say_it: Pretend to jump out a window. "Hah-ah-LEH-leh!"
words.picture: "Ha, ah, lele!" out the window
story_paragraphs: You are at the most boring party of all time. You grab the jumping flea with the ʻukulele from lele, laugh "HA!", gasp "AH!" and jump out the window. "LELE!" You fly over Diamond Head and never come back.
Ha, ah, lele. You left.

words.english: to leave something, to put down
words.say_it: Drop something on the table. "Why-ho."
words.bonus: Haʻalele is you leaving. Waiho is you leaving something behind.
words.picture: "Why, Ho?" Santa dumps presents
story_paragraphs: Santa from noho finally moves out of your house. On his way out, he dumps all his presents in the middle of the street and just walks off. You chase him and yell "WHY, HO? WHY?" He does not answer. He just left them there.
Why, Ho. Waiho.

words.say_it: Toss an invisible letter into the sky. "Ho-ʻo-OO-nah!"
words.picture: Pelican mail carrier, "Whoa, Oona!"
story_paragraphs: The post office fired all its workers and replaced them with a pelican named Oona. You hand her a letter and she swallows it and flies off. You hand her a couch and she swallows that too. Every time someone sends something, the whole line yells "WHOA, OONA!"

words.say_it: Hold out an invisible mug. "Koh-KOO-ah!"
words.bonus: You will see "Please kōkua" on signs all over Hawaiʻi.
words.picture: Lifeguard throwing hot cocoa
story_paragraphs: A lifeguard at Hanauma Bay does not use a rescue board. When someone is in trouble, he throws them a giant steaming mug of hot cocoa. It floats. They grab it and he reels them in. Every rescue he yells "COCOA!" and the whole beach cheers.
Cocoa, stretched out, is kōkua.

words.say_it: Raise your eyebrows like you just got it. "Ah... oh!"
words.bonus: Kumu is teacher. Haumāna is student.
words.picture: Owl class, "Ah... oh!"
story_paragraphs: An owl teacher stands in front of a class of mongooses. She explains something, and the second a student gets it, its eyes go wide and it says "AH... OH!" Then that student turns around and teaches the one behind it, who also goes "AH... OH!" The whole room is a chain of light bulbs.
Learning and teaching are the same word. That "ah, oh" moment goes both ways.

words.say_it: Open your hands like a book. "Heh-loo-HEH-loo."
words.bonus: Helu alone means to count. Reading is counting your way through the words.
words.picture: Book that says "Hello hello!"
story_paragraphs: You open a library book and it says "HELLO HELLO!" in a squeaky voice. Every page you turn, it says it again. "HELLO HELLO!" You try to read quietly. The librarian keeps shushing the book. You finish the whole thing in one night just to make it stop.

words.say_it: Write in the air with your finger. "Kaah-kow."
words.bonus: Kākau is also the traditional word for tattoo, writing on skin.
words.picture: Cow writing on cars, "Car! Cow!"
story_paragraphs: A cow breaks into a parking lot with a can of spray paint tied to its tail. It swishes its tail and writes its name on every car. The owners come out screaming "CAR! COW!" The cow has beautiful handwriting.
Car, cow. Kākau.

words.say_it: Hand over invisible money. "Koo-eye."
words.bonus: Kūʻai mai is to buy (the thing comes to you). Kūʻai aku is to sell (the thing going away).
words.picture: Glass eyeball store, "Cool eye"
story_paragraphs: There is a store at the mall that only sells glass eyeballs. Remember the eating eyeball from ʻai? This is its cousin. You walk in, the eyeballs all turn to look at you, and the cashier says "Cool eye, yeah?" You buy one. Then you sell it back. Then buy it again.

words.say_it: Count out invisible coins. "Oo-koo."
words.bonus: Careful. ʻUku with an ʻokina is a flea, like in ʻukulele. Uku without it is pay.
words.picture: Pigeon paying in crumbs, "Oooh, coo"
story_paragraphs: A pigeon walks up to the register at a plate lunch place. It orders a loco moco. When the cashier asks for money, the pigeon pays in bread crumbs, one at a time. The cashier counts them and says "Oooh... coo." Paid in full.
This is the same pigeon from kū. It stopped standing long enough to eat.

words.say_it: Hand over your eyes like a lookout. "Ee-mee?"
words.bonus: ʻImi naʻauao means to seek knowledge.
words.picture: Kid searching for "Emmy"
story_paragraphs: A kid is playing hide and seek, but he is the one who is lost. He is running through the house yelling "EE-MEE? EE-MEE?" like he is calling for someone named Emmy. Nobody is named Emmy. He is just searching for everyone.

words.english: to get, to have, to find
words.say_it: Pretend to open a chest. "Lo-AH-ah!"
words.bonus: Loaʻa works backward from English. Loaʻa iaʻu means I have it, or literally, it was gotten by me.
words.picture: Diver finds treasure, "Low, ah ah!"
story_paragraphs: A treasure diver goes low, low, low to the bottom of the ocean. Down there she finds a chest, opens it, and it is full of gold. "LOW... AH! AH!" she screams into her regulator, so loud a turtle swims over to look.

words.say_it: Point at yourself with fake innocence. "Eye-HOO-eh?"
words.picture: Thief says "I? Who, eh?"
story_paragraphs: A guy is caught walking out of your house carrying your TV, your fridge and your dog. You point at him. He looks around with the most innocent face in history and says "I? WHO, EH?"
I, who, eh. ʻAihue.

words.english: to join, to meet, to gather
words.say_it: Wave people over. "Hoo-ee!"
words.bonus: Hui as a noun is a club, group or company. You see it in names all over Hawaiʻi.
words.picture: Canoe clubs yelling "Hoo-ee!"
story_paragraphs: Two canoe clubs are on opposite ends of the beach. One paddler cups his hands and yells "HOO-EE!" The other side yells it back. Everyone runs to the middle and joins into one giant club. By sunset the whole beach is one team.

words.say_it: Tag the person next to you. "Paah-ah-nee!"
words.picture: "Pa! Annie!" playing tag
story_paragraphs: Pa and his little girl Annie are playing tag at a family party. Pa is 300 pounds and slow. Annie is fast. She tags him and runs. He chases her through the buffet line, over the cooler and through the bouncy house, yelling "PAAA! ANNIE!" every time he misses.
Pa, Annie. Pāʻani.

words.say_it: Sway your hips. "Hoo-lah."
words.picture: Uncle with 50 hula hoops
story_paragraphs: A 90 year old uncle gets up at a party and starts spinning 50 hula hoops at once. Arms, legs, neck, all of them. Then he stops, drops every hoop, and does a slow, perfect hula that makes the whole room cry.
Hula is the dance and it is also the verb, to dance it.

words.english: to sing, to chant; a song
words.say_it: Sing it. "Meh-leh!"
words.picture: Carolers make it snow
story_paragraphs: It is December and a choir of carolers shows up on your lawn in aloha shirts. They sing "Mele Kalikimaka" so loud that snow starts falling on Honolulu. Tourists panic. The carolers keep singing.
Mele is the "merry" in that song, but on its own it means song, and to sing.

words.say_it: Strum an air ʻukulele. "Ho-ʻo-KAH-nee!"
words.bonus: Kani means to make a sound, so hoʻokani is making it sound. Hoʻokani pila means play music.
words.picture: "Whoa, Connie!" flaming ʻukulele
story_paragraphs: Connie picks up a ʻukulele at a backyard party and plays so fast the strings catch fire. The whole party yells "WHOA, CONNIE!" She does not stop. She switches to a steel guitar. It also catches fire. The fire department shows up and starts dancing.
Whoa, Connie. Hoʻokani.

words.say_it: Hand on your heart. "Mah-HAH-lo."
words.picture: "Ma, hollow!" bunny gets a hug
story_paragraphs: The hollow chocolate bunny from holo shows up at your mom's door with flowers. She is so touched she hugs it and says "Ma... HOLLOW! Thank you!" The hug is a little too tight and the bunny cracks. She thanks it anyway.
Ma, hollow. Mahalo.

words.say_it: Hands together. "Poo-leh."
words.bonus: Pule also means week. Lāpule, Sunday, is literally prayer day, and one explanation is that the week was counted from one church day to the next.
words.picture: Praying for parking at Ala Moana
story_paragraphs: It is the Saturday before Christmas at Ala Moana and you have been circling the parking lot for an hour. You finally put your hands together and pray for a stall. You pray so hard your car starts to float. "POOO-LEH!" A spot opens right in front of you.

words.english: to give birth, to be born
words.say_it: Arms up like a newborn. "Haah-NOW!"
words.bonus: Lā hānau is a birthday. Remember hauʻoli lā hānau? Happy birthday.
words.picture: Newborn yelling "Haah! Now!"
story_paragraphs: A baby is born already talking. The doctor holds her up and she looks around the room, laughs "HAAAH!" and then demands "NOW! Milk NOW! Phone NOW!"
Haah, now. Hānau.

words.english: to live, to be healthy, to heal
words.say_it: Wave hello. "Oh-lah!"
words.bonus: Ola is also the word for life and health.
words.picture: Skeleton says "Hola!"
story_paragraphs: A skeleton is lying in a museum case. Somebody sneezes. The skeleton sits up, looks around, jumps out of the case and waves at everyone. "HOLA!" It is alive. It dances out the front door. Spanish "hola" has a silent H, and it sounds just like ola.

words.say_it: Clutch your chest and fall on the couch. "Mah... keh."
words.bonus: Ola and make are the life and death pair. You might hear make in local pidgin too.
words.picture: 45 minute death scene
story_paragraphs: Warning. This is not the English word "make." Say every vowel.

A very dramatic actor is doing a death scene. It lasts 45 minutes. He staggers, clutches his chest, falls, gets back up, falls again. Every time he falls he moans "MAH... KEH..." The audience goes home. He is still dying.

words.say_it: Hide behind your hand. "Peh... eh."
words.picture: Uncle behind a skinny pole
story_paragraphs: A 300 pound uncle is playing hide and seek. He hides behind a skinny telephone pole. His whole body sticks out on both sides. He holds his breath (that is the ʻokina) and whispers to himself "Peh... eh..." Everyone can see him. Nobody says anything. He thinks he is winning.

words.english: to move along, to scoot over
words.say_it: Scoot your butt one inch along your chair and bleat. "NEH-eh."
words.bonus: Neʻe mai means scoot this way, toward me. Neʻe aku means scoot away from me.
words.picture: Goat in aloha shirt scooting down pew
story_paragraphs: You squeeze into the last spot on the church pew on Easter Sunday. The pew is packed tight like a can of Vienna sausage. Then the back door opens and in walks Aunty Pua carrying three casseroles, and she needs a seat.
Right next to you sits a goat. A real goat, 180 pounds, wearing a little aloha shirt. Nobody knows whose goat it is. Everybody leans over and whispers, "Scoot over."
The goat bleats "NEH... eh!" and slides exactly one inch down the pew. The whole row slides with it. "NEH... eh!" Another inch. Hymnals fall on the floor.
A baby rolls to the end of the pew like a bowling ball and a cousin catches it. It takes 23 bleats and 23 inches, but Aunty Pua finally sits down. The goat looks at you like it did you a big favor.

words.english: to move something, to shift it
words.say_it: Push an imaginary couch with both hands and grunt. "Ho-oh-NEH-eh!"
words.bonus: Hoʻo- in front of a word usually means to make it happen. Neʻe is to scoot yourself. Hoʻoneʻe is to make something else scoot.
words.picture: Pushing a couch with goat on it
story_paragraphs: The goat from neʻe is back, and this time it will not scoot. It is sitting on your couch, and you are moving to a new apartment today. The movers quit. It is just you, a 400-pound koa couch and a goat that weighs as much as a refrigerator.
You squat, grab the couch and heave. "HO!" Your back pops. "OH!" The couch slides one foot. The goat bleats "NEH-eh!" like a coach cheering you on. Ho! Oh! Neh-eh!
You shove that couch down the hall, down three flights of stairs, across the parking lot and up the ramp into the truck. 211 heaves. The goat never lifts one hoof.
When you finally slam the truck door, it bleats one last proud "Neh-eh" and falls asleep. You moved it. It did not move itself.

words.english: to move, to stir, to wiggle
words.say_it: Catch your breath, then bounce your knee under the table. "OH-nee!"
words.bonus: Mai ʻoni means don't move, what a teacher or a photographer might say.
words.picture: Wiggling knee ruins wedding photo
story_paragraphs: You are the ring bearer at your cousin's wedding at a fancy hotel in Waikīkī. The photographer is a very serious man with a camera the size of a microwave. He says, "Nobody moves. Not one hair."
Everybody freezes. 140 guests, stiff as statues. Then your left knee starts to wiggle. Just a little. Then more. Then it is bouncing like it has its own heartbeat, 90 bounces a minute.
You gasp with a little catch in your throat. "(gulp) Oh... KNEE!" Your knee stirs the air like a spoon in a pot of stew. It bumps the ring pillow. The rings fly. The groom dives for them.
The cake wobbles. The photographer screams. The only photo from the whole wedding is 140 frozen people and one blurry knee.

words.english: to shake, to tremble, to sway
words.say_it: Shake both hands like jelly on a plate. "Nah-OO-eh."
words.picture: Trembling 12-foot haupia tower
story_paragraphs: Uncle Keoni built a haupia tower for the family party. It is 12 feet tall, pure white, coconut pudding stacked on coconut pudding, and it sits on a card table in the carport.
Then the trade winds pick up. The tower starts to tremble. It shakes. It sways left, then right, like a hula dancer who had too much coffee.
Aunty asks, "Is it going to fall?" Uncle folds his arms. "Nah."
The tower sways so far it almost touches the mango tree. The whole party goes "Ooooh." Uncle looks less sure. "...Eh?"
Nah. Ooh. Eh? Nah. Ooh. Eh? For three hours the tower shakes, and every guest shakes with it, knees wobbling, plates trembling. It never falls. But nobody eats it either. Too scared.

words.english: to turn, to flip over; to search
words.say_it: Flip your hand palm up, then palm down. "HOO-lee!"
words.bonus: Huli huli chicken is chicken turned over and over on the grill. Huli also means to search, like Lee hunting for his keys.
words.picture: Lee flipping his truck upside down
story_paragraphs: Your friend Lee lost his car keys. Lee does not search like a normal person. Lee flips things over.

He flips the couch. He flips the fridge. He flips the dog, gently, and the dog does not mind. Then he goes outside and flips his whole pickup truck onto its roof, wheels spinning in the air like a dead cockroach.
The neighbors run out in their slippahs. "WHO flipped the truck?!" Everybody points. "LEE!" Who? Lee! Huli! Then Lee flips the neighbor's car too. "WHO?" "LEE!"
He flips the mailbox, the trash can, a picnic table and a canoe. After flipping 41 things, he finds the keys in his own pocket. Then he flips his hat and walks home.

words.english: to turn something over; to change someone's mind
words.say_it: Flip a huge invisible sign with both hands. "Ho-oh-HOO-lee!"
words.bonus: Huli is to turn over yourself. Hoʻohuli is to turn something or someone else over, even their opinion.
words.picture: Lee flipping a giant CLOSED sign
story_paragraphs: Lee from huli is back, and he has a new talent. He can turn things over, and he can turn people's minds.
Uncle Boy is standing at the beach park swearing it is closed today. He is so sure he bets his cooler on it. There is a giant sign on a pole that says CLOSED.
Lee walks up, grabs the 30-foot sign, grunts and turns the whole thing over. The back side says OPEN, BRING YOUR COOLER. Everybody gasps. "Ho! Oh!" Then they ask, "Who?" "LEE!" Ho! Oh! Who? Lee!
Uncle Boy stares at the sign for a long time. Then he changes his mind and says the beach was always open. He hands over his cooler. Lee just smiles and turns over his plate for seconds.

words.english: to go out for fun, to cruise around
words.say_it: Knock twice on the table and grin. "Ho-lo-HO-lo!"
words.bonus: Holo means to run, sail or ride. Doubling it makes it loose and wandering. Ask "Where you going?" and a local might answer "Just holoholo."
words.picture: Uncle cruising in a hollow watermelon
story_paragraphs: It is Saturday. You have no plans, no money and no car. Then Uncle Sonny pulls into the carport driving a watermelon.
It is a watermelon the size of a minivan. He scooped out the inside, cut out windows and bolted on four wheels. He knocks on the side and it goes "hollow, hollow." He grins. "Get in. We go holoholo."
Nobody knows where you are going. That is the point.
You cruise to Haleʻiwa for shave ice. You cruise to Kailua to look at the water. You drive past Makapuʻu twice because the view was nice the first time.
Every time somebody asks where you are going, Uncle knocks on the dashboard. Hollow, hollow! You get home at 11 at night, sticky, sunburned and happy. You went nowhere and everywhere.

words.say_it: Draw a big circle in the air with one finger. "Kah-ah-POO-nee!"
words.bonus: Kaʻa means to roll or turn, and today it is also the word for a car. Puni means all the way around.
words.picture: Tiny pony pulling tour wagon around island
story_paragraphs: You sign up for a round the island tour. You expect a big air conditioned bus. What shows up is a pony. One pony, about as tall as your hip, pulling a wagon with 30 tourists in it.
The tour guide stands on the wagon with a microphone. Somebody asks, "Is this a car?" The guide hiccups into the mic. "Car? (hic) AH... PONY!" Car, ah, pony! Kaʻapuni! The pony takes off.
That pony goes around the whole island. Around Diamond Head. Around Makapuʻu. Around the North Shore and all the way back to town. Then it goes around again, because it likes it.
Round and round, three times, 330 miles. When it finally stops, the tourists have beards. The pony stamps its hoof. It wants to go around one more time.

words.english: to travel, to take a trip
words.say_it: Grab an invisible suitcase handle and wave down a car. "Kah-ah-HEH-leh!"
words.bonus: Hele means to go. Kaʻahele is traveling about from place to place, a trip or a tour. It is close to kaʻapuni, which stresses going all the way around.
words.picture: Tūtū and mongoose traveling the world
story_paragraphs: Tūtū Rose is 84 and has never left Oʻahu. Then she wins a trip. She packs one suitcase and one travel buddy, a mongoose named Leh who rides in the side pocket.
She goes to Japan. She goes to Italy. She goes to Egypt and makes the mongoose climb a pyramid. Nine countries in 14 days.
Every morning she stands outside a new hotel, waves down a car and hollers, "CAR! (gulp) AH! Hey, LEH, let's go!" Car, ah, hey, Leh! Kaʻahele!
Leh jumps in the pocket. The car zooms off.
At the airport back home the whole family waits with leis. Tūtū Rose walks out with a tan, a French hat, a passport full of stamps and a mongoose wearing sunglasses.

words.say_it: Lie back with your arms out like you are floating. "LAH-nah."
words.picture: Uncle floating on his lawn
story_paragraphs: Last night it rained so hard in Mānoa that Uncle Dennis's whole front lawn slid off the hill. This morning it is floating in the ocean off Waikīkī, 200 feet out. A perfect square of green grass, bobbing on the waves.
Uncle is still on it. He is sitting in his lawn chair with his coffee. The sprinkler is still going. His dog is chasing a seagull across the grass.
People on the beach point and scream. Uncle stands up, sees the shore getting smaller and yells, "My LAWN! AH!" Lawn, ah! Lana!
Then he shrugs, sits back down and floats. He floats past surfers. He floats past a cruise ship. By sunset his lawn is floating near Molokaʻi, and he is mowing it.

words.say_it: Drop down on one knee. "Koo-KOO-lee!"
words.picture: Cuckoo clock bird kneeling on one knee
story_paragraphs: Grandpa's old cuckoo clock has a problem. When it strikes the hour, the little wooden bird pops out, but it does not cuckoo. It kneels.
At 3 o'clock the tiny door flips open. The bird slides out, drops down on one tiny knee and sings, "Coo-KOO-lee!" Then it stares at you. Nobody in the house can move until everybody kneels too.
So you kneel. Grandma kneels in the kitchen with the rice paddle in her hand. The dog kneels. Your cousin kneels on a toy block and screams. The mailman outside hears it and kneels on the lawn.
At midnight the clock goes 12 times. "Coo-KOO-lee! Coo-KOO-lee!" The whole family kneels up and down in their pajamas like a crazy exercise video. Your knees are purple by morning.

words.say_it: Bow your head slowly and hold the first sound long. "KOOOO-loh."
words.bonus: Kūlou is bowing just the head. Kukuli is going all the way down on your knees.
words.picture: Seven-foot cousin bowing under doorway
story_paragraphs: Your cousin Big Mike is 7 feet 4 inches tall. Tūtū's house in Kalihi was built in 1952 for people about 5 feet tall. Every doorway is low. Every ceiling fan is at nose level.
Every time Big Mike comes for Sunday dinner, the whole family yells the same thing at the front door. "Cooool... LOW!" Stay cool, head low. Coooo, low! Kūlou!

He bows his head under the front door. He bows under the kitchen doorway. He bows under the fan, the hanging plants, the wind chimes and the framed picture of Tūtū's wedding. By the end of the night he has bowed his head 64 times.
He looks like the most polite man in Hawaiʻi. Then one night he forgets. BONK. Now the doorway has a dent shaped like his forehead.

words.say_it: Tip over sideways onto the couch. "HEE-nah!"
words.bonus: Hina can also mean gray, like gray hair.
words.picture: Laughing hyena toppling off a rock
story_paragraphs: You take your nephew to the zoo. At the hyena yard, a hyena the size of a golf cart is standing tall on a rock, looking proud.
Then somebody tells it a joke. You do not hear the joke.
The hyena starts to laugh. "HEE! HEE! HEE!" It laughs so hard it starts to lean. It leans like a tree that just got chopped.
Your nephew asks the keeper, "Is he going to fall?" The keeper says "Nah." The hyena goes "HEE!" The keeper says, "...nah?" Hee! Nah! Hina! And TIMBERRR.
It topples straight over, stiff as a board, right off the rock. It lands with a boom that shakes the snack stand. It lies there on its back with its legs in the air, still giggling.

words.say_it: Stretch one arm to the ceiling and sing the first part long. "Laaaah-lau!"
words.picture: Reaching for the last malasada
story_paragraphs: There is one malasada left at the bakery. It is on the very top shelf, up near the ceiling, and it is still warm. Sugar is falling off it like snow.

You reach for it. You stretch your arm up so far your shirt comes untucked. You go up on your toes, and because stretching makes you sing, you sing. "Laaaaa... laaaaa..." Two more inches. One more inch.
Then your shoulder goes pop. "OW!" Laaa-laaa-OW! Lālau!
You grab it anyway. You come down on your heels holding the malasada high like a trophy. Everybody in line claps. Your arm is now 3 inches longer than the other one, and you do not care one bit.

words.say_it: Creep your fingers across the table like a crawling baby. "KO-lo."
words.picture: Baby army crawling toward the cola
story_paragraphs: Grandpa sets his cold cola on the coffee table and goes to find the bottle opener. Across the living room, 40 feet away, baby Kaimana sees it.
Kaimana is 10 months old and she cannot walk yet. But she can crawl.
She drops to her belly like a soldier and creeps. Under the dining table. Under the sleeping dog. Between the legs of three uncles watching football.
Slow. Silent. Elbows and knees. Grandpa comes back and sees her one foot from the table, reaching up with one sticky hand. He yells, "My COLA!" Cola! Kolo!
She freezes. He freezes. Then she grabs the bottle and crawls backward, faster than any baby in history, all the way to her blanket. She pretends to be asleep, hugging the cola.

words.say_it: Kick the air in front of you like a kung fu rooster. "PEH-koo!"
words.picture: Karate rooster kicking a coconut
story_paragraphs: Next door lives a rooster named Sensei. He wears a tiny black belt. He trained in the mountains for 7 years.
You kick a soccer ball over the fence by accident. Sensei walks up to it. He pecks it once. "PECK!" Then he spins in the air and kicks it with one yellow foot. "OOH!" Peck! Ooh! Peku!
The ball flies 90 yards, over your house, over the street, into the school field. The whole neighborhood comes out.
Somebody tosses him a coconut. PECK! OOH! It sails over the church. Somebody tosses a slippah. PECK! OOH! It lands on the roof of the store.
By sunset Sensei has kicked 26 things into the next town. Then he crows once and goes to bed.

words.say_it: Stomp your foot on the floor and giggle. "HEH-hee!"
words.picture: Aunty stomping a yard of bubble wrap
story_paragraphs: Aunty Lani ordered a new TV and it came wrapped in bubble wrap. A LOT of bubble wrap. Enough to cover the whole backyard, 2,000 square feet of fat plastic bubbles.
She steps on one. POP. She giggles. "Heh!" She stomps on another. POP. "Hee!" Heh! Hee! Hehi! Now she cannot stop. She stomps across the yard, knees up high, slippahs slapping, giggling at every pop.
The neighbors think it is fireworks. The dogs on the street start howling. Uncle comes out, steps on one by accident, POP, and starts giggling too. Now two grown adults are stomping in circles.
It takes them 4 hours to step on every single bubble. When they finish, they look at each other and call the store to order another TV.

words.english: to climb aboard, to get on
words.say_it: Hop up like you are getting on a bus, with a catch in the middle. "Eh-(catch)-eh!"
words.bonus: You eʻe a bus, a canoe, a plane or a horse. Anything you climb onto to ride. Pukui-Elbert spells it eʻe. You may also see it written ʻeʻe, but Pukui-Elbert uses ʻeʻe for a different word meaning hard or stiff.
words.picture: 22 cousins climbing aboard a pickup
story_paragraphs: It is the last ride to the beach and Uncle's old pickup is the only ride left. There are 22 cousins, one cooler and a truck bed made for maybe six.
Uncle yells, "Everybody climb aboard!" The first cousin jumps on the bumper and says "Eh!" Then he hiccups, that little catch in the throat. "Eh... (hic) eh!"
The next one climbs on. "Eh! (hic) eh!" Every cousin who climbs aboard hiccups the same way.
They climb on the tailgate. They climb on the roof. They climb on each other's shoulders. One little cousin climbs on the cooler and sits there like a king. Eh (hic) eh! Eʻe!
Twenty-two hiccups later the truck is full. It sinks so low the tires squeal. Uncle drives 4 miles an hour all the way to the beach.

words.say_it: Pinch your nose and bend forward like you are diving. "LOO-oo!"
words.bonus: Luʻu is diving down under the water. Jumping feet first off a cliff into water is lele kawa.
words.picture: Loon in goggles diving at Hanauma Bay
story_paragraphs: A loon from the continent is on vacation at Hanauma Bay. It is a big black and white diving bird the size of a canoe, wearing tiny swim goggles.
The lifeguard walks over. "Sir, be careful out there." The loon ignores him.
It stands up tall, takes a huge breath and calls out, "LOOO..." Then its head hits the water with a gulp. "...(glub) OO!" Loo-oo! Luʻu! Down it goes.

The crowd waits. One minute. Five minutes. Eleven minutes. Tourists start to worry. Then the loon shoots up out of the water holding a lost slippah, a gold ring, a waterproof camera and a very confused sea cucumber.
It drops the treasure at the lifeguard's feet. It says "Loo-oo" one more time and dives again.

words.say_it: Paddle three strokes on one side, then switch. "HO-eh!"
words.bonus: Hoe is also the paddle itself. The famous canoe race across the channel from Molokaʻi is called the Molokaʻi Hoe.
words.picture: Canoe team paddling with garden hoes
story_paragraphs: It is the big canoe race from Molokaʻi to Oʻahu. Your team is ready. The canoe is ready. Then you open the truck and there are no paddles. None. Somebody forgot.
Aunty Mae marches into her garden and comes back with six garden hoes. Rusty ones, with dirt still on them. She hands them out. "You paddle with this."

The gun goes off. Everybody digs in. "HOE!" you yell on every stroke. "EH!" Hoe! Eh! Hoe! Eh! The hoes chop the water like it is a vegetable patch. One cousin accidentally plants a row of onions in the ocean.
But the team keeps rowing, 41 miles, blisters on blisters. You finish last, but you finish. The coach says you are the best weeders the ocean has ever seen.

words.say_it: Stand sideways, bend your knees, arms out. "Heh-eh-NAH-loo!"
words.bonus: Heʻe means to slide and nalu means wave, so heʻe nalu is wave sliding. You will also see it written as one word, heʻenalu. Heʻe is also the word for octopus.
words.picture: Old man surfing ironing board on huge wave
story_paragraphs: It is a giant day at the North Shore. The waves are 40 feet high and the whole beach is watching. Then out walks Lou.
Lou is 78 years old and weighs 310 pounds. He is carrying an ironing board.
The crowd starts yelling. "HEY! EH! NAH, LOU!" Everybody means don't do it. Hey, eh, nah, Lou! Lou just waves.

He paddles out on the ironing board. A mountain of water stands up behind him. He jumps up and slides down the face of it, arms out, ironing board rattling, aloha shirt flapping. He carves left. He carves right. He irons a wrinkle right out of the wave.
He rides it all the way to the sand and steps off dry. The crowd is silent. Lou shrugs. "What? It's just surfing."

words.english: to jump off a cliff into water
words.say_it: Hold your nose and jump in place, feet together. "Leh-leh-KAH-vah!"
words.bonus: Lele means to jump or to fly. Lele kawa is the feet first leap off a cliff into water, done so cleanly there is almost no splash.
words.picture: Aunty jumping off cliff with guavas
story_paragraphs: At the jump rock, a line of kids waits to leap feet first into the deep water. Then Aunty Florence pushes to the front. She is 71. She is holding a basket of fresh guavas from her yard.

"Aunty, what are you doing?" She does not answer. She takes three steps and jumps off the 25-foot cliff, feet first, basket held high over her head, yelling the whole way down, "LEH-LEH... ka-GUAVA!" Lele, ka guava! Lele kawa!

She slices into the water feet first, straight as a pencil, with barely a ripple. No splash at all. A second later 30 guavas rain down on everybody like pink hail. Aunty pops up, spits out water and floats on her back eating a guava.
The kids look at each other. Then all 14 of them jump off together, screaming "LEH-LEH-KAH-VAH!"

words.say_it: Sway side to side like you are drifting, with a little catch at the start. "Ow-AH-nah."
words.bonus: Hula ʻauana is the modern, free flowing style of hula. The older style is hula kahiko.
words.picture: Uncle drifting on pool noodle to Molokaʻi
story_paragraphs: Uncle Roy falls asleep on a pool noodle at Waikīkī at 2 in the afternoon. The current does the rest.
He drifts. No plan, no map, no paddle. He bumps into a buoy. There is a little catch in his throat. "(hic) OW!"
He opens one eye and looks around. "Ah... nah." Too much work. He closes the eye. Ow! Ah, nah! ʻAuana!

He drifts past Diamond Head. He bumps a surfer. "OW! Ah, nah." He drifts past Hawaiʻi Kai and bumps a buoy full of seabirds. "OW! Ah, nah." He wanders across the whole channel, snoring, one arm dragging in the water.
The next morning he washes up on a beach on Molokaʻi. A fisherman asks how he got there. Uncle scratches his head. "Ah, nah. I just wandered."

words.say_it: Slide your hand toward your face, one inch at a time. "Ho-oh-ko-KO-keh!"
words.bonus: Kokoke means near. Hoʻokokoke is to get near, to come closer.
words.picture: Coconut creeping closer on the beach
story_paragraphs: You are lying on your towel at the beach. Twenty feet away sits a coconut. Brown, hairy, normal. You close your eyes.
When you open them, the coconut is fifteen feet away. You did not see it move. You close your eyes again. Now it is ten feet away, and it has a face.
You sit up and yell, "HO! OH!" The coconut whispers, "My name is Coco Kay." Ho! Oh! Coco-KAY!
You blink. It is five feet away. You blink. Three feet. It comes closer every time you look away, like the scariest game ever, and it is humming.
Finally it is right next to your face. You hold your breath. Coco Kay smiles. "Sorry. I just wanted some shade." It snuggles under your umbrella and falls asleep.

words.say_it: Slide two things on the table far apart. "Ho-oh-kah-ah-VAH-leh!"
words.bonus: Kaʻawale means apart or free. Hoʻokaʻawale is to make things apart, to separate them.
words.picture: Lunch man separating rice with tweezers
story_paragraphs: At the school cafeteria there is a lunch man named Wally. Wally believes food should never touch. Ever.
You hand him your plate lunch. Two scoops rice, one scoop mac salad, teri beef. He pulls out tweezers and a tiny ruler.
He separates every grain of rice so it sits apart from the others. He moves the mac salad two inches away and builds a little wall out of a napkin.
Then he separates each macaroni, one by one. The line behind you is now 300 kids long. You finally yell, "HO! OH! Cut it! Ah... WALLY!" Ho! Oh! Cut, ah, Wally! Hoʻokaʻawale!
He hands back your plate. Every single thing on it is sealed in its own separate bag. Your lunch took 48 minutes.

words.english: to be apart; to be free, available
words.say_it: Hold your nose and scoot far away. "Kah-ah-VAH-leh."
words.bonus: Kaʻawale also means free or available, like a free seat or a free afternoon. Hoʻokaʻawale is to separate things.
words.picture: Stinky Wally alone on crowded beach
story_paragraphs: Wally the lunch man from hoʻokaʻawale has a day off, so he goes to Ala Moana Beach on the Fourth of July. There are 10,000 people there. Towels touch towels. Umbrellas touch umbrellas.
There is not one free spot of sand. Except one. Around Wally there is an empty circle 40 feet wide.
Why? Wally brought his lunch, which is a three-week-old fish in a bucket, and he smells exactly like it.
Every family that walks up to the free spot sniffs, gags and backs away. "Car? (gulp) Ah! WALLY!" they cry, and run back to their cars. Car, ah, Wally! Kaʻawale!
So Wally sits happily apart from everybody, in the biggest, freest, most available spot on the whole beach. The seagulls do not even land near him.

words.english: to lay down, to put to bed
words.say_it: Lay an imaginary baby down very gently. "Ho-oh-MO-eh."
words.bonus: Moe is to lie down or sleep yourself. Hoʻomoe is to lay someone else down, like putting a baby to bed.
words.picture: Tucking giant calf into swimming-pool crib
story_paragraphs: The giant sleepy cow from moe had a baby. The calf is only two weeks old, but it is already the size of a delivery truck, and it will not go to bed.
You are the babysitter. It is 11 at night. The calf is running laps around the ranch. You grab it around the belly and lift. "HO!" Your knees shake. "OH!"
You carry it to a crib the size of a swimming pool and lay it down on 300 pillows. The calf blinks. It tries to moo, but it is too sleepy to finish. "Mo... eh." Ho! Oh! Mo... eh! Hoʻomoe!
You tuck a blanket made of 16 bedsheets under its chin. You turn off the light. You lie down on the floor next to the crib, and you fall asleep first.

words.english: to seat, to set in place, to install
words.say_it: Point at a chair and press down with both hands. "Ho-oh-NO-ho!"
words.bonus: Noho means to sit or to live somewhere. Hoʻonoho is to make someone sit, or to set something in its place.
words.picture: Crane lowering Santa onto his chair
story_paragraphs: Santa from noho is back, and this year he is working at the mall. He weighs 600 pounds. Nobody asks why. His big red chair is on a stage three feet high, and he cannot climb up.
So they bring a crane. A real yellow construction crane, 80 feet tall, parked in the middle of the mall. They strap Santa into a harness. The crane lifts him slowly into the air above the food court.
He swings over the kids in line. He waves. "HO!" He swings the wrong way. "OH! NO! HO!" Ho, oh, no, ho! Hoʻonoho!

It takes 45 minutes to set him in place. The crane lowers him inch by inch until his big bottom lands perfectly on the chair. The workers bolt the chair to the stage so he stays installed. Then he says he needs the restroom.

words.say_it: Push something into an imaginary bag. "Ho-oh-KO-mo!"
words.bonus: Komo means to enter. E komo mai means come in, welcome. Hoʻokomo is to put something in.
words.picture: Grandma's purse swallowing a kayak
story_paragraphs: Grandma's purse is black, shiny and small. It is also bottomless. Everything you put in it disappears, and the purse always wants more.

You put in her phone. Fine. The purse clicks open by itself and calls out in a deep voice, "Come, oh!" So you put in her umbrella. "COME, OH!" You put in a ʻukulele, a rice cooker and a bag of 40 manapua. "Ho! Oh! COME, OH!" Hoʻokomo!
Grandma just nods. You put in a surfboard, a folding table, the dog's bed and a cousin who volunteered. You slide in a kayak, one inch at a time. The purse burps.
At church Grandma opens it to find a tissue. She pulls out the cousin. He blinks, waves at the pastor and asks when lunch is.

words.english: to bring out, to say out loud, to issue
words.say_it: Reach into your pocket, pull out your hand and announce it loud. "Ho-oh-POO-kah!"
words.bonus: Puka means a hole, and also to come out or appear. Hoʻopuka is to bring something out, including words said out loud.
words.picture: Uncle pulling a canoe out of a hat
story_paragraphs: Uncle Ikaika does magic at every birthday party. His trick is simple. He has a black hat with a puka, a hole, in the bottom. He reaches into the puka and brings things out.
At your 9th birthday he reaches in and yells, "HO! OH! From the PUKA!" He pulls out a rabbit. Everybody claps.
He reaches in again. "Ho! Oh! PUKA!" He brings out a live pig. Then a lawnmower. Then a 20-foot canoe, still dripping wet.
Every time he pulls something out, he announces it out loud like a radio man. "A CANOE, ladies and gentlemen!" The neighbors come over to see.
At the end he reaches in one last time and pulls out your report card, the one you hid under your bed. He reads it out loud to everybody. Worst trick ever.

words.english: to give back, to return something
words.say_it: Hold out both hands like you are giving something back. "Ho-ee-HO-ee!"
words.bonus: Hoʻi is to go back yourself, like going home. Hoʻihoʻi is to send something back where it belongs.
words.picture: Forklift returning 312 food containers
story_paragraphs: Twenty-six years ago you borrowed one plastic food container from Aunty Momi. You filled it with her chicken long rice, took it home and never gave it back.

Every evening since then, Aunty Momi stands at the end of your street and calls out, "HOY! HOY!" like a fisherman calling in a boat. Twenty-six years. Rain or shine. "Hoy! Hoy!" Ho-ee! Ho-ee! Hoʻihoʻi!

One day you open your cupboard and find out you did not borrow one container. You borrowed 312. Every family party, every graduation, a little more. So you rent a forklift. You stack them on a pallet eight feet high and drive them down the street.
She counts every single lid. Then she fills them all with food and makes you take them home again.

words.english: to throw; to put a lei on someone
words.say_it: Toss an invisible lei across the room like a ring toss. "Ho-oh-LAY!"
words.bonus: Hoʻolei means to throw anything, and it is also the word for putting a lei on someone.
words.picture: Aunty ring-tossing leis at the airport
story_paragraphs: Aunty Gwen greets visitors at the airport, and she is the fastest lei thrower in the Pacific. She does not walk up and place leis on people. She throws them.

The doors open. 200 tourists come out of the gate. Aunty Gwen stands 50 feet back with a mountain of plumeria leis on her arm, like a ring toss champion. "HO!" she winds up. "OH!" she spins. "LEI!" Ho! Oh! Lei! Hoʻolei!
FLING. A lei sails across the room and lands perfectly around a man's neck. FLING. A grandma. FLING. A baby in a stroller. FLING. A pilot. She never misses. She even rings a dog in a pet carrier.
By the end, 200 people are wearing leis and smiling. The security guard is wearing three, because she likes him.

words.english: to place, to hang up; to get on (a ride)
words.say_it: Hang an invisible hat on a hook. "KOW!"
words.bonus: Kau has many meanings. It can also mean a season, like kau wela, the hot season.
words.picture: Cow riding the Ferris wheel
story_paragraphs: At the county fair a cow walks up to the Ferris wheel and waits in line like everybody else. She has a ticket in her mouth.
The ride man looks at her. She looks at him. He shrugs.

He places her carefully in the seat, all four legs sticking out the sides. He takes her straw hat and hangs it up on the hook by the ticket booth. Then he yells to the crowd, "COW!" Kau! And he pulls the lever.
Up she goes, 90 feet in the air, over the whole fairground. She moos all the way around. The wheel turns 8 times while people take pictures.
When she gets off, she walks over to the hook, takes her hat back and gets right back in line to ride again.

words.english: to put on top of, to impose
words.say_it: Put your hand flat on top of your head like a heavy load. "Ho-oh-KOW!"
words.bonus: Kau is to put something somewhere. Hoʻokau is to put it on top of something, or to put a burden on someone.
words.picture: Boss setting a cow on your desk
story_paragraphs: The cow from kau is back, and now she works at your office. Your boss thinks this is funny.

Friday, five minutes before quitting time, you are packing up to go home. Your boss rolls in with a forklift. On the forklift is the cow. He sets her right on top of your desk, on top of your keyboard, on top of your 400-page report. "HO! OH! COW!" you scream. Ho! Oh! Cow! Hoʻokau!
"She is your job this weekend," he says, and just like that he puts the whole load on you. The desk creaks. The cow chews your sticky notes.
All weekend the cow sits on top of everything you own. Your couch. Your bed. The roof of your car. On Monday you set her on top of your boss's desk. Fair is fair.

words.english: to cling, to stick to; to be related
words.say_it: Grab your own arm tight and try to peel your hand off. "PEE-lee!"
words.bonus: Pili also means close or related, like family. Pili is also the name of the grass that old Hawaiian houses were thatched with.
words.picture: Little cousin clinging to your leg
story_paragraphs: Your cousin Kekoa is four years old and he clings. To be exact, he clings to your left leg, arms and legs wrapped around it like a sticky octopus.
