You try to walk. He comes with you. You try to peel him off like a stuck sticker. "Peel-y! PEEL-Y!" He sticks harder. You shake your leg. He laughs. Peel-y! Pili!
You go to the beach. He clings. You go into the water. He clings, snorkeling. At dinner you eat with a 38-pound cousin hanging off your leg under the table.
Finally Aunty says, "Leave him. He's family." That is the other meaning. You are stuck together because you are related. By bedtime he is asleep, still on your leg, snoring.

words.english: to attach; to copy, to imitate
words.say_it: Copy the last thing someone said, in their voice. "Ho-oh-PEE-lee."
words.bonus: Pili is to stick. Hoʻopili is to make something stick, or to copy someone so closely you are stuck to their words.
words.picture: Mynah on your head copying you
story_paragraphs: A mynah bird lands on your head at the bus stop and attaches itself there. Its claws grip your hair like a sticker. It will not leave.
Worse, it copies you. You say, "Get off." It says, "Get off."
You sneeze. It sneezes. You tug at it and yell, "HO! OH! PEEL-Y!" The bird yells back in your exact voice, "HO! OH! PEEL-Y!" Hoʻopili!
It copies everything all day. At work your boss asks for the report. The bird says, "Report? Nah."
You get in trouble. At dinner with your crush it repeats your nervous laugh 50 times.
After a week you give up. The bird is part of your look now. People think you are wearing a very realistic hat that does impressions.

words.say_it: Turn your whole head slowly toward the door and hold the first sound. "Haaah-LEE-oo."
words.picture: Ballroom turning toward a yawning lion
story_paragraphs: You are at a fancy dinner in a hotel ballroom. 200 people in their best aloha wear, all facing the stage, all bored by a long speech.

Then, in the back of the room, a lion walks in. His name is Leo. Nobody invited him. He sits down at table 14 and opens his mouth in a giant, slow yawn. "HAAAAAAH..." Then he burps. "...LEO!" Haaah, Leo! Hāliu!

Every head in the room turns. Like a field of sunflowers turning toward the sun, 200 heads swivel slowly away from the stage and toward the lion. The speaker turns. The waiters turn. Even the fish on the buffet turn.
Leo loves it. He yawns again, "HAAAAH... LEO," just to watch the whole room turn toward him one more time.

words.say_it: Duck your head fast, with a catch in the throat. "AH-lo!"
words.bonus: Careful. Alo, with no ʻokina, means the front or the face, like being in someone's presence. ʻAlo, with the catch, means to dodge.
words.picture: Dodging poi balls from runaway machine
story_paragraphs: Uncle Walter built a poi machine for the family lūʻau. It was supposed to scoop poi into bowls. Something went wrong. Now it fires poi balls across the yard at 90 miles an hour.
SPLAT. A poi ball hits the tent. SPLAT. One knocks the hat off an aunty. The machine swings toward you. You catch your breath with a little gulp and scream, "(gulp) AH! LOW!" You duck. Ah! Low! ʻAlo!
A ball whooshes over your head. You dodge left. You duck under the table. You roll behind the imu. "AH! LOW!" The whole family is dodging and ducking now, like the world's stickiest dodgeball game.
Finally Grandma pulls the plug. There is poi on the roof, poi on the dog and poi on the mango tree. You did not get hit once.

words.english: to step over; to break a rule
words.say_it: Lift your foot high and step over an invisible line, with a catch. "AH-eh!"
words.bonus: ʻAʻe means both to step over something and to break a rule, which is really stepping over a line.
words.picture: Foot stepping over Tūtū's chalk line
story_paragraphs: Tūtū has drawn a white chalk line across the kitchen doorway. The rule is simple. Nobody steps over the line while she is cooking. For 40 years, nobody has.

But the smell of her shoyu chicken is drifting through the door, and you are hungry. You lift one foot. Slowly. Over the line. "Ah..." Your foot hangs in the air. There is a catch in your throat. "...EH!" Ah, eh! ʻAʻe!
Your toe touches the kitchen floor. Every pot lid in the house rattles. The lights flicker. The dog hides. From the stove, without turning around, Tūtū says, "I heard that."
You step back over the line so fast you fall on the rug. The rule is broken. Your dinner is now mostly rice.

words.english: to follow along, to tag along
words.say_it: Walk two steps behind someone, then sigh. "Oo-KAH-lee."
words.bonus: Ukali also means a follower or attendant, like a governor's aide. In modern Hawaiian, ukali is also the word for a satellite, which follows a planet around.
words.picture: Little cousin tagging along to job interview
story_paragraphs: Your cousin Carly is five, and she tags along everywhere you go. Everywhere.
You go to the store. Carly follows two steps behind. You go to the beach. Carly follows, dragging a boogie board twice her size.
You go to your job interview downtown and sit down across from the manager. Carly sits down right next to you in a tiny chair she brought herself.
The manager asks, "Who is this?" You sigh. "Ooh... CARLY." Ooh, Carly! Ukali!
You walk into the ocean to get away. Carly follows in goggles. You climb a tree. Carly follows.
You sneak out at 5 in the morning. Carly is already in the car with her seatbelt on.
You get the job. Carly gets a name tag too.

words.say_it: Point at the floor and tiptoe like you are following footprints. "Hah-HAI!"
words.bonus: Hahai covers both following along and a real chase, even hunting. Hoʻohahai is to lure someone into following you.
words.picture: Following tiny footprints to a crab
story_paragraphs: At sunrise you find footprints in the sand at Waimānalo. Tiny ones, in a neat line. You decide to follow them.
You follow them past the lifeguard tower. Past a sleeping uncle. Past a family setting up a tent.
The footprints go on and on, three miles down the beach, around a rock and into the bushes. You are sweating now. You have to know.
At the very end of the trail there is a crab. It is wearing tiny slippahs, one on each of its eight feet. It turns around, raises one claw and says, "HA! HI!" Ha! Hi! Hahai!
Then it walks off, and you follow it again. Then it follows you back. For the next two hours, a crab and a person follow each other up and down the beach, saying hi.

words.say_it: Run in place, pumping your arms. "Ah-loo-AH-loo!"
words.bonus: Alualu is also used for running for political office, chasing after votes. Alualu loloa is to keep chasing and never give up.
words.picture: Family chasing a runaway porta-potty
story_paragraphs: Your family is having a picnic on top of Tantalus. The only restroom is a portable toilet, a big blue plastic box, parked at the edge of the lookout.
Then somebody bumps it. It tips. It starts to roll. Down the road it goes, bouncing and spinning, door flapping open and shut.
The whole family takes off after it. Uncle in his slippahs. Aunty holding a plate of chicken. Grandpa on a skateboard.
"A LOO! A LOO!" they scream all the way down the mountain. A loo! A loo! Alualu!
The loo takes 17 hairpin turns. It passes a tour bus and a man on a bike.
The family chases it for 5 miles. At the bottom it rolls gently into a parking stall and stops. Uncle opens the door and goes inside.

words.english: to stop, to put an end to
words.say_it: Hold up one hand like a crossing guard and stretch the middle. "Ho-OOOH-kee!"
words.bonus: Pau means finished. Hoʻōki is when someone makes it stop.
words.picture: Aunty pulling the karaoke plug
story_paragraphs: It is Uncle Clyde's birthday party, and Uncle Clyde found the karaoke machine. He started singing at 6 in the evening. It is now 8 in the morning. He has sung the same love song 211 times.
The neighbors called. The police came, listened and left. The birds outside have learned the words. Uncle's voice sounds like a rusty gate, but he will not stop.
Finally Aunty Leilani walks across the room. She grabs the cord. She holds up her other hand like a crossing guard and yells, "HO! OOOOOH-KEY!" Ho! Okey! Hoʻōki! And she pulls the plug.
Silence. Beautiful silence. Everybody cheers. Uncle Clyde stands there with the dead microphone for a long time. Then he starts singing without it.

words.say_it: Plant your feet, cross your arms and puff out your chest. "Kooo-EH!"
words.bonus: Kūʻē is to stand against something. You hear it at protests, for people standing in opposition.
words.picture: Pigeons refusing to give up the bench
story_paragraphs: The city wants to take out the old bench at the park and put in a new one. Nobody asked the pigeons.
The workers show up at 7 in the morning with a truck. On the bench sits one pigeon, a big gray one with a torn ear. It does not move.
The worker says, "Shoo." The pigeon puffs out its chest and says, "COOOO..." Then a sharp catch in its throat. "...EH!" Coo, eh! Kūʻē!
The worker tries to lift the bench. More pigeons land. 40. 90. 300. They cover the bench, the truck and the worker's hard hat, all puffed up, all going "COOOO... EH!" in one angry choir.
By noon the workers give up. The old bench stays. The pigeons hold a meeting on it to celebrate.

words.english: to meet, to have a meeting
words.say_it: Yawn two long yawns, then throw your hands in the air. "Haaah-laaah-VAI!"
words.bonus: The same word is also a noun. A meeting at work is a hālāwai.
words.picture: Office yawning through a stapler meeting
story_paragraphs: It is Monday at 9 in the morning. Your boss has called a meeting. It is about the stapler.
There are 14 people around the table. The meeting has slides. 86 slides. Slide 12 is a photo of the stapler. Slide 13 is the same photo, closer.

By hour two, everybody is yawning long, loud, slow yawns. "Haaaah..." Somebody else. "...Laaaah..." Then from the back of the room one voice cries out what everybody is thinking. "WHY?!" Haaah! Laaah! Why! Hālāwai!
The boss says you will all meet again tomorrow to discuss why. By Friday you have had 11 meetings about the stapler. On Saturday the stapler quits.

words.say_it: Knock twice on the table like you are dropping by. "KEE-pah!"
words.bonus: Kipa is a quick visit. Hoʻokipa is when you are the one hosting the visitors.
words.picture: Zookeeper and elephant visiting on Sunday
story_paragraphs: Your doorbell rings on a Sunday afternoon. It is the zookeeper. Nobody knows how he got your address.
He is just dropping by for a visit, he says. He brought a friend. The friend is an elephant. The elephant is holding a plate of cookies.
You yell back into the house, "Ma! It's the KEEPAH!" Keepah! Kipa! Ma yells back, "Tell him take off his shoes!" So the keeper takes off his shoes. The elephant takes off four giant slippahs.

They stay for two hours. The keeper drinks coffee and talks about the weather. The elephant sits on the lanai, which is now a little lower. When they leave, the keeper says, "Same time next week?" He means it.

words.say_it: Open your arms wide like you are standing at the front door. "Ho-oh-KEE-pah!"
words.bonus: Hoʻokipa is the island spirit of hospitality. There is also a famous windsurfing beach on Maui called Hoʻokipa.
words.picture: Zookeeper hosting a lūʻau for animals
story_paragraphs: The zookeeper from kipa decides it is his turn to host. He invites everybody to his house for a lūʻau. He means everybody.
You arrive and he is standing at the gate with an armful of leis, greeting each guest. "HO! OH! Welcome to the KEEPAH'S!" Ho, oh, keepah! Hoʻokipa!
Behind you come the other guests. The elephant from last week. Two giraffes, ducking under the tent.
A family of flamingos. 16 tortoises. A hippo who brought potato salad. The keeper puts a lei on every single one.

He brings every guest a plate. He refills every drink. He even gives the hippo seconds. At midnight he stands at the gate and waves as each animal goes home, telling every one of them to come back soon.

words.say_it: Hold out your hand, palm up, and ask. "NOY!"
words.bonus: When you ask for something, add "e ʻoluʻolu," which means please.
words.picture: Kid asking for everything in the store
story_paragraphs: You take your nephew Bronson to the drugstore for one thing. Toothpaste.
He starts asking the second you walk in. "Can I get gum? The robot? The pool float shaped like a shark? The big bag of li hing mui?"
He asks for things in every aisle. He asks the cashier. He asks a lady who does not even work there.
By aisle 9 he has asked for 214 things. You are about to explode. You turn around and hiss, "You are so a-NOY-ing!" Annoy! Noi!
He looks up at you with big eyes and asks for one more thing. "Can I have a hug?" You give him the hug. Then he asks for the shark float again.

words.say_it: Hold out an imaginary ice cream cone to a friend. "KO-no!"
words.picture: Party invitation written on ice cream
story_paragraphs: Aunty Tessie does not mail her invitations. She sends them in ice cream cones.
One day a delivery man hands you a waffle cone with a scoop of lychee sherbet. Written on the sherbet in chocolate is PARTY SATURDAY 5 PM BRING ICE. You stare at it. "A cone? OH!" Cone, oh! Kono!
You want to say you are busy. But the only way to say no is to not eat the cone, and it is already melting down your arm. So you eat it. Now you are going.
She invites 300 people this way. Cones arrive at offices, schools and one fire station. On Saturday the whole island shows up, sticky, happy and carrying ice. Nobody has ever turned her down.

words.english: to show, to reveal, to demonstrate
words.say_it: Whip off an invisible sheet and reveal what is under it. "Hooo-EE-keh!"
words.bonus: Hōʻike also means a test or a recital, a time to show what you know. ʻIke means to see or to know.
words.picture: Kid revealing an erupting volcano
story_paragraphs: It is show and tell in the third grade class. The first kid shows a shell. The second shows a rock.
Then Kaleo walks up with something under a bedsheet. It is six feet tall and it is humming.
He pulls off the sheet. It is a volcano. He built it himself, and it is smoking.
The class leans in. Kaleo presses a button.
BOOM. Red goo shoots up to the ceiling. The whole class screams, "HOOOO! EEK! EH!" Hoooo, eek, eh! Hōʻike! The goo rains down on the desks, the goldfish tank and the teacher's glasses.
When it stops, Kaleo bows. "That," he says, "is my demonstration." He gets an A. The janitor gets a raise.

words.say_it: Cup your hands around your mouth and sing it out. "Ho-oh-LAH-hah!"
words.bonus: Hoʻolaha is also the word for an ad or a notice. Laha means to spread, so an announcement makes news spread.
words.picture: Opera aunty announcing sale over loudspeaker
story_paragraphs: Aunty Rosalind works at the grocery store, and today she finally gets to use the loudspeaker. She used to sing opera. She has been waiting 20 years for this.
She grabs the microphone. "HO! OH!" The whole store stops. Then she sings the announcement at the top of her lungs. "SPAM IS ON SALE IN AISLE SIIIX! LAAAA-HAAAAAA!" Ho, oh, la-ha! Hoʻolaha!
The windows shake. The produce misters turn on by themselves. Her voice rolls out the door, across the parking lot and down the whole street. Drivers on the freeway hear it and take the next exit.
In 10 minutes there are 800 people in aisle six. By closing time she has announced sales on rice, eggs and slippahs, and the store has no windows left.

words.say_it: Laugh twice and point at the person next to you so they catch it. "LAH-hah!"
words.bonus: Laha is to spread out, like news or a cold going around. Hoʻolaha is to make news spread, to announce it.
words.picture: A laugh spreading across a stadium
story_paragraphs: It is the quietest moment of the big football game. 30,000 fans are holding their breath. Then one man in section 12 laughs. "LA-HA!"

Nobody knows why. But the lady next to him catches it. "La-ha!" Then her whole row. "LA-HA! LA-HA!" It spreads across section 12, then 13, then 14, then all the way around the stadium like a wave. La-ha! Laha!
The players start laughing. The referees laugh so hard they drop their flags. The laugh spreads out the gates into the parking lot, where the tailgaters catch it too.
By 9 at night it has spread to Pearl City. By midnight people are laughing in Kona. The next morning the news says it is everywhere. It all started with one "La-ha!"

words.say_it: Push both hands forward like you are unrolling a mat. "Ho-HO-lah!"
words.picture: Beach mat unrolling three miles long
story_paragraphs: Uncle Ben bought a new beach mat at the swap meet. It is rolled up tight, about the size of a paper towel roll. He sets it on the sand at Kaimana Beach and gives it a little push.
It unrolls. And unrolls. And keeps unrolling. It rolls down the whole beach, past the hotels, over sandcastles. It rolls across Kalākaua Avenue and stops traffic. It keeps going for three miles.

The whole family runs after it. At the very end it finally spreads out flat, right at the feet of a tourist from Spain eating a malasada. He looks at the mat. He looks at the 40 people running toward him. He waves. "Ho... HOLA!" Ho, hola! Hohola!
Uncle now owns the biggest beach mat in Hawaiʻi. It takes 9 hours to roll it back up.

words.say_it: Fold a piece of paper in half and hold out your hand. "PEH-loo!"
words.picture: Lou folding a pickup truck
story_paragraphs: Lou the ironing board surfer from heʻe nalu has retired. Now he runs a folding shop. He folds anything, for a price.
You bring him a fitted sheet, the kind nobody on Earth can fold. Lou folds it into a perfect square in 4 seconds. You say, "Wow." He holds out his hand. "Pay Lou." Pay, Lou! Pelu!
The line behind you is long. A lady brings a tent, and Lou folds it into a wallet. A man brings a map of the whole island, and Lou folds it into a paper crane that flies away.

A guy drives up in a pickup truck. Lou folds the truck in half, then in half again, and hands it back the size of a lunch box. Every time, he holds out his hand. "Pay Lou." Nobody argues. Nobody wants to get folded.

words.say_it: Roll your hands over each other like rolling up a mat. "Ohhh-VEE-lee!"
words.bonus: ʻŌwili is rolling something up into a bundle, like a mat or a sleeping bag. Wili is twisting or winding.
words.picture: Willy rolled inside giant sushi roll
story_paragraphs: It is sushi night at your friend Willy's house. Willy wants to make the world's biggest sushi roll. He buys a sheet of nori as big as a garage door and lays it on the lawn.
He spreads 200 pounds of rice on it. He adds cucumber, crab, egg and a whole row of spam. Then he lies down on top to press it flat.

He is still lying there when his three cousins start to roll it up. They roll. And roll. Willy disappears inside. His head sticks out one end and his feet stick out the other. You catch your breath and gasp, long and slow, "Ohhhhh... WILLY!" Oh, Willy! ʻŌwili!
They slice the roll into pieces for 60 guests. Very carefully. Around Willy.

words.english: to wind, to twist, to grind
words.say_it: Twist an invisible jar lid round and round. "VEE-lee!"
words.bonus: A lei wili is made by winding leaves or flowers around each other instead of stringing them, like a maile lei. Do not mix up wili, to twist, with kāwili, to mix.
words.picture: Spinning Willy grinding coffee in the ground
story_paragraphs: Willy from ʻōwili has just been unrolled from the sushi, and he is so dizzy he cannot stop spinning.
He spins on the spot. Faster. Faster. His body twists up like a wet towel being wrung out.
His arms wind around his body three times. His legs wind around each other. He looks like a giant corkscrew with a head.
The cousins yell, "WILLY! WILLY!" but he is spinning too fast to hear. Willy! Wili! He drills down into the lawn and grinds a hole 6 feet deep.

Aunty is smart. She drops a bag of coffee beans into the hole. Willy grinds them into perfect coffee in 30 seconds. She scoops it up and makes coffee for everybody. Willy finally stops, twisted, dizzy and very proud.

words.say_it: Braid three fingers together, over and under. "HEE-lee."
words.bonus: A lei hili is a braided lei, often made with ferns.
words.picture: Grandkids braiding Tūtū's two-mile hair
story_paragraphs: Tūtū Hattie has not cut her hair since 1961. It is gray, it is shiny and it is 2 miles long. Every morning it has to be braided.

She sits on her porch at the bottom of the mountain road. Her hair runs all the way up the hilly road behind her, around 14 curves, over 3 hills and down the other side. Three grandkids stand along the road twisting it together. Over, under, over, under.
Cars drive by and honk. A tourist leans out the window and yells, "Why is this road so HILLY?" The grandkids yell back, "It's not the road! It's her HAIR!" Hilly! Hili!
It takes 5 hours. The finished braid is so thick that birds nest in it. At night Tūtū coils it up in the yard like a giant rope and sleeps with her feet on it.

words.say_it: Weave your fingers over and under each other. "Oo-LAH-nah."
words.bonus: Ulana lauhala is weaving mats, hats and baskets from hala leaves.
words.picture: Spider weaving a web across H-1
story_paragraphs: A spider named Lana moves in under an overpass on the H-1. She is the size of a dinner plate and she is an artist.
One night she starts weaving. Over, under, over, under. By morning her web stretches across all six lanes of the freeway. It has a pattern like a lauhala mat, with little flowers woven in.
The morning traffic stops. Hundreds of drivers get out of their cars to look. Nobody is mad. They all say the same thing. "Ooooh... LANA!" Ooh, Lana! Ulana!
Lana keeps weaving. She weaves a little welcome sign. She weaves a hammock for a tired commuter. By noon the city puts up a sign that says SLOW, WEAVING AHEAD, and everybody takes the back roads.

words.say_it: Push fabric through an invisible sewing machine and hum deep. "HOO-moo."
words.picture: Grandma sewing one giant family muʻumuʻu
story_paragraphs: Grandma's sewing machine is 70 years old, and it is loud. When she turns it on, it hums so deep the whole house shakes. "HUMMM... ooo. HUMMM... ooo." Hum, ooo! Humu!
This week she is sewing a muʻumuʻu for the biggest wedding in family history. The bride wants one dress so big the whole family can wear it at the same time.
Grandma sews for five days straight. The needle goes up and down 1,000 times a minute.
Flowered fabric pours off the table, out the window and across the yard. The neighbors think it is an earthquake. The dog hums along.
At the wedding, 43 relatives stand inside one giant muʻumuʻu, heads poking out of 43 holes, humming together. Grandma cries into her tissue. "HUMMM... ooo."

words.say_it: Push an invisible needle through a flower. "KOO-ee!"
words.bonus: Careful. Kui, smooth, is to string a lei. Kuʻi, with the catch, is to pound, like pounding poi.
words.picture: Aunty stringing plumerias with a giant needle
story_paragraphs: Aunty Noe has to string a lei for every graduate at the high school. That is 5,000 plumerias, and her lei needle is as long as a broom handle.
She pokes the needle through the middle of the first flower. White sap oozes out all over her fingers. "GOOEY!" she says. She threads the next one. "GOOEY!" Gooey! Kui!
She strings flowers all day on the lanai. Her fingers are sticky. Her arms are sticky. Her hair is stuck to the needle.
By sunset she has strung one lei that is 400 feet long. It wraps around the house twice.
At graduation she cuts it into pieces and gives one to every kid. She puts the extra 30 feet on the principal. She is still sticky on Tuesday.

words.say_it: Sprinkle glitter over everything with both hands. "Ho-oh-NAH-nee!"
words.bonus: Nani means beautiful. Hoʻonani is to make something beautiful, and also to praise or glorify.
words.picture: Nanny with glitter cannon beautifying Dad
story_paragraphs: Your family hires a nanny. She is five feet tall and carries a glitter cannon on her back. She believes everything should be beautiful.

On the first day she walks into the kitchen and sees a dirty pot. She yells "HO! OH!" and fires the glitter cannon. The pot sparkles. She finds the garbage can. HO! OH! Now it has pink flowers painted on the side.
She finds Dad asleep on the couch in his old shorts. HO! OH! He wakes up in a tuxedo with a flower behind his ear. The whole family runs around yelling, "HO! OH! NANNY!" Ho, oh, nanny! Hoʻonani!
By Friday she has made the garbage truck look like a parade float. The street is so beautiful the mail carrier cries.

words.english: to dress up, to wear finery
words.say_it: Straighten an invisible bow tie and hold the first sound. "Kaaah-HEE-ko!"
words.bonus: Do not mix it up with kahiko, no long vowel, which means old or ancient, like hula kahiko. Kāhiko, with the long ā, is dressing up.
words.picture: Gecko in tuxedo on dressed-up car
story_paragraphs: You wake up on the morning of the Christmas parade and walk out to your car. It is not your car anymore.

Overnight, it got all dressed up in finery. There are 800 plastic flowers glued to the hood. There are 90 strings of lights. There is a disco ball hanging from the mirror and a pink feather boa around every tire.

On the roof stands a gecko. He is wearing a tiny tuxedo, a bow tie and a sequin hat. He is dressed up for the parade too. You stare at him and stretch out the first sound. "Caaaar... GEE-ko!" Caaar, gecko! Kāhiko!
You drive in the parade. You win first prize. The gecko rides on the dashboard, waving at the crowd, taking all the credit.

words.english: to get dressed, to put on clothes
words.say_it: Pull an invisible shirt over your head, with a catch. "Ah-AH-hoo!"
words.bonus: ʻAʻahu is also the noun for clothing or a garment.
words.picture: Family wearing every piece of clothing in snow
story_paragraphs: Your family goes to see snow for the first time. You land on the continent and it is 5 degrees outside. Nobody owns a coat.

So Dad makes everybody put on every piece of clothing in the suitcases. Three t-shirts. Two aloha shirts. Four pairs of shorts over one pair of jeans. Socks on your hands and a beach towel for a scarf. Grandma wears six muʻumuʻus, one on top of the other.
You walk out of the airport looking like a pile of laundry with eyes. Mom looks around and gasps with a catch in her throat. "Ah! (catch) AH! WHO is that?" Ah! Ah! Who! ʻAʻahu!
It is Dad. He is wearing 19 layers. He cannot bend his arms. He tips over in the snow and has to be rolled to the car like a snowball.

words.say_it: Scrub your forearm hard with the other hand. "Aaah-NAI!"
words.picture: Uncle getting scrubbed in a car wash
story_paragraphs: Uncle Gordon has not showered since the canoe race. Nine days. He smells like fish, sunscreen and old rubber slippahs. The family drives him to the car wash.
He stands in the middle of the car wash in his swim shorts. The giant spinning brushes come at him.
They scrub his back. They rub his belly. They scrub behind his ears. Soap flies everywhere.
Uncle closes his eyes, catches his breath and lets out one long happy sigh. "Aaaaaah..." Then he grins. "...NICE!" Aaah, nice! ʻĀnai!
The brushes scrub so hard they rub off three layers of dirt, a tattoo that turned out to be marker and some of his eyebrows. He comes out shiny as a new truck. He pays extra for the wax.

words.say_it: Stir an invisible bowl fast, then lift your front wheels up. "Kaaah-VEE-lee!"
words.bonus: Kāwili is mixing things together. Wili, without the kā, is twisting or winding.
words.picture: Smoothie mixer truck popping a wheelie
story_paragraphs: There is a cement mixer truck on the H-1, but it is not full of cement. Aunty Josie rented it for the family party. It is full of mango, guava, pineapple, poi, ice cream and three whole papayas.
The drum spins, mixing and blending, round and round. Everything turns into one giant orange smoothie. But Aunty wants it smoother.
She hits the gas. The truck goes faster and the drum spins faster.
The front wheels lift off the road. The whole truck pops a wheelie down the freeway. People in other cars point and yell, "Caaaar... WHEELIE!" Caaar, wheelie! Kāwili!
She pulls into the party still on two wheels. She opens the chute and pours out 400 cups of perfectly mixed smoothie. The line goes around the block.

words.say_it: Poke an imaginary chicken with a fork. "Ho-oh-MO-ah!"
words.bonus: Moa means chicken. Moʻa, with the catch, means cooked. So hoʻomoʻa is to make something cooked.
words.picture: Chicken cooking on a truck engine
story_paragraphs: Uncle Kalani's oven is broken, and he has a chicken to cook for dinner. So he wraps the chicken in foil, straps it to the engine of his old truck and drives around the island.
He drives from Kāneʻohe to Haleʻiwa and back. The engine gets hotter.
At every stoplight he jumps out, opens the hood, pokes the chicken and yells, "HO! OH! MO... AH!" with a catch in the middle. Ho, oh, mo, ah! Hoʻomoʻa!
By Kailua it smells so good that three cars follow him home. People roll down their windows and sniff.

He pulls into his driveway, pops the hood, and the chicken is cooked perfectly, crispy on the outside and juicy inside. He serves it to the whole block. It tastes a little like motor oil. Nobody complains.

words.english: to bake in an underground oven (imu)
words.say_it: Pretend to dig a hole, then pat the dirt down on top. "Kaaah-LOO-ah!"
words.bonus: Kālua pig is pork baked in an imu until it falls apart. You can kālua other foods too, like turkey or sweet potato.
words.picture: Dog named Lua digging an imu
story_paragraphs: Your family has a dog named Lua. Lua is a digger. She has dug 300 holes in the yard, and your dad is tired of it.

Then comes the graduation lūʻau, and Uncle needs an imu, an underground oven, big enough for a whole pig. Nobody wants to dig. Uncle stands in the middle of the yard and yells, "Caaall... LUA!" Caaall, Lua! Kālua!

Lua comes running, ears flapping. She digs. Dirt flies over the fence. In 10 minutes the pit is 6 feet deep and perfectly round. Uncle fills it with hot rocks and banana leaves, lays in the pig, covers it up and lets it cook all night.
The next day the pig comes out smoky, soft and falling apart. Everybody eats. Lua gets the biggest plate, and she buries half of it for later.

words.say_it: Flip an imaginary steak over hot coals and hold the first sound. "Poooo-LEH-hoo!"
words.bonus: Traditionally pūlehu meant roasting foods like sweet potato, breadfruit or banana right on hot embers. Today you will also see pūlehu steak and ribs at local parties.
words.picture: Uncle grilling steaks in empty pool
story_paragraphs: The hotel pool has been drained for repairs. Uncle Frank sees an opportunity.

Overnight, he fills the whole empty swimming pool with kiawe charcoal. 6,000 pounds of it. By morning the coals are glowing orange from the shallow end to the deep end. He lays a giant metal grill across the top and puts on 400 steaks and 90 sweet potatoes.
Smoke rises into the sky. The lifeguard shows up for work, stares at the pool and yells, "POOOOL... EH? WHO did this?" Poool, eh, who? Pūlehu!
Uncle flips a steak with a canoe paddle. "Broiling," he says. The lifeguard thinks about it for 3 seconds. Then he grabs a plate.

words.say_it: Shake an invisible frying pan. "Pah-LAI!"
words.bonus: Palai is also the name of a native Hawaiian lace fern.
words.picture: Pa lying next to a fried remote
story_paragraphs: Pa loves to fry. And Pa lies about it.
You come home and the TV remote is golden brown and crispy. "Pa, did you fry the remote?" Pa shakes his head. "No." You point at him and shout, "Pa... LIE!" Pa, lie! Palai!
The next day the mail is fried. The dog's chew toy is fried. The newspaper is in tempura batter.
There is a whole fried pineapple on the table like a trophy, and Pa is standing next to it with a spatula and oil on his shirt. "I don't know who did this."
"PA, LIE!" the whole family yells. By Friday he has fried a slippah, a ʻukulele and your homework. The homework actually tastes pretty good with ketchup.

words.say_it: Wiggle your fingers up from the table like bubbles rising. "Ho-oh-lah-pah-LAH-pah!"
words.bonus: Lapalapa is the bubbling itself. Hoʻolapalapa is to make it bubble, to boil it.
words.picture: Grandma boiling peanuts in a hot tub
story_paragraphs: Grandma is boiling peanuts in the backyard. Her pot is not a pot. It is an old hot tub.

She fills it with water, salt, star anise and 900 pounds of peanuts, and she lights a fire under it. At first nothing happens. Then little bubbles come up and pop with a tiny sound. "Lapa... lapa..." Then bigger bubbles. "LAPA! LAPA!"

Now the whole tub is boiling hard, bubbles the size of beach balls popping and splashing. Grandma stands over it with a canoe paddle, stirring and yelling, "HO! OH! LAPA LAPA!" Ho, oh, lapa lapa! Hoʻolapalapa!
A wave of boiling water sloshes over the side and cooks the grass. By dinner the peanuts are perfect. The whole neighborhood lines up with bags, and the yard smells like peanuts for a year.

words.english: to draw a line, to mark; to slice open
words.say_it: Karate chop the air in one straight line. "KAH-hah!"
words.bonus: Kaha is to draw a line or mark, and also to cut open, like a fish. Kaha kiʻi means to draw a picture.
words.picture: Karate master slicing an ʻahi
story_paragraphs: The fish market has a new worker. He is a karate master in a white uniform and a black belt.
A fisherman brings in a 60-pound ʻahi. The master bows to it. He raises one hand high. "KA..." he says quietly.
Then he chops down. "...HAH!" Ka-HAH! Kaha! The ʻahi slices open, clean and straight, right down the middle.
The crowd gasps. He does it again with a mahimahi. KA-HAH! Then he draws a line in the sawdust on the floor with one finger, perfectly straight, and says, "Line starts here." KA-HAH!
Soon he is marking the price on each fish with one karate chop. The line of customers goes out the door and down the street. Everybody wants their fish opened with a yell.

words.say_it: Point at things around you and count them. "HEH-loo!"
words.bonus: Helu also means a number. Your phone number is your helu kelepona.
words.picture: Store greeter counting every customer
story_paragraphs: The new store greeter is a man named Mr. Bill, and he takes his job very seriously. He counts every customer who walks through the door, and he says hello to each one.
"HEL-LOO! One!" "HEL-LOO! Two!" "HEL-LOO! Three!" Hello! Helu! By lunchtime he is at 2,400. He does not stop to eat.
A tour bus pulls up and 60 people get off at once. He counts every one, so fast he sounds like a woodpecker. "Hel-loo-hel-loo-hel-loo!"
A pigeon walks in. He counts the pigeon. A gecko runs in. He counts the gecko.
At closing time he stands at the door and announces the total. "8,812." Then someone walks out, and he counts backward. He is still out there at midnight, counting the lights in the parking lot.

words.say_it: Clap your hands together, like joining two things. "Ho-oh-HOO-ee!"
words.bonus: Hui is a club or a group, or to join. Huʻi, with the catch, is an ache or a chill. Hoʻohui is to put things together or add them up.
words.picture: Cousins joining into a giant human tower
story_paragraphs: It is the big family reunion at the park, and the cousins want to build the tallest human tower in Hawaiʻi.

The biggest uncle stands at the bottom. The next cousin climbs onto his shoulders and yells, "HO! OH! HOOEY!" Another cousin joins. "HO! OH! HOOEY!" Ho, oh, hooey! Hoʻohui! Every person who joins adds another level to the tower.
10 cousins. 20. 31. The tower is taller than the banyan tree. It sways in the wind. The tiniest cousin climbs all the way up and adds herself to the very top, and the whole tower cheers, "HOOEY!"
Then Grandma adds one plate of chicken to the top cousin's hands, and the whole thing wobbles. They add, they join, they hold. They do not fall. For about 8 seconds.

words.say_it: Slide your voice from high to low while you count out invisible money. "Ho-oh-LEE-lo."
words.bonus: Hoʻolilo is to make something gone, like spending money, or to turn something into something else. Lilo is being gone, or becoming.
words.picture: Spending money at swap meet, voice dropping
story_paragraphs: It is Saturday at the swap meet and you have 100 dollars. You feel rich. Your voice is high and happy. "Ho! Oh! LEEEEE!"
You spend 20 on a hat. You spend 15 on a coconut with a face painted on it. You spend 30 on a lamp shaped like a fish.
Every time you spend, the money in your pocket gets lower, and so does your voice. "Leeee... low." Ho, oh, lee, low! Hoʻolilo!
By noon you have 3 dollars left. Your voice is so low it sounds like a foghorn. "LOOOOOW."

Then you catch yourself in a mirror at one of the booths. You have turned into a totally different person. Fish lamp. Coconut face. Hat with a propeller on top. You spent everything, and it turned you into a swap meet uncle.

words.english: to be gone, to be taken; to become
words.say_it: Wave goodbye as your voice fades from high to low. "LEE-lo."
words.bonus: Lilo is used when something is lost or taken, and also when something becomes something new. Compare hoʻolilo, to spend or to turn into.
words.picture: Bus driving away with your slippahs
story_paragraphs: You leave your favorite slippahs on the bus seat. You notice the second the bus pulls away.
You run after it barefoot. The bus honks its horn, and the sound fades away down the street like a sad whistle. "LEEEEE..." It turns the corner. "...looooow." Lee, low. Lilo! Gone.
You stand on the hot sidewalk at 2 in the afternoon, hopping from foot to foot like a frog. The slippahs are gone. Taken. On a trip around the island without you.
Three weeks later you see the same bus. The driver is wearing your slippahs. They have become his lucky slippahs now.
He honks, "LEEEE... looow," waves and drives off. They are gone for good, and they have become somebody else's.

words.say_it: Hide something behind your back and shake your head slowly. "Hoo-NAAAH."
words.picture: Uncle hiding a musubi in his cheek
story_paragraphs: There is one spam musubi left on the plate at the party. Then there are zero. Everybody turns to look at Uncle Kimo.
Uncle Kimo is standing very still. His left cheek is huge, the size of a softball. A little corner of nori is poking out of his mouth.
Aunty points at him. "Who took the musubi?" Uncle Kimo shakes his head slowly and says, through a full mouth, "Hoo? NAAAAAH." Who? Nah! Hūnā!
The kids check his pockets. Three more musubi. They check his hat. Two more.
They check his slippahs. One more, a little flat. He has hidden 11 musubi on his body.
Still he says, "Hooo? Naaaaah." Nobody believes him, but nobody can prove it, because he eats the evidence.

words.english: to practice, to get used to
words.say_it: Say it slowly five times in a row, like you are practicing. "Ho-oh-mah-ah-MAH-ah."
words.bonus: Maʻa means used to it. Hoʻomaʻamaʻa is doing something over and over until you are used to it.
words.picture: Baby practicing ma-ah in high chair
story_paragraphs: Baby Leilani is ten months old, and she has decided today is the day she says her first word. She will practice until she gets it right.
She sits in her high chair and concentrates. "Ma." A tiny catch in her throat. "Ah." Again. "Ma... ah. Ma... ah." Her big brother cheers every try. "HO! OH!" Ho, oh, ma, ah, ma, ah! Hoʻomaʻamaʻa!
She practices all morning. She practices through lunch with rice on her face. She practices at the beach, at the store and in the bath.
By the end of the week she has said "Ma-ah" 10,000 times. Her voice is strong. She sounds like a little coach.
Finally her mom walks in the door. Baby Leilani looks right at her, takes a big breath and says, perfectly, "DAD." All that practice.

words.english: to be used to, to be accustomed
words.say_it: Shrug and sip your drink like nothing could ever surprise you. "MAH-ah."
words.bonus: Maʻa is being used to something. Hoʻomaʻamaʻa is practicing until you get used to it.
words.picture: Calm mom sipping tea in total chaos
story_paragraphs: Your mom has 11 kids, 4 dogs and a pet chicken. Nothing surprises her anymore. She is used to it.
The ceiling fan falls. She sips her tea. The twins ride the dogs through the kitchen. She turns the page of her magazine.
Your brother sets the toaster on fire. She hands him the extinguisher without looking up.
You run in screaming, "MA!" She raises one eyebrow. There is a little catch in her throat. "Ah." Ma! Ah. Maʻa.
"MA! THE CAR IS IN THE POOL!" "Ah." "MA! GRANDPA IS ON THE ROOF!" "Ah." "MA! THERE IS A PIG IN YOUR BED!" She thinks about it. "Ah."
She has heard it all before, 10,000 times. At this point she would be surprised if nothing happened.

words.say_it: Flex both arms and grunt out every sound. "Ho-oh-ee-KAI-kah!"
words.bonus: Ikaika means strong. Hoʻoikaika is to make strong, and people also say it to mean try hard, keep going.
words.picture: Skinny uncle lifting a canoe overhead
story_paragraphs: Uncle Pono is the skinniest man in Waiʻanae. His arms look like two chopsticks. But he has decided he will lift his own canoe over his head by summer.
Every morning he trains on the beach. He grabs a coconut and lifts it. "HO! OH! EEE! KAI! KAH!" Ho, oh, ee, kai, kah! Hoʻoikaika! He grunts so loud the fish swim away.
He lifts a bucket of sand. He lifts a cooler. He lifts his neighbor, who did not agree to this.
He tries hard every single day for 190 days. His arms grow. His legs grow. His grunt gets deeper.
On the first day of summer he grabs the canoe, all 400 pounds of it, and lifts it over his head. The whole beach cheers. Then he carries it into the ocean and goes fishing.

words.say_it: Stretch your hands apart, wider and wider. "Ho-oh-NOO-ee!"
words.bonus: Nui means big. Hoʻonui is to make bigger. The opposite is hoʻēmi, to make smaller.
words.picture: Machine making a giant malasada
story_paragraphs: Your cousin builds a machine in his garage that makes things bigger. It has a funnel on one end and a door on the other, and when it runs it groans, "NOOO-EEE."

He drops in a malasada. The machine shakes. "HO! OH! NOOO-EEE!" Ho, oh, nui! Hoʻonui! Out rolls a malasada the size of a car tire. He drops in a gecko. Out comes a gecko the size of a dog, and it licks your face.
Everybody gets excited. You put in a shave ice, and out comes a snow mountain. You put in a dollar, and out comes a dollar the size of a bedsheet that no store will take.
Then the machine accidentally makes itself bigger. "NOOOO-EEEE!" It grows right through the roof. Now the whole garage is the machine, and you live inside it.

words.say_it: Pinch your fingers closer and closer together. "Ho-EH-mee!"
words.bonus: Hoʻēmi is to make smaller or cut down. The opposite is hoʻonui, to make bigger.
words.picture: Plate lunch shrunk to one grain
story_paragraphs: You order a plate lunch at your favorite lunch wagon. Two scoops rice, one scoop mac, chicken katsu. The same thing you have ordered every day for 9 years.
But there is a new manager, and he is cutting down. He takes your plate and scrapes off one scoop of rice. Then half the other one.
He trims the katsu with scissors until it is the size of a postage stamp. The mac salad is now one macaroni.
He hands it back. You stare at it. You look up at him. "HO! EHHH? ME?" Ho! Eh? Me? Hoʻēmi!
He nods. Then he takes back the one macaroni. Now it is a plate with a single grain of rice on it. "Price is the same," he says. You eat it in one bite and stay hungry for 9 more years.

words.say_it: Swing an imaginary rope over your head and whoop. "Ho-oh-PEE-hah!"
words.bonus: Paniolo are Hawaiian cowboys. Piha means full, so hoʻopiha is to make something full.
words.picture: Paniolo filling a barn with fire hose
story_paragraphs: Up on a ranch in Waimea there is a paniolo named Jimmy who fills things up. That is all he does, and he yells the whole time.
The water trough is empty. Jimmy grabs a fire hose. "HO! OH! PEE-HAH!" Ho, oh, pee-hah! Hoʻopiha!
In 4 seconds the trough is full to the top. He fills the horse's bucket. He fills the rain barrel.

He fills his hat and puts it back on his head. He cannot stop. He fills the bed of the pickup until the fish from the pond jump in. He fills his boots. He fills the barn so high the hay bales float out the door.
The boss rides up and asks what is going on. Jimmy grins, soaking wet, and fills the boss's coffee cup to the brim. "PEE-HAH!"

words.say_it: Pat your belly and lean way back. "PEE-hah."
words.bonus: Piha means full, of food, water or people. A packed room is piha too.
words.picture: Paniolo burping after 14 plate lunches
story_paragraphs: Jimmy the paniolo from hoʻopiha has finished work, and he is at the plate lunch place with a coupon for all you can eat.

He eats one plate. Two plates. Six plates. Loco moco, beef stew, chili pepper water on everything. By plate 13 his belt pops off and shoots across the room. By plate 14 his cheeks are round like a pufferfish.
He cannot fit one more bite. He is full to the top, full like a water balloon. He leans back, pats his giant belly and lets out a burp that sounds like a cowboy yell. "PEE-HAH!" Pee-hah! Piha!
The windows rattle. The cook peeks out of the kitchen and takes the coupon sign off the wall. Jimmy has to be rolled out to his horse.

words.say_it: Tip an imaginary pitcher and make a siren sound. "Nee-NEE-nee!"
words.picture: Fire truck pouring gravy on loco moco
story_paragraphs: At the diner, Aunty Carol is in charge of the gravy for the loco moco. She does not use a ladle. She uses a fire truck.
The fire truck backs up to the kitchen window. The siren goes on. "Nee-NEE-nee! Nee-NEE-nee!" Aunty grabs the hose and starts pouring. Nee, nee, nee! Ninini!
Brown gravy arcs across the room and lands on the rice, the patty and the egg. She pours it on every plate. She pours it on the counter. She keeps pouring until the gravy is up to everybody's ankles.
Customers lift their feet. A kid floats by on a menu. When the siren finally stops, everybody agrees it is the best loco moco they ever had. It just needs a little less gravy.

words.say_it: Wave your hand in a long, flowing S shape. "KAH-heh."
words.bonus: Kahe is used for any liquid flowing, even tears running down your face.
words.picture: Stream carrying Uncle's couch down the street
story_paragraphs: The little stream behind Uncle Sam's house in Mānoa has always stayed in its bed. Today it gets bored.
It climbs up the bank. It flows under the back door, across the kitchen floor, around the table legs and down the hall. It chuckles as it goes. "KAH-heh! KAH-heh!" Kah-heh! Kahe!

Uncle Sam is asleep on the couch. The stream flows right under the couch, lifts it up and carries it, with him on it, out the front door. "KAH-heh!" It flows down the driveway, past the school and past the store.
Uncle wakes up floating past the zoo. He waves at a monkey. The stream flows all the way to Waikīkī, sets him gently on the sand, then turns around and flows back home.

words.english: to swell, to rise, to overflow
words.say_it: Puff up your cheeks and slowly raise both arms. "HOOOOO!"
words.bonus: Hū is used for dough rising and for water swelling up and spilling over.
words.picture: Sweet bread dough swelling out the windows
story_paragraphs: Aunty Helen makes sweet bread for the church bake sale. She puts the dough in a big bowl, covers it with a towel and goes to sleep. She put in too much yeast. 40 times too much.
At midnight the dough starts to rise. It swells over the bowl. It swells over the counter. It pushes the kitchen door open and swells down the hallway like a big soft whale.
At 3 in the morning Aunty wakes up because the dough is in her bed. She screams, one long sound, "HOOOOOOOO!" Hū!

By sunrise the dough has swelled out every window and overflowed into the yard. It is rising up the telephone pole. The neighbors come out and cut off pieces with a knife. The bake sale sells out by 7.

words.say_it: Puff up your cheeks, then pop them with both hands. "Po-HAAAH!"
words.bonus: Pohā is also the name of the cape gooseberry. You will see pohā berry jam in local stores.
words.picture: Giant water balloon bursting at the fair
story_paragraphs: The biggest water balloon in the world is being filled on the lawn at the school fair. It is filling from a fire hydrant. It is already the size of a minivan, green and wobbly, and it is shaking.
The crowd steps back. The principal keeps saying it is safe. The balloon gets bigger.
The rubber is so thin you can see through it. Every kid holds their breath.
Then a mosquito lands on it. "Po..." says the principal. The balloon bursts. "...HAAAAAAH!" Po, HAAAH! Pohā!

A wall of water 20 feet high knocks over the cotton candy stand. It sweeps the principal off his feet and slides him down the lawn like a waterslide. Every kid is soaked. It is the best day in school history.

words.say_it: Stare at an imaginary cracked phone and let out a long sigh. "Nah-HAAAH."
words.bonus: Nahā is for something cracked or broken, like a dish or a phone. Haki is for something that snaps in two, like a stick.
words.picture: Uncle staring at his cracked phone
story_paragraphs: Uncle Rudy just bought a brand new phone. It cost more than his car. He is showing it off on the balcony of his apartment on the 14th floor.
Then he drops it. It falls 14 floors and smacks the sidewalk. Everybody runs downstairs. Uncle picks it up and slowly turns it over.
His nephew asks, "Is it broken?" Uncle looks at the front. It looks OK. "Nah."
Then he flips it. The back is cracked into 800 pieces, like a spiderweb. He lets out a long, sad sound. "HAAAAAAH." Nah... HAAAH. Nahā.
He tries to make a call and the screen cracks more. He tries to take a picture and it cracks more. Now the sidewalk under his feet is cracked too. He puts the phone in a bag of rice and cries.

words.english: to break (like a stick), to snap
words.say_it: Snap an invisible stick over your knee. "HAH-kee!"
words.bonus: Haki is for things that snap in two, like sticks and bones. For a cracked dish, use nahā.
words.picture: Grandma snapping hockey sticks over her knee
story_paragraphs: Grandma needs firewood for the imu. The hardware store is closed. But the kid next door plays hockey and has a garage full of hockey sticks.
Grandma walks over. She picks up a hockey stick. She holds it with both hands, raises it over her knee and SNAP! Breaks it in half like a pencil. "HOCKEY!" she yells. Hockey! Haki!
She snaps another. SNAP. "HOCKEY!" She snaps 70 sticks. She snaps a broom, a curtain rod and a pool cue. The kid watches with his mouth open.
By the end the garage is empty and Grandma has a pile of wood as tall as a truck. She pays the kid with a plate of kālua pig from the imu. He says it was worth every stick.

words.english: to break open, to tear down
words.say_it: Cry like a baby, then smash your fist down and giggle. "Vaaah-VAH-hee!"
words.picture: Giant baby knocking down a building
story_paragraphs: The city wants to tear down the old building on the corner. They bring a wrecking ball. It does not work.
The building is too strong. So they call in a specialist.
The specialist is a baby. A giant baby, 50 feet tall, in a diaper, cranky from her nap. She sits down in front of the building and starts to cry. "WAAAH! WAH!"
Then she swings one chubby arm. BOOM. A whole floor falls off. She giggles. "HEE!"
Waaah, wah, hee! Wāwahi! She knocks down the next floor. "WAAAH! WAH! HEE!" She pulls the roof off like the lid of a cookie tin. She breaks open a wall and finds a snack machine inside.
By lunchtime the building is a pile of bricks, and the baby is asleep on top of it with a bag of chips.

words.say_it: Throw your hands open from your chest like a blast. "Pah-HOOO!"
words.bonus: Careful. Pahu, with no long ū, means to push, and also a box or a drum. Pahū, with the long ū, means to explode.
words.picture: Pa lighting a giant firecracker
story_paragraphs: It is New Year's Eve, and Pa from palai has put down the frying pan. Tonight he is in charge of fireworks.

Pa has one firecracker. It is 9 feet long and as thick as a telephone pole. He bought it from a man at the swap meet who said, "Don't ask." The whole neighborhood gathers at a safe distance, which is two streets away.
Pa lights it with a very long stick. He walks back very, very slowly. Everybody counts down. Three. Two. One. Pa turns around and yells, "PAAA..." Then it explodes. "...HOOOOO!" Pa! Hooo! Pahū!
The blast knocks every mango off every tree for a mile. Car alarms go off in the next town. Pa stands in the smoke with his hair straight up and yells, "Happy New Year!"

words.say_it: Let your whole body slump down, lower and lower. "Hee-OH-lo."
words.picture: Hotel-sized sandcastle collapsing
story_paragraphs: Twelve cousins spent all day building a sandcastle at Waimānalo. It is the size of a hotel. It has towers, a moat, a drawbridge made from a boogie board and a flag made from somebody's t-shirt.
At sunset everybody steps back to admire it. It is perfect. Then one sand crab walks out of the main tower.

The tower starts to lean. Somebody whispers, "He..." It leans more. "...OH..." It starts to fall. "...LOOOW!" He, oh, low! Hiolo! The main tower collapses into the next tower, which tumbles into the next, which falls into the wall.
The whole thing slumps down, lower and lower, into one giant wet pile. The crab walks away. The cousins stand in silence. Then everybody starts building again.

words.say_it: Hold your hands toward a pretend fire, catch your breath and let it out long. "AAAAH!"
words.bonus: Ahi means fire. ʻĀ can also mean rough ʻaʻā lava. Hoʻā is to set something on fire.
words.picture: 99 candles blazing on Tūtū's cake
story_paragraphs: It is Tūtū Violet's 99th birthday. Her grandkids bake a cake the size of a coffee table and put 99 candles on it.
They light the first candle. They light the second. By the time they light number 99, the cake is burning like a campfire.
The flames are 3 feet high. The smoke alarm is screaming. The paper plates catch fire.
Everybody in the room opens their mouth at the same time. There is a tiny catch in every throat, and then one long, loud scream. "(gulp) AAAAAAAH!" ʻĀ!
Tūtū just sits there, warm and happy, holding her hands out to the fire like it is a cold night. "Nice," she says. "Burning bright. Just like me."

words.english: to blow; to burn; to smoke
words.say_it: Blow out an invisible candle as hard as you can. "POO-hee!"
words.bonus: Puhi is also the word for an eel. Same sound, totally different thing.
words.picture: Tūtū blowing out 99 candles
story_paragraphs: The cake from ʻā is still burning. 99 candles. Three-foot flames. The fire alarm is still screaming. Tūtū Violet decides it is time to blow them out.
She stands up. She takes the biggest breath of her whole life. Her chest puffs up like a balloon. Then she blows. "POOOH!" The flames bend over flat. "HEE!" The last candle goes out. Pooh! Hee! Puhi!
The smoke rolls across the room. The curtains fly up. The dog slides across the floor. The front door blows open, and Uncle's hat sails out and lands in the neighbor's mango tree.
She sits back down, calm as can be, while the smoke puffs out the windows. "Done," she says. "Who wants cake?"

words.english: to light, to set on fire
words.say_it: Strike an invisible match and jump back. "Ho-AAAH!"
words.bonus: ʻĀ means to burn. Hoʻā is to make it burn, to light it.
words.picture: Uncle lighting torches with a giant match
story_paragraphs: It is the grand opening of the new beach hotel, and Uncle Makoa gets the honor of lighting the first tiki torch. A big crowd is watching.

They hand him a match. It is not a normal match. It is the size of a telephone pole, and it takes four men to carry it. Uncle braces his feet, lifts the giant match and drags it across a matchbox as big as a garage door.
SSSKRRRT. FWOOM. A fireball blooms. Uncle yells, "HO!" Then he feels the heat on his eyebrows and screams a long, long "AAAAAH!" Ho, aaah! Hoʻā!
He runs down the beach with the flaming match, lighting all 300 torches one after another. By the last torch the whole beach is glowing, and his eyebrows are gone.

words.say_it: Point far away with one squinting eye, then dump an invisible bucket. "Kee-NAI!"
words.bonus: Kinai ahi means a firefighter, or a fire extinguisher. Ahi means fire.
words.picture: Old firefighter dumping shave ice on grill
story_paragraphs: The fire station has a new firefighter. She is 80 years old and has the keenest eyes on the island. She can spot a fire from 30 miles away.

She sits on the station roof with a cooler of shave ice. Suddenly she points at the mountains. "Somebody's grill is burning on the other side!" The crew squints. They see nothing. "Keen eye!" they yell. Keen eye! Kinai!
She jumps in the truck. They race over the mountain. She leaps out, runs to the burning grill and dumps the whole cooler of shave ice on it. Strawberry, lemon, blue. HSSSSS. The fire is out.
She does this 14 times a day. The whole island smells like rainbow shave ice and wet charcoal.

words.english: to protect, to shelter; to keep calm
words.say_it: Spread your arms over something to shelter it and speak softly. "Ho-oh-MAH-loo."
words.bonus: Malu means shade or shelter. Hoʻomalu is to give shelter, to protect and to keep things calm.
words.picture: Mall guard sheltering the whole town
story_paragraphs: A big storm is coming. The radio says winds of 90 miles an hour. People are running in circles in the street, holding their dogs and their rice cookers.
Then Aunty Dee, the security guard at the shopping mall, gets on her megaphone. She is calm like a lake. "Everybody come inside the MALL."
The whole town cheers, "HO! OH! MALL! OOH!" Ho, oh, mall, ooh! Hoʻomalu!
5,000 people pack into the mall. She locks the big doors. Outside the wind howls and the palm trees bend flat. Inside she hands out blankets, puts on soft music and gives every kid a free pretzel.
Nobody panics. People nap in the furniture store. Aunties play cards in the food court. The storm passes by morning, and nobody wants to leave.

words.say_it: Stand with your arms crossed in front of a door. "Kee-AH-ee!"
words.bonus: A kiaʻi is also a guard or a guardian, the person who watches over.
words.picture: Chihuahua guarding the snack cabinet key
story_paragraphs: In Grandma's kitchen there is a snack cabinet with a big padlock. The only key hangs from the collar of Grandma's chihuahua, Peanut. Peanut is the guard.
Peanut weighs 4 pounds. She sits in front of the cabinet all day and all night. She never sleeps. When you walk near, she lifts her lip and growls a tiny growl.
You tiptoe up at midnight. "Key..." you whisper, reaching for her collar. She snaps her head around. "AH!" you gasp, and there is a gulp in your throat. She barks. "EEE!" Key! Ah! Eee! Kiaʻi!
The whole house wakes up. Grandma comes out in her curlers and finds Peanut sitting on your chest like she caught a burglar. She guards that cabinet for 17 years. Nobody ever gets a cracker.

words.say_it: Hold up an invisible camera and click it twice. "Maah-kah-ee-KAH-ee!"
words.bonus: A visitor or newcomer who comes to go sightseeing is a malihini.
words.picture: Mom photographing everything, even mailboxes
story_paragraphs: Your Ma comes to visit you for one week, and she wants to see EVERYTHING.
She has a camera around her neck the size of a toaster. Every time she takes a picture, she yells "MAAA!" to get your attention, and the camera goes "ka-EE, ka-EE." Maaa! Ka-ee! Ka-ee! Mākaʻikaʻi!

She sightsees Diamond Head. Ka-ee, ka-ee. She sightsees the Pali Lookout. Ka-ee, ka-ee. Then she sightsees a stop sign, a mailbox, a pigeon, a man eating a plate lunch and the inside of a gas station restroom.
By the end of the week she has taken 14,000 pictures. When she gets home she shows them all to her friends. Nine thousand of them are of her own thumb.

words.english: to relax, to pass the time pleasantly
words.say_it: Lean back, put your hands behind your head and sigh it out. "Ho-oh-nah-NEH-ah."
words.bonus: Nanea means relaxing and enjoyable. Hoʻonanea is to spend time that way.
words.picture: Grandpa relaxing in hammock for 11 years
story_paragraphs: Grandpa Bully has been lying in the same hammock between two coconut trees in Lāʻie for 11 years. He is the most relaxed man in history.
When anyone asks him to do anything, he answers in one long lazy sigh. "Ho... oh... nah... NAY... ahhh." Ho, oh, nah, nay, ah! Hoʻonanea!

"Grandpa, you have a phone call!" "Ho... oh... nah... nay... ahhh." "Grandpa, the tide is coming in!" "Ho... oh... nah... nay... ahhh." A coconut falls and bounces off his belly. He does not even open his eyes.
Moss grows on his feet. A bird builds a nest in his hair. Tourists take photos of him like he is a statue.
He is not sleeping. He is just passing the time, very pleasantly.

words.english: to be at leisure, to take it easy
words.say_it: Lean back like you are in a hammock. "Loo-AH-nah."
words.bonus: Luana is also a popular name in Hawaiʻi.
words.picture: Lou relaxing while house flies overhead
story_paragraphs: Your whole family is moving house today. Forty cousins, three trucks, one crane. Everybody is sweating. Everybody except your cousin Lou.
Lou is in a hammock between two coconut trees. He is holding a coconut with eleven straws in it. He has sunglasses on his face and a second pair resting on his belly button.
Grandma yells "LOU! Grab the couch!" Lou lifts one finger. "Ahh... nah."

The crane lifts the entire house into the air and swings it right over his hammock. A refrigerator falls out and lands next to him. Lou opens it, takes a cold drink, and closes the door with his foot.
"LOU!" "Ahh... nah." Lou, ah, nah. By sunset the house is gone, the trees are gone, and Lou is still swinging in his hammock, now held up by two tired cousins. He is the king of taking it easy.

words.say_it: Bounce on your toes twice. "Leh-ah-LEH-ah!"
words.bonus: Leʻa by itself means joy or pleasure. Doubling it to leʻaleʻa gives you fun and games.
words.picture: Hen laying eggs in a bounce house
story_paragraphs: You rent a bounce house for your birthday. Before any kids arrive, a big red hen named Pua sneaks inside.

Pua bounces once and lays an egg. She loves it. She bounces again, higher, and lays another. Every time she goes up she screams with joy. "LAY (hic) AH! LAY (hic) AH!" There is a little hiccup in the middle every time because she is laughing so hard.
Soon she is bouncing 20 feet high. Eggs shoot out the door like popcorn. The neighbors run over with bowls. Somebody sets up a scrambled egg station on the lawn.
The kids arrive and nobody wants to leave. A grandpa is bouncing. The mailman is bouncing. Pua is having the best day of her whole life. "LAY, AH! LAY, AH!" That is what fun looks like.

words.say_it: Throw both arms in the air. "Oh-lee-OH-lee!"
words.bonus: ʻOli by itself also means joy or happy. Doubling it makes the joy even bigger.
words.picture: Giant dog tackling Lee with joy
story_paragraphs: Your friend Lee has been away at college on the continent for two years. His dog Moku has waited by the front door the whole time. Every morning. Every night. Just staring at the door.
Today the door opens. Lee walks in.

Moku weighs 160 pounds. He hits Lee like a truck. They both fly across the living room and land in the laundry basket. Moku's tail wags so fast it knocks three pictures off the wall. He is so glad he forgets how to bark. All that comes out is "Oh (gulp) LEE! Oh (gulp) LEE!"

He runs laps around the house. He licks the ceiling. He licks the neighbor. He licks the mailman, who was only walking by. The whole street hears it. "OH, LEE! OH, LEE!" That is pure joy on four legs.

words.say_it: Tickle the air with one finger. "Ho-oh-how-OH-lee."
words.bonus: Hauʻoli means happy, as in Hauʻoli lā hānau, happy birthday. Put hoʻo in front and you make someone happy.
words.picture: Gecko tickling grumpy neighbor's foot
story_paragraphs: Your neighbor, Old Man Lee, has not smiled since 1994. The whole street decides today is the day. Everybody stands in his yard and yells "HO! OH! HOW (hic) OH, LEE? HOW do we make you happy?"
First try. A marching band of 80 kids plays in his driveway. Nothing.
Second try. Forty puppies are let loose in his living room. He pets one. Still no smile.
Third try. A tower of malasadas taller than his house. He eats one. His left eyebrow moves a little.

Finally a tiny gecko climbs up his pant leg and tickles the bottom of his foot. Lee explodes. He laughs so hard his dentures fly out and land on the roof. He laughs for 45 minutes. The whole street cheers and hugs. You made someone happy. It just took a gecko.

words.english: to be sad; to be heavy
words.say_it: Slump your shoulders like you are carrying a cow. "Kow-MAH-hah."
words.bonus: Kaumaha covers both heavy and sad, like a heavy heart. Kaumaha au means I am sad.
words.picture: Sad giant cow on Ma's lap
story_paragraphs: The ranch beauty contest is over. The prize cow, all 2,000 pounds of her, came in last place. Her ribbon just says "Participant." She is crying big cow tears, each one the size of a water balloon.
She walks straight into your house and climbs onto Ma's lap in the rocking chair.

You scream "COW! MA!" Ma can only wheeze out a tiny "...hah." The rocking chair sinks through the floor. The cow is so heavy and so sad she does not even notice. She lays her big head on Ma's shoulder and sniffles.
Ma pats her ear. "Cow... Ma... hah." Two meanings, one cow. She is heavy. She is sad. And now Ma is stuck under her until the cow feels better, which could take a while.

words.say_it: Reach out toward something far away. "Mee-nah-MEE-nah."
words.bonus: Minamina is the feeling of holding tight to something precious that you might lose, or already did.
words.picture: Chasing Mina and Grandpa's surfboard
story_paragraphs: You are having a yard sale. A lady named Mina picks up Grandpa's old dented surfboard. You say "Three dollars." She pays and walks away.
Ten seconds later you remember. Grandpa rode that board on the North Shore in 1971. He carved his initials in it. He told you it was the most precious thing he ever owned.

You run down the street yelling "MINA! MINA!" You jump a fence. You run straight through a car wash. You chase her across two parking lots and onto the beach. Mina is already paddling out on the board, waving.
You stand in the water up to your knees. "Mina... Mina..." That sick feeling in your stomach is regret. And the reason it hurts so much is that you treasure that board. Minamina is both at once.

words.say_it: Raise your hand slowly and wince. "MEE-hee."
words.bonus: Mihi is a real, from the heart apology. Its partner is kala (#208), to forgive.
words.picture: Breadfruit through window, hand raised
story_paragraphs: You are playing catch in the yard with a breadfruit. Big mistake. It weighs 12 pounds. You throw it way too hard. It sails over the fence and CRASH, through the neighbor's front window and into his fish tank.
The neighbor storms out holding a goldfish in a coffee mug. He is dripping wet. "WHO DID THIS?"
Your hand goes up all by itself. "Me!" Then a scared little giggle sneaks out. "...hee." Me, hee.

You feel so bad you get down on your knees. Then on your belly. You crawl across the grass to him holding a sign that says SORRY in 14 colors. You offer him your allowance, your bike, and your little brother. "Me... hee. I apologize."
He thinks about it for a long time. He takes the bike.

words.english: to forgive; to loosen, to release
words.say_it: Unclip an invisible collar. "KAH-lah."
words.bonus: E kala mai means excuse me or I am sorry. Careful, kālā with long vowels means money, a totally different word.
words.picture: Loosening a frosting-faced pig's collar
story_paragraphs: Your pet pig Kiko ate your birthday cake. The whole thing. Three layers. You are furious. You grab her by her little pink collar and give her a long lecture.
Kiko looks up at you with frosting on her snout and the saddest eyes in the world. One tear rolls down her nose.

You can't stay mad. You sigh. You reach down and loosen her collar. Click. Then you take it off completely. "COLLAR! Off! You're free!" Kiko runs down the beach at full speed, ears flapping, doing happy little hops.
That is kala. You forgave her. You loosened the collar. You released the pig. All the same word.
She comes back an hour later and eats your other cake.

words.english: to hurt, to be in pain
words.say_it: Grab your toe and hop. "EH-hah!"
words.bonus: ʻEha koʻu poʻo means my head hurts. The next word, hoʻeha (#210), is hurting somebody else.
words.picture: Giant crab clamped on your toe
story_paragraphs: You are walking barefoot on the beach feeling great. You step on a crab the size of a mini fridge. It grabs your big toe with one claw.
"EH!" The pain stops your breath for a second, a little catch in the throat. Then "HAH!" You start hopping. "EH! HAH! EH! HAH!"

The crab does not let go. You hop down the beach. You hop across the parking lot. You hop up the road, past the church, past the shave ice stand, two whole miles. The crab rides along like it paid for a ticket.
At urgent care the nurse looks up. "What hurts?" You point at the crab. "EH! HAH!"
Your toe stays purple for a week. Every time you bump it on the table leg, it comes right back out. "EH! HAH!"

words.say_it: Swing an invisible pillow. "Ho-EH-hah!"
words.bonus: ʻEha is to hurt or be in pain yourself. Put hoʻ in front and it becomes causing the pain.
words.picture: Aunty's rice pillow launching champions
story_paragraphs: It is the World Pillow Fight Championship at the high school gym. Your opponent is Aunty Leilani, 72 years old, five feet tall. Her pillow is stuffed with a 25 pound bag of rice.
The bell rings. She winds up like a baseball pitcher. "HO!" The pillow swings. "EH!" It smacks last year's champion. "HAH!" He flies through the gym doors and lands in the parking lot.
Next guy. "HO! EH! HAH!" Into the bleachers.
Next guy. "HO! EH! HAH!" Into the scoreboard, which now reads 0 to AUNTY.
You are last. Your knees are shaking. You hold up your fluffy little pillow. She smiles sweetly and says "Don't worry, this won't hurt a bit." Then she hurts you. "HO! EH! HAH!"

words.say_it: Hold your forehead and moan. "MAH-ee."
words.bonus: Maʻi can also be a noun, sickness. A hale maʻi, a sick house, is a hospital.
words.picture: Sick green goat on the couch
story_paragraphs: Your pet goat Pilipo is sick. Really sick. His face is a little green, like a lime. He is lying on the couch under three blankets with a thermometer in his mouth. The thermometer beeps, then explodes.
He tries to bleat like a normal goat. "Maaaah..." Then his voice catches in his throat and turns into a tiny squeak. "...eee." Maaah... eee.

You bring him soup. He sneezes in it. You bring him a heating pad. He eats it. You call the vet. The vet says "Put him on the phone." Pilipo moans into the phone. "Maaah... eee." The vet says "Yup. He's sick."
He stays on that couch for four days watching cooking shows. Every hour you hear it from the living room. "Maaah... eee."

words.english: to treat with medicine, to heal
words.say_it: Spray an invisible bottle at your knee. "Lah-pah-OW!"
words.bonus: Lāʻau lapaʻau is traditional Hawaiian medicine made from plants.
words.picture: Wrestler nurse spraying giant medicine
story_paragraphs: You crash your bike into a mango tree and scrape your whole knee. You limp to the school nurse. She is a retired pro wrestler, six foot five, with forearms like tree trunks.
She picks you up like a baby and sets you on her lap. Then she pulls out a bottle of medicine the size of a fire extinguisher.
"Lap," she says, patting her knee. "A..." she says, aiming the nozzle. PSSSHHHT. "OW!" you scream. Lap, a, OW.
Then something amazing happens. The scrape zips shut like a jacket. The bruise fades. Your hair looks better. Your math grade goes up. She hands you a lollipop and says "Next!"
There is a line of 30 kids out the door. Every thirty seconds you hear "Lap... a... OW!" and another kid walks out healed.

words.english: to save, to heal, to bring back to life
words.say_it: Sing one long note. "Ho-OHHHH-lah."
words.bonus: Ola means life or to live. Hoʻōla means to make live, so to save or heal.
words.picture: Opera cousin reviving the dead fern
story_paragraphs: Everything in your house is dead. The fern on the lanai is brown and crunchy. The goldfish is floating. The lei from graduation looks like old spaghetti.

Your cousin Kainoa, who sings opera in the shower, walks in. He takes a deep breath. His chest puffs up like a balloon. "HO..." Then he holds the next part. "OHHHHHHHHHHHH..." Ten seconds. Twenty seconds. The windows start to shake. "...LA!"

The fern springs up green. The goldfish flips over and starts swimming laps. The lei puffs up fresh and smells like a flower shop. A dead cockroach under the fridge gets up and walks out the door, which is a mistake, but still.
Kainoa bows. That long OHHHH is the healing part. The longer he holds it, the more things come back to life.

words.say_it: Cover your mouth and cough. "KOO-noo."
words.bonus: Kunu is to cough. Its gross twin kihe (#215) is to sneeze.
words.picture: Coughing steersman jet-powering a canoe
story_paragraphs: You are in a six person canoe race off Waikīkī. Your steersman, Big Keoni, has the worst cough on the island. Every cough sounds exactly the same. "KOO... NOO!"
Here is the secret. Every time Keoni coughs, the blast shoots out behind him like a jet engine and the canoe jumps forward 50 feet.
The race starts. You paddle. He coughs. "KOO... NOO!" You are in first. He coughs twice. "KOO... NOO! KOO... NOO!" You pass a surfer, a sailboat and a very confused turtle.
At the finish line the judges ask what your secret is. The whole crew points at Keoni. He opens his mouth to answer and coughs instead. All three judges get blown into the water.
Now whenever you hear a cough, you hear a canoe.

words.say_it: Scrunch your face and sneeze. "KEE-heh!"
words.bonus: When someone sneezes, some families answer "Kihe, a mauli ola," wishing them life and good health.
words.picture: Sneeze blasting 400 keys down hallway
story_paragraphs: Uncle Walter is the janitor at your school. He carries 400 keys on a ring the size of a hula hoop. He jingles when he walks. You can hear him coming from two floors away.
Today he gets pepper up his nose. His face scrunches. His eyes close. He takes a huge breath. "KEEEEE..."
Everybody in the hallway ducks.

The sneeze rips the key ring right off his belt. Four hundred keys fly down the hallway like a swarm of bees. Keys stuck in the ceiling. Keys in the fish tank. One key lands inside a malasada a kid was eating. Another flies out the window and locks a car in the parking lot.
Everyone turns and looks at Uncle Walter. He sniffs. "Key... heh." Now he has to find every single one.

words.say_it: Grab your stomach and run in place. "Loo-AH-ee."
words.bonus: Lua means a hole or pit, and locals use it for the bathroom. The two words only sound alike, but picture luaʻi as what happens when you do not make it to the lua in time. Luaʻi is also used for a volcano erupting.
words.picture: Plate lunch champ racing for the lua
story_paragraphs: Your cousin Kimo takes on the Plate Lunch Challenge at the diner. Twelve plates. Two scoops rice each, mac salad, and a mountain of kalbi. He eats all twelve in 20 minutes. The whole diner cheers. He raises his arms like a champion.
Then his face turns the color of a kiwi.
He looks at you in panic. "LUA!" That is the local word for the bathroom. He takes off running. "LUA! AH..." He gulps, a hard catch in the throat. "...EE!"
He runs past the counter. He runs past the cook. People jump out of his way. There is a line of six people at the bathroom door. Kimo does not make it to the lua.
He makes it to the trash can by the door. The trash can will never be the same. Twelve plates, going back where they came from.

words.say_it: Zip up an invisible backpack, fast. "Pah-KEH-leh!"
words.bonus: Pakele is getting away safe yourself. Its bigger sibling hoʻopakele (#219) is rescuing someone else.
words.picture: Escaping Aunty's slideshow down bedsheets
story_paragraphs: You and your cousin Kelly are trapped at Aunty's house. She is showing slides from her cruise. Slide 1,204 is a picture of a buffet. Slide 1,205 is the same buffet from the left. There are 3,000 slides to go.
Aunty steps into the kitchen for more pūpū. You lean over and whisper "PACK, KELLY!"

Kelly already has her backpack on. You tie six bedsheets together. You open the bathroom window. You slide down the sheets into the mango tree, drop into the hedge, and army crawl under the carport. Kelly is right behind you with her slippahs in her mouth.
From inside you hear Aunty. "Slide 1,206!" The projector keeps clicking. You hop the fence and run all the way to the beach.
"Pack, Kelly." You got away. You escaped.

words.say_it: Dart your hand away like a fish. "Mah-HOO-kah!"
words.bonus: Pakele (#217) is escaping safe. Mahuka is the running part, fleeing like a runaway.
words.picture: Fish school fleeing a giant hook
story_paragraphs: You are a small fish, a manini, cruising the reef with your mom and 400 brothers and sisters. Life is good. You are nibbling algae. You are blowing bubbles.
Then you look up. A fishhook is coming down through the water. It is as big as a coat hanger. It is shiny. It has a whole sardine on it.
You scream "MA! HOOK... AH!"

The whole school hears it. Four hundred fish turn at once and flee so fast the water stays shaped like fish for a second after they leave. The coral shakes. An eel slams its door. A crab gets spun around three times.
You are gone. Ten miles gone. Up on the boat, the fisherman reels in an empty hook and scratches his head. "Ma, hook, ah." When you see a hook, you run away.

words.say_it: Reach up and pull someone into your arms. "Ho-oh-pah-KEH-leh!"
words.bonus: Pakele is escaping yourself. Hoʻo makes it happen to someone else, so hoʻopakele is to rescue.
words.picture: Fire truck ladder rescuing Kelly
story_paragraphs: Kelly from pakele is in trouble again. She ran from Aunty's slideshow by climbing the tallest mango tree in the yard. Now she is 60 feet up, stuck on a branch, hugging a mango, and Aunty is at the bottom aiming the projector at the tree.
You call the fire department. A fire truck pulls up with a ladder that stretches 70 feet. You ride the bucket up. The wind is blowing. A mynah bird is screaming at you.
You reach her and yell "HO! OH! PACK, KELLY!" Kelly throws her backpack into the bucket, then her slippahs, then herself. The ladder swings back down like a giant arm.
Aunty clicks to the next slide. Too late. You drive off with Kelly on the fire truck, sirens going. You saved her. That is a rescue.

words.say_it: Stand at an imaginary edge, gulp, then jump. "AH-ah!"
words.bonus: Watch the marks. ʻaʻa, to dare, has two ʻokina. aʻa, with only the middle ʻokina, means root or vein. ʻaʻā, with a long a at the end, is the rough, jagged lava.
words.picture: Gulping at the edge of a cliff
story_paragraphs: You are standing on top of a rock 40 feet above the water at Waimea Bay. Your cousin, floating below, yells up. "I DARE YOU!"
You walk to the edge. You look down. The water looks the size of a postage stamp. You open your mouth to say "AH..." and your throat freezes. A gulp. A catch. Your knees knock like coconuts.
Your cousin yells "I DOUBLE DARE YOU!" A crowd of tourists holds up their phones. A dragonfly lands on your nose to watch.
You take one breath. "AH!" Gulp. "AH!" And you jump. You fall for what feels like 17 minutes, screaming the whole way. SPLASH.
You pop up, spit out water, and point at your cousin. "Your turn. I dare you." ʻAʻa always starts with a gulp.

words.say_it: Pump your fist over your head. "Lah-nah-KEE-lah!"
words.bonus: Ua lanakila mākou means we won.
