words.picture: Tiny aunty winning the musubi contest
story_paragraphs: It is the Spam musubi eating contest at the school carnival. Twelve contestants. Big guys, football players, a sumo wrestler. And at the very end of the table, a tiny aunty named Lana in a flowered muʻumuʻu and a visor.
The horn blows. The football players eat 5 musubi each. The sumo wrestler eats 9. Lana eats 41. She eats them two at a time. She finishes, wipes her mouth with a napkin, and asks "Is there more?"
The crowd loses its mind. "LANA! KILLA! LANA! KILLA!"

They lift her onto their shoulders. She holds a trophy the size of a refrigerator over her head. Confetti falls. A marching band plays. She wins. She triumphs. She wins again next year, and the year after that, and the sumo wrestler asks for her autograph.

words.english: to be beaten, captured; to go out (like a fire)
words.say_it: Blow out an invisible candle. "PEE-oh."
words.bonus: Ua pio ke ahi means the fire went out. You can say pio about a light, a candle, or a team that lost.
words.picture: Dragon losing staring contest to Grandma
story_paragraphs: Your uncle bought a pet dragon at the swap meet. It is the size of a golden retriever and it breathes fire. It lights the grill. It lights the tiki torches. It lights Uncle's eyebrows twice.
At the family party it gets cocky. It challenges Grandma to a staring contest.
Grandma does not blink. The dragon's eyes water. Its lip shakes. After four minutes it blinks, and its fire goes out with a sad little whistle like a teakettle. "PEEEEEE... oh."
It is beaten. Its fire is out. Grandma drops a laundry basket over it. Captured.
For the rest of the night it sits under the basket. Every time it tries to make a flame, only a puff of smoke comes out. "Peee... oh." Beaten, captured, and fire out, all in one little word.

words.say_it: Flap your elbows and squawk. "Hah-kah-KAAAH!"
words.bonus: Hakakā can be a real fight or just a loud quarrel, like two siblings in the back seat.
words.picture: Two mynahs fighting over one fry
story_paragraphs: You drop one french fry in the beach park parking lot. Just one.
Two mynah birds land on it at the exact same second. They look at each other. The fight begins.

"HA!" says the first one, grabbing the fry. "Ka-KAAAAAAH!" screams the second one, grabbing the other end. That last part is long and loud and it never seems to end. They pull. They flap. They roll across the hot asphalt in a ball of feathers.
Other mynahs show up to cheer. One is selling tickets. The fight rolls under a car, over a picnic table, and into the lifeguard tower. The lifeguard hides.
After 45 minutes they drop the fry so they can yell at each other better. A pigeon walks up, eats it, and leaves. The mynahs keep fighting anyway.

words.say_it: Throw an invisible pie across the room. "PAI-oh!"
words.bonus: Paio also means an argument or a struggle, not only a fight with weapons.
words.picture: Bakery armies launching pies by catapult
story_paragraphs: The bakery on one side of the street and the bakery on the other side have hated each other for 30 years. Today it is war.

Both armies line up in aprons. Each side has a catapult made from a canoe paddle and a trampoline. Your general is a 90 year old baker with a wooden spoon. She raises it and screams "PIE!" Everybody answers "OH!"

Custard pies fly across the street by the hundreds. Coconut cream. Lemon. Chocolate haupia. People slip, get up, get hit again. You try to lift a 200 pound sweet potato pie onto the catapult and it takes four of you, groaning and struggling.
"PIE! OH! PIE! OH!" The battle lasts until sunset. Nobody wins. Everybody is sticky. Tomorrow morning they battle again.

words.english: to compete, to hold a contest
words.say_it: Pop your head out like a cuckoo bird and hold it. "Ho-oh-koo-KOOOO!"
words.bonus: Hoʻokūkū is also a noun, a contest or competition, like a hula competition or a spelling bee.
words.picture: Giant cuckoo bird winning clock contest
story_paragraphs: Welcome to the first ever Cuckoo Clock Contest at the community center. Fifty clocks sit on a long table. Their owners stand behind them, sweating. It is one minute to noon.
The judges hold up scorecards. The rules are simple. Loudest bird, longest call, best form.
The clocks strike noon. Fifty little doors fly open. Fifty wooden birds shoot out. "Koo koo! Koo koo!" Most of them are done in two seconds.

But one clock, built by a retired ship captain, is different. His bird comes out the size of a chicken. It takes a breath. "KOO..." Then it holds the second one. "KOOOOOOOOOOOO!" For a full minute. Windows crack. A judge's hat flies off.
The crowd chants "HO! OH! KOO KOOOO!" The captain wins a trophy shaped like a bird. The other 49 demand a rematch. The competition continues next year.

words.say_it: Stand tall, take a huge breath, and hold one steady tone. "OH-lee."
words.bonus: An oli is a chant that is not danced to, like one asking permission to enter a place or one that welcomes guests. Careful, ʻoli with an ʻokina means glad, as in ʻoliʻoli.
words.picture: Little Ollie chanting, cheeks puffed
story_paragraphs: Your little cousin Ollie is eight years old and just joined a hālau. Before class starts, the kumu calls out "Ollie! Time to chant!"
Ollie stands tall. He plants his bare feet. He takes the biggest breath of his life. His chest swells. His cheeks puff out like a pufferfish. The whole room waits.

Then the chant comes out, strong and steady, one long line of voice rising and falling with no stopping. Ten seconds. Twenty. Thirty. The windows hum. The dog outside sits down to listen. A mynah bird on the fence goes quiet.
When Ollie finally finishes, his face is bright red and he gasps like he just swam up from the bottom of a pool. The kumu nods once and smiles. "Ollie. That is how you chant."

words.say_it: Hold one long high note, then drop down. "Heeee-MEH-nee."
words.bonus: Hīmeni comes from the English word hymn. Hawaiian church choirs have been singing them since the 1800s.
words.picture: Aunty choir singing forty seven hymns
story_paragraphs: Sunday morning at a little country church. Twelve aunties in matching muʻumuʻu fill the choir. The pastor smiles and says "Let's sing one hymn."
The lead aunty starts. "HEEEEEEEEE..." She holds that first note like a car alarm. The windows rattle. Then the whole choir comes in. "...MANY!" Many hymns, it turns out. Not one.

They sing hymn number 1. Then 2. Then 47. The ʻukulele player's fingers go numb. The pastor checks his watch. Someone brings in plate lunches and the choir eats between verses. A family of chickens wanders in and sits in the back row to listen.
At 4 in the afternoon they finally stop. The pastor wipes his forehead and says "Next week, just one hymn." The aunties smile sweetly. "HEEEE... MANY."

words.say_it: Point left, then right, arguing with yourself. "Ho-oh-pah-ah-PAH-ah!"
words.bonus: Hoʻopaʻapaʻa can also be a noun, an argument or a debate. A school debate team does hoʻopaʻapaʻa.
words.picture: Two grandpas debating mac salad placement
story_paragraphs: At the family reunion, two grandpas sit at opposite ends of the picnic table. Both of them are called Pa. The question is serious. Does the mac salad go on the left of the rice or the right?
"PA!" says one, pointing left. "AH!" says the other, slapping the table. "PA!" "AH!" Every word has a little hiccup in it because they are so worked up.

It turns into a full debate. Somebody brings two podiums and a microphone. A cousin keeps time with a stopwatch. There are charts. There is a poster board with glitter. Grandma is the moderator and she keeps ringing a cowbell.
Six hours later the plate lunches are cold, the sun is down, and the two Pas are still going. "PA! AH! PA! AH!" Nobody remembers what they were arguing about.

words.say_it: Cross your arms and groan. "Oh-HOO-moo."
words.bonus: ʻŌhumu can also mean to plot or scheme in secret, like two grumblers whispering in a corner.
words.picture: Grumpy rodeo bull complaining in dirt
story_paragraphs: At the rodeo, the whole crowd is waiting for the famous bull, Thunder. The gate bangs open. Thunder walks out slowly, sighs, and sits down in the dirt.
"Ohhhhhhhh," he groans, long and low. "Hoo... moo." He is not bucking. He is grumbling.

The dirt is too dusty. "Ohhhhhh... hoo moo." The cowboy's hat is too big. "Ohhhhhh... hoo moo." The music is too loud, the sun is too hot, the popcorn smells funny, his hooves hurt, and his cousin never calls.
The cowboy climbs on his back and waits. Thunder complains about that too. The rodeo clown tries to cheer him up. Thunder complains about the clown's shoes.
The buzzer rings. The cowboy wins, because Thunder never moved. Thunder grumbles all the way back to the barn. "Ohhhhhh... hoo... moo."

words.english: to act stuck up, to be arrogant
words.say_it: Lift your nose high and sniff. "Ho-oh-KAH-no."
words.bonus: The opposite is haʻahaʻa, humble.
words.picture: Snob with nose up, gold canoe
story_paragraphs: There is one guy at the beach who thinks he is better than everybody. He owns a canoe painted gold. Real gold. It has a leather seat and two cup holders.
He walks everywhere with his nose so high in the air that when it rains, his nostrils fill up with water. He does not look at people. He looks over them.
A kid asks "Can I touch it?" He sniffs. "Ho, oh... my CANOE." A tourist asks for a photo. "Ho, oh, my CANOE." A crab crawls onto the front. He shoos it away with a tiny silk fan.

Then he paddles out, nose up, not looking where he is going, and runs straight into the reef. The gold canoe sinks in three feet of water. He is standing there, waist deep, nose still pointed at the clouds.

words.say_it: Wave off a compliment, twice. "Ho-oh-hah-no-HAH-no."
words.bonus: Hanohano by itself means glorious or honored. Hoʻo turns it into giving that honor to someone.
words.picture: Bus driver buried in thirty lei
story_paragraphs: Uncle Sonny drove the same city bus route for 42 years. He never missed a day. He learned every rider's name. He let kids ride free with a smile when they forgot their fare.
On his last day, the whole route is waiting at the final stop. Four hundred people. A band. A banner. A pile of lei.

Uncle Sonny is way too humble. As they put the first lei on him he waves his hands. "HA, NO! HA, NO!" Another lei. "Ha, no!" Another. "HA, NO!" By lei number 30 he is covered up to his eyeballs. Only his bus driver hat sticks out. He keeps saying it, muffled under all the flowers.
The kids sing to him. The riders hug him. They honor him until the sun goes down, and he cries a little into the flowers.

words.english: to congratulate, to praise, to bless
words.say_it: Pat someone on the back. "Ho-oh-mai-KAH-ee!"
words.bonus: Hoʻomaikaʻi ʻana! means Congratulations! Maikaʻi by itself means good.
words.picture: Beach cheering Kai and his giant ʻahi
story_paragraphs: Your friend Kai paddles out on a stand up board just to fish for fun. He comes back towing a 200 pound ʻahi. It is bigger than the board. It is bigger than Kai.

The whole beach runs down to the water screaming. "HO! OH MY, KAI!" Grandmas hug him. A lifeguard gives him a high five that leaves a mark. Somebody's tutu says a little blessing over Kai and the board.

Somebody makes him a trophy out of a cooler lid. Somebody else writes KAI IS THE BEST in the sand in letters 20 feet tall. Everyone wants to shake his hand. His hand gets so tired he starts shaking with his foot.
"Oh my, KAI!" That is praise. That is congrats. That is blessing him for a good day. That is hoʻomaikaʻi.

words.say_it: Hold one soft note, with a little catch in it. "Ho-oh-LAH-ah."
words.bonus: Laʻa means sacred or set apart. Hoʻolaʻa is to make something that way, like blessing a new building or a new canoe. At blessings the maile lei is untied, not cut.
words.picture: Hiccuping choir at library blessing
story_paragraphs: Your school just finished building a new library. Before anyone walks in, there is a dedication. The elders offer a blessing, and a maile lei hangs across the doorway, waiting to be untied.
Your class is the choir. The teacher asks everyone to hold one soft, steady note the whole time. "Ho... oh... LAAAAAA..."

Everyone holds it. It sounds beautiful. Then the boy next to you gets the hiccups. "LAAAA (hic) AH." He tries again. "LAAAA (hic) AH." He turns bright red. You try not to laugh so hard that your ears pop.
Nobody minds. The blessing is finished, the maile is gently untied, and the building is set apart for learning. Dedicated. Made special. Ho, oh, la, ah.
Every time you walk through those doors now, you remember that hiccup.

words.say_it: Slap the table once. "PAH-ee!"
words.bonus: Paʻi kiʻi means to take a photo. Careful, pai with no ʻokina is the Hawaiian word for pie. Watch the family, paʻi (slap), paʻipaʻi (clap, #235), hoʻopaʻi (punish, #250).
words.picture: Slapping a printer that prints pies
story_paragraphs: The printer in your office is 40 years old. It is the size of a car. It only works if you slap it.
You press print. Nothing. You slap the side. WHACK. "PIE!" it groans, and a page slides out. But the page is not your report. It is a picture of a pie.

You slap it again. WHACK. "PIE!" Another pie picture. Apple. Then coconut cream. Then a picture of a pie hitting your boss in the face. You slap it harder. WHACK WHACK WHACK. "PIE! PIE! PIE!" Paper pours out like a waterfall.
By lunch the whole office is buried in pie pictures up to the ceiling. Your boss climbs out of the pile, stares at the printer, and slaps it himself. "PIE!"
Slap. Print. Same word.

words.say_it: Clap twice, then twice again. "Pah-ee-PAH-ee!"
words.bonus: Hawaiian often doubles a word to repeat the action. Paʻi is one slap. Paʻipaʻi is slapping over and over, clapping.
words.picture: Octopus clapping eight arms for pie
story_paragraphs: You are at the aquarium show. The star is Big Momi, an octopus with eight very long arms. The trainer holds up a whole pie and asks "Momi, what do you want?"

Momi gets so excited she starts clapping. With all eight arms. Two at a time, then four at a time, then all eight together. SLAP SLAP SLAP SLAP. It sounds like popcorn in a metal pot. Water splashes the first ten rows.
While she claps she chants "PIE! PIE! PIE! PIE!" The whole crowd joins in, clapping and yelling "PIE! PIE!"
The trainer tosses her the pie. Momi catches it, eats it in one bite, and gives herself a standing ovation, which for an octopus looks like a wet umbrella flapping.
One slap is paʻi. Slap slap, again and again, is a clap.

words.say_it: Knock three times on a table, slow and long. "Kee-keh-KEH."
words.bonus: Kī by itself is the word for a key, borrowed from English. Handy when you are locked out.
words.picture: Locked out, knocking the house sideways
story_paragraphs: You come home from the beach in wet shorts and sandy feet. You reach for your key. No key. It is in the car. The car is locked. The car key is in the house.
You knock on the door. Your little brother is inside playing video games with headphones on.
You yell "KEY?" and knock twice more. "KEEEEY! KEH! KEH!" Each knock you hold a little longer, stretching the sound out like chewing gum. "KEEEEE... KEEEEH... KEEEEH!"
Nothing. You knock harder. The mangoes fall off the tree. The neighbor's dog starts howling. You knock so hard the whole house hops two inches to the left.
Finally your brother opens the door. "Oh. Hi." He was never wearing the headphones. He just liked hearing you knock.

words.english: to poke, to pierce, to stab with a fork
words.say_it: Stab an invisible fork down, then gasp. "OHHH."
words.bonus: The same spelling ʻō also means over there, as in maʻō. And ʻōʻō, doubled, is the old digging stick.
words.picture: Fork popping a beach ball malasada
story_paragraphs: Your friend brings a malasada to the party. It is the size of a beach ball. It is so full of custard it wobbles whenever anyone talks.
Everyone gathers around. You pick up a fork. You raise it high like a spear. The room goes quiet.

You poke. The fork pierces the skin with a tiny pop. For one second, nothing. Then everyone in the room catches their breath at once, a little gulp, and then "OHHHHHHHHHHHH!" as custard shoots straight up like a geyser.
It hits the ceiling fan. The fan spins custard across the whole room. The dog is custard. Grandpa is custard. Your little sister stands there with her mouth open, catching it like rain.
"OHHHHHHH!" The gasp lasts twelve seconds. One poke with a fork. That is ʻō.

words.say_it: Shake out your foot, fast. "NAH-hoo!"
words.bonus: Nahu is a hard bite or a sting. Do not mix it up with nau (#239), which is just chewing.
words.picture: Centipede biting toe inside shoe
story_paragraphs: You wake up late for work. You shove your foot into your shoe. Something inside it moves.
A centipede. Seven inches long. Orange. Angry. It bites your big toe as hard as it can.
"NAH..." you say, because this cannot be happening. Then the pain arrives. "...HOOOOOOOOO!"

You jump nine feet straight up. Your head pokes through a ceiling tile. You come down, hop across the kitchen, and kick the shoe across the yard. It lands in the neighbor's pool. The centipede climbs out, dries itself off on the diving board, and gives you a dirty look.
Your toe swells up like a cherry tomato. All day at work you limp. Every time someone asks what happened, you say it again. "Nah... HOOOO." That is a hard bite. That is nahu.

words.say_it: Chew slowly and loudly. "NOW. NOW. NOW."
words.bonus: Nau is chewing. Nahu (#238) is biting down hard. Chew nicely, don't bite.
words.picture: Tūtū timing fifty chews of jerky
story_paragraphs: Tūtū has one rule at her table. Every bite gets chewed 50 times. No exceptions.
Today she is serving pipikaula, dried beef so tough it could be a slippah. You put a piece in your mouth. Tūtū starts her stopwatch and stands over you like a drill sergeant.

"NOW!" You chew. "NOW!" You chew again. "NOW! NOW! NOW!" Every time she says it, your jaw goes up and down. By chew 20 your cheeks are burning. By chew 35 your ears are moving. By chew 49 your whole head is bobbing like a chicken.
"NOW!" Chew 50. You swallow. Tūtū nods. Then she puts another piece on your plate.
That night in bed, your jaw keeps going on its own. Now. Now. Now.

words.say_it: Suck hard through an invisible straw. "OH-mo."
words.picture: Mo sucking the food court into straw
story_paragraphs: Your cousin Mo orders the thickest mango smoothie at the food court. It is so thick a spoon stands straight up in it. He gets the skinniest straw in the building.
He starts to suck. His cheeks cave in. His eyes bulge. His face turns purple. Nothing moves.
He sucks harder. The cup crumples. Napkins fly off the next table and stick to his face. A man's toupee lifts off his head. Everybody yells "OH, MO!"
He keeps going. The straw starts pulling in french fries, a fork, somebody's slippah, a pair of sunglasses. The table cloth is sliding toward him. "OH, MO! OH, MO!"
Finally, SHHLOOOORP. The whole smoothie shoots up the straw in one gulp. Mo leans back, very happy. Somewhere inside him is a pair of sunglasses.

words.say_it: Hold out a spoon again and again. "Ho-oh-mo-MO-nah."
words.bonus: Momona means fat, and also sweet or fertile. Hoʻomomona makes something fat, or makes soil rich.
words.picture: Grandpa fattening pig, giant tomatoes
story_paragraphs: Grandpa is getting his pig ready for the county fair. Her name is Honey and she is going to win Biggest Pig.
Every hour he brings her a bucket of leftover rice, poi and papaya. "Mo'?" he asks. Honey eats it. "MO'?" Honey eats more. He looks at her. "Nah?" Honey never says nah.

Then he goes out back and does the same thing to his garden. He shovels in a mountain of horse manure. "Mo'? MO'? Nah?" The tomatoes grow to the size of beach balls. The zucchini is longer than his truck.
By fair day, Honey is so fat she has to be rolled into the trailer. The tomatoes need their own trailer. Grandpa wins two ribbons. He fattened the pig. He fertilized the dirt. Mo', mo', nah.

words.say_it: Rub your belly and moan. "Poh-LO-lee."
words.bonus: Pōloli is hungry. Its opposite is māʻona (#243), full. Pōloli au means I am hungry.
words.picture: Hungry climber on a butter pole
story_paragraphs: You skipped breakfast. You skipped lunch. It is 4 in the afternoon at the county fair and you are so hungry your stomach growls like a motorcycle. People turn around to see who is revving.
Then you see it. The greasy pole game. A 30 foot pole covered in butter, and at the very top, a lollipop the size of a trash can lid.
You point and moan "POOOOOOLE..." You hold it long because your stomach is too empty to talk fast. "...LOLLY!"

You climb. You slide down. You climb. You slide down. Twelve times. People start cheering. Your stomach roars so loud it scares a toddler. On the thirteenth try you reach the top and bite the lollipop right off the stick while still hugging the pole.
Pōloli. Hungry enough to climb a butter pole.

words.say_it: Lean back, pat your belly, and wave off more food. "Maah-OH-nah."
words.bonus: Ua māʻona au means I am full. The pair to remember, pōloli (hungry) and māʻona (full).
words.picture: Full sumo wrestler rolled out the door
story_paragraphs: It is the all you can eat buffet. A sumo wrestler sits at the table next to yours. He has eaten 14 plates. The stack of empty plates is taller than he is.

The waiter comes by with a tray of chocolate cake. The sumo wrestler leans back. His belt pops off and flies across the room like a slingshot. He lets out a long, happy sigh. "MAAAAAAAAAH." Then a little gulp catches in his throat. He waves the cake away. "...Oh, nah."
He tries to stand up. He can't. The chair is stuck to him. Three waiters roll him out the door like a barrel.
On the way out he pats his belly and says it one more time, very satisfied. "Maaaah. Oh, nah." He is full. Totally, completely, perfectly full.

words.say_it: Take an invisible bite, then look scared. "OH-no."
words.bonus: Locals use ʻono in everyday English for tasty food. The fish called ono, the wahoo, is spelled without the ʻokina.
words.picture: Licking the empty butter mochi pan
story_paragraphs: Your coworker brings in a pan of butter mochi. It is still warm. It is golden on top and chewy in the middle and the whole office smells like coconut.
You take one little square. You bite it. You freeze. You whisper "Oh no."

Because now you know. You are going to eat the whole pan. You eat another square. "Oh no." Another. "OH NO." You are hiding squares in your desk drawer, in your pockets, in your shoes. By 10 am the pan is empty and you are licking it.
That night at 3 in the morning you wake up craving it so badly you drive to your coworker's house in your pajamas and knock on her door. She opens it holding a fresh pan. "Oh no," you both say.
Delicious, and craving it. Both are ʻono.

words.english: to give a drink; to water (plants)
words.say_it: Tip an invisible watering can. "Ho-oh-EE-noo."
words.bonus: Inu means to drink. Hoʻo makes it happen to someone else, so hoʻoinu is giving water to people, animals or plants.
words.picture: Thirsty plants cheering at the hose
story_paragraphs: You come back from a two week trip. Every plant on your lanai is flat, crispy and gasping. The fern is lying on its back with one frond on its forehead like it fainted.
You grab the hose. The second the water hits, the plants start slurping. The fern sits up and gulps like a camel. The orchid grabs the hose and drinks straight from it.
Then the tomato plant, dripping wet, turns to the others and whispers "Ho... oh... he KNEW!" He knew we were thirsty! They all start cheering and waving their leaves.
The neighbor's horse leans over the fence with its tongue hanging out. You give it a drink too. Then the mailman. Then a gecko who looks very thirsty. "He KNEW!" they all shout.
You give a drink to anything that asks. That is hoʻoinu.

words.english: to feed, to raise, to adopt
words.say_it: Hold out a baby bottle. "Haaah-NAI."
words.bonus: A hānai child is raised by someone other than the birth parents, a common and loving tradition in Hawaiian families.
words.picture: Tūtū bottle feeding a giant horse
story_paragraphs: Tūtū lives at the end of a long dirt road in Waimānalo. She raised 14 kids. Only 3 were born to her. The rest just showed up one by one, and she fed them, and they stayed.

She also raised a baby horse whose mother could not feed him. She gave him a bottle every three hours for six months. She sang to him. She let him sleep on the lanai. He is now 1,200 pounds and still thinks he is a lap dog.
Every morning when Tūtū comes out with breakfast, the horse throws his head back and neighs as loud as he can. "HAAAAAAH... NAY!" A long happy start, then the neigh.
All 14 kids come running too. Tūtū feeds everybody. The kids, the horse, the neighbor kids, and a mailman who retired years ago but still comes by for breakfast.

words.say_it: Walk your fingers across the table like crabs. "Ho-oh-lee-mah-LEE-mah."
words.bonus: Lima means hand, and also the number five. Hoʻolimalima can also be a noun, a lease or a rental.
words.picture: Rented hands carrying a piano upstairs
story_paragraphs: You have to move a piano to the eighth floor. The elevator is broken. Your friends suddenly all have plans.
So you go to a rental shop at the end of an alley. The sign says HANDS FOR RENT. The old man behind the counter asks how many. You say "A lot." He hands you a box.
You open it at home. Two hundred wooden hands crawl out like crabs. They line up in rows. They lift the piano. As they carry it up the stairs they chant in tiny voices "LIMA! LIMA! LIMA!"

Up they go. Floor three. Floor five. Floor eight. They set the piano down, play a little song on it, and crawl back into the box. You pay the old man 40 dollars and 6 lima beans, because that is his price.
You rented hands. That is hoʻolimalima.

words.english: to let go, to release, to dismiss
words.say_it: Open your hands like you are releasing a bird. "Ho-oh-KOO-oo."
words.bonus: Hoʻokuʻu is used for dismissing a class or releasing a prisoner. Its short cousin kuʻu (#249) is to let down or let go.
words.picture: Six hundred pigeons released at a wedding
story_paragraphs: Your cousin's wedding is on the beach. The plan is simple. At the end, release twelve white doves.

Somebody ordered wrong. The box is the size of a shipping container. The groom opens the door. Six hundred pigeons pour out at once, cooing so loud it sounds like an airplane. "KOO... (gulp) OOO! KOO... OOO!"
They let go of the box. They let go of the groom's jacket. One of them snatches Uncle's toupee on the way up and lets it go right over the cake.
Then the pastor looks at the crowd and says "Okay. Everybody is dismissed." Six hundred pigeons and two hundred guests all scatter in different directions at the same time.
Letting go of the birds. Letting everybody go home. Ho, oh, koo, oo.

words.english: to let down, to lower, to release
words.say_it: Lower an invisible rope, hand over hand. "KOO-oo."
words.bonus: Kuʻu also means my, in a loving way, like kuʻu ipo, my sweetheart, in old love songs.
words.picture: Basket lowered on a squeaky rope
story_paragraphs: The lady upstairs in the old Chinatown building is 90 years old and does not do stairs. Every morning she lowers a basket on a rope from her third floor window.
The rope runs over a squeaky old pulley. As the basket goes down, the pulley sings "KOOOOOOO..." Then the rope catches for a second, a little hiccup, and keeps going. "...oooooh."
The whole street knows that sound. The malasada man puts in six malasadas. The fish man puts in a whole ʻahi. The mailman puts in her mail. A kid puts in his homework for her to check.
Today the basket is so heavy she has to let it down inch by inch, arms shaking, the pulley singing the whole time. "Kooooooo... ooooh." It lands on the sidewalk with a thump.
Lowering it down. Letting it go. That is kuʻu.

words.say_it: Shake your finger at someone. "Ho-oh-PAH-ee."
words.bonus: Paʻi, paʻipaʻi, hoʻopaʻi. Slap, clap, punish, all from the same little word. Hoʻopaʻi can also mean a fine or penalty.
words.picture: Brother punished while family eats pie
story_paragraphs: Your little brother ate the whole coconut cream pie meant for the church bake sale. All of it. He even licked the tin. He has whipped cream in his eyebrows.

Mom decides the punishment. He has to sit in a chair in the middle of the kitchen while the entire family eats pie in front of him. Nine pies. Apple, lemon, chocolate haupia, sweet potato. Everyone chews slowly and makes happy noises.
He whimpers. "Ho... oh... no PIE." Mom takes another bite. "Nope. No pie." He howls. "HO! OH! NO PIE!"
The punishment lasts three hours. The neighbors come over to watch. Somebody brings popcorn. By the end he promises he will never touch another pie as long as he lives.
The next morning, the last pie is missing.

words.english: to put on trial, to investigate
words.say_it: Bang an invisible gavel twice. "Ho-oh-ko-lo-KO-lo."
words.bonus: A courthouse is a hale hoʻokolokolo. Kolo by itself means to creep or crawl, like a detective creeping around for clues.
words.picture: Mongoose judge putting cola on trial
story_paragraphs: Court is in session. The judge is a mongoose in a tiny black robe. The accused is a can of cola.
The charges are serious. Yesterday the cola exploded inside Aunty's purse and soaked her wallet, her lipstick and her bingo cards.

The detective, a crab with a magnifying glass, investigates. He sniffs the purse. He pokes the can. He plays a slow motion video that shows someone shaking the can before putting it in the purse. It was Aunty's grandson.
The courtroom gasps and chants "COLA! COLA! COLA!" The mongoose bangs a gavel made from a macadamia nut. Ho, oh, cola, COLA.
The cola is found not guilty. It is so happy it fizzes a little. The grandson is sentenced to buy Aunty a new purse. Investigate, put on trial, find the truth.

words.english: to sue, to accuse, to complain
words.say_it: Point an accusing finger. "Ho-oh-PEE-ee!"
words.bonus: Piʻi by itself means to climb or go up. Think of hoʻopiʻi as taking your complaint up to someone higher.
words.picture: Seventh grader suing P.E. class
story_paragraphs: Kawika is in seventh grade and he hates P.E. more than anything. Today the coach made him run 40 laps in the rain.
So Kawika sues. He shows up at the principal's office in his dad's suit, four sizes too big. He carries a briefcase. The briefcase has a sandwich in it.
He points at the coach and says "HO! OH! I accuse... P.E.!" His voice cracks on the E, a little squeak in the throat. "P... EE!"

He reads his complaints from a scroll that unrolls across the floor. The laps were too long. The rain was too wet. The dodgeball hit him in the face three times, and one time was on purpose. He demands 5 million dollars and new shoes.
The principal reads it all, nods seriously, and makes him run five more laps.

words.say_it: Point and pinch your nose. "Ho-aah-HEH-vah."
words.bonus: Hoʻāhewa is strong blame, like a judge condemning someone. The whole car blaming Heather counts too.
words.picture: Family blaming Heather for the smell
story_paragraphs: You are on a long family road trip. Six people in one car, windows up, AC on high. Somewhere in the second hour, a smell arrives. A terrible smell. A smell that could peel paint.
Every head in the car turns toward your little cousin Heather.
"HO!" says Dad. "AAAAAAAH, HEATHER!" says everybody else, with that long disgusted ahh. Mom points. Grandma points. The baby points.
Heather's eyes go wide. "It wasn't me!" Nobody believes her. They condemn her to the far back seat, alone, windows down, with a clothespin on her nose.
Ten minutes later the dog, curled under the seat, lets out a small happy sigh. Another smell. Heather sits up. "HO! AAAAH, DOG!"
Too late. The family already blamed her. The dog gets away with it forever.

words.say_it: Hand over an invisible cup, proudly. "Ho-oh-KOH."
words.bonus: Hoʻokō is keeping your word or carrying out an order all the way to the end.
words.picture: Carrying shave ice up 44 floors
story_paragraphs: The shave ice delivery guy made a promise. "Your order will arrive cold, no matter what."
Your order is going to the roof of the tallest hotel in Waikīkī. Forty four floors. The elevators are broken. It is August.

He starts up the stairs holding a rainbow shave ice with a snow cap on top. Floor 10, he is sweating. Floor 20, he takes off his shoes. Floor 30, he balances the cup on his head and fans it with his hat. Floor 40, he is crawling, blowing on it the whole way so it will not melt.
He kicks open the roof door. He holds it out. You take a bite. He yells "HO! OH! COOOOOOOLD!" and holds that long O until he runs out of air.
Promise kept. Order carried out. Fulfilled.

words.say_it: Tap an invisible putter, then throw up your hands. "Ho-oh-HO-lo!"
words.bonus: Holo means to run or to sail. Hoʻoholo, to decide, is like finally making the plan run.
words.picture: Council deciding a law by golf putt
story_paragraphs: The town council has argued about the same law for three years. Should chickens be allowed on the golf course? Half say yes. Half say no. They cannot decide.
So the chairwoman stands up and says "Let the hole decide."
The whole council marches out to the 18th green in their suits. She places a golf ball 60 feet from the cup. If it goes in, the law passes.
She swings. The ball rolls over a hill. It bounces off a chicken. It circles the cup three times. The whole council leans in and holds their breath.
It drops. "HOLE! OH!" The council screams and hugs like they just won a championship. Papers fly everywhere. The law passes. Seventeen chickens immediately walk onto the golf course.
Decided. Passed. Ho, oh, hole, oh.

words.english: to choose, to vote; to guess
words.say_it: Mark an X on an invisible ballot. "KO-ho."
words.bonus: Koho covers every kind of picking, from voting to guessing on a quiz. Koho is choosing, ʻāpono (#257) is giving the thumbs up.
words.picture: Salmon winning the fish market election
story_paragraphs: It is election day at the fish market. For the first time ever, the fish are running for mayor of the market.
The candidates lie on the ice. A mullet with a bad haircut. A tuna wearing a tie. And a coho salmon who flew in from the continent with a campaign bus and signs everywhere that say VOTE COHO.
You have to choose. You stare at them. You try to guess which one will win. The tuna blinks. The mullet tells a joke. The coho salmon stands up on its tail and shouts "CO... HO!"
That does it. You mark your ballot. Everybody marks their ballot. The whole market chants "COHO! COHO! COHO!"
The salmon wins. His first act as mayor is to lower the price of salmon, which is a strange choice for a salmon.

words.say_it: Stamp the table with your fist. "Aah-PO-no."
words.bonus: Pono means right, good, proper. ʻĀpono is like saying yes, this is pono, I approve.
words.picture: Principal stamping approved potluck dishes
story_paragraphs: The church potluck has one judge. She is a retired school principal who has never smiled in public. She carries a rubber stamp the size of a hubcap.

She walks down the long table. She tastes the chicken long rice. She chews. Everybody holds their breath. She lets out a long, low sound. "AAAAAAAAH." A little gulp. "...PONO." Then BAM, she slams down the stamp. Approved.
The lomi salmon. "AAAAAH... pono." BAM. The kālua pig. "AAAAAH... pono." BAM. The whole table jumps each time.
Then she tastes your macaroni salad with raisins in it. Silence. She puts the stamp back in her purse and walks away.
Your mom is crying. The other aunties nod quietly. Some dishes get ʻāpono, and some dishes do not.

words.english: to set right, to fix; to resolve a conflict
words.sound_hook: Oh no, oh no... pono, pono.
words.say_it: Fit your two hands together like puzzle pieces. "Ho-oh-po-no-PO-no."
words.bonus: Hoʻoponopono is also a traditional Hawaiian family practice of talking things through, with prayer and forgiveness, to make relationships right again.
words.picture: Two brothers making peace at the table
story_paragraphs: Two brothers stopped talking eleven years ago over a borrowed fishing pole that came back broken. Since then they sit at opposite ends of every party. At Christmas they pass the rice through three cousins so they never touch the same bowl.
This year their mom has had enough. She sits them down at the kitchen table, knee to knee, with the whole family around them.
At first all anybody says is "Oh no. OH NO." Oh no, this is awkward. Oh no, here we go. The older one crosses his arms. The younger one stares at the ceiling fan.
But they talk. Hour after hour. One says sorry. Then the other. Somebody cries. Somebody brings out a brand new fishing pole with a bow on it.
By midnight the words have changed. "Oh no, oh no" has turned into "pono, pono." Right again. Set right.

words.say_it: Wave your hand like a magic wand. "Ho-oh-LO-lee."
words.bonus: Loli means to change by itself. Hoʻololi is to make a change, to alter something.
words.picture: Chameleon Lolly changing everything around
story_paragraphs: Your pet chameleon is named Lolly. She is green, with three little horns, and she rides on your shoulder all day.
Whenever you yell her name, she changes color. "LOLLY!" Purple. "LOLLY!" Orange with pink stripes. "LOLLY!" Plaid.

Then it gets weird. You yell "LOLLY!" and the couch changes from brown to yellow. "LOLLY!" Your dad's plain shirt turns into an aloha shirt. "LOLLY!" The family car is now a boat. The dog is now a cat, and she is not happy about it.
You panic. "HO! OH! LOLLY! Change it back!" Everything flips back except the car, which stays a boat. Your dad just shrugs and drives it down the road anyway.
Ho, oh, Lolly. Anything she looks at changes.

words.say_it: Yank an invisible string. "Oo-NOO-hee!"
words.bonus: Translating is pulling the meaning out of one language and setting it down in another. Same word, unuhi.
words.picture: Yanked tooth, suddenly translating everything
story_paragraphs: You have a loose tooth that has been wiggling for three weeks. The dentist ties it to a string. He ties the other end to the bumper of his truck.
He drives off. The string pulls tight. "OOO!" Tighter. "NOOOOO!" POP. The tooth flies out the window. "HEE!"

Then something strange happens. The dog barks, and you understand it perfectly. "Is that a tooth? Can I eat it?" A mynah bird on the wire says "Nice tooth, kid." Visitors at the bus stop ask for directions in four different languages, and you answer every one of them.
You even understand what the baby is saying. It is mostly complaints about socks.
The dentist pulled out your tooth, and now you can translate everything. Oo, noo, hee. Both meanings in one yank.

words.sound_hook: This WAY, hey! That WAY, hey!
words.say_it: Point this way, then that way. "Veh-heh-VEH-heh."
words.bonus: Wehe means to open. Wehewehe is opening an idea up until it makes sense. The online Hawaiian dictionary is called Wehewehe Wikiwiki.
words.picture: Uncle explaining TV remote on whiteboard
story_paragraphs: Grandpa got a new TV remote. It has 64 buttons. Your uncle has been explaining it to him for three hours.

He has a whiteboard. He has a laser pointer. He has drawn a map of the remote with arrows and colors. "This WAY, hey!" he says, pointing at the volume. "That WAY, hey!" pointing at the channels. "WAY, hey! WAY, hey!"
Grandpa nods. Grandpa presses a button. The garage door opens. Uncle explains again, slower. Grandpa presses a button. The neighbor's garage door opens.
Uncle brings out a slideshow. He acts it out with hand puppets. He makes a song about it. By hour six, Grandpa finally changes the channel by himself. Uncle falls to his knees and cries with joy.
Then Grandpa asks "Now how do I turn it off?"

words.say_it: Wipe a foggy window in a big circle. "Ho-aah-KAAH-kah."
words.bonus: Akāka by itself means clear, easy to see or understand. Hoʻākāka makes it that way, like explaining until it clicks.
words.picture: Toddler wiping a foggy windshield clear
story_paragraphs: It is pouring rain on the H-1. The inside of Dad's windshield is so fogged up it looks like milk. He is driving with his head out the window like a dog.
In the car seat in the back, your two year old brother is yelling the only words he knows. "AAAAAH! CAAAR CAR!"
Nobody understands. Dad says "Yes, buddy, car car." The baby gets madder. "HO! AAAAAAH! CAAAAAR CAR!"

So the baby leans forward as far as his straps allow, stretches out one sticky arm, and wipes one big circle on the glass with his sleeve. Suddenly everyone can see. There is a car right in front of you. Dad hits the brakes. Everyone is fine.
The baby folds his arms. He made it clear. He made the windshield clear. Ho, ah, car car.

words.say_it: Point this way, then that way. "Koo-hee-KOO-hee."
words.bonus: Kuhi means to point or gesture. Doubled, kuhikuhi is pointing over and over, giving directions.
words.picture: Old man's stretchy finger pointing directions
story_paragraphs: You are lost downtown. Your phone is dead. You stop a tiny old man on the sidewalk and ask how to get to the bakery.

He smiles, lifts one finger, and points. His finger starts to stretch. It stretches like a telescope. Out across the street. Past the bank. Around a corner. Down two blocks. It stops, tapping on the bakery window.

"Cookie?" you ask. "COOKIE!" he says, grinning. "Cookie, cookie!" Every time he says it, the finger bends to point at the next turn. Left at the church. Right at the mango tree. Straight past the sleeping dog.
You walk 12 blocks with your hand on his finger like a handrail. At the bakery, the finger holds the door open for you.
The old man is already inside, eating a cookie. Cookie, cookie. Point, point. Kuhikuhi.

words.say_it: Put both hands out and push. "Kaah-KO-oh!"
words.bonus: Kākoʻo is also used for supporting a cause, a team or a person running for office. Mahalo for your kākoʻo means thanks for your support.
words.picture: Thirty strangers pushing a dead truck
story_paragraphs: Uncle's old truck dies on the H-1 at rush hour, right in the middle lane. It will not start. Cars are honking for a mile.

Then something beautiful happens. A construction worker gets out of his car and pushes. A nurse gets out and pushes. A grandma in a muʻumuʻu. A football team off their bus. A guy in a gorilla suit. Thirty strangers get behind the truck, backing Uncle up.

They push together and yell "CAAAAAR... GO..." Somebody's voice catches in a little gulp. "...OH!" The truck rolls. "CAAAAR! GO! OH!" It rolls faster. They push it all the way down the off ramp and into a gas station.
Uncle cries. He hands out spam musubi to all thirty of them. That is support. You get behind someone and push.

words.say_it: Raise your hand from low to high. "Ho-oh-OO-loo."
words.bonus: Ulu means to grow (#266). Hoʻoulu is making something grow, from a garden to a kid's courage.
words.picture: Coach with megaphone making a kid grow
story_paragraphs: Lou is 11 years old and the shortest kid on the basketball team. Four foot one. He cannot touch the net even standing on a chair.

The coach does not give up on him. Every morning she stands in front of Lou with a megaphone. "HO! OH! OOH, LOU! You can do it! You are a giant inside!" She plays loud music. She shows him videos of redwood trees growing.
Lou believes her. And he starts to grow. Two inches a week. Then six inches a week. By March he is six foot four. His pants are shorts. His shirts are belly shirts. He dunks on everybody.
The rest of the team begs the coach to yell at them too. She does. Now the whole team is growing. The gym ceiling has to be raised twice.
She inspired him. She made him grow. Both at once.

words.say_it: Stretch up on your toes. "OO-loo."
words.bonus: Ulu, to grow, has no ʻokina. ʻUlu, with the ʻokina, is breadfruit. Luckily, breadfruit trees ulu pretty fast.
words.picture: Lou growing through the reunion tent
story_paragraphs: Remember Lou from hoʻoulu? It is summer and he is at the family reunion. Every aunty who walks in grabs his cheeks and screams "OOOH, LOU! You GREW!"

Here is the thing. He is still growing, right there, during the party. You can watch it happen. While the first aunty pinches his cheeks, he gets two inches taller. By the time the sixth aunty reaches him, she has to stand on a cooler.

"OOOH, LOU!" He grows through the tent. "OOOH, LOU!" His head is in the mango tree. By dessert the aunties are yelling up at him through a bullhorn, and he is picking mangoes off the top branch and handing them down.
At the end of the party the family has to drive him home lying down in the back of a flatbed truck, feet hanging off the end.

words.say_it: Push one finger slowly up out of your fist like a sprout. "KOO-poo."
words.bonus: Kupu, mohala, oʻo, pala, popopo. Sprout, bloom, mature, ripe, rot. A plant's whole life in the next five words.
words.picture: Sprout lifting chicken coop into sky
story_paragraphs: You toss a handful of old seeds into the chicken coop and forget about it.
The next morning there is a rumbling under the coop. The chickens are nervous. One hen is standing on her tiptoes.

Then a sprout pushes up through the floor. A little green curl, right under the fattest hen. It keeps coming. It lifts the hen. It lifts the whole coop. The coop rises into the air on top of a giant green stalk. 20 feet. 40 feet. 60 feet. Chickens cluck out the windows.
The neighbors run outside and point. "COOP! OOOOO!"
By noon the coop is above the clouds and the chickens are laying eggs that fall into your yard like hail. All from one tiny sprout. Coop, ooo.

words.say_it: Open your fist slowly, one finger at a time. "Mo-HAH-lah."
words.bonus: A pua mohala is a flower in full bloom.
words.picture: Giant flower bud unfolding like a tent
story_paragraphs: At the botanical garden there is one flower bud that has refused to bloom for 12 years. It is shaped like a closed fist. The gardeners call it Mo.
Today the whole island shows up to cheer it on. They bring drums. They bring signs. They stand in a circle around it and scream "MO! HOLLA! MO! HOLLA!"

The bud shivers. Then it unfolds. One petal. Two petals. It keeps opening. The petals spread like an umbrella, then like a beach tent, then like a circus tent. It is 40 feet wide and hot pink. It smells so good that three tour buses pull over.
The crowd goes crazy. Someone sets up a snack stand underneath it. A band plays in its shade.
Mo bloomed. Mo unfolded. All it needed was a holla.

words.say_it: Gasp twice, with a little gulp between. "OH-oh."
words.bonus: Oʻo is mature, full grown, like fruit ready to pick. Pala (#270) is the next step, ripe and soft. Different from ʻōʻō, the old digging stick.
words.picture: Nine year old brother suddenly an adult
story_paragraphs: Your little brother is nine. Yesterday he ate a crayon and put a gecko down your shirt.
This morning you walk into the kitchen and he is sitting at the table in a suit and tie. He is reading the newspaper. He has a mustache. He is drinking black coffee and paying the electric bill.
You stare. "OH!" A catch in your throat. A gulp. "OH!"
He looks up over his reading glasses. "Good morning. I made breakfast. Please rinse your plate." He folds his napkin into a perfect triangle. He talks about his retirement plan.
At school he politely corrects the teacher. At lunch he eats a salad. You follow him around all day going "Oh! Oh!"
He is mature. Like a mango that is finally full size, he is done growing. In one night.

words.say_it: Squeeze an invisible banana. "PAH-lah!"
words.bonus: Oʻo (#269) is mature but still firm. Pala is ripe and soft. Popopo (#271) has gone too far.
words.picture: Aunty Paula squishing ripe bananas
story_paragraphs: There is a lady at the farmers market named Aunty Paula who tests every banana. She squeezes them.
She picks up a banana. It is brown with black spots. It is so ripe and soft that when she squeezes it, banana squirts out of both ends like toothpaste. It hits the guy at the next stand.
"PAULA!" the banana man yells.
She squeezes a mango. SPLAT. "PAULA!" A papaya. It collapses in her hand like a water balloon. "PAULA!" An avocado. It turns into guacamole on the spot.
She nods, very happy. "Perfect. Soft. Ripe." She buys all of them. The banana man mops his table and yells after her as she walks away. "PAULA!"
When fruit is so ripe it squishes, it is pala.

words.say_it: Pinch your nose and pop your lips three times. "Po-PO-po."
words.bonus: Popopo is used for rotten fruit, rotten wood, even a rotten tooth. Pala (#270) is ripe and soft, popopo is way past that.
words.picture: Rotten mango soup bubbling in trunk
story_paragraphs: In August you forget a bag of mangoes in the trunk of the car. Then you leave on a trip for three weeks.
When you come back, the car is bulging. The trunk is humming. The back tires are flat.

You open it. Inside, the mangoes have rotted into a brown, bubbling soup. Big stink bubbles rise to the top and burst. "po... POP... po." Each pop lets out a smell that makes your eyebrows curl. "po POP po."
The mynah birds fly away screaming. The neighbors close their windows. A fly zooms in, takes one sniff, and flies back out holding its nose. The paint on the trunk lid peels off in long strips.
You slam the trunk. You put a sign on the car. FOR SALE. Inside you can still hear it. "po... POP... po." That is rot.

words.say_it: Lick your dry lips and gulp. "Mah-LO-oh."
words.bonus: Iʻa maloʻo is dried fish, a local favorite. Maloʻo is dry, pulu (#274) is wet.
words.picture: Empty water tank, fish with umbrellas
story_paragraphs: It has not rained in 200 days. The grass is crunchy. The stream is a dusty path. The fish are walking across the dirt carrying tiny umbrellas.
You climb the ladder on the side of the water tank to check it. You knock. It sounds empty. You look inside. One sad raindrop is sitting at the bottom.
You yell down to the house "MA! LOW!" Then you catch your breath, a hard gulp. "...OH!" Ma, low, oh.
Everything is dry. The laundry dries in four seconds. The dog's water bowl is a dust bowl. Your lips are so dry that when you smile they crack like old paint. Even the cactus looks thirsty.
That night one single cloud floats over. Everyone runs outside holding up buckets. It does not rain. It just looks at you.

words.say_it: Blow on your hands like a hair dryer. "Ho-oh-mah-LO-oh."
words.bonus: Maloʻo is to be dry. Hoʻomaloʻo is to make something dry, like dishes, laundry, or fish in the sun.
words.picture: Industrial hair dryer puffing up a cat
story_paragraphs: Ma from maloʻo finally got rain. Too much rain. The cat, Mochi, got caught in it and is now soaked, skinny and dripping on the carpet, looking furious.
Ma grabs a hair dryer. Not a normal hair dryer. An industrial one, the kind used to dry airplanes. She cranks it to HIGH.
WHOOOOSH. Mochi lifts off the ground like a kite. You scream "HO! OH! MA! LOW! OH!" You mean put it on LOW. She cannot hear you over the roar.

Mochi floats around the living room, drying fast. Her fur puffs out. She gets bigger and fluffier until she looks like a giant dandelion. When Ma finally clicks it off, Mochi drifts slowly down onto the couch, perfectly dry and three times her normal size.
Ma dried the cat. That is hoʻomaloʻo.

words.say_it: Shake water off your hands. "POO-loo."
words.bonus: Pulu pē means soaking wet, drenched. Pulu is also the soft fluff from the hāpuʻu tree fern, once used to stuff pillows.
words.picture: Uncle's cannonball soaking the whole party
story_paragraphs: It is your cousin's graduation party in the backyard. Everybody is dressed nice. Aunties in new muʻumuʻu. Uncles in pressed aloha shirts. A three layer cake on the table right next to the pool.
Then Uncle Bula, 380 pounds, climbs onto the roof of the house. Everybody looks up. He yells "POOL!" and jumps.

He does a cannonball. The pool empties in one second. A wave twelve feet tall rolls across the yard. Every single guest is soaked. The cake is soaked. The neighbor, who was just mowing his lawn, is soaked.
Uncle Bula stands up in the empty pool and yells "OOH!"
Forty people stand there dripping, hair flat, shoes squishing, cake floating in the grass. POOL. OOH. Everyone is pulu.

words.say_it: Aim an invisible hose. "Ho-oh-POO-loo!"
words.bonus: Pulu is to be wet. Hoʻopulu is to make something wet, from watering a plant to dunking your brother.
words.picture: Old lady with fire hose flooding street
story_paragraphs: Every summer the kids on your street have a water balloon war. This year the old lady on the corner decides to join. Nobody has ever seen her leave her porch.
She walks out holding a fire hose. A real one. It is hooked up to the hydrant. She turns the valve and yells "HOSE! OH!"

The first blast knocks three kids into a hedge. She soaks the ice cream truck. She soaks the mailman so hard his letters come out like wet noodles. The water fills the street. It rises over the curb. It rises to your knees.
She yells "POOL!" By the end, the whole street is one big swimming pool, and she is floating in the middle of it on an inner tube, wearing sunglasses.
She wet everybody. She soaked the whole block. Hose, oh, pool.

words.say_it: Rub your hands together and blow on them. "Ho-oh-mah-HAH-nah."
words.bonus: Mahana means warm. Its opposite in this list is hoʻomaʻalili (#277), to cool down.
words.picture: Frozen cowboy thawing on Waikīkī sand
story_paragraphs: A cowboy from Montana steps off the plane in Honolulu. He has been cold for 40 years. He is wearing three coats, two hats, and a scarf wrapped around his neck eleven times. There are icicles in his mustache.
He walks out into the sunshine, throws his arms wide, and shouts "HO! OH! MONTANA!" like he is saying goodbye to it forever.

He lies down on the hot sand at Waikīkī. Steam rises off him. The icicles melt and drip. He peels off one coat. Then the second. Then the third. His toes turn from blue to pink. His frozen belt buckle thaws and falls off.
After six hours he is finally warm all the way through. He sits up, smiles, and orders a hot chocolate anyway, because old habits die hard.
He warmed up. Ho, oh, Montana.

words.say_it: Fan your face fast. "Ho-oh-mah-ah-LEE-lee."
words.bonus: Maʻalili means cooled off, like hot food that has cooled or anger that has calmed. Hoʻomaʻalili is cooling something down on purpose.
words.picture: Chili judge steaming in a lily pond
story_paragraphs: It is the chili cook off. The final judge takes one spoonful of the hottest chili ever made. It has 90 peppers in it.
His face turns red. Then purple. Then a color no one has ever seen. Steam blows out of his ears like a train whistle. His hair stands straight up and smokes.

He staggers out of the tent looking for anything cold. Then he spots the pond behind the tent, covered in lily pads. He points and croaks "MA..." His throat catches, a little gulp. "...AH... LILY!" He means the lily pond.
He dives in head first. SSSSSSSSSS. A cloud of steam rises 30 feet. The frogs leap out. The water starts bubbling like a hot tub.
Finally he floats on his back, cooled down, while the frogs fan him with little leaves.

words.say_it: Shake your whole body like a wet dog. "LOOOO."
words.bonus: Lū is also used for scattering seeds on the ground or flinging something off. The long ū is the long shake.
words.picture: Wet dog shaking sand on the lūʻau
story_paragraphs: The lūʻau is perfect. Two hundred guests. White tablecloths. The kālua pig just came out of the imu.
Then the host's dog, Keiki, a 150 pound fluffy monster, comes running up from the beach. He is dripping wet and covered in sand.
He stops right in the middle of the tables. Everybody knows what is coming. The whole party tries to yell "LOOK OUT!" but only the first part comes out, long and slow. "LOOOOOOOOOO..."

Keiki shakes. He shakes from nose to tail like a washing machine. Water and sand scatter in every direction. It hits the guests, the pig, the band, the dessert table, the dancers and the roof of the tent.
He shakes one more time for good measure. "LOOOOOOO!" Everybody is sandy. Keiki is dry and happy. He scattered everything.

words.say_it: Sprinkle salt from your fingertips. "Kaah-pee-PEE."
words.bonus: Lū (#278) is a big shake or scatter. Kāpīpī is a light little sprinkle, like salt on a tomato or water on plants.
words.picture: Tiny car sprinkling the whole neighborhood
story_paragraphs: Every Saturday a tiny rainbow car drives through your neighborhood. It is the size of a golf cart. On its roof is a giant salt shaker, but it is full of rainbow sprinkles.
You hear it before you see it. "CAAAAAR! BEEEEEP! BEEEEEP!" Every sound held long, like an old horn.
It drives slowly past each house, sprinkling everything. Sprinkles on the lawns. Sprinkles on the cats. Sprinkles on the bald man washing his car. He does not mind. He licks his head.
Kids chase it with bowls of ice cream. Birds follow it like a parade. By the end of the block, the whole street looks like a birthday cake.
Then it drives away. "CAAAR... BEEEEP... BEEEEP..." It never dumps. It never pours. Just tiny little sprinkles. That is kāpīpī.

words.sound_hook: Old MA had a farm... EE (gulp) EYE!
words.say_it: Hoe an invisible row. "Mah-hee-AI!"
words.bonus: A mahiʻai is also a farmer. Growing kalo, taro, is the classic Hawaiian kind of farming.
words.picture: Ma singing on her new farm
story_paragraphs: Your Ma quits her office job, sells the car, and buys a farm up in Kula. She has never grown anything except mold on leftovers.

On day one she stands in the field in rubber boots and sings as loud as she can. "Old MA had a farm... EE..." Then she gets choked up and gulps. "...EYE!" She stops right there because she is too happy to finish.
She plows the field with a rototiller that drags her 40 feet. She plants taro, sweet potato and cabbage in perfectly straight rows. She buys six chickens and a goat that eats her hat.
Every morning at sunrise you hear her out in the field. "Ma... ee... EYE!" The cabbages grow to the size of beach balls. The sweet potatoes come up purple and huge. Ma is a farmer now.

words.say_it: Reel in an invisible fish. "Lah-VAI-ah!"
words.bonus: A lawaiʻa is also a fisherman.
words.picture: Uncle singing, hauling up giant ulua
story_paragraphs: Uncle sits at the end of the pier with his fishing pole. He sings the same little song every time he goes fishing. "La, la, la..."
Nine hours. Nothing. Not one nibble. The sun goes down. He looks up at the sky and sings "La... WHY?" His voice catches in his throat.

Then his pole bends in half. Something huge is on the line. "AH!" He braces his feet. He pulls. The fish pulls back. The pier creaks. Uncle leans back so far he is almost lying down. People come running with flashlights.
"LA! WHY! AH!" He hauls up an ulua bigger than a surfboard. It flops onto the pier, knocks over his cooler, and looks at him like it is annoyed.
Uncle sits back down, opens a soda, and starts singing again. "La, la, la..." He will be back tomorrow.

words.say_it: Chip at an invisible block with a chisel. "Kaah-LAI."
words.bonus: Kālai kiʻi means to carve an image or statue. Kālaiʻāina, carving up the land, is the word for politics.
words.picture: Old carver drives off in wooden car
story_paragraphs: There is a 90 year old woodcarver down the road who can carve anything. A bowl. A canoe paddle. A spoon so thin you can see through it. A perfect wooden pineapple.
One day he tells the neighborhood kids "Today I carve a car."
The kids laugh. "CAAAAR? LIE!"

He does not argue. He picks up a mango log the size of a school bus and starts carving. Chips fly. Sawdust fills the air like snow. He carves wheels. He carves seats. He carves a steering wheel, a mirror and a pair of fuzzy dice.
At sunset he blows off the last of the dust. The kids are still saying "Car? LIE!" He climbs in, turns the wooden key, and drives off down the road at 40 miles an hour, honking a wooden horn.
The kids stand there with their mouths open. Not a lie. He carved a car.

words.say_it: Press your two palms together like gluing. "Kaah-PEE-lee."
words.bonus: Kāpili is used for building a house or a boat, and for gluing a broken plate back together.
words.picture: Sister hot gluing a race car mid-race
story_paragraphs: Soapbox derby day. You built your race car out of 10,000 popsicle sticks and every tube of glue in the house. It took you all summer.
You line up at the top of the hill. The flag drops. You roll. Faster. Faster. Then you hear it. The car is peeling apart. "CAAAAR!" you yell as a board flies off. "PEEEEL!" Another one. "EEEEEE!"

But your little sister is running right next to you holding a hot glue gun like a firefighter with a hose. She glues the wheel back on. She glues the seat back on. She glues the steering wheel back on. She glues your hat to your head by accident.
You cross the finish line with half a car and a sister stuck to the side of it. First place.
Build it. Glue it together. Kāpili.

words.say_it: Pick up whatever is near you and pretend it is a phone. "Ho-oh-HAH-nah."
words.bonus: Hana means work, or to do. Hoʻohana makes a thing do work, so it means to use.
words.picture: Hannah fixing car with musubi wrapper
story_paragraphs: Your friend Hannah can use anything for anything.

The TV remote is lost? She uses a spatula. The front door won't stay open? She uses a slippah. A gecko gets in the house? She catches it with a colander. She uses a cooler as a chair, a surfboard as a table, and a rice paddle to fix the lawn mower.
Every time she does it, everybody yells "HO! OH! HANNAH!"

Today your car breaks down on the side of the road. Hannah opens the hood, looks inside, and pulls a musubi out of her purse. She eats the musubi. Then she uses the plastic wrapper to fix the fan belt. The car starts.
"HO! OH! HANNAH!" Around her, nothing goes to waste. Everything gets used.

words.say_it: Line up invisible chairs in a row. "Ho-oh-no-ho-NO-ho."
words.bonus: Noho means to sit, or a chair. Hoʻonohonoho is putting things in their place, like chairs, flowers, or your whole schedule.
words.picture: Wedding planner arranging six hundred chairs
story_paragraphs: The wedding planner has a clipboard, a whistle and a headset. She has 600 folding chairs to set up on the lawn in exactly 60 rows.

Your family is helping. That is the problem. Uncle sets a chair facing backward. "NO! HO!" she yells, blowing the whistle. Your cousin stacks three chairs in a pyramid. "NO! HO! NO! HO!" Grandma drags her chair into the shade under a tree, far from everything. "NOOOO! HO!"
She marches through the rows with a tape measure. She moves each chair a quarter inch. She lines up the legs with a laser. She makes every flower face the same direction.
By sunset the rows are so straight you could use them as a ruler. She lowers the whistle and smiles. Then the wind blows one chair over. "NO! HO!"

words.say_it: Throw two practice punches. "Ho-oh-maah-kow-KOW."
words.bonus: Hoʻomākaukau is getting ready. Mākaukau (#287) is being ready, or being skilled.
words.picture: Tūtū training with rice bag and futon
story_paragraphs: Tūtū has signed up for the boxing tournament. The fight is in one month. She is 81.

She gets ready. Every morning at 4 am she runs up the Koko Head stairs with a 25 pound bag of rice on her back. She jumps rope with a garden hose. She does pushups with a grandchild sitting on her back.
Then she does mock fights in the carport against a punching bag made from an old futon. "MOCK! Ka-POW! MOCK! Ka-POW!" Each punch is louder. One punch sends the futon flying into the neighbor's yard.
She prepares her meals. She prepares her gloves. She prepares a playlist. She even prepares a victory speech and practices it in the bathroom mirror.
The night before the fight everything is laid out on the bed. Shoes. Gloves. Mouthguard. Two musubi. She is prepared.

words.english: to be ready; to be skilled
words.say_it: Flap your elbows and squawk. "Maah-kow-KOW!"
words.bonus: Teachers ask "Mākaukau?" meaning Ready? and the class answers "Mākaukau!"
words.picture: Macaw that can do everything
story_paragraphs: The pet store has a parrot. A big red and blue macaw named Captain.
Captain can do everything. It can juggle three mangoes. It can flip pancakes with its feet. It can play the ʻukulele, badly, and do your taxes, very well.
When it is ready for the next trick, it screams "MAAAAAA... CAW! CAW!" A long start, then two sharp caws. Everybody knows that means it is ready.
Today a kid brings in a wooden puzzle box that nobody has ever opened. Captain looks at it. It stretches its wings. It cracks its neck. "MAAAAAA... CAW! CAW!" It opens the box in four seconds.
The kid asks "Can you do my homework?" Captain is already on page two. Ready. Skilled. Ma, caw, caw.

words.say_it: Stack invisible boxes higher and higher. "Ho-oh-LAH-ko."
words.bonus: Lako means well supplied, having plenty. Hoʻolako is giving people what they need.
words.picture: Old man's truck supplying the valley
story_paragraphs: There is one old man in the valley who supplies everybody. Nobody knows where he gets it all.
When a storm is coming, he drives down the road in an old flatbed truck piled 20 feet high. Rice. Water. Batteries. Toilet paper. Canned sardines. A generator. A spare canoe.

He stops at every house. "How much rice you need?" You say "Uh, a little?" He shakes his head. "HO! OH! A LOT, OH!" He throws three bags on your porch. "Batteries?" "A few?" "HO! OH! A LOT, OH!" Forty batteries.
By the end of the road, every family has enough for a year. The truck is empty. He drives home whistling.
The next morning the truck is full again. Nobody asks how. He supplies. He provides. A lot, oh.

words.say_it: Hold up your palm to say stop. "LAH-vah!"
words.bonus: Ua lawa means that is enough. Just Lawa! by itself works like Enough! or That's plenty. Listen to the ending. Lawe (take) ends in "eh." Lawa (enough) ends in "ah," like a happy sigh after a big plate. Ahh, enough.
words.picture: Gravy lava flowing off a loco moco
story_paragraphs: You order a loco moco at the diner. Rice, hamburger patty, fried egg. Then you grab the gravy pitcher.
You pour. Brown gravy flows over the egg like lava. It covers the patty. It buries the rice. It spills over the edge of the plate. It creeps across the table like a slow river, bubbling.
The waitress yells "LAVA! LAVA!" meaning stop, enough. You keep pouring. The gravy reaches the floor. It flows out the front door. A man on the sidewalk has to jump over it.
"LAVA! LAVA!" she yells again, and grabs the pitcher right out of your hands. She points at your plate. "That is enough."
You look down. She is right. It is enough. You never need more gravy than that. Well. Maybe a little more.

words.say_it: Push an invisible mower forward, and do not stop. "Ho-oh-MOW."
words.bonus: Hoʻomau is often used as a motto, meaning keep going, persevere, never give up.
words.picture: Uncle mowing across the whole island
story_paragraphs: Uncle starts mowing his lawn on Saturday morning. He finishes the front yard. But it feels so good he keeps going.
He mows the neighbor's lawn. He mows the park. He mows across the school field and down the side of the H-1. Traffic slows down to watch. "HO! OH! MOW!" he shouts, waving.

He mows through the night with a flashlight taped to his hat. He mows past Ala Moana. He mows a golf course. He does not stop for lunch. His wife drives next to him and passes him musubi through the car window.
On Sunday he is in Waimānalo. On Monday he reaches the North Shore. Behind him the grass looks perfect for 60 miles.
When people ask him why he doesn't stop, he just yells "HO! OH! MOW!" and keeps going.

words.english: to finish off, to use up, to waste
words.say_it: Clap once, loud, like something just ran out. "Ho-oh-POW!"
words.bonus: Pau means done or finished, and locals use it in everyday English, like pau hana for after work. Hoʻopau means to make something pau.
words.picture: Brother emptying the fridge, POW
story_paragraphs: Your big brother is home from college for the weekend. That means everything in the house is about to disappear.

He opens the fridge. POW. The rice pot is empty. POW. A gallon of ice cream, gone. POW. The whole family pack of chicken katsu, gone. Every time he finishes something off, there is a little explosion of crumbs and a POW.
He takes a 45 minute shower. POW. No hot water for anyone. He uses the last roll of toilet paper. POW. He leaves every light in the house on. POW POW POW.
Mom stands in the kitchen staring at the empty cabinets. "HO! OH! POW!"
By Sunday he has finished off everything, used up everything, and wasted whatever was left. He hugs everybody goodbye and asks for gas money.

words.english: to save some for later, to leave some
words.say_it: Push half your plate aside. "Ho-oh-KO-eh."
words.bonus: Koe (#293) is what is left over. Hoʻokoe is making sure some is left, saving it on purpose.
words.picture: Giant koi waiting for saved leftovers
story_paragraphs: Dad has one rule at dinner. Always save some for the koi.

He has a pond in the backyard with 12 koi. After every meal, before anyone can finish, he takes one scoop off every plate. Rice. Noodles. Half a musubi. He drops it all in a bucket and says "HO! OH! KOI... EH!"
He has done this for 20 years. The family has learned. Nobody eats the last bite. They leave it on the plate for later.
The koi are now enormous. Each one is the size of a golden retriever. They wait at the edge of the pond with their mouths open at 7 pm sharp. One of them has learned to ring a bell.
When Dad passes you a slice of cake, you already know what to do. You eat half. You leave some. "Koi, eh!"

words.say_it: Point at the last piece on an invisible plate. "KO-eh."
words.bonus: Koe also means the rest, what remains. Hoʻokoe (#292) is leaving some on purpose, koe is whatever ends up left.
words.picture: Last chicken piece nobody takes
story_paragraphs: It is the end of the party. On the long table there is one piece of fried chicken left over in the tray. Just one.
Forty people want it. Nobody takes it. Everybody is being polite. Everybody is being coy. Aunty looks at it, then looks away. Uncle reaches for it, then pretends he was scratching his arm.
Somebody whispers "Coy, eh?" Everybody laughs nervously.
An hour goes by. The chicken is still there. The party ends. People go home. The chicken stays on the table, alone, under a paper towel.

Three days later it is still there. It gets a name. The kids visit it. Somebody builds a little fence around it. Five years later it sits in a glass case at the family reunion with a sign that says LEFT OVER. Nobody ever took it.

words.say_it: Wave a lazy hand and push something away. "Ho-oh-pah-NEH-eh."
words.bonus: Neʻe means to scoot or move along. Hoʻopaneʻe is like scooting a date further down the calendar.
words.picture: Pa rafting across flooded living room
story_paragraphs: There is a leak in the roof over the living room. Mom asks Pa to fix it.
Pa is on the couch. He waves his hand. "Pa? NAY..." A little hiccup. "...eh. Tomorrow."
Tomorrow comes. "Pa, the roof?" "NAY, eh. Next week." Next week comes. "NAY, eh. After football season." The bucket under the leak fills up. Then a second bucket. Then a kiddie pool.

Eleven years pass. The living room is now an indoor pond. There are fish in it. Pa paddles an inflatable raft across the room to get to the fridge. Every time someone mentions the roof, he pushes it back again. "Nay, eh. Next year."
Finally the whole roof falls in. Pa looks up at the open sky and says "Tomorrow." Ho, oh, Pa, nay, eh.

words.say_it: Snip invisible scissors close together. "Ho-oh-poh-KO-leh."
words.bonus: Pōkole means short. Loa means long. Hoʻopōkole makes something short, like cutting a long story short.
words.picture: Shaved collie looking like a chicken
story_paragraphs: Your neighbor's collie, Duke, has the longest fur on the island. It drags behind him like a wedding dress. He sweeps the sidewalk when he walks. Birds nest in it.
Summer comes. It is 92 degrees. Duke is overheating. So the neighbor takes him to the groomer.

The groomer brings out the clippers. BZZZZZ. Off comes the fur, pile after pile, until it fills the shop to the ceiling. When she is done, Duke is tiny and skinny and pink. He looks like a chicken with ears.

Everybody on the street sees him and says "Poooooo' COLLIE!" holding that oh sound long out of pity. The groomer shortened his fur. She also shortened his leash, his tail bow, and his name. Now he is just Du.
Ho, oh, pooo' collie. Everything about him is shorter.

words.say_it: Hunch over like you are carrying someone heavy. "Ho-oh-LOO-hee."
words.bonus: Luhi (#297) is to be tired. Hoʻoluhi is to make someone tired, to wear them out or weigh them down.
words.picture: Louie riding piggyback all day
story_paragraphs: Your nephew Louie is three. He has more energy than a power plant.

He wants a piggyback ride. You say okay. He climbs on your back at 9 in the morning and never gets off. You carry him around Ala Moana. He points left. "HO! OH! LOUIE!" you gasp, and go left. He points up the escalator. You go up. He points down. You go down.

By noon your legs are shaking. By 2 pm you are crawling on your hands and knees, and he is still riding you like a horse, kicking your sides, yelling "Faster!" He also has three shopping bags on his lap that you are somehow carrying too.
By 5 pm you lie face down on the food court floor. Louie climbs off, fresh as a daisy, and asks "Again?"
He wore you out. He was the burden. HO, OH, LOUIE.

words.say_it: Let your head drop slowly onto your hands. "LOO-hee."
words.bonus: Luhi can also mean tiring or tedious, a burden that wears you out.
words.picture: Louie asleep face down in mac salad
story_paragraphs: Remember Louie from hoʻoluhi? After wearing out the whole family, it finally happens. Louie runs out of power.
It happens at dinner. He is holding a spoon of rice halfway to his mouth. His eyes start to close. His head starts to drop. Slower. Slower. His whole body goes soft like melted butter.
Everybody at the table leans in and whispers "Louie..."
He lets out one tiny, tired giggle. "...hee." Then his face lands in his mac salad. FLOMP. Asleep. Snoring. Mac salad on his cheek.

They carry him to bed. He is so worn out he sleeps for 16 hours straight. A rooster crows right on the windowsill. He does not move. The dog licks his face. Nothing. He is totally, completely worn out. Louie... hee.

words.say_it: Cup your hands around your mouth. "Oo-AAAAH!"
words.bonus: Three ways to be loud in this list. ʻUā is shouting, hea (#299) is calling out to someone, hoʻōho (#300) is crying out in surprise.
words.picture: Tiny old fan's yell bending goalposts
story_paragraphs: At the high school football game there is one fan everybody knows. He is a tiny old man, 80 pounds, four foot ten, with a foam finger bigger than he is.
When the home team scores, he climbs up on the bleachers. He takes a breath. There is a little catch in his throat. Then he yells.
"OOH... AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAH!"

The long AAAAH goes on for 20 seconds. The goalposts bend. The ref's whistle flies out of his mouth. The quarterback's helmet spins around backward. Car alarms go off in the parking lot. A flock of birds turns around.
The team scores again. "OOH... AAAAAAAAAAH!" Windows in the school rattle. The principal crawls under his desk.
Nobody knows how that much yell fits inside such a tiny man. But everybody on the island has heard it.

words.say_it: Cup your hands and call across a valley. "HEH-ah!"
words.bonus: The same spelling hea also means where, as in Aia i hea? Where is it?
words.picture: Neighbor calling the whole island to dinner
story_paragraphs: The lady next door calls her kids home for dinner the same way every night. She stands on her porch, takes a breath so big her apron lifts, and yells "HEY, AH! KEONI! HEY, AH! MALIA!"

Her kids are two miles away at the beach. They hear it. Surfers out at the reef hear it and start paddling in, just in case. A fishing boat turns around. A dog at the park drops its ball and runs toward her house.
Then she calls everybody by name, one at a time. The kids. The cousins. The dog. The cat. The chickens. The mailman. "HEY, AH! Pualani! HEY, AH! Uncle! HEY, AH! Mister Rooster!"
In five minutes her dinner table has 32 people and 3 animals around it. Only 2 of them are her kids.

words.say_it: Throw your hands up in surprise. "Ho-OHHH-ho!"
words.bonus: Locals shout Ho! for everything, good food, big waves, bad traffic. Hoʻōho is the proper word for crying out like that.
words.picture: Horse jumping out of birthday cake
story_paragraphs: It is your birthday. You come home after a long day. The house is dark. You flip on the light.
Sixty people jump out. "SURPRISE!" You drop your bag and scream "HO!"
Then the giant cake on the table starts shaking. The top pops off and a full grown horse jumps out, covered in frosting, wearing a party hat. You gasp and hold it long. "OHHHHHHHHHHH!"

The horse gallops across the living room, knocks over the punch bowl, and does a little dance. The confetti cannon goes off. The dog starts howling. Grandma faints onto the couch, then sits right back up to take a picture.
You stand in the middle of it all with both hands on your head and let out the biggest exclamation of your life. "HO! OHHHHH! HO!"
That is hoʻōho. A cry of surprise with a long oh in the middle.

words.say_it: Cup one hand behind your ear and lean in. "Ho-oh-LO-no."
words.bonus: Lono means news or a rumor, the thing you hear. Hoʻolohe is another common word for to listen.
words.picture: Party freezing to hear a tiny radio
story_paragraphs: You are the DJ at a backyard party in Waimānalo. Your speakers are as big as refrigerators and the bass is making the chicken long rice hop off the paper plates.
Uncle Boy runs over waving both arms like he is landing a plane. "HO! OH! LOW! NO!" Turn it low. No more music. Right now.

You kill the sound. Uncle holds up a tiny radio the size of a matchbox. They are about to read the winning number for a free pickup truck. Two hundred people lean in at the same time. Nobody chews. A baby stops crying halfway through. The dog tilts one ear at the radio.
"Ho, oh, low, no," Uncle whispers again. Listen. Pay attention.
The number is read. It is on your ticket. Two hundred heads turn and stare at you. You were listening so hard you forgot to breathe.

words.english: to talk, to chat, to chatter
words.say_it: Flap your hand open and shut like a mouth that won't stop. "Vah-lah-OW."
words.bonus: Local folks sometimes use walaʻau in everyday talk too, meaning to just chat and talk story.
words.picture: Two aunties chattering across your face
story_paragraphs: You get the middle seat on a five hour flight to the continent. On your left is Aunty Lei. On your right is Aunty Pua. They have not seen each other in 11 years.

They talk across you the whole way. Words fly past your nose like popcorn. Cousins, weddings, a guy who owes somebody $40 since 1996, a dog that ate a whole ham. They talk through takeoff. They talk through the snack. They talk through the movie and nobody is watching the movie.
By hour three your left ear is ringing. By hour four your right ear goes numb. You finally cry out "WAH... LA... OW!"
They do not even notice. Aunty Lei hands you a cracker without looking and keeps going. When the plane lands they are still chattering on the jet bridge.

words.say_it: Hold an invisible mic and hiccup twice. "Hah-ee-oh-LEH-lo."
words.bonus: Haʻi means to tell and ʻōlelo means words or language. So a speech is telling words.
