words.picture: Graduation speaker with loud hiccups
story_paragraphs: You are the class speaker at graduation. The stadium holds 10,000 people. Every one of them has a lei and an air horn.
You walk up to the podium. You tap the microphone. It booms like thunder over Aloha Stadium. And then, right there, you get the hiccups.
"Hi! (hic) Oh! (hic) HELLO!"

Ten thousand people yell back "HELLO!" Somebody's tutu blows an air horn. You try again. "Hi! (hic) Oh! (hic) HELLO!" Every hiccup is a little catch in your throat, right where the word has its ʻokina.

You give up on fixing it and just go. You give the whole speech with hiccups. Forty five minutes about dreams and hard work and thanking your mom. When you finish, the crowd stands and chants "HI! OH! HELLO!" like it is your name.

words.say_it: Stamp your foot four times, then bray. "Hoh-oy-ah-EE-oh."
words.bonus: ʻOiaʻiʻo means truth or true. Hōʻoiaʻiʻo is to show that something is true, to prove or confirm it.
words.picture: Donkey in glasses stamping out math
story_paragraphs: Uncle Kimo swears his donkey can do math. Nobody at the feed store believes him. "Prove it," they say. "Prove it or buy everybody lunch."
So Uncle backs up his truck and out comes the donkey. It is wearing reading glasses. Uncle holds up a chalkboard. Two plus two.
"HŌŌŌ! OY!" Uncle yells, a long proud shout. The donkey stamps its hoof. One. Two. Three. Four. Then it throws back its head and brays "AAAH, EE-OH!"

The feed store goes silent. Somebody tries seven plus five. Twelve stamps. "AAAH, EE-OH!" Nine times nine. The donkey stamps for three minutes straight while a guy counts on his fingers. Eighty one. "AAAH, EE-OH!"
It is confirmed. Uncle proved it. The feed store buys him lunch, and the donkey gets a whole bag of carrots.

words.say_it: Close your eyes, lean forward like you're jumping. "Mah-nah-oh-EE-oh."
words.bonus: Manaʻo means thought and ʻiʻo means true or real, so to believe is to hold a thought as true. Same ʻiʻo as in hōʻoiaʻiʻo.
words.picture: Kid on a zipline shouting yee-oh
story_paragraphs: You are nine years old, standing on the top platform of a zipline in the mountains. The line runs 2,000 feet across a valley. Down below, the trees look like broccoli.
Your mom is already on the other side, waving. She calls over the radio, "You gotta believe, baby. The rope going hold. Just trust and go."
Your knees knock. You grip the handle. "Ma... NOW?" You gulp so hard it makes a little click in your throat. "Oh..."
Then something in your chest decides to believe. You jump. "YEE-OH!"
You fly over the valley like a bird with a helmet on. A goat on a cliff watches you go by. You land in your mom's arms, and she says "See? Ma, now, oh, yee-oh. You believed."

words.say_it: Lean back a little, then squeal. "Hee-lee-NAH-ee."
words.bonus: Hilinaʻi is also a noun, trust or confidence. You can hilinaʻi a friend, a plan, or a rope.
words.picture: Twelve coworkers catching a falling uncle
story_paragraphs: Company picnic at Magic Island. The boss decides everyone must do the trust fall.
First up is Big Uncle Sonny. He is 350 pounds and made of pure plate lunch. He climbs onto the picnic table. Behind him, twelve coworkers lock arms and hold a beach towel.
"You gotta trust us!" they shout. Uncle Sonny closes his eyes. He starts to tip back. Everyone yells "He LEAN! He LEAN!"
Halfway down, his faith runs out. "NAH... EEEEE!"
Too late. He falls like a tree. The twelve coworkers catch him. Their knees shake. The towel rips. One guy's slipper flies into the ocean. But Uncle Sonny does not touch the grass.
He opens his eyes and smiles. "Okay," he says. "I trust you guys now." And from that day on, he relies on them for everything.

words.say_it: Wave at a paint can and turn away. "Ho-oh-kah-oo-LOO-ah."
words.picture: Paint cans ignored while you party
story_paragraphs: Your mom says the house needs painting. One gallon for each wall. The brushes are right there. You say sure, you'll start today.
Then your phone buzzes. A cousin's baby is turning one. "Ho, oh... gotta go lūʻau," you say, and you leave.

Next day, brush in hand. Buzz. A graduation party. "Ho, oh... gotta go lūʻau." Next day, a retirement party. Then a wedding. Then a party for a guy's new boat. You go to 31 lūʻau in 31 days. You eat so much kālua pig that you have to buy new shorts.
The paint cans sit on the porch. A family of geckos moves into one of them. Moss grows on the brushes. Your mom paints the whole house herself while you are out.
When you finally come home, she hands you a brush. "Ho, oh... gotta go lūʻau?" she says. "Not today."

words.english: to give hope; to float something
words.say_it: Hug an invisible floatie. "Ho-oh-LAH-nah."
words.bonus: Lana by itself means to float. Hoʻo makes something else float, and hope works the same way. It keeps you up.
words.picture: Giant pink llama floatie saving you
story_paragraphs: Your fishing boat sank in the middle of Kāneʻohe Bay. You are treading water, and your arms feel like cooked noodles. No boats in sight. You start to lose hope.
Then from the shore, a little kid throws something. It lands with a SPLOOSH next to you. It is a giant pink inflatable llama named Lana, the size of a pickup truck, with sunglasses painted on.
"HOLD ON, LANA!" the kid yells. You grab her neck. Lana floats you. She floats you so well your head is dry. The sun comes out. You feel hope come back into your whole body.
You ride Lana like a parade float all the way back to the sandbar. People cheer. You wave. Lana smiles her painted smile. She floated you, and she gave you hope. Hold on, Lana.

words.say_it: Clap twice and chant. "Pai-PAI!"
words.picture: Crowd chanting pie at a kid on a bike
story_paragraphs: Your little cousin Keoni is learning to ride a bike on a hill in Mānoa. He is scared. He wobbles. He stops. He wants to quit.
So the whole family lines the street. Forty people. Grandpa, the aunties, the neighbors, a guy delivering mail. And at the bottom of the hill, Tūtū holds up a coconut cream pie as big as a car tire.
"PIE! PIE! PIE! PIE!" everybody chants, clapping. Keoni pushes off. He wobbles. "PIE! PIE!" He pedals harder. "PIE! PIE! PIE!" The mailman is jumping. The dog is barking in rhythm.
Keoni rolls all the way down and crashes face first into the pie. He comes up covered in cream, grinning. That is what encouragement looks like. A whole street yelling "Pie, pie!" until you go.

words.say_it: Copy someone's move and add a long sigh. "Ho-oh-haah-LEE-keh."
words.bonus: Like means alike or the same. Hoʻohālike is to make yourself like something else, to copy it. The long ā is that big sigh.
words.picture: Mynah bird copying your every move
story_paragraphs: A mynah bird moves onto your lanai and starts copying you. Everything.

You yawn. It yawns. You scratch your ʻōkole. It scratches its tail feathers. You sneeze, and it does a perfect fake sneeze. You say "Ho, oh," and it says "Ho, oh." You sigh a big long "HAAAH," and it sighs "HAAAH."
By Tuesday it is wearing tiny slippers. By Friday it has learned to walk like you, a little bowlegged, with a musubi in one claw.
Your friend comes over and looks back and forth between you and the bird. "Ho, oh, haaah... like eh! Alike!" You two are exactly alike. The bird imitates the shocked look on your face.
It even answers your phone now. Your aunty cannot tell the difference.

words.say_it: Hold your hands out like a scale, up and down. "Ho-oh-haah-lee-keh-LEE-keh."
words.bonus: Hoʻohālike can mean to copy or to compare. Doubled, hoʻohālikelike is a comparison, holding two things side by side to see how alike they are.
words.picture: Aunty judging two identical giant pumpkins
story_paragraphs: County fair, the giant pumpkin contest. Two farmers wheel in two orange monsters, each one the size of a small car. They look exactly the same.
The judge is a tiny old aunty with a clipboard and a measuring tape. She walks around pumpkin one. She walks around pumpkin two. She holds her hands up like a scale, one hand for each.
"Haaah... like-eh... like-eh?" she mutters. Are they alike? She measures the stems. She knocks on each one like a door. She sniffs them. She lies down on the grass and compares the bottoms.
The crowd waits two hours. The mynah from hoʻohālike lands on top of pumpkin one and copies her.
Finally she finds it. Pumpkin two has one extra freckle. She holds up the blue ribbon. "Compared!" The crowd goes wild.

words.say_it: Hold out an open hand to everyone. "Kah-AH-nah."
words.bonus: Kaʻana like means to share equally, everyone getting the same.
words.picture: Tūtū cutting 80 malasadas for everyone
story_paragraphs: Your little brother gets a box of 80 malasadas for his birthday. He hugs the box like a baby. His cheeks are already full of sugar.
Your cousin walks up. "Can I ka..." Before he even finishes, your brother goes "AH! NAH!"
Another cousin. "Ka...?" "AH! NAH!" The dog walks over. "AH! NAH!" A neighbor, the mailman, a pigeon. "AH! NAH! AH! NAH!"

Then Tūtū steps out of the kitchen. She is holding a bread knife the size of a canoe paddle. She takes the box, cuts every malasada into four, and walks around the yard handing out pieces to all 26 people and the dog. There is just enough for everyone.
Your brother stares. Tūtū hands him the last piece. "That," she says, "is how we share."

words.say_it: Pretend to hand something over and grab something back. "Koo-AH-po."
words.bonus: Kuapo works for any trade, like swapping seats, swapping shifts, or swapping lunches.
words.picture: Pigeon in a visor running swap trades
story_paragraphs: There is a pigeon who runs a booth at the swap meet. Nobody knows how he got the spot. He wears a tiny visor and keeps his cash in a fanny pack.
You bring a broken toaster. The pigeon looks at it. "COO!" Then he slaps down a surfboard. "AH... POH!" That is how he seals a deal, with a little pop of his beak. Swap done.
You swap the surfboard for a ʻukulele. "COO! AH... POH!" The ʻukulele for a rice cooker. "COO! AH... POH!" The rice cooker for a lawnmower, the lawnmower for a goat, the goat for a canoe.
By noon you have traded your way up from one broken toaster to a used ice cream truck. The pigeon pats you on the shoulder with one wing. "Coo, ah, poh." Pleasure doing business.

words.english: to owe, to be in debt
words.say_it: Scratch the back of your head, nervous. "Ai-EH." Stretch that last eh.
words.bonus: Don't mix it up with ʻai, to eat. The long ē at the end is the groan of someone who owes.
words.picture: Cousin unrolling a giant debt scroll
story_paragraphs: In third grade you borrowed $5 from your cousin Makana to buy shave ice. You forgot about it. Makana did not.

Every birthday since then, he shows up with a bill. With interest it keeps growing. At age 15 you owe him $80. At age 25 you owe him $900. Now you are 40 and he hands you a scroll that rolls out across the whole yard and into the street. It says $4,312.50.
Everyone at the party turns to look at you. You open your mouth, you catch your breath, and all that comes out is "I... ehhhhh..."
That is the sound of owing money. Makana nods. "I, eh. Yeah. You ʻaiʻē me."
You pay him back with a shave ice. He sighs and accepts. The interest keeps going.

words.say_it: Put something on an imaginary shelf behind you. "Kaah-PAI." Hold the kaah long.
words.bonus: Kāpae is also used for putting a plan on hold or setting an idea aside for later.
words.picture: Pie buckled into the front seat
story_paragraphs: Thanksgiving at Aunty Noelani's. There are 30 pies on the table. Apple, pumpkin, sweet potato haupia, chocolate, you name it.

But Aunty is smart. Before anybody arrives, she takes the best one, the sweet potato haupia with the extra thick crust, and walks it out to her car. She buckles it into the front seat with a seatbelt.
"That one," she says, "is the CAAAR PIE." Set aside. Nobody touches the car pie.

All night 60 relatives destroy the other 29 pies. Crumbs everywhere. A cousin licks a pie tin. When the last guest leaves, Aunty walks out to the car in her slippers, opens the door, and eats the car pie alone in the dark, with the radio on.

words.say_it: Scoop up an armful, then throw it forward. "Ho-oh-OO-kah!"
words.bonus: Hoʻouka kaua means to attack, to start a battle. On a computer, hoʻouka is to load or upload, and hoʻoili, next, is to download.
words.picture: Kid on a tailgate yelling oo-kah
story_paragraphs: Summer water balloon war on your street. Your side is the kids from the even numbered houses.

Step one, you load. You fill 600 water balloons and pile them into Grandpa's old pickup. Each time a bucket goes in, your captain, a six year old named Bula, yells like a caveman, "HO! OH! OO-KAH!" Load it! Another bucket. "OO-KAH!" The truck sags down to the tires.
Step two, you attack. Grandpa drives slowly down the street at 3 miles an hour. Bula stands on the tailgate and screams "HO! OH! OO-KAH!" and all 12 kids throw at once.
The odd numbered houses never had a chance. One kid gets hit so many times he just lies down on the lawn like a starfish. You load up again. Attack again. Load. Attack. OO-KAH!

words.english: to transfer, to hand over; to pass down
words.say_it: Pass an imaginary slimy thing to the person next to you. "Ho-oh-EE-lee."
words.bonus: Hoʻoili is moving something from one holder to another, like cargo set on shore, money moved between bank accounts, a football handed off, or a family treasure passed down in a will. On a computer it means to download.
words.picture: Grandpa handing over eels, then his old trap
story_paragraphs: Grandpa's fishing boat pulls into the harbor riding low in the water. It is full of eels. Hundreds. Slimy, grumpy, snapping eels.

Time to transfer them to the dock. Grandpa stands in the boat and hands the eels over to you one at a time. "Ho, oh, EEL-EE!" Every time, one slips out of your hands. It slides down your shirt. It goes up your shorts. You dance around the dock like you're on fire. "EEL-EE!"
Three hours later the boat is empty. Grandpa climbs out, wipes his hands, and gives you his old eel trap. It is made of wood and wire and it smells like 60 years of the ocean.
"This was my father's," he says. "Now it is yours." He is passing it down. You hold it like gold, even though it stinks. Hand over the eels, pass down the trap. Ho, oh, eel-ee.

words.say_it: Point forward like you're leading a line. "Ah-lah-KAH-ee."
words.bonus: Alakaʻi is also a noun, a leader or guide. Older dictionaries explain it as ala, road or path, plus kaʻi, to lead, so it is the one who leads you along the path.
words.picture: Mother hen leading 60 chicks across highway
story_paragraphs: A mother hen decides it is time. She has 60 chicks and she needs to get them across Kalanianaʻole Highway to the other side, where somebody dropped a whole bag of rice.
She steps into the road. She does not look left or right. She just leads. Sixty fluffy chicks follow in one perfect line behind her, like a train.
A traffic guy in an orange vest sees them and throws up both hands. "ALL A' CAR... STOP!" Brakes squeal. "EEEEE!" Every car stops. A bus stops. A cement truck stops.

The hen marches the whole line across, slow and proud. At the end, one chick gets lost and runs in a circle. She turns, clucks once, and guides it back into line. The traffic guy wipes a tear. "All a' car... eee," he whispers.

words.say_it: March in place with your knees high. "KAH-ee!" Hiccup in the middle.
words.bonus: Kaʻi is not the same as kai, the sea. The ʻokina splits it into two beats, KAH-ee. Callback to alakaʻi, which is leading in general.
words.picture: Toddler with baton leading a parade
story_paragraphs: It is the big parade down Kalākaua Avenue. Pāʻū riders on horses, a marching band, 12 floats covered in flowers. And who leads the whole thing? A three year old boy with a baton.
He marches in front, knees up high, very serious. The whole procession follows him. Every time he lifts the baton, the band plays. Every time he stops, 400 people behind him stop.

Then he gets the hiccups. "KAH! (hic) EE!" He turns left. The whole parade turns left, down a side street. "KAH! (hic) EE!" He turns into a parking lot. The horses follow. The band follows. The floats squeeze in.
He leads them through the drive-thru of a burger stand and out the other side. Nobody questions it. He is the leader of the procession. When he stops for a juice box, everybody waits.

words.say_it: Grip an invisible paddle and lean. "Ho-oh-KEH-leh."
words.bonus: Hoʻokele also means a navigator or helmsman, the person who steers, like the navigators of voyaging canoes.
words.picture: Tiny tutu steering canoe with a musubi
story_paragraphs: You are on a voyaging canoe in the middle of the Pacific. It is night. The wind is howling. Waves the size of houses.
At the back, holding the big steering paddle, is Tūtū Kelly. She is 91. She weighs about as much as a bag of rice. She has one hand on the paddle and a spam musubi in the other.
A wave hits. The canoe tips. The whole crew screams "HOLD 'ER, KELLY!" She leans on the paddle and the canoe swings straight. Another wave. "HOLD 'ER, KELLY!" She doesn't even put down the musubi.
She looks up at the stars, points at one, and turns the canoe a little to the right. No map. No phone. Just stars. At sunrise, land appears exactly where she said it would. She finishes her musubi.

words.say_it: Grip an invisible steering wheel and turn. "Kah-LAI-vah."
words.bonus: Kalaiwa came from the English word driver, sounded out the Hawaiian way. It can also mean the driver.
words.picture: Station wagon coming alive and driving
story_paragraphs: You are sitting in the driver's seat of Uncle's old station wagon in the driveway. The keys are not even in it. You are just pretending to drive, making engine noises.
Then the car coughs. The headlights blink like eyes. The steering wheel turns by itself.
"CAR! ALIVE! AH!" you scream.

The car backs out of the driveway and takes off down the street. It drives. It drives really well. It signals. It lets a grandma cross. It merges onto the H-1 like a pro. You are just holding the wheel with your eyes wide open while it drives you to the beach, to the drive-in, to Ala Moana, and back home.
It parks perfectly. The headlights wink at you. Uncle comes out. "You drove?" You nod. You did not drive. The car did.

words.say_it: Slide your hand flat across the table and stop. "PAI."
words.bonus: Pae ʻāina means a group of islands. Ka pae ʻāina o Hawaiʻi is the Hawaiian island chain.
words.picture: Pa sliding up the beach on his belly
story_paragraphs: Pa has been bodysurfing at Makapuʻu all afternoon. He catches one last wave. It is the biggest one of the day, a monster, 15 feet of white water.

He rides it in like a torpedo, arms out in front, cheeks puffed. The wave carries him, and carries him, and does not stop at the sand. It shoots him right up the beach, past the towels, past the coolers, past the lifeguard tower.
The whole family watches him slide by on his belly. "PA! EH!" everybody yells.

He finally comes to a stop in the parking lot, right next to the car, still in his bodysurfing pose. Sand in his hair. Seaweed on his ear. He stands up, bows, and says "Landed." Pa, eh. He came ashore all right.

words.say_it: Grab an invisible rope and pull hard. "Kow-OH!" Hold that long ō.
words.bonus: Kauō is for heavy hauling, the kind of pulling where your feet dig in.
words.picture: Truck dragging a lazy cow off the road
story_paragraphs: There is a cow lying in the middle of the only road to your house. She is 2,000 pounds and she refuses to move. She is chewing slowly and looking at you like you are the problem.
You get a rope. You loop it around her. You pull. "COW! OHHH!" Nothing. You get your brother. You both pull. "COW! OHHH!" She moves one inch and burps.

You get Uncle's truck. You tie the rope to the hitch. The truck strains. Smoke comes off the tires. Slowly, slowly, you drag her across the road. She does not stand up. She just slides on her side like a giant furry sled, still chewing, never once looking worried.
Twenty minutes later she is in the grass. You untie the rope. She stands up by herself and walks right back into the road.

words.say_it: Tug an invisible kite string up into the sky. "Ho-oh-LEH-leh."
words.bonus: Lele means to fly or jump. ʻUkulele is often said to mean jumping flea, from ʻuku, flea, and lele, to jump.
words.picture: ʻUkulele flying like a kite and playing
story_paragraphs: Windy day at Kapiʻolani Park. Everybody is flying kites. You forgot your kite. All you have is Grandpa's old ʻukulele.
So you tie fishing line to the neck. You run. "HO! OH!" The wind grabs it. Up it goes. "UKU... LELE!"

The ʻukulele flies higher than all the kites. Fifty feet. A hundred feet. The wind blows across the strings and it starts playing music by itself, a sweet little song floating over the whole park. People stop their picnics. A dog howls along. A kid drops his plate lunch.
Grandpa walks up, looks way up at his ʻukulele in the sky, and just nods. "Good launch." You let out more line. The ʻukulele plays louder. By sunset there are 20 more ʻukuleles flying next to it.

words.english: to beat, to strike; to kill
words.say_it: Whack the table twice with an open hand and squeal. "Peh-PEH-hee."
words.bonus: Pepehi is a strong word. It can mean to beat or to kill, so save it for cockroaches and not your brother.
words.picture: Aunty killing a flying cockroach with slipper
story_paragraphs: It is 11 at night. Aunty is watching her show. Then she sees it. A flying cockroach, as big as a matchbox car, sitting on the wall above the TV. Its antennas are waving at her like it owns the place.
Aunty takes off one slipper. Slowly. She stands. The whole house holds its breath.
The roach takes off and flies straight at her face. Aunty swings. "PEH!" Miss. It lands on the lampshade. "PEH!" Direct hit. The roach drops to the carpet like a rock.
Aunty lets out a high little victory squeal. "HEEEE!"
She puts her slipper back on, sits down, and turns her show back up. Two strikes and it's over. Peh, peh, hee.

words.say_it: Flick your fingers out like you're squirting water. "Pah-KEE!" Short pah, long kee.
words.bonus: Watch the marks. Pakī, with a short a, is to splash or squirt. Pākī, with a long ā, means to smash or crush.
words.picture: Sea cucumbers squirting you in tide pool
story_paragraphs: You are tide pooling at low tide, barefoot, stepping from rock to rock. You step on something soft. It is a sea cucumber, fat and brown and as long as your arm.
It does not like that. "PAH!" It squirts a jet of water straight up your leg, into your shorts, and across your face. You shriek "KEE!"

You jump back and land on another sea cucumber. "PAH!" Squirt. "KEE!" And another. The whole tide pool is full of them. Every step is a squirt. PAH, KEE. PAH, KEE. You splash around like you are dancing on a trampoline made of water guns.
Your friends on the beach are laughing so hard they cannot breathe. You crawl out soaked from hair to toenails. Somewhere behind you, one last sea cucumber goes "pah" just to be mean.

words.say_it: Throw both arms up like you're at a party. "Ho-oh-lau-LEH-ah!"
words.bonus: A hoʻolauleʻa is also a big street party or festival, like the block parties in Waikīkī. Leʻa means joy.
words.picture: 100-year-old tūtū dancing on a table
story_paragraphs: Great-grandma Tūtū Lani turns 100. The whole family rents the park. Five hundred people. Twelve imu pigs. A band with three ʻukuleles, two guitars, and one very old trumpet.
The party is so loud the plates rattle on the tables. Car alarms go off down the block. Birds leave the trees and do not come back until Tuesday.
At 9 p.m. Tūtū Lani climbs up onto the picnic table with her walker. Somebody hands her the microphone. She raises one fist and shouts "HO, OH, LOUD, LAY-AH!" The crowd roars back "LOUD, LAY-AH!"
She dances hula on the table for 20 minutes. Nobody can stop her. The trumpet player passes out from happiness. That is how you celebrate. Loud, all night, and grandma on the table.

words.say_it: Tap your forehead and then light up. "Ho-oh-nah-ow-AH-oh."
words.bonus: Naʻauao means learned or wise. Naʻau is the gut and ao is daylight, so learning puts light inside you.
words.picture: Octopus teacher with eight pieces of chalk
story_paragraphs: Night school in a portable classroom. The teacher is an octopus. She holds eight pieces of chalk in eight arms and writes on eight chalkboards at the same time. Math, history, science, Hawaiian, all at once.
You are trying to keep up. The octopus taps her board with one arm and says "Now!" Then she taps your head with another arm. "OW!" Then she writes the answer.
You stare at it. Something clicks. "AHHH... OH!"
That is the sound of learning. Now, ow, ahh, oh. All night long the room is full of it. Forty students getting bonked and understanding. "Now... OW... AHHH, OH!"
At graduation the octopus hands out 40 diplomas at the same time, eight at a time, and every student yells "AHH, OH!" together. She educated all of you.

words.say_it: Wag your finger slowly, like giving advice. "Ah-oh-AH-oh."
words.bonus: Aʻo means to teach or learn. Doubled, aʻoaʻo is to give advice, and it can also mean the advice itself.
words.picture: Parrot on shoulder warning ah-oh
story_paragraphs: You have a small green parrot who lives on your shoulder. His whole job is to give you advice. He has only one piece of advice, and he says it every time you are about to do something dumb.
You reach for the fourth plate of kālua pig. "AH-OH! AH-OH!" You think about texting your ex at 2 a.m. "AH-OH! AH-OH!" You try to fix the toilet yourself with a butter knife. "AH-OH! AH-OH! AH-OH!"
At first you ignore him. The toilet floods the bathroom. The kālua pig gives you a stomachache for two days.

So now you listen. Before any big choice, you look at the parrot. If he stays quiet, you go. If he says "Ah-oh, ah-oh," you sit down and think. Best counselor you ever had, and he works for sunflower seeds.

words.english: to talk it over, to consult
words.say_it: Lean your head toward a friend, like discussing a plan. "Koo-KAAH."
words.bonus: Kūkākūkā means to discuss or hold a meeting. You will hear it for any sit-down talk story about a problem.
words.picture: Dove and crow discussing your car engine
story_paragraphs: Your car will not start. You open the hood and stare at the engine like it is a puzzle in another language.

Up on the power line, two birds are watching. A dove and a big black crow. The dove leans over. "Coo?" The crow thinks. "KAAAH." The dove shakes her head. "Coo, coo." The crow points a wing at the battery. "KAAAH."
They talk it over for two hours. They argue. They draw diagrams in the dirt with their feet. Other birds come by to listen. A mynah gives an opinion and gets ignored.

Finally the dove and the crow shake wings. They fly down, land on your engine, and the crow tightens a loose wire with his beak. You turn the key. VROOM. Coo, kaaah. They consulted, they decided, and they did not even send you a bill.

words.say_it: Hold a fist up to someone's mouth like a microphone. "Nee-now-EH-leh." Hold the nee long.
words.bonus: Nīnau means to ask a question. A nīnauele is an interview, a lot of questions in a row.
words.picture: Reporter interviewing a kneeling elephant
story_paragraphs: A TV reporter shows up at the zoo to interview Ellie the elephant. Ellie is famous. She paints pictures with her trunk.

Problem. The reporter is five feet tall. Ellie is eleven feet tall. He holds the microphone up as high as he can and asks, "Ellie, what inspires you?" Ellie cannot hear him. She is looking at a banana.
He jumps. He stands on a bucket. Nothing. Finally he yells, long and loud, "KNEEEEE, NOW, ELLIE!"

Ellie folds her front legs and kneels down. Now her giant ear is right next to his microphone. He asks his questions. She answers with a trunk toot for yes and two toots for no. It is the best interview of the year. They run it on the six o'clock news. Knee, now, Ellie.

words.say_it: Carry an invisible hot plate with both hands. "Lah-veh-LAH-veh."
words.bonus: Lawe means to take or carry. Lawelawe is to serve, and also to handle or take care of things, like handling your business.
words.picture: Waiter running plates from a lava flow
story_paragraphs: You get a job as a waiter at the world's hottest restaurant. It is built right on the edge of a lava flow on the Big Island. The cook does not have a stove. He just holds a pan over the lava.
When an order is ready, he rings the bell and yells "LAVA! LAVA!" That means serve it now, before it melts the plate.
You run out with a sizzling steak in fireproof gloves. "LAVA! LAVA!" Another order. You juggle four plates of glowing hot garlic shrimp. Your eyebrows are gone by 7 p.m. Your shoes are smoking by 8.

But you serve 300 people and handle every table like a pro. Nobody waits. Nobody gets cold food. How could they? At closing time the cook pats your back and slides you a lava dessert. "Lava, lava," you say. You served it.

words.english: to catch, to grasp; to embrace
words.say_it: Snap your hand shut like catching a ball, then hug yourself. "AH-po."
words.bonus: ʻApo means to catch and also to embrace. Watch for ʻaʻapo later in the list (#396), which is to catch on fast, to learn quick.
words.picture: Catching a sky-high softball, then hugged
story_paragraphs: Family softball game at the park. The batter is Uncle Tiny, who is not tiny. He swings, and the ball goes UP. Way up. Higher than the coconut trees. Out of sight.
Everybody looks at you. You are playing catcher. You swallow hard, a little catch in your throat. "UP... OH!"
You wait. Ten seconds. Twenty. A plane goes by. Then the ball comes screaming down like a meteor. You put out your glove. SMACK. You catch it. The ball is smoking.

The whole park goes crazy. Uncle Tiny runs over. He is not mad. He picks you up in a giant embrace and spins you around three times. First you caught the ball. Then he caught you. Up, oh, twice in one day.

words.say_it: Wrap your arms around yourself and squeeze. "Poo-LEE-kee." Stretch the poo.
words.bonus: Pūliki is the hug. ʻApo can also mean to embrace, but pūliki is the everyday word for a squeeze.
words.picture: Tūtū hugging so hard everything leaks
story_paragraphs: You land at the airport after two years away. Tūtū is waiting at the gate. She is five feet tall and four feet wide, and she has been waiting for this hug since 2 a.m.
She grabs you. She squeezes. Your ribs creak. Your juice box, still in your hand, bursts and squirts across the floor.

"POOOO..." you wheeze, all the air leaving you in one long sound. Then your eyes start leaking. Then Tūtū's eyes start leaking. Then the shave ice in your little cousin's hand starts leaking down his arm. "LEAKY!"

She holds the hug for eleven minutes. A security guard walks by and starts crying too. A family from the next flight joins in. When she lets go, everybody is damp and happy. Poo, leaky. Best hug of your life.

words.say_it: Draw a big circle around yourself with your finger. "Ho-oh-POO-nee."
words.bonus: Puni means surrounded, and also to be fond of something. Hoʻopuni is to make a circle around.
words.picture: Hundreds of ponies circling you
story_paragraphs: You go out to feed your one pony on the farm in Waimea. You open the gate with one bucket of oats.
You hear hooves. Then more hooves. Then thunder. Over the hill come three hundred ponies. Brown ones, white ones, spotted ones, one wearing a hat. You have no idea where they came from.
"Ho, oh... PONY!" you whisper.

They form a circle around you. Then another circle around that one. Then another. You are surrounded, ten ponies deep in every direction. You can't see the fence. You can't see your truck. All you see is pony faces staring down at your one bucket of oats.
You hold it up. "Ho, oh, pony," you say again, very politely. Three hundred ponies lean in at once. You are going to need more oats.

words.say_it: Rub slow circles on your arm like lotion. "Kaah-HEE-noo."
words.bonus: Hinu means oily, greasy, or shiny. Kāhinu is to rub that oil on.
words.picture: Uncle rubbing coconut oil on rusty truck
story_paragraphs: Uncle Walter has a 1978 pickup truck that is more rust than truck. One day he decides to fix it up. Not with paint. With oil.

He buys five gallons of coconut oil. He rubs it on the hood with his bare hands, slow circles, like he is waxing a surfboard. He rubs the doors, the tires, the bumper. He rubs oil into the steering wheel. The whole street smells like a suntan.
By sunset the truck shines like a mirror. The neighbors gather. "Kaaah!" one says. "HE... NEW!"

Then Uncle gets in, starts it, and the truck slides right down the driveway on its own oily tires, into the street, and parks itself sideways against the mailbox. Uncle climbs out, grinning, and rubs a little more oil on the dent.

words.say_it: Swipe your hand back and forth like spreading butter. "HAH-mo."
words.bonus: Kāhinu is rubbing with oil. Hamo is any smear or spread, like glaze, butter, lotion, or paint.
words.picture: Uncle paint-rolling glaze on a huge ham
story_paragraphs: Christmas Eve. Uncle is in charge of the ham. It is the size of a canoe. He needs to smear pineapple glaze all over it, and he does not own a brush big enough.
So he uses a paint roller.

He dips the roller in a bucket of glaze and rolls it across the ham. "HAM!" Another roll. "OH!" The glaze drips on the floor. He rolls faster. "HAM! OH! HAM! OH!" Glaze on the counter. Glaze on the fridge. He slips and smears a stripe across the dog.

By the time dinner starts, the ham is perfect and shiny. So is the kitchen. So is the dog, who is sticky and very proud of it. Uncle is glazed from his elbows to his eyebrows. "Ham, oh," he says, and licks a finger.

words.say_it: Hunch forward like you're carrying a heavy backpack. "Haah-AH-veh."
words.bonus: Hāʻawe is carrying on the back. Next, ʻauamo is carrying with a pole across the shoulder.
words.picture: Tiny ant carrying spam musubi on back
story_paragraphs: Family picnic at the beach. A tiny ant finds a spam musubi that fell in the sand. The musubi is about 500 times bigger than the ant.
The ant does not care. She crawls under it, braces her six legs, and lifts the whole thing onto her back. "HAAAH..." she grunts in a tiny voice. Then she starts walking. "AWAY!"

She carries it on her back across the sand. Up and over a slipper. Around a bucket. Through a forest of beach umbrella poles. Kids stop to watch. A crab offers to help and she waves him off with one leg.
It takes her four hours. At the ant hole, 200 cheering ants help her set it down. The musubi feeds the whole colony for a year. She carried it on her back the whole way. Haaah, away.

words.english: to carry on the shoulder with a pole
words.say_it: Put a broom across your shoulders and bounce. "Ow-AH-mo."
words.bonus: ʻAuamo is carrying with a pole on the shoulder. Hāʻawe is carrying on your back. ʻAuamo can also mean a responsibility you carry.
words.picture: Uncle carrying watermelons on a bamboo pole
story_paragraphs: The kids want to take the watermelons from the farm stand down to the beach party. Uncle Sol grabs a long bamboo pole and sets it across his shoulders. A net hangs on each end.
A cousin drops a watermelon in the left net. "OW!" says Uncle. Another in the right. "OW!" Then he smiles. "Ah... mo'?" More?
So they give him more. Two more. "OW! Ah, mo'?" Four more. The pole bends into a big smile shape. Eight watermelons. Twelve. A cousin climbs in one net for a ride. A dog jumps in the other.

Uncle walks the whole mile to the beach, pole on his shoulder, bouncing with every step, saying "Ow... ah, mo'?" the whole way. When he sets it down, he stands up straight and asks if anybody needs anything else carried.

words.english: to hold a child in the arms
words.say_it: Cradle an invisible baby and rock it. "HEE-ee." Little hiccup in the middle.
words.bonus: Hiʻi is holding a child in the arms. A related word, hiʻialo, means a beloved one, a child held close.
words.picture: Baby passed arm to arm at lūʻau
story_paragraphs: Baby Kaiʻa is turning one. The first birthday lūʻau is huge. Four hundred guests. And every single one wants to hold the baby.

Aunty holds her first, rocking her in her arms. Baby squeals "HEE! (hic) EE!" Then Uncle. "HEE! (hic) EE!" Then Grandpa, then the neighbors, then the band leader. She gets passed down the line like the most precious package in the world.
Every person cradles her the same way, one arm under, one arm around, careful as if she is made of glass. And every time, she giggles that same little hiccup giggle. "Hee! (hic) Ee!"
At midnight she finally comes back to her mom, who holds her in her arms and sways. Baby is asleep. Four hundred people whisper "hee, ee" at the same time, very softly.

words.say_it: Pump your fist once. "Koo-LEH-ah!"
words.bonus: Kū means to stand and leʻa means joy. Kūleʻa is used for any success, like passing a test or finishing a big job.
words.picture: Forty layer cake finally standing
story_paragraphs: You decide to make a 40 layer cake for Aunty's retirement party. Nobody has ever done it. You watched one video.
Try one. You get to layer 12 and the cake leans like a drunk palm tree and falls on the floor. Try two. Layer 20, the cat jumps on it. Try three. Layer 31, an earthquake. Not a big one, just enough.
You try 39 times. The kitchen is a disaster. There is frosting on the ceiling fan.
On try 40, you stack the last layer. It holds. The cake is as tall as you. It does not lean. It does not wobble. Your whole family is holding their breath.
Your little brother says it first, quietly. "Cool... layer." Then everyone screams it. "COOL! LAYER!" You succeeded. You eat a piece off the top with a ladder.

words.english: to move forward, to make progress
words.say_it: Take one step forward and kiss the air. "Ho-lo-MOO-ah."
words.bonus: Holo means to run or sail, and mua means forward or in front. E holomua means go forward, keep making progress.
words.picture: Walking through a line of kissing aunties
story_paragraphs: Family reunion. The food table is at the far end of the yard. Between you and the food are 45 aunties. They are standing in a line like a gauntlet.
You take one step forward. The first aunty grabs your face. "HELLO! MWAH!" Big kiss on the cheek. One step. "HELLO! MWAH!" Another aunty. Lipstick on the other cheek.

You keep moving forward. Slowly. Every step is a hello and a mwah. Aunty number 20 pinches your cheek. Aunty number 31 asks when you're getting married. Aunty number 38 kisses you twice to make up for last year.

It takes you two hours to cross the yard. Your face is covered in lipstick. But you keep going. Inch by inch. Hello, mwah. You make progress. Finally you reach the food table and there is exactly one scoop of mac salad left.

words.english: to track, to follow a trail
words.say_it: Bend down and follow an invisible trail with your finger. "Ho-oh-KO-lo."
words.bonus: Kolo means to creep or crawl, like a gecko on the trail. Hoʻokolo is to follow along after something.
words.picture: Gecko detective tracking cola drips
story_paragraphs: Somebody stole the last can of cola from the fridge. Grandpa is furious. It was his.
So he hires a detective. The detective is a gecko named Sly, wearing a tiny trench coat. Sly sniffs the fridge. He finds a drop of cola on the floor. "Ho, oh... COLA."

He follows it. Another drop by the door. "Cola." Another on the steps. A sticky print on the garage. A drip on the lawn. He follows the trail through the neighbor's yard, under a fence, over a wall, up the mango tree.

At the top, sitting on a branch, is the neighbor's cat with the empty can and a guilty burp. "Ho, oh, cola," says Sly, and snaps his little notebook shut. He tracked it all the way. Grandpa pays him in fruit flies.

words.say_it: Straighten your back and smooth your shirt. "Ho-oh-po-lo-LAY."
words.bonus: Pololei means straight or correct. You will hear "Pololei!" for "That's right!"
words.picture: Aunty ironing a polo and your posture
story_paragraphs: Aunty Marlene is the queen of straight. She cannot stand anything crooked.
Your polo shirt is wrinkled. She takes it right off you, lays it on the ironing board, and yells "HO, OH, POLO, LAY!" She irons it so flat and straight you could cut paper with the collar.

Then she looks at you. You are slouching. "Polo, lay!" She lays you on the ironing board too. Not with the iron, don't worry. She just pulls your shoulders back and presses your spine against the board until you are straight as a surfboard.

Then she hears you talk. "Me and him went..." she says "He and I went." She corrects your grammar. She straightens the pictures on the wall. She straightens the dog's ears. By the time you leave, even your car is parked straighter.

words.english: to trim, to cut (hair), to pluck
words.say_it: Snip your fingers like scissors, with a stop-sneeze. "AH-ko."
words.bonus: You can ʻako hair, a hedge, or flowers for a lei. It is any kind of trimming or plucking.
words.picture: Sneezing barber trimming chunks of hair
story_paragraphs: You go to a new barber. He has the worst allergies on the island. His eyes are red. His nose is running. He picks up the scissors.

He leans in. "Ahhh..." Snip. "...KO!" The sneeze stops in his throat halfway, with a hard little catch, and his hand jerks. A chunk of hair is gone. "Ahhh... KO!" Another chunk. "AHHH... KO!" Snip snip.
He trims your eyebrows by accident. He plucks one hair out of your ear with a sneeze. Behind you, the hedge outside the window is somehow trimmed too.
Twenty minutes later you look in the mirror. You look like a pineapple. But he did cut and trim everything. The barber blows his nose, holds out his hand, and says, "That will be $12."

words.say_it: Pretend to tie a big knot and yank it tight. "Nah-kee-NAH-kee."
words.bonus: Nakinaki works for any tying or binding, from shoelaces to a boat at the dock.
words.picture: Retired sailor uncle tying up everything
story_paragraphs: Your Uncle Rex was a sailor for 40 years. Now he is retired and he cannot stop tying things.

You wake up and your shoes are tied to your slippers. The dog is tied to the mango tree. The mango tree is tied to the fence. Uncle walks through the house with a big coil of rope, humming to himself, "Knotty, knotty. Knotty, KNOTTY."
He ties the car to the house. He ties the rice cooker lid shut. He ties the TV remote to the couch so nobody loses it. He ties a bow on the cat.

By dinner the whole house is one giant web of rope and knots. You have to crawl under the lines to get to the table. Uncle sits down, very happy, and ties his napkin around his neck with a sailor's knot you will never get off.

words.say_it: Drape an invisible lei over someone's neck. "MAH-leh."
words.bonus: Male comes from the English word marry, sounded the Hawaiian way. Don't read it like the English word male.
words.picture: Groom buried in 200 leis
story_paragraphs: It is your wedding day on the beach. You are standing under the arch. The minister is ready. Your future spouse is walking down the sand.

Then Ma steps up. "Ma! LEI!" somebody yells, and she puts a lei on you. Then another. Then another. Ma brought a whole shopping bag. Pīkake, tuberose, orchid, maile, candy lei, money lei, a lei made of spam musubi.
By the time the minister says "Do you take," there are 200 leis around your neck. They go up past your nose. He can't find your face. "Ma! LEI!" people keep shouting as she adds more.
You say "I do" through a foot of flowers. You kiss your spouse through a maile lei. You are married. You smell amazing. Ma is crying and looking for more lei.

words.say_it: Drop down on one knee and hold up a ring. "Ho-oh-pah-LOW."
words.bonus: First comes hoʻopalau, getting engaged. Then comes male, getting married.
words.picture: Proposal kneeling so low he sinks
story_paragraphs: Your friend Kainoa is going to propose on the sand at sunset. He has the ring in his pocket. All his buddies are hiding behind a lifeguard tower.

He gets down on one knee. His buddies whisper, "Ho, oh, pal... LOW! Go low!" He wants it to be romantic, so he goes lower. The sand is soft. His knee sinks. "LOW!" He sinks to the thigh. "LOWER!" Now he is in the sand up to his belly button.
He holds up the ring with sand in his hair. "Will you marry me?"

His girlfriend looks down at him, at the ring, at the giant hole. "Yes!" she laughs. She takes the ring and pulls him out of the sand by both arms. They are engaged. The buddies jump out cheering, and one falls in the hole.

words.english: to come loose, to come off; to be divorced
words.say_it: Pull an invisible loose thread and watch it go. "HEH-mo."
words.bonus: Hemo is also used for being divorced, when two people come loose from each other. Next, hoʻohemo is taking something off on purpose.
words.picture: Aloha shirt unraveling from a door
story_paragraphs: You are at a fancy party at a hotel. You are wearing your best aloha shirt. You walk past a door and a thread from your hem catches on the doorknob.
You don't notice. You keep walking. The thread keeps coming. "HEM!" says a guy behind you, pointing. You turn around. "OH!"

Your shirt is unraveling. Slowly the bottom disappears. Then the pockets. Buttons pop loose one at a time, tink, tink, tink, rolling across the ballroom. The sleeves come off by themselves. The collar hangs on by one thread and then lets go too.
By the time you reach the buffet, you are standing in your undershirt with a long thread trailing all the way back to the door. Everything came loose. Everything came off. Hem, oh.

words.say_it: Pull hard on an invisible boot. "Ho-oh-HEH-mo!"
words.bonus: Hemo is coming off by itself. Hoʻohemo is you taking it off, like shoes, a lid, or a bandage.
words.picture: Family pulling off muddy boots
story_paragraphs: You spent all day working in the loʻi, planting kalo up to your knees in mud. Now your rubber boots are stuck to your legs. The mud is like glue. They won't come off.
Grandpa grabs one boot with both hands. He braces his foot on your butt. "HO! OH! HEAVE... OH!"
Nothing. You are sliding across the porch. Your cousin grabs Grandpa's waist. Your aunty grabs your cousin. "HO! OH! HEAVE... OH!"
SCHLOOP. The boot pops off with a sound like a giant kiss. Everybody flies backward into a pile. Mud sprays the whole house. There is a gecko in the boot. It looks surprised.
"One more," Grandpa says. "HO! OH! HEAVE... OH!" The second boot pops off, flies over the roof, and lands in the neighbor's yard. Both boots removed.

words.english: to mourn, to chant a lament
words.say_it: Put your hand over your heart and say it low and slow. "Kah-nee-KOW."
words.bonus: A real kanikau is a traditional Hawaiian chant of grief for a loved one who has died, often naming the places shared together. Kani means sound.
words.picture: Grandpa chanting goodbye to the old truck
story_paragraphs: Connie is the family truck. She is a 1983 pickup, faded blue, and she carried this family for 41 years. First day of school, every beach day, every trip to the hospital when a baby was born, every move, every funeral, every graduation.
One Sunday morning she will not start. The mechanic shakes his head. Connie is done.

The whole family gathers around her in the driveway. Grandpa takes off his hat. In a low, slow voice, he starts to chant a goodbye. He names every place she took them. Makapuʻu. Kaʻena Point. The old house in Kalihi. The hospital. The cemetery. Every line ends the same. "Connie... ciao."
By the end, everybody is crying, even the teenagers, even the mechanic. The kids pat her hood one last time. Connie, ciao. That is mourning. You name what you shared, and you say goodbye out loud.

words.say_it: Lift both hands gently, like singing in church. "Ho-oh-MAH-nah."
words.bonus: Hoʻomana also means religion. Inside it is the word mana, spiritual power.
words.picture: Little boy singing loud in church pew
story_paragraphs: Palm Sunday in a small wooden church up in the country. The windows are open. Chickens wander past the door. Tūtū has sat in the same pew for 62 years, and she sings louder than the organ.

Next to her is her great-grandson, four years old, in a tiny aloha shirt. He is trying very hard. The choir sings "Hosanna!" and he belts it out with his whole chest, but it comes out wrong. "HO... OH... MAH-NAH!"
The whole church hears it. People smile. The minister smiles. The kid does not care. He sings it again, even louder, arms up. "HO, OH, MAH-NAH!"
After the service Tūtū kneels down and fixes his collar. "You know what?" she says. "You said it right. Hoʻomana. That's what we do in here. We worship." He grins. He sings it all the way to the car.

words.say_it: Hold up your hand like a stop sign. "Ho-oh-KAH-poo."
words.bonus: Kapu means sacred or forbidden. Hoʻokapu is to make something kapu, and hoʻonoa, the next word, is to lift it.
words.picture: Cop knocking on a mannequin's head
story_paragraphs: It is 6 a.m. on the H-1 and traffic is not moving. You look over at the zipper lane. Empty. Beautiful. But it is only for carpools. Forbidden to drivers alone.
So you get an idea. You put a mannequin in your passenger seat. You give it sunglasses, a lei, and a straw hat. You slide into the zipper lane.

Two minutes later, lights flash behind you. The officer walks up, looks at your passenger, and taps the mannequin on the head. Knock knock. "HO! OH!" he says. "CAR POOL!" Meaning, this lane is for car pools. Kapu for solo drivers like you.
He writes you a ticket as long as your arm. The mannequin gets a warning. You drive the rest of the way in the slow lane, and the mannequin will not even look at you.

words.english: to lift a kapu, to make free
words.say_it: Snip an invisible rope and throw up your arms. "Ho-oh-NO-ah!"
words.bonus: Noa means free of kapu, open to everyone. Hoʻonoa is to make something noa again.
words.picture: Dad cutting the rope around new pool
story_paragraphs: Dad put in a brand new pool in the backyard. Then he said the scariest word. "No." The cement has to cure. Three weeks. Nobody goes in.
He puts a rope around it. He hangs a sign that says KAPU. Every day the kids stand at the rope and stare at the blue water like hungry dogs at a steak. Every day Dad says "No."
Twenty one days go by. On the morning of day 22, the whole family is lined up in swimsuits. Dad walks out with scissors. He cuts the rope. He takes down the sign.
"Ho, oh..." he says. "NO more no." Everybody screams "AHHH!" Nine people cannonball in at once. Water flies over the fence. The neighbor's cat gets wet. The rule is lifted. The pool is free.

words.say_it: Bow your head a little. "Ho-oh-poh-mai-KAH-ee."
words.bonus: Pōmaikaʻi by itself means blessed or fortunate. In Hawaiʻi many new homes and businesses get a blessing, often with a ti leaf and salt water.
words.picture: Everyone bowing at a food truck blessing
story_paragraphs: Your friend Kekoa just bought his first food truck. It is shiny and yellow and smells like garlic chicken. Before he sells one plate, he asks the kahu to come bless it.
Thirty people stand around the truck. The kahu dips a ti leaf in a bowl of salt water. Everyone goes quiet.

Except Kekoa's nephew, six years old, who is staring at a mynah on the roof. Kekoa leans over and whispers, "Ho, oh... BOW, my GUY!" The nephew drops his head. So does the dog. So does a delivery guy who was just walking by. Even the mynah looks down.
The kahu says a gentle prayer and sprinkles water on the truck, the grill, the cash box, and Kekoa. It feels like sunshine. That afternoon Kekoa sells 400 plates. Blessed.

words.say_it: Lift both hands up high like presenting something. "Moh-HAI." Hold that long ō.
words.bonus: Mōhai can also be a noun, an offering or a sacrifice.
words.picture: Boy lifting his treasure box up high
story_paragraphs: It is the keiki Christmas program at church. Each child walks up to the manger scene and gives an offering. Most bring a canned good or a dollar.

Then comes Kapono, five years old. He is carrying a shoebox with both hands like it holds the crown jewels. Inside is everything he owns that matters. His loose tooth in a baggie. His favorite smooth rock from the beach. A half eaten malasada. A photo of his dog.
He does not just set it down. He lifts it. Higher. "MOOO' HIGH!" he says, stretching his arms as far as they go, standing on his tiptoes. The whole church can see it.
He places it down very gently. The pastor wipes his eyes. Kapono gave his best, and he held it up high first so it would count. The malasada is gone by the end of the service, though.

words.say_it: Hold your hands out together, palms up, giving something. "Ho-oh-KOO-poo."
words.bonus: Kupu means to sprout or grow. One popular explanation is that a hoʻokupu is a gift that makes something grow, like respect between people.
words.picture: Little girl carrying ti leaf bundle slowly
story_paragraphs: A voyaging canoe is coming home after months at sea, and the whole community will gather at the beach to welcome it. Your little cousin Leilani, five years old, hears that everyone brings a hoʻokupu.
She thinks hard. "Can I give a... coupon?" she asks. She has one for a free shave ice. She is very proud of it.
Aunty laughs gently. "Not a coupon. A hoʻokupu. A gift from your heart, given with respect." She shows Leilani how to wrap a sweet potato in ti leaves and tie it with a string.

On the day of the ceremony, Leilani carries her little bundle with both hands. She walks down the beach so slowly and so carefully that it takes her ten minutes to go 200 feet. She sets it down and bows. The crew bows back. She never forgets that day. Her coupon is still in her pocket.

words.say_it: Pop your head up from behind your hands. "Oh-EE-lee!"
words.bonus: Don't mix ʻōʻili, to pop up, with hoʻoili, to transfer or pass down. The long ō at the start is the scream.
words.picture: Cousin popping out of the fridge
story_paragraphs: Your cousin Lee has a talent. He appears. Out of nowhere. Anywhere.

You open the fridge. Lee is sitting inside next to the mayonnaise. "OHHH! EEE! ...Lee." You close it fast. You open the mailbox. Lee pops up like a jack in the box. "OHHH! EEE! ...Lee." You pull back the shower curtain. Lee. You lift the lid of the rice cooker. Lee, holding a spoon.
Nobody knows how he does it. He shows up at your job interview behind the potted plant. He pops up at the bottom of the pool when you dive in, waving.

It happens so much that your scream is now just "OHHH, EEE, LEE." Long ō, gasp, and then the name. Last week you went on a plane to Kauaʻi. The overhead bin opened. You didn't even scream. "Oh, eee... Lee."

words.say_it: Hold up your forearm like a shield. "PAH-leh."
words.bonus: Palekana, built on pale, means safe or safety. Say PAH-leh, not like the English word pale.
words.picture: Aunty blocking chickens with canoe paddle
story_paragraphs: You sit down at the beach park with your plate lunch. Garlic chicken, two scoops rice, mac salad. Then you hear them. Chickens. Twenty wild chickens coming across the grass like a gang.
They surround the table. A rooster jumps on the bench. Your plate is in danger.

Then Aunty Nani stands up. She grabs her canoe paddle. She plants her feet. "PADDLE, EH!" she shouts, and swings it in a big circle over the table. The chickens scatter. The rooster comes back. "PADDLE, EH!" She holds the flat side up like a shield and blocks him in mid flight. He bonks off it and lands in a trash can.
For the next hour she guards your lunch like a warrior. Every chicken that comes near gets "Paddle, eh!" You finish every grain of rice.

words.english: to ring, to make a sound
words.say_it: Cup your hands around your mouth and ring it out. "KAH-nee!"
words.bonus: Kani is any sound, like a bell ringing, a phone ringing, or a rooster crowing.
words.picture: Tiny rooster crowing loud as a bell
story_paragraphs: The farm in Kula gets a new rooster. He is tiny. The size of a coffee mug. The other roosters laugh at him.
At dawn, all the animals gather. "Can he?" whispers a goat. "Can he even crow?" the cows ask each other. "CAN HE?"
The little rooster climbs onto the fence post. He puffs out his chest. He opens his beak. And the sound that comes out is enormous. "KAAAH-NEEEE!"

It rings like a church bell. It rings like a fire alarm. Forty car alarms go off in town. Windows buzz. The church bell down the road starts ringing by itself. People hear it all the way over on Lānaʻi.
The other roosters never laugh again. Every morning at 5:30 the tiny one rings out, and the whole island wakes up. Can he? Yes. He can.

words.say_it: Curl your fingers and pull the air toward you. "OO-meh."
words.bonus: ʻUme is a pull toward you. Pale, from before, pushes things away. So ʻume pulls in and pale shields off.
words.picture: Magnet belt pulling every fork in mall
story_paragraphs: You buy a belt from a guy at the swap meet. He says it is a magnet belt. It is good for your back. You put it on and walk into Ala Moana.
A fork flies out of the food court and sticks to your stomach. "Ooh... me?" Then a spoon. Then 40 forks. A shopping cart rolls across the parking lot and slams into your side. "OOH... ME?"

Keys fly out of people's pockets. Coins shoot out of the fountain. A security guard's flashlight. A little kid's toy truck. Every metal thing in the mall is pulled toward you like you are the center of the universe.
By the time you get to the exit, you are wearing a giant ball of metal like a shell. You can only move one inch at a time. Somewhere inside it, your phone is ringing.

words.say_it: Grip invisible bars and look sad. "Ho-oh-pah-ah-HAH-oh."
words.bonus: Paʻahao means a prisoner, and hale paʻahao is a jail. Inside it is paʻa, meaning stuck.
words.picture: Pa locked in the dog kennel
story_paragraphs: Your niece Malia is seven, and she just got a toy sheriff badge. She takes her job very seriously.
At the party, someone eats the last spam musubi. Malia investigates. There is rice on Pa's shirt. There is nori in his teeth. Case closed.
She marches him to the backyard and locks him in the big dog kennel. She puts the padlock on and tucks the key in her sock. The dog is inside too. The dog looks at Pa. Pa looks at the dog.

"Ho, oh... PA... AH... HOW?" he says. How did he end up in jail? Everyone at the party walks by and waves. Somebody hands him a plate through the bars. Three hours later Malia lets him out on good behavior. He has to promise to share next time. He does not.

words.say_it: Stomp your feet like a tiny monster. "LOO-koo!"
words.bonus: Luku is a big word for total wipeout, like a storm flattening a town. For one broken thing you would use a smaller word.
words.picture: Toddler stomping a giant sandcastle flat
story_paragraphs: Your whole family spent nine hours at Waimānalo building a sandcastle. It is nine feet tall. Towers, a moat, a drawbridge made of a boogie board, little flags made of chopsticks. People are taking pictures.
Then two year old Kaleo wakes up from his nap.
He toddles over. He stares up at the castle with big eyes. "LOOK!" he says, pointing. Everyone smiles. "OOOO!" he says.
Then he raises both fists like a tiny monster and charges. He stomps the moat. He knocks down the east tower. He sits on the drawbridge. He bites a flag. Nine hours of work, wiped out in 45 seconds.
When the dust clears there is nothing but a flat patch of sand and one proud baby in the middle. "Look! Oooo!" he says again. He totally destroyed it.

words.say_it: Wince like you just heard a crash. "Ho-oh-poh-EE-no."
words.bonus: Pōʻino means harm or misfortune. Don't mix it with hōʻino, the next word, which is harming with insulting words.
words.picture: Uncle's truck denting your new car
story_paragraphs: You just bought your first car. It is used but it is shiny and yours. You park it in the driveway and stand there admiring it.
Uncle is backing his truck out next door. He has three surfboards, a kayak, and a ladder sticking out the back. He is looking at his phone.
"Oh-oh," you say. POH! The ladder hits your windshield. POH! The kayak hits your door. POH! POH! The surfboards hit the side mirror.
"EEE... NO!" you scream.

Uncle finally looks up. Your car has a cracked windshield, a door shaped like a taco, and a mirror hanging by a wire. He gets out, looks at it for a long time, and says "Ho, sorry, eh." Then he backs up again and hits the mailbox. Harm, damage, POH, eee, no.

words.say_it: Look someone up and down and shake your head. "Hoh-EE-no."
words.bonus: Hōʻino is insulting or disrespecting with words. Hoʻopōʻino is harming things. Both share ʻino, which means bad.
words.picture: Rude robot vacuum insulting everyone
story_paragraphs: Your aunty buys a new robot vacuum. It is smart. Too smart. It rolls around the house and it judges everybody.

It rolls up to your cousin's shoes. It stops. It looks up with its little blue light. "Hōōō... eee... no." It rolls away. It rolls up to Uncle's aloha shirt, the one with the flamingos. "HŌŌŌ... EEE... NO." It rolls over your plate lunch and refuses to clean it. "Hōōō... eee... no."
It insults the couch. It insults the cat. It insults Grandma's new hairdo, and Grandma chases it around the house with a broom for twenty minutes.
Now nobody will walk past it. It sits in the corner going "Hōōō, eee, no" at the wall. Aunty wants to return it, but the box just says No Refunds.

words.english: to look down on, to scorn
words.say_it: Look down your nose and laugh long. "Ho-oh-vah-haah-vah-HAAH."
words.picture: Monster truck driver laughing at a moped
story_paragraphs: You pull up to the red light on your little moped. It is pink. It has a basket. It goes 25 miles an hour, 30 downhill.
Next to you rolls a monster truck. Tires taller than you. The driver sits 30 feet up, wearing mirrored sunglasses. He looks down at you. All the way down.
"Ho, oh," he says. Then he laughs a big, long, scornful laugh. "WAH-HAH, WAH-HAAAAH!" He looks at your basket. "WAH-HAAAH!" He looks at your helmet with the stickers. "WAH-HAH, WAH-HAAAAAH!"
The light turns green. He roars off in a cloud of smoke and drives straight into a huge mud puddle, where he gets stuck up to the doors.
You putt putt past him at 25 miles an hour. You do not laugh. You just ring your little bell. Ding ding.

words.english: to tease, to make fun of
words.say_it: Wiggle your fingers by your ears and sing it. "Ho-oh-heh-neh-HEH-neh."
words.picture: Hens teasing a bald rooster
story_paragraphs: There is one bald rooster on the farm. He lost all his neck feathers in a fight with a mango. He looks like a plucked hot dog with legs.

The hens will not let it go. Every morning they line up on the fence, all eleven of them, and sing their teasing song. "Heh-neh, HEH-neh! Heh-neh, HEH-neh!" The same sing song you used on the playground.

He tries to crow. "Heh-neh, HEH-neh!" He struts. "HEH-neh!" One hen puts a tiny pink bow on her own neck just to make fun of him. The goats laugh. The pig laughs. Even the eggs look like they are giggling.
He finally gets a little knitted scarf from the farmer's wife. He wears it proudly. The hens stop for exactly one day. Then, "Heh-neh, HEH-neh!" They tease the scarf.

words.english: to be naughty, to act up
words.say_it: Duck down low, look both ways, and grin. "Ko-LO-heh."
words.bonus: Kolohe is used all the time in local English for a rascal, a playful troublemaker. Calling a kid kolohe is usually said with a smile. There is no kahakō, so every o is short.
words.picture: Kids tying wedding guests' shoes together
story_paragraphs: Big fancy wedding. White tablecloths down to the floor. Under the head table crawl two little rascals, your nephews, five and seven.

"Go low, hey!" whispers the big one. They slide along on their bellies. One by one, they tie guests' shoelaces together. Uncle's shoe to Aunty's shoe. The groom's to the best man's. Grandma's to the table leg. The nakinaki uncle would be proud.
Then the dad of the bride taps his glass. "Everybody, please stand for a toast!"
Forty people stand up. Forty people fall down. Glasses fly. Cake lands on the minister. The best man is hopping in a circle, tied to the groom.
Under the table two little faces giggle. "Go low, hey!" They are already crawling toward the dessert table. That is kolohe. Pure naughty, with a big grin.

words.say_it: Pump your arms like you're running late. "Vee-kee-VEE-kee!"
words.bonus: The Honolulu airport shuttle was named the Wiki Wiki, and that shuttle is where the web word wiki got its name.
words.picture: Grandma sprinting through airport with fish cooler
story_paragraphs: Your flight leaves at 9:15. It is 9:02. You are just getting out of the car at the airport with Grandma, who is 84 and has three suitcases and a cooler full of frozen fish.
"QUICKY, QUICKY!" she yells. She grabs two suitcases and takes off running. You did not know she could run.

She goes through security like a bowling ball. She jumps over a luggage cart. "Quicky, QUICKY!" She dodges a family of six and a guy with a surfboard. She runs down the terminal so fast her slippers make smoke.

At 9:14 she reaches the gate. The door is closing. She sticks the cooler in the gap. The door opens. She turns around, fish cooler under one arm, and waves you in. "Quicky, quicky," she says, not even out of breath.

words.english: to be slow; to be late
words.say_it: Move your hand across the table, super slow. "LO... hee."
words.bonus: Lohi means both slow and late. Next comes hoʻolohi, to slow something down.
words.picture: Sea turtle driving the city bus
story_paragraphs: You are already late for work. You jump on the bus. The driver is a sea turtle. A big old honu with a little driver's cap.
He turns the key. Very slowly. He checks the mirror. Very slowly. He puts on the blinker. It blinks four hundred times. He pulls out into traffic at one mile an hour.
You lean over. "Uh, can we go faster?" He turns his head. It takes 45 seconds. He opens his mouth to say "slowly," but he is so slow that he misses the S completely. "...LOW... HEE."
It takes four hours to go one block. You are late. The bus is late. Everybody on the bus is late. A snail passes you on the sidewalk and waves. Low, hee. That is lohi. Slow and late.

words.say_it: Pull back on invisible reins. "Ho-oh-LO-hee."
words.bonus: Lohi is being slow. Hoʻolohi is making something slow. Good for traffic, horses, and people who talk too fast.
words.picture: Paniolo stopping runaway horse at cliff
story_paragraphs: You are a paniolo up in Waimea. The ranch gives you a new horse. His name is Rocket. You should have asked why.
You climb on. Rocket takes off. Seventy miles an hour. You fly past cows. You fly past fences. A tourist's hat flies off. You are headed straight for the edge of a cliff.
You pull back on the reins with everything you've got. "WHOA! OH! LOW! HEE!"

Rocket starts to slow down. "WHOA! OH!" Slower. Slower. He slows so much he ends up at turtle speed, the same speed as the bus driving honu from lohi. His front hooves stop one inch from the edge. A pebble falls off and takes eight seconds to hit the bottom.
You slide off. Your legs are jelly. From now on you ride Rocket very, very slowly.

words.english: to join together; to crash into
words.say_it: Smack your fists together and keep them stuck. "Ho-oh-KOO-ee!"
words.bonus: Hoʻokuʻi can mean to join and also to crash into, and bumper cars do both. Next, hoʻokuʻikahi joins things into one.
words.picture: Bumper cars stuck together with cotton candy
story_paragraphs: Bumper cars at the county fair. Right before your turn, you drop your cotton candy all over the front of your car. The bumper is pink and sticky.

The ride starts. You crash into Aunty. BONK. Your cars stick together. "Ho, oh, GOO... EE!" You can't get loose. You crash into your cousin. BONK. Stuck. Into a guy from Kāneʻohe. Stuck. Into a kid with a shave ice, who adds more goo.
Every crash joins another car. By the end of the ride there are twelve bumper cars glued together into one giant bumper car blob, spinning in a circle, everybody laughing and screaming "GOO... EE!"
The ride operator has to use a spatula to pull you apart. It takes an hour. Now they post a sign. No cotton candy on the bumper cars.

words.say_it: Hook two pinky fingers together and shake. "Ho-oh-koo-ee-KAH-hee."
words.bonus: Kahi means one, so hoʻokuʻikahi is to join into one. It is used for making peace and uniting people.
words.picture: Two uncles making peace over sweet coffee
story_paragraphs: Uncle Ben and Uncle Kalani have been fighting for 20 years. It is about a mango tree on the property line. Whose mangoes? Nobody knows. They do not wave. They do not talk. One built a fence. The other built it higher.

One morning Aunty has had enough. She sets up a card table right on the property line. She makes a pot of coffee. She pours in a whole can of sweet condensed milk. It is so thick it barely pours. Gooey coffee.
"Ho, oh," she says. "GOOEY KAH-HEE. Sit."

They sit. They sip. They get sticky. Neither one can stay mad while drinking something that sweet. Uncle Ben laughs first. Uncle Kalani laughs second. By noon they are picking mangoes together. They tear down both fences. Two families, one yard.

words.say_it: Spread your fingers open like a light turning on. "Ho-oh-maah-lah-mah-LAH-mah."
words.bonus: Mālamalama means light or clear. Don't mix it up with mālama, to take care of. Hoʻomālamalama also means to enlighten a person, to help them understand.
words.picture: Glowing llama lighting up the house
story_paragraphs: Remember Mom's spoiled llama from mālama? He got bored one night and ate a whole box of glow sticks. Four hundred of them.
At 8 p.m. the power goes out on the whole street. Pitch black. You cannot see your hand. Then the llama walks into the living room. He is glowing. Green, pink, blue, like a disco ball with legs.
"Ho, oh, MAAA!" you yell. "LLAMA, LLAMA!" The whole house lights up.

The neighbors come over. Everybody sits around the llama like a campfire. Kids do homework by llama light. Grandpa reads the newspaper. A lost moth flies in from outside and thinks it has found heaven.
When the power comes back on, nobody turns on the lights. Why would they? The llama lights up the room, and the room likes it.

words.say_it: Hold out an invisible bowl, shy and hopeful. "Ho-oh-NEE-po."
words.bonus: Hoʻonipo is to court, to try to win someone's heart. The next word, nipo, is the feeling itself, being in love or longing.
words.picture: Fish market guy offering poke every day
story_paragraphs: Kainalu works at the fish market. Every day at 11:45, a woman in a green visor comes to buy fish. He is in love. He cannot talk.

On day one he holds out a little bowl of ʻahi poke. "Oh... need poke?" She takes it and smiles. On day two, shoyu poke. "Oh... need poke?" Day three, limu poke. Day ten, spicy. Day forty, a poke bowl shaped like a heart.
He writes her a song. He leaves flowers on her car. He learns to play the ʻukulele just to sing "Need poke? Need poke?" under the window of her office.
On day one hundred, she walks in holding her own bowl. She holds it out to him. "Oh... need poke?" He drops a whole tuna. That is courting. One hundred bowls of poke.

words.english: to long for, to be in love
words.say_it: Put a hand on your heart and let your knees wobble. "NEE-po."
words.bonus: Nipo is the feeling, longing or being in love. Hoʻonipo is acting on it, courting.
words.picture: Lovesick cousin collapsing by the mailbox
story_paragraphs: Your cousin Makoa is in love. The girl moved to the continent for college, 2,500 miles away, and now he just misses her. All day. All night.
Every afternoon at 2:15 he waits by the mailbox for her letter. He stares down the street. He sighs so hard the mailbox flag goes up by itself.
When the mail truck finally turns the corner, his knees go weak. Literally. "KNEE..." they buckle, "...POP!" You can hear them crack from the house. He drops to the sidewalk every single day.

One Tuesday there is a pink envelope with a heart on it. Makoa's knees do not just pop. They pop, pop, POP, like popcorn in a microwave, and he lies in the grass holding the letter to his chest for an hour. That is nipo. Longing so hard your knees give out.

words.english: to be patient, to hang in there
words.say_it: Take a deep breath, stand on one leg, stay calm. "Ho-oh-mah-nah-vah-NOO-ee."
words.bonus: Manawa can mean heart or disposition, and nui means big, so a big, steady heart. Many people also remember it as manawa, time, plus nui, giving it lots of time. People say E hoʻomanawanui to each other for be patient, hang in there.
words.picture: Kid and heron both waiting on one leg
story_paragraphs: There is a new malasada shop in town, and the line is 300 people long. It wraps around the block twice. You are number 287. Your little brother is seven.
After ten minutes he starts. "Oh, maaan... ah, wahhh... noo-eee!" It is the sound of a kid falling apart. Twenty minutes. "OH, MAAAN... AH, WAHHH... NOO-EEE!"
Grandpa does not get upset. He just takes the whine and finishes it for him, calm as a rock. "Hoʻo... manawa... nui." Hang in there.
Across the street, a heron has been standing on one leg by the drain for six hours waiting for a fish. It does not move. It does not whine. Your brother watches it. He stands on one leg too.
Two hours later you get to the window. The malasadas are still warm. The heron gets its fish at the same time.

words.english: to think it over, to reflect
words.say_it: Tap your chin and look up at the ceiling. "No-oh-NO-oh."
words.bonus: Noʻonoʻo is thinking something over. It can also mean the mind or a thought. Manaʻo is more like an opinion or idea.
words.picture: Uncle thinking 45 minutes over plate lunch
story_paragraphs: Uncle Kawika walks up to the counter at the plate lunch place. There are 38 choices on the board. He has been coming here for 30 years. It does not matter. He still has to think.
He strokes his chin. "Chicken katsu? No... oh... NO... oh." He nods slowly. "Loco moco? No... oh..." His eyes go up to the ceiling. His lips move. He counts on his fingers.

The line behind him grows. Twenty people. Forty. Somebody orders a pizza to the line. A lady knits a whole sweater. Uncle is deep in thought, bobbing his head with a little catch each time. "No... oh... NO... oh."
Forty five minutes later he looks up, very sure. "I'll have the usual." The cashier already made it. It's been sitting on the counter for 40 minutes.

words.say_it: Lower both hands slowly, like letting out a rope. "Ho-oh-EE-ho."
words.bonus: Iho means down or downward. Hoʻoiho is to bring something down.
words.picture: Firefighters lowering a cat in a bucket
story_paragraphs: A cat named Biscuit is stuck at the top of a 60 foot coconut tree. She has been up there all day, yelling at everyone.

The fire truck comes. The ladder is too short. So the firefighters try something else. One climbs the tree like a gecko, puts Biscuit into a bucket, and ties it to a rope. Now they have to lower her. Slowly.
Six firefighters hold the rope. "HO! OH!" they chant together, and let out a little rope. The rope squeaks. "EEEEE..." The bucket drops a foot. "HO!" Another foot. "HO! OH! EEEEE... HO!"

It takes half an hour. The whole neighborhood counts along. Biscuit sits in the bucket like a queen being carried down from her throne. When she touches the ground, she hops out, licks one paw, and walks away. Not one thank you.

words.say_it: Flick your eyes to the side and back, fast. "Ah-LAH-vah."
words.bonus: ʻAlawa is a quick sideways look. Kilo, the next word, is the opposite, watching closely for a long time.
words.picture: Diner glancing at a larva in salad
story_paragraphs: You are at a fancy lunch. The waiter sets down a beautiful salad. Greens from Waimānalo, edible flowers, tiny tomatoes like jewels.
You pick up your fork and give the plate one quick look. Just one. A glance. And there, curled on a lettuce leaf, is a fat little white bug baby, waving at you.
"Ah... LARVA!"

That is all you need. One glance. You do not need to study it. You do not need a second look. You put the fork down. You look out the window. You look at the ceiling. You glance back one more time, super quick, like touching a hot stove. Still there. "Ah, larva."
The waiter comes by. He glances at the plate. He glances at you. He takes it away without a word and brings you fried rice instead.

words.english: to watch closely; to read the stars
words.say_it: Lean in close and stare without blinking. "KEE-lo."
words.bonus: A kilo hōkū is a star watcher, someone who reads the stars. Kilo is also used for reading the weather and the ocean.
words.picture: Uncle staring at the fish scale needle
story_paragraphs: Uncle Masa has been buying fish at the early morning auction for 50 years. He can guess any ʻahi within one kilo just by looking. But today the numbers matter. A big one is on the scale.
He leans in with a magnifying glass. He watches the needle. It wobbles. "Kee-lo... kee-lo..." He does not blink. He watches the needle for two minutes. Four minutes. Ten.
A fly lands on his eyeball. He does not blink. The other buyers get bored and go get coffee. The fish gets bored. Uncle keeps watching, eyes wide, nose one inch from the dial.
Finally the needle stops. Uncle nods. "Forty two kilo, 300 grams." He was right before it even stopped. He always watches that closely. At night he goes home and watches the stars the same way.

words.say_it: Peek over the top of your hands like binoculars. "Haah-KEE-lo."
words.bonus: Hākilo has kilo inside it. Kilo is watching closely. Hākilo is watching when you're not supposed to be, spying.
words.picture: Aunty in a hawk costume spying from tree
story_paragraphs: Aunty Winnie wants to know everything happening on her street. Binoculars are not enough anymore. So she buys a hawk costume. Brown feathers, yellow beak, big fake wings.
At dawn she climbs the mango tree across from the neighbor's house and settles in on a branch. She whispers to herself, "Hawk... ee..." and sinks lower into the leaves, "...LOW."
She watches everything. Who got a new car. Who is dating who. Which cousin came home at 3 a.m. She writes it all down in a tiny notebook tucked under her wing.

When the neighbor steps outside, she freezes and goes "Hawk, ee, low," and slides down even lower. Her feathers are shaking. The neighbor looks up, sees a giant hawk with reading glasses, and waves. "Morning, Aunty Winnie." She pretends she did not hear.

words.english: to be alert, to watch out
words.say_it: Snap your eyes wide open and look side to side. "Mah-kah-AH-lah."
words.bonus: Maka means eye. Older dictionaries explain the rest as ala, awake, so eyes awake, on the lookout. Notice the ʻokina in makaʻala.
words.picture: You wide-eyed from all-night car alarm
story_paragraphs: Your car alarm is broken. It goes off every four minutes, all night, for no reason. WEE-OO WEE-OO WEE-OO.
At 11:04 p.m. you jump out of bed. "My CAR! Ah... LAAARM!" You run outside. Nothing. At 11:08 again. At 11:12 again.

By 2 a.m. you are the most alert person on the island. Your eyes are as wide as pie plates. You hear a leaf fall two streets away. You can see in the dark like an owl. You catch a mosquito with chopsticks while standing in the driveway in your boxers.

At dawn the neighbors come out to complain, and you already know what they're going to say before they say it. You do not sleep for three days. You become a lifeguard. Nobody has ever been more alert.

words.english: to be careful, to go easy
words.say_it: Hold out both hands flat and walk like you're on ice. "Ah-kah-HEH-leh."
