words.bonus: Hele means to go. Akahele is going with care, and people say it the way you'd say drive safe or take it easy.
words.picture: Cousin carrying giant cake down steep stairs
story_paragraphs: Your cousin Lehua, everybody calls her Leh, has one job. Carry the six tier wedding cake down 40 steep concrete steps from the house to the backyard. The cake is taller than she is. It wobbles like jello.
The whole family lines the stairs, whispering, "Uh-kah... hey, Leh!" Easy, Leh. Careful, Leh.
She takes one step. The cake leans. "HEY, LEH!" She stops. She leans the other way. One step. "Uh-kah... hey, Leh." A gecko runs across her foot. Everyone gasps. She freezes for a full minute.

It takes her an hour and ten minutes to go down 40 steps. Grandma prays. Uncle can't watch. But Leh sets the cake down on the table, perfect, not one flower out of place. The whole family collapses on the grass. Then the ring bearer runs straight into the table.

words.english: to get to know, to get familiar
words.say_it: Lower an invisible camera and relax your shoulders. "Ho-oh-kah-mah-AAH-ee-nah."
words.bonus: A kamaʻāina is a local, someone born or long settled in a place. Kama means child and ʻāina means land, so child of the land.
words.picture: New neighbor putting camera down for rainbow
story_paragraphs: Your new neighbor, Brad, moves from the continent. The first week he takes pictures of everything. The rainbow. The mango tree. A chicken crossing the road. His plate lunch. Your aunty. He takes 4,000 photos in seven days.

But then he starts learning. He learns your names. He learns which beach is safe. He learns to take off his shoes at the door. He learns the shortcut to Kalihi and how to say "shoots." He learns that the chicken crossing the road happens every day at 7 a.m.

A year later you are all at the beach. A double rainbow comes out. You hand him your phone. "Camera?" He looks at it. He looks at the rainbow. "Ahhh... ee... nah." He just sits and enjoys it. He knows this place now. He got familiar.

words.say_it: Hold out an open hand from one friend toward another. "Ho-oh-LAU-nah."
words.bonus: Hoʻolauna is to introduce. The next word, launa, is to be friendly and hang out. Hoʻolauna is what gets the hanging out started.
words.picture: Dog howling introductions at the dog park
story_paragraphs: You take your dog Kolohe Boy to the dog park for the first time. You are new here. You don't know anybody.
Kolohe Boy walks you straight up to a big poodle. He sits, lifts his head, and howls. "HOOO... OH... LOWWW... NAH!" The poodle's owner laughs and shakes your hand. That's an introduction.

He walks you to a husky. "HOOO... OH... LOWWW... NAH!" The husky's owner says hi. To a tiny chihuahua in a sweater. "HOOO... OH... LOWWW... NAH!" To a guy with three pugs. A lady with a pig on a leash. Kolohe Boy howls at each one, then sits back like a proud emcee.
By sunset you know 34 dogs and 29 people. You have been invited to two birthday parties and a barbecue. Your dog introduced you to the whole park.

words.english: to be friendly, to hang out with
words.say_it: Lean back in your chair and put your hands behind your head. "LAU-nah."
words.bonus: Launa is being friendly and getting along with people. Hoʻolauna, with hoʻo in front, is to introduce people.
words.picture: Friendly crab in a tiny beach chair
story_paragraphs: You set up your beach chair at Kailua. Umbrella, cooler, a bag of chips. You lean back. "Lounge, ah."
A ghost crab pops out of the sand next to you. He is dragging a tiny beach chair of his own, the size of a matchbox. He sets it up right next to yours. He leans back. "LOUNGE, AH."

He is very friendly. He waves at every dog. He offers you a crumb. You offer him a chip. He shares his tiny cooler, which has one drop of water in it. You talk story all afternoon. He tells you about the time he got carried off by a wave.
At sunset he folds his chair and waves one claw. The next Saturday he is waiting for you. You hang out every weekend now. You even bring him a tiny umbrella.

words.say_it: Put a hand over your eyes like a pirate spotting something. "Hoy-HOY!"
words.bonus: Hoihoi can mean interested and also interesting or enjoyable. Next, hoʻohoihoi is making something fun for others, to entertain.
words.picture: Pirate captain excited by a shave ice raft
story_paragraphs: A pirate ship is sailing past Waikīkī. The captain is bored. He has seen a hundred islands. He has seen gold. Nothing interests him anymore.
Then his telescope stops. Floating on a raft in the middle of the ocean is a shave ice stand. Rainbow syrup. Li hing powder. A little sign that says Ice Cream On Bottom.
"AHOY! HOY!" he shouts, leaning so far over the rail that his hat falls in. He is very interested. "HOY! HOY!"

He turns the whole ship around. He rows over himself. He tries every flavor, all 24 of them. He asks the shave ice guy how the machine works, where the syrup comes from, if he could learn. He stays for three days. His crew sails off without him. He does not even notice.

words.say_it: Spread your arms like a showman. "Ho-oh-hoy-HOY!"
words.bonus: Hoihoi is being interested. Hoʻohoihoi is making others interested, entertaining them.
words.picture: Pirate juggling pineapples at a birthday party
story_paragraphs: Remember the pirate who fell in love with shave ice? He needs money now, so he takes a job as the entertainment at kids' birthday parties.
First party. Thirty bored kids sitting on the grass, looking at their phones. The pirate jumps out of a cardboard box. "HO! OH! HOY-HOY!"

He juggles five coconuts. He juggles three pineapples and a watermelon. He tells a story about a shark with a toothache. He does a magic trick where the birthday boy's slipper turns into a chicken. The chicken runs away. The kids scream with joy.

By the end, the kids are dancing on the picnic tables and the parents are filming. The pirate bows so low his hook gets stuck in the grass. "HO! OH! HOY-HOY!" He entertained them all, and he did not use a single phone.

words.say_it: Jump out and throw up your hands. "Ho-oh-mah-KAH-oo!"
words.bonus: Makaʻu means afraid or scared. Hoʻomakaʻu is to make someone afraid, to scare them.
words.picture: Kid bursting out of the laundry basket
story_paragraphs: Your little brother wants to scare Ma. So he hides in the laundry basket. He waits. Under the dirty towels. For two hours. He falls asleep once.
Finally, Ma walks in to do laundry. She hums a song. She reaches into the basket.
He explodes out of the towels. "MA! KA..." a gulp as he takes a breath, "...BOOOO!"

Ma jumps so high her head hits the ceiling fan. She screams so loud the neighbor's dog starts howling. She drops the detergent. Soap bubbles fill the whole laundry room. She runs out the door and halfway down the street before she stops.
When she comes back, she is holding her chest and laughing. Your brother is so proud. Then she sits down, very calm, and says, "Okay. Now you do all the laundry." That scared him more.

words.say_it: Poke the air three times, then make a train whistle. "Ho-oh-hoo-HOO!"
words.bonus: Huhū means angry. Hoʻohuhū is to make someone angry. Ukiuki, next, covers being annoyed, irritated or peeved.
words.picture: Steam whistling out of an angry uncle's ears
story_paragraphs: Uncle Keola is trying to take a nap on the couch. Your little cousin decides to poke him. Once on the arm. Uncle's eye opens a little.
Poke. Uncle's ears turn pink. Poke. His face turns red. Poke poke poke. Now his face is purple, like a plum.

At poke number 40, steam starts coming out of both his ears. It gets louder and louder until it sounds just like an old train whistle. "HOO-HOOOOOOO!" The windows fog up. The smoke detector goes off. The cat hides in the rice cooker.

Your cousin looks up, very innocent. "What?" Uncle stands up, still whistling steam. "HOO-HOOOOO!" He chases your cousin around the house three times, then outside, then down the block. The steam trail hangs in the air for an hour. That is how you make somebody angry.

words.say_it: Twitch one eye and grit your teeth. "Oo-kee-OO-kee."
words.bonus: Ukiuki covers being annoyed, irritated, peeved or resentful. Hoʻoukiuki is to irritate someone on purpose.
words.picture: Neighbor kid strumming one wrong chord at dawn
story_paragraphs: The kid next door got a ʻukulele for his birthday. He knows one chord. It is the wrong chord.
At 5 a.m. he starts. "Ukey, ukey. Ukey, ukey." Strum strum. Strum strum. The same chord. Over and over.

At 6 a.m. your left eye starts to twitch. At 7 a.m. your jaw is tight. At 8 you are eating breakfast with your teeth clenched. "Ukey, ukey, ukey, ukey." At 9 you put a pillow on your head, then two pillows, then the couch cushions.

At noon you walk over, knock on the door, and politely offer to teach him a second chord. He learns it. Great. Now he plays two chords. Wrong ones. "UKEY, UKEY!" Your eye is twitching so hard it is keeping the beat. That is ukiuki. Annoyed, all the way down to your eyelid.

words.say_it: Blow an imaginary whistle, then jump. "Pee-hoy-HOY!"
words.bonus: Pīhoihoi is being all stirred up, excited, worried or alarmed. Hikilele, next, is the jump that comes with a shock.
words.picture: Aunty launched from hammock by a whistle
story_paragraphs: Aunty Momi is asleep in the hammock on a Sunday afternoon. Snoring. A plate of half eaten poke on her belly.
Her grandson finds a whistle in the junk drawer. He tiptoes up. He puts it right next to her ear. He blows as hard as he can. "PEEEEEEEE!"

Aunty launches out of the hammock like a rocket. "HOY! HOY!" She flies over the fence. The poke flies over the roof. She lands in the kiddie pool with a big SPLASH. She sits there in six inches of water, heart pounding, eyes as big as plates. "HOY! HOY!"

Then she sees the ice cream truck turning onto the street, playing its song. Now she is excited instead of scared. She jumps up, dripping wet, and runs after it. "PEEEE! HOY! HOY!" Alarmed, then excited, all stirred up in one minute. Pīhoihoi.

words.say_it: Jump a little in place with both hands up. "Hee-kee-LEH-leh!"
words.bonus: Lele means to jump or fly, like in hoʻolele and ʻukulele. Hikilele is the jump that comes with a fright.
words.picture: You stuck to ceiling from centipede scare
story_paragraphs: You slide your foot into your slipper by the back door. Something inside moves. Something with a hundred legs. It is a centipede, seven inches long, and it is not happy.
"HEE!" you squeal. "KEE!"

Then your body jumps without asking you. "LEH-LEH!" Remember lele, to jump or fly? You jump so high you hit the ceiling and stick there, flat, arms and legs out like a cat in a cartoon. Your slipper stays on the floor.
The centipede crawls out, looks around, and walks off into the garden. Nobody chases it.

Your mom walks into the kitchen. She sees you stuck to the ceiling. She looks at the slipper. She knows. "Centipede?" You nod. She hands you a broom to help you climb down. That is hikilele. Jumping out of your skin.

words.say_it: Open your mouth wide and gasp three times, each one longer. "Kaah-haah-HAAH!"
words.bonus: Kāhāhā is the big wow. It is used when you are amazed or astonished, and the long ā sounds are the gasps.
words.picture: Magician pulling a whole car from his hat
story_paragraphs: A magician comes to the school carnival. He is wearing a top hat and a cape. He looks at the crowd. "For my last trick," he says, "I will pull something out of this hat."
He reaches in. He pulls out a steering wheel. Then a bumper. Then a whole front tire. Then, very slowly, he pulls out an entire car. A red station wagon. Full size. With a surfboard on top.
Three hundred people stare with their mouths hanging open. "CAAAR!" gasps one kid. "HAAAH!" says her mom. "HAAAAH!" says the principal, who drops his shave ice.
Nobody claps. They are too amazed. Then the car honks. Then the magician climbs into it, waves, and drives away out the gate. Everyone is still standing there with their jaws on the ground.

words.english: to catch on fast, to be quick to learn
words.say_it: Snap your fingers like you just got it. "Ah-AH-po!"
words.bonus: ʻApo means to catch. ʻAʻapo is catching on, being quick to learn, just like English says you catch on.
words.picture: Baby hippo acing second grade
story_paragraphs: A baby hippo enrolls in the second grade. Nobody expects much. He is gray and round and he sits on two desks at once.

Monday, the teacher writes long division on the board. The hippo looks at it once. He solves it. "Ah! A hippo!" the kids say. Tuesday, he learns to play ʻukulele in 20 minutes. "AH! A HIPPO!" Wednesday he learns hula. By Thursday he is teaching the teacher how to fix the printer.
Every time he picks up a new thing in about five seconds, the whole class shouts "Ah! A HIPPO!" He catches on faster than anybody ever has. He catches on so fast he graduates by Friday.
The principal gives him a diploma. He eats it. He learned everything else fast, but table manners take longer.

words.say_it: Tap your belly and then your head. "Ho-oh-pah-ah-nah-OW."
words.bonus: Paʻa means stuck and naʻau means gut. Hoʻopaʻanaʻau is making something stick in your gut, learning it by heart.
words.picture: Kid eating flash cards before spelling bee
story_paragraphs: It is the night before the spelling bee. You have 400 words to learn. Pa is quizzing you at the kitchen table with a pile of flash cards.

"Pa! Ah..." you say. "I can't remember." Pa has an idea. The old folks say you learn things by heart in your gut, not your head. So he hands you a flash card. You eat it. "Now!" he says. Another card. Chew. Swallow. "Now!"
By card 200 your stomach hurts. "OW!" By card 400 you are round as a ball. "Pa! Ah... now... OW!"

Next morning at the spelling bee, the judge says "necessary." You burp. The word comes up spelled perfectly. N, E, C, E, S, S, A, R, Y. You win the whole thing. You memorized it all. Every word is stuck in your gut forever.

words.english: to fasten; to study; to book
words.say_it: Click an invisible seatbelt with a snap. "Ho-oh-PAH-ah."
words.bonus: Hoʻopaʻa has three everyday meanings. You hoʻopaʻa a seatbelt, you hoʻopaʻa for a test, and you hoʻopaʻa a table at a restaurant.
words.picture: Aunty strapping you in with 14 seatbelts
story_paragraphs: You climb into the front car of the biggest roller coaster at the fair. The ride operator is a seven foot tall aunty with a whistle. She takes safety very seriously.

She pulls down your lap bar. "HO! OH! PAH!" It locks. You gasp, "AH!" She adds a seatbelt. PAH. AH. Another seatbelt. A strap across your chest. A clip on your ankle. She fastens you in with 14 straps. You can't move your eyebrows.
Then she hands you a thick textbook. "You gonna study while you ride," she says. "Test is Monday." You read chapter one while the coaster goes upside down.
When it stops, she checks her clipboard. "I booked you for nine more rides." PAH. AH. That is hoʻopaʻa. Fasten, study, and book, all in one day at the fair.

words.english: to be solid, stuck; to be done
words.say_it: Grip one fist with the other hand and pull hard. "PAH-ah."
words.bonus: Paʻa also means finished or done. Ua paʻa ka hana means the work is done.
words.picture: Dog's paw stuck in peanut butter jar
story_paragraphs: Your dog, Tank, finds the peanut butter jar on the floor. He shoves his whole front paw inside to get the last bit. Now it is stuck. Solid. Like it was cemented in.
"PAW!" you yell. He looks at you. He shakes his paw. The jar stays on. "(hic) AH!" You grab the jar and pull. Tank slides across the floor with you. Nothing. The jar is on there tight as a bolt.
Your brother pulls Tank. You pull the jar. Your mom holds the couch. Everyone counts to three. Pull. The jar will not budge. It is paʻa.
Then Tank does the only smart thing anyone does all day. He licks the jar clean from the inside, and his paw slides right out. The jar is empty. Totally finished. Paʻa. Stuck, and then done.

words.english: to wake someone up; to revive
words.say_it: Shake an invisible sleeper by the shoulder. "Ho-AAH-lah!"
words.bonus: Ala means to wake up. Hoʻāla is to wake someone else up, and it can also mean to stir up, revive or restore. A mele hoʻāla is a chant to wake a sleeper.
words.picture: Rooster alarm clock waking the whole street
story_paragraphs: Your cousin Kainoa sleeps like a rock. Fire trucks do not wake him. Thunder does not wake him. Last year he slept through his own birthday party.
So Tūtū buys the loudest alarm clock on the island. It is shaped like a rooster, and instead of beeping, it yells. At 6 a.m. it goes off. "HO! AAAH-LA(RM)! HO! AAAH-LA(RM)!"
Kainoa rolls over. Tūtū turns the knob up to ten. "HO! AAAAAAH-LA!" The windows rattle. The neighbor's dogs wake up. The whole street wakes up. A cat napping on Maui opens one eye.
Ho, aaah, la. Hoʻāla. To wake someone up.

Finally Kainoa sits up, hair sticking straight out. "Okay, okay, I'm awake." Tūtū hands him a cup of coffee. The rooster clock even revives the wilted plant on the windowsill. It stands up straight and looks around.

words.say_it: Tip your flat hand over like a flipping canoe. "Kah-HOO-lee!"
words.bonus: Hoʻokahuli means to tip something over on purpose.
words.picture: Crow, owl and Lee flipping a canoe
story_paragraphs: You are paddling a tiny two seat canoe off Kailua, but somehow three passengers climbed in. A crow up front. An owl in the middle. Your cousin Lee in the back, eating a family size bag of chips.
A little wave comes. The crow leans left and screams "KAH!" The owl leans right and hoots "HOO!" Lee leans way out over the side to grab a floating chip and yells "LEE!"
Kah. Hoo. Lee. The canoe flips completely upside down. Now all four of you are under it in a little air pocket. The crow is soaked, the owl is furious, and Lee is still chewing.
You flip it back over and everybody climbs in. Then Lee spots another chip. "KAH! HOO! LEE!" Over you go again. Kahuli. Round two.

words.english: to cover; to break (like a wave)
words.say_it: Curl your hand over like a breaking wave, and catch your breath in the middle. "Po... ee!"
words.bonus: Poʻi (with the ʻokina catch) is not poi (the food). As a noun, poʻi is also a lid, like the cover on a pot. Compare uhi (403), another word for cover.
words.picture: Giant purple poi wave covering the beach
story_paragraphs: Sunset Beach, winter. A wave rises up 40 feet tall, and it is not water. It is purple. It is poi. Somebody dumped the biggest bowl of poi in history into the ocean, and now it is coming for the beach.
The wave curls high over everyone's heads. People start yelling "POI!" but right at the top the wave gets a hiccup and freezes for one full second. "PO..." freeze... "EE!"
SPLOOSH. It breaks. Poʻi. It covers everything. The cars, the lifeguard tower, the guy selling shave ice, the shave ice. The whole beach is under two feet of sticky purple blanket.
You dig yourself out and lick your arm. Honestly? Not bad. A little sour. Two day poi.

words.say_it: Pull an invisible sheet of plastic over the table. "Oo-hee!"
words.bonus: Uhi is also the word for a yam, a starchy food plant grown across the Pacific. Poʻi (402) is more like a lid on top, uhi is spreading a covering over something.
words.picture: Aunty plastic wrapping the whole house
story_paragraphs: Aunty Pua just bought a roll of plastic wrap one mile long. She has a mission. Cover everything.

She covers the couch. She covers the TV. She covers the rice cooker, the fan, the mailbox and the mailman. Every time she stretches the plastic over something new, it squeaks "OOH... HEE!" Ooh, hee. Uhi.
By lunchtime she has covered the car, the mango tree and the whole house, like a giant leftover plate in the fridge. The neighbors walk by and their voices sound muffled.

The next morning you wake up and try to get out of bed. Squeak. You can't move. She covered you too, tucked in tight like a plate of chow fun. "Ooh-hee!" says the plastic. "Keep you fresh," says Aunty.

words.say_it: Snatch at the air fast, then gasp. "Kaah... EE-lee!"
words.bonus: Kāʻili is a quick grab. Pōā (405) is a full robbery.
words.picture: Car eel snatching fries at drive thru
story_paragraphs: There is an eel living in the cup holder of your car. Nobody knows how it got in there. It is nine feet long, and it is fast.

You pull up to a drive thru. The worker holds out your fries. Before your hand even moves, the eel shoots out the window and SNATCHES them. You scream the longest scream of your life. "CAAAAAR..." Then a little hiccup of shock. "...EEL-EE!" Caaar eely. Kāʻili.
It doesn't stop. It snatches the worker's hat. It snatches a malasada from the car behind you. It snatches the sunglasses off a guy on a moped at the red light. Snatch, snatch, snatch.
By the time you get home, the back seat is full of stolen stuff, and the eel is wearing all the hats.

words.say_it: Pat your empty pockets and wail. "Pohhh-AAAH!"
words.bonus: Pōā can also be the noun, a robber.
words.picture: Masked mongoose gang robbing plate lunch
story_paragraphs: You are sitting at a beach park with the best plate lunch of your life. Two scoop rice, mac salad, kalbi. Then, out of the naupaka bushes, come 30 mongooses wearing tiny black masks.

They rob you. Completely. They take the plate lunch. They take your wallet, your phone, your slippahs, your car keys and the cooler. One of them takes the shirt right off your back and puts it on. They leave you exactly one grain of rice.
You stand there in your shorts and let out the longest scream of your life. "POOOOO'! AAAAAAH!" As in, I am po' now. Poor. AAAAH. Pōā. Both vowels long, because the robbery was that thorough.
Far away in the bushes, you hear 30 tiny mongooses chewing kalbi.

words.say_it: Shake your fist at an invisible goat. "Ho-oh-pee-lee-KEE-ah!"
words.bonus: Pilikia means trouble. In pidgin you hear "No make pilikia," don't make trouble. Hoʻo- turns it into causing the trouble.
words.picture: Goat Pili swallowing the car key
story_paragraphs: Your cousin has a goat named Pili. Pili makes trouble every single day. He eats the laundry. He headbutts the mailbox. He climbs onto the car roof and dents it into a bowl.

Today you have a job interview, and Pili eats your car key. Just swallows it. Gulp. You chase him around the yard yelling "HO! OH! PILI! KEY! AH!" He runs through Aunty's orchids, tips over the pūpū table, jumps the fence and stops traffic on Kamehameha Highway.
Ho, oh, Pili, key, ah. Hoʻopilikia. To bother. To make pilikia, trouble.
The whole neighborhood joins the chase. Pili is having the best day of his life. Three days later the key comes back out on its own. You don't want to talk about it. You take the bus.

words.say_it: Lift both hands up slowly, like raising a chair. "Ho-oh-hee-vah-HEE-vah!"
words.bonus: Hiwahiwa alone means precious, dearly loved.
words.picture: Uncles lifting Tūtū's recliner up high
story_paragraphs: Tūtū turns 100 today, and the whole neighborhood wants to honor her. Not with a card. Not with a cake. Something bigger.

Forty uncles grab the legs of her recliner. She is sitting in it with 60 lei stacked up to her nose. The uncles lift together and chant "HO! OH! HEAVE-AH! HEAVE-AH!" Hee-vah, hee-vah. Up she goes. Above their heads. Above the carport. Level with the mango tree.
They carry her down the street like royalty. Traffic stops. Cars honk. A little kid runs up and offers a spam musubi, and Tūtū raises it high like a trophy.
Every time the uncles get tired, somebody yells "Heave-ah! HEAVE-AH!" and she rises again. That is how you cherish your Tūtū. Hoʻohiwahiwa.

words.say_it: Reach for something tiny with a trembling finger. "Ee... EE-nee!"
words.bonus: ʻIʻini is a strong craving or yearning. Ake (409) is another word for wanting, being eager or yearning for something.
words.picture: Floating toward the last butter mochi
story_paragraphs: There is one tiny piece of butter mochi left at the potluck. It is the size of a dice. You want it more than you have ever wanted anything. More than a new car. More than summer vacation.
You point at it with a shaking finger. Your throat catches. "EE!" Hiccup. "EEEE-NY!" The eeny one. The teeny eeny one. "Ee... EE-nee!"

Your wanting gets so strong that you start to float. Your feet leave the floor. Your eyes turn into two little mochi squares. The whole room goes quiet as you drift across the table toward it, whimpering "ee... EE-nee..." like a puppy at the door.
Just as your fingers reach it, Uncle leans in and eats it. You float there, crying, for three hours.

words.english: to desire, to yearn, to be eager
words.say_it: Put your hand on your heart and sigh at the window. "AH-keh."
words.bonus: Ake is also the word for the liver.
words.picture: Lonely slippah staring at the sea
story_paragraphs: Two slippahs went to Ala Moana Beach. Only one came home. The right slippah was carried off by a wave in 1998.

The left slippah has been sitting in the window by the front door ever since, staring at the ocean. Every sunset it lets out a long sigh. "Aaaah... KEH." Its little rubber heart aches. "My heart... it ACHE, eh."

Ake. Wanting something back so much it aches. The slippah has written 4,000 letters. It dreams about the right slippah every night. Some mornings it hops, alone, all the way to the beach, and just stands in the sand, looking out.
So if you ever find a lonely right slippah on a beach, bring it home. Somebody is waiting.

words.english: to knead, to massage, to press
words.say_it: Knead invisible dough with both hands. "LO-mee, LO-mee."
words.bonus: Lomilomi is Hawaiian massage. Lomi salmon is salted salmon mashed by hand with tomato and onion.
words.picture: Octopus kneading you like dough
story_paragraphs: You go to a massage place in Chinatown. The massage therapist is a giant octopus named Aunty. Eight arms. Every one of them strong like a forklift.

She kneads your back like bread dough. Push, fold, roll. Two arms on your shoulders, two on your legs, one on your head, and three kneading the air just to warm up. You try to say "Lower, please," but you are so squashed it comes out "LOW... ME! LOW... ME!"
Lomi, lomi, lomi. She rolls you out flat like a pizza. She presses you into a ball. She kneads you so long you forget your own name.
After one hour you walk out loose, soft and floppy, like a wet noodle with a smile. You tip her eight dollars. One for each arm.

words.say_it: Press your palm flat down on the table, hard. "Kah-OH-mee!"
words.bonus: Kaomi is pressing straight down. Lomi (410) is kneading and rubbing.
words.picture: Cow sitting on a sandwich
story_paragraphs: There is a food truck in Haleʻiwa that makes the flattest sandwiches on the island. Their secret is not a grill. It is a 1,400 pound cow named Bessie.
You order a grilled cheese. The cook lays the bread down, whistles, and Bessie sits on it. The whole truck tips sideways. The cook yells "COW! OH ME!" Kaomi. Pressed down.

The sandwich comes out as thin as paper. You can read the menu through it. So you ask for another one, extra pressed. Bessie climbs the ladder to the roof of the truck and does a cannonball onto the bread. "COW! OH ME!"
The sandwich goes six inches into the ground. You dig it out with a shovel and eat it anyway. Best sandwich of your life.

words.say_it: Pinch your own earlobe and yelp. "OOO... MEE... ee!"
words.bonus: As a noun, ʻūmiʻi can also mean a clamp or pincers.
words.picture: Car tire crab clamped on your toe
story_paragraphs: You are walking on the reef at low tide, minding your business. A crab the size of a car tire is waiting under a rock. It has been waiting there for eleven years for exactly your big toe.
CLAMP. You scream a long "OOOOOOOOH!" Then your breath catches. "ME!" Catches again. "EE!" Ooooh, me, ee. ʻŪmiʻi.
You hop all the way up the beach with the crab hanging off your foot like a heavy slippah. You shake it. It pinches harder. You try to bribe it with a spam musubi. It pinches harder.

A lifeguard tries to pry it off with a surfboard. The crab clamps the surfboard with its other claw. Now you have a crab, a surfboard and a lifeguard all attached to your foot, hopping together toward the tower.

words.say_it: Scrub the air in fast circles. "Ho-oh-mah-eh-MAH-eh!"
words.bonus: Maʻemaʻe (468) means clean. Add hoʻo- and it means to make clean.
words.picture: Ma pressure washing the whole house
story_paragraphs: Company is coming in ten minutes, and Ma switches into cleaning mode. Her eyes glow. Steam comes out of her ears. She has a mop in one hand, a vacuum in the other, and a pressure washer strapped to her back.

You walk in and ask "Ma, eh?" She doesn't hear you. "MA, EH!" She blasts the couch clean. She vacuums the dog. She scrubs the ceiling. She polishes the goldfish bowl until the goldfish can see its own face.
Ho, oh, Ma, eh, MA, EH! Hoʻomaʻemaʻe. To make clean.
Then she sees your dirty slippah feet. She lifts you by the collar, dips you in the sink, and scrubs behind your ears until they squeak. The doorbell rings. The house is so clean it echoes.

words.say_it: Pin an invisible shirt on a line. "Kow-LAH-ee."
words.bonus: Kaulaʻi lole means to hang clothes out to dry.
words.picture: Wet koala on the clothesline
story_paragraphs: Aunty brings home a koala from a trip. Don't ask. On the very first day it falls into the fishpond. It comes out soaked and smells like a wet carpet.

So Aunty does what she does with anything wet. She hangs it on the clothesline. The koala grabs the line with both arms, because that is what koalas do, and Aunty clips a few clothespins on its fur for style. It swings there in the trade wind, dripping, slowly getting fluffy.
The neighbor looks over the fence and yells "IS THAT A KOALA? EE!" Koala, ee. Kow-LAH-ee. Kaulaʻi. Hung out to dry.
By afternoon it is so dry and fluffy it looks like a cloud. It refuses to come down. Now Aunty hangs her sheets right next to it, and it hugs them.

words.english: to recede, to pull back (of the sea)
words.say_it: Pull both hands back toward your chest slowly. "Mee-MEE-kee."
words.bonus: A real safety lesson. If the ocean suddenly pulls back far from shore, a tsunami may be coming. Get to high ground right away.
words.picture: Ocean pulling back, key on the sand
story_paragraphs: You drop your car key off the end of the pier. Plop. Gone. You stand there with your mouth open.

Then the ocean does something strange. It pulls back. Way back. The water slides away from the beach like someone pulled the plug in a giant bathtub. A hundred feet. Five hundred feet. Half a mile. Fish flop on the sand. And there, glittering way out on the wet reef, is your key.
You yell "ME! ME! KEY!" and start to run for it. Then you stop. Tūtū taught you this one. When the sea pulls back like that, you do not run toward it. You run UP.
So you and everyone on the beach race to high ground, still yelling "Me, me, key!" because you are still sad about the key. Mimiki. The sea pulling back.

words.say_it: Sway and pat the air softly. "Ho-oh-maah-LEE-eh."
words.bonus: Mālie (494) means calm. Hoʻo- makes it to calm someone down.
words.picture: Calming a twelve foot baby at the mall
story_paragraphs: There is a baby at Ala Moana Center who is twelve feet tall, and she is having a tantrum. Her name is Molly. She is throwing strollers. She is kicking the fountain. Security is hiding behind the pretzel stand.

You walk up slowly. You do not yell. You sway side to side and hum, very low and very soft. "Hooo... ohhh... MAAAAH-lee... eh..." Ho, oh, Mah-lee, eh. The long maaah wraps around her like a warm blanket.
Molly stops. Her lip shakes. You keep going. She sits down with a boom that rattles every window in the mall. Her eyes close. She sucks her giant thumb. The whole mall goes silent.
Two thousand shoppers tiptoe out holding their bags over their heads. Hoʻomālie. To calm down, to quiet.

words.say_it: Put a finger to your lips and hiss long. "HAAAH... mow."
words.bonus: Hāmau! works as a command, like Shh! Be quiet! Don't mix it up with hāmama (475), wide open.
words.picture: Librarian hissing 40 cats silent
story_paragraphs: It is 3 in the morning. Outside your window, 40 cats are having a singing contest. "MEOW! MREEEOW! MAAAOW!"

The retired librarian next door steps outside in her robe. She walks to the middle of the street, plants her feet, and lets out one long, giant hiss. "HAAAAAAAAH!" Every cat freezes. The loudest one opens its mouth, and all that comes out is a tiny little "...mow."
Haaa... mow. Hāmau. Hush.

She points one finger at each cat. They sit down in a neat row like kids at church. The dogs stop barking. A gecko on the wall stops chirping and holds its breath. The neighbors' lights go off one by one. She goes back inside. The whole valley sleeps.

words.say_it: Puff out your chest and crow. "Hah-ah-HEH-oh!"
words.bonus: The song Aloha ʻOe starts with Haʻaheo ka ua i nā pali, proudly the rain on the cliffs.
words.picture: Uncle strutting with a tiny fish
story_paragraphs: Uncle catches a fish. It is four inches long. It may be the smallest fish ever caught at Magic Island.

He holds it over his head like an Olympic gold medal. He puffs up his chest until his shirt buttons pop off. He struts down the beach like a rooster, knees high, and crows at every person he passes. "HA! AH! HEY-OHHH!" Ha, ah, hey, oh. Haʻaheo.
He makes everybody take a picture. He calls the newspaper. He has the fish framed. He wears a T-shirt with the fish on it for three years.
He tells the story at every party, and every time the fish gets bigger. At Christmas it was a marlin. By New Year's it was a whale. "HA! AH! HEY-OH!" Proud, proud, proud.

words.english: to be humble; to be low
words.say_it: Bow low and give a tiny laugh. "Hah-ah-HAH-ah."
words.bonus: Haʻaheo (418) is proud, haʻahaʻa is humble. Haʻahaʻa also just means low, like low land.
words.picture: Uncle flat under the limbo bar
story_paragraphs: Remember proud Uncle with the four inch fish? He enters the limbo contest at the family lūʻau, still strutting, still crowing.
Then he meets Tūtū. Tūtū has won the limbo 52 years in a row. She goes under a bar two inches off the ground without spilling her fruit punch.

Uncle goes low. Lower. His back cracks like popcorn. He ends up flat on the grass like a dropped beach towel, and his big rooster crow shrinks into a tiny little laugh. "ha-ah... HA-ah." Haʻahaʻa. Low. Humble.
He crawls out and bows to Tūtū, lower than the bar. The crowd claps. From that day on, when people ask about the fish, Uncle just smiles and says, "Small one."

words.say_it: Pump an invisible jack handle. "Ho-oh-kee-eh-KEE-eh!"
words.bonus: Kiʻekiʻe (448) means high. Hoʻo- makes it to raise something up.
words.picture: Squeaky jack lifting truck to the clouds
story_paragraphs: Uncle wants to look under his truck, so he slides a jack under it. It is an old squeaky jack. Every pump screams "kee-eh... KEE-EH!"

Pump. "Kee-eh!" The truck goes up a foot. Pump. "KEE-EH!" Up past the carport roof. Uncle is enjoying this. He keeps pumping. The truck rises above the mango tree, above the power lines, above the clouds. A plane flies under it. Birds build a nest in the tire well.
"Ho, oh, kee-eh, KEE-EH!" Hoʻokiʻekiʻe. To lift up, to raise high.
Now the truck is so high the neighbors on Maui can see it. Uncle stands underneath with a flashlight, squinting up at the tiny dot. "Yup," he says. "Needs one oil change."

words.say_it: Pinch your nose and hold a pillow far away. "Pee-LOW!"
words.bonus: People use pilau in pidgin too, for stink, and for somebody acting rotten, as in "That's pilau, brah."
words.picture: Stinky pillow held with tongs
story_paragraphs: Your brother has had the same pillow since fifth grade. It has never been washed. Not once. Not in 14 years.
It smells like old fish, gym socks and a dead mongoose had a party inside it. It is yellow. It is crunchy. Flies fly toward it and then faint. When he leaves it in the sun, the grass under it dies.
Your sister finally picks it up with barbecue tongs, holds her breath, and runs outside screaming "PILLOW! PEE-LOW! PILAU!" She throws it in the ocean. The ocean throws it back.
So she buries it in the backyard, six feet deep. Nothing grows there now. But on hot nights, when the wind is right, you can still smell it.

words.english: to smell sweet, to be fragrant
words.say_it: Sniff a flower, then sing it out. "AH-lah!"
words.bonus: The opposite of pilau (421). Watch the ʻokina. ʻAla is fragrant, but ala means path or road.
words.picture: Whole bus singing at a plumeria lei
story_paragraphs: You are on a crowded city bus on a hot afternoon. It smells like the bus. Then a lady gets on wearing a lei made of 900 plumeria and pīkake flowers.

The smell hits you like a wave. You catch your breath, close your eyes, breathe in, and cannot stop yourself. You belt it out like an opera singer. "AAAAH... LAAAA!" Everybody on the bus breathes in too. "AAAAH... LAAAA!" The driver sings. A guy in the back with headphones sings. Ah, la. ʻAla.

By the next stop the whole bus is a choir, floating two inches off the road, carried by the sweet smell. People at the bus stop sniff the air and start singing too. The lady just smiles and fixes her lei.

words.say_it: Tap an invisible clipboard and sing. "Ho-oh-laah-LAAH!"
words.bonus: Lālā means branch. A good plan branches out every which way.
words.picture: Aunty's wall of lūʻau plans
story_paragraphs: Aunty is planning your cousin's first birthday lūʻau. The baby is two months old. The party is ten months away. Aunty has been planning for a year already.

The whole living room wall is covered in charts. A seating plan. A food plan. A parking plan. A backup plan for the backup plan. She has a color coded pen for every aunty and a map showing where each cooler goes. As she writes, she sings, holding each note forever. "Ho, oh, LAAAA... LAAAA!"
Hoʻolālā. To plan. The two long laaa's are the two long kahakō.

The big day comes. It pours rain. Aunty calmly pulls Plan R, the rain plan, from folder 47. Three hundred guests eat under 30 tents that were already set up. Nobody gets wet. "LAAA... LAAA," she sings.

words.say_it: Set an invisible stone down firmly. "Ho-oh-KOO-moo!"
words.bonus: Kumu means base, foundation or source, and also teacher.
words.picture: Pigeon and cow laying the first stone
story_paragraphs: A long time ago, a pigeon and a cow wash up together on a raft on an empty island. There is nothing there. No houses, no roads, no plate lunch.

The pigeon says "COO." The cow says "MOO." They look at each other and decide to start a town. The pigeon lays down the very first stone. The cow sits on it to make it level. "COO!" "MOO!" Koo, moo. Hoʻokumu. To found, to set up from the base.
They build a school, a post office and a very small bank. The pigeon is the mayor. The cow is the whole police force.
Today 12,000 people live there. In the town square stands a bronze statue of a pigeon on a cow's head. Every morning the town bell rings. "Coo. Moo."

words.say_it: Cup your hands around your mouth. "Koo-KAH-lah!"
words.bonus: Kū means to stand. Picture standing up tall on the roof when you kūkala.
words.picture: Uncle proclaiming mangoes by megaphone
story_paragraphs: Uncle's mango tree finally has ripe mangoes. This is the biggest news in the history of the valley. So at 5 in the morning he climbs onto the carport roof with a megaphone the size of a canoe.
He holds the first sound forever. "KOOOOOOOO..." Dogs wake up. Chickens fall off fences. Then "CALL-AH EVERYBODY! MANGO TIME!" Kooo, call-ah. Kūkala. To proclaim, to announce to the public.
People hear it in Kaimukī. They hear it on Maui. A fishing boat 60 miles out turns around.

By six there is a line down the block with empty bags. Uncle announces every single mango as he hands it out. "KOOOO... CALL-AH! THIS ONE FOR AUNTY LEI!" A news helicopter hovers overhead to catch every word.

words.say_it: Point back and forth between you and a friend. "Ho-oh-kah-ah-EE-keh."
words.bonus: Inside it hides ʻike, to see or to know. Communicating is passing ʻike back and forth.
words.picture: Parrot, mouse, baby and uncle in elevator
story_paragraphs: Four strangers are stuck in an elevator at the Ala Moana building. A parrot, a mouse, a tired baby, and your uncle, who only talks in sighs. Nobody speaks the same language. They need to communicate to get out.
The parrot says "CAW!" Uncle says "AH." The mouse says "EEK!" The baby says "EH?" Caw, ah, eek, eh. And somehow, it works. They understand each other perfectly.
The parrot explains the button is stuck. Uncle sighs that he has a butter knife. The mouse squeaks that he can fit behind the panel. The baby asks everyone to please hurry, she needs a nap.
Ten minutes later the doors slide open. They walk out chattering a mile a minute in four different noises. Hoʻokaʻaʻike. To communicate.

words.say_it: Slide one hand along the other like a blade on a stone. "Hoh-OY!"
words.bonus: ʻOi (428) means sharp. Hō- in front makes it cause, so hōʻoi is to make sharp. Hoʻokala is another word for sharpening.
words.picture: Swap meet man sharpening a whole car
story_paragraphs: There is a man at the swap meet with a sign that says I SHARPEN ANYTHING. He has a grinding wheel as big as a Ferris wheel. You walk over to ask about scissors. He sees your car.

Before you can stop him, he pushes your whole car against the wheel. Sparks fly for a block. "HOOOOOOO..." he howls, holding the note the whole time like a man on a roller coaster. Then he steps back and points. The front bumper now comes to a point like a kitchen knife. "OY!"
Hooo, oy. Hōʻoi. To sharpen.

You pay him twelve dollars and drive home. The car slices through traffic cones like butter. It splits a coconut clean in half at a red light. You pull into the driveway and it cuts right through the garage door. Very sharp. Very bad for parking.

words.english: to be sharp; to be the best
words.say_it: Hold up an invisible knife, tiny gasp, then say it. "OY!"
words.bonus: ʻOi aku means more than, surpassing. ʻOi aku ka maikaʻi means better.
words.picture: Old chef's knife cutting a sunbeam
story_paragraphs: There is a knife contest in Hilo. Every chef on the island brings their sharpest knife. One slices a tomato in midair. One cuts a single sheet of paper into 40 sheets.

Then a tiny 93 year old retired sushi chef steps up with his old kitchen knife. He holds it to the light. It is so sharp it cuts the sunbeam in half, and half the room goes dark. The whole crowd catches its breath and gasps "OY!"
He waves it gently. It splits the wind. A fly zooms past and comes out the other side with the best haircut of its life.
The judges don't even vote. They just yell "OY!" and hand him the trophy. The sharpest one is the best one. ʻOi. Sharp. The best.

words.say_it: Slap your knee and cackle. "Ho-oh-mah-keh-AH-kah!"
words.bonus: ʻAkaʻaka means to laugh.
words.picture: Gecko doing stand up on the rice cooker
story_paragraphs: There is a gecko living behind your fridge who thinks he is a comedian. Every night at 10 he climbs onto the counter, taps the rice cooker like a microphone, and tells jokes.

"Why don't geckos pay rent? Because we just stick around!" Terrible. But the way he tells it, you laugh so hard rice comes out your nose. Then he yells his catchphrase, "Ho, oh, MAKE a... AH-KAH!" which is how he says make a cackle. Everybody cackles. "AH-KAH! AH-KAH!"
Ho, oh, make a, ah-kah. Hoʻomakeʻaka. To be funny, to make people laugh.
By the end of the week he has a real show. Forty geckos come to watch. They sit on the walls chirping with laughter, and one laughs so hard it falls into the sink.

words.english: to be a hypocrite, to act fake
words.say_it: Flash fake money, then hide it behind your back. "Ho-oh-kah-MAH-nee."
words.bonus: Don't mix it up with hoʻokano, which means stuck up or conceited.
words.picture: Fake gold cardboard car melting in rain
story_paragraphs: Your neighbor gives a speech at every block party. "Never waste money on fancy things," he says, wagging his finger. "Money is for saving." Then he walks home and parks a shiny gold sports car in his driveway.

Except it isn't real. It is made of cardboard, painted gold, and covered in fake money he printed himself. There's no engine. He sits inside and pushes it with his feet. He waves at everybody yelling "HO! OH! CAR! MONEY!"
Then it rains. The cardboard melts. The fake bills slide off in a gold puddle. There he is, sitting in the rain, still pedaling with his feet, still pretending. "Car... money..." he whispers.
Hoʻokamani. Kah-MAH-nee. Fake. Saying one thing, doing another.

words.say_it: Scoop invisible breadfruit into a pile. "Hoh-oo-loo-OO-loo!"
words.bonus: ʻUlu (breadfruit) is a separate word, but piling up ʻulu makes a great hook for collecting and summing up.
words.picture: Breadfruit pile as tall as a church
story_paragraphs: A storm blows through Kona in the night. In the morning, 4,000 breadfruit are scattered all over the neighborhood. On roofs. In pools. One is on top of a stop sign. One is inside a mailbox.

Your job is to collect every single one and add them up. You drag a red wagon everywhere. Each time you find one you yell "HO! ʻULU! ʻULU!" with a catch in your throat, because they are heavy. You roll them all into one giant pile at the park.
By sunset the pile is as tall as a church. You climb to the top and give the neighborhood your summary. "Total. Three thousand nine hundred ninety nine. One is still in Uncle's truck."
Hōʻuluʻulu. Collected, counted, summed up.

words.say_it: Wave everyone in with both arms. "Aah-ko-ah-KO-ah!"
words.bonus: Don't mix it up with kōkua (help), which also sounds like cocoa. ʻĀkoakoa is when everyone comes together.
words.picture: Grandpa calling 300 cousins with cocoa
story_paragraphs: The family is spread all over the island. Cousins in Waiʻanae, cousins in Kāneʻohe, and one cousin who has been lost somewhere in Waikīkī since 2019.
Grandpa steps onto the porch with a pot of hot cocoa the size of a hot tub. He bangs a ladle on it and hollers "AAAAAH! COCOA! COCOA!"

Within four seconds, 300 people assemble on his lawn. They come on bikes, in trucks, on surfboards. One uncle arrives by parachute. The lost cousin shows up in a wetsuit, still holding a snorkel. Everyone gathers in one big circle with their cups held out.
Ah, cocoa, cocoa. ʻĀkoakoa. To gather. The long aaah at the start is Grandpa's lungs warming up.

words.english: to be loyal, to stand firm
words.say_it: Plant your feet wide and cross your arms. "Koo-PAH-ah."
words.bonus: Kū means to stand and paʻa means firm or stuck. Stand stuck.
words.picture: Pa holding umbrella through a wave
story_paragraphs: Pa sets up the family beach umbrella at Waimānalo at 7 in the morning and says, "Nobody takes this spot." Then the wind comes.

Forty mile an hour gusts. Pa grabs the pole and plants his feet. A beach cleaning tractor rolls up and beeps. Pa does not move. A giant wave hits him, soaks him, and goes around him. Pa does not move. A tour group asks him to scoot for a photo. Pa does not move.
The kids cheer from the car. "COOL PA! AH!" Cool, Pa, ah. Kūpaʻa. Stand firm. Loyal to the spot, loyal to the family.
At sunset everyone else has gone home. Pa is still standing there, sandy and grinning, holding the umbrella like a flag. "Told you," he says.

words.say_it: Fling your arms open like a door bursting. "Koo-oh-KO-ah!"
words.bonus: Lā Kūʻokoʻa, November 28, marks the day in 1843 when Britain and France recognized the Hawaiian Kingdom as an independent nation.
words.picture: Cuckoo bird breaking out of the clock
story_paragraphs: For 80 years a little wooden bird has lived in Grandma's cuckoo clock. Every hour the door opens, it sings "coo-coo," and the door slams shut. Every hour. For 80 years.
Tonight at midnight it pops out, and something is different. It sings "COO... OH..." and then it breaks right out of the clock. "...KO-AH!" It flies out the window, free.
Coo, oh, KO-ah. Kūʻokoʻa. Independent.

The bird gets its own apartment in Mōʻiliʻili. It gets a job at a bakery. It buys its own groceries, does its own taxes and pays its rent on time. Now it sings whenever it wants, which is mostly at a quarter to four in the afternoon. Nobody tells that bird what to do anymore.

words.say_it: Hold both hands out like a scale and level them. "Ho-oh-kow-LEE-keh."
words.bonus: Like (492) means alike or the same. Kaulike means equal or fair.
words.picture: Barber leveling two matching cowlicks
story_paragraphs: A kid walks into a barbershop in Kalihi with the worst cowlick in history. The left side of his hair sticks straight up like a palm tree. The right side is flat. He looks like he's always leaning.

The barber is very serious about being fair. He can't fix the cowlick, so he gives the other side one too. Now both sides stick up, but the left is taller. So he adds gel to the right. Now the right is taller. Back and forth, back and forth, with a level and a ruler, muttering "Cowlick-eh... cowlick-eh..."
Ho, oh, COWLICK-eh. Hoʻokaulike. To make it fair, to balance.
After three hours the kid has two perfectly equal cowlicks, like horns. The barber checks them with a laser level. Dead even.

words.say_it: Hold out your open hand like you're giving away your keys. "Lo-ko-mai-KAH-ee."
words.bonus: Loko means inside and maikaʻi means good. Good on the inside.
words.picture: Uncle handing his car keys to a neighbor
story_paragraphs: Uncle Kimo is the most generous man in Kaʻaʻawa. If you say you like his shirt, he takes it off and gives it to you. If you say his dog is cute, you walk home with a dog.
One day a neighbor says, "Nice car." Uncle hands over the keys. The whole street screams "LOCO!" Uncle just shrugs and says, "My car? EH! Take!" Loco, my car, eh. Lokomaikaʻi.
He keeps going. He gives his canoe to the canoe club, his ladder to the church, and his lunch to a hungry cat. By sunset he is sitting on the beach in borrowed shorts, happy as a clam.
Then 40 neighbors show up, each one carrying something back for him, plus a plate lunch. That is how kindness works around here.

words.say_it: Hug an invisible pile of food to your chest. "Aah-LOO-noo!"
words.bonus: The opposite is lokomaikaʻi (436), generous.
words.picture: Greedy loon sitting on the prime rib
story_paragraphs: A loon bird escapes from a zoo on the continent and somehow ends up at a hotel buffet in Waikīkī. It is greedy beyond belief.

It stuffs its beak with every crab leg on the table. It hides shrimp under both wings. It drags the whole prime rib to the corner, sits on it, and hisses at anyone who comes near. The dessert table disappears down its neck. It is now shaped like a beach ball.
The manager runs out and yells "AAAH! A LOON! OOH!" Aaah, loon, oo. ʻĀlunu. Greedy. That long aaah is the manager seeing the empty buffet.
The loon doesn't care. It waddles out the front door dragging the chocolate fountain behind it by the cord, burping. It leaves one sprig of parsley for the other 200 guests.

words.say_it: Move your hands in a fast blur like stringing flowers. "Eh-LEH-oo!"
words.bonus: ʻEleu is quick and full of energy. Its opposite is moloā (439), lazy.
words.picture: Blur of lei flying through the airport
story_paragraphs: There is a lei maker at the airport named Aunty Mapuana. She is so fast your eyes can't follow her hands. Flower, needle, string, done. One lei per second.

A plane lands with 400 passengers. She yells "EH! LEI! OOH!" and a blur of flowers shoots across the terminal. Every single passenger has a lei on before their foot touches the carpet. Eh, lei, ooh. ʻEleu.
She doesn't stop. She makes lei for the pilots, the luggage, the security dog and the parking meters. She puts a tiny lei on a pigeon as it flies past.
Then she sits down and sips her coffee. It is still hot. The whole thing took eleven seconds.

words.say_it: Slump way down in your chair and sigh. "Mo-lo-AAAH."
words.bonus: You hear it in pidgin too, as in "No be moloā!"
words.picture: Brother sinking under the house
story_paragraphs: Your brother lies down on the couch Saturday morning. By noon he is lower. "Mo' low," he sighs, and slides deeper into the cushions. By dinner he is under the couch. "Mo' low... aaaaah."

He does not get up for a week. He slides under the rug. He slides through the floorboards. Now he is under the house, lying in the dirt with the geckos, eating chips you drop down to him through a crack. "Mo' low... AAAAAAH."
Mo' low, aah. Moloā. Lazy. That long aaah at the end is the sound of someone who has decided to never get up again.
Ma finally calls a construction crew to dig him out. When they reach him, he asks if they can carry him to the car.

words.say_it: Flex both arms and grunt. "Ee-KAI-kah!"
words.bonus: Ikaika is also a popular name for boys in Hawaiʻi.
words.picture: Aunty carrying twelve kayaks on her head
story_paragraphs: Aunty Leilani is 72, and she is the strongest person in Kailua. Every morning she walks to the beach carrying her kayak. Not on a cart. On her head.

Then she started carrying more. Two kayaks. Five kayaks. Today she strolls down the beach with twelve kayaks stacked on her head, a canoe under each arm, and her grandson riding in the top kayak, waving. Tourists scream "EEE! KAYAK-AH!" Ee, kai, kah. Ikaika.

She sets them all down gently and paddles to the Mokulua islands and back before breakfast. On the way home she carries a stalled car out of the road and parks it for the owner. She is not even breathing hard. Strong.

words.say_it: Let your arms hang limp like noodles. "Naah-vah-lee-VAH-lee."
words.bonus: The opposite of ikaika (440), strong.
words.picture: Wally pinned under a single leaf
story_paragraphs: Meet Wally. Wally is the weakest man in the world. His arms are wet noodles. His legs are wet noodles. He tries to open a jar of pickles, and the jar wins.

Today Wally is trying to lift the TV remote. He grunts. He sweats. His face turns purple. The remote does not move. His wife walks by and sighs "NAAAH, Wally. Wally." like she has said it ten thousand times. Naah, Wally Wally. Nāwaliwali. Weak.

A single leaf falls on Wally and pins him to the grass for an hour. A gentle breeze pushes him into the neighbor's yard. A butterfly lands on his shoulder, and he tips over. Wally lies there and sighs. He's used to it.

words.english: to be good, to be well
words.say_it: Give a big thumbs up, voice cracking a little. "Mai-KAH-ee!"
words.bonus: Ask Pehea ʻoe? (How are you?) and the usual answer is Maikaʻi. (Good.)
words.picture: Proud dad yelling My Kai at the park
story_paragraphs: A dad at the park keeps yelling "MY KAI!" His son Kai is the best kid anyone has ever seen.

Kai helps a grandma cross the street. Then he helps her cross back, because she forgot her purse. He returns 40 shopping carts in a rainstorm. He gives his last spam musubi to a hungry dog. He picks up trash off the whole beach and sorts it by color.
Every time Kai does something good, his dad's chest puffs up and he yells "MY KAI!" Then his breath catches, he tears up, and a little "EE!" squeaks out. My Kai, ee. Maikaʻi. Good.
By sunset the whole park is chanting along. "My Kai-ee! My Kai-ee!" Kai is embarrassed. He goes to help somebody fix a flat tire.

words.say_it: Frame your face with your hands and pose. "NAH-nee."
words.bonus: Nani ʻoe means you are beautiful.
words.picture: Glowing nanny goat winning the pageant
story_paragraphs: The county fair holds a beauty contest for goats. Most of them look like goats. Then a nanny goat walks out on stage.

She is so beautiful the stage lights get brighter by themselves. Her coat shines like silk. Flowers bloom wherever her hooves touch the floor. A rainbow appears indoors, right over her head. The judges cry. The other goats cry. The farmer who owns her faints into a hay bale.
The announcer grabs the microphone and can only say one thing, over and over. "NANNY! NANNY!" Nani, nani. Beautiful.
She wins every prize at the fair, including Best Pie, which she did not enter. As she walks off the stage, three photographers follow her all the way home.

words.english: to be big; to be many
words.say_it: Stretch your arms as wide as they go. "NOO-ee!"
words.bonus: Mahalo nui loa means thank you very much.
words.picture: Giant gnu towering over Waikīkī
story_paragraphs: The Honolulu Zoo gets a gnu. On the first day it is normal gnu size. Then it eats. All the hay, all the bananas and the zookeeper's lunch. The next morning it is the size of a bus.
The zookeeper screams "GNU! EEE!" Gnu, ee. Nui. Big.

It keeps growing. By Friday its head is above the clouds. When it sneezes, it rains in Kaimukī. And it gets worse, because nui also means many. The gnu has 400 babies. Four hundred giant gnus, all standing on Kalākaua Avenue, all going "GNU! EEE!"
Traffic is terrible, but honestly, not that much worse than usual.

words.say_it: Squeeze your thumb and finger almost together and squeak. "Lee-ee-LEE-ee."
words.bonus: The opposite of nui (444), big.
words.picture: Tiny Lee on a musubi wrapper
story_paragraphs: Remember cousin Lee from kahuli, the one who flipped the canoe for a chip? He finds a strange glowing chip on the beach and eats it. Then he starts to shrink.
Now Lee is the size of a grain of rice. He lives inside a spam musubi wrapper. He surfs on a drop of water. A gecko keeps looking at him like he is lunch.

You can barely hear him anymore. He stands on the kitchen table waving his tiny arms and squeaking "LEE! ee! LEE! ee!" which is how he says his name now. Every word comes out with two tiny hiccups in it.
Lee, ee, Lee, ee. Liʻiliʻi. Small.
You feed him one grain of rice for dinner. He is full for a week.

words.say_it: Slide your hand way, way out in front of you. "LOOOH-ee-hee!"
words.bonus: Lōʻihi was the name of the undersea volcano growing off the Big Island, now called Kamaʻehuakanaloa.
words.picture: Nine mile long water slide
story_paragraphs: The water park opens a new slide. It starts at the top of a mountain and ends in the ocean nine miles away. It is the longest slide ever built.

You sit down at the top and push off. "LOOOOOOOOOO..." You slide past cows. Past a school. Past a whole town. "OOOOOOOOOO..." You stop for lunch on a flat part. You take a nap. Still sliding. "OOOOOOOOO..." Two days later you finally shoot out the bottom and hit the water. "EE! HEE!"
Looooo, ee, hee. Lōʻihi. Long. That long ō is the whole nine miles.
You climb out, wet and happy. The lifeguard is seven feet tall. He points at the line for the next ride. It is also very lōʻihi. It is a week long.

words.say_it: Hold your hand down near your knee. "Poh-KO-leh."
words.bonus: The opposite of lōʻihi (446), long or tall.
words.picture: Two foot rodeo clown poking a bull
story_paragraphs: At the rodeo in Waimea, the new rodeo clown is two feet tall. His hat is bigger than he is. The bull can't even find him.

The bull charges straight over his head. The little clown pops up and pokes the bull in the ankle with one finger. The crowd jumps to its feet. "POOOOKE! OLÉ!" Poke, olé. Pōkole. Short. Hold that pooo long, because it's the only long thing about him.
The bull spins around, confused. It looks left. It looks right. The clown is standing between its front hooves, waving a red napkin. "Poke! Olé!"
He wins the whole rodeo. His trophy is taller than he is, so the trophy carries him out.

words.say_it: Point straight up at the sky. "Kee-eh-KEE-eh!"
words.bonus: Hoʻokiʻekiʻe (420) means to raise something up high.
words.picture: Fish kite whistling past the moon
story_paragraphs: Your little sister gets a fish shaped kite with a whistle on it. Every time it climbs, the whistle screams "KEE-EH! KEE-EH!"

She lets out the string. The kite goes over the trees. "KEE-EH!" Over the clouds. Airplanes swerve. "KEE-EH!" She has 40 miles of string. It goes past the moon. Astronauts on the space station look out the window and see a fish kite fly by, screaming.
Kee-eh, kee-eh. Kiʻekiʻe. High.
She reels it in for dinner. It takes three days. When it finally comes down, it is covered in frost, and a note is taped to the tail. It says, "Nice kite."

words.say_it: Hop from foot to foot on invisible hot sand. "VEH-lah! VEH-lah!"
words.bonus: Wela ka hao, the iron is hot, is a saying for a wild, good time.
words.picture: Hot sand dance on black sand
story_paragraphs: It is August. It is noon. You are at a black sand beach on the Big Island, and your slippahs are in the car, 200 feet away.

You take one step. Your foot sizzles like bacon. "VEH!" You hop to the other foot. "LAH!" VEH! LAH! VEH! LAH! You are doing a hot sand dance in front of 60 tourists, and they think it's a show. They start clapping to the beat.
Like "well, AH!" with a V. Wela. Hot. So hot.

Halfway to the car you pass a raw egg someone dropped. It is fried. Sunny side up. A mynah bird is eating it with a tiny fork. You give up on the car and dive into the ocean instead, and the water hisses and steams around you.

words.say_it: Hug yourself, shiver, and let your teeth chatter. "Ah-noo-AH-noo."
words.bonus: The opposite of wela (449), hot.
words.picture: Frozen in shorts on Mauna Kea
story_paragraphs: You drive up Mauna Kea in winter wearing shorts and a tank top. Big mistake. At the top there is snow and wind, and you are the only person without a jacket.
Your teeth start to chatter. They chatter so hard they make words. "AH-NOO-AH-NOO! AH-NOO-AH-NOO!" Ah, noo, ah, noo. Anuanu. Cold.
Icicles grow from your nose. Your shorts freeze solid and stand up by themselves. Your eyebrows turn white. A kid builds a snowman next to you, then looks closer and realizes you ARE a snowman.
You shuffle back to the car like a penguin, still chattering. You turn the heater all the way up. It takes until Hilo for your teeth to stop.

words.say_it: Rub your hands together over a cozy fire. "Mah-HAH-nah."
words.bonus: Mahana is nice warm. Wela (449) is too hot and anuanu (450) is cold.
words.picture: Giant fluffy dog warming you in bed
story_paragraphs: You get home from Mauna Kea still frozen. You crawl into bed under six blankets and you are still an ice cube. Your teeth are still going ah-noo, ah-noo.
Ma pokes her head in and hollers "HANNAH!" Hannah is the family dog, a 200 pound fluffy mountain dog. She thunders down the hall and flops right on top of you.
Warm. Instantly warm. Not hot, not cold. Just right, like a heater made of fur that snores. You mumble "Ma... Hannah..." and drift off smiling.
Ma, Hannah. Mahana. Warm.
In the morning you wake up toasty. Hannah is still lying on you. You can't move. You don't care one bit.

words.say_it: Open an invisible box, gasp, close it, open again. "HO-oo! HO-oo!"
words.bonus: Hana hou! means do it again. It's how you shout encore in Hawaiʻi.
words.picture: Opening a new shoe box again and again
story_paragraphs: Your little cousin Keoni just got brand new shoes. They are so white they glow. He opens the box and yells "HO! OOOO!"
Then he closes the box. Then he opens it again. "HO! OOOO!" He can't stop. They're new every time. He takes them out, smells them, puts them back. "HO! OOO!" Again. Again. Again.
He wears them to the store. Every time he looks down, "HO! OOO!" Strangers start joining in. By closing time the whole store shouts it every time he takes a step. Ho, oo. Hou. New. And again.
At midnight you hear it through the wall. He's opening the box one more time.

words.say_it: Cough like an old engine starting. "Kah... HEE... ko!"
words.bonus: Hula kahiko is the older, traditional style of hula. Hula ʻauana is the modern style.
words.picture: Ancient rusty truck coughing to life
story_paragraphs: The oldest truck in Hawaiʻi lives in a farmer's yard in Waimānalo. It is so old it came with a spot to tie a horse. The rust has rust. A mango tree is growing up through the floor.
Every morning the farmer turns the key and the truck coughs like a grumpy old man. "KAH! HEE! KO!" Kah, hee, ko. Kahiko. Old. Ancient.

The license plate is a carved stone. The radio only plays one station, and it is the news from 1920. The farmer says his great great grandpa bought it used. Top speed is five miles an hour. Chickens pass it.
But every morning, "KAH! HEE! KO!" and off they go, one more time.

words.say_it: Sink back into your chair and sigh happily. "Oh-loo-OH-loo."
words.bonus: Ke ʻoluʻolu ʻoe means please (literally, if you would be so kind).
words.picture: Singing recliner lulling a whole store
story_paragraphs: There is a recliner at a furniture store in Kapolei that nobody can get out of. It is the most comfortable chair on earth. It is soft, it is warm, and it smells like fresh laundry.
You sit down. It shapes itself to your back. A tiny voice inside the cushion starts to sing. "Oh... LULL-oh-LULL... oh LULL-oh-LULL..." Oh, lull, oh, lull. ʻOluʻolu.

Your shoulders melt. Your troubles float away. The salesman is asleep in the next chair. So is a security guard, three kids and a delivery driver still holding a box. The whole store is sleeping and smiling.
The chair is so pleasant, so kind, that when the store closes it gently tucks a blanket over you.

words.say_it: Tap your temple with one finger. "Ah-kah-MAI."
words.bonus: Akamai is used in local pidgin too, as in "Eh, you akamai, brah!"
words.picture: Mynah bird doing math homework
story_paragraphs: There is a mynah bird at the bus stop in Kalihi who is smarter than everybody. He does the crossword in pen. He fixes the broken crosswalk light with a paper clip. He tells a lost man which bus to take and shows him a shortcut.

A kid is crying over his math homework. The mynah hops down, looks at the page, and squawks every answer in order. Then he explains fractions using a pizza. The kid's mouth drops open. "AH-KAH-MYNAH!" Akamai. Smart.
By noon there is a line down the block of people asking about taxes, car loans and how to cook rice without a rice cooker. The mynah charges one french fry per question. He's retired by Friday.

words.english: to be wrong, to make a mistake
words.say_it: Make an X with your arms and buzz. "HEH-vah!"
words.bonus: Hewa can also mean a wrong in the moral sense. Its opposite is pono (457).
words.picture: Wrong answer buzzer dropping you in poi
story_paragraphs: You are on a game show, and you are terrible. The host asks, "What color is the sky?" You say, "Tuesday."
A giant buzzer goes off. "HEHHHH-VAAAHHH!" Heh, vah. Hewa. Wrong.
The floor tips and you slide into a tank of cold poi. You climb out. Next question. "How many legs does a chicken have?" You say, "Seven." "HEHHH-VAAAHH!" Into the poi again.

You get every single question wrong. By the end the studio is covered in poi, the host is quietly crying, and the audience is chanting along with the buzzer. "HEH-VAH! HEH-VAH!" You go home with the grand prize, which is the buzzer.

words.say_it: Push an invisible wallet away, then stand up tall. "PO-no."
words.bonus: The state motto uses it. Ua mau ke ea o ka ʻāina i ka pono, the life of the land is perpetuated in righteousness.
words.picture: Returning a found wallet, Po', no
story_paragraphs: You are broke. Totally po'. Your pocket has a button and some lint in it. Then, on the sidewalk outside the drugstore, you find a wallet with 900 dollars inside.
Your stomach says take it. That's 900 malasadas. A little voice in your head whispers "you're po'..." and then you say out loud, very firm, "Po'... NO." Po', no. Pono.
You walk it to the address on the ID. It belongs to a tiny old lady. She hugs you so hard your back cracks straight.
Suddenly everything in your life lines up. Your posture is perfect. Your checkbook balances. The picture frames in your room hang level by themselves. Doing the right thing feels exactly right.

words.say_it: Slice your hand forward in a perfectly straight line. "Po-lo-LAY."
words.bonus: Say Pololei! when someone gets an answer right. It means correct.
words.picture: Aunty laying a 900 foot pole straight
story_paragraphs: Aunty Rose can lay anything down perfectly straight. She has never owned a ruler. She just squints.
The city asks her to put down a 900 foot pole along Kalākaua Avenue. She picks it up, squints once, and lays it down. "POLE-oh-LAY." Pole, o, lay. Pololei. Straight.

Engineers come with lasers to check. The beams line up exactly. Not off by a hair. So they quiz her too. "What is 47 times 12?" "Five sixty-four." Correct. "Is this line straight?" "Pololei." Correct again.
Now she lines up the plate lunch line at the beach park every weekend. It's so straight you can look through 200 heads from one end to the other.

words.english: to be light (not heavy); to be quick
words.say_it: Blow a feather off your palm. "Maah-MAAH!"
words.bonus: The opposite, heavy, is kaumaha, which also means sad.
words.picture: Light mama running across the ocean
story_paragraphs: Your mama weighs about as much as a paper plate. When the trade winds blow, she has to hold on to the mailbox. She is also the fastest person in Waipahu.

She runs to the store so quick and so light she leaves no footprints. She runs across the top of the swimming pool without getting wet. When she's late for a lūʻau on Molokaʻi, she just runs across the ocean, hopping from wave to wave, and gets there before the plane.
People on the beach look up and shout "MAAAA-MAAAA!" as she floats by like a kite. Māmā. Light and quick. Two long vowels, like the wind carrying her.
At the party, she lifts a whole roast pig and it feels light too.

words.say_it: Squint into the dark like you lost your cat. "Eh-leh-EH-leh."
words.bonus: Pōʻeleʻele (484) is the dark of night. You can see ʻeleʻele hiding inside it.
words.picture: Pitch black cat dimming the room
story_paragraphs: The Nakamura family has a cat named Ellie. Ellie is black. Not dark gray. Not almost black. Ellie is so black that when she walks into a room, the lights go dim.

She sits on the white couch, and it looks like somebody cut a hole in the couch. She stares at a birthday candle and the candle goes out. You try to take her picture, and the phone shows nothing but two yellow eyes floating in space.
Everybody calls her with a little catch in the throat. "Eh! Ellie! EH-leh!" ʻEleʻele. Black.
At night the family can only find her by her purr. Even her shadow has a shadow.

words.say_it: Throw a punch, then raise your arm. "Keh-oh-KEH-oh!"
words.bonus: Keʻokeʻo is white and ʻeleʻele (460) is black.
words.picture: Glowing white rice boxer, K.O.
story_paragraphs: It is the big fight at the arena downtown. In one corner stands a boxer made completely of white rice. Not brown rice. Sticky white rice, packed tight, the color of a brand new sheet of paper.
He is so white the crowd has to wear sunglasses. Under the lights he glows like the full moon. His opponent can't even look at him. He squints, swings, and misses by a foot.
The rice boxer throws one punch. Rice everywhere. The other guy goes down. The ref counts to ten and yells "K.O.! K.O.!" Kay-oh, kay-oh. Keʻokeʻo. White.
The whole arena is covered in white rice like snow. The champ holds up his belt, missing a little bit of his shoulder. Somebody in row nine eats it with shoyu.

words.say_it: Fan your hot red cheeks. "Oo-lah-OO-lah!"
words.bonus: The shorter form ʻula also means red.
words.picture: Sunburned visitor glowing red
story_paragraphs: A visitor from the continent falls asleep on Waikīkī Beach at 8 in the morning. No sunscreen. He wakes up at 5 in the afternoon.

He is red. Not pink. RED. Red like a fire truck, like a cherry, like the inside of a watermelon. Boats think he is a warning light and turn around. A bull on a ranch 40 miles away sees him glowing and starts to charge.
He stands up and walks down the beach, and everyone he passes stares and says "OOOH-la, OOOH-la!" Ooh la, ooh la. ʻUlaʻula. Red.
He goes back to his hotel. He is so red the elevator thinks he is the emergency button and stops on every floor.

words.english: to be dark blue or deep green
words.say_it: Cup your hands like a whale singing through the water. "Oo-lee-OO-lee."
words.bonus: Don't mix it up with ʻulīʻulī, the feathered gourd rattle used in hula.
words.picture: Humpback singing in deep blue water
story_paragraphs: You are diving off Kona, and you go deep. The water changes from light blue to blue to dark blue to deep green, the color of a swimming pool at midnight.

Out of the dark, a humpback whale the size of a school bus glides up to your mask. It looks at you with one huge eye. Then it sings. "OOOO-lee... OOOO-lee..." Oo, lee, oo, lee. Uliuli. Dark blue, deep green.
The song fills the whole ocean. Your mask buzzes. Fish stop to listen. The water around you gets darker and bluer and greener, like the song is painting it.
You float there in the deep blue, and the whale sings to you until your air runs low and you slowly rise back to the light.

words.say_it: Lean back all relaxed and wave a lazy hand. "Meh-leh-MEH-leh."
words.bonus: Mele alone means song. Melemele is yellow.
words.picture: Mellow uncle glowing in a yellow house
story_paragraphs: The mellowest man in Kailua lives in a yellow house. It has a yellow door, yellow curtains and yellow grass that he painted himself. He drives a yellow truck. He has a yellow dog and a yellow canary on his shoulder. He eats only bananas, pineapple and lemons.
He never hurries. He never frowns. When somebody cuts him off in traffic, he just smiles and waves a little yellow flag. Everybody in town calls him "Mellow Mellow."
Mellow mellow. Meh-leh-MEH-leh. Melemele. Yellow.
After 50 years of lemons and bananas, he is yellow too. At night he glows softly in his yellow hammock like a nightlight, humming.

words.say_it: Push an invisible mower and whine. "Ohhh-mah-oh-MAH-oh."
words.picture: Mowing a glowing green lawn forever
story_paragraphs: Your family's lawn is the greenest in the state. Too green. It glows. Airplanes use it as a runway light at night.

It also grows two feet every hour. Ma hands you the lawnmower. "Ohhhh, Ma..." you whine. "Oh, MOW!" she says. You mow the whole thing. You turn around. It's already grown back. "Ohhhh, Ma!" "Oh, MOW!"
Oh, ma, oh, mow. ʻŌmaʻomaʻo. Green. Hold that first oh long, like a sigh.

By sunset you have mowed the lawn 60 times. The clippings are piled into a green mountain. Your hair is green. Your arms are green. A lost goat wanders in, looks at the mountain, and decides to live there forever.

words.english: to be purple; to crown, to anoint
words.say_it: Place an invisible crown on your own head. "PO-nee."
words.bonus: Poni can mean purple, and it can also mean to crown or anoint someone.
words.picture: Purple pony being crowned
story_paragraphs: At the county fair there is a purple pony. Not lavender. Purple like ube, like a slice of purple sweet potato, deep and shiny.

The fair decides this pony is so special it must be crowned. A marching band plays. Somebody gently pours sweet coconut oil on its mane. A little girl climbs a ladder and sets a gold crown between its purple ears. The whole crowd bows and cheers "PONY! PONY!"
Pony. Poni. Purple. And also to crown, to anoint. Both happen to this pony at the same time.
The purple pony trots around the fairgrounds, crown shining, and eats an entire ube cake in one bite. Now its teeth are purple too. It doesn't mind. Royalty.

words.say_it: Squint into the fog and do a quiet hyena laugh. "Aah-hee-nah-HEE-nah."
words.bonus: ʻĀhinahina is also the name of the Haleakalā silversword, the silvery gray plant that grows near the summit.
words.picture: Gray hyena laughing on Haleakalā
story_paragraphs: It is 5 in the morning on top of Haleakalā, waiting for sunrise. Everything is gray. Gray fog. Gray rocks. Gray cinder. Your gray hoodie. The sky itself, gray.
Then out of the fog walks a hyena, gray from nose to tail. Gray like old ash. It sits down on the cinder and starts to laugh. "AAAAH... HYENA-HYENA-HYENA." The long aaah rolls across the crater.
Ah, hyena, hyena. ʻĀhinahina. Gray.
It laughs until the sun comes up. As the sky turns orange, it tiptoes over to a spiky silver gray plant, curls up beside it and matches it perfectly. Gray on gray on gray. You blink, and it's gone.

words.say_it: Bleat like a very clean sheep. "Mah-eh-MAH-eh!"
words.bonus: Hoʻomaʻemaʻe (413) means to make clean.
words.picture: Sparkling sheep under a sprinkler
story_paragraphs: There is a sheep on a ranch upcountry who takes four showers a day. She uses coconut shampoo. She blow dries her wool. She has her own tiny toothbrush.

She is so clean she sparkles. Mud jumps out of her way. When the other sheep roll in the dirt, she stands under the sprinkler bleating "MAAH-eh! MAAH-eh!" Maʻemaʻe. Clean. The little catch between maah and eh is her spitting out shampoo bubbles.

Flies won't land on her because they would get washed. Rain falls on her and comes off cleaner than it went on. You can see your face in her wool. The rancher uses her as a mirror to shave every morning.

words.say_it: Hold your arms out, dripping, and grimace. "Peh-lah-PEH-lah!"
words.bonus: The opposite of maʻemaʻe (468), clean.
words.picture: Muddy dog shaking at a lūʻau
story_paragraphs: Your dog Pella found the pig pen at the lūʻau. She rolled in the mud, then in some old poi, then in something nobody wants to name. She is now brown, gray and green, with a mango peel stuck to her head.
She runs straight toward 300 guests in their nicest aloha wear. You chase her yelling "PELLA! PELLA!" Too late. She stops in the middle of the dance floor and shakes.
Pella, Pella. Pelapela. Dirty. Gross.

Now everybody is covered. Aunty's white muʻumuʻu is spotted like a cow. The kālua pig has a paw print on it. The band keeps playing, but mud drips out of the ʻukulele. Pella lies down under the dessert table, very proud of herself.

words.english: to be fat; to be sweet
words.say_it: Pat your full belly and nod. "Mo-MO-nah."
words.bonus: ʻĀina momona means rich, fertile, abundant land.
words.picture: Endless butter mochi, Mo'? MO'!
story_paragraphs: Aunty Mae thinks you look too skinny. She sets a plate of butter mochi in front of you. You eat it. She says "Mo'?" You say "MO'!" She brings more. "Mo'?" "MO'!" You keep waiting for yourself to say "nah," but it never comes.
Hours pass. Mo', mo', mo'... the nah never shows up. Mo, mo, nah. Momona.

Your cheeks puff out. Your shirt buttons fly off like popcorn. You roll instead of walk. And everything about you is sweet. You sweat sugar. Bees follow you home. When you smile, your teeth sparkle like frosting.
Aunty Mae stands back with her arms crossed, very satisfied. "Now you look healthy."

words.say_it: Pucker your whole face and wail. "Ah-vah-AH-vah!"
words.bonus: ʻAwa is kava, the bitter root drink. A handy reminder.
words.picture: Face folding from bitter melon
story_paragraphs: Your uncle grows bitter melon. He says it's good for you. He cuts you a slice and watches you closely.

You bite. Your face folds in half. Your eyes water. Your tongue tries to crawl out of your mouth and hide under the table. You make a sound like a baby who just dropped her ice cream. "Aw-VAH! AW-VAH!" Aw, vah, aw, vah. ʻAwaʻawa. Bitter.
The bitterness spreads. Your ears curl. Your hair stands straight up. The dog licks your hand, tastes it, and runs out the door.
Uncle eats three slices in a row without blinking. "Good for you," he says, and his face doesn't move at all.

words.english: to be hard, difficult; to be stubborn
words.say_it: Cross your arms and shake your head hard. "Pah-ah-kee-KEE!"
words.bonus: Its opposite is maʻalahi (473), easy.
words.picture: Stubborn Pa chipping a wall with a spoon
story_paragraphs: Pa locked himself out of the house. Ma has the spare key right there. She holds it out. Pa will not take it. He is stubborn. "I can do it myself."
