He tries the window. Stuck. He tries a credit card in the door. It snaps. He climbs onto the roof looking for a way in, and the house doesn't even have a chimney. The kids are screaming "PA! AH! KEY! KEEEY!" Pa, ah, key, key. Paʻakikī. Hard. Stubborn.

So he starts chipping through the wall with a spoon. Nine hours later he crawls into the living room, covered in dust. Ma is on the couch, spinning the key on her finger. Pa brushes off his shirt and says, "See? Easy."
It was not easy.

words.say_it: Brush off your hands like it was nothing. "Mah-ah-LAH-hee."
words.bonus: The opposite of paʻakikī (472), hard.
words.picture: Aunty fixing a car with a chopstick
story_paragraphs: Your car breaks down on the H-3, in the rain, in the tunnel. You panic. Aunty Pua, riding in the back, just climbs out humming a little tune. "Mah, ah, LA-HEE... la-hee..." It's the sound of somebody not trying at all.

She lifts the front of the car with one hand. She fixes the engine with a chopstick and a hair tie. She changes a flat tire while eating a spam musubi. Then she pushes the whole car out of the tunnel with her pinky. All while humming. "Mah, ah, LA-HEE."
Maʻalahi. Easy. Like la-dee-dah.
She gets back in, buckles up, and starts the crossword. You still haven't finished panicking.

words.say_it: Turn your pockets inside out. "Ee-lee-HOO-neh?"
words.bonus: If a pōā (405) robs you, you end up ʻilihune.
words.picture: Couple sharing one grain of rice
story_paragraphs: A couple is so poor they share one grain of rice for dinner. They cut it in half with a razor blade. Their TV is a cardboard box with a TV drawn on it. Their dog is a sock puppet.

The husband opens his wallet. A moth flies out. "Honey," he says, "we're broke. Again." The wife looks up from patching her one sock and says "EE-lee... HOO-neh?" Really, honey? Ee-lee, HOO-neh. ʻIlihune. Poor.
They try to pay the rent with seashells. The landlord says no. They offer him the sock puppet. He takes it.
They're happy anyway. They split their grain of rice and toast each other with two empty cups.

words.say_it: Open your mouth and arms as wide as they go. "Haah-MAH-mah!"
words.bonus: Pani means to close. And don't mix it up with hāmau (417), to hush.
words.picture: Hippo mama's mouth wide open
story_paragraphs: A mother hippo at a wild animal park yawns. It is the biggest yawn in history. "HAAAAAAAH..." Her mouth opens wider, and wider, and wider. A bus could drive in. A tour bus actually does drive in, by mistake, then carefully backs out.
The keeper stares up and yells "HAAAH... MAMA!" Haaa, mama. Hāmama. Wide open.
Her mouth stays open for a full hour. Birds fly in one side and out the other. A family spreads a mat and has a picnic on her tongue. The keeper parks his golf cart in there.
Finally she closes it, very slowly, with a sound like a garage door. Everybody claps. Then she yawns again.

words.say_it: Point down, down, way down, and wail. "Ho-HO-noo!"
words.bonus: Hohonu can also mean profound, like deep knowledge. He kanaka hohonu o ka ʻike is a person of deep knowledge.
words.picture: Phone falling into a bottomless hole
story_paragraphs: You are standing on the end of the pier taking a selfie. The phone slips. It falls into a hole in the ocean floor that nobody knew was there. The deepest hole in the world.
You yell as it drops. "HO! HO! NOOOOOOO!" Ho, ho, noo. Hohonu. Deep.

You lean over and listen. You can hear your phone ringing, getting softer, and softer, and softer. Three hours later you can still hear it falling. A submarine goes down to look for it. A week later the submarine comes back up with a note taped to the hatch. "Too deep."
Somewhere down there, your phone is still getting texts from your aunty. A glowing fish is reading them.

words.say_it: Dip one toe in and pull it right back. "Paah-PAH-oo!"
words.bonus: The opposite of hohonu (476), deep.
words.picture: Pa swan diving into two inches of water
story_paragraphs: Pa sees the water at the beach, runs down the sand, and yells "Watch this!" He leaps into a huge swan dive, arms out, toes pointed, like an Olympic diver.
The water is two inches deep. SPLAT. "PAAAA-PA... OW!" Paa, pa, ow. Pāpaʻu. Shallow.

He sits up with sand on his face and a small crab sitting on his nose. He tries surfing. The board just sits on the sand. He tries snorkeling and sees his own knees. He tries a cannonball and makes one tiny ripple and a big dent.
The kids are crying laughing. The crab climbs down and checks the water. It doesn't even come up to the crab's ankles.

words.say_it: Pull hard on an invisible stuck spoon. "Maah-no-ah-NO-ah!"
words.bonus: One finger poi is the thickest poi, thick enough to scoop with just one finger.
words.picture: Spoon standing straight up in thick poi
story_paragraphs: Grandpa makes his poi so thick you don't eat it, you climb it. A spoon stands straight up in it. A fork stands up in it. A small child could stand up in it.

A visitor tries to stir it. The spoon won't move. He grabs it with both hands and pulls. He puts his foot on the bowl. His face turns red. "MAAAAAN! NO-AH! NO-AH!" Maaan, no-ah, no-ah. Mānoanoa. Thick.
The spoon stays put. The bowl lifts right off the table with him. Somebody hands him a pry bar. The pry bar gets stuck too.
Grandpa walks over, sticks one finger in, twirls, and eats a perfect bite. "One finger," he says. "Good poi."

words.say_it: Turn sideways and suck in your cheeks. "Lah-hee-LAH-hee."
words.bonus: The opposite of mānoanoa (478), thick.
words.picture: Skinny cousin hiding behind a chopstick
story_paragraphs: Your cousin Pua is so thin she can hide behind a chopstick. When she turns sideways, she disappears. She mails herself to Hilo in a regular envelope for one stamp.

Pua has a tiny thin giggle, like air squeaking out from under a door. "La-HEE, la-HEE." When the trade wind blows, she flutters on the clothesline next to Aunty's koala from kaulaʻi. She slides under doors. She reads the newspaper by standing inside it.
La hee, la hee. Lahilahi. Thin.
At the beach she uses one strand of saimin as a boogie board. A frigate bird once picked her up by mistake, thinking she was a ribbon, and dropped her off on Lānaʻi. She giggled the whole way.

words.say_it: Sweep both arms out as wide as you can. "Lau-LAAAH!"
words.bonus: Don't mix it up with laulau, the pork wrapped in taro leaves. Lau means leaf.
words.picture: Laulau as wide as the H-1
story_paragraphs: The biggest party in history needs the biggest laulau in history. Forty uncles wrap one in ti leaves the size of parachutes. When they finish, it is as wide as the H-1. All six lanes. Both directions.
They have to shut down the freeway. The laulau sits there steaming. Cars line up just to look at it. It is so wide you can't see around it. A small plane lands on it by accident.
Everyone stands on the overpass and sings "LAU... LAAAAAA!" holding that last note as long as the laulau is wide. Lau, laaa. Laulā. Wide.
It takes 3,000 people a week to eat it. They start from both sides and meet in the middle.

words.say_it: Squeeze your palms close together, almost touching. "Oh-lo-LEEE."
words.bonus: Laulā (480) is wide and ʻololī is narrow.
words.picture: Family stuck in a four inch alley
story_paragraphs: There is a shortcut to the beach through an alley between two buildings. The alley is four inches wide. Everybody tries it anyway. Nobody fits.

Uncle tries it sideways and gets stuck with his cheek smooshed against the wall. Aunty gets stuck by her purse. The dog gets stuck. A pizza delivery gets stuck. Now there is a whole line of people wedged in there, groaning.

Then skinny cousin Pua from lahilahi walks up, looks at the gap and says "Oh, LOLLY!" because it's as narrow as a lollipop stick. Oh, lolly. ʻOlolī. Narrow. She slides right through, holding the long leee the whole way.
She waves from the beach while everyone else waits for the fire department to bring butter.

words.say_it: Creep your fingers closer and closer to your ear. "Ko-KO-keh!"
words.bonus: Its opposite is mamao (483), far.
words.picture: Chicken crowing right in your ear
story_paragraphs: You are sleeping on the lanai at your aunty's house on Kauaʻi. Far away you hear a chicken. "ko-ko-KEH..." Very soft.

A minute later, closer. "Ko-ko-KEH." Closer. "KO-KO-KEH." Now it's on the steps. Now it's on the railing. Now it's on your pillow. Now its beak is right in your ear, closer than anything has ever been to your ear.
"KO! KO! KEH!" Kokoke. Near.

You open your eyes. It is 4 in the morning. There are actually 60 chickens, all near, all touching you. One is sitting on your face like a hat. They are all staring at you. They all take a deep breath together.

words.say_it: Shade your eyes and call to the horizon. "Mah-MAH-oh!"
words.bonus: Kokoke (482) is near and mamao is far.
words.picture: Yelling for Ma across the ocean
story_paragraphs: Ma moved really far away. Not to the next town. To the very tip of the Big Island. And you are on the far end of Kauaʻi.

You need to ask her where the rice cooker is. So you climb to the top of a mountain and yell "MA! MA-OH!" Your voice flies out across the ocean. It takes three days to get there. Seabirds carry it part of the way.
On Thursday Ma hears a tiny faraway "...ma-oh." She yells back. Her answer reaches you on Sunday. "It's in the cupboard!" By then you've already eaten at the drive in every night.
Ma, ma-oh. Mamao. Far.

words.say_it: Shut your eyes, wave your hands in front of you, and bonk. "Poh-eh-leh-EH-leh."
words.bonus: Pō means night and ʻeleʻele (460) means black. Black night.
words.picture: Searching for a black cat at midnight
story_paragraphs: Ellie the black cat from ʻeleʻele got out, and it's midnight. No moon. No streetlights. It is the darkest night Kaimukī has ever had. You can't see your own hand.

The Nakamuras are out in the yard in their pajamas. Little Kenji walks face first into the mango tree. "POH!" Then he catches his breath and calls, "Eh, Ellie? EH-leh?" Pō, eh, Ellie, eh-leh. Pōʻeleʻele. Dark, like night.
The dark is so thick you could spread it on toast. Somebody switches on a flashlight, and the dark just eats the beam.
Then a pair of yellow eyes blinks open, right in front of your nose. Ellie was sitting on your head the whole time.

words.say_it: Squint and shield your eyes from the glow. "Maah-lah-mah-LAH-mah!"
words.bonus: Don't mix it up with mālama (to care for). Mālamalama has an extra lama and a lot more light.
words.picture: Glowing llamas lighting up a valley
story_paragraphs: There's a llama farm on the Big Island where the llamas glow. Nobody knows why. They are brighter than headlights. When they walk into the pasture, the sun looks dim.

The farmer's little boy loves them. Every night he runs outside and shouts "MA! LLAMA! LLAMA!" and his mother has to put on sunglasses before she opens the door. Ma, llama, llama. Mālamalama. Bright. Clear.

At night the whole valley is lit up like noon. Boats use the llamas as a lighthouse. Moths fly in from three islands away. The neighbors complain they can't sleep, so the farmer puts a thick blanket on each llama. They glow right through it.

words.say_it: Freeze completely, arms stiff, then crack a smile. "Oh-oh-LEH-ah!"
words.bonus: The opposite of palupalu (487), soft.
words.picture: Frozen Leah used as a coat rack
story_paragraphs: Leah is playing freeze tag in the park. She gets tagged. She freezes. And she takes it very, very seriously.
She stays frozen for three days. Stiff as a board. Arms sticking straight out. Her friends poke her and yell "Oh! Oh! LEAH!" with a little hiccup between each oh. Oh, oh, Leah. ʻOʻoleʻa. Hard. Stiff.

Her dad carries her home under his arm like a surfboard. He leans her in the corner and uses her as a coat rack. Aunty hangs her purse on Leah's arm. A gecko climbs onto her head. You knock on her elbow and it goes tock, tock, like wood.
On day four somebody finally tags her back. She blinks and says, "Did I win?"

words.say_it: Squish an invisible marshmallow between your fingers. "Pah-loo-PAH-loo."
words.bonus: The opposite of ʻoʻoleʻa (486), hard or stiff.
words.picture: Pa sinking into a super soft bed
story_paragraphs: A mattress store in Kapolei gets a new bed. The sign says SOFTEST BED IN THE WORLD. Pa lies down to test it.
He sinks. Slowly at first, like into warm pudding. Then deeper. The kids watch his feet disappear. They scream "PA! LOO(K)! PA! LOO(K)!" Pa, loo, pa, loo. Palupalu. Soft.
Only his nose is showing. Then just a bubble. The salesman pokes the bed and his arm sinks in up to the shoulder. The bed is so soft it's more like a cloud with a price tag.
After an hour Pa floats back up, sleepy and smiling. "We'll take it," he says. They deliver it in a bucket.

words.english: to be bad; to be stormy
words.say_it: Hold onto an invisible doorframe against the wind. "Ee-no-EE-no!"
words.bonus: ʻIno alone means bad or wicked. Doubled, ʻinoʻino is extra bad.
words.picture: Trampoline flying past in a storm
story_paragraphs: The worst storm in 100 years hits the North Shore. The rain goes sideways. Then upward. Palm trees bend flat. A whole chicken coop flies past your window with the chickens still sitting inside, looking bored.
Your little brother watches the neighbor's trampoline float by and screams "EE! NO! EE! NO!" Ee, no, ee, no. ʻInoʻino. Bad. Stormy.

The roof of the shed lands in the ocean, and a surfer rides it. The wind strips the mango tree and sticks every mango to the side of the house like magnets. The dog's ears turn inside out and stay that way.
When the storm finally passes, the sun comes out, and your brother is still yelling "Ee, no!" out of habit.

words.say_it: Twirl your finger next to your ear. "Poo-POO-leh!"
words.bonus: Pupule is common in local pidgin too, as in "You pupule or what?"
words.picture: Crazy poodle driving a golf cart
story_paragraphs: There is a poodle in Waikīkī who has completely lost its mind. It wears sunglasses at night. It drives a golf cart through a hotel lobby. It jumps off the pier holding an umbrella like it's going to fly.
It barks at the ocean, and the ocean barks back. It orders a plate lunch in perfect English, then eats the plate. It sings opera to the pigeons. It tries to adopt a mongoose.
Everyone on Kalākaua points and yells "POO-POODLE-EH!" Poo, poodle, eh. Pupule. Crazy.
At sunset it paddles out on a boogie board, catches a wave, and stands on its head the whole ride. Honestly, it's the best surfer on the beach.

words.say_it: Smack your own forehead. "Hoo-POH."
words.bonus: Hūpō is foolish in the sense of not knowing better, literally swelling darkness. Pupule (489) is crazy.
words.picture: Cousin rolling downhill in 400 hoops
story_paragraphs: Your cousin buys 400 plastic hoops at a garage sale. He has a plan. He will put all 400 on at once, spin them all together, and become famous.

He steps into them. He can't move. He looks like a giant slinky. He tries to spin, tips over, and starts rolling down the driveway like a spring. Then down the street. Then down the hill. He's yelling the whole way. "HOOOOOP! OHHHH!" Hoop, oh. Hūpō. Foolish. Both vowels long, like his scream.

He rolls past the school, past the store, across the beach and into the ocean. He floats there, 400 rings around him, like a jellyfish. When the lifeguard pulls him out, he looks up and says, "Next time, 500."

words.say_it: Wave to your adoring fans. "Kow-LAH-nah!"
words.bonus: Kaulana Nā Pua, Famous Are the Flowers, is a beloved Hawaiian song from 1893.
words.picture: Famous cow Lana signing autographs
story_paragraphs: There's a cow named Lana on a ranch in Kula. One day a visitor posts a video of Lana tap dancing on a wooden bridge. Overnight, Lana is famous.
By Monday there are cameras everywhere. By Wednesday she has sunglasses and a manager. Fans scream from the fence "COW! LANA! COW! LAAANA!" Cow, Lana. Kaulana. Famous.

She's on a cereal box. She's on a billboard over the H-1. She has a red carpet leading to her water trough. She signs autographs by dipping her hoof in poi. Even the other cows line up for selfies with her.
Lana just chews her grass, cool as ever, while a helicopter films her from above.

words.say_it: Point at two things and nod. "LEE-keh."
words.bonus: It's spelled like the English word like, and it even means alike. Its opposite is ʻokoʻa (493), different.
words.picture: Forty identical uncles in the same shirt
story_paragraphs: Forty uncles show up to the family reunion, and they are all wearing the exact same aloha shirt. Same blue flowers. Same shorts. Same slippahs. Same sunglasses on the same bald head.
They look at each other for a long time. Then all forty say, at the same moment, "LIKE, EH?" Like, eh. Like. Alike. Same.

They all reach for the same piece of chicken. They all sneeze together. When one laughs, all 40 laugh the same laugh at the same time. Aunty tries to find her husband and gives up after twenty minutes. She just picks one to drive home. He's fine. They're all the same.

words.say_it: Point at the odd one out, with a little catch first. "Oh-KO-ah!"
words.bonus: Like (492) is same and ʻokoʻa is different. It also hides inside kūʻokoʻa (434), independent.
words.picture: Koa tree in a line of identical uncles
story_paragraphs: The same 40 uncles from like are lined up for the family photo. Same shirts, same slippahs, same smile. The photographer counts. "38... 39... 40... 41?"

There is a forty first. At the end of the line stands a koa tree. It is not wearing the shirt. It does not have slippahs. It does not have arms. Everyone turns to stare. "OH! KOA!" Oh, koa. ʻOkoʻa. Different.
The tree just stands there, rustling a little. Somebody says it must be Uncle Boy's cousin from Hilo. Nobody argues.
The photo comes out with 40 matching uncles and one tall koa tree right in the middle. It's the only thing anyone ever looks at.

words.say_it: Lower both palms slowly, like smoothing water. "Maah-LEE-eh."
words.bonus: Hoʻomālie (416) means to calm someone down. Mālie is the calm itself.
words.picture: Calm lifeguard soothing a hurricane
story_paragraphs: Remember baby Molly from hoʻomālie, the twelve foot baby at the mall? She grew up. She is now a lifeguard, and she is the calmest person on the planet.

A hurricane comes. Everyone runs. Molly sits in her tower sipping tea. The wind reaches her and turns gentle, like a fan on low. The waves reach her and lie flat. Even the hurricane slows down to listen. "Maaah-lee... eh," she says softly to the storm. Maah, lee, eh. Mālie. Calm. Gentle.
The hurricane curls up on the sand like a sleepy dog and turns into a nice little breeze. Molly pats it on the head. Everyone comes back and finishes their picnic.

words.english: to rotate the hips (a hula step)
words.say_it: Hands on hips, circle them slowly. "AH-mee."
words.bonus: ʻAmi and kāholo (496) are two of the first hula steps students learn.
words.picture: Army soldiers doing the hula ʻami
story_paragraphs: A drill sergeant stands in front of 500 soldiers on the parade field. He blows his whistle. "ARMY!" They snap to attention. "ʻAMI!"

Five hundred soldiers put their hands on their hips and rotate them in a slow, smooth circle. Around and around. Perfect hula. The sergeant watches, very serious. "Army! ʻAmi! Other way!" Five hundred hips turn the other way, all together.
Ah, mee. Army. ʻAmi. The hip circle of hula.

By lunch the whole base is moving together like a hālau. The trucks sway. The flag sways. And later that night, alone in his office, the sergeant is secretly practicing too. He signs up for hula class that weekend.

words.english: to step side to side (a hula step)
words.say_it: Step right, right, left, left, swaying. "Kaah-HO-lo!"
words.bonus: Holo means to run, sail or ride.
words.picture: Car stepping side to side around potholes
story_paragraphs: The road to your house has so many potholes the city gave up. Some are small. Some are the size of a swimming pool. One has fish in it.

Your car has learned to dance. When it sees a hole, it steps to the side. Step, step, together, step. Then back the other way. Everyone inside yells "CAAAR! HOLE! OH!" Caaar, hole, oh. Kāholo. The side to side hula step.
It keeps rhythm the whole way home. Four steps right, four steps left, never misses a beat. The tires stay perfectly in time.
A kumu hula waiting at the bus stop watches it go by and nods. "Good kāholo," she says. "Now watch your hands." The car does not have hands.

words.say_it: Fan yourself hard, then sigh with relief. "Peh-AH-hee!"
words.bonus: Peʻahi is also the name of the famous big wave surf spot on Maui's north shore.
words.picture: Giant fan cooling the whole beach
story_paragraphs: It's the hottest day of the year. A visitor on the beach is melting like a candle. A man walks up carrying a fan the size of a garage door and says, "Pay, and I fan."
The visitor pays. The man waves the giant fan. WHOOSH. The visitor's hat blows to Molokaʻi. His face ripples. He lets out a long "AHHH... HEE!" of pure relief. Pay, ah, hee. Peʻahi. To fan. To wave.

Now there's a line. Pay, fan, "Ahhh-hee!" The waves start rolling the wrong direction. Sailboats go backward. After an hour the whole beach is so cool people are putting on jackets. The fan man waves goodbye with the same fan and blows a family's umbrella into the parking lot.

words.say_it: Curl one finger toward you slowly. "AH-nee."
words.bonus: Peʻahi (497) is to fan or wave. Ani is to beckon, and also a breeze blowing softly.
words.picture: Gentle breeze Annie beckoning you
story_paragraphs: There is a breeze that lives on the North Shore named Annie. You can't see her, but you always know when she's around. She is the softest, gentlest breeze on earth.

When she wants you to come over, she curls her little fingers of wind. Come here. Come here. The palm leaves lean toward her. Your hair lifts gently. Even a strawberry shave ice drips in her direction. Everybody on the beach smiles and whispers "Ahh... Annie."
Ah, nee. Ani. To beckon. To blow gently.
You follow her down the beach, pulled softly by the back of your shirt. She leads you to the perfect spot, in the shade, facing the sunset. Then she smooths your towel flat and floats away.

words.say_it: Roll over on a lumpy invisible rock and groan. "Ho-oh-mo-AH-nah."
words.bonus: Moana alone means the open ocean.
words.picture: Moaning in a tent on a rock
story_paragraphs: Your family goes camping at the beach park for Easter weekend. It's tradition. Forty people, twelve tents, three generators and a pig.

The first night you lie in your sleeping bag on a rock the shape of a fist. A mosquito sings in your ear. Somebody's uncle snores like a leaf blower. The chickens start at 3 in the morning. You moan. "Ho... oh... MOAN... ah." Ho, oh, moan, ah. Hoʻomoana. To camp.
Every night you moan louder. By Sunday the whole campsite is moaning together in harmony, like a choir.
Then on Monday you pack up the tent, and you already miss it. You can't wait for next year.

words.english: to give freely, to be generous
words.say_it: Hold out both open hands like you're giving something away. "Mah-nah-vah-LEH-ah!"
words.bonus: Manawa here means heart or feelings, and leʻa means joy or pleasure. A joyful heart that gives. Hui manawaleʻa is a relief society.
words.picture: Aunty cleaning a whole valley for free
story_paragraphs: There's an aunty in Mānoa who gives her time and help to everyone for free. The food bank, the beach cleanup, the church bake sale, school crossing guard, all before breakfast. She never takes a dime.
One day somebody sighs, "The whole valley needs cleaning." Aunty rolls up her sleeves. People laugh. "Man! A VALLEY? AH!" Man, a valley, ah. Manawaleʻa. To give freely, with a generous heart.
She starts at the top. She picks up every piece of trash, pulls every weed and paints every fence. She fixes 900 potholes, plants 4,000 trees and hands every kid a free musubi.
By Sunday the valley sparkles. And the people who laughed are right behind her, carrying rakes, giving their time freely too.

words.say_it: Point at your own chest like the robot. "Kah-NAH-kah."
words.bonus: With a long first vowel, kānaka is the plural, people. Kanaka Maoli means Native Hawaiian people.
words.picture: Robot scanning beachgoers for humans
story_paragraphs: A robot lands at Ala Moana Beach Park. It is 9 feet tall, shiny as a new rice cooker, and it has one job. Find a human being.
It rolls up to a sandcastle shaped like a man and scans it. "Kah?" it beeps. Long pause. "Nah." The sandcastle falls over from embarrassment.
It scans a mannequin outside a surf shop. "Kah? Nah." It scans a mongoose, a boogie board and a coconut wearing sunglasses. "Nah. Nah. Nah."
Then it points its big glass eye at you. You are sandy, sunburned and eating a spam musubi. Lights flash. Bells ring. "Kah? Nah... KAH!" Human confirmed. A real, breathing, snack-eating person.
The robot is so happy it hugs you, prints a certificate that says PERSON, and flies home.

words.say_it: Hold invisible reins, bounce in your seat. "Vah-HEE-neh!"
words.bonus: With a long first vowel, wāhine is the plural, women. You will see Wahine on the women's restroom door in Hawaiʻi.
words.picture: Tiny woman riding a giant bucking horse
story_paragraphs: It is the big rodeo in Waimea on the Big Island. Out of the chute comes a horse the size of a delivery truck. It has thrown 214 cowboys this year. On its back is one small woman in a lauhala hat, holding on with one hand and her coffee with the other.
The horse bucks. It spins. It jumps so high it scares a passing airplane. Every time it lands it screams "VAH! HEE-NEIGH!"
She does not spill one drop. After 9 minutes the horse gives up, lies down and lets her use it as a couch.
The whole crowd stands and chants the horse's own sound back at her. "Vah-HEE-neh! Vah-HEE-neh!" Her husband yells "That's my wife!" and faints.

words.say_it: Flex both arms and hold the long vowel. "KAAAAH-neh."
words.bonus: Kāne is on the men's restroom door, wahine is on the women's. Do not mix them up at the beach park.
words.picture: Groom yelling Caaan, eh at his wedding
story_paragraphs: It is a beach wedding at sunset. The groom is a big man with a neck like a tree stump. He has practiced his line for weeks. The minister asks, "Can you promise to love her, carry her groceries, and open every stuck jar for the rest of your life?"
The groom takes a breath so big his shirt buttons pop off. "CAAAAAAN... EH!" He holds that long "caaan" for 31 seconds. The seagulls leave. A wave stops halfway up the beach to listen.
To prove it, he opens a stuck pickle jar with two fingers, then crushes a soda can flat on his own forehead. Everybody cheers. She has a husband. A real man who caaan.

words.say_it: Wipe invisible frosting off your face. "KAY-kee."
words.bonus: You will see keiki all over Hawaiʻi, like a keiki menu or a keiki hula class. For many children, see kamaliʻi.
words.picture: Baby face deep in a birthday cake
story_paragraphs: It is a baby's first birthday lūʻau in a rented hall with 300 guests. In the middle of the room is a cake 3 feet tall, covered in frosting flowers.

The birthday child crawls across the table, stands up, and dives face first into the cake like it is a swimming pool. SPLOOSH. Frosting hits the ceiling fan. The fan throws it onto Aunty's hair, Uncle's aloha shirt and the DJ.
The kid comes up for air with a face like a frosted donut. Only two eyes blinking. The whole room screams "CAKEY! CAKEY!"
That is a child. Loud, sticky, happy, and completely cakey. Every family party in Hawaiʻi has at least 12 of them running around under the tables.

words.say_it: Hands out like you are stopping a stampede. "Kah-mah-LEE," little hiccup, "ee."
words.bonus: Kamaliʻi means children, a whole bunch of them. One child is a keiki. The cakey kid from keiki is probably in there somewhere.
words.picture: 23 kids named Molly freezing mid-chaos
story_paragraphs: You agree to babysit for one hour. You open the door and 23 children run in. Every single one of them is named Molly. Nobody can explain this.
They climb the curtains. They put the cat in the rice cooker (it is off, the cat is fine). One Molly is on the roof. Another Molly is inside the piano.
You stand on a chair and yell "CALM, MOLLY!" All 23 Mollys freeze at once. Total silence. Then all 23 hiccup at the same time. "EE!" That hiccup is the ʻokina, a tiny catch in the throat.
Then they go wild again. You spend the rest of the hour yelling "CALM, MOLLY! EE!" over and over. Children. So many children.

words.say_it: Look back over your shoulder like you are asking permission. "Mah-KOO-ah?"
words.bonus: Makua can be a parent or any relative of the parents' generation, like an aunt or uncle. It is also the front half of makuahine (mother) and makua kāne (father).
words.picture: Teen on cliff asking parents for permission
story_paragraphs: You are 16 and standing on a rock 40 feet above the ocean. Your friends are already in the water yelling at you to jump. But first you need permission.

You turn around. Way back on the beach, your mother sits in a lawn chair with a clipboard. Next to her is your father with a whistle. Behind them sit your aunty, your uncle, and a grandma holding binoculars. Every grown-up relative you have, lined up like judges at a surf contest.
You cup your hands and scream "MA! COOL, AH?"
The parents huddle. They argue for 11 minutes. Finally your mother holds up a sign that says NO. Your aunty holds up one that says MAYBE. Grandma is asleep. You climb down and eat a sandwich.

words.say_it: Laugh like a horse, then point to the sky. "Mah-koo-ah-HEE-neh."
words.bonus: Makua (parent) plus wahine (woman) makes makuahine. Once you see the pieces, it builds itself.
words.picture: Lost kid following mom's horse laugh
story_paragraphs: You are 6 years old and lost at Ala Moana Center on the Saturday before Christmas. There are 10,000 people. All you can see is knees and shopping bags. You start to cry.
Then, far away, over all the noise, you hear it. A laugh like a happy horse. "HEE-NEIGH! HEE-NEIGH!" Only one person on Earth laughs like that. Your mother.

You follow the sound past the food court, past the koi pond, up the escalator. There she is, laughing at a joke from a lady selling socks. She scoops you up. You sniff and ask "Ma, cool, ah?" and she laughs again. "HEE-NEIGH!"
Makua plus wahine. The parent who is a woman. Your mother.

words.say_it: Lift an invisible truck and hold the long vowel. "Mah-KOO-ah KAAAH-neh."
words.bonus: Makua (parent) plus kāne (man) makes makua kāne, father. Pukui-Elbert writes it as two words, while makuahine (mother) is one word. Makua kāne can also mean an uncle or any man of your parents' generation.
words.picture: Dad lifting stuck truck out of sand
story_paragraphs: Your family truck is stuck in soft sand at the beach. The tide is coming in. Eight cousins push. Two aunties push. The dog pushes. Nothing.
You run to your mother. "Ma, cool, ah, if we just leave it?" She points. "Ask your father."
Your father puts down his plate lunch. He walks over in rubber slippahs. He squats, grabs the back bumper, and says "CAAAAAN... EH!" He holds that long "caaan" the whole time he lifts.
The truck rises one foot, two feet, four feet. Sand pours out of the tires like a waterfall.
He carries the whole truck up to the parking lot, sets it down gently, and goes back to his lunch. It is still warm. Makua plus kāne. The parent who is a man. Your father.

words.say_it: Hold up an invisible coupon proudly. "Koo-POO-nah."
words.bonus: With a long first vowel, kūpuna is the plural, elders or ancestors. You will hear kūpuna used with deep respect all over Hawaiʻi.
words.picture: Grandma with a giant coupon book at the register
story_paragraphs: Your grandma takes you shopping at the drugstore. She walks in carrying a coupon book 4 inches thick, held together with a rubber band older than your father.
At the register the total is $412. Tūtū does not blink.
She licks her thumb and flips. "Coupon, ah!" Rice, minus two dollars. "Coupon, ah!" Toilet paper, half off. "Coupon, ah!" Dried mango, buy one get one.
The cashier starts to sweat. A line of 30 people forms, and nobody complains, because they are taking notes.
Final total, $3.18. The store manager comes out and shakes her hand.
In the car she tells you she learned it from her own grandmother, who learned it from hers. The wisdom of the elders, handed down, one coupon at a time.

words.say_it: Pull an invisible train whistle. "Toooo-TOOOO." Hold both long.
words.bonus: Tūtū works for grandma or grandpa. Tūtū wahine is grandma, tūtū kāne is grandpa. Pukui-Elbert lists it under the spelling kūkū, usually pronounced tūtū.
words.picture: Grandma on scooter yelling Toot toot
story_paragraphs: Your grandma is 91 and just got a red electric scooter for her birthday. Big mistake. She has taken off the speed limiter with a butter knife.

She rips through the swap meet at 30 miles an hour with a basket full of mangoes. Instead of a horn, she just yells. "TOOOOO-TOOOOO!" Long and loud like a train, both vowels held forever. People dive out of the way. A man selling T-shirts jumps into a cooler.

Later that day your grandpa gets one too. Now there are two of them, racing each other around the church parking lot, both yelling "TOOOO-TOOOO!" The pastor just waves. Every grandkid in the family runs behind them trying to catch a ride.

words.say_it: Sniff the air, gulp, then shake your head. "Mo-oh-POO-nah."
words.bonus: Moʻo can mean a lizard, and also a line or series, like a family line. Your grandchild continues the line.
words.picture: Grandpa sniff-checking the baby
story_paragraphs: Grandpa is babysitting his grandchild for the first time in 30 years. He has forgotten everything. He is holding the baby like a bowling ball.

Something smells. Grandpa lifts the baby up to his nose very slowly, like he is defusing a bomb. He sniffs. "Mmmmmo..." He freezes with a gulp. That is the ʻokina. "...OH!" He checks the diaper. "Poo?" Long pause. "...NAH." It was the dog the whole time.

The baby grabs Grandpa's nose and laughs so hard it hiccups. Grandpa laughs too. By the time Grandma gets home, the grandchild is asleep on his chest and he is asleep in the recliner, both snoring in the same rhythm. Mo, oh, poo? Nah.

words.say_it: Cross your arms like a big brother. "Kai-koo-ah, AH-nah."
words.bonus: Kaikuaʻana is only for the same gender. A boy's older brother, or a girl's older sister. The younger one is kaikaina.
words.picture: Big brother saying ah, nah to everything
story_paragraphs: Your big brother is named Kai. He is 17. You are 11. He has a car, a job, and a room with a lock on it. You have none of those things.
Every day you ask him something. "Kai, cool, ah, if I borrow your skateboard?" He does not even look up. "Ah..." he says, stopping with a little catch in his throat. "...nah."
"Kai, cool, ah, if I sit in the front seat?" "Ah... nah." "Kai, cool, ah, if I eat the last malasada?" "AH... NAH." He eats it in one bite while looking at you.
One day you ask 44 times in a row just to see. He answers every time. That is an older sibling. Same gender as you, a little bigger, and always saying "ah, nah."

words.say_it: Point at the ocean, then fold your arms. "Kai-KAI-nah."
words.bonus: Kai means sea. Kaikaina is a younger sibling of the same gender. The older one is kaikuaʻana.
words.picture: Little sister in kayak refusing to paddle
story_paragraphs: You and your little sister rent a two person kayak in Kailua. The plan is to paddle 3 miles out to the islands. You sit in back. She sits in front with a paddle she has no plans to use.
You push off. She points at the ocean and yells "KAI! KAI!" which just means sea. Yes. It is the sea. We are on it. "Paddle!" you say. She thinks about it. "Nah."
For 3 miles she yells "KAI! KAI!" at every wave, every fish, and one very confused turtle. Every time you ask her to paddle, "Nah." You arrive with arms like cooked noodles. She arrives with a tan.
That is a younger sibling. Same gender as you, rides for free, and never paddles.

words.say_it: Mime braiding hair with huge clumsy hands. "Kai-koo-NAAAH-neh."
words.bonus: Only a girl uses kaikunāne for her brother. A boy calls his brother kaikuaʻana (older) or kaikaina (younger).
words.picture: Football player braiding his little sister's hair
story_paragraphs: A girl in third grade has a big brother who is 6 foot 5 and plays on the high school football team. His neck is wider than her whole head.

Every morning he braids her hair into perfect double French braids. He packs her bento with a smiley face made of nori. He walks her to class carrying her unicorn backpack, which looks like a coin purse on his giant shoulder.
The other girls stare. One whispers, "That guy?" Her friend nods slowly. "Cool naaaanny." They say it long, with their mouths open. "Guy... cool... NAAAH-nee."
That is a girl's brother. Big, scary looking, and the best nanny in the whole school.

words.say_it: Hand someone an invisible drink, then giggle. "Kai-koo-ah-HEE-neh."
words.bonus: Only a boy uses kaikuahine for his sister. A girl calls her brother kaikunāne. Notice the -hine ending, like wahine, woman.
words.picture: Little sister giving big brother pickle juice
story_paragraphs: Remember Kai, the big brother who says "ah, nah" to everything? He has a sister. She is 9, and she has been planning her revenge for years.
It is a hot day. She walks up with a tall glass of what looks like lemonade, with ice and a little umbrella. "Kai, cool, ah?" she asks, sweet as a malasada.
He grabs it and chugs. It is pickle juice. Pure pickle juice, with a spoon of hot mustard. His face folds up like a paper fan.
His ears turn purple. Steam may come out.
She runs away giggling "HEE-HEH! HEE-HEH!" all the way down the street. That is a boy's sister. Sweet voice, evil giggle, perfect memory.

words.say_it: Wobble your knees, then fall into a chair. "Ho-ah-haaah-NOW."
words.bonus: Hoa means companion, and hānau means birth. Your cousin is a companion from the same birth line. It can also mean a fellow church member.
words.picture: Pyramid of cousins collapsing on the beach
story_paragraphs: It is the family reunion at the beach park and the cousins decide to build a human pyramid. There are 28 of them. The oldest is 44. The youngest is 5. Most of them met today.
Cousin Boy is on the bottom because he is the biggest. Cousins climb onto cousins onto cousins. It gets 5 stories high. A small cousin at the top waves a flag.

Cousin Boy starts to shake. "Whoa... ah..." His knees wobble. "HAAAAAH..." he gasps, holding the long breath. "NOW!" The whole pyramid collapses into the sand in a pile of cousins, slippahs and potato chips.
Everyone is laughing. Nobody is hurt. Aunty takes a picture. That is cousins. A giant pile of people who share grandparents and fall down together.

words.say_it: Throw up your hands and then pull out a chair. "Oh-HAH-nah."
words.bonus: One popular explanation links ʻohana to ʻohā, the young taro shoot that grows from the older corm. The family grows from the same root.
words.picture: Aunty Hannah bringing a goat to dinner
story_paragraphs: It is Sunday dinner at Grandma's house. There are 11 chairs and 14 people already. Then the door opens and Aunty Hannah walks in with more people.

She brought the neighbor. "Oh, HANNAH!" She brought the mailman. "Oh, HANNAH!" She brought the guy who fixed her tires, his wife, their three kids, and a goat that followed them from the park. "OH, HANNAH!"
Everyone groans. And then everyone scoots over. Grandma cooks another pot of rice. Somebody finds more chairs. The goat gets a bowl of poi.

By dessert there are 43 people squeezed into a 3 bedroom house and the mailman is calling Grandma "Mom." That is family. Everyone yells "Oh, Hannah," and then everybody makes room. Start with a small catch in your throat, the ʻokina, before the "oh."

words.say_it: Open your arms wide for a crash hug. "Ho-ah-LO-hah."
words.bonus: Hoa (companion) plus aloha (love) makes hoaloha, literally a beloved companion. You may also see it written hoa aloha, or hoaaloha in older writing.
words.picture: Friend in 40 lei sliding across the airport
story_paragraphs: You come home to Honolulu after 2 years on the continent. You walk out into the airport, and at the far end, 200 feet away, is your best friend.
She is wearing 40 lei. Carnation, plumeria, candy lei, one made of dried cuttlefish. She sees you and runs. Full speed. Her slippahs hit the shiny floor and she starts to slide.
"WHOA... AH..." She is sliding sideways past the baggage claim. "...ALOHAAAA!" She crashes into you at 20 miles an hour. You both go down in a pile of flowers.
She puts every one of the 40 lei on your neck. You cannot see. You smell like a flower shop that sells jerky. That is a friend. A loved companion who crashes into you on purpose.

words.say_it: Grip invisible handlebars and lean. "HO-ah!"
words.bonus: Hoa is the root in hoaloha (friend), hoahānau (cousin) and hoalauna (neighbor). Spot it and you know it is a kind of companion.
words.picture: Two people screaming on a tandem bike downhill
story_paragraphs: You and your partner rent a tandem bicycle, the long one with two seats. You are in front. Your partner is behind you, and his job is to pedal and trust you.
You take it up Tantalus. Then you point it down. There are no brakes on the back seat. There are barely brakes on the front seat.
You pick up speed. 20 miles an hour. 35. 50.
Your partner holds on and yells one word through every single curve. "WHOA! WHOA! WHOOOAAA!" A tour bus pulls over to watch. A mongoose covers its eyes.

At the bottom you coast to a stop. Your partner's hair is straight back like a broom. He climbs off, shakes, and gets right back on. That is a partner. Your mate. The one who yells "whoa" and still rides with you.

words.say_it: Lean over an invisible fence. "Ho-ah-LAU-nah."
words.bonus: Hoa (companion) plus launa (friendly, getting along). A neighbor is a companion you get along with, hopefully.
words.picture: Neighbor with giant speaker at 5 a.m.
story_paragraphs: It is 5 in the morning. Your new neighbor has a speaker the size of a refrigerator on his lanai. He is playing ʻukulele through it. The same three chords, over and over, at a volume that shakes the mangoes off your tree.
You climb on a bucket and look over the fence. "Whoa, ah..." you say, trying to be nice. "LOUD, nah?"
He smiles big and says "NAH!" and turns it up. Your windows rattle. Your dog howls along.

But then he hands a plate of banana bread over the fence. Warm. With butter. The next day he fixes your gate. The day after that he feeds your cat when you go to Maui. Loud, nah? Yes, loud. But that is your neighbor. Say "whoa, ah, loud-nah" fast and it slides into the word.

words.say_it: Push up invisible glasses, then moo politely. "KOO-moo."
words.bonus: Kumu hula means hula teacher. Kumu can also mean the source or base of something, like the trunk of a tree.
words.picture: Cow teacher at chalkboard with calves
story_paragraphs: There is a school on a farm upcountry on Maui, and the teacher is a cow. A big brown one wearing reading glasses. She stands at a chalkboard holding a piece of chalk in her mouth.
The students are 30 baby calves in tiny desks. One raises a hoof. "Where does milk come from?" The teacher leans in and says softly, "Coo..." then louder, "MOOOO." She points at herself.
"Where does cheese come from?" "Coo... MOOOO." "Why is there ice cream?" "Coo... MOOOO."
She is the teacher. She is the source. She is the reason. Every answer in that classroom is the same big brown cow. Coo-moo.

words.say_it: Shoot your hand up in the air. "How-MAAAH-nah."
words.bonus: A kumu teaches, a haumāna learns. Put the two words together in your head like a teacher and a student in one room.
words.picture: Student stuck to ceiling with hand raised
story_paragraphs: There is one student in the front row whose hand is always up. Always. He raised it on the first day of school and it has not come down since. His arm is now very strong.
The teacher explains fractions. His hand shoots up. "How, MAAAAAA'AM?" She explains again. He thinks. "...Nah." She draws a pizza. "How, MAAAAAA'AM?" She draws a bigger pizza. "...Nah."
He asks 212 times in one day. Once his hand shoots up so fast it launches him out of his chair and he sticks to the ceiling like a gecko. He asks from up there too.
By June he knows more than anyone in the school. That is a student. Hand up, always asking how. Stretch the middle like he does. "How... MAAAH... nah."

words.say_it: Point proudly at an invisible machine. "Kai-kah-mah-HEE-neh."
words.bonus: Kaikamahine means girl or daughter. Notice the -hine ending again, like wahine and makuahine. It is a hint the word is female.
words.picture: Girl riding a giant musubi machine
story_paragraphs: Your daughter is 8. She has been locked in the garage for 3 days. You hear banging, drilling, and one small explosion.
On the fourth morning the garage door opens. Out rolls a machine the size of a pickup truck, made from a rice cooker, 600 rubber slippahs, a lawnmower engine, and your good toaster.
It stomps into the kitchen and starts making spam musubi. 50 a minute. Perfectly wrapped.
She sits on top of it like a queen, wearing welding goggles. You fall to your knees. "My tyke... a MACHINE, EH!"
The neighbors come over. The news comes over. By noon she has a line down the block and a business license.
That is a girl. That is your daughter. Tyke, a machine, eh. Kaikamahine.

words.say_it: Tap your forehead with an invisible can. "KAY-kee KAAAH-neh."
words.bonus: Keiki (child) plus kāne (male) makes keiki kāne, a boy or a son. Pukui-Elbert writes it as two words. The same pieces you already know.
words.picture: Cakey boy bonking a can on his forehead
story_paragraphs: Remember the cakey kid from keiki? Now he is a boy of 6, and he has watched his uncles crush soda cans on their foreheads at every party. He wants to be a man. Today is the day.
He still has birthday cake on his face. He picks up a full, unopened can of soda. He stares at it with total confidence. "Caaaan, eh?" he asks himself. He decides yes.
BONK. The can does not dent. BONK. Nothing. BONK. The can is fine. The boy has three little frosting prints on his forehead and he is a bit dizzy.
His uncle takes the can and pops it open for him instead. The soda sprays all over his cakey face. He laughs. Half keiki, half kāne. Still cakey, still asking if he can.

words.say_it: Hold out your palm like a tiny boss. "Pehhh-PEHHH."
words.bonus: Both e's in pēpē are long, so stretch them. Short and quick sounds wrong.
words.picture: Baby holding out palm for pinch money
story_paragraphs: There is a new baby in the family, and every aunty in Hawaiʻi wants to pinch its cheeks. The line goes out the front door, down the driveway and around the block.
The first aunty reaches in. The baby opens its eyes, holds out one tiny hand, palm up, and says "PEHHH. PEHHH." It sounds exactly like "pay, pay." Long and slow, both vowels stretched.

The aunty laughs and puts a dollar in the little hand. The baby lets her pinch. Next aunty. "PEHHH. PEHHH." Another dollar. By dinner the baby has $340 stuffed in its diaper bag and is wearing a tiny money lei.
That is a baby. Chubby, bald, and already running the family business.

words.say_it: Pump your fist like a teenager. "Oh-PEE-oh!"
words.bonus: Think teenager. A kupuna is an elder, and an ʻōpio is a young person with energy to burn.
words.picture: Teens exploding onto the P.E. field
story_paragraphs: Grandpa is 78 and says he is still young. To prove it, he signs up for high school P.E. for one day.
He walks onto the field in knee socks. 30 teenagers are waiting.

The coach blows the whistle and the teenagers explode like popcorn in a pot with no lid. One runs laps backward. One does a backflip off the bleachers. One does 200 push-ups while eating a bag of chips. They all scream the same thing. "OHHHHH! P.E., YO!"
That first "oh" is long, and it starts with a tiny catch in the throat, the ʻokina.

Grandpa does one jumping jack. His knee makes a noise like a stick breaking. He sits down in the shade with a juice box and watches them run circles until sunset. That is youth. So much energy it bounces off the fence.

words.say_it: Lower yourself slowly into an invisible cooler. "Eh-leh-mah-KOO-leh."
words.bonus: An ʻelemakule is an old man. An old woman is a luahine, the next word.
words.picture: Old man sitting in a cooler of ice
story_paragraphs: It is 98 degrees at the beach park in Waiʻanae. No wind. The slippahs are melting. Everyone is hiding under the pop-up tent.

Then the old man gets up. He is 94, with white hair, suspenders and a cane made from a guava branch. He walks to the family's giant 120 quart cooler. He takes out every drink, one at a time, and lines them up on the sand. 48 cans in a row.
Then he climbs in. He sits down in the ice, up to his neck, and sighs. "Eh... lemme COOL, eh." He pulls the lid halfway shut like a garage door.
For 3 hours the kids knock on the lid to bring him snacks. He comes out fresh as a head of lettuce, beats everyone at cards, and goes back in. That is an old man. He has earned the cooler.

words.say_it: Kiss an invisible lure and cast it far. "Loo-ah-HEE-neh."
words.bonus: Luahine is an old woman, and ʻelemakule is an old man. Say them as a pair.
words.picture: Old woman landing a giant fish off the rocks
story_paragraphs: It is 4 in the morning on the rocks at Kaʻena. Thirty young fishermen have been casting all night. They have caught nothing but seaweed and one slippah.

Then an old woman shuffles out. She is 88, with her hair in a bun and a bucket that says DO NOT TOUCH. From her pocket she takes a fishing lure that is older than everyone there. She kisses it. "LURE, AH!"
She casts 200 feet. Before the lure even lands, the water explodes. A 90 pound ulua. She fights it with her tiny arms for 20 minutes while the young guys hold their breath.
She drags it onto the rocks and giggles. "HEE-heh." Then she goes home to make breakfast. That is an old woman. Wrinkled, patient, and better than all of you.

words.say_it: Lift two invisible kids by their collars. "Ah-nah-KAH-lah."
words.bonus: ʻAnakala comes from the English word uncle, said with Hawaiian sounds. Its partner, ʻanakē, comes from aunty.
words.picture: Uncle lifting nephews by their collars
story_paragraphs: Your uncle is on the living room floor, and 11 nephews are piled on top of him. The rule is simple. He has to say "UNCLE!" to give up.
"Say uncle! Say uncle!" they scream. The pile is 5 kids high. One is sitting on his head. One is chewing on his ankle.
Uncle does not say uncle. He is too proud.

He takes a deep breath and roars "AH, NAH!" Then he stands up. All 11 nephews slide off like laundry off a chair. He grabs the two biggest by the backs of their shirts. "COLLAR!" He holds them up in the air, one in each hand, feet kicking.
Then he lets them go and asks who wants shave ice. That is an uncle. Ah, nah, collar. ʻAnakala. Start it with a little catch in the throat.

words.say_it: Wave off an invisible plate, then accept it. "Ah-nah-KEHHH."
words.bonus: ʻAnakē comes from the English word aunty. Pair it with ʻanakala, uncle.
words.picture: Aunty stacking cake on a full plate
story_paragraphs: Every family has this aunty. She comes to every party with a cake. It does not matter what the party is. A funeral. A garage sale. A dog's graduation. She has a cake.
You are already full. She holds up a knife. "Cake?" You politely say "Ah, nah." She does not hear the "nah." She only hears the "cake."
"Ah, nah... CAAAAAKE!" She cuts you a slice the size of a phone book and slams it on your plate. The table bends.
You say it again. "Ah, nah." Another slice lands on top. Then another. Now you have a tower of cake as tall as a fire hydrant and Aunty is smiling like an angel.
Hold the end long like she does. "Ah-nah-KEHHH." That is your aunty. You will eat that cake.

words.say_it: Point at an invisible car and look around. "KAH-hoo?"
words.bonus: A kahu can be a pastor, or anyone who is the keeper or caretaker of something, like a special place.
words.picture: Old pastor pushing a truck from the gate
story_paragraphs: The little country church has one man who does everything. He preaches on Sunday. He mows the lawn on Monday. He fixes the roof, feeds the church cat, unclogs the sink and visits every sick person in the valley. He is the caretaker of the whole place and everyone in it.
Today there is a wedding. 300 guests. The bride's car is coming. And somebody has parked a rusty truck right across the gate.
The old man walks out with a rake in one hand and a Bible in the other. He looks at the truck. He looks at the crowd. "CAR?" Long pause. "WHO?"
Nobody talks. So he puts the truck in neutral and pushes it out of the way himself, all 70 years of him, and still gets back in time to start the song. That is the one who takes care.

words.say_it: Say it slowly and with respect. "Kah-HOO-nah."
words.bonus: Kahuna kālai waʻa is a canoe carving expert, and kahuna lapaʻau is a healer who uses medicine.
words.picture: Master craftsman fixing a cracked ʻukulele
story_paragraphs: Great-grandpa's old koa ʻukulele has a crack down the front. It is the most precious thing in the family. Everyone is at the kitchen table, panicking.
"Call WHO?" says your cousin. "The music store?" "Nah." "The guy who fixed the fence?" "Nah." "Look it up online?" "NAH." Call who? Nah. Call who? Nah. This goes on for an hour.

Finally Tūtū speaks. "Call the master." Two days later an old woodworker arrives. He has built 2,000 instruments. He closes his eyes, runs one finger along the crack, and knows the whole story of that wood. He fixes it without a single mark. When he plays it, the room goes quiet.
In old Hawaiʻi, the kahuna were trained experts and priests, the true masters of their craft. Not a joke title. Call who? Call the one who really knows.

words.say_it: Stand up straight, chin up. "Ah-LEE," tiny hiccup, "ee."
words.bonus: Aliʻi nui means high chief. The aliʻi were the ruling chiefs of old Hawaiʻi.
words.picture: Nervous boy leading the May Day court
story_paragraphs: It is May Day at the elementary school. The whole field is covered in lei. 400 parents are in folding chairs, filming on their phones. The teachers have chosen one quiet 7 year old named Lee to lead the royal court.
He wears a lei of yellow flowers and a cape. The announcer calls his name into the microphone. "Ah... LEE!" Lee is so nervous he hiccups right into the mic. "ʻEE!" That little hiccup is the ʻokina.
Then he stands tall. He walks slow and proud across the field, chin up, like the chiefs his teacher told him about. A little girl drops her lei. He stops, picks it up, and puts it back on her.
Everyone stands. That is what a chief does. Takes care of the people first.

words.say_it: Lift an invisible chess king high. "Mooooh," catch, "EEEE."
words.bonus: Hawaiʻi had its own mōʻī. ʻIolani Palace in Honolulu was home to the last Hawaiian monarchs.
words.picture: Tūtū raising the chess king to the sun
story_paragraphs: Tūtū has played chess on the lanai every afternoon for 50 years. She teaches you when you are 6. She picks up the tallest piece, the one with the little cross on top, and holds it up to the sun.
"This is the king," she says. Then, every time she moves him, she announces it like a royal horn. "MOOOOOOW..." She freezes for a split second. That is the ʻokina. "...ʻĪĪĪĪ!"
The neighbor's rooster answers every time. The mail lady starts saying it too. You lose 212 games in a row.
Then one day, at age 12, you trap her king. Checkmate. Tūtū stands up, bows to your king, and says it one more time, softly. "Mōʻī." Hold both vowels long.

words.say_it: Sit tall and proud like the rider, then whinny. "Moh-EE vah-HEE-neh."
words.bonus: Mōʻī (monarch) plus wahine (woman) makes mōʻī wahine, queen, written as two words. The same wahine from the rodeo.
words.picture: Horse in 200 lei whinnying at a parade
story_paragraphs: It is the big floral parade in Waikīkī. Thousands of people line the avenue. The pāʻū riders come first, women on horses, each wearing a long flowing skirt, each horse covered in flowers.
At the very front is the queen of the riders. Her horse is white, draped in 200 lei.
Her skirt is so long it flows down past the stirrups like a waterfall. She sits perfectly still. The crowd goes quiet and someone whispers "Mōʻī..." like she is royalty.
Then her horse lifts its head and adds the rest. "Vah-HEE-NEIGH!" Loud, proud, perfectly on time.
The whole avenue laughs and cheers. King plus woman. The horse did the second half. Mōʻī, wahine.

words.say_it: Pat all your pockets in a panic. "Kee-ah-AAH-ee-nah."
words.bonus: Kia means a pillar or post, and ʻāina means land. The governor is like a pillar holding up the land.
words.picture: Governor hunting for a giant golden key
story_paragraphs: It is the new governor's first day. On the steps of the State Capitol, 40 reporters wait with cameras. Someone hands the governor a golden ceremonial key to the state. It is 4 feet long and weighs as much as a small dog.
The governor gives a speech, poses for photos and goes inside. Then stops at the office door. Pats every pocket. "KEY?" Freezes with a gasp. "AHHH!" Checks behind the potted plant. "I... nah."
For 2 hours the whole staff searches. Under desks. Inside the koi pond. A police dog sniffs the elevators.

Then a little kid on a school tour points. The 4 foot golden key is hanging from the back of the governor's lei the whole time. Key? Ahh! I... nah. That is the governor. Holds up the whole state, cannot find a 4 foot key.

words.say_it: Tip your head back and howl at the sky. "LOO-nah!"
words.bonus: Luna also means up or above. I luna means upward, and its opposite is i lalo, downward.
words.picture: Boss in a crane cab high above workers
story_paragraphs: At the construction site in Kakaʻako, the boss never comes down. He sits in the crane, 200 feet up, in a little glass box. From down there he looks like a peanut.
He runs the whole job with a megaphone. "MORE CEMENT! LEFT! NO, THE OTHER LEFT!" His bento goes up in a bucket on a rope. When it rains, he opens an umbrella inside the box.
The workers have a nickname for him. He is so high up he is basically on the moon. So when they need him, they all tip their heads back and howl at the sky like wolves. "LOOOO-NAAAA!" Like lunar.
That is the boss. The supervisor. The one way up above. Luna.

words.say_it: Clap once, then coo softly. "HAH-koo."
words.bonus: Haku also means to braid or compose. A haku lei is a braided lei worn on the head, and a haku mele is a composer of songs.
words.picture: Uncle covered in 400 pigeons
story_paragraphs: On a rooftop in Kalihi lives an uncle with 400 racing pigeons. He built the coop himself out of old doors. He owns every bird and every bird knows it.

At sunset he steps out in his undershirt and claps once. "HAH!" All 400 pigeons blast into the sky at once, like somebody shook a pillow the size of a bus. They circle the whole neighborhood in one giant swirl. The laundry on the lines flaps like flags.
Then he whistles. The whole cloud turns and lands on him. His head. His arms. His shoulders. His belly. He is a man-shaped pile of birds, and all of them say "COO."
"HAH!" "COO." "HAH!" "COO." He is the master. The owner. The lord of the rooftop.

words.say_it: Point at three invisible workers fast. "Lee-mah-HAH-nah."
words.bonus: Lima means hand and hana means work. A limahana is a worker, somebody whose hands do the work.
words.picture: Three workers slamming out rainbow shave ice
story_paragraphs: There is a tiny shave ice shack on the North Shore with a line of 300 people. It has exactly three workers. Lee, a teenager. Ma, who is 70. And Hannah, the same Aunty Hannah who brought the goat to Sunday dinner.

When the owner rings the bell at 10 a.m., she yells roll call. "LEE! MA! HANNAH!" All three jump into action. Lee shaves the ice. Ma pours the syrup, three colors, never a drop wasted. Hannah takes the money and talks to every single customer like they are family, which they will be soon.
By 3 p.m. they have made 2,400 shave ice. Their hands are rainbow colored. Their arms are shaking. Lee, Ma, Hannah. Workers.

words.say_it: Cough like a cow into your elbow. "KOW-kah."
words.bonus: Kauka comes from the English word doctor, said with Hawaiian sounds. D and t both become k.
words.picture: Cow coughing in a doctor's waiting room
story_paragraphs: At the little clinic in the country town, the waiting room is full. An aunty with a sore wrist. A boy with a bean in his ear. And a cow. A whole brown cow, sitting in a plastic chair, holding number 14.
The cow has a cold. Every few seconds it coughs, and a cow cough sounds just like this. "KOW-KAH! KOW-KAH!" The magazines fly off the table. The fish tank sloshes.

The doctor comes out in a white coat. She takes one look, puts a stethoscope the size of a garden hose on the cow's chest, and hands it a cough drop as big as a hockey puck. The cow stops coughing and moos politely.
Then she calls "Number 15" and fixes your sprained ankle too. That is the doctor. She takes whoever walks in.

words.say_it: Stand up fast and yodel an objection. "Lo-EE-oh!"
words.bonus: Loio comes from the English word lawyer, reshaped with Hawaiian sounds.
words.picture: Lawyer yodeling in a courtroom
story_paragraphs: It is a big court case. A farmer is suing his neighbor over a runaway pig. The courtroom is packed. The judge looks tired already.

The farmer's lawyer stands up in a shiny suit and a tie with little pigs on it. The other side says something wrong. The lawyer jumps up, throws back his head and yodels. "LO-EE-OHHHHH!" Like a mountain goat herder. The windows buzz. The court reporter drops her pen.
The other side says something else wrong. "LO-EE-OHHHH!" He yodels every objection. He yodels his whole closing argument. The jury starts swaying.
He wins. The pig is returned. The judge secretly yodels in the parking lot on the way home. That is a lawyer. Always objecting, and very, very loud.

words.say_it: Hold out a hand like a traffic stop. "Maah-KAH-ee."
words.bonus: Do not mix it up with mākaʻikaʻi, which means to go sightseeing or visit around.
words.picture: Cop on a bicycle chasing a runaway car
story_paragraphs: Your mother parks at the top of a steep hill in Mānoa and forgets the parking brake. The car starts rolling. Nobody is in it. It picks up speed straight down toward a bakery.
You scream "MAAAAA! CAR!" and then you gulp so hard it catches in your throat. "EE!"

Out of nowhere comes a police officer on a tiny bicycle. Full uniform, shiny badge, sunglasses. He pedals so fast his legs are a blur. He catches the car, jumps off the bike onto the hood, climbs in through the window, and pulls the brake 3 inches from the bakery door.
The baker hands him a malasada. He writes your mother a ticket and hands her a malasada too. That is a police officer. Maaa, car, ee.

words.say_it: Take a fighting stance and strum hard. "KO-ah!"
words.bonus: Koa wood is famous for ʻukulele and canoes. The same word means warrior and brave. Do not mix it up with kua, back.
words.picture: Koa ʻukulele fighting off a thief
story_paragraphs: In a little ʻukulele shop in Kaimukī, the most expensive ʻukulele sits on the top shelf. It is made of koa wood, golden with dark stripes, like a tiger that plays music.
One night a thief sneaks in through the back. He reaches for the cash drawer. The koa ʻukulele jumps off the shelf. It lands in a fighting stance. It strums one loud chord like a war cry. "KO-AH!"
The thief freezes. The ʻukulele leaps and bonks him on the head with its neck. "KO-AH!" Bonk. "KO-AH!" Bonk. The thief runs out the door and all the way to Kapahulu.
In the morning the owner finds the shop safe and the ʻukulele back on its shelf, perfectly in tune. Made from the koa tree. Brave as a warrior.

words.say_it: Squawk like a parrot on your shoulder. "Kaaah-PEH-nah!"
words.bonus: Kāpena comes from the English word captain.
words.picture: Parrot fetching the captain's pen from the sea
story_paragraphs: The captain of the fishing boat has a white beard, a salty hat, and a big green parrot on his shoulder. The captain is in charge of everything. The boat, the crew, the course, the fish.
But he always loses his pen. He needs it to write in the ship's log. So the parrot helps. Every morning it screams "CAAAAAAAH! PEN-AH!" with a long, long first sound, until somebody finds a pen.
Today the pen falls into the ocean. The parrot dives in after it, swims under the boat, and comes back up with the pen in its beak and a small octopus on its head.
The captain writes, "Day 44. Parrot better than crew." The crew agrees. Hold that long first sound. That is the captain.

words.say_it: Sway side to side like you are on a deck. "Keh-lah-MO-koo."
words.bonus: Kela sounds like sailor, and moku means ship (it also means island). A kelamoku is a ship's sailor.
words.picture: Wobbly sailor ordering 14 loco mocos
story_paragraphs: A sailor comes home after 9 months at sea. His beard is crusty with salt. His arms have anchor tattoos. He has not stood on dry land since last year.
He walks off the ship and his legs still think they are on the ocean. He sways left. He sways right. He walks sideways down the pier like a crab, bumping into poles.
He wobbles all the way into a diner and slams his hand on the counter. "Hey, lah! MOCO!" One loco moco. Then another. Then 14 more. Rice, hamburger, egg, gravy. Stacked like a tower.
He eats all 14 without sitting down, because the stool keeps rocking like a boat. That is a sailor. Hey, lah, moco. Kelamoku.

words.say_it: Hold an invisible steering yoke and click a lock. "Pai-LAH-kah."
words.bonus: Pailaka comes from the English word pilot.
words.picture: Coconut pies flying through a plane cabin
story_paragraphs: You are on a small plane from Honolulu to Kona. The pilot comes on the speaker. "Good morning, this is your pilot. I have 30 coconut pies up here with me. Nobody touch my pies."
Then you hear a click. "PIE... LOCK... AH!" She has locked the pies in a special cabinet.
Halfway there, the plane hits a bump. The pie lock breaks. The cockpit door flies open. 30 coconut pies float down the aisle like flying saucers.
The pilot does not panic. She tips the plane left, then right, then does a gentle loop. Every pie lands back in its box. She locks them up again. "PIE, LOCK, AH!"
The plane lands softly. Everyone claps. She gives each passenger one slice. That is a pilot. Flies the plane, saves the pies.

words.say_it: Balance invisible plates up your arm. "Koo-EH-neh."
words.picture: Waiter on skates serving a long line
story_paragraphs: The new restaurant in town is so popular that the line of people, the queue, goes out the door, around the block, and back again. 400 people, standing in the sun, hungry and grumpy.
Then the waiter comes out. He is on roller skates. He looks at the long line. "Queue, eh?" he says. Then he shakes his head. "NAY!"
He will not let anybody wait. He skates up and down the whole line with plates stacked up both arms, all the way to his shoulders.
Saimin for the grandma. Fried rice for the surfers. Pancakes for the baby. He pours coffee while skating backward. He takes orders by pointing.
In one hour he serves all 400 people without anyone sitting down. That is a waiter. Queue, eh? Nay.

words.say_it: Raise one hand like you are being sworn in. "Peh-leh-kee-KEH-nah."
words.bonus: Pelekikena comes from the English word president. Hawaiian turns r into l, and s, d and t into k. That is how president becomes pelekikena.
words.picture: Pelican in a bow tie winning election
story_paragraphs: The school is voting for student council president. One of the candidates is a pelican. A big white one with a bow tie. His name, it says right on the poster, is Pelly Key Kenna.
He gives a speech by flapping. He promises longer recess and free fish on Fridays. The kids go crazy. They chant his full name. "PELLY! KEY! KENNA!"
On voting day, he carries the ballot box around in his giant beak pouch so nobody can cheat. 400 votes in there. When they count, he wins all 400.
He is sworn in on the lunch table, one wing raised. His first act is to eat the principal's sandwich. That is a president. Pelly Key Kenna. Say it fast and it becomes pelekikena.

words.say_it: Hop from foot to foot on hot sand. "Mah-lee-HEE-nee."
words.bonus: The opposite of malihini is kamaʻāina, somebody from here. That is the next word.
words.picture: Visitor hopping on burning hot sand
story_paragraphs: Molly just landed from Minnesota, where it snowed yesterday. It is her first hour in Hawaiʻi and she runs straight to the beach, kicks off her shoes, and steps onto the sand.

It is noon. The sand is 140 degrees. Her feet start to cook. She hops. "HEE!" She hops on the other foot. "NEE!" Her friends scream "MOLLY!" as she hops in a zigzag all the way to the water, 50 yards, "HEE! NEE! HEE! NEE!"
She jumps in the ocean and her feet sizzle like bacon. A turtle swims away from the steam. Then she gets out and does it all again, because she forgot her towel.
That is a visitor. A newcomer. Fresh off the plane, and hopping. Molly, hee, nee.

words.say_it: Dig your toes in slowly and sigh. "Kah-mah-AAH-ee-nah."
words.bonus: Kama means child and ʻāina means land. A kamaʻāina is a child of the land. Many businesses in Hawaiʻi give a kamaʻāina discount to residents.
words.picture: Barefoot local strolling across hot sand
story_paragraphs: Molly the visitor is still hopping on the hot sand. "HEE! NEE!" Then she sees an aunty strolling toward her across the same sand. Barefoot. Slow. Holding a hot coffee.
The aunty has walked this beach every day for 60 years. Her feet are like old leather. She does not hop. She does not sweat. She stops right next to Molly and says, "Calm, ma'am."
Then she digs her toes into the burning sand and sighs happily. "AAAAAH." Molly stares. "Don't you need slippahs?" The aunty sips her coffee. "I? Nah."
She shows Molly the shady path, the good shave ice place, and the rock where the turtles nap. That is a local. Calm, ma'am. Ah. I? Nah.

words.say_it: Tip your head back and howl softly. "HOW-leh."
words.bonus: Long ago haole meant any foreigner or foreign thing. Today it often means a white person. It also shows up in plant names like koa haole, an introduced shrub whose name means foreign koa.
words.picture: Coworker and husky howling in the heat
story_paragraphs: Your new coworker just moved here from Alaska. He brought his sled dog, a huge fluffy husky. Neither of them has ever felt 88 degrees with no wind.

The first afternoon, they sit on the curb outside the office, both panting. The husky tips its head back and howls at the sun. "HOOOWL!" Your coworker, sweating like a glass of iced tea, tips his head back too. "Howl, eh," he agrees.

Aunty from the corner store walks over with two shave ice, one for him and one for the dog. She shows them the shady side of the street and where the trade winds come through. By summer the husky sleeps on cold tile and your coworker says "shoots" like he was born here.
Long ago haole just meant someone or something from outside. From somewhere else. Howl, eh.

words.say_it: Hold a small plant with care. "Oh-EE-vee."
words.bonus: ʻŌiwi contains iwi, bone. Native to the bone. Kanaka ʻŌiwi means Native Hawaiian people.
words.picture: Kids planting a native flower
story_paragraphs: The 3rd grade class is weeding the school garden with a volunteer uncle who is 75 and has dirt permanently under his nails. A girl finds a vine climbing the fence. It is 15 feet long. "OHHH, IVY!" she yells.
It takes 20 kids to pull it. They tug like it is a rope in a tug of war. It snaps and all 20 land on their ʻōkole in the mud.
The uncle laughs and holds up a small plant with little yellow flowers. "Not ivy. This one is ʻōiwi." He says it slow. A little catch in the throat, a long "ohhh," then "EE-vee."
He explains. The ivy came from far away. This ʻilima was here long before any of us. It belongs. Its roots go deep, like bones in the land. The kids plant it in the best spot.

words.say_it: Sing one long note, then cheer. "Laaah-HOO-ee!"
words.bonus: Lāhui Hawaiʻi means the Hawaiian nation, the Hawaiian people as a whole.
words.picture: Huge crowd singing one long note
story_paragraphs: It is a free concert at the park. 30,000 people are on the grass. Tūtū in folding chairs. Babies on shoulders. Surfers, nurses, farmers, kids from every island, all packed in with coolers and mats.

The singer starts the last song. She hits the big note and holds it. "LAAAAAAAAH..." She holds it for 20 seconds. Then 30,000 people join her on the same note. The ground hums. A bird in a tree stops to listen.
When the note ends, the whole crowd shouts together. "HOO-ee!" So loud the ocean feels it.
Look around. Every face is different and every voice is the same song. That is a people. A nation. Stretch that first sound long. "Laaaah... HOO-ee."

words.say_it: Grab an invisible bus pole and lurch. "PO," gulp, "eh."
words.bonus: Ka poʻe means the people. Put poʻe in front of a word to talk about a group, like the fishing people or the singing people.
words.picture: 64 people clinging to one bus pole
story_paragraphs: It is rush hour on the city bus. There is one metal pole in the middle. And there are 64 people holding it.

They are stacked like spam musubi. A nurse. A guy with a surfboard. Two grandmas with shopping carts. A kid holding a fish in a bag. Hands on hands on hands, all the way from the floor to the ceiling.
A new guy climbs on and looks for something to hold. "Pole?" he asks. Then the bus brakes hard. Everyone lurches forward at once and catches with a gulp. "EH!" That gulp is the ʻokina.
All 64 swing back together like a school of fish. Not one lets go. That is a group of people. Pole, eh. Poʻe.

words.say_it: Pat yourself from head to toe. "KEE-no."
words.picture: Person doing a handstand to find keys
story_paragraphs: You are locked out of your car at the beach. The sun is going down. The keys are somewhere on your body. Probably.
You start at the top. You pat your head. "Key?" Nothing. "NO!" Your ears. "Key? NO!" Your shirt pocket, your armpits, your belly button. "Key? NO! Key? NO!"
You check your shorts, all 6 pockets. Your socks. Inside your slippahs. You bend over and shake your whole body like a wet dog. Sand flies everywhere. A family nearby covers their plate lunch.
Finally you do a handstand. CLINK. The key falls out of your hair. Every part of you got checked. Head, arms, chest, legs, feet. That is your body. Key? No. Kino.

words.say_it: Tap the top of your head, freeze, then groan. "PO," catch, "oh."
words.bonus: Poʻo also means the top or the leader, the head of anything, like the head of a group.
words.picture: Coconut bonking a head at the beach
story_paragraphs: You are lying on the beach under a coconut tree, 60 feet tall. Everybody knows not to do this. You do it anyway. You close your eyes.
Way up at the top, a coconut the size of a bowling ball lets go. It falls for 2 full seconds. Then it lands right on the top of your head. POW!
Everything freezes. Birds stop. Waves stop. Your eyes cross. There is a tiny pause, a catch, and then it hits you. "...OHHHH."
A bump grows on your head as big as a musubi. Tūtū comes over, puts a frozen bag of peas on it, and sits you somewhere else. POW, freeze, OH. Head.

words.say_it: Run your fingers through your hair. "Lau-OH-ho."
words.bonus: Lauoho is the hair on your head. Hair on the body, or fur and feathers, is hulu.
words.picture: Aunty spinning by her hair under a fan
story_paragraphs: Aunty has not cut her hair since 1987. It is 30 feet long. She keeps it wrapped around her body like a shiny black bath towel. She sweeps the floor with it by walking backward.
One hot day, she unwraps it to cool off. The ceiling fan is on high. The tips of her hair float up. The fan grabs them.
It starts winding her hair like fishing line on a reel. Aunty rises up off the couch.
"TURN IT LOW!" she screams. Her feet leave the ground. "OH-HO!" Now she is spinning under the fan like a tetherball. The cousins are laughing too hard to help.
Finally Uncle unplugs it. Aunty drops back onto the couch, hair perfectly braided by the fan. She says it is the best it has ever looked.

words.say_it: Point at your own eye, then your face. "MAH-kah."
words.bonus: Maka also means raw, so iʻa maka is raw fish. And maka is inside kuʻemaka, eyebrow.
words.picture: Staring contest with a macaw
story_paragraphs: At the zoo there is a big red macaw with a yellow face. It hops down to the fence, puts its face one inch from yours, and stares. Its eye is the size of a quarter. Round and shiny with a little black dot in the middle.
You stare back. A staring contest. Five minutes. Ten minutes. A crowd gathers. Your eyes are drying out like raisins. The macaw does not blink. It does not even breathe.
At minute 40, you blink. The macaw leans back, flaps both wings and screams in your face, "MAH-KAW!"
You go home and every time you close your eyes you see that face and that eye. Eye. Face. Macaw. Maka.

words.say_it: Wrinkle your nose, then sneeze. "EE-hoo!"
words.bonus: The old Hawaiian greeting called honi touches nose to nose and shares breath. Ihu to ihu.
words.picture: Giant sneeze blowing lei across the room
story_paragraphs: You walk into the lei stand at the airport. There are 800 lei hanging from the ceiling. Plumeria, pīkake, tuberose, ginger. The smell is like being punched by a garden.
Your nose starts to twitch. It gets bigger. It turns red. The pollen crawls up inside it and starts a party. You try to hold it in. You cannot. "AH... EEEE... HOO!"

The sneeze blows every lei off every hook. They fly across the room like frisbees and land on the heads of 40 surprised tourists getting off a plane. The lady who runs the stand just shrugs and charges them.
Your nose is fine. It is proud of itself. Ee-hoo. That is your nose.

words.say_it: Open your mouth wide and laugh. "VAH-hah!"
words.bonus: In Hawaiʻi slang, someone with a big waha talks too much. "Eh, no be big waha."
words.picture: Uncle laughing with a giant open mouth
story_paragraphs: Uncle has the biggest mouth on the island. Not because he talks too much. Well, also that. But mostly because it is physically huge.
He can fit a whole spam musubi in there sideways. Three at once, if nobody is watching. At the lūʻau, he eats a scoop of rice without chewing, like a hippo.

But the best part is his laugh. When somebody tells a joke, his mouth opens so wide you can see his lunch, his dinner, and what he had last Tuesday. "WAH-HAH! WAH-HAH!" The sound echoes off the mountains. The dog hides.
One time a moth flew in, looked around, and flew back out. Too big in there. That is a mouth. Wah-hah. Waha.

words.say_it: Kick one leg out fast. "NEE-ho!"
words.bonus: Niho manō means shark tooth. Old Hawaiian tools and weapons used rows of them.
words.picture: Uncle kicking a tooth out on a string
story_paragraphs: Your little cousin has a loose front tooth. It has been hanging there for 3 weeks, wiggling like a door on one hinge. Nobody can get it out.
So Uncle ties one end of a string to the tooth. He ties the other end to his own knee. He stands in the yard like a football kicker. He counts. "One... two..."
On three he swings his leg and shouts "KNEE... HO!" The tooth rockets out, sails over the carport, over the mango tree, and lands on the neighbor's roof 40 feet away. PING.
