The neighbor climbs up with a ladder, finds it in the gutter, and brings it back in a little plastic bag. Your cousin grins, one tooth short. Knee, ho. Niho. Tooth.

words.say_it: Stick out your tongue, then pull it back in. "Ah-LEH-lo."
words.bonus: Alelo can also mean a language, the same way English says tongue. The everyday word for language is ʻōlelo, as in ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi.
words.picture: Tongue flopping out to wave hello
story_paragraphs: You are at the doctor. She holds a wooden stick and says "Open wide and say AHH."

You open wide. "AHHHH." And your tongue keeps going. It slides out of your mouth like a pink carpet unrolling. One foot. Two feet. Three. It flops onto the doctor's desk, lifts its tip like a little head, and waves at her.
Then it talks. "...LLO!" So you said "Ah," and your tongue said "hello." Ah, hello. Alelo.
The doctor does not even blink. She shakes the tip of your tongue like a hand and writes something on her clipboard. The kid in the waiting room faints.

words.say_it: Tug on your ear, then wince. "Peh-pay-OW!"
words.bonus: Local bakeries and manapua shops sell pepeiao, a folded bun named for its ear shape.
words.picture: Grandpa getting his ears pierced
story_paragraphs: Grandpa is 80 and has decided he wants his ears pierced. The whole family comes to the mall to watch. He sits in the tall chair at the kiosk like it is a throne.
The girl with the piercing gun tells him the price. He pays. She does the left ear. CLICK. "OW!" She says the right ear costs extra. He grumbles and pays again. CLICK. "OW!"
Pay, pay, OW. That is how he tells the story for the rest of his life. "Pay! Pay! OW!"
He walks out with two tiny gold studs, both ears glowing red like stoplights, grinning at his reflection in every store window. That is an ear.

words.say_it: Puff both cheeks, then pop them. "Pah-PAAAH-lee-nah."
words.picture: Grandpa with huge puffed cheeks inflating a float
story_paragraphs: Your grandpa is blowing up a pool float for his granddaughter, Lina. It is a unicorn. It is 12 feet long. He does not own a pump.

He takes a giant breath and blows. His cheeks puff out like two watermelons. They turn red. Then purple. Then a color that does not have a name. Every time he stops to breathe, his lips pop. "Pa... PAAAAAH..." And then he gasps her name. "...Lina."
It takes 45 minutes. At the end his cheeks are so stretched that they stay puffed for the rest of the day. He looks like a squirrel storing nuts. When he smiles, they bounce.
Lina rides the unicorn all afternoon. Grandpa sits in the shade and pats his tired cheeks.

words.say_it: Blow air through loose lips like a horse. "Leh-heh-LEH-heh."
words.bonus: Lehelehe is a doubled word, like lihilihi (eyelashes) and manamana (fingers). Lots of body words double up.
words.picture: Skydiver with lips flapping in the wind
story_paragraphs: You are skydiving over the North Shore. You jump out of the plane at 13,000 feet. You are falling at 120 miles an hour, and the wind hits your face like a fire hose.

Your lips have never been through this. The wind grabs them and flaps them like two flags in a hurricane. They make a sound all on their own. "LAY-HEY-LAY-HEY-LAY-HEY!" The top lip goes up to your nose. The bottom lip slaps your chin.
People on the beach look up and wonder what that noise is.
When you land, your lips are still flapping on their own for 10 minutes. You cannot eat your plate lunch. The rice keeps flying off. That is lips.

words.say_it: Roll your head slowly, then wince. "Aaah," catch, "EEE."
words.picture: Tiny tutu massaging a giraffe's stiff neck
story_paragraphs: The giraffe at the zoo slept wrong. Its whole neck is stuck, bent sideways, 7 feet of stiff neck. It cannot reach its leaves. It walks around looking at the world tilted.
So the zoo calls in a tūtū who does massage. She is 4 foot 10. She climbs up a ladder, then another ladder on top of that ladder, and gets to work. She pushes her thumbs into the giraffe's neck.
Every time she presses, the giraffe groans, long and deep, then squeaks at the end. "AAAAAAAH..." little catch... "EEEEEE!" She works her way from the top to the bottom. Crack. Crack. Crack.
When she is done, the giraffe stands up straight, happy, and eats every leaf in the zoo. Neck. Long sounds, both of them.

words.say_it: Lift an invisible kid onto your shoulders and groan. "Po-oh-HEE-vee."
words.bonus: Poʻohiwi starts with poʻo, head. Your shoulders sit right under it.
words.picture: Kid eating snacks on sinking shoulders
story_paragraphs: It is New Year's Eve and the fireworks are about to start. Your nephew Po is 5 and cannot see. So you put him up on your shoulders.

He weighs 40 pounds. No problem. Then Aunty hands him a malasada. Then another. Then a bag of popcorn, a musubi and a whole plate of fried noodles. He eats everything up there like a king on a throne.

Every time he takes a bite, your shoulders sink a little lower. "Po!" you say. "Oh... HEAVY!" By midnight your shoulders are down by your hips. Your knees are shaking. Po is asleep up there with sugar on his face.
Po, oh, heavy. Say it fast and that is where the kids ride. Shoulders.

words.say_it: Hold up your hand and spread all five fingers. "LEE-mah."
words.bonus: Lima means hand or arm, and also the number five, because a hand has five fingers.
words.picture: Lima beans exploding from a high five
story_paragraphs: Tūtū makes lima beans for dinner. You hate lima beans. You have hated them since you were born.

So you get sneaky. You hide one bean between each finger. Thumb, pointer, middle, ring, pinky. Five fingers on one hand, five lima beans, squeezed tight. You keep your hand under the table, very calm, very innocent.
Then Grandpa says, "Good job cleaning your plate! Up high!" He raises his hand for a high five. You cannot say no to Grandpa. You slap his hand. SPLAT.
Five lima beans explode across the kitchen. One sticks to the ceiling. One lands in the rice cooker.
Tūtū stares at you. "LIMA," she says. Hand. Five fingers. Five beans. Lima.

words.say_it: Wiggle all your fingers in front of your face. "Mah-nah-MAH-nah."
words.bonus: Manamana lima is a finger and manamana wāwae is a toe. Lima is hand, wāwae is foot.
words.picture: Whole family with feet on the dinner table
story_paragraphs: Your little cousin is learning to count. She gets to 10 on her fingers. But her homework says count to 100. So she takes off her slippahs and puts both feet on the dinner table. Now she has 20.

Not enough. She makes her brother put his feet up too. Then her mom. Then Uncle, whose toes look like 10 little sweet potatoes. Soon 5 people have their hands and feet on the table. 100 fingers and toes, all wiggling.
Tūtū walks in carrying a pot of stew. She stops. She looks at all those toes next to the rice. "MAN-A-MAN-AH!"
Everyone freezes with their feet in the air. Man oh man, ah. Fingers and toes, all over the table.

words.say_it: Scratch the air with curled fingers, then cringe. "Mai-OO-oo."
words.picture: Aunty's long nails on a chalkboard
story_paragraphs: Aunty just came back from the nail salon. Her nails are 3 inches long, gold, with little rhinestones and a tiny palm tree on each one. They click when she walks.
She comes to the school fundraiser to help. Somebody asks her to write the prices on the old chalkboard. She lifts one hand, sets her nails on the board and drags them down, slow.
SKREEEEEEEEE. Every kid in the room grabs their ears. "MY!" Their bodies shake. "ʻOO! ʻOO!" Each "oo" starts with a little gulp, a catch in the throat. The class cat hisses and shows its own claws.
Aunty looks at the cat. The cat looks at Aunty. They respect each other. Fingernails. Claws. My, ʻoo, ʻoo.

words.say_it: Puff your chest and thump it. "Oo-mah-OO-mah!"
words.picture: Buff cousin popping his shirt buttons
story_paragraphs: Your cousin has been lifting weights every day for 2 years. Today he walks out onto the beach and takes a deep breath. His chest puffs out like two slabs of kālua pig.
He wants his mother to see. "Ooh, MA!" he calls. Puff. "OOH, MA!" Puff, puff. His chest keeps getting bigger. He thumps it with both fists. BOOM, BOOM, like a drum.
His shirt buttons cannot take it. They pop off one at a time like bullets. PING. One hits a seagull. PING. One lands in a lady's shave ice. PING. One goes so far it may still be flying.
His mother looks up from her magazine for one second. "Very nice, dear," she says. Chest.

words.say_it: Pat your stomach and sigh. "Ohhh-POOOO."
words.bonus: People in Hawaiʻi use opu in everyday English, like "my opu is full."
words.picture: Uncle too full to eat the haupia
story_paragraphs: Uncle at the lūʻau. Plate number one, kālua pig and rice. Plate two, lomi salmon and poi. Plates three through seven, everything else. His belly grows with each plate like a beach ball being pumped up.
By plate seven it is so round the kids use it as a table for their cards. When he laughs, the cards bounce. His belt has given up and gone home.

Then Aunty walks by with a tray of haupia, cold, sweet, perfect. His favorite. He looks at the haupia. He looks down at his giant stomach. He sighs, long and sad. "Ohhhhh... POOOOH." Like when you miss the bus.
That is a belly. It has limits. Hold both long sounds, the long o and the long u.

words.say_it: Lift the bottom of your shirt an inch. "PEE-ko!"
words.bonus: Piko also means the center of something, the summit of a mountain, or the top of the head.
words.picture: Toddler flashing his belly button at sunrise
story_paragraphs: Your little nephew is 3 and has one trick. He lifts up his shirt, shows you his belly button, and yells "PEEK-O!" Like peekaboo, but for belly buttons. He does it to everyone. The mailman. The pastor. A dog.
One morning the whole family hikes to the top of the mountain for the sunrise. It takes 2 hours in the dark. He rides most of it on your back.
At the very top, the summit, the sun pops up over the clouds. Everyone goes quiet. And your nephew stands on the highest rock, lifts his shirt at the sun, and shouts "PEEK-O!"
The sun, as far as anyone can tell, laughs. Belly button. Summit. Both of them are a piko.

words.say_it: Reach over your shoulder and pat your back. "KOO-ah."
words.bonus: Kua (KOO-ah) is back. Koa (KO-ah) is warrior or the koa tree. One little vowel.
words.picture: Koala clinging to someone's back
story_paragraphs: A koala escapes from a visiting zoo show and climbs straight onto your back. It wraps its arms around your neck and its legs around your waist. It will not let go. It makes a little sound in your ear. "KOO-AH."
You go to work with a koala on your back. You go to the bank. You go to the dentist. You lie on your stomach at the beach so it can nap. It eats a lei off a lady walking by.
Every time you try to peel it off, it squeezes tighter and says "KOO-AH!" louder, right in your ear.
After 3 days you just give up and name it. You sleep on your stomach now. That is your back. Koo-ah. Kua.

words.say_it: Hold your knee and wince. "KOO-lee."
words.bonus: Kuli can also mean deaf. Context tells you which one.
words.picture: Aunty dumping a cooler on a scraped knee
story_paragraphs: You slide into second base at the family softball game. Bad idea. You are wearing shorts. Your knee drags through the dirt for 6 feet. It looks like a hamburger patty.

Aunty runs out from the bleachers carrying the whole 50 quart cooler. She does not bother with a bag of ice. She dumps the entire cooler right on your knee. Ice, cans, two pieces of fried chicken, everything.
First you feel the cold. "COOOOL!" Then the sting. "EEEEEEEE!" Your voice gets higher and higher until only the dogs can hear it.
Your knee is now the coldest knee in history. It has a can of soda sitting on it like a trophy. Cool, eee. Knee.

words.say_it: Lift one foot and hop in pain. "Vaaah-VAI!"
words.bonus: Wāwae means the whole leg and foot, the same way lima means the whole arm and hand.
words.picture: Barefoot hopping on toy blocks at 3 a.m.
story_paragraphs: It is 3 in the morning. You get up for a glass of water. You walk barefoot into the dark living room. You do not know that your nephew left 2,000 plastic building blocks on the floor.
Your right foot comes down on the first one. The pain shoots up your whole leg like lightning. "WAAAAAAAAH!" You hop onto your left foot. It lands on three more. "WHY?!"
Now you are hopping through the dark, foot to foot, leg to leg. "WAAAAH! WHY?! WAAAAH! WHY?!" The neighbor's lights come on. A dog two streets away starts barking. The cat leaves home.
You finally reach the kitchen, drink your water, and realize you have to go back the same way. Leg. Foot. Waaah, why.

words.say_it: Hold up the bottom of your foot like a stop sign. "Kah-poo-AH-ee."
words.bonus: Kapuaʻi means both the sole of the foot and the footprint it leaves behind.
words.picture: Car full of bare feet and footprints
story_paragraphs: Eleven cousins, one tiny car, one trip to the beach. It is a carpool. You got there last, so you get the worst seat, the back corner, squished against the window.

Everyone takes off their slippahs. Suddenly there are 22 bare feet in the car, and all of them are in your face. Sandy soles. Stinky soles. One sole with a sticker stuck to it. A foot rests on your head like a hat.
"CARPOOL?" you gasp. A heel lands on your cheek. "AH!" A big toe goes up your nose. "EE!"
When you finally get out at the beach, the car windows are covered in footprints. The ceiling too. The sole of every foot, printed everywhere. Carpool, ah, ee. Kapuaʻi.

words.say_it: Put your hand on your chest and sniff. "Poo-oo-VAI."
words.bonus: Puʻu means a hill or lump, and wai means water. Hawaiians also speak of the naʻau, the gut, as a deep seat of feeling.
words.picture: Aunty sobbing into a heart pillow
story_paragraphs: It is Saturday and Aunty has invited you over for a Korean drama marathon. 14 episodes. She has 3 boxes of tissues, a bag of dried mango and a heart shaped pillow.

By episode 9 the two main characters finally meet in the rain. By episode 12 one of them forgets who the other one is. Aunty is squeezing the heart pillow so hard it pops. She is crying. You are crying. The cat is crying.
"BOO-HOO..." Aunty hiccups mid-sob, a little catch in the throat. "...WHY?"
You feel it right in your chest, thumping and aching and full. At 2 in the morning the last episode ends happy and you both scream with joy. That is the heart. Boo, hoo, why. Puʻuwai.

words.say_it: Draw a V in the air with one finger. "EE-vee."
words.bonus: Iwi kūpuna means the bones of ancestors. They are sacred and cared for with deep respect in Hawaiian culture.
words.picture: X-ray of an arm bone with a V crack
story_paragraphs: You tried to skateboard down the steepest street in Mānoa. It did not go well. Now you are at the clinic with your arm in a sling and your helmet still on.
The doctor clips the x-ray to the glowing board. There it is. Your arm bone, long and white. And right in the middle, a crack. It is shaped exactly like the letter V. A perfect V.
You lean in and squint. "EE..." you say, because it hurts. "...VEE!" Because it really is a V.
The doctor puts on a bright green cast. 60 people sign it. In 6 weeks the bone knits back together, stronger than before. You keep the x-ray on your wall. EE, VEE. Bone.

words.say_it: Sip from an invisible mug. "KO-ko." Both o's short.
words.picture: Chicken-size mosquito sipping blood like cocoa
story_paragraphs: It is dusk at a backyard party in Hilo. The mosquitoes come out. One of them is the size of a chicken. It lands on your arm with a thump.
It pokes its long straw nose into your arm, closes its eyes, and slurps. Loud. Like a kid at the bottom of a milkshake. Then it smacks its lips and sighs, "Mmmm... COCOA."
To it, your blood is hot cocoa. It even drops in two tiny marshmallows it brought from home. It sips slowly, pinky out, like a fancy lady at a tea party.
When it is done, it pats you on the head, burps, and flies off wobbling, too full to fly straight. Cocoa. Koko. That is blood.

words.say_it: Rub your arm like it is slippery. "EE-lee."
words.bonus: ʻIli also means a land section, a smaller piece of land inside an ahupuaʻa.
words.picture: Kid shooting out of hands like soap
story_paragraphs: Before the beach, Aunty grabs you for sunscreen. She does not do a little. She does three whole bottles. Face, neck, ears, the back of your knees, between your toes. You shine like a glazed donut.
You step onto your towel and slide right off it. You slide down the sand, 30 feet, straight into the water. A fish bumps into your leg and shoots away like it hit ice.
Your cousin tries to grab your arm to pull you out. You squirt out of his hands like a wet bar of soap. He tries again. Squirt. "EELY!" he yells. "Your skin is EELY!"
Say it with a little catch in the throat first. ʻIli. Skin. The slippery stuff that holds you together.

words.say_it: Put your hand on your belly and listen. "Nah," catch, "OW."
words.bonus: In Hawaiian thinking the naʻau, the gut, is where deep feeling and knowing live, much like English uses heart.
words.picture: Uncle holding a steering wheel from his truck
story_paragraphs: Uncle is at a used car lot. A salesman with very white teeth shows him a shiny red truck. "Only $900," he says. Deep in Uncle's belly, something speaks up. "Nah."
Uncle ignores it. He buys the truck. He drives it off the lot. After one block the engine falls out onto the road. Then the doors fall off. Then the steering wheel comes off in his hands. "OW."
He walks home carrying the steering wheel. Grandma is on the porch. She does not even ask. She just pats his stomach twice. "Next time," she says, "listen to your naʻau."
That gut feeling, that deep knowing in the middle of you, that is the naʻau. It said nah. You went anyway. Ow. Put a little catch between them.

words.say_it: Tap your head like a dead battery. "LO-lo."
words.bonus: Do not mix up lolo (brain) with lōlō, with two long vowels, which means numb, paralyzed or crazy. The local slang "No act lolo" comes from lōlō.
words.picture: Student with a low battery brain
story_paragraphs: It is 2 p.m. in math class, right after lunch. You ate two plates of chicken katsu. Suddenly you hear a beep in your head. Your brain has a battery, and it just hit 3 percent.
"LOW... LOW..." says a robot voice inside your skull. Your eyes get heavy. Your head drops toward the desk.
The teacher asks you what 7 times 8 is. Your brain answers, "Low... low..." and then shows you a picture of a sandwich.
You try to plug your ear into the wall socket. It does not work. A classmate hands you a juice box and your brain goes up to 11 percent, just enough to spell your name.
That is the brain. Lolo, with two short, quick vowels. When it runs low, all you hear is low, low.

words.say_it: Say it once deep, once tiny. "LEH-oh."
words.bonus: Leo can also mean any sound or tone, not just a person's voice.
words.picture: Lion with a mouse voice
story_paragraphs: The traveling animal show has a lion named Leo. He weighs 500 pounds. His mane is like a giant golden bush. Kids hide behind their parents when he walks out.
The trainer says, "Leo, ROAR!" Leo opens his huge mouth, shows every tooth, and out comes a tiny squeaky voice. "leh-oh." Like a mouse whispering its own name.
Then a real mouse walks out behind him, opens its tiny mouth, and ROARS. The bleachers shake. Popcorn flies. Somebody's hat blows off.
They switched voices. Leo is embarrassed. The mouse is thrilled. The show sells out for 3 years. That is a voice. Big or small, it is yours. Leo.

words.say_it: Brush invisible feathers off your arms. "HOO-loo."
words.bonus: Hulu (feather) and hula (dance) differ by one vowel. A lei hulu is a feather lei.
words.picture: Boy covered in feathers after a pillow fight
story_paragraphs: Nine kids at a sleepover. One pillow fight. One pillow that cannot take it. It bursts, and 90,000 feathers explode into the room. It looks like a snow globe that somebody shook too hard.
The door opens. Mom stands there. "WHO?" she says. Every kid points at the same boy. "LOU!"
Lou is covered from head to toe in feathers. They are stuck to his hair, his eyebrows, his pajamas, even the hair on his arms. He looks like a chicken who lost a bet. He flaps his arms. Feathers fly.
Then the family dog runs in, shakes its fur, and adds its own hair to the pile. Feathers, fur, body hair. Who? Lou. Hulu.

words.say_it: Tap your forehead. "LAI."
words.bonus: Lae also means a cape or point of land. Many coastal place names start with Lae.
words.picture: Kid's forehead glowing like a lighthouse
story_paragraphs: Your little brother has a very big forehead. Big and shiny. And it has a problem. Every time he tells a lie, it lights up. Bright white, like a lighthouse.
"Did you eat the last malasada?" "No." FLASH. His forehead beams a light that sweeps across the room. "LIE!" everyone yells. "Did you feed the dog?" "Yes." FLASH. "LIE!"
At night, ships out at sea see the light coming from your house and think it is the lighthouse on the point. One fishing boat turns and heads for your yard.
So now your family uses him. He stands out on the cape at night and tells little lies to guide the boats in. Forehead. Point of land. Both lae. Lie.

words.say_it: Raise one eyebrow slowly. "Koo-eh-MAH-kah."
words.bonus: Kuʻemaka ends with maka, eye. The eyebrow is part of the eye family.
words.picture: Pigeon nesting in grandpa's eyebrow
story_paragraphs: Grandpa's eyebrows are so bushy that one of the pigeons from the rooftop uncle moved in. It built a nest in his left eyebrow. It lives there now. Grandpa does not mind.

He walks into the coffee shop. The pigeon says "COO!" The girl at the counter stares. Grandpa raises his left eyebrow at her, the pigeon riding up with it like an elevator. "EH?" he says, like what are you looking at.
Then he orders. "MOCHA."
She makes it with a little heart on top. And a tiny cup for the pigeon. Coo, eh, mocha. And notice it ends with maka, eye. The eyebrow sits right over it.

words.say_it: Flutter your eyelashes and giggle. "Lee-hee-LEE-hee."
words.bonus: Lihi means edge or border. Lihilihi, the eyelashes, grow along the edge of the eyelid.
words.picture: Camel tickling someone with long eyelashes
story_paragraphs: At the county fair there is a camel. The camel has eyelashes 2 feet long. Thick, curly, beautiful. Every lady walking by is jealous.
You get close to pet it. The camel looks at you and blinks. The lashes sweep across your face like two feather dusters. It tickles so much you giggle. "Lee-hee!" It blinks again. "LEE-hee!"
The camel likes this. It blinks faster and faster. Flutter flutter flutter. You are laughing so hard you fall down in the hay. "LEE-HEE! LEE-HEE!" The breeze from its lashes blows three hats off.
Eyelashes. Right on the edge of the eye. Lihilihi.

words.say_it: Tap your chin twice. "Ow-VAI."
words.bonus: ʻAuwae (ow-VAI) is chin. Wāwae (vaah-VAI) is leg. They rhyme, so hear the start.
words.picture: Mangoes falling on a chin
story_paragraphs: It is mango season. You lie down on the grass under Tūtū's mango tree. You tilt your head back, chin up, and close your eyes.
PLOP. A ripe mango lands right on your chin. "OW!" Another one. PLOP. "WHY?" Then another. The tree is aiming. It hits the same spot every time. "OW! WHY? OW! WHY?"
By the end there are 11 mangoes around your head and your chin is sticky, yellow and shaped a little bit like a mango.
Start with a tiny catch in your throat, then ow, why. That is your chin. Different from wāwae, the leg, which starts with a long "waaah."

words.say_it: Flex your arm and strain. "EE," catch, "oh!"
words.bonus: Do not confuse ʻiʻo (flesh, meat) with ʻio, the Hawaiian hawk.
words.picture: Skinny cousin's muscle popping out
story_paragraphs: At the beach party the grill is loaded with 50 pounds of meat. Short ribs, chicken, hot dogs, a whole fish. It has to move out of the wind. Skinny Cousin Kimo says he got it.
He grabs both sides. He lifts. His face goes red. "EEEEEEEEEE..." His arms shake like a washing machine. Then a little catch in his throat. And then "...OH!"
At that exact moment, his arm muscle pops up out of nowhere, like a softball jumping out from under his skin. Everyone gasps. Nobody knew it was in there.
He carries the grill 20 feet, sets it down, and stares at his new muscle. The meat is fine. Muscle. Meat. Flesh. Eee, oh.

words.say_it: Trace the veins on your wrist. "AH," catch, "ah."
words.bonus: Aʻa (vein, root) is different from ʻaʻā, the rough, sharp, crumbly kind of lava.
words.picture: Vein on arm looking like banyan roots
story_paragraphs: You are at the blood drive. The nurse needs a vein. She taps your arm. Nothing. She slaps your arm. Nothing. She calls another nurse. They both slap.

Then it rises. A vein pops up on your arm as thick as a garden hose. It keeps going. It branches out across your elbow and down your wrist, twisting and splitting like the roots of the giant banyan tree outside the window.
The nurse looks at the vein. She looks out the window at the banyan roots. She looks back at the vein. "Ah..." she says, then a catch in her throat. "ʻAH!" She found it.
Vein. Root. They even look the same. Aʻa.

words.say_it: Wave to someone right in front of you. "AH-lo."
words.bonus: A popular way to explain aloha is alo (face, presence) plus hā (breath). Face to face, sharing breath.
words.picture: Sunflower always facing you
story_paragraphs: There is a giant sunflower in Tūtū's yard, 9 feet tall, and it has decided you are the sun. Wherever you go, its big yellow face turns to face you.
You walk to the mailbox. The flower turns. "ʻALLO!" it squeaks, dropping the h because it has no lungs.
You walk around to the back of the house. It twists all the way around. "ʻALLO!" You hide behind the water tank. It leans over the tank, face first. "ʻALLO!"
It will not show you its back. Ever. Only its front. Only its face.
You give up and eat your lunch in front of it. It watches every bite. ʻAllo. Alo. Front and face.

words.say_it: Bump your hip to one side. "Kee-KAH-lah!"
words.picture: Aunty's hip bump launching uncle into hay
story_paragraphs: It is a paniolo party upcountry. There is a barn, a band, and 200 people in cowboy boots doing a line dance. The caller has a microphone and a very loud voice.
"KICK!" Everyone kicks. "HOLLER!" Everyone hollers. "HIP!" Everyone swings their hip to the side and bumps the person next to them.

Then Aunty gets in the line. Aunty has been doing hip bumps at parties for 50 years. She swings her hip. Uncle next to her flies 12 feet into a stack of hay bales. The hay explodes. A horse looks in through the window.
"KICK! HOLLER!" Bump. Two more cousins go flying. Aunty keeps dancing. That is the hip. The most powerful thing in the barn.

words.say_it: Suck in your waist, then let it all go. "Poo-HAH-kah!"
words.picture: Uncle's belt buckle flying off at a photo
story_paragraphs: It is the big family photo on the beach. 60 people. Uncle is in the front row and he is sucking in his waist so hard his belt is loose.
The photographer's camera jams. "Hold on, one more minute." Uncle holds his breath. One minute. Ten minutes. Thirty minutes. His face turns blue like a mahimahi. His waist is as thin as a coffee can.

At minute 45 the photographer says "Okay, done!" Uncle lets it all out. "POOOOOOOO... HAH!" His waist springs back out like a spring. His belt buckle shoots off with a "KA!" and knocks a coconut out of a tree.
In the photo, 59 people are smiling and Uncle is a blue blur. That is the waist. Pooo, hah, ka.

words.say_it: Slap both thighs and hold it long. "Oooo-HAAAH!"
words.picture: Cousin slapping giant watermelon thighs
story_paragraphs: Your cousin has done leg day at the gym every day for a year. No arms. No chest. Only legs. Now his thighs are the size of two watermelons.
He cannot find jeans that fit. He wears two pairs of shorts, one per leg. When he walks, the thighs rub and make a sound like a squeaky balloon.
He is very proud. He slaps both thighs with both hands and yells "OOOOOO-HAAAAA!" The slap is so loud the car alarms go off down the street. Both sounds long, the long u and the long a.
Then he tries to walk down the stairs. The thighs are too big to bend. So he slides down the railing. Thigh.

words.say_it: Flap your arms like wings. "Eh-HEH-oo!"
words.picture: Uncle with paper plate wings in a kiddie pool
story_paragraphs: Uncle has built wings. He made them from 400 paper plates, a roll of duct tape and two broom handles. Each wing is 10 feet long. He has been flapping them in the carport for a week.
Today he climbs onto the carport roof. The whole street comes out. A neighbor lady drops her hose and yells "EH! HEY, YOU! Get down!"

He does not get down. He jumps. He flaps. For one magic second, he flies. He goes up 2 feet. The chickens in the yard gasp. Then the wings fold like a taco and he drops straight into the kiddie pool. SPLOOSH.
He climbs out and shakes the water off his wings. "Tomorrow I going use more plates." Wing. Eh, hey, you.

words.say_it: Swish your hand behind you like a tail. "Hoo-EH-lo."
words.bonus: Huelo is also the name of a place on Maui.
words.picture: Cat's giant tail swishing in the dark
story_paragraphs: You are house sitting for the neighbor. It is dark. The power went out. You are feeling your way down the hallway.
Something soft and furry swishes across your cheek. You freeze. "WHO?" Silence. "'ELLO?" It swishes again, across your neck this time. "WHO? 'ELLO?"

You find the flashlight and turn it on. It is the neighbor's cat, sitting on the bookshelf. It has a tail 4 feet long, fluffy as a feather duster. It is swinging it back and forth across the hallway like a windshield wiper, dusting everything.
It looks at you like you are the weird one. Tail. Who, 'ello. Huelo.

words.say_it: Squat like a hen, then stand up proud. "HAH-leh!"
words.bonus: Hale shows up in many words. Hale pule is a church, a house of prayer. Hale kula is a schoolhouse.
words.picture: Giant hen laying a whole house
story_paragraphs: There is an empty lot at the end of your street. One morning a chicken the size of a tour bus walks in and sits down on it. The whole street comes out to watch.
The giant hen closes her eyes. She grunts. "HAH!" Everyone leans in. She strains. "LAY!"
She stands up and walks away. Behind her is a house. A whole house. Three bedrooms, two bathrooms, a lanai and a carport. Still a little warm. The mailbox already has the family name on it.
By dinner a family has moved in and they are grilling on the lanai. Hah, lay. Hale. House. Building.

words.say_it: Spread your arms and touch both walls. "LOO-mee."
words.bonus: Lumi comes from English room. Lumi moe is a bedroom and lumi ʻauʻau is a bathroom.
words.picture: Tiny apartment where the door hits the bed
story_paragraphs: You found an apartment in Honolulu. The ad says "ROOMY!" in big letters. It costs $2,400 a month. You sign right away.
You open the door. It hits the bed. The bed hits the wall. The wall is the kitchen. The kitchen is also the closet.
The toilet is under the sink. To turn around, you have to go outside.
The landlord squeezes in behind you and spreads his arms. His elbows touch both walls. "Roomy, eh!" he says. He says it with a Hawaiian L. "LOO-mee!"
You sleep standing up, like a horse. Still, it is a room. Lumi.

words.say_it: Walk through an invisible doorway with arms out. "Ee-POO-kah."
words.bonus: Puka means a hole or opening, or to pass through. An ʻīpuka is the opening you pass through.
words.picture: Uncle-shaped hole used as a door
story_paragraphs: Uncle is late for the lūʻau. The front door is locked and the key is lost. He does not wait. He backs up to the end of the driveway, puts his head down and runs straight at the living room wall.
CRASH. He goes right through. There is now a hole in the wall in the exact shape of Uncle, arms out, one slippah shape at the bottom.
Tūtū looks up from her chair and screams long and high. "EEEEEEE!" Then she points. "PUKA!" Puka means hole.
Nobody ever fixes it. The family uses the Uncle-shaped hole as the new front door. Guests have to hold their arms out to come in. That is a door, a gateway. Eee, puka.

words.say_it: Poke one finger through an invisible window. "Poo-kah-ah-nee-AH-nee."
words.bonus: Puka means hole or opening and aniani means clear, like glass, so a window is literally a transparent opening. Aniani by itself means mirror or glass.
words.picture: Coconut hole in window, twin Annies
story_paragraphs: Your neighbor has twin girls, and for some reason he named both of them Annie. Today the Annies are playing baseball in the living room with a coconut and a rolling pin.

CRACK. The coconut flies straight through the front window and punches a perfect round hole in the glass, 9 inches wide. The wind starts whistling through it. A myna bird flies in, looks around, and flies back out.
Dad storms in, sees the hole, and jabs his finger at the glass. "PUKA! ANNIE! ANNIE!" Both Annies point at each other.

He never fixes it. He glues a little wooden frame around the hole and calls it the new window. Now every time the trade winds blow, the whole house whistles "Puka, Annie, Annie" at the girls all night.

words.say_it: Pretend to shove a grandpa sled across the floor. "Pah-pah-HEH-leh!"
words.bonus: Papa is a flat surface or board, and hele means to go. The floor is the flat surface you go on.
words.picture: Grandpa sliding on waxed floor like a sled
story_paragraphs: Papa is 78 and he waxes the floor every Saturday like it is his religion. Nine hours on his hands and knees. When he is done, the floor is so shiny you can see up your own nose in it.
The grandkids have figured out the best part. Papa lies flat on his belly with wax rags tied to his elbows and knees. Three kids grab his ankles, run, and shove. "PAPA, HEH-LEH!" Papa, go!

He zooms down the hallway like a sled, spinning slowly, arms out, buffing 60 feet of floor as he goes. He shoots past the kitchen, out the back door, across the lanai, and stops with a splash in the koi pond.
He climbs out dripping and says the floor still has a spot. "Again. Papa, HEH-leh."

words.say_it: Point up at your ceiling. "Kow-PAH-koo." Spit on the PAH, coo on the koo.
words.bonus: Kaupaku is really the peak or ridge of the roof, the very top line of the house.
words.picture: Cooing cow on the roof ridge
story_paragraphs: You wake up at 5 in the morning because the ceiling is creaking. Something very heavy is walking around on top of your house. Thump. Thump. Plaster sprinkles on your face.
You run outside in your slippahs and look up. There is a full grown cow standing on the very top of your roof, balanced on the ridge like a tightrope walker. Nobody knows how it got up there.

It chews a roof shingle, makes a face, and spits it out. "PAH!" The shingle lands in your cereal. Then it tucks its legs under itself and settles in with the 40 pigeons that live up there, and it starts to coo like them. "Cooo. Cooo."
You call the neighbors over and point. "COW! PAH! COO!" Nobody believes you until the roof sags 2 feet in the middle.

words.say_it: Slap a wall with your palm. "Pah, EE, ah." Get louder on the EE.
words.picture: Ninja cousin running up the wall
story_paragraphs: Your cousin has watched too many ninja movies. He is convinced he can run straight up the living room wall, flip backwards, and land on the couch.

He backs up to the kitchen. He runs full speed in his socks. First foot hits the wall. "PAH!" Second foot, third foot, he is actually going up. "EEEEEE!" Four steps, five steps, his head is almost touching the ceiling fan.
Then the wall does what walls do. Nothing. It just stands there, flat and hard, and gravity remembers him. "AHHHHH!" He peels off and lands in the laundry basket.

There are now five sock prints going up the wall in a perfect line. Aunty was going to be mad, but instead she framed them. Now every guest asks about the wall, and your cousin tells the story like he won.

words.say_it: Karate chop the nearest table, gently. "Paaah... kow-KOW!" Hold that first paaah long.
words.picture: Karate Tūtū chopping the koa table
story_paragraphs: Tūtū is 83 years old and a black belt in karate. At Thanksgiving somebody says she is getting soft. The whole house goes quiet.

She walks over to the dining table. It is solid koa, 11 feet long, built by her own grandfather, and it weighs more than a pickup truck. The turkey is on it. The rice is on it. Eleven plates are on it.
She raises her hand, takes a long breath, and lets out the longest yell you have ever heard. "PAAAAAAAH!" Then she chops. "KOW!" Again. "KOW!"

Every plate jumps 2 feet in the air, spins once, and lands back exactly where it was. Not one grain of rice spills. The table does not even crack. Tūtū bows to the table. The table, somehow, bows back.

words.say_it: Flop down on an invisible mat. "Mo-EH-nah." Yawn on the nah.
words.bonus: Moe means to sleep, so a moena is the thing you sleep on. The old style moena is woven from lauhala (pandanus leaves).
words.picture: Lauhala mat unrolled over tall grass
story_paragraphs: Dad told you to mow the lawn a month ago. You did not. The grass is now 4 feet tall and a family of chickens has moved in.

Today you finally go out there, but not with a lawn mower. You drag out Aunty's giant lauhala mat, woven by hand, 40 feet long, and you unroll it right over the jungle. FLOOMP. The grass folds flat under it like a mattress. It is the softest bed in Hawaiʻi.
You lie down. The sun is warm. The chickens climb on too.
Dad comes home, sees the mat on the lawn, and yells from the car. "Did you MOW?" You do not even open your eyes. "Mow? Eh... nah." Then you snore so loud the chickens leave.

words.say_it: Fluff your pillow and whisper at it. "Oo-LOO-nah."
words.bonus: Moena (mat) and uluna (pillow) go together. That is your whole bed.
words.picture: Glowing moon pillow floating over rooftops
story_paragraphs: You buy a pillow at the swap meet from a man who will not tell you what is inside it. It is perfectly round, 4 feet across, and it glows a soft white, like the full moon.
That night you put your head on it. It puffs up. And up. It lifts off the bed with you still on it, floats out the open window, and drifts over the whole neighborhood at rooftop height.
Down below, people are in their yards having barbecues. They look up, see this big glowing circle crossing the sky, and gasp. "OOOH, LUNA!" One uncle starts howling at it.
You float over the H-1 until sunrise, drooling on your moon. At 6 a.m. it gently sets you back in bed, and a little bit of drool falls on a dog.

words.say_it: Pound your fist on your knee twice. "KAH-pah. KAH-pah."
words.bonus: Kapa is beaten from wauke (paper mulberry) bark with a wooden beater called an iʻe kuku. Do not mix it up with kapu, which means forbidden or sacred.
words.picture: Aunty beating bark into a house blanket
story_paragraphs: Aunty sits on the lanai with a strip of soaked bark about as wide as your hand. She puts it on a smooth log and starts beating it with a wooden beater.
KA. PA. KA. PA. That is the sound. It echoes up the whole valley. The roosters start nodding to the beat. The neighbor's dog stops barking and just listens.
She does not stop for three days. KA, PA, KA, PA. The bark gets thinner and wider and softer. By day two it covers the lanai. By day three it hangs off the roof and spills into the street.

That night it rains hard. Aunty throws the giant cloth over the whole house like a blanket and tucks the corners under the steps. Everyone inside sleeps warm, and all night the rain on the roof sounds like ka, pa, ka, pa.

words.say_it: Hold your nose over an imaginary gourd. "EE-poo."
words.bonus: An ipu is also the gourd drum used in hula. An ipu heke is a double gourd, one on top of another.
words.picture: Kid inside a giant smelly gourd
story_paragraphs: Your neighbor grew a gourd so big it broke the trellis. It is 5 feet tall, round on the bottom, shaped like a giant bottle, and it has been drying on his carport for a year.

Your little cousin, age 6, crawls inside it through the hole on top. It still has old dried seeds and pulp in the bottom, and it smells like a gym bag that went to a fish market. From deep inside you hear a hollow, echoing voice. "EEEE... POOOO!"

He climbs out green. The neighbor laughs, scrapes the whole thing clean, and now it is the most useful container on the street. It holds rice. It holds fishing gear. It holds the TV remote. On weekends it holds your cousin, who has decided he likes it in there after all.

words.say_it: Hold up both hands like you are cradling a big bowl. "PO-lah."
words.bonus: Pola comes from the English word bowl. Ipu is the older word for any kind of container.
words.picture: Polar bear drinking saimin from a hot tub bowl
story_paragraphs: A polar bear walks into a little saimin stand in Waipahu. It is sweating. It is 88 degrees. It has come a very long way for noodles.
The cook asks what size. The bear cannot say the letter R, so it just pounds its chest. "PO-LAH. Big. PO-LAH." Then it spreads its arms as wide as they go.

The cook goes out back and comes in rolling a bowl the size of a hot tub. He fills it with 80 gallons of saimin, 400 slices of kamaboko and a whole green onion field. The bear lifts the bowl with both paws and drinks it in one long slurp. Then it climbs into the empty bowl, curls up, and falls asleep because the bowl is cool on its belly.
The stand now sells a Po-lah size.

words.say_it: Run a wet finger around a real glass. "Keeee," tiny catch, "AH-hah."
words.bonus: Kīʻaha can be a cup, a glass or a mug. The long ī is that high keeeee note held out.
words.picture: Uncle playing 40 water glasses, then chugging
story_paragraphs: At the family party, Uncle lines up 40 drinking glasses on the table, each filled with a different amount of water. He wets his finger and starts rubbing the rims.

"KEEEEEEEEE." It is a high, thin, glassy sound. It goes right through your teeth. The dogs in the whole neighborhood start howling. A light bulb flickers. Uncle plays for three straight hours in the hot garage, moving down the row of glasses like a piano player.

When he finally finishes, he is so thirsty he picks up the first glass and chugs it. Gulp. He stops dead for a second, that little catch in his throat. Then "AHHH-HAH!" He does it 39 more times. Keeeee, gulp, ahh-hah. Keeeee, gulp, ahh-hah. By the end he is sloshing when he walks.

words.say_it: Dig with an imaginary spoon. "POO-nah!"
words.bonus: Puna means both a spoon and a spring of water. The Puna district on Hawaiʻi Island carries the same word.
words.picture: Baby with spoon striking a water spring
story_paragraphs: Your baby niece is 2 and she cannot say the letter S. Her favorite thing in the world is a big metal soup spoon. She carries it everywhere and holds it up to strangers. "POONA!"

One afternoon she takes her spoon to the backyard and starts digging. Everybody laughs. She digs for three hours without stopping. The hole gets knee deep, then waist deep. Tiny scoop, tiny scoop, tiny scoop.
Then her spoon goes clink on a rock, and a spring of cold fresh water shoots 30 feet into the air. It makes a rainbow over the carport. The water keeps coming, clean and cold, and it never stops.
She stands in the spray with her spoon held high like a trophy and yells "POONA!" Now the whole block fills their water jugs in your backyard.

words.say_it: Chop the air with a flat hand. "PAH-hee." Giggle on the hee.
words.bonus: Pahi kaua, a fighting knife, is a word for sword.
words.picture: Giggling knife chopping 200 onions
story_paragraphs: The family is cooking for a lūʻau for 300 people, and your job is chopping onions. Two hundred onions. Everyone in the kitchen is crying like it is a sad movie.

Except the knife. Aunty's big old kitchen knife has been in the family for 60 years, and somewhere along the way it learned to laugh. Every time it chops, it hits the board with a "PAH!" and then it giggles. "Hee!"
PAH. Hee. PAH. Hee. PAH. Hee hee hee.

The faster you chop, the harder it laughs. By onion 150 it is cackling so hard it vibrates in your hand. You are sobbing, snot running, and this knife is having the best day of its life. When you finish, it winks at you in the light and says "Pah... hee," one last time, very pleased with itself.

words.say_it: Stir a huge pot with both arms. "EE-poo HOW."
words.bonus: Ipu means container and hao means iron, so an ipu hao is literally an iron container. Today it means any cooking pot or saucepan, even one made of aluminum or glass.
words.picture: Burning gourd next to giant iron pot
story_paragraphs: Remember the giant gourd from ipu? Your cousin decides to cook beef stew in it. He sets it right on the campfire at the beach.

The gourd catches fire in about 9 seconds. Black smoke everywhere. It smells like burnt hair and old socks. Your cousin backs away holding his nose. "EEE, POO!" Then he looks at the pile of raw beef and carrots. "HOW are we supposed to cook now?"

Six uncles come walking up the beach carrying something on two poles. It is a black iron pot, 4 feet wide, heavy as a car engine. They hang it over the fire, dump in the whole cooler of stew stuff, and it bubbles for five hours without a problem.
Your cousin looks at the iron pot, then the ashes of his gourd. "Iron ipu. Ipu... HOW. Ohhh."

words.say_it: Flick an imaginary match and jump back. "Kah-poo-AH-hee!"
words.bonus: Ahi means fire. Do not mix it up with ʻahi, with an ʻokina, which is the yellowfin tuna.
words.picture: Grandpa's stove fireball, smoking hair
story_paragraphs: Grandpa's gas stove is older than your parents. The pilot light has been broken since 1994, so to light it he turns the knob, waits, looks for the matches, finds the matches, drops the matches, picks up the matches, and THEN strikes one.
By then the kitchen is full of gas.

"KA-POOF!" A fireball the size of a beach ball rolls up to the ceiling. Grandpa's eyebrows are gone. His comb-over is standing straight up and smoking. "AH!" Then he pats his head, sees he is fine, and starts giggling. "Hee hee hee."
The burner is lit, blue and perfect. He puts on the rice pot like nothing happened. Every morning, same thing. Ka-POOF, AH, hee. The neighbors set their clocks by it.

words.say_it: Hold your hands out to catch snowflakes. "HOW?!"
words.bonus: Snow really does fall on the tall mountains of Hawaiʻi Island in winter. Hau is also the hau tree with yellow flowers. Do not mix it up with hao, which is iron.
words.picture: Shave ice machine snowing on Ala Moana
story_paragraphs: It is 91 degrees at Ala Moana beach park. A shave ice truck is parked by the lagoon with a line of 200 kids. The owner has just bought a brand new shave ice machine that is way too powerful.
He flips it on. The machine shudders. Then it explodes out the side of the truck like a snow cannon.

It snows. Actual snow, all over the park. It piles up 3 feet deep on the grass and on the picnic tables. The kids stop, look up, and scream "HOW?!" A lady in a bikini is building a snowman. An uncle slides down the little hill on a boogie board.
The owner does not panic. He walks around pouring strawberry, lilikoʻi and blue vanilla syrup on the whole park, and sells it by the scoop.

words.say_it: Hold up an imaginary torch. "Koo-KOO-ee!" like a cuckoo.
words.bonus: Old Hawaiians strung oily kukui nuts on a stick and burned them one at a time for light. Kukui is the state tree of Hawaiʻi.
words.picture: Cuckoo bird holding a kukui nut torch
story_paragraphs: A storm knocks out power on the whole island. Your house is pitch black. You cannot find the flashlight. Your little brother is crying because the refrigerator stopped humming.
Then, at exactly 9 o'clock, the old cuckoo clock on the wall clicks. The tiny door swings open and out pops the little wooden bird. But tonight it is holding a burning nut on a stick, like a torch.
"KOO-KOO-EE!"

The whole living room lights up warm and orange. The bird does not go back inside. It just stays out there, holding up its little lamp, for five hours. The family plays cards by cuckoo light. Every hour it adds another burning nut to the stick and yells "KOO-KOO-EE!" a little louder, very proud of itself.

words.say_it: Wiggle your fingers like sparks. "Oo-EE-lah!" Hit that EE high.
words.bonus: Uila means lightning and electricity. Hekili is thunder.
words.picture: Aunty struck by lightning at karaoke
story_paragraphs: Aunty is singing karaoke in the backyard during a thunderstorm, which everyone told her not to do. She is holding a metal microphone on a long metal stand. She is going for the big note.
The sky flashes. A bolt of lightning comes straight down and hits the microphone.
Aunty's hair shoots 3 feet straight up. Her eyes glow blue. Sparks jump off her earrings. And she hits the note of her life. "OOOOOH... EEEEEEE... LAAAAAH!"
Every light on the street turns on at once. The garage door opens by itself. The neighbor's TV turns on. The rice cooker starts cooking. The karaoke machine gives her a score of 100 and then melts.
Aunty is totally fine. She says she has never sounded better. She now sings only in storms.

words.say_it: Hold up a key between two fingers and stretch it out. "Keeeee."
words.bonus: Ti leaves are what wrap laulau. The same short word kī means both the key and the plant.
words.picture: Key wrapped in a ti leaf in the hedge
story_paragraphs: You are locked out of the house. You call Mom. She says she hid the spare key in the kī. You think she means "in the key," which makes no sense, so you hang up.
Then you turn around and see the hedge. It is 300 ti plants, tall green and red leaves, all around the yard. She meant the ti. The key is somewhere in there.
You dig through the leaves for an hour. Leaf after leaf after leaf. Finally you just stand in the middle of the hedge and scream "KEEEEEEEEEY!" and hold it as long as you can.
Every ti plant rustles. One of them slowly lowers a leaf. Tied inside it, wrapped up like a tiny laulau, is the key. You unwrap it and it smells faintly like dinner.

words.say_it: Point a remote at the TV. "Kee-VEE." The w sounds like a v.
words.bonus: Hawaiian uses a k where English has a t, so TV became kīwī. The w here sounds like a v.
words.picture: Giant kiwi fruit hogging the TV
story_paragraphs: A kiwi fruit the size of a beanbag chair rolls in through your front door. Brown, fuzzy, smelling a little sour. It rolls straight to the couch and plops down in front of the television.

You reach for the remote. The kiwi rolls on your hand. Squish. You try again. Squish. It will not let you change the channel. It only wants cooking shows, and only the ones about fruit salad, which is honestly a little dark.
When you unplug the television, the kiwi starts vibrating and screaming. "KEE-VEE! KEE-VEE! KEE-VEEEE!" The fuzz stands straight up. The windows rattle.
You plug it back in. It settles down, fuzz flat, happy. It has now watched 14 straight hours. It is getting a little fuzzy around the eyes. It does not have eyes.

words.say_it: Hold your fist to your ear like a phone. "Keh-leh-PO-nah."
words.bonus: Hawaiian turns T into K and F into P, so telephone became kelepona.
words.picture: Sister yanked home by a 3 mile phone cord
story_paragraphs: The old phone hangs on the kitchen wall with a curly cord. Your sister Kelly is 15 and she has stretched that cord all the way down the hall, into her room, out her window, down the street, and around the corner to the bus stop. It is 3 miles long now.
Every time the phone rings, Mom picks up and screams down the hallway. "KELLY! PHONE-AH!" Then she yanks the cord.

Somewhere in Kaimukī, Kelly gets pulled off a bench and dragged backwards through a plate lunch line, across a parking lot, and past three mongooses, the cord snapping back like a giant rubber band. She lands in the kitchen, grabs the phone, says "Hello?"
It is a wrong number. She walks back to the bus stop.

words.say_it: Turn an invisible radio knob. "Leh-kee-OHHH." Hold the ō.
words.bonus: Radio became lekiō the same way telephone became kelepona. R turns into L, and D turns into K.
words.picture: Dump truck of musubi from a radio contest
story_paragraphs: You are stuck in traffic on the H-1 with the radio on. The DJ says caller number 9 wins a year of free spam musubi.
You dial. You get through. You are caller number 9. The DJ yells "You are the LUCKY caller!" and you scream so loud the car shakes. "LUCKY... OHHHHHHHH!"
You hold that OH for so long that the cars around you start honking along. The radio dial spins by itself. The antenna shoots up 20 feet like a periscope.

The next morning a dump truck backs into your driveway and pours out 3,650 spam musubi, a hill of them taller than the house. The radio on your kitchen counter keeps saying "Lucky, oh... lucky, oh..." by itself for a week.

words.say_it: Twist an imaginary pepper grinder. "PEH-pah."
words.bonus: Pepa comes from the English word paper. Nūpepa is newspaper. Pepa can also mean playing cards, and even pepper, so the grinder in the story is not totally wrong.
words.picture: Pepper grinder spewing paper blizzard
story_paragraphs: Uncle Sonny gets a fancy pepper grinder for his birthday. It is 3 feet tall and made of shiny black wood. At dinner he holds it over his steak and twists.
Instead of pepper, out comes paper. Little white squares, like confetti, pouring onto the steak. He twists harder. Now whole sheets come curling out, then notebook paper, then a phone book.
Everyone yells "PEPPER!" and Uncle yells back "No! PEH-PAH!"
Then he sniffs the grinder and sneezes. A giant sneeze. FWOOSH. Five hundred sheets of paper blast out and fill the dining room like a blizzard. It is up to your knees.
The kids are thrilled. They do all their homework on the table right there, and Uncle keeps grinding out more paper whenever they need it.

words.say_it: Wag your finger at a dog. "POO-keh." Two soft syllables, not the English word for throwing up.
words.bonus: Puke comes from the English word book. B turned into P.
words.picture: Poi dog eating a dictionary
story_paragraphs: Your dog is named Pook. Pook is a fat brown poi dog and Pook eats books. Not shoes. Not slippahs. Books.

He ate a whole cookbook in one afternoon. He ate the phone book. He ate a 900 page dictionary and now he burps big words. You come home and there are shredded pages all over the living room and a library sticker stuck to his nose.
You scream "POOK! EH!" and he looks up at you with a mouth full of chapter 7.

The library now knows him by name. When you walk in to return a chewed-up book, the librarian just sighs and says "Pook, eh?" Pook sits by the shelf, very calm, reading the spines. Deciding what is for dinner.

words.say_it: Click an imaginary pen three times. "PEH-nee."
words.bonus: Peni is a pen or pencil. Pukui-Elbert also lists peni for a penny, but the usual word for a cent is keneka.
words.picture: Aunty Penny with 312 pens in her bun
story_paragraphs: Aunty Penny works at the post office and she never loses a pen, because she keeps all of them in her hair. She has a tall bun on top of her head with 312 pens stuck in it, pointing out in every direction.
When anybody in the line needs to sign something, they just yell "PENNY!" and she leans over. You pull one out. Blue, black, red, a gold one that lights up, one that is also a tiny flashlight.

Once a customer took the last pen from the middle and the whole bun collapsed. Pens rained down onto the counter for a full minute. Aunty Penny did not flinch. She scooped them up and stacked her hair back up in 40 seconds flat.
When she clicks all 312 at once, it sounds like popcorn.

words.say_it: Pull an imaginary pencil out of your collar. "Peh-nee-KAH-lah."
words.bonus: Peni is a pen and penikala is a pencil. Both came from English.
words.picture: Aunty Penny with pencils around her collar
story_paragraphs: Aunty Penny from peni has run out of room in her hair. So now she keeps her pencils in her shirt collar. Eighty-eight yellow pencils, sharpened to needle points, sticking straight up all around her neck like a sea urchin.
Today she is subbing for a fourth grade class on test day, and 30 kids forgot their pencils. The regular teacher panics and yells across the room. "PENNY! COLLAH!"
Aunty Penny walks slowly down each row and bends her neck. Each kid pulls one pencil out of her collar. Pip, pip, pip. By the end her collar is bare and her neck is covered in little gray dots.
At lunch she sits in the corner with an electric sharpener and reloads. Grrrrr. Grrrrr. Eighty-eight times.

words.say_it: Flick an invisible envelope across the room. "LEH-kah!"
words.bonus: Leka comes from the English word letter.
words.picture: Mailman flinging letters like ninja stars
story_paragraphs: The mailman on your street is Uncle Leh, and Uncle Leh does not get out of his car. Ever. He delivers every letter by flinging it out the window at 60 miles an hour.

The envelopes spin through the air like ninja stars and stick into your front door. Thunk. Thunk. Thunk. Birthday cards, electric bills, a letter from Grandma in Hilo, all stuck in the wood in a neat row.
When the kids on the street hear his engine, they scream the warning. "LEH! CAR!" Everyone dives behind a wall. The cats run. A letter slices through a hedge and trims it perfectly.
Grandma writes back every week. She always adds a note at the bottom of her letter that says "Tell Leh to slow down." He reads it. He speeds up.

words.say_it: Pat your pocket, hiccup, then "EH-keh!"
words.bonus: ʻEke can be a bag, a sack or a pocket in your clothes. That little catch at the start is the ʻokina.
words.picture: Birthday cake pulled from a shorts pocket
story_paragraphs: You are at the bus stop digging in your shorts pocket for bus fare. Your hand keeps going down. Past your wrist. Past your elbow. Your whole arm is in your pocket, and it is still going.
You pull things out one by one. A slippah. A mango. A live crab that pinches you and runs away. A ʻukulele. A fishing pole. A cousin you have not seen since 2019.
Then your fingers touch something soft and sticky. You pull out a whole birthday cake, three layers, chocolate, with nine candles already lit.

You get such a shock you hiccup, a little catch in your throat, and then you yell "EH... CAKE!" The bus pulls up. The driver sees the cake. He lets you ride free if you share, and you pull out paper plates from the same pocket.

words.say_it: Bleat like a goat with a bucket on your head. "Paaah-KEH-keh."
words.bonus: Pākeke comes from English bucket. It rhymes with lākeke, which is a jacket.
words.picture: Goat with a bucket stuck on its head
story_paragraphs: A wild goat wanders down from the hills into your backyard. It is thirsty. It finds the mop bucket by the hose, full of soapy water, and sticks its whole head in.
Now the bucket is stuck on its head.

The goat panics and runs in circles around the yard, bleating. "PAAAAAAH!" But inside the metal bucket, the sound bounces around and comes out as this weird echo. "Keh-keh-keh-keh." PAAAAH, keh-keh. PAAAAH, keh-keh.

It runs into the car. Clang. It runs into the fence. Clang. It runs into Dad, who was carrying a plate of barbecue chicken. The chicken goes flying. The goat, still wearing the bucket, somehow catches a drumstick in the bucket.
It stands still for a second, chewing inside its bucket. Then it goes back up the mountain with it. Keh-keh.

words.say_it: Cup your hands into a round bowl. "Oo-MEH-keh."
words.bonus: An ʻumeke is the classic bowl for poi. It can be carved from wood like koa or made from a gourd.
words.picture: Carving a koa calabash in a pile of chips
story_paragraphs: You ask the old master carver down the road if you can buy one of his wooden bowls. He looks at you for a long time. Then he rolls a koa log into your arms. It is 3 feet wide and weighs as much as you do. He hands you a stone adze.
"YOU MAKE, EH!"
So you carve. Every day after school for six months. The wood chips pile up to the ceiling of your garage. Your arms get so big your shirt sleeves rip. You dream about wood grain.
Finally you hold it up. A smooth, round calabash, shining like honey, big enough to hold poi for the whole family. The carver taps it with one knuckle and it rings like a bell. He nods.
Then he rolls another log over. "Good. Now you make ANOTHER, eh."

words.say_it: Hug a huge imaginary pile of stuff. "Vai-HO-nah."
words.bonus: Hale waihona puke means library, a house for storing books.
words.picture: Hermit crab with a shell full of files
story_paragraphs: Hona is a hermit crab who lives under your lanai, and Hona cannot throw anything away. His shell used to be small. Now it is the size of a rice cooker, and it is packed.

Inside it he stores 4,000 bottle caps, 60 keys, every receipt from the corner store since 2011, and a whole metal filing cabinet somehow folded up. The shell creaks when he walks. It is so heavy he leaves a trench in the sand.
You lift the shell and look in. "WHY, HONA? WHY?"

But the neighbors started trusting him. They drop off their spare change and he keeps it in a little drawer inside his shell. He is basically the neighborhood treasury now, a safe place for everyone's savings. When you need your money back, he digs through his files for ten minutes and hands you exactly the right coins.

words.say_it: Point at your feet with a guilty face. "Kaah-MAH," tiny catch, "ah."
words.bonus: The long ā is the drawn out Kaaar, and the ʻokina is your guilty gulp before the last ah.
words.picture: Stolen sneakers marching you back at 3 a.m.
story_paragraphs: At Aunty's birthday party there are 300 pairs of shoes piled at the front door, like everyone in Hawaiʻi does. A mountain of slippahs, sneakers and work boots.
When you leave, you do not take your own old slippahs. You take the shiny new sneakers on the very top. Nobody sees.

At 3 a.m. the sneakers wake you up by kicking you. They tie their own laces onto your feet. Then they march you out of bed, out the door, and down the street in your pajamas. Five miles. Uphill. In the rain.
As you pass the corner store, the night clerk shakes his head. "Kaaaar-MA." You gulp. "...ah."
The shoes walk you right back to Aunty's porch, kick themselves off, and hop neatly onto the pile. Your old slippahs are sitting there waiting.

words.say_it: Tip an imaginary hat. "Paah-PAH-leh." Stretch the first paah.
words.bonus: A lei pāpale is a lei made to wrap around the band of a hat.
words.picture: Pa's glowing pale forehead, hat flying off
story_paragraphs: Pa has worn the same lauhala hat every single day for 31 years. He wears it fishing. He wears it to church. He sleeps in it. Nobody in the family has ever seen his forehead.
Then one day at Makapuʻu the wind comes screaming over the cliff and rips the hat right off his head. It sails away over the ocean like a frisbee, 2 miles out.

The whole beach goes silent. Pa's face is brown as a coconut. But his forehead is WHITE. Glowing white, like powdered sugar on a malasada. It is so bright the lifeguards put on sunglasses. A plane circles, thinking it is a landing light.
The kids scream "PAAAA! PALE!"
Pa slaps both hands on his forehead, runs into the ocean, and swims after his hat.

words.say_it: Roll an invisible shirt tight between your hands. "LO-leh."
words.bonus: Lole means clothes in general and also a dress. Lole wāwae (leg clothes) means pants.
words.picture: Navy aunty rolling clothes into tiny logs
story_paragraphs: You are packing for a trip to the continent. You throw everything in the suitcase. It will not close. You sit on it. It still will not close.
Then Aunty walks in. She was in the Navy for 22 years. She looks at your suitcase like it insulted her family. "ROLL, EH!"

She dumps it out and grabs every piece of clothing you own. Shirts, shorts, your good dress, your pajamas, your socks. She rolls each one into a tight little log, like a musubi, in about half a second. Roll, roll, roll. Forty-seven pieces of clothes.
They all fit in a lunch box. She hands it to you. Then she looks at your big suitcase, rolls that up too, and puts it in your pocket.

words.say_it: Cover your ears and point at someone's shirt. "Paah-LOO-leh." Stretch the first paah.
words.bonus: Pālule is a shirt. Lole is clothes in general. Keep the long ā at the front, because palule with a short a is a rare word for a commoner.
words.picture: Pa's aloha shirt squawking and honking
story_paragraphs: Pa is back with a new aloha shirt from the swap meet. It is the loudest shirt ever made. Not loud colors. Loud. It makes noise.
The parrots printed on it squawk. The hibiscus flowers honk like car horns. The little ʻukuleles on the pocket strum by themselves. There is a volcano on the back and every few minutes it rumbles.

At the family party nobody can hear anything. Grandma is trying to say grace and a parrot on Pa's shoulder is screaming over her. Ma finally stands up and points at him across the yard. "PAAA! LOUD, EH!"
Pa buttons his jacket over the shirt. It is still loud. He goes and sits in the car. You can still hear it from the car. Grandma finishes grace with earplugs.

words.say_it: Throw an imaginary cape over one shoulder. "Kee-HAY!"
words.bonus: A kīhei is traditionally worn tied over one shoulder. It is still worn for hula and special events. Kīhei is also a town on Maui.
words.picture: Flying over a Maui beach on a cape
story_paragraphs: You are on the beach in Kīhei on Maui, which has the same name as this word, and the afternoon wind is blowing 35 miles an hour. You tie a big kapa cloth over one shoulder, knotted at the side, the old style way.
A gust grabs it. The cloth fills up like a sail. Your feet leave the sand.
"KEEEEEEEE!" You are 20 feet up. Then 40. The cape is flapping behind you, and you are flying over the beach like a kite with no string. The ʻiwa birds fly next to you and look annoyed.
You see your family below and wave. "HEY! HEY!" They wave back and keep eating their plate lunch.
The wind finally drops you gently in the ocean. You swim to shore with your cape and your family says you missed the mac salad.

words.say_it: Stand up tall and proud. "MAH-lo." Short and strong.
words.bonus: The malo was the everyday garment for men in old Hawaiʻi, and it is still worn for hula kahiko and canoe events.
words.picture: Tiny cousin proudly wearing a red malo
story_paragraphs: Your cousin is 4 years old. At the canoe festival he watches the paddlers come in, strong men wearing malo, long strips of cloth wrapped around the waist and between the legs, with a flap hanging in front.
He is in love. He has one question, and he asks it loud enough for the whole beach. "Where do I get a MARSHMALLOW?"
The steersman, a big uncle with arms like tree trunks, laughs so hard he almost tips the canoe. He kneels down. "Not marsh-mallow. MAH-lo. Malo."

Then he takes a strip of red cloth and wraps a tiny malo for your cousin, right over his swim trunks. Your cousin stands up proud as a chief, grabs a boogie board, and paddles out 200 yards. He will not take it off for three weeks. He sleeps in it.

words.say_it: Spread your arms wide like a skirt in the wind. "Paaah," catch, "OOOH."
words.bonus: Pāʻū riders on horseback wear long wrapped skirts in parades, each in a color for one island. Hula dancers also wear a pāʻū.
words.picture: Parade rider's giant skirt catching the wind
story_paragraphs: Aunty is riding her horse in the big flower parade in Honolulu. She is wearing a pāʻū, a long wrapped riding skirt made from 16 yards of bright yellow satin. It drapes down over both sides of the horse almost to the ground.
They turn the corner onto Kalākaua, and a huge gust of wind comes off the ocean. The skirt catches it. "PAAAAAH!" It snaps open like a ship sail.

For one second everything freezes. Then Aunty, the horse and 16 yards of satin get pushed backwards down the street at walking speed. The horse is still walking forward. They are just going the wrong way.
The whole crowd goes "OOOOOOOH!" The parade marshal just points her the right direction. She sails back to the start and does the whole thing again.

words.say_it: Moo like a polite cow, with a tiny catch. "Moo-oo-MOO-oo."
words.bonus: A muʻumuʻu is loose and flowing. A holokū is a long fitted dress, often with a train.
words.picture: Cow in a red muʻumuʻu at the buffet
story_paragraphs: A cow shows up at your family lūʻau wearing a muʻumuʻu. A giant one, bright red with white hibiscus, long enough to reach the grass, loose enough to fit a cow. Nobody knows where she got it. It looks great on her.

She walks straight to the buffet. She eats the whole tray of lomi salmon, then the poi, then the haupia. Her belly gets bigger and bigger, but the muʻumuʻu is so loose it just flows. No problem. That is the whole point of a muʻumuʻu.
The aunties are jealous. They want to know where she got it. The cow just shakes her head, making tiny catches in her throat. "Moo? (hic) Oo. MOO? (hic) Oo."
By the end of the night she is doing hula with the aunties in a line, all in muʻumuʻu, all eating.

words.say_it: Drape an invisible lei over someone's head. "LAY."
words.bonus: May 1 is Lei Day in Hawaiʻi. Lei can also mean to wear a lei.
words.picture: Graduate buried in 60 lei
story_paragraphs: It is your graduation. You walk off the stage and your family is waiting on the grass with a mountain of lei. Plumeria, orchid, ti leaf, candy, money lei, a lei made of spam musubi.
Aunty puts the first one on. Then the next. Then Uncle yells "LAY another one on!" and everyone starts piling them over your head. LAY. LAY. LAY.

By lei 30 they are up to your chin. By 45 they are over your nose. By 60 you are just a walking tower of flowers with two feet sticking out the bottom. You cannot see. You smell like a flower shop. A bee has moved in.
You try to walk to the car and wander into the wrong family's photo. They put one more lei on you too.

words.say_it: Wave at yourself in a mirror. "Ah-nee-AH-nee."
words.bonus: Aniani means mirror and also glass. Pukaaniani, a window, is a hole in the glass.
words.picture: Twin Annies copying each other in a mirror
story_paragraphs: The twin Annies from pukaaniani are back. Their dad just put up a huge new mirror in the hallway, 8 feet tall.
One Annie walks down the hall, sees her reflection, and stops. She thinks it is her sister. "Annie?" The reflection says "Annie?" right back. "ANNIE!" "ANNIE!"

She sticks out her tongue. The reflection sticks out its tongue. She does a dance. It does the same dance, perfectly, at the same time. She is furious. They copy each other for 45 minutes. Hopping, spinning, making faces.

Then the real other Annie walks up behind her. Now there are two Annies in the hallway and two Annies in the glass, all yelling "ANNIE! ANNIE!" at each other. Their dad walks by, looks at four Annies, and goes back to bed.

words.say_it: Throw a slippery punch and then spit. "KO-pah!"
words.bonus: Kopa comes from English soap. Careful, kōpaʻa with a long ō and a catch is sugar.
words.picture: Soap bar wrestling champ in the bathtub
story_paragraphs: Every night in your bathtub there is a secret wrestling league. The champion is a big white bar of soap. Nobody can beat him, because nobody can hold him.

Tonight the challenger is a plastic army man. The rubber duck is the referee. The bell rings. The army man charges and grabs the soap in a headlock. The soap squirts out of his arms, shoots across the tub, bounces off the faucet, and slams into the army man. He flies out of the tub and lands in the sink.
The rubber duck squeaks over the edge and counts. One, two, three. "K.O.!" The soap blows a bubble, pops it, and spits a little foam. "PAH!"
He has won 312 matches in a row. He is getting smaller every week, but he says that is just him cutting weight.

words.say_it: Dry your hair with an invisible towel. "Kaah-VEH-leh."
words.bonus: The w in kāwele is often said like a v, which is why the whale hook works. It came from English towel, with T turned to K.
words.picture: Humpback whale drying off on a beach towel
story_paragraphs: You lay out the biggest beach towel in the world at Waikīkī. It is 50 feet long and has a picture of a sunset on it. You go get a shave ice.

When you come back, a humpback whale is lying on your towel. It flopped all the way up the beach. It is rolling back and forth, drying its belly, then its back, then its tail. Sand sticks everywhere. It sighs a big fishy sigh.
The lifeguard walks up next to you and just stares with his mouth open. "Kaaaaaa... WHALE, eh!"

The whale finishes drying, wraps the towel around its head like a turban, and scoots back into the ocean. You watch your towel swim out past the reef. Every winter it comes back and waves at you from the water, still wearing it.

words.say_it: Sweep the floor with big strokes. "Poo-LOO-mee." Stretch the first poo.
words.bonus: Pūlumi comes from the English word broom. B turned to P, R turned to L. Keep the long ū, because pulumi with a short u is a flume or gutter.
words.picture: Giant broom sweeping a huge dust bunny
story_paragraphs: The lady next door sweeps her lanai every morning at 6 a.m. with a broom that has bristles 4 feet long. It is the biggest broom on the island. She calls it her car.

Under her couch lives a dust bunny named Loomy. Loomy is the size of a golden retriever, gray and fluffy, made of hair, sand and old rice. Every morning she sweeps him. WHOOSH. Loomy tumbles across the lanai, bounces down the steps, rolls down the driveway, and stops in the middle of the street.
The kids waiting for the school bus all say it together. "Poooor LOOMY!"
By lunch Loomy has rolled all the way back up the driveway, picked up a few more crumbs, and is hiding under the couch again. He gets bigger every day. The broom is getting nervous.

words.say_it: Hug yourself and chatter your teeth. "Laah-KEH-keh."
words.bonus: Lākeke comes from English jacket. It rhymes with pākeke, a bucket.
words.picture: Shivering in slippahs at a mountain sunrise
story_paragraphs: Your friends drag you up to the top of Haleakalā to watch the sunrise. You wear shorts, a tank top and slippahs because you live in Hawaiʻi and you think it is always warm.
It is 3 a.m. and 36 degrees. The wind is blowing sideways. You are 10,000 feet up and your legs are turning blue.
You try to ask the guy next to you if you can borrow his jacket. "Laaaaaa..." But your teeth start chattering so hard nothing else comes out. "Keh-keh-keh-keh-keh." "LAAAA... keh-keh-keh."

He understands. He unzips his puffy jacket, which is the size of a sleeping bag, and zips you inside it with him. You watch the whole sunrise from inside the jacket like two peas in a pod. It is beautiful. Your teeth are still going keh-keh.

words.say_it: Pull invisible socks up to your knees. "Kaah-KEE-nee."
words.bonus: Kākini came from the English word stocking. Do not mix it up with kini, which is a can.
words.picture: Uncle in knee-high khaki socks with slippahs
story_paragraphs: Uncle Bully shows up at the beach wearing slippahs with socks. Not just socks. Tan khaki socks pulled all the way up to his knees. Tight. Crisp. Ironed.
The whole beach stops. A surfer falls off his board. A man drops his plate lunch. The kids point and chant. "KHAKI KNEE! KHAKI KNEE!"

Uncle does not care. He says socks keep the sand off. He walks right into the ocean in them. When he comes out, each sock is holding about 4 pounds of water and sloshing like a water balloon. Squish. Squish. Squish.
He lies down on his towel, and a crab crawls out of the left sock and waves at him. He says it was in there before he went in the water.

words.say_it: Pretend to lift a very heavy suitcase. "Oo-KAH-nah."
words.bonus: Ukana is any luggage, baggage, or cargo that gets carried somewhere.
words.picture: Tower of 14 suitcases on your back
story_paragraphs: Aunty is coming home from a week in Las Vegas. You go to pick her up at the airport. She left with one small bag.

She comes back with 14 giant suitcases. Every single one is stuffed with snacks from the casino gift shop, plus six boxes tied with string and a cooler that is making noise. The baggage carousel is groaning under it.
She points at the pile, then at you. You are 5 feet tall. "YOU CAN, AH?"

You stack all 14 suitcases on your back in a tower 20 feet high. You wobble through the airport like a camel. You go through the automatic doors sideways. People film you. At the car you realize none of it will fit, so Aunty just sits on top of the pile and you push the whole thing home down the street.

words.say_it: Whistle a falling sound, then catch it low. "Poo," catch, "OH-lo!"
words.bonus: A pūʻolo is often a bundle wrapped in ti leaves, like food wrapped up to carry home.
words.picture: Diving catch of Grandma's ti leaf bundle
story_paragraphs: Grandma in Hilo always sends you home with a bundle. Dried fish, mochi, sweet bread, all wrapped in ti leaves and tied up with string. This time she is late. Your plane is already boarding.
She runs up to the fence by the runway and throws the bundle like a football. It goes up, up, 200 feet into the sky. On the way down it whistles like a bomb in a cartoon. "POOOOOOOOOOO..."
You run under it. You see it dropping fast. Your throat catches. "OH... LOW!" You dive across the tarmac, slide on your belly past two luggage carts, and catch the bundle 1 inch from the ground.
The whole plane cheers through the windows. The dried fish smell follows you all the way to Honolulu. Nobody sits next to you.

words.say_it: Pinch a teeny can between two fingers. "KEE-nee."
words.bonus: Kini comes from English tin. The T turned into K, just like kīwī from TV.
words.picture: Teeny can pouring out 40 pounds of sausage
story_paragraphs: You find a can in the back of the pantry. It is teeny. It is the size of your thumbnail. The label just says "Vienna Sausage."
You laugh. "TEENY!" You peel back the lid with your pinky.

Out comes a Vienna sausage. Then another. Then 40 more. They keep coming out of that teeny can like clowns out of a tiny car. They pour onto the counter, off the counter, onto the floor. Two hundred. Five hundred. They fill the kitchen up to your waist. The dog swims through them in pure joy.
After 40 pounds of sausage, the can finally goes quiet. You look inside. There is one more at the bottom. It waves at you.
You quickly close the lid and put it back in the pantry for next time.

words.say_it: Hold up an invisible bottle and peek in. "Oh-MO-leh." Start with a little catch.
words.bonus: Kini (can) and ʻōmole (bottle) are the two words you need at the recycling bin.
words.picture: Mole in goggles climbing out of a giant bottle
story_paragraphs: A glass bottle washes up on the North Shore. It is 9 feet long. There is a cork in the top as big as a tree stump, and you can see something moving inside.

It takes three surfers and a tow rope to pull the cork. POP. Out climbs a mole. A little brown mole, wearing tiny swim goggles and a captain's hat, with a sunburn on his nose. He has sailed that bottle all the way from California. He is very tired.
Everyone on the beach steps back. You gasp and hold your breath for a second, then point. "OHHHH... MOLE, EH!"
He asks where he can get a plate lunch. Then he climbs back into the bottle to sleep because it is the only home he knows. It is still parked there on the sand.

words.say_it: Fan out an imaginary deck of cards. "Kaah-LEH-kah."
words.bonus: Kāleka comes from the English word card.
words.picture: Ceiling fan blasting cards everywhere
story_paragraphs: Family game night. Uncle Dennis wants to show off his fancy card shuffle. He bends the whole deck into an arch and lets it fly between his hands.
