Except he is standing right under the ceiling fan, which is on high.

FFFWAPPP. Fifty-two cards get sucked up into the blades and shot out in every direction like a machine gun. One sticks in the wall. One lands in the rice pot. One goes in Grandma's coffee. One slices a banana in half in midair. The queen of hearts is somehow stuck to the dog.

Uncle stands there with empty hands. Then he points at the kids and yells "CAAAH... COLLECT-AH! COLLECT-AH!" The kids run around the house for 40 minutes picking up cards. They find 51. The last one shows up a week later in somebody's slippah.

words.say_it: Tap your wrist where a watch goes. "Oo-AH-kee."
words.bonus: Uaki comes from English watch. To ask the time, people say Hola ʻehia kēia?
words.picture: Grandpa's clock hands spinning and fighting
story_paragraphs: Grandpa's big wall clock has been perfect for 50 years. Today it goes wacky.

At noon, the hour hand starts spinning like a helicopter blade. The minute hand goes backwards. Then the two hands start fighting each other, slapping back and forth. The clock chimes 47 times in a row. The cuckoo from kukui pops out of the clock next door, looks at this mess, and goes back inside.
Everyone checks their watch. Every watch in the house is spinning too. Dad's watch says it is Tuesday of next year. Your little sister's watch is playing music.
Grandpa stares at the wall and just says "Ooooh... WACKY."
He smacks the side of the clock once with his palm. Everything stops. It says a quarter past three. It is actually a quarter past three. Nobody ever finds out why.

words.say_it: Tap your head, then wiggle your fingers like sparks. "Lo-lo, oo-EE-lah."
words.bonus: Lolo means brain (and also crazy), and uila means electricity. A computer is an electric brain.
words.picture: Crazy computer singing karaoke with Aunty
story_paragraphs: The karaoke aunty from uila is back. Since the lightning hit her, she has too much electricity in her fingers. Today she tries to check her email on the family computer.

She touches the keyboard. ZAP. The computer screen flashes. The fan starts spinning so fast the computer slides across the desk. Then it goes totally lolo. It opens 900 windows at once. It orders 60 pounds of rice online. It starts talking to the printer, and the printer is printing pictures of cats.
Then it starts singing, in her voice. "Ooooh... EEEEE... LAAAAH!"
The whole family stands in the doorway. Your cousin shakes his head. "Lolo. Ooh-ee-lah."
Now the computer and Aunty sing duets every Saturday. It is better at the high notes than she is.

words.say_it: Snap open a big newspaper with both hands. "Noo-PEH-pah." Stretch the noo.
words.bonus: Nūhou means news. Nūpepa came from English newspaper, and pepa by itself is paper.
words.picture: Dad swallowed by a giant Sunday paper
story_paragraphs: The Sunday newspaper kid in your neighborhood is 11 years old and has an arm like a cannon. This week the paper is 900 pages thick and weighs 40 pounds.
He winds up on his bicycle and throws. It smashes through your screen door, skids across the kitchen floor, and slams into Dad's chair at breakfast. Dad is launched 3 feet into the air.
Dad picks it up and opens it. The paper unfolds and unfolds. It covers the table. It covers the kitchen. It covers Dad. You cannot see him anymore. You can only hear crinkling.
Then from somewhere deep inside the pages you hear a muffled voice, very happy. "Nuuuuuu... PAPER!"
He does not come out until Tuesday. He has finished the crossword.

words.sound_hook: KEE! (hic) EE! Oh, KNEE! (hic) Oh, KNEE!
words.say_it: Grab your knee and hop. "Kee-ee, oh-nee, OH-nee." A little catch before each ee and oh.
words.bonus: Kiʻi means picture and ʻoniʻoni means moving. A movie is a moving picture.
words.picture: Man banging his knee down a dark theater row
story_paragraphs: You are at the movie theater. The movie is about a giant crab attacking Honolulu, and it is right at the scariest part. The theater is pitch dark.

A big guy with a bucket of popcorn the size of a trash can is climbing over the whole row to get to his seat. He bangs his knee on the first seat. "KEE!" Hiccup. "EE!" He bangs it on the next one. "OH, KNEE!" Hiccup. "OH, KNEE!"
He does this all the way down a row of 20 seats. Every bang has a little hiccup in the middle. Kee, ee, oh knee, oh knee.
Everyone in the theater is watching him now instead of the movie. When he finally sits down, the whole crowd claps. On the screen, even the giant crab turns around and claps.

words.say_it: Hold out both hands and beg. "Mah-KAH-nah?"
words.bonus: Makana is also the name of a mountain on Kauaʻi. Makana aloha is a gift given with love.
words.picture: 12 foot present with 40 boxes inside
story_paragraphs: There is a present in the living room that is 12 feet tall. It is wrapped in gold paper and it has your name on it. Your birthday is in three days.
You stand next to it. You look at Ma. "Ma, CAN, ah?" She says no. You ask again after dinner. "Ma, can, ah?" No. You ask 700 times over three days. You ask in your sleep.

Finally the day comes. You tear it open. Inside is another box, a little smaller. And another. And another. There are 40 boxes, each one inside the last, and the living room fills up with gold paper to the ceiling.
The last box is the size of a matchbox. You open it. One perfect, warm malasada. It is the best malasada you have ever eaten. You would ask 700 times again.

words.say_it: Rub your thumb and fingers together like money. "Kaah-LAAAH." Both vowels long.
words.bonus: Kālā came from English dollar. ʻEhia kālā? means how much money?
words.picture: Chihuahua wearing a collar of dollar bills
story_paragraphs: There is a tiny Chihuahua in Kāhala who is richer than everyone on your street. His owner made him a dog collar out of real dollar bills. Hundreds of them, folded into little fans, going all the way around his neck.
The collar is so big the dog looks like a lion. It rustles when he walks. When the wind blows, dollar bills flutter off it and float down the sidewalk.
Every kid in the neighborhood follows him on his walk like a parade, picking up loose bills. They sing a little song. "Collaaaah, dollaaaah! Collaaaah, dollaaaah!"

The dog does not care about money. He only wants the bread crust your little brother is holding. They trade. Your brother walks home with the whole collar around his neck, looking like a very rich lion.

words.say_it: Flip an invisible penny. "Keh-NEH-kah."
words.bonus: Keneka comes from English cent. One hundred keneka make one kālā. Peni can also mean penny, but keneka is the usual word for a cent.
words.picture: Kid bent over by a 30 pound penny necklace
story_paragraphs: Your classmate Kenny has been saving every penny he finds for eight years. He has 5,000 pennies. He does not trust piggy banks. So he drilled a hole in every penny and strung them all into one giant necklace.
It weighs 30 pounds. When he wears it to school, he walks bent over like an old man. It clanks like a pirate.
His teacher looks at him and gasps. "Kenny, your NECK, ah!"

In P.E. he tries to run and the necklace swings out and knocks over three kids. When he sits down, his chair cracks. In the hallway, other kids toss pennies at him and they stick to the necklace like magnets.
He finally cashes it in at the bank. It is fifty dollars. He buys a neck brace.

words.say_it: Pull on an invisible rope, hand over hand. "KOW-lah."
words.bonus: Hawaiian style beef jerky is called pipi kaula, rope beef, because it dries in long strips.
words.picture: Singing cow lowered off a roof by rope
story_paragraphs: Remember the cow sitting on top of your roof from kaupaku? She is still up there. It has been a week. She has made friends with the pigeons. The fire department says it is not their problem.
So the old paniolo from up the road comes over with a rope. It is 200 feet long and as thick as your arm. He swings it three times over his head and lassos the cow on the first try.
Then the whole neighborhood holds the other end, like tug of war, and they lower her down slowly off the edge of the roof. She dangles there, spinning gently.
The cow is not scared at all. She loves it. As she floats down she starts to sing like an opera singer. "COWWWW... LAAAAAAA!" Her hooves touch the grass and everyone claps.

words.say_it: Throw an invisible net in a big circle. "Oo-PEH-nah!"
words.bonus: An ʻupena can be any net, from a small hand net for the tide pools to a huge net for a whole school of fish.
words.picture: Tiny lady's throw net covering the harbor
story_paragraphs: The best throw net fisherman on the island is a tiny old lady who is 4 feet 10 inches tall. She stands on the rocks at the harbor, folds the net over her arm, and spins.
She holds her breath for a second, a little catch in her throat. Then she lets it go and yells "OOOO... PEN-AH!" Open, ah!
The net flies out and opens into a perfect circle. It keeps opening. Bigger and bigger. Soon it is as wide as the whole harbor. It comes down over everything.

When she pulls it in, she has 300 fish, an octopus, two confused kids on boogie boards, a canoe, a lifeguard in his chair, and an ice cream cart. She lets everything go except the fish and one ice cream.
Then she folds the net back over her arm like it was nothing.

words.say_it: Flap your arms and squawk. "Mah-KOW!"
words.bonus: Carved fishhook pendants called makau are popular necklaces in Hawaiʻi.
words.picture: Macaw fishing off the pier with a hook
story_paragraphs: Your neighbor has a big red and blue macaw parrot, and the macaw loves to go fishing. Every morning it flies down to the pier holding a fishhook in its beak on a long line.
It hovers over the water and drops the hook down. It waits. Very patient. Then a fish bites and the macaw screams "MACAW!" and flaps up hard. A fish comes flying out of the water.
It catches 30 fish before breakfast. MACAW. MACAW. MACAW. The fishermen on the pier with their fancy poles have caught nothing. They are so mad.
One morning the hook snags a fisherman's hat instead. The macaw screams "MACAW!" and flies off with the hat. It wears it now. It is a very good fisherman and it knows it.

words.say_it: Throw an invisible spear. "EEEE," as it flies, "heh!" as it lands.
words.bonus: Spear throwing at a target is one of the old Makahiki games that people still play today.
words.picture: Tiny aunty spearing a banana trunk
story_paragraphs: At the Makahiki games there is a spear throwing contest. The target is a banana trunk stuck in the ground, far away. Big strong guys go first. They grunt, they throw, the spears wobble and fall short.
Then your Aunty Mele steps up. She is 70 years old and 5 feet tall. She is still holding her purse.
She throws the spear so hard and so fast it screams through the air. "EEEEEEEEEEE!" It flies for 90 yards. The crowd turns their heads to follow it.
Then "HEH!" It sinks right into the center of the banana trunk and hums there, shaking.
The big guys are silent. Aunty Mele just says "Heh," fixes her hair, and goes back to her lawn chair. The banana tree gives up and falls over.

words.say_it: Cup your hands to your mouth and hold one long note. "POOOOOO." The ū is extra long.
words.bonus: Pū also means gun, from the loud blast.
words.picture: Uncle blowing a conch shell for 4 minutes
story_paragraphs: It is the start of a big canoe race. Twelve canoes are lined up in the water. The paddlers are ready. A big uncle stands on the beach with a conch shell as big as a football to blow the start.
He lifts it to his lips. "POOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO..."
He does not stop. One minute. Two minutes. His face turns red, then purple. The paddlers are still holding their paddles in the air. A kid's shave ice melts. A cloud passes.
Three minutes. Out in the ocean, a humpback whale lifts its head out of the water and answers. "POOOOOOOO..."
Four minutes. Uncle finally runs out of air and sits down in the sand. The race starts. Nobody remembers who won. They only remember the POOOO. The whale still calls back every year on race day.

words.say_it: Swing an invisible adze down. "KO," freeze, "ee!"
words.bonus: Old koʻi blades were made from hard basalt stone lashed onto a wooden handle.
words.picture: Giant koi fish carving a canoe with an adze
story_paragraphs: In the pond at the botanical garden lives a koi fish the size of a canoe. Orange and white, with whiskers like an old man. Everybody thinks it is just a fish.
One night it hops out of the pond. It grabs a stone adze in its fins. It flops over to a huge log that has been lying by the path for years.
Then it gets to work. CHOP. Wood chips fly 20 feet. CHOP. CHOP. It carves in a blur, faster than any machine, for four minutes straight. When it stops, the log is a perfect canoe, smooth and shiny.
The night guard sees the whole thing. He freezes halfway through saying the name. "KO..." Freeze. "...EE?"
The koi puts down the adze, hops back into the pond, and pretends to eat a lily pad.

words.say_it: Stab the ground with an invisible stick twice. "Oh," catch, "OH." Both long.
words.bonus: ʻŌʻō is also the name of a black forest bird with yellow feathers that is now extinct.
words.picture: Grandpa jabbing holes with a digging stick
story_paragraphs: Your grandpa wants to plant sweet potatoes, but he refuses to use a shovel. He uses a long wooden digging stick, sharp at one end, as tall as he is. He says it is how they did it long ago and it works better.
He jabs it into the ground. Every jab, he makes the same noise. A catch in his throat, and then a long "OHHH!" Catch, "OHHH!" Catch, "OHHH!" OH, OH. OH, OH.
He digs 200 holes in one afternoon. Perfect straight rows. The neighbor with the gas powered tiller only did 30.

On hole 201 the stick hits something hard. Grandpa digs it out. It is an old cooler somebody buried in 1987. He opens it. Inside are four cans of soda and a musubi that has turned to stone. "OH... OH."

words.say_it: Play an invisible recorder. "PEEE," squeak, "lah."
words.bonus: Pila means any musical instrument and also a bill you have to pay. Kanikapila means to play music together, a jam session.
words.picture: Forty kids squeaking recorders, windows cracking
story_paragraphs: It is the third grade recorder concert. Forty kids, each holding a plastic recorder, standing on the risers. The parents are smiling nervously.
The music teacher lifts her hands. Forty kids blow at once. "PEEEEEEEEE!" A horrible squeak. Then they find the note. "LAAAAAAAH." Then squeak again. PEEEE. LAAAAH. PEEEE. LAAAAH.
Every dog in Kalihi starts howling. The school windows crack, one by one, in a line. A car alarm goes off. A myna bird falls out of a tree.
They play for 22 minutes. Everybody claps very hard because they are so glad it is over.
The next day the school gets a bill for 34 broken windows. The principal sends that bill home with every kid, rolled up and stuck inside each little recorder.

words.say_it: Air guitar one big windmill strum. "Kee-KAAAH!"
words.bonus: Kī hōʻalu, slack key, is the famous Hawaiian style of guitar where the strings are loosened.
words.picture: Guitar feedback blasting chickens onto roof
story_paragraphs: Backyard jam session. Everybody has an ʻukulele and they are playing sweet slow songs. Then your cousin shows up with an electric guitar and an amplifier the size of a refrigerator.
He plugs in. He turns every knob all the way up. He stands too close to the amp. It screams with feedback.
"KEEEEEEEEEEEEE... KAAAAAAAAAAH!"
The sound knocks the chickens onto the roof. The ʻukuleles all go out of tune at once. Aunty's wig spins around backwards. The lid flies off the pot of chili.

Your cousin thinks this is amazing. He jumps in the air and does it again. "KEEEEEE... KAAAAH!" Then the amp blows up in a puff of smoke, and he finishes the song on a regular guitar with no plug, very quiet, like a gentleman.

words.say_it: Wiggle your fingers like they are hopping on strings. "Oo-koo-LEH-leh." Start with a tiny catch.
words.bonus: ʻUku means flea or louse and lele means to jump, so ʻukulele is literally the leaping flea. Pukui-Elbert says the name probably came from the nickname of a small, quick man who helped make the instrument popular. Another popular explanation is fingers hopping on the strings.
words.picture: Hamster sized flea jumping on uke strings
story_paragraphs: You look closely at your ʻukulele and realize there is a flea living inside it. A flea the size of a hamster. It pops its head out of the sound hole and says "Ooh, koo!"

It climbs out onto the strings. It starts jumping. Its legs hit the strings on the way up and on the way down, bouncing so fast it plays a song. Boing, strum, boing, strum. Jump, jump, jump. It is playing the fastest ʻukulele solo you have ever heard.
As it jumps it sings along in a squeaky voice. "Ooh, KOO! LAY-lay! LAY-lay!"
The whole family comes to watch. The flea bows. Then it jumps onto the dog and starts playing him too. The dog does not know what is happening, but he is humming.

words.say_it: Bounce an invisible ball, one bounce per syllable. "Kee-nee-poh-POH." Hold both ō sounds.
words.bonus: Pōpō by itself means a round ball or lump.
words.picture: Tiny dog pushing a giant beach ball
story_paragraphs: Popo is a scruffy little mutt who weighs 3 pounds. He is teeny. He fits in a coffee cup. But he has one dream, and it is a beach ball that is 8 feet tall.

At the beach he gets behind it and pushes with his little head. It does not move. He backs up and charges. It rolls. Just an inch. He pushes again. It rolls a foot. Then it starts going downhill toward the water, and Popo is running full speed behind it, legs spinning.
The whole beach cheers him on. "TEENY POPO! TEENY POPO!"

The ball hits the water and bounces over a wave. Popo swims after it. Twenty minutes later he comes back pushing it up the beach like a champion, then lies down on top of it and falls asleep, rolling slowly back and forth.

words.say_it: Walk stiff like a robot. "MEE. KEE. NEE." Then say it smooth. "Mee-KEE-nee."
words.bonus: Mīkini comes from English machine. Mīkini holoi lole is a washing machine, a machine for washing clothes.
words.picture: Garage robot machine firing out musubi
story_paragraphs: Uncle builds a machine in his garage out of a lawn mower, a washing machine, a rice cooker, two old fans and a car battery. It is taller than the garage door. It hums.
He flips the switch. The lights in the whole house dim. Two headlight eyes open on the front. Then it talks in a flat robot voice. "MEEE. KEE. NEE."

It rolls to the kitchen. It starts making spam musubi. One every second. Then ten every second. Rice is flying, nori is flying, musubi are shooting out the side and stacking themselves on the counter. Five hundred a minute.
By dinner there are 20,000 musubi in the house, on the stairs, in the bathtub. Uncle cannot find the off switch. The machine just keeps saying "MEEE. KEE. NEE." The neighbors are not complaining.

words.say_it: Lift something heavy over your head. "HAH-oh," said fast, "HOW."
words.bonus: Hao sounds a lot like hau (ice, snow, and the hau tree). Hao ends in o, hau ends in u. An ipu hao, literally an iron container, is a cooking pot.
words.picture: Strongman's iron bar drooping like a noodle
story_paragraphs: At the beach park, a big strongman flexes next to a solid iron bar that weighs 800 pounds. A crowd gathers. He chalks his hands. He squats. He grabs it.
"HAH!" He lifts it over his head in one move. The crowd screams. His arms are shaking. His face turns red.
Then the iron starts to bend. Very slowly, it droops on both sides like a cooked noodle, until the ends are touching the sand. He looks up at it. "...oh."
HAH, oh. Said fast it is just HOW.
He sets it down. Now it is shaped like a horseshoe. A little girl walks up and uses it as a bench. The strongman sits next to her and eats a musubi. He says the iron was probably cheap.

words.say_it: Shrug, then fan your burning mouth. "Meh-ah," catch, "AI!"
words.bonus: Mea means thing and ʻai means to eat, so meaʻai is the thing you eat.
words.picture: Picky kid eating chili peppers at a lūʻau
story_paragraphs: Your nephew is the pickiest eater in the family. At the lūʻau there are 40 feet of food on the table. Kalua pig, poke, chicken long rice, lomi salmon, haupia. He walks down the whole line and looks at every dish.
"Meh." "Meh." "Meh." "Meh."
At the end of the table there is a tiny bowl of little red chili peppers. He thinks they are candy. He pops a whole handful in his mouth.
"Meh... ah..." A little catch in his throat. Then "AIIIIIIIII!"

Smoke comes out of his ears. He runs back down the line and eats everything to put out the fire. The poke, the rice, the pig, a whole tray of haupia. By the end he is lying on the grass, stuffed, holding his belly, whispering "Food..."

words.say_it: Lean back from a pair of chopsticks. "AI-nah." Start with a tiny catch.
words.bonus: ʻAina (meal) is not ʻāina (land), which has a long ā. ʻAina kakahiaka is breakfast, ʻaina awakea is lunch, ʻaina ahiahi is dinner.
words.picture: Tūtū offering a fish eye on chopsticks
story_paragraphs: Sunday dinner at Tūtū's house. The whole family is squeezed around the table. The main dish is a giant steamed fish, 3 feet long, with the head still on.
Tūtū reaches over with her chopsticks and pops out the fish eye. It is big and white and wobbly. She says it is the best part and the guest of honor gets it. You are the guest of honor.
She holds it right in front of your face. It stares at you. "EYE?"
You freeze. Little catch in your throat. "...NAH."

She waits. The eye waits. The whole table is waiting. The meal cannot go on until somebody eats that eye. Finally Grandpa leans over and slurps it off her chopsticks. "Mmmm." The family cheers, and the meal finally starts.

words.say_it: Make a disgusted face, then a surprised one. "Paah," catch, "EE-nah."
words.bonus: A pāʻina is a small party with food. The bigger versions are ʻahaʻaina and lūʻau.
words.picture: Hyena in a lei at a backyard party
story_paragraphs: Your sister's graduation party in the backyard. Thirty people. Folding tables, a tent, pans of chicken wings, mac salad, a cooler of drinks. Nice and small.
Then a hyena shows up. Nobody invited it. It is wearing a plumeria lei. It walks right under the tent and starts laughing that crazy hyena laugh. "Hee hee hee HEE!"
It laughs at every joke Uncle tells, even the bad ones, which Uncle loves. It eats all 90 chicken wings. It does the limbo. It dances with Grandma.
When your dad walks in from parking the car, he sees it on the dance floor and makes a disgusted face. "PAH!" Then he looks closer. Catch in his throat. "...HYENA?"
The hyena waves at him with a chicken wing. By the end of the night it is his best friend.

words.say_it: Point at someone and shout. "Ah-HAH," catch, "AI-nah!"
words.bonus: ʻAha means a gathering, and ʻaina means a meal. A feast is a gathering meal.
words.picture: Tūtū finding you at the feast with a huge eye
story_paragraphs: Remember Tūtū and the fish eye from ʻaina? You thought you escaped. Now it is the giant family feast. Eight hundred people. Tables a quarter mile long. Twelve whole pigs from the imu. A fish as big as a canoe.
You hide at the very end of the last table, behind a tower of poi bowls, wearing sunglasses and a hat.

Tūtū walks the whole quarter mile, checking every face. Then she spots you. She points. "AHA!" From the pocket of her muʻumuʻu she pulls out chopsticks holding an eye. It is the size of a baseball this time.
"EYE?"
You gulp. "...NAH."
The entire feast goes quiet. Eight hundred people are staring. Grandpa, bless him, walks the whole quarter mile to eat it for you.

words.say_it: Grab your itchy throat. "Looo," catch, "OW!"
words.bonus: The feast called a lūʻau is named after the taro leaf dish served there. Raw taro leaves really do itch, so they must be cooked a long time.
words.picture: Scratching your throat after raw taro leaves
story_paragraphs: You are helping cook for the big party, and your job is the taro leaves. Aunty says to cook them for at least an hour. You get impatient after 10 minutes and taste one.
It is dark green and soft and smells great. You chew. You swallow.

Then your throat starts to itch. Not a little. It feels like you swallowed a cactus wearing a wool sweater. You open your mouth to say "Looks done," but all that comes out is "LOOOOOO..." Then a catch in your throat. "OW! OW! OW!"
You run around the yard scratching your neck with a fork. Aunty does not even look up. She just says "Told you. One hour."
An hour later the leaves are cooked in coconut milk, creamy and perfect, and you eat three bowls. No itch. Just happiness.

words.say_it: Hold up two fingers like you are scooping. "POY."
words.bonus: Poi is made by pounding cooked kalo (taro) and adding water. It is described as one finger, two finger or three finger poi depending on how thick it is.
words.picture: Pirate patching his ship with three finger poi
story_paragraphs: A pirate ship sails into Honolulu harbor. The captain climbs up on the rail, raises his hook, and instead of "Ahoy!" he bellows "A-POI!"
He only eats poi. The whole ship smells like it. There are barrels of purple gray poi in the hold, some fresh and sweet, some three days old and sour.

The captain tests it by fingers. One finger poi is thin and drippy, for the cabin boy. Two finger poi is for the crew. Three finger poi is so thick it holds your fingers together when you scoop it. That is for the captain.

Then a cannonball blasts a hole in the side of the ship. Water pours in. The captain does not panic. He scoops a big glob of three finger poi and slaps it on the hole. It seals. "A-POI!" The crew cheers.

words.say_it: Crouch down low like a sinking car. "KAH-lo."
words.bonus: In Hawaiian tradition kalo is the elder brother of the Hawaiian people, which is why it is treated with so much respect.
words.picture: Tiny car sparking under 900 pounds of taro
story_paragraphs: Uncle spent all day pulling kalo from the wet patch in the valley. Big purple corms, each one as heavy as a bowling ball, still muddy, with the green leaves sticking up like elephant ears. He has 900 pounds of it.
He loads it all into his little old two door car. The trunk. The back seat. The front seat. His lap.
The car sinks. And sinks. The tires squash flat. The bottom of the car is 1 inch off the road. When he drives onto the freeway, sparks shoot out from underneath like a fireworks show.

Every car he passes honks and people lean out the windows yelling "CAR! LOW!" He waves at everyone. He drives slowly and carefully. Not one taro gets bruised. He gets home and the car sighs and rises back up 6 inches.

words.say_it: Kiss your fingers like a fancy chef. "Oo-AH-lah!" Start with a tiny catch.
words.bonus: The purple sweet potatoes so popular in Hawaiʻi are often called Okinawan sweet potatoes.
words.picture: Fancy chef amazed by a purple sweet potato
story_paragraphs: A very fancy chef from Paris comes to a farmers market in Hawaiʻi. He wears a tall white hat and has a mustache that curls up at both ends. He does not believe anything here can impress him.
Then he picks up a sweet potato. Brown and dusty on the outside. He cuts it open with a tiny silver knife.
Inside it is bright purple. Glowing purple, like a sunset. The chef takes a step back. His mustache uncurls. "Oooooooh..."
He roasts a slice right there on a camp stove and takes a bite. It is soft and sweet and melts in his mouth. He holds it up to the sky. "AHHHH... LAAAAH!"
He buys all 400 pounds of them. He opens a restaurant that only serves purple sweet potato and never goes home.

words.say_it: Duck like something is falling on you. "OO-loo." Tiny catch at the start.
words.bonus: ʻUlu with the ʻokina is breadfruit. Ulu without it means to grow, which breadfruit trees do very well.
words.picture: Breadfruit bombing a beach portable toilet
story_paragraphs: At the beach park there is one portable toilet, the loo, parked right under a giant breadfruit tree. The tree is 60 feet tall and loaded with fruit. Each breadfruit is green, bumpy, and as big and heavy as a bowling ball.
Uncle goes in. He shuts the door. The wind blows.
BOOM. A breadfruit drops 60 feet and hits the roof of the loo. The whole thing rocks. From inside you hear "OOOH!"
BOOM. BOOM. BOOM. Fourteen breadfruit, one after another, like drums. The roof dents in. The door rattles. "OOOH! MY LOO! OOOH! MY LOO!"
When it stops, Uncle opens the door slowly. There is breadfruit piled up to his knees all around the loo. He walks out, picks up the two best ones, and takes them home to roast.

words.say_it: Hug an invisible bunch of bananas. "MAI," catch, "ah!"
words.bonus: The short sweet apple bananas are a backyard favorite in Hawaiʻi.
words.picture: Toddler hugging a 140 banana bunch
story_paragraphs: Tūtū has a banana tree in the backyard, and today the bunch is finally ripe. It is huge. One hundred and forty little yellow bananas all in one bunch, hanging down like a giant chandelier.
Your 2 year old nephew toddles out in his diaper. He sees it. His eyes get huge. He has just learned one word, and it is "MY."
He wraps both arms around the whole bunch, which is bigger than him. "MY!" Then he hiccups, that little catch. "...AH!"

He drags the whole thing across the yard. It takes him 20 minutes. He will not let anyone help. He gets it into the living room and sits down next to it and eats bananas one by one, saying "My... ah. My... ah," until he falls asleep on the peels.

words.say_it: Grab your knee and wince. "NEE-oo!"
words.bonus: Niu Valley on Oʻahu carries the same word.
words.picture: Coconut bonking your knee from 70 feet
story_paragraphs: Your cousin climbs a coconut tree that is 70 feet tall. No rope. No ladder. Just his hands and feet, walking up it like a gecko. At the top he waves.
He starts twisting coconuts off and dropping them. They are big, green and as heavy as bowling balls. You are standing underneath to collect them.
The first one lands right on your knee. BONK.
"KNEE! OOOOOOH!"
You hop around the yard holding your knee. He drops another one. BONK. Other knee. "KNEE! OOOOH!" Now you are hopping on no legs, somehow.
Finally he climbs down, cracks one open, and hands it to you with a straw. The coconut water is cold and sweet. You sip it with both knees wrapped in ice, and you forgive him. A little.

words.say_it: Wipe your hands on a rag like a mechanic. "Mee-KAH-nah."
words.bonus: Papaya with a squeeze of lime is a classic Hawaiʻi breakfast.
words.picture: Mechanic opening a papaya car full of seeds
story_paragraphs: A papaya grows so big in your neighbor's yard that he decides to drive it. It is 12 feet long, orange and green, shaped like a fat little car. He cuts a door in the side, puts a seat inside, sticks four wheels on the bottom and drives it to the store.
Halfway down the street it breaks down. It starts leaking orange juice and making noises.
He calls the mechanic. "MECHANIC, AH!" The mechanic comes out, rolls under it, frowns, and opens the hood.
Out pour 10,000 shiny black papaya seeds, like ball bearings, rolling down the whole street. Kids slip on them. A bus slides sideways.
The mechanic shakes his head and says the engine is fine, it is just ripe. He scoops out a piece with a spoon and squeezes lime on it. Best repair he ever did.

words.say_it: Put on an invisible helmet and charge. "Mah-nah-KOOOH!" Hold the ō.
words.bonus: Manakō came from the English word mango.
words.picture: Ma charging the mango tree in a helmet
story_paragraphs: It is mango season. The tree in the backyard is so overloaded that the branches are touching the ground. Mangoes are dropping every ten seconds. THUD. THUD. THUD.
You want to go out and pick them. You ask Ma. She says "NAH." She is scared. Last year a mango knocked out the mailman.

Then a mango crashes right through the kitchen window and lands in her hand. She looks at it. Red and gold, the size of a football, smelling like heaven. She takes one bite. Juice runs down to her elbow.
She grabs a laundry basket and a helmet. She looks at you. You say "Ma?" She says "Nah..." and then she yells "GOOOOOOO!"
You both charge into the yard with baskets, dodging falling mangoes like it is a war, and you come back with 300.

words.say_it: Cup your hands and holler across a field. "HAH-lah kah-HEE-kee!"
words.bonus: Hala is the pandanus tree, whose fruit looks a lot like a pineapple, and kahiki means a foreign land. So pineapple is the foreign hala.
words.picture: Hunting a car key in a pineapple field
story_paragraphs: You are driving through the pineapple fields in central Oʻahu. You stop to take a picture. You drop your car key.
It bounces once and disappears into the field. Two million pineapples, in rows, all the way to the mountains. Each one has a spiky crown on top. Each one looks exactly like the one next to it.

You start searching. You pick up one pineapple. No key. Another. The spiky leaves scratch your arms. Your legs are cut up. You get more and more desperate and start hollering across the field. "HOLLA! CAR KEY! CAR KEEEEEY!"
After three hours, one pineapple starts jingling. You lift it. Your car key is stuck right in its crown, like a little flag.
You buy that pineapple. You also buy 40 more, because you are too tired to explain.

words.say_it: Take a bite and wipe your eye. "Oh-HEE-ah AI." A little catch before each vowel sound that has one.
words.bonus: ʻŌhiʻa ʻai means the ʻōhiʻa you eat. It is different from ʻōhiʻa lehua, the native tree with the red lehua flowers.
words.picture: Mountain apple squirting juice in a hiker's eye
story_paragraphs: A friendly visitor from Ohio is on a rainforest hike with you. Along the trail there is a tall tree with little red fruit hanging off the trunk, shaped like tiny bells, shiny like they were painted.
You tell him the name. He lights up. "OHIO? Like me?"
You hand him one. He bites it. The skin is thin and the inside is white and crunchy and so full of water that the juice squirts sideways 6 feet and hits him right in the eye.
"OHIO... EYE!"
He is laughing and crying at the same time. He eats 30 more. He fills his backpack. He says they taste like a pear and a rose had a baby. He tries to take one home to Ohio but eats it at the airport.

words.say_it: Pat your own cheek. "EE," catch, "ah."
words.bonus: Iʻa can mean fish or meat, the main dish you eat with poi. Do not mix it up with ia, with no catch, which means he, she or it.
words.picture: Fish slapping you in the face
story_paragraphs: You are standing knee deep in the water at the beach, minding your own business. A fish jumps out of the ocean. A big one, 3 feet long, silver, very wet, very angry.
It flies through the air and slaps you across the face with its tail.
"EE!" SLAP. For a second you just freeze, a catch in your throat, water dripping off your nose. Then "AH!"
Another fish jumps. SLAP. "EE! AH!" Then another. It is a whole school of fish, taking turns slapping you, like they have been planning this for years.
You run up the beach. The last fish jumps out, lands in your cooler, and the lid snaps shut. You take it home and grill it with rice and shoyu. That fish did not think it through.

words.say_it: Hold your nose, then jump back. "Poo," catch, "AH-ah!"
words.bonus: Kālua puaʻa is kālua pig, roasted in an imu. Do not mix up puaʻa with pua, which means flower.
words.picture: Wild pig with its head in the rice cooker
story_paragraphs: You wake up at 2 in the morning because something smells terrible. Mud, garbage, and old wet dog. You sniff the air. "Poo?"
You tiptoe into the kitchen and turn on the light. A wild pig is standing on the counter. It is 300 pounds, hairy, with little tusks, and it has its whole head inside the rice cooker.
You freeze. A catch in your throat. Then "AH! AH!"

The pig looks up with rice all over its face and grunts. It knocks over the fridge. It eats a whole pan of mac salad. It drinks from the sink like a dog. Then it walks out the front door, which it opens with its nose.
In the morning, Dad finds its muddy hoof prints on the ceiling. Nobody can explain the ceiling.

words.say_it: Flap your elbows like wings. "MO-ah!"
words.bonus: Kauaʻi really is famous for its wild chickens. Moa is also the name of a giant extinct bird of New Zealand, the same old Polynesian word.
words.picture: Hundreds of chickens following you on Kauaʻi
story_paragraphs: You land on Kauaʻi for vacation. At the airport parking lot, one chicken walks up to you. A pretty rooster with red and gold feathers. Cute.
Then another. Then 10 more.

They follow you to the rental car. They follow you to the hotel. When you open your hotel room door, there are 40 chickens on the bed. You look at them. "MORE?!" A rooster crows right in your ear. "AHHHH!"
They are on the beach. They are at the restaurant. One climbs onto your plate lunch and steals your fried chicken, which is a lot to think about.
On the last day you have 400 chickens following you to the airport like a parade. At the gate you turn around and say goodbye. One follows you onto the plane. You still do not know how.

words.say_it: Say it in the tiniest chick voice you have. "PEE-pee." Then say it normal.
words.bonus: Pipi came from English beef. Paniolo are Hawaiian cowboys.
words.picture: Huge cow peeping like a baby chick
story_paragraphs: Up on a ranch on the Big Island there is a cow that weighs 1,400 pounds. Black and white, huge shoulders, horns as long as your arm. The toughest looking cow on the whole ranch.
But it does not moo. It peeps. Like a baby chick. "Peep peep. Peep peep."
It was raised by a hen when it was a calf, and nobody ever told it. It follows the chickens around. It tries to sit on eggs. It tried to roost in the chicken coop once and the whole coop fell over.
The paniolo ride out to round up the herd. Two hundred cows go "MOOOO." One giant cow in the middle goes "peep peep."
The paniolo just tip their hats to it. Nobody is going to be the one to tell it.

words.say_it: Look around confused with your hands out. "HOO-ah?"
words.bonus: Hua moa is a chicken egg. Hua can mean the egg, the fruit, or the seed, the whole cycle in one word.
words.picture: Car sized egg hatching a fruit tree
story_paragraphs: You wake up and there is an egg in your backyard the size of a car. White, smooth, and a little warm. There was nothing there last night.
The whole neighborhood comes over. Everybody looks around at the sky, at each other. "WHO... AH?" Who laid this? The chickens all back away slowly.
At noon it starts to crack. Everyone ducks. The shell falls open. Inside there is no bird. There is one giant seed, as big as a beanbag.
The seed rolls out, sinks into the grass, and a tree shoots up out of the ground in 30 seconds, loaded with fruit. Mangoes, lychee, oranges, all on the same tree.
Everyone stands there holding fruit. Nobody knows who to thank. "WHO... AH?" The chickens take the credit.

words.say_it: Spit out seawater, catch, then gasp. "Pah," catch, "ah-KAI."
words.bonus: One popular explanation splits paʻakai into paʻa (hard, solid) and kai (sea), so salt is hardened sea. Red ʻalaea salt is mixed with a red clay.
words.picture: Spitting out a mouthful of salty ocean
story_paragraphs: You are bodysurfing at the beach and you get caught under a big wave. You come up with a mouth full of ocean. You spit. "PAH!" You freeze with that catch in your throat, then gasp "AH..." and cough out "KAI!" which is Hawaiian for the sea, the thing that is currently in your mouth.
Your tongue is so salty it has turned white. You lick your arm. Salty. You lick your hair. Salty.
An aunty on the beach is scraping salt out of shallow pans by the shore, where the sea water dried in the sun. She hands you a crunchy pinch of it. You crunch it with a slice of raw fish.
It is the best thing you ever tasted. You spit the ocean out again, "Pah, ah, kai," but now in a happy way.

words.say_it: Shovel invisible rice into your mouth. "LAI-kee!"
words.bonus: Laiki came from English rice, with the R turned into an L.
words.picture: Baby eating her way through a rice pot
story_paragraphs: Your baby niece is 1 year old, and she has discovered rice. She is sitting in her high chair at the plate lunch place, with two scoops of rice in front of her. She grabs a fistful and shoves it in her mouth.
"LIKE-EE!"
She finishes both scoops. She points at your plate. You give her your rice. "LIKE-EE!" She points at the next table. The whole restaurant starts passing her their rice. "LIKE-EE! LIKE-EE! LIKE-EE!"
The cook brings out the giant rice pot, the one that holds 60 cups. She climbs out of her chair, into the pot, and eats her way to the bottom like a tiny bulldozer.
She pops her head out with rice on her eyebrows and one grain on her nose. "Like-ee." Then she burps.

words.say_it: Pull dough between your hands. "Pah-lah-OH-ah."
words.bonus: Palaoa means both bread and flour. It also means sperm whale and whale ivory, as in the lei palaoa, a whale tooth pendant worn by chiefs.
words.picture: Stretching bread dough across the street
story_paragraphs: Grandma has been making sweet bread dough since 4 in the morning. She dumps a whole 50 pound sack of flour on the kitchen table, and the kitchen disappears in a white cloud. When it clears, Grandpa is white from head to toe, like a ghost.
She works the dough and hands you one end. "Pull."

You pull. It stretches. You walk backwards. It keeps stretching. Out the kitchen, down the hall, out the door, down the driveway. "PULL-a... WHOA-ah!" It is 200 feet long now, a soft golden rope across the whole street. Cars stop to wait.
Finally Grandma yells "Enough!" and it snaps back like a rubber band. It pulls you all the way back into the kitchen and you land in the flour sack. She bakes it. It is the fluffiest bread on Oʻahu.

words.say_it: Hold your nose like milk is coming out. "Vai-OOOO." Hold the ū.
words.bonus: Wai is fresh water, and waiū is milk. Waiūpaka is butter.
words.picture: Milk shooting out of cousin's nose
story_paragraphs: Your cousin bets he can chug a whole gallon of milk in 20 seconds. The whole family gathers in the kitchen. He tips the jug up. Glug glug glug glug. Eleven seconds. Empty. Milk mustache all the way up to his eyebrows.
Then your uncle tells a really dumb joke.
Your cousin tries not to laugh. His cheeks puff up. His eyes water. Then it comes. Milk shoots out of both his nostrils in two white jets, 8 feet across the kitchen, and hits the refrigerator.
The whole family jumps back. "WHY... OOOOOOOOH!"
The cat walks in, sees milk all over the fridge, and thinks it is the best day of its life. It licks the fridge for an hour. Your cousin has to lie down. He smells like milk until Friday.

words.say_it: Hold a mug with two shaky hands. "KO-peh."
words.bonus: Kope came from the English word coffee. Coffee grown in the Kona district of Hawaiʻi Island is world famous.
words.picture: Uncle drinking coffee from a mop bucket
story_paragraphs: It is 5 a.m. and your uncle has not had his coffee. He is not a person yet. He is a grumpy lump in a bathrobe. He walks into the wall. He tries to open the fridge with the TV remote. He says good morning to the dog in the wrong language.
He cannot cope.
He shuffles to the kitchen and fills a mug. Not a mug. A bucket. A whole mop bucket of hot black coffee from the farm in Kona. He lifts it with both hands and drinks.
His eyes pop open. His hair stands up. He starts vacuuming, doing push-ups, and fixing the roof at the same time. He mows the lawn in 4 minutes.
He looks at you, twitching, and gives you a thumbs up. "COPE, EH!"

words.say_it: Hold your palms up and shrug. "VAI?" Then shake off the water.
words.bonus: Wai is fresh water and kai is salt water. Waiwai, doubled, means wealth. One popular explanation is that fresh water was the greatest riches.
words.picture: Water dumping on a kid who asks why
story_paragraphs: Your little cousin is 4 and he asks "WHY?" about everything. Why is the sky blue. Why do dogs lick. Why is Uncle bald. He asks 900 times a day.
One day at the stream in the valley, something changes. He asks "WHY?" and SPLOOSH, a bucket of cold, clear stream water dumps on his head out of nowhere. He blinks. "...Why?" SPLOOSH.
Nobody is holding a bucket. It just happens. Every "why" comes with fresh cold water from the mountains. It is so clean he can drink it as it falls, and it tastes like rain.
By sunset he is soaked and shivering and very, very refreshed. He opens his mouth to ask one more question. He stops. He thinks about it. He just nods.

words.say_it: Stick out a numb tongue. "AH-vah." Tiny catch before the ah.
words.bonus: ʻAwa is often served in a coconut shell cup. Awa without the ʻokina is the milkfish.
words.picture: Numb tongue after a coconut cup of ʻawa
story_paragraphs: You are at a gathering in a friend's backyard, and his uncle offers you a drink of ʻawa. It is served in a coconut shell cup. It is brown and cloudy, like muddy water, and it smells like a root dug up out of the ground, because it is one.
You drink it. It tastes earthy and peppery. You say thank you.
Then your tongue goes numb. Totally numb, like after the dentist. Your lips tingle. You try to say "That was great" and only two sounds come out.
"Ahhhh... vahhhh."

You try again. "Ahhhh... vahhh." The uncle laughs a big warm laugh and says you just said its name perfectly. You sit back in your chair, calm and relaxed, and listen to the ʻukulele under the stars, saying "ahhh, vahhh" every time someone asks you anything.

words.say_it: Crouch like a runner at the starting line. "KOHHHH!" Hold the ō long.
words.bonus: Kōpaʻa, sugar, is built from kō, sugarcane, plus paʻa, hard or solid.
words.picture: Sugarcane sugar rush blasting down the street
story_paragraphs: Your neighbor has a patch of sugarcane taller than the house. He cuts you a stalk. It is 12 feet long, with rings on it like bamboo. He peels a piece and tells you to chew it.
You bite in. Sweet juice floods your mouth. So much sugar. You chew harder. You feel it go to your legs. Your knees start bouncing. Your hair stands up. Your ears are ringing.
The neighbor counts down like a rocket launch. "Three, two, one..."
"KOHHHHHHHHHHH!"
You blast off down the street. You run around the block 11 times in four minutes. You pass a moped. You pass a bus. Dogs give up chasing you.
You finally flop in his yard, still holding the stalk, chewing. "Koh." Then you ask for another piece.

words.say_it: Pump your fists like a cheering crowd. "Koh-PAH," catch, "ah!"
words.bonus: Kōpaʻa is kō (sugarcane) plus paʻa (hard), so sugar is hardened cane. Do not mix it up with kopa, which is soap.
words.picture: Pa sugar-rushing laps around the block
story_paragraphs: Remember Pa with the pale forehead and the loud shirt? Pa has been told to stop eating sugar. Today Ma is out, and he finds the sugar bag. The 25 pound one.
He eats one spoonful. Then ten. Then he just pours it straight into his mouth like a waterfall of white crystals.
His eyes spin. His mustache curls. He kicks open the front door and starts running laps around the neighborhood. The kids line the street and cheer like it is a marathon. "GOOOO, PA!"
On lap 30 he sees Ma's car turning the corner. He stops dead. That catch in his throat. "...AH!"
He runs back inside, hides the empty sugar bag in the rice pot, and sits on the couch pretending to read. He is still vibrating. The couch is vibrating.

words.say_it: Lick imaginary honey off your finger. "MEH-lee."
words.bonus: Nalo meli means honeybee.
words.picture: Giant bee Melly dripping honey in your car
story_paragraphs: You open a jar of honey at the farmers market and a bee the size of a golden retriever climbs out. Her name is Melly. She is sticky from her antennas to her stinger, and she loves you right away.

She follows you to the car. She rides in the back seat with her head out the window, dripping honey all the way down the H-1. Everything she touches turns gold and sticky. The steering wheel. Your slippahs. Your cousin's hair.

At every red light you yell "MELLY! NO!" and she buzzes happy and leaves another puddle on the dashboard. By the time you get home there are 6 pounds of honey in your car and 40 regular bees following it like a parade.
Melly. Meli. Honey and bee, one word, one sticky mess.

words.say_it: Pull invisible slime off your chin. "LEE-moo."
words.bonus: Limu covers lots of plants that grow in water, even moss. Limu kohu is a favorite red seaweed for poke.
words.picture: Cow named Lee with a seaweed beard
story_paragraphs: There is a cow on the North Shore named Lee, and Lee has given up grass. Lee only eats seaweed. Every morning at low tide she walks down to the reef, sticks her whole face in a tide pool and comes up with a green and brown slimy beard three feet long.
The farmer stands on the sand with a bucket of good hay, begging her to come home and act like a normal cow. "LEE! MOO!"

Lee turns around with seaweed hanging off both ears and answers "Mooooo," and a little crab falls out of her mouth. Tourists take pictures. Lee chews. Green slime drips off her chin onto her hooves, and she looks like the happiest cow in the state.
Lee, moo. Limu.

words.say_it: Wiggle a finger like you're tickling a shell. "oh-PEE-hee."
words.bonus: ʻOpihi is a prized pūpū at a lūʻau, often eaten raw with a little salt.
words.picture: Ticklish limpet giggling off the rock
story_paragraphs: You are on the wet rocks at low tide with a butter knife, trying to pop an ʻopihi off. It is a little cone shaped shell stuck down harder than superglue. You push. Nothing. You pry. Nothing. You sit on the knife with your whole body. It does not move one millimeter.
Then you notice something. When you poke the edge of the shell, it wiggles. You poke again. It lets out a tiny gasp and then a giggle. "(gasp) Oh! PEE-HEE-HEE!"
It is ticklish. So you tickle it for ten straight minutes. "Oh! Pee-hee! Oh! Pee-hee-hee!" It laughs so hard it loses its grip and plops into your bucket, still giggling.
That little gasp at the front is the ʻokina. And keep one eye on the ocean the whole time, because the waves out there do not joke around.

words.say_it: Wave with both hands and hiccup in the middle. "HEH-eh."
words.bonus: Heʻe also means to slide or to surf. Heʻe nalu means surfing, sliding on a wave.
words.picture: Octopus waving eight arms at the bus stop
story_paragraphs: You are waiting at the bus stop when an octopus the size of a beanbag chair slides up and sits next to you on the bench. It is very friendly. It waves one arm. "Hey..." Then it hiccups. "...eh!"

It waves a second arm. "Hey... eh!" Then a third. By the time the bus comes it is waving all eight arms at everybody on the sidewalk, "HEY... eh! HEY... eh!", with a hiccup in the middle of every single one.

The bus door opens. The octopus squeezes through a gap the size of a coin and takes over the whole back row. Every stop, it waves at the new people getting on. "Hey... eh!" An aunty waves back with her umbrella.
That little hiccup in the middle is the ʻokina. Heʻe.

words.say_it: Shake an invisible shovel over your plate. "ee-nah-MO-nah."
words.bonus: ʻInamona, limu and salt are the classic seasonings for old style poke.
words.picture: Aunty Mona shoveling relish on a birthday cake
story_paragraphs: Aunty Mona runs the poke counter and she has one rule. Everything gets ʻinamona. That is the crunchy brown relish made from roasted kukui nuts pounded with salt. She keeps a bucket of it the size of a trash can behind the counter, and she sprinkles it with a garden shovel.
ʻAhi poke? ʻInamona. Rice? ʻInamona. Your cousin's birthday cake? She is already reaching for the shovel. The whole line screams "EEE! NAH, MONA!"

Too late. The cake is covered. Your cousin takes one bite, freezes, and slowly says "...Mo', Mona." Now everybody wants it on everything. A kid puts it on his shave ice. The line goes out the door and around the block.
Eee, nah, Mona. ʻInamona.

words.say_it: Stare at a pie in shock. "Ohhh... PAI!"
words.bonus: ʻŌpae ʻula are tiny red shrimp that live in brackish ponds near the shore.
words.picture: Shrimp exploding out of a fair pie
story_paragraphs: It is the pie contest at the county fair. The judge is a very serious man in a bow tie. He lifts the crust of the last pie, and three thousand tiny shrimp come boiling out like popcorn.
They are everywhere. On the table, in his bow tie, in the lemonade. Little pink and see-through shrimp doing backflips across the tablecloth.
The judge gulps. That little catch is the ʻokina. Then he opens his mouth slow. "Ohhhhhhhh..." It takes him five full seconds to finish. "...PIE!"
The whole crowd joins in. "Ohhhh... PIE!" A shrimp jumps onto his tongue. He chews. He thinks. He gives it first place.
Hold that ō long like the judge did. ʻŌpae.

words.say_it: Point at a crab in terror. "Paah-PAH-ee!"
words.bonus: ʻAʻama is the black rock crab you see running along the shoreline rocks.
words.picture: Hubcap crab staring at sleeping Papa
story_paragraphs: You are at the beach with Papa. Papa is asleep in his beach chair with his mouth open and his toes in the sand. Out of a hole next to him walks a crab the size of a hubcap.
It walks sideways right up his leg, across his belly, and parks on his chest. Its two eyes pop up on little sticks and stare at his face from one inch away.
You try to warn him, but you are so scared it comes out in pieces. "PAAAA... PA... (gulp) EEE!"

Papa opens his eyes. He is nose to nose with the crab. The crab clicks its claws. Papa goes "EEE!" The crab goes click. They both panic. The crab runs off sideways with his slippah, and Papa runs off sideways too, because now he thinks that is how you run.
Paaa, pa, eee. Long ā, then the gulp before the ee.

words.say_it: Strike a pose with lobster claws. "OO-lah."
words.bonus: Don't mix it up with ʻula, with an ʻokina, which means red. That is the color a lobster turns when you cook it.
words.picture: Fashion lobster in a beret on Waikīkī
story_paragraphs: A lobster the size of a canoe crawls out of the water at Waikīkī. She has a tiny beret on her head and a silk scarf around her neck, and she walks down the sidewalk like it's a fashion show.

She stops. She poses. She lifts one giant claw. The whole crowd goes "OOOH... LA!" She lifts the other claw. "OOOH... LA!" She spins around, and her long feelers whip three sun hats off three tourists. "OOH-LA!"

At the end of the sidewalk she climbs up the lifeguard stand, blows a kiss with her claw, and belly flops back into the ocean with a splash that soaks the whole first row. People clap for ten minutes.
Ooh, la. Ula. The lobster.

words.say_it: Jerk back on a pretend fishing rod. "(tiny catch) AH-hee!"
words.bonus: Keep the ʻokina. ʻAhi with the ʻokina is the tuna. Ahi without it means fire.
words.picture: Water skiing behind a giant yellowfin tuna
story_paragraphs: You are fishing off the Waiʻanae coast. Your line goes tight and something pulls so hard the whole boat turns around. You hold on. It pulls you right over the side. Now you are water skiing on your slippahs behind a 200 pound yellowfin tuna.
It is fast. It zigzags. Salt water keeps splashing in your mouth, so every scream starts with a gulp. "(gulp) AH! HEE!" "(gulp) AH! HEEEE!"
After five miles the tuna slows down, pokes its long yellow fin out of the water, and looks back at you like "You done?" Then it takes off again. "(gulp) AH! HEE!"
That gulp at the start of every scream is the ʻokina. ʻAhi.

words.say_it: Flip your imaginary long hair back. "ah-NAI!"
words.bonus: ʻAmaʻama is the young mullet. ʻAnae is the full grown one.
words.picture: Mullet fish with a mullet haircut neighing
story_paragraphs: In the old fishpond there is one giant gray mullet, as long as your arm and fat like a football. It has the haircut to match. Short in front. Long in the back. A real mullet. It is very proud of that hair.
Every morning it jumps out of the water, flips its hair back, and makes a sound like a horse. First a little hitch in the throat, then "Ah... NEIGH!"

The baby mullets swim in circles under it. They don't have hair yet. They are too young. Only the full grown fish gets the haircut, and only the full grown fish gets to neigh. The little ones practice anyway. "Ah... neigh," in tiny squeaky voices.
Ah, neigh. ʻAnae. The big grown-up mullet.

words.english: wrapped bundle of food cooked in leaves
words.say_it: Hug yourself tight like you're wrapped. "lau-LAU."
words.bonus: Lau by itself means leaf.
words.picture: You wrapped up as a giant laulau
story_paragraphs: Aunty is making laulau for a graduation party of 300 people, and you are the practice laulau. She lays ti leaves on the table and says "Lie down." You lie down. She puts a lūʻau leaf on your chest, a chunk of pork belly in your hand and a piece of butterfish on your forehead.
Then she wraps you. You complain. "Too tight!" She says "Too LOUD. Too LOUD," and wraps another leaf. You complain again. Another leaf. "LOUD, LOUD."

After 20 complaints you are a green bundle the size of a sleeping bag, tied up with a ti leaf string, and the only thing sticking out is your nose. Two uncles carry you to the steamer. You smell amazing.
Loud, loud. Laulau.

words.say_it: Wave off a plate like it's nothing. "Poo-POO."
words.bonus: Pūpū also means shell. A lei pūpū is a shell lei, like the tiny Niʻihau shell lei.
words.picture: Uncle pooh-poohing then eating the whole pūpū table
story_paragraphs: Uncle Rodney shows up at the party and looks at the pūpū table. Shoyu chicken wings, poke, fried wontons, edamame. He waves his hand. "Pooh-POOH. That's just snacks. I'm saving room for the real food."

Then he eats one wing. Just one. Then 60 more. Then the whole tray of wontons. Every time somebody walks by he waves them off again, "Pooh-pooh, just pūpū," with sauce on his face and a toothpick behind each ear.
When the main food finally comes out, Uncle is lying on the grass holding his stomach. He looks at the kālua pig and the lomi salmon and whispers "...pooh-pooh."
Hold both ū's long, like his sad little whisper. Pūpū.

words.say_it: Nod slow like you're too cool. "Kooo-LO-lo."
words.bonus: Kūlolo is made from grated kalo and coconut milk, baked or steamed for hours.
words.picture: Lowrider truck sagging under 400 pounds of kūlolo
story_paragraphs: Your uncle drives a shiny lowrider truck that can bounce up and down. Today he is delivering kūlolo to a party. Kūlolo is dense. Taro and coconut cooked together until it's sticky and brown and heavy like a brick of fudge. He has 400 pounds of it in the back.
He pulls up to the party and the whole truck sinks. The tires squish flat. The bumper scrapes the road. Sparks. Everybody comes out to look.
Uncle leans out the window with his sunglasses on, nods slow and says "Cooool. Low. Low." He hits the switch to bounce. The truck will not bounce. It just groans.
It takes 12 cousins to carry the trays inside. Cool, low, low. Kūlolo. Hold that first ū long and cool.

words.say_it: Wobble your head like jello. "how-PEE-ah."
words.bonus: Haupia was first thickened with pia, Polynesian arrowroot. Today most people use cornstarch.
words.picture: Wobbly haupia square asking "How be ya?"
story_paragraphs: At the lūʻau there is a square of haupia on your plate. White, smooth, cold, cut perfect. You poke it with your fork and it jiggles. Then it jiggles back. Then it opens two little eyes.
"HOW be ya?" it says, wobbling.

You say fine. It says "How be ya?" again, wobbling harder, like it didn't hear you. Now the whole tray of haupia on the buffet table is wobbling and asking "HOW be ya? HOW be ya?" in tiny coconut voices.
Grandma walks over and eats three of them in one bite. The rest go quiet. You look at yours. It looks at you. You eat it. It's so good you feel a little bad.
How be ya. Haupia.

words.say_it: Clasp your hands and beg. "kah-nah-KEHHH?"
words.bonus: Kanakē comes from the English word candy. Hawaiian has no d, so the sounds shifted.
words.picture: Kid begging for candy, "Can a... KAAAY?"
story_paragraphs: You are six years old in the checkout line, and there is a wall of candy right at eye level. You grab the biggest chocolate bar. You look up at your dad with the biggest eyes in history.

"Can a...? 'Kay?" He says no. "Can a... KAAAAY?" He says no. You keep going. The KAAAY gets longer every time, until one "Kaaaaaaaaaaay" lasts so long the people behind you start buying candy just to make it stop.

The cashier hands you a free lollipop. The man behind you buys you gum. A lady buys you a whole bag of gummy bears. You walk out of there with more candy than the store. Dad has no idea what just happened.
Can a... KAAAY? Kanakē. Stretch that last ē like a begging kid.

words.sound_hook: Ice... cream... ah (with a frozen tongue)
words.say_it: Stick your tongue out like it's frozen. "ai-kah-LEE-mah."
words.bonus: ʻAikalima is borrowed from the English words ice cream, reshaped to fit Hawaiian sounds.
words.picture: Frozen tongue ordering a thirteenth scoop
story_paragraphs: You order the biggest ice cream in the shop. Twelve scoops, taller than you. You eat six scoops in two minutes. Your brain freezes. Then your lips freeze. Then your tongue turns into a popsicle.

You want a thirteenth scoop. You open your mouth to say "ice cream," but your frozen tongue can't make the sounds. First a little catch in your throat, then it comes out "AI... kah... LEE... mah." The worker stares. You point at the tub and try again. "AI-kah-LEE-mah!" Your cheeks are so cold they crackle.
She gives you the scoop. It worked. Now everybody in line is ordering the frozen tongue way. "Ai-kah-LEE-mah, please." The owner changes the menu board.
Frozen tongue ice cream. ʻAikalima.

words.say_it: Pop a grape in your mouth. "VAI-nah."
words.bonus: Waina means both the grapes and the wine made from them. It comes from the English word wine.
words.picture: Grapevine feeding you grapes in bed
story_paragraphs: You leave your window open one night. In the morning there is a grapevine coming through it. A thick green vine, 90 feet long, curling across your floor, up your bed and around your ankle. It is heavy with purple grapes the size of golf balls.
You yell "VINE! AHHH!" It squeezes a little. A grape falls into your open mouth. It is sweet. You yell again. "VINE! AHHH!" Another grape. You start to see how this works.
By lunch you are still in bed, wrapped up in vine, yelling "VINE, AH!" every 30 seconds and eating grapes. Your mom walks in, looks at you, and closes the door.
Vine, ah. Waina. The w can sound like a v here.

words.say_it: Gasp, then clap. "ah-LAH-nee!"
words.bonus: ʻAlani comes from the English word orange. Wai ʻalani is orange juice.
words.picture: Orange peel ribbon running down the driveway
story_paragraphs: Uncle Lonnie has one talent. He can peel an orange in a single long spiral without breaking the peel. At the family party the kids line up and bring him the biggest orange they can find, one the size of a basketball.

He starts at the top. His thumb goes around and around. The peel comes off in one orange ribbon. Ten feet, twenty feet, thirty feet, out the door and down the driveway. The neighbors come outside. A car stops to watch.
When the last inch comes off in one piece, the whole yard gasps and cheers. "(gasp) AH! LONNIE!"
He bows. He hands out slices. There is juice running down every chin in the yard.
Ah, Lonnie. ʻAlani. The little catch at the front is that gasp.

words.say_it: Open wide and hold it. "Aaaah-PAH-lah."
words.bonus: The mountain apple, the pink fruit that grows in Hawaiʻi valleys, is ʻōhiʻa ʻai.
words.picture: Dentist popping an apple in your mouth
story_paragraphs: You go to the dentist. He says "Open wide, pal. Say AAAAH." You say "Aaaaaaah." You hold it. You hold it longer. That long ā is important.
While your mouth is wide open, he reaches over and pops a whole red apple in there, like the roast pig on a fancy platter. "PAL, ah," he says, "that's how wide I need you."

Now you are stuck in the chair with an apple in your mouth and a little paper bib. He goes to lunch. You sit there for an hour. You get bored. You eat the apple from the inside out. When he comes back the apple is gone and your teeth are the cleanest he has ever seen.
Aaah... pal, ah. ʻĀpala.

words.say_it: Reach out and grab. "LEH-mee!"
words.bonus: Lemi comes from the English word lemon.
words.picture: Twelve cousins squeezing one giant lemon
story_paragraphs: Twelve cousins are standing around one lemon on the picnic table. It is the size of a watermelon and it is the only lemon at the party. Everybody wants to squeeze it into their drink.
"LEMME!" "No, LEMME!" "LEMME, LEMME!" Twelve hands grab it at once. They all squeeze together.

The lemon explodes. A wave of sour juice shoots across the yard. It hits Aunty in the eye. It hits the dog. It fills the cooler. Every cousin is soaked, puckered and blinking, twelve little sour faces with their lips sucked all the way in.
Only one person says anything. From under the table, dripping, Grandpa whispers "...lemme next time."
Lemme. Lemi. The lemon.

words.say_it: Crunch a pretend carrot, loud. "Kaah-LO-keh." Hold the kaah like a car horn.
words.bonus: Kāloke comes from the English word carrot.
words.picture: Giant carrot car that is not low-key
story_paragraphs: You buy a used car from a lot at the edge of town. It is not really a car. It is a giant carrot, 14 feet long, bright orange, with four wheels bolted on and leafy green tops sticking up like antennas.
Your cousin rides with you wearing sunglasses and a hat pulled down low. He does not want anybody to see him. "It is just a CAAAR," he whispers. "Keep it LOW-KEY."

It is not low-key. At the first red light a horse leans in the window and bites off a piece of the hood. Two rabbits chase you down the highway. A kid on the sidewalk points and yells "CAAAR! LOW-KEY!" and the whole bus stop laughs.
By the time you park, half the carrot is gone and there is a trail of orange crumbs behind you.
Caaar, low-key. Kāloke. Hold that ā long like a car horn.

words.say_it: Wipe your eyes and hiccup. "ah-kah-ah-KAI."
words.bonus: Hawaiʻi's famous sweet onions grow upcountry in Kula on Maui.
words.picture: Whole family sobbing over a giant onion
story_paragraphs: You have to chop one onion for the family stew. It is the size of a bowling ball. The first cut, your eyes sting. The fifth cut, your nose runs. By the tenth cut you are sobbing so hard you hiccup between every sound.
"Ah... (hic) ka... (hic) ah... CRY!"

The dog walks in and starts crying. The neighbor walks past the window and starts crying. Your whole family comes in to see what's wrong, and they all start sobbing and hiccuping too. "Ah-ka-ah-CRY!" Fifteen people crying over one cutting board.
The stew comes out great. A little salty from the tears.
Those hiccups are the two ʻokina. ʻAkaʻakai.

words.say_it: Throw your hands up at the mess. "Ohhh-LEH-nah!"
words.bonus: ʻŌlena is a canoe plant brought by early voyagers, used for yellow dye and for medicine.
words.picture: Yellow dog Lena leaving paw prints on the couch
story_paragraphs: Your golden retriever Lena sneaks into the kitchen while Mom is grating fresh ʻōlena for tea. The bowl of bright orange turmeric falls off the counter. SPLAT. Lena rolls in it. When she stands up, she is not golden anymore. She is school bus yellow.
She is so happy about it. She runs through the house wagging, leaving yellow paw prints on the white couch, the white rug and the white wall. You chase her down the hall screaming "OHHHH, LENA!"
Mom washes her three times. Still yellow. Your hands are yellow from grabbing her. Lena stays yellow for two weeks and glows in every family photo.
Ohhh, Lena. ʻŌlena. Hold that long ō like you mean it.

words.say_it: Put your palm flat on the ground and breathe out. "Aaah-ee-nah."
words.bonus: Many teachers explain ʻāina as "that which feeds," from ʻai, to eat. Aloha ʻāina means love for the land.
words.picture: Tūtū handing you a shovel instead of lunch
story_paragraphs: You show up at Tūtū's house on a Saturday, starving. "Tūtū, can I eat?" She hands you a shovel. "Eat? Nah. First we plant."

So you plant. Kalo in the wet corner. ʻUala along the fence. A banana stump by the water tank. Every weekend for months you dig, you weed, you haul water. You get blisters. You ask again. "Now can I eat?" "Nah. Not yet."

Then one morning the ground gives it all back. Bananas hanging heavy. Sweet potatoes as long as your forearm. Kalo ready to cook. Tūtū makes lunch, you take the first warm bite, and you let out the longest sigh of your life. "Aaaaah."
That long sigh, then "eat? nah." Aaah, eat, nah. ʻĀina. The land feeds you when you take care of it first.

words.say_it: Spread your arms like you're holding a globe. "ho-NOO-ah."
words.bonus: Mālama honua means care for the earth. It was the name of Hōkūleʻa's voyage around the world.
words.picture: Alien amazed by everything at Ala Moana
story_paragraphs: A small green alien lands his spaceship in the Ala Moana parking lot. It is his first time on Earth, and everything amazes him.

He sees a rubber slippah. "HO! NEW, ah!" He sees a spam musubi. "HO! NEW, AH!" He sees a pigeon, a shopping cart, a lady with 40 shopping bags. "HO! NEW AH!" He takes pictures of all of it with his three eyes.

He buys a shave ice and gets rainbow syrup all down his antennas, and he decides this whole planet is the best thing he has ever seen. When he flies home he takes a bag of dirt, a coconut and one slippah. His friends back home don't believe a word.
Ho, new, ah. Honua. The whole world, brand new to him.

words.say_it: Point straight up. "LAH-nee."
words.bonus: Lani shows up in lots of names, like Leilani, heavenly lei. Don't confuse it with ʻalani, the orange.
words.picture: Your lawn floating up into the sky
story_paragraphs: You are mowing the front lawn on a hot Saturday. The grass is thick and green. You get to the last strip, the mower jerks, and the whole lawn peels up off the ground like a giant green carpet.
It floats. It rises past the fence, past the roof, past the power lines. You grab the edge and now you are going up too. You yell down to your dad. "My LAWN! EEEE!"

Up and up, past the birds, through the clouds, into the wide blue sky. You lie back on the grass and look around. It's quiet up here. Somebody's kite drifts past. A plane waves its wings. Your lawn floats over the whole island like a magic carpet, and you never want to come down.
Lawn, eee. Lani. The sky.

words.say_it: Lift your arms and sing one long note. "LAAAAH."
words.bonus: Lā also means day. Hauʻoli lā hānau means happy birthday.
words.picture: The sun singing one long note all day
story_paragraphs: Every morning the sun comes up over Diamond Head and starts to sing. One note. "LAAAAAAAAAAH." It holds it. It holds it through breakfast. It holds it through school. You can hear it all day long.
The sun never takes a breath. That's its job. As long as it's singing, it's day. Surfers ride waves to it. Aunties hang laundry to it. Chickens dance to it in the yard.

Around 7 o'clock the sun gets tired. The note starts to wobble. It sinks lower and lower toward the ocean, and the "LAAAAH" gets quieter and quieter until the sun dips into the water with a little fizz and goes silent. Night.
Next morning, same note. "LAAAAH." Lā. The sun, and the day it sings.

words.say_it: Look up at the ceiling and howl. "mah-HEE-nah."
words.bonus: Hawaiians named every night of the moon's cycle. Māhealani is one of the full moon nights.
words.picture: Hyena laughing at the full moon on your roof
story_paragraphs: Every full moon a hyena shows up on your roof. Nobody knows where it comes from. It stands on the peak of the roof, looks up at the big round moon, and laughs like crazy. "HEE-HEE-HEE-HAAA!"
You run into your mom's room. "MA! HYENA!" She pulls the pillow over her head. "It's the moon again. Go back to sleep."

It happens every month, like clockwork. The moon gets fat and round, the hyena appears, you yell "MA! HYENA!" Then the moon shrinks back to a skinny sliver and the hyena is gone for weeks. You start marking it on the calendar. Pretty soon you count your whole year in hyenas.
Ma, hyena. Mahina. Moon, and month, same word.

words.say_it: Coo softly at the ceiling. "Hohh-KOOO."
words.bonus: The voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa is named for a star, Arcturus. The name means star of gladness.
words.picture: Fallen star cooing like a pigeon
story_paragraphs: You are lying on the grass at night counting stars. One of them starts to wobble. Then it falls. It lands in your yard with a soft thump. It is about the size of a microwave, glowing gold and warm like fresh bread.
It is also cooing. Like a pigeon. "Hooo... COOOO."

You pick it up. It snuggles under your arm. "Hooo... COOO." It's shy. Your whole yard is lit up gold. The neighbor's cat comes over to stare. You feed it a little rice, which is probably wrong, but it eats it.
At midnight it floats up out of your arms, gives one last "Hooo-COOO," and zooms back to its place in the sky. Now every time you look up, one star is cooing at you.
Both vowels are long. Hōkū.

words.say_it: Rub the top of your head. "OW."
words.bonus: Ao and pō are a pair. Ao is daylight and pō is night. Ao can also mean the world.
words.picture: Hard cloud bonking beachgoers on the head
story_paragraphs: It is a perfect beach day until a cloud drops out of the sky. Not rain. The actual cloud. It comes down low and slow and bonks you right on the head.
"OW!"

Clouds are supposed to be soft. This one is not. This one is solid, like a 50 pound bag of rice. It floats back up and comes down again. "OW!" It bonks your uncle. "OW!" It bonks a surfer, a lifeguard and the guy selling shave ice. "OW! OW! OW!" The whole beach is rubbing their heads.
Finally it floats away. The sun comes out bright. Daylight everywhere. Everybody goes back to swimming, still going "ow" under their breath.
Ow. Ao. The cloud, the daylight after it, all of it.

words.say_it: Look up and hold your palms out. "OO-ah."
words.bonus: Hawaiian has hundreds of names for different rains. Kanilehua is a famous rain of Hilo.
words.picture: Neighborhood oohing at raindrops like fireworks
story_paragraphs: It has not rained for 40 days. The grass is brown. The dogs are grumpy. The whole neighborhood is sitting outside staring at the sky.
Then one fat raindrop falls. It lands on a little boy's nose. Everybody gasps like it's a fireworks show. "OOOOH!"
Then another drop. "AAAAH!"

Then the sky opens up and it pours. Buckets. Sheets. People stand in the street with their arms out and faces up, going "OOOH! AHHH!" like it's New Year's Eve and every raindrop is a firework. An aunty opens her umbrella, then throws it away. Uncle dances in the gutter in his slippahs. The dogs roll in the mud.
Ooh, ah. Ua. The rain.

words.say_it: Hold your hair down against the wind. "mah-KAH-nee."
words.bonus: Many places in Hawaiʻi have their own named winds. A Kona wind blows from the south and brings sticky weather.
words.picture: Little brother flying like a kite
story_paragraphs: It is the windiest day of the year at the beach. Fifty mile trade winds. Your little brother weighs 40 pounds and he wants to fly the big kite. You look over at Ma. "Ma, CAN he?"
Ma says "Sure, just hold on tight."

He grabs the string. The wind grabs the kite. The kite grabs him. Up he goes like a flag on a pole, feet kicking, cheeks flapping, laughing his head off. You grab his ankle and walk him down the beach like a balloon at a parade. His slippahs fall off one at a time.
Ma jumps up. "WHO SAID HE CAN?" You yell back over the wind. "Ma, CAN HE? You SAID!"
Ma, can he. Makani. The wind.

words.say_it: Shake your head at a mountain. "MOW-nah."
words.bonus: Mauna Loa means long mountain. Mauna Kea is the tallest mountain in Hawaiʻi.
words.picture: Pushing a lawn mower up a snowy mountain
story_paragraphs: Dad hands you a lawn mower and points out the window. Not at the yard. At the mountain. Thirteen thousand feet of mountain.
"Go mow that."
You look at the mower. You look at the mountain. There is snow on top. There are clouds halfway up. There are rocks the size of trucks. "MOW? NAH."

Dad does not accept nah. So you start. Mow at the bottom. Mow up the side. By the end of week one your legs are huge. By week three you are above the clouds and a goat is following you. At the very top, freezing, you look down at the whole island and whisper one more time. "Mow? ...Nah."
Mow, nah. Mauna. The mountain.

words.say_it: Hunch over like you're carrying a piano. "koo-ah-HEE-vee."
words.bonus: Kua by itself means back, the part of you carrying that piano.
words.picture: Hauling a piano over peak after peak
story_paragraphs: Aunty Pua wants her piano moved. Not to the next room. To her sister's house, on the other side of the mountains. She does not trust the moving company. So it's you.

They strap the piano on your back. You hike up the ridge trail, one peak, then another, then another, a whole long line of peaks like the spikes on a dragon's back. Every step you groan the same thing.
"Koo... ah... HEAVY!"

At the top of each peak you stop and rest, and a hiker plays a song on the piano on your back. Then you keep going. "Koo... ah... HEAVY!" Twelve peaks later you set it down at her sister's door. Her sister says "Oh, I don't play."
Koo, ah, heavy. Kuahiwi. The high mountains, peak after peak.

words.say_it: Hand on your throat, gulp in the middle. "POO-oo."
words.bonus: Lots of place names start with Puʻu, like Puʻu ʻUalakaʻa, the park high above Honolulu.
words.picture: Kid gasping on top of a steep hill
story_paragraphs: There is a hill behind your school so steep that nobody has ever made it to the top without stopping. You decide today is the day. You run straight up. Your legs burn. Your lungs burn. Your slippahs are smoking.
You reach the top. You bend over, hands on your knees, and let out the biggest "PHEW!" of your life. Then a gulp gets stuck in your throat. "...OOH."
"PHEW... (gulp) OOH."

Everybody down below hears it echo off the hill. Now every kid who makes it up there does the same thing at the top. "Phew... ooh." Somebody sticks a flag up there with a cartoon of a kid holding his throat.
Phew, ooh. Puʻu. The hill, and the throat where that gulp got stuck. The ʻokina is the gulp.

words.say_it: Cup your hands and sing into a valley. "ah-VAAAH-vah."
words.bonus: Don't mix it up with awa, which means harbor. Awāwa is the valley.
words.picture: Frog singing group echoing in a valley
story_paragraphs: Deep in a green valley, with walls so tall the sun only shows up for a couple of hours a day, lives a singing group of 40 frogs. They stand on rocks in matching bow ties. Every night they sing the same song.
"Ahhh... WAAAAH... vah."
The valley walls bounce it back. "WAAAH-vah... WAAH-vah... wah-vah." The echo lasts ten minutes. Hikers stop on the trail and snap their fingers. The waterfall keeps the beat.
One night a frog tries a solo, "Ah-WAAAAH-vah," so loud the echo wakes up a herd of wild pigs on the far side of the valley. They join in. Now it's 40 frogs and 12 pigs singing till sunrise.
Ah, waaah, vah. Awāwa. Stretch that middle ā like the frogs.

words.say_it: Laugh, then shrug hard. "kah-hah-VAI."
words.bonus: Wai means fresh water. Look for it in kahawai, wailele, pūnāwai and muliwai.
words.picture: Stream running through the living room
story_paragraphs: You wake up and there is a stream running through your living room. Clear, cold, fresh water, knee deep, coming in the front door and going out the back. There are little fish in it. There is a frog on your couch.
