Your dad walks in, stands in the water holding his coffee, and starts laughing. "Ka, ha ha!" Then he stops. "...WHY?"
"Ha ha... WHY?" Your mom comes in. "Ha ha... WHY?" Grandma floats past on an inner tube. "Ha ha, WHY?"
Nobody knows why. The stream stays for a week. You catch ʻōpae under the TV. Then one morning it's gone, and the carpet smells like a river forever.
Ka, ha... WHY? Kahawai. The stream.

words.say_it: Jump in place with your arms up. "vai-LEH-leh!"
words.bonus: Wai is fresh water and lele means to jump or fly. A wailele is water that leaps.
words.picture: Scared water drop at the top of a waterfall
story_paragraphs: At the top of a 300 foot waterfall, a million tiny drops of water are lined up at the edge like skydivers. One by one they jump. "WHEEE!" They sparkle all the way down into the pool.
Except one little drop named Layla. She stands at the edge, shaking. She won't jump. The line behind her backs up for miles, all the way up the stream. Every drop is yelling at her.
"WHY, LAYLA? JUST JUMP!" "Why, Layla? WHY?!"
She takes a breath. She closes her eyes. She jumps. She screams the whole way down, lands in the pool with a plip, pops back up, and runs straight back to the top to get in line again.
Why, Layla. Wailele. Water that jumps.

words.say_it: Spin a finger next to your ear. "LO-ko."
words.bonus: Loko iʻa means fishpond. I loko means inside.
words.picture: Fishpond gone loco on coffee
story_paragraphs: Uncle's fishpond is usually calm. Today it has gone completely loco. The fish are jumping. The crabs are doing cartwheels. The big mullet with the mullet haircut from ʻanae is spinning on its tail like a breakdancer.
Uncle stands on the stone wall with his arms out. "The pond is LOCO!"

You look closer. Somebody dropped a 40 pound bag of coffee beans in there. Every fish inside is wired. The ducks won't land. The frogs are singing too fast. Bubbles are coming up from inside the pond like a hot tub.
It takes three days to calm down. Uncle puts up a sign. NO COFFEE IN POND.
Loco. Loko. The pond, and everything going crazy inside it.

words.say_it: Sink down slowly and squeak. "LO-ee!"
words.bonus: A loʻi kalo is a wetland taro patch. Cool water flows in from a ditch called an ʻauwai.
words.picture: Sinking knee deep in the taro patch mud
story_paragraphs: It's a work day at the loʻi. The aunties and uncles have been at it since before sunrise, and now it's your turn. You step off the bank into the taro patch.

The mud is cold. The mud is deep. You sink. Lower. Lower. Past your ankles, past your shins, up to your knees. You freeze. The cold mud squishes up between your toes and you let out one little squeak.
"Low... EEE!"

The aunty next to you laughs with you, not at you. She shows you how to walk, slow, knees high, feet flat. By lunch you are pulling weeds around the big heart shaped kalo leaves like you were born here. You're muddy to the belly button. Best day of your summer.
Low... eee. Loʻi. That little freeze in the middle is the ʻokina.

words.say_it: Shake sand out of your shoe. "OH-neh!"
words.bonus: One here is sand, not the number. The number one is ʻekahi.
words.picture: Sand pouring out of everything for weeks
story_paragraphs: You go to the beach for one afternoon. One. That's all.

Three weeks later there is still sand everywhere. In your shoes. "Oh, NEH!" In your ears. "Oh, NEH!" In your rice at dinner. "OH, NEH!" Under your pillow, in your toothbrush, inside a sealed jar of peanut butter that never even went to the beach.
You shake out your towel and a whole beach falls out of it, about 400 pounds of sand, burying the vacuum cleaner. You take a shower and the drain clogs. You open your wallet. Sand. "OH, NEHHH!"
You will be finding sand from that one afternoon until you are 80.
Oh, neh. One. Not the English number. Oh-neh, the sand.

words.say_it: Breathe in slow, chop the air, then wince. "poh-HAH-koo."
words.bonus: ʻIliʻili are small smooth stones clicked together like castanets in some hula.
words.picture: Karate chop on a rock that doesn't break
story_paragraphs: A karate master stands in front of a big smooth rock on the beach. Black belt. Serious face. A crowd gathers.
He breathes in slow. "Pohhhhhhh..." That breath lasts forever, just like the long ō. Then he raises his hand and brings it down on the rock with all his power. "HAH!"
The rock does not break. The rock does not even notice. There is a long silence. Then, very quietly, he holds his hand and makes a tiny sad sound. "...koo."
"Pohhh... HAH... koo."
The rock just sits there being a rock. A crab walks across it. The master bows to it with respect and goes to find some ice.
Pōhaku. The stone always wins.

words.say_it: Spit out imaginary dirt. "LEH-po."
words.bonus: Lepo is the dirt on your slippahs and also the good soil that kalo grows in.
words.picture: Tug of war team sliding into a dirt pit
story_paragraphs: Tug of war at the family picnic. Thirty cousins on one side, thirty on the other, and a giant pit of loose dirt in the middle. You are at the very front of your team, closest to the pit.
The rope goes tight. Your feet slide. You feel yourself going. You scream to your team, "LET GO! LET GO!"

They do not let go. They pull harder. You go face first into the dirt, and your whole team slides in after you like dominoes, thirty people in one big brown pile. Dirt in your ears. Dirt in your teeth. Dirt in your belly button. You spit out enough dirt to plant a tree.
Let go. Lepo. The dirt you'll be washing out of your hair for a week.

words.say_it: Peek down into a deep hole. "LOO-ah."
words.bonus: Lua also means two, as in ʻelua.
words.picture: Giant hole with a toilet seat at camp
story_paragraphs: Camping trip at the beach park. The bathrooms are closed. Uncle Kimo grabs a shovel and says "No worries, I'll make one."

He digs. And digs. He doesn't stop. By sunset the hole is 12 feet deep and as wide as a hot tub. He lays a plank across the middle, sticks a toilet seat on it, and hangs a shower curtain around the whole thing.
You walk over with your flashlight. "Uncle... where's the loo?"
He points proudly at the giant hole. You look down. It is very, very deep. Something down there echoes. "The LOO?... AHHH."
You decide you can wait until morning.
Loo, ah. Lua. The hole, and the toilet. Same word.

words.say_it: Cup your hands and yell into a cave. "AH-nah!"
words.bonus: Many caves in Hawaiʻi are lava tubes, tunnels left behind when flowing lava drained out.
words.picture: Yelling "Anna!" into an echoing lava tube
story_paragraphs: You are exploring a lava tube cave with a flashlight, and your cousin Anna went ahead. The walls are black and bumpy. Water drips from the ceiling. The tunnel keeps going deeper.
You can't see her. You cup your hands and yell. "ANNA!"

The cave yells back. "ANNA... Anna... anna... anna..." Forty times. It bounces all the way to the end and comes back again. Then from somewhere deep inside you hear Anna yell "WHAT?" and the cave answers "WHAT... what... what..." for another ten minutes.
You finally find her. She is sitting on a rock eating a musubi in the dark. She says the echo was the best part.
Anna. Ana. The cave.

words.say_it: Lean forward into the wind. "PAH-lee."
words.bonus: The Pali Lookout on Oʻahu sits on top of the Koʻolau cliffs and is famous for wind strong enough to lean on.
words.picture: Parrot blown backwards at the cliff lookout
story_paragraphs: You are standing at the Pali Lookout with a parrot named Polly on your shoulder. The wind up here is famous. It comes screaming up the cliff so hard you can lean into it and not fall down.
Polly spreads her wings to show off. Big mistake. The wind catches her and she flies backwards while flapping forwards, like a bird on a treadmill. "POLLY!"

She shoots up over the edge of the cliff and hangs there in the air, wings out, not moving at all, staring at you. Then the wind flips and blows her straight back onto your head. Your hair is sticking straight up. So are her feathers.
Polly. Pali. The cliff where the wind lives.

words.say_it: Rub your arms like you're freezing. "KOO-lah."
words.bonus: A kula kaiapuni is a Hawaiian language immersion school.
words.picture: School inside a giant cooler in an open field
story_paragraphs: Upcountry, in a wide open field with nothing but grass, cows and sky for miles, there is a school. It is inside a giant cooler. A red and white cooler the size of a gym, with the lid propped up for a door.

The kids come to class in jackets and beanies. Inside it's cold like a fridge. The teacher writes on the board in mittens. At recess everybody runs out into the warm open field to thaw, and at the bell they all run back into the cooler.
A new kid shows up on the first day, looks at it, and says "The school... is a COOLER?"
"Yup," says the teacher. "COOLER."
Cooler. Kula. School, and all that open country around it.

words.say_it: Hold your hands up to a fire. "AH-hee."
words.bonus: Ahi with no ʻokina is fire. ʻAhi with the ʻokina is the tuna. A menu that says ahi poke is, strictly speaking, selling you fire poke.
words.picture: Giant bonfire curling your eyebrows
story_paragraphs: Uncle builds a bonfire at the beach. He keeps adding wood. Pallets. Driftwood. An old chair. By 9 o'clock it is 30 feet tall and you can see it from a plane.

You walk up with a marshmallow on a stick. You get within 20 feet and the heat hits you like opening an oven. "Ah! HEAT!" You get closer. Your eyebrows curl. "AH, HEAT!" Your marshmallow catches fire, then the stick, then the bottom of your slippah.
Everybody at the beach is standing in a big circle 40 feet away, holding their hands up to the glow, going "Ah, heat... ah, heat..."
Ah, heat. Ahi. The fire. No ʻokina on this one.

words.say_it: Wave smoke away from your face and cough. "oo-AH-hee."
words.bonus: Uahi has ahi inside it. Where there is smoke, there is fire.
words.picture: Smoke chasing you around a bonfire
story_paragraphs: Remember the 30 foot bonfire from ahi? Now it's smoking. And the smoke picks you. Only you.

You move left. The smoke moves left. You move right. The smoke follows. You run around the fire three times and the smoke chases you like a puppy. It gets in your eyes, your nose, your hair, your hoodie.
You cough so hard it comes out in three pieces. "OOH! ...AH! ...HEE!" Everybody else is sitting happy in clean air. You are the only one inside a cloud. "OOH-AH-HEE!"
Next morning your pillow smells like a barbecue.
Ooh, ah, hee. Uahi. And look, ahi, fire, is hiding right inside it.

words.say_it: Feel warmth on your face and say it softly. "PEH-leh."
words.bonus: Pele is also the name of the volcano goddess. People there speak of her with respect and don't take lava rocks home.
words.picture: Pale face glowing orange at the crater
story_paragraphs: You just came home from four years of college on the continent, and you are pale. Pale like rice. Pale like the inside of a coconut. Your uncle takes one look at you and drives you to the volcano.

At night you stand at the overlook with a hundred other people, all quiet. Down in the crater the lava is glowing and rolling, bright orange, breathing heat you can feel on your cheeks from far away. It is the most powerful thing you have ever seen. Nobody talks loud here.
The glow lights up your whole face. Your uncle looks at you, orange from forehead to chin, and gives a small nod. "Not so PALE now, eh?"
Pale, eh. Pele. The lava and the volcano, a place you visit with respect.

words.say_it: Slide your feet like you're on ice. "paah-ho-eh-HO-eh."
words.bonus: Pāhoehoe and ʻaʻā are Hawaiian words that geologists all over the world use for these two kinds of lava.
words.picture: Pa sliding on smooth lava in his socks
story_paragraphs: Pa goes for a walk across an old lava flow in his socks. Not the sharp kind. The smooth kind. Shiny gray-black, with ripples and ropes in it, like somebody poured brownie batter over the land and it froze.

It is so smooth that Pa starts to slide. His arms go out. His knees wobble. You scream "PAAAA!" and he yells back "WHOA, EH! WHOA, EH!" He slides down a long lava ripple like a kid on a water slide, spinning in circles, socks smoking a little.
He comes to a stop at the bottom and stands up very slow. He brushes off his shorts. He says he meant to do that. Nobody believes him.
Paaa... whoa eh, whoa eh. Pāhoehoe. The smooth, ropy lava.

words.say_it: Tiptoe on sharp rocks. "ah... AAAH!"
words.bonus: Don't mix it up with aʻa, which means a small root or a vein.
words.picture: Barefoot Pa yelling on sharp lava
story_paragraphs: Pa lost his socks on the pāhoehoe. Now he has to cross a different lava field barefoot, and this one is ʻaʻā. Jagged, sharp, crumbly, like a field of broken flowerpots and burnt cornflakes.
He takes one step. "Ah!" He freezes. Then the pain arrives. "AAAAAAAH!"
Every step is the same. A short "Ah!", a frozen stop, then a long "AAAAH!" You can hear him a mile away. A mongoose pokes its head out of a crack and starts copying him. "Ah! AAAAH!"
It takes Pa forty minutes to go a hundred feet. At the end he sits down, looks at the bottoms of his feet, and swears he will never leave home without slippahs again.
Ah... AAAH. ʻAʻā. The ʻokina is the freeze, the ā is the long scream.

words.say_it: Push a branch out of your face. "nah-HEH-leh."
words.bonus: The ʻōhiʻa lehua is one of the most important trees in Hawaiʻi's native forests.
words.picture: Following Haley's phone into a thick forest
story_paragraphs: Your friend Haley has a new phone with a map app, and she says she knows a shortcut. The map says turn left. Left is straight into the forest.
"Nah, Haley."

She goes anyway. You follow. The trees close in. Ferns taller than trucks. Vines hanging down like jump ropes. Moss on everything. Birds you have never heard in your life. Every ten feet she says "It says keep going," and you say "NAH, HALEY."
Three hours later you come out the other side covered in leaves, with a spider in your hair and mud up to your knees, 50 feet from where you started. The phone chirps. "You have arrived."
Nah, Haley. Nahele. The forest, the wild green place where maps give up.

words.say_it: Puff out your chest and brag. "MO-koo."
words.bonus: Moku can also mean cut or broken apart. Mokupuni is another word for island.
words.picture: Cargo ship turned into a floating island
story_paragraphs: Two brothers each buy a boat. The first brother gets a little fishing boat. The second brother, Uncle Keoni, buys a huge old cargo ship and parks it right next to his brother's. He leans over the rail. "Mine is MO' COOL."
His brother adds a cooler and a flag. Keoni plants 60 coconut trees on his deck. "MO' COOL." His brother adds a hammock. Keoni adds a sandy beach, a fishpond and a family of chickens. "MO' COOL."
By summer his ship is basically an island floating in the harbor. It has its own zip code. It holds an election and picks its own mayor. It is officially its own district.
Mo' cool. Moku. Ship, island and district, all in one word.

words.say_it: Hold your thumb and finger a little bit apart. "mo-koo-POO-nee."
words.bonus: Hawaiʻi is a pae ʻāina, a chain of islands, with eight main mokupuni.
words.picture: Tiny four foot island with one tree
story_paragraphs: Remember Uncle Keoni and his mo' cool ship island from moku? His little brother is jealous. So he goes online and buys his own private island. Twelve dollars, free shipping.

It shows up in a box. He carries it to the beach and sets it in the water. It is four feet across. One coconut tree, about as tall as a fire hydrant. One hermit crab. That's the whole island. He has to stand on one foot.
He waves up at Keoni with a tiny flag. Keoni looks down from his giant ship island, tilts his head, and says "Mo' cool... but PUNY."
The hermit crab nods. The coconut tree drops its one coconut. The island tips over.
Mo' cool, puny. Mokupuni. The everyday word for island. Big or puny, every island is a mokupuni.

words.say_it: Spit and make a sour face. "KAI!"
words.bonus: Kai is salt water and wai is fresh water. Makai means toward the sea.
words.picture: Kayaker swallowing a mouthful of sea water
story_paragraphs: You go kayaking. The very first wave hits the front of your kayak and a big splash of sea water goes straight into your open mouth.
It is salty. It is SO salty. Your whole face scrunches up. "KAI... YAK!"

Another wave. Another mouthful. "KAI-YAK!" You paddle harder. The ocean keeps slapping salt water at you like it's a game. By the time you reach the sandbar you have swallowed half a gallon of ocean, your lips are crusty white with salt and your tongue is dry like beef jerky. You drink three bottles of water and it still tastes like the sea.
Now every time you see a kayak, you taste salt.
Kai. The sea. The salty stuff.

words.say_it: Moan low like a whale. "mo-AH-nah."
words.bonus: Moananuiākea is a name for the vast Pacific Ocean.
words.picture: Whales moaning across the open ocean
story_paragraphs: You are in a small boat in the middle of the ocean. Nothing but blue in every direction. Blue below, blue above, blue forever. No land for a thousand miles.
Then from deep, deep down comes a sound. A whale as long as a city bus is moaning. "MOOOOAN... AH."

It rattles your cooler. It shakes the spam musubi in your hand. The whole ocean seems to hum. Then another whale answers from 50 miles away. "MOOOOAN-AH." They moan back and forth all night across all that open water, the loudest conversation on earth, and you are a tiny speck in the middle of it.
You lie on the deck and listen until sunrise.
Moan, ah. Moana. The big open ocean.

words.say_it: Paddle hard with both arms. "NAH-loo."
words.bonus: Heʻe nalu means to surf, to slide on a wave. Remember the octopus from heʻe?
words.picture: Old Uncle Lou riding a giant wave
story_paragraphs: North Shore, winter, biggest day of the year. A wave rolls in as tall as a five story building. Everybody on the beach takes a step back.
Out in the water, one old man is already paddling for it. Uncle Lou. Seventy-four years old, tank top, longboard, no fear at all.
The lifeguard grabs the megaphone. "NAH, LOU! NOT THIS ONE!"

Lou ignores him. He catches it anyway, stands up, and rides that giant wave all the way in, arms out, gray hair flying. The wave curls over his head like a blue roof. The lifeguard yells the whole time. "NAH, LOU! NAH, LOUUU!" Lou steps off onto the sand and hands the lifeguard his board.
Nah, Lou. Nalu. The wave.

words.say_it: Point at the ocean and laugh. "kah-hah-KAI."
words.bonus: Kahakai ends in kai, sea. Kahawai, the stream, ends in wai, fresh water. Salty beach, fresh stream.
words.picture: Giant shark kite dragging you down the beach
story_paragraphs: You buy the biggest kite at the swap meet, shaped like a shark, 20 feet wide. You take it to the beach. The wind grabs it and you hold on.

It drags you. Down the beach on your butt, through the wet sand, past umbrellas and coolers and a man sleeping under a newspaper, digging a trench the whole length of the shoreline, right where the waves meet the sand.
Everybody on the beach points and laughs. "HA HA! KITE!"
Two miles later the kite finally drops. You sit up in the ditch you just dug. The tide comes in and fills it. Now it's a canal. Kids are floating down it on bodyboards. "Ha ha, kite."
Ka ha KITE. Kahakai. The beach, the edge of the sea.

words.say_it: Lie flat and stiff as a board. "PAH-pah."
words.bonus: A papa heʻe nalu is a surfboard, a board for sliding on waves.
words.picture: Grandkids surfing on Papa on the reef flat
story_paragraphs: Papa lies down flat on the reef flat at low tide, stiff as a board. The water is shallow and warm. Six grandkids climb onto his back.
"Papa is the board!" He does not move. A little wave comes, he floats, and they stand up on him, wobbling, arms out, screaming "PAPA! PAPA!" One falls off. Another climbs on.

Then Papa lifts his head and starts teaching. He is the board, he is the surf teacher, and this is class. "Knees bent. Look forward. Paddle." Six kids sit in a row on the reef flat, taking notes with their fingers in the wet sand. A turtle swims up to listen.
Papa. Papa. Papa. Board, class and reef flat. Papa is all three.

words.say_it: Blow bubbles, then gasp. "aah-ko-ah-KO-ah."
words.bonus: Coral is alive. Don't stand on it or touch it, and use reef safe sunscreen.
words.picture: Coral shaped like a koala, snorkel flooding
story_paragraphs: You go snorkeling with your cousin. Down on the reef she spots a coral head shaped exactly like a koala hugging a tree. Brown and bumpy, round ears, little nose, arms wrapped around a branch of coral. Fish are swimming in and out of its ears.
She pops up to tell you. "Ah! A koa..." A wave floods her snorkel. She coughs. "(gulp) KOA...!" Another splash. She never gets to say the "la." "Ah! Koa... (gulp) KOA...!"

Now you both keep diving down to look at it and coming up choking. "Ah-koa-KOA!" The coral has towers and fans and antlers and brains, a whole underwater city, and all you two can say is half a koala.
Every gulp is an ʻokina. ʻĀkoʻakoʻa. Coral.

words.say_it: Push your hands up like a fountain. "poo-naah-VAI."
words.bonus: Spot the wai, fresh water, at the end. A pūnāwai is a spring of fresh water.
words.picture: Spring bursting up in the backyard
story_paragraphs: Your kid wants a swimming pool. Every single day. "Can we get a pool?" And every day you say the same thing. "Pool? Naaaah."

One morning you're watering the garden and the ground under your feet starts to bubble. Then gurgle. Then cold, clear, fresh water comes shooting up out of the grass like a fountain, straight out of the earth. It fills the yard. It fills the sandbox. It floats the lawn chairs.
Your kid runs out in goggles and cannonballs in. You stand there soaked, staring at the spring in your backyard. "Pool? Naaah... WHY?!"
Pool, naaah, why. Pūnāwai. A spring, fresh water coming up from the ground.

words.say_it: Put one foot forward and one foot back. "moo-lee-VAI."
words.bonus: At a muliwai, fresh water, wai, meets salt water, kai. The mix is called brackish water.
words.picture: Cow standing half in the stream, half in the sea
story_paragraphs: Lee the cow from limu is back. She got tired of eating seaweed on the reef, so she walked up the beach to where the stream runs into the ocean. Now she stands there with her front legs in the salty sea and her back legs in the fresh stream water. Half and half.
She won't move. She just chews and looks happy. The farmer comes running down the beach waving his hat. "Moo, Lee! WHY?"

She stays right there in the mixed-up water where fresh and salty meet, with little fish around her ankles, some from the stream and some from the sea. Then she moos, a mullet jumps over her tail, and a duck lands on her back.
Moo, Lee, why. Muliwai. The river mouth.

words.say_it: Wince, then shrug. "ow-VAI."
words.bonus: The water in an ʻauwai flows through the loʻi and then goes back to the stream.
words.picture: Water drop bouncing down a stone ditch
story_paragraphs: Layla the water drop from wailele is back. After the waterfall she floats down the stream, and a little stone ditch scoops her up. It's an ʻauwai, and it carries water off the stream toward the taro patches.
It's narrow. It's fast. It's twisty. Layla shoots down it like a water slide, bouncing off every stone. "OW! WHY? OW! WHY?" Right before every bump she gulps. "(gulp) OW! WHY?"

Then she pops out into the calm, cool water of the loʻi and floats in circles around the big green kalo leaves. The kalo drinks. When she's done, she flows back out the other side and home to the stream, ready to do it all again.
Ow, why. ʻAuwai. The gulp is the ʻokina.

words.say_it: Wave boats in like a harbor master. "AH-vah!"
words.bonus: Don't mix up awa, the harbor, with ʻawa, the kava plant and drink, or awāwa, the valley.
words.picture: Three hundred boats named Ava jammed in the harbor
story_paragraphs: The harbor is packed. Three hundred boats. Fishing boats, sailboats, a tugboat, a canoe, an old yacht with a hot tub on the deck. And every single one is named Ava. Say it like the harbor master does, AH-vah.
He stands on the dock with a megaphone. "AVA! You're up!"
All three hundred boats start their engines at the same time. Horns blast. Seagulls scatter. They all try to leave at once and jam up at the harbor mouth like the H-1 at five o'clock.
The harbor master sighs into the megaphone. "The BLUE Ava." Two hundred of them are blue.
Ava. Awa. The harbor where all the boats come home.

words.say_it: Draw a big arc across the sky with your arm. "aah-noo-eh-NOO-eh."
words.bonus: A rainbow is on Hawaiʻi's license plates.
words.picture: Aunty unrolling a rainbow from the swap meet
story_paragraphs: Aunty comes home from the swap meet with a rainbow. A real one, 90 feet long, rolled up under her arm like a carpet, the price tag still hanging off the end. She unrolls it across the yard. Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple, glowing.
She is so proud. She shows the neighbor. "Aaah! NEW, EH? NEW, EH?"
The neighbor says "Wow." She shows the mailman. "Aaah! NEW, eh? NEW, eh?" She drapes it over the carport. She hangs it off the mango tree. She makes the whole family stand under it for a photo.
That night it sprinkles a little, and the rainbow gets even brighter. Aunty's eyes shine. "NEW, eh?"
Aaah, new eh, new eh. Ānuenue. The rainbow.

words.say_it: Roll an invisible bowling ball, then say it like a boom. "heh-KEE-lee!"
words.bonus: Hekili is thunder and uila is lightning.
words.picture: Giant named Keely bowling in the clouds
story_paragraphs: Ever wonder what thunder is? Up in the clouds there is a bowling alley for giants. And the best bowler up there is a giant named Keely.

Every time she steps up, her whole team yells "HEY, KEELY!" She rolls a ball the size of a house down a lane made of cloud. BOOOOOM. The pins crash. The whole sky rattles. Down below, dogs hide under beds and windows shake in their frames.
"HEY, KEELY!" Strike. BOOM. "HEY, KEELY!" BOOM. She bowls a perfect game, and all of Hilo is awake at 2 in the morning listening to every frame.
Hey, Keely. Hekili. The thunder.

words.say_it: Wipe drops off a windshield with your hand. "keh-HOW?"
words.picture: Staring at a dew covered car at 4 a.m.
story_paragraphs: Every night you park your car in the driveway. Every morning it is covered in tiny drops of water. Thousands of them. On the windshield, on the mirrors, on the hood. It did not rain. The ground is dry. The sky was clear all night.
You stand there in your slippahs with your coffee. "Oookaaay... HOW?"

So one night you stay up to watch. You sit in a lawn chair with a flashlight. Midnight, nothing. Two o'clock, nothing. Around 4 a.m. the air gets cool, and one by one, little drops just appear out of nowhere, like the car is sweating. "Kaaaay... HOW?"
You fall asleep in the chair. In the morning you are covered in drops too.
Kay, how. Kēhau. The dew. Stretch that ē like you're confused.

words.say_it: Pat your hair down in a panic. "NO-eh!"
words.bonus: The name Noelani means heavenly mist, noe plus lani.
words.picture: Prom hair poofing up in the mist
story_paragraphs: You spent two hours on your hair for prom. Perfect. Flat. Shiny. Not one hair out of place. You step outside.
The mist is waiting for you. Not rain. Just a soft, fine, floating mist, so light you can barely see it. It hangs in the air like a ghost of water. You take one step into it.
Your hair goes POOF. Twice as big. Then three times. "NO, EH!" You run back inside. Too late. You look like a dandelion. "NO! EHHHH!"
Your date shows up. Their hair is poofy too. Everybody at prom is poofy. The photographer says it's the best group photo he has ever taken.
No, eh. Noe. The mist.

words.say_it: Stick your hands out like you're blind. "OH-hoo?"
words.bonus: Noe is a fine mist. ʻOhu is fog, or a low cloud sitting on the mountain.
words.picture: Bumping into strangers in thick fog
story_paragraphs: You're driving up the mountain road at night and the fog rolls in so thick you can't see your own hood. You pull over and get out to look around. You can't see your own hands.
You walk forward with your arms out. You bump into something warm. Something with a face. First a little catch in your throat, then "OH! WHO?"

"Me," it says. It's your cousin. He got lost in the fog too. You walk together. You bump into another face. "OH! WHO?" It's a man selling boiled peanuts. Another bump. "OH! WHO?" A very confused nēnē. Then a lady walking her pig.
By the time the fog lifts, there are 12 of you standing in a clump on the side of the road, holding hands, all going "Oh. Who?"
Oh, who. ʻOhu. The fog.

words.say_it: Point at a sunbeam. "koo-KOO-nah."
words.bonus: Kukuna o ka lā means the rays of the sun.
words.picture: Caterpillar wrapped in a ray of light
story_paragraphs: In the garden a moth caterpillar is getting ready to change. Most of them make their cocoon out of silk. Not this one. This one waits for the morning sun and grabs a single ray of light shining through the leaves.
It wraps that golden ray around and around its body like tape. The light is warm and bright. When it's done, there is a glowing gold cocoon hanging from the branch like a little lantern.

Your little sister sees it and screams "Co-COON, ah! COCOON, AH!" Every neighbor comes to look. At night it lights up the whole yard. A week later a moth bursts out with shining gold wings, and a hundred little rays of light fly out with it.
Co-coon, ah. Kukuna. A ray of light.

words.say_it: Stretch, then grab your foot. "vah-nah-OW!"
words.bonus: Wanaʻao is the first light of dawn, before the sun is fully up.
words.picture: Stepping on a toy block at dawn
story_paragraphs: It's 5 in the morning. Pitch dark. Your dad shakes you awake and whispers "Wanna see the sunrise?"
You're half asleep. You say "Wanna..." and roll out of bed and stomp straight onto a toy block. First a gasp. Then "...OW!"
"Wanna... OW!" You hop down the hall. You bang your knee on the door. "OW!" You walk into the screen door. "OW!" You trip on the pile of slippahs by the step.

Then you get outside, and the whole sky over the mountain is turning pink and gold. The first light of the day. You forget all about your foot. You and Dad stand there in the cool air with your mouths open.
Wanna... OW. Wanaʻao. The dawn. The gasp before the ow is the ʻokina.

words.say_it: Flap your elbows and crow. "kah-kah-hee-AH-kah!"
words.bonus: Aloha kakahiaka means good morning.
words.picture: Rooster on a fence crowing "Kah-kah-hee-AH-kah!"
story_paragraphs: Your neighbor's rooster has one job. Crow in the morning. Every day at sunrise he climbs up on the fence, puffs out his chest, and gives it everything he's got.
But he doesn't do cock-a-doodle-doo. He never learned it. He does his own.
"KAH-KAH-HEE-AH-KAH!"

Every window on the street flies open. Dogs start howling. The garbage truck driver honks along. By the third crow the whole neighborhood is up, making coffee, grumbling, and saying it to each other over the fence like a greeting. "Kah-kah-hee-AH-kah." The rooster struts back and forth, very proud, until noon.
Kakahiaka. Morning.

words.say_it: Stretch and yawn big. "ah-vah-KEH-ah."
words.bonus: Twice a year in Hawaiʻi the noon sun is straight overhead and your shadow disappears. People call it Lāhainā Noon.
words.picture: Teenager waking up at noon with pineapple hair
story_paragraphs: Your teenage cousin is sleeping over. Morning comes. He sleeps. Breakfast comes. He sleeps. Somebody mows the lawn right outside his window. He sleeps. A marching band goes by. He sleeps.
At twelve noon, sun high in the sky, he walks out of the room with his hair sticking up like a pineapple and one sock on.
Your dad looks up from the table. "Oh. AWAKE, ah?"

Your cousin blinks. "Is it morning?" "It's NOON." "Awake, ah?" says Grandma. "Awake, ah?" says the neighbor through the window. Even the dog looks at him like "Awake, ah?" He eats breakfast for lunch.
Awake, ah. Awakea. Noon. The w can sound like a v too.

words.say_it: Slide your hand down in a slow arc. "ow-ee-nah-LAAH."
words.bonus: ʻAuina means to slope down, and lā is the sun. Aloha ʻauinalā means good afternoon.
words.picture: The sun sliding down a slide in the sky
story_paragraphs: Remember the singing sun from lā? By afternoon it gets bored of just hanging up there. So it climbs onto a giant slide made of sky and lets go.

It starts slow. It bumps over a cloud. "OW!" Then it picks up speed. "WHEEE!" Halfway down it grabs the edge because it doesn't want the day to end. "Nah..." Then it slips, and slides the rest of the way toward the ocean singing its long song. "LAAAAAH!"
"Ow! Whee! Nah... LAAAH!" All afternoon long the sun slides down the sky, the shadows stretch out long, and the heat goes soft and golden.
ʻAuinalā. The afternoon, when the sun slopes down. Hold that last ā like the sun's song.

words.say_it: Light two pretend torches, one after the other. "ah-hee-AH-hee."
words.bonus: Aloha ahiahi means good evening.
words.picture: Torch lighter running down the beach at sunset
story_paragraphs: It's evening at the beach. The sun just went down and the sky is purple. A guy with a long torch comes running down the sand to light the row of tiki torches, a hundred of them, all the way to the rocks.

Every time he lights one, the flame jumps up and the heat hits him in the face. "AH, HEAT!" Next torch. "AH, HEAT!" He goes faster and faster. "Ah, heat! Ah, heat! Ah, heat!" It turns into a song. The tourists start clapping to the beat. A little kid runs behind him doing it too.
By the last torch the whole beach is glowing orange, and a hundred little fires flicker in the dark.
Ah heat, ah heat. Ahiahi. It even looks like ahi, fire, twice.

words.say_it: Blow out a candle, slow and long. "POHHH."
words.bonus: In the Kumulipo, the Hawaiian chant of creation, life begins in pō, the deep darkness.
words.picture: Giant blowing out the sun like a candle
story_paragraphs: It's 7 p.m., the sun is still up, and the baby can't sleep. So a giant as tall as Diamond Head stomps down to the beach, leans over the ocean, and looks at the sun like it's a birthday candle.
He takes a huge breath. He blows. "POHHHHHHHHHH."

The sun goes out like a candle. A little puff of smoke curls up off the ocean. Everything goes dark. Deep, black, starry dark. The frogs start singing. The streetlights click on one by one. Somebody down the street yells "HEY! I was reading!"
The giant whispers "Good night," tiptoes off, and the baby is snoring before he gets home.
Pō. Night. Hold that ō long, like the giant's breath.

words.say_it: Stub your toe, then slump asleep. "ow-MO-eh."
words.bonus: Aumoe hides the word moe, to sleep. Midnight is sleeping time.
words.picture: Sleeping standing up at the fridge at midnight
story_paragraphs: It's midnight. The whole house is dark. You sneak into the kitchen for the last spam musubi in the fridge. On the way you stub your toe on the rice cooker. "OW!"

You grab the musubi. You take one bite. And the sleep hits you all at once, like a wave. Your eyes close. Your knees bend. You try to say "more," but it comes out "Mo... eh." You are asleep standing up, right there in front of the open fridge, holding the musubi.
"OW! Mo... eh."
In the morning Mom finds you curled up on the kitchen floor with rice on your face and the fridge still open. The musubi has one bite out of it.
Aumoe. Midnight. There is moe, sleep, hiding in it.

words.say_it: Point at a clock and holler. "HO-lah!"
words.bonus: ʻEhia ka hola? means what time is it?
words.picture: Grandpa's clock hollering every hour
story_paragraphs: Grandpa's old clock in the hallway doesn't ding and it doesn't bong. It hollers. Every hour, on the hour, a little door pops open, a tiny wooden man leans out and HOLLERS.
"HO-LAH!"

One o'clock, one holler. Two o'clock, two. At noon it's twelve in a row, "HO-LAH! HO-LAH! HO-LAH!", and the whole street sets their watches by it. Midnight is the worst. Twelve hollers in the dark, and the dog howls along with every one.
In Spanish, hola means hello, so visitors think the clock is being friendly. It isn't. It's telling you the hour.
Holler. Hola. The hour, the o'clock.

words.say_it: Punch in one minute on a pretend microwave. "mee-NOO-keh."
words.bonus: Minuke comes from the English word minute.
words.picture: Uncle microwaving a turkey one minute at a time
story_paragraphs: Uncle Wendell nukes everything in the microwave for exactly one minute. Leftover laulau? One minute. Cold coffee? One minute. His slippahs when they're wet? One minute. Beep beep beep.
Every time he reaches for the button, the whole family yells "ME! NUKE, EH?!" because they know what's coming, and he yells back "ONE MINUTE!"

One day he puts in a whole frozen turkey. One minute. It comes out still frozen solid. He puts it back in. "ONE MINUTE." Again. "ONE MINUTE." After 300 minutes, one at a time, the turkey is finally done and the whole house smells like Thanksgiving in June.
Me, nuke, eh. Minuke. A minute.

words.say_it: Stare at an empty cone. "keh-KO-nah."
words.bonus: Kekona comes from the English word second. Hawaiian has no s sound, so it changed to fit.
words.picture: Shave ice melting in one second
story_paragraphs: The hottest day of the year in Kona. You buy a rainbow shave ice, the biggest one, piled high on a paper cone.
You turn around. One second. The whole thing melts. One second, and it's a puddle of red and blue and yellow syrup on your slippahs, and you're holding an empty soggy paper cone.
"HECK! CONE, AH!"

You buy another one. One second. Melted. "HECK... CONE, AH!" A kid behind you starts timing it on his phone. One second, every time. The shave ice man gives up and starts handing them to you already in a cup with a straw.
Heck, cone, ah. Kekona. One second.

words.say_it: Tap your wrist where a watch goes. "mah-NAH-vah."
words.bonus: I kēlā me kēia manawa means all the time, at every moment.
words.picture: Kid fighting a giant hourglass at bedtime
story_paragraphs: Bedtime is 8 o'clock, and Ma has a timer. It's a giant hourglass the size of a refrigerator, standing in the middle of the living room. The sand is almost gone.

You beg. "Ma! NAH! WAIT!" She says time's up. You grab the hourglass and try to flip it over. It weighs 400 pounds. "Ma, NAH, WAIT!" You try to hold the sand up with your hand. It pours through your fingers.
The last grain drops with a tiny click. Ma points down the hall. You drag yourself to bed yelling "Ma, nah, wait!" the whole way, like there's any time left.
Ma, nah, wait. Manawa. Time.

words.say_it: Cry like a baby, one long note. "VAAAH."
words.bonus: I ka wā kahiko means in the old days, in ancient times.
words.picture: Baby crying through a whole season
story_paragraphs: When your baby cousin turned two, the family started calling it "the WAAAH era." For a whole season, from summer all the way to Christmas, he cried. At breakfast. "WAAAAH." At the beach. "WAAAAAH." At birthday parties, at the car wash, at graduations, at the zoo.
Every cry was long. Very long. Grandma timed one at four minutes. The family's whole history is split into two parts, before the waaah and after the waaah.
Then one day he stopped. Just like that. The era was over. Now he's 16, and at every party somebody still says "Remember the waaah?"
Wā. A period of time, an era, a season. Hold it long like the baby.

words.say_it: Hold out your hand for keys and squeal. "mah-kah-HEE-kee!"
words.bonus: Hauʻoli Makahiki Hou means Happy New Year. Makahiki is also the traditional season of harvest, games and peace in honor of Lono.
words.picture: Kid crossing off 365 days for the car keys
story_paragraphs: You are 15. Ma says you can have the car keys when you turn 16. One year. Exactly one year. So you make a calendar with 365 boxes and tape it to the fridge.
Every night you cross one off. Day 1. Day 90. Day 200. Rainy season, dry season, rainy again. You grow two inches. Your voice cracks. On day 364 you can't sleep.
Day 365. You run into the kitchen at 6 a.m. with your hand out. "MA! CAR!" You squeal. "HEEE!" Then, "KEY!" Ma hands them over. You're so excited you just keep saying it. "Ma! Car! HEE! KEY!"
Ma, car, hee, key. Makahiki. One whole year.

words.say_it: Hug yourself and shiver. "ho-oh-EE-lo."
words.bonus: The old Hawaiian year has two seasons, kau for the warm dry months and hoʻoilo for the cool wet ones.
words.picture: Islanders in parkas at 64 degrees
story_paragraphs: It's winter in Hawaiʻi. The temperature drops to 64 degrees. The whole island panics.

Your neighbor comes out in a parka, snow boots and earmuffs. Your uncle has three hoodies on and a beanie. The dog is wearing a sweater. Somebody at the bus stop is standing inside a sleeping bag with holes cut out for the arms. The rain has been coming down for a week, gray and steady.
The weatherman on TV is shivering. He points at the number and yells "HO! OH! EEE... it's LOW!"
The whole island says it together, teeth chattering. "Ho, oh, EEE, LOW!" Everybody makes chili. Somebody lights a fireplace they didn't know they had.
Ho, oh, ee, low. Hoʻoilo. The winter, the rainy season. The ʻokina is the shiver between ho and oh.

words.say_it: Laugh like a horse. "neh-hee-NAY!"
words.bonus: Nehinei is yesterday, i kēia lā is today, and ʻapōpō is tomorrow.
words.picture: Horse laughing about yesterday's lunch disaster
story_paragraphs: Yesterday you tripped in the school cafeteria and your whole plate lunch went flying. Mac salad on the principal. Rice in the fish tank. Gravy on the ceiling fan.

Today there is a horse outside your classroom window. Nobody knows whose horse it is. Every time you walk past, it looks right at you and laughs. "NEH-HEE-NAAAY!" It's laughing about yesterday. It saw the whole thing.
You try to explain. "That was YESTERDAY!" It does not care. "Neh-hee-NAAAY!" It follows you to the bus stop. "NEH-HEE-NAAAY!" It's still out there when you go to bed.
Neh, hee, nay. Nehinei. Yesterday. The horse will never let it go.

words.say_it: Stomp on pretend bubbles. "ah-poh-POH!"
words.bonus: Pair it with nehinei, yesterday. ʻApōpō is always one day away.
words.picture: Kids jumping on giant bubble wrap
story_paragraphs: A box shows up at your house. Inside is a sheet of bubble wrap as big as a football field. Every kid on the street comes running.
Ma says "Not today. Tomorrow."
So everybody waits. Nobody sleeps. Twelve kids lie on the lawn all night staring at the bubble wrap in the moonlight. At sunrise Ma opens the door and nods. You all jump on it at once.
"AH! POP! POP!" You're so excited there's a little gulp before every "ah." "(gulp) AH! POPPP! POPPP!" It sounds like fireworks. The neighbors think it's New Year's.
Halfway through, Ma yells "Save the rest for tomorrow!" Everybody groans.
Ah, pop, pop. ʻApōpō. Tomorrow. Hold the pops long.

words.say_it: Scream high, then call a dog. "eee-LEE-oh!"
words.bonus: Take off the ʻī and you get lio, the horse. ʻĪlio is the dog.
words.picture: Tiny dog dragging a whole kālua pig
story_paragraphs: Leo is a tiny dog. He weighs 4 pounds. At the family lūʻau, while everybody is dancing, he slips into the kitchen and comes out dragging the whole kālua pig. It's 30 times bigger than him. He's walking backward, pulling it with his teeth, tail going crazy.
Aunty sees him. She screams so high the glasses on the table crack. "EEEEEE! LEO!"

He keeps pulling. "EEEEEE! LEO!" He gets it all the way under the house. Twenty people crawl under after him with flashlights. They find him lying on top of the pig, belly round as a ball, sound asleep.
Eee, Leo. ʻĪlio. The dog. Hold that ī long, like Aunty's scream.

words.say_it: Poke the air with one finger. "poh-PO-kee."
words.bonus: Pōpoki is the cat and ʻīlio is the dog.
words.picture: Cat poking your face before sunrise
story_paragraphs: Your cat wants breakfast. It's half past four in the morning. She climbs onto your chest, sits on your face, and starts poking.
Poke. Your cheek. Poke. Your eyelid. Poke. Up your nose. Soft paw, tiny claws, zero mercy. You pull the blanket over your head. She pokes through the blanket.
"Pohhh... POKEY!" you groan. "Stop being so POKEY!"

She keeps going. Poke, poke, poke. Fifteen minutes later she knocks your phone off the table. Five minutes after that she pokes your ear so hard you sit straight up. One minute later she is eating breakfast, purring, and you are awake forever.
Pohhh, pokey. Pōpoki. The cat. Hold that first ō like a long sleepy groan.

words.say_it: Gallop in place. "LEE-oh!"
words.bonus: A paniolo is a Hawaiian cowboy, and paniolo ride lio.
words.picture: Horse named Leo pretending to be a lion
story_paragraphs: Leo is a horse. A huge one. Brown, shiny, 2,000 pounds. But Leo thinks he is a lion.

He lies in the sun on the ranch in Waimea with his mane all fluffed out. He practices roaring. It comes out "NEIGH-RRRR." He tries to sneak up on the chickens through the tall grass. He is eight feet tall. They see him coming from a mile away and don't even stop pecking.
The paniolo just call him by name. "LEO! Come!" And he trots over proud, mane blowing in the wind, sure he's the king of the jungle. There is no jungle. There is a pasture. He is a horse.
Leo. Lio. The horse. Not the tiny dog from ʻīlio, the big one.

words.say_it: Make goat horns with your fingers. "KOW."
words.bonus: The real cow is pipi, which also means beef.
words.picture: Goat on a truck roof insisting it's a cow
story_paragraphs: There is a goat on the roof of your truck. Nobody knows how it got up there. It is standing on the very top, looking down at everybody, chewing on your windshield wiper.
You tell it to get down. It looks you right in the eye and says, very clearly, "COW."

"You're a goat." "COW." You show it a picture of a cow on your phone. It licks the phone. "COW." A real cow walks by. The goat looks at the cow. The cow looks at the goat. The goat says "COW." The cow walks away very confused.
The goat is still up there. It ate the antenna. It is now wearing your sun shade like a cape.
Cow. Kao. It sounds like cow, but it's the goat.

words.say_it: Stack your hands one on top of the other. "HEE-pah."
words.bonus: Hipa comes from the English word sheep.
words.picture: Heap of sheep piled on your car
story_paragraphs: You come out in the morning and your car is gone. In its place there is a heap. A heap of sheep. Forty sheep piled on top of each other in the shape of a car, fluffy, warm and chewing.
"HEAP, AH!" you yell. Forty heads turn and look at you.

Somewhere under there is your car. You can see one side mirror sticking out of the wool. You start digging. More sheep. "HEAP, AH!" Every sheep you pull off, another one climbs back on. They like it up there. The hood is warm from the sun.
You take the bus to work. When you come home, the heap is on your couch watching TV.
Heap, ah. Hipa. The sheep.

words.say_it: Flap your arms like wings. "MAH-noo."
words.bonus: Manu is also the name for the carved end pieces at the front and back of a canoe.
words.picture: Ma's new hat flies off, it was a bird
story_paragraphs: Ma buys a new hat for the big party. It's gorgeous. Round, feathery, bright green and yellow, with a little beak on the front. Wait.
At the party everybody compliments her. "Ma, NEW hat?" "Ooh, Ma, NEW!" She beams and turns her head so everybody can see.

Then, in the middle of the speeches, the hat stands up. It stretches its wings. It flies off her head, lands in the mango tree, and starts to sing. It was a bird the whole time. It just liked sitting on her head.
The whole party stares. Ma, very calm, pats her hair down. "Yes. New."
Ma, new. Manu. The bird.

words.say_it: Shake your head slow and honk. "nehh-NEHH."
words.bonus: The nēnē is Hawaiʻi's state bird. Slow down for them on the road.
words.picture: Goose stopping 50 cars with "nay nay"
story_paragraphs: You're driving slow through the national park, and a goose is standing in the middle of the road. Gray and brown, stripes down its neck, little black face. It doesn't move. You roll forward one inch. It shakes its head.
"NEHHH-NEHHH." Like, "Nay, nay." No. Not today.

You wait. Another car pulls up behind you. The goose gives them a look too. "NEHHH-NEHHH." A tour bus comes. A motorcycle. A guy on a bike. By the time the goose decides to cross, there's a line of 50 cars, and it walks across the road like a queen, one flat foot at a time, not hurrying at all.
Nay, nay. Nēnē. Stretch both ē's, like the goose.

words.say_it: Swoop your hand down fast. "poo-EH-oh."
words.bonus: For some Hawaiian families the pueo is an ʻaumakua, a family guardian, and it is treated with deep respect.
words.picture: Owl diving in daylight, uncle saying "Oh."
story_paragraphs: Sunny afternoon in an open field upcountry. A little mouse is sitting in the grass eating a crumb of malasada it found. Feeling good. No worries.
Most owls hunt at night. Not this one. High above, a brown and white owl hangs in the wind with big yellow eyes, perfectly still. Then it folds its wings and drops.
"PEW!"
Like a laser. The grass shakes. The mouse is gone. The owl is already gliding away low over the field.
Your uncle, sitting on the fence with his lunch, looks at the empty spot. "Eh?" Then he looks up and sees it. "...OH."
Pew, eh, oh. Pueo. Hawaiʻi's own owl, hunting in broad daylight.

words.say_it: Snatch something out of the air. "EE-vah!"
words.bonus: Because this bird steals fish from other birds, ʻiwa is also used to mean a thief.
words.picture: Diva frigatebird stealing a fish midair
story_paragraphs: Out over the ocean, a big black seabird with long pointy wings and a forked tail glides around like she owns the sky. Her name is Eva. She is a diva.

Eva can catch her own fish, but why bother? Eva waits. When a smaller bird catches a fish, Eva dives at it, chases it, tugs its tail, until it drops the fish. Then she snatches the fish out of the air before it hits the water. She doesn't even get her feet wet.
Every bird on the beach screams at her. "EEE! EVA!" She doesn't care. She tilts her long wings and floats away with lunch, not flapping once.
Eee, Eva. ʻIwa. The frigatebird, the best thief in the sky.

words.say_it: Squeak like a rusty hinge. "ee-EE-vee."
words.bonus: The ʻiʻiwi's red feathers were used in featherwork like capes and cloaks for aliʻi. Don't mix it up with ʻiwa, the frigatebird.
words.picture: Red bird squeaking back at a screen door
story_paragraphs: Great aunty's house up in the rainforest has a rusty screen door. Every time it opens, it squeaks. "Ee... EEE-vee."

One morning a small bright red bird lands on the gate. Red like a fire truck, black wings, and a long curved orange beak like a hook. It looks at the screen door. Aunty opens it. "Ee... EEE-vee." The bird opens its beak and answers with the exact same squeak. "Ee... EEE-vee."
Now they talk every day. Door squeaks. Bird squeaks. Door. Bird. Aunty names the bird Evie. "Eee, EVIE!" she says when it shows up. She refuses to ever oil that door again.
Eee, Evie. ʻIʻiwi. The scarlet honeycreeper. The squeak in the middle is the ʻokina.

words.say_it: Wave your arms like a car alarm going off. "ah-lah-LAAAH!"
words.bonus: The ʻalalā is one of the rarest birds on earth. Conservation programs are working to bring it back to Hawaiʻi's forests.
words.picture: Crow copying car alarms on a wire
story_paragraphs: Every car on the street has an alarm, and there is a big black crow sitting on the telephone wire listening to all of them.

One morning it starts copying. "Uh-la-LAAAAH! Uh-la-LAAAAH!" A perfect car alarm. Everybody runs outside in their pajamas to check their cars. Nothing wrong. They go back in. "UH-LA-LAAAAH!" Everybody runs out again.
It's the crow. A smart, loud, show-off crow. By lunch it can also do the ice cream truck, a rooster and your mom calling you for dinner.
"Is that an ALARM?" "No. It's the crow." "Uh-la-LAAAAAH!"
Uh-la-LAAAH. ʻAlalā. The Hawaiian crow. Hold that last ā like the alarm.

words.say_it: Waddle and burp. "ko-LO-ah!"
words.bonus: The koloa maoli is the native Hawaiian duck.
words.picture: Duck burping after drinking two liters of cola
story_paragraphs: At the family picnic somebody leaves a two liter bottle of cola open on the grass. A little brown duck waddles over, sticks its bill in and drinks the whole thing. Glug glug glug. Two liters. The duck is about the size of the bottle.
It sits back. Its eyes go wide. It shakes. Then it lets out a burp so big the paper plates blow off the table. "CO-LOOOAH!"
It waddles around the picnic burping. "Co-LOAH!" Each one bigger than the last. The kids are rolling on the grass laughing. The duck jumps into the pond and burps a bubble the size of a beach ball.
Cola. Koloa. The duck.

words.say_it: Swoop your hand down and grab. "EE-oh!"
words.bonus: The ʻio lives only on Hawaiʻi Island and was seen as a symbol of royalty.
words.picture: Hawk stealing the singing farmer's hat
story_paragraphs: An old farmer is out in his field singing the farm song. "Old farmer had a farm, EE-I-EE-I-OH." He has a big straw hat on and a chicken under each arm.
High above him, a brown hawk circles. Slow. Patient. Waiting for the right moment.
The farmer gets to the end of the song. "EE-I-EE-I..." On the last "EE" the hawk dives and snatches the straw hat right off his head. "...OH!"
"EE... OH!" The hawk flies up to the top of a tall tree and sits there wearing the hat. The chickens are fine. The farmer is bald, sunburned and still singing. "EE... OH!"
Ee, oh. ʻIo. The hawk. A little catch before the ee.

words.say_it: Wave at the sky like Aunty. "Kooooh-leh-ah."
words.bonus: Kōlea fly between Alaska and Hawaiʻi every year, arriving around August and leaving around April.
words.picture: Aunty waving at a fat golden bird
story_paragraphs: Every August a small golden bird lands on the exact same patch of grass in Aunty Momi's front yard. Same patch. Same bird. He just flew nonstop from Alaska, about 3,000 miles, and he looks skinny and tired, like he drove all night.

Aunty has been waiting in her folding chair since 5 in the morning. She named him Cole. When he lands she jumps up and yells "Coooooole! Eh! Ah!" She holds that first sound so long the neighbors come out to check on her.

All winter Cole walks around her yard, bobbing his head and eating bugs. By April he is so fat he looks like a golf ball with legs. Then one morning he is gone, back to Alaska. Aunty sits in her chair and waves at the sky anyway.

words.say_it: Swing an invisible towel to the side. "Ee-OH-leh!"
words.bonus: Do not skip the ʻokina at the front. ʻIole is the rat. Say the little catch before the ee.
words.picture: Grandma bullfighting a giant rat
story_paragraphs: It is midnight and you go to the kitchen for leftover rice. You flip on the light. In the middle of the floor is a rat the size of a corgi, holding a whole spam musubi in its little hands.
It sees you. It drops the musubi. It lowers its head and scrapes the floor with one foot like a bull.

Before you can run, Grandma bursts in with a red dish towel. She plants her feet and holds the towel out to the side. The rat charges. Grandma swings the towel away at the last second and screams "Eeeee! OLÉ!" The rat shoots past her, slides across the floor and bonks into the rice cooker.
It charges again. "Eee! OLÉ!" Nine times. Three little mice cheer from the doorway. Finally the rat gets dizzy, bows, and leaves through the cat door with the musubi.

words.say_it: Gulp, then say it with a catch in the middle. "MO-ʻoh."
words.bonus: Moʻo as succession hides inside moʻolelo (a story passed along) and moʻokūʻauhau (genealogy).
words.picture: Line of lizards ending in a dragon
story_paragraphs: A tiny gecko sits on your bedroom wall. You point and say "Mo." You don't know why. It just looks like a Mo.

Then you notice a bigger lizard behind it. And a bigger one behind that. They go out your window in a line, each one bigger than the last, like a family photo. A cat-sized lizard. A dog-sized lizard. One as long as a canoe.
You follow the line out into the yard. At the very end, lying on the lawn and crushing the mango tree, is a dragon the size of a city bus. It blinks one yellow eye at you.
You gulp so hard your throat clicks. "Mo... ʻoh!"
A lizard, a dragon, and a whole succession of them lined up in a row. That is moʻo.

words.say_it: Duck under an invisible slippah. "NAH-lo."
words.bonus: Nalo also means to vanish or be lost, which is what every fly does the second you swing. Nalo meli is the honeybee.
words.picture: Uncle swinging slippah at giant fly
story_paragraphs: Family beach potluck. Forty people. One fly. But this fly is the size of a guava and it has a plan.
It lands on the potato mac salad. Uncle Kimo raises his slippah high over his head and swings. The fly just says "Nah... LOW!" and dives under the table.
Uncle ducks under the table and swings low. The fly zips up to the tent roof, waits, then dives again. "Nah, LOW!" It lands in the chili. Uncle smashes the chili. Chili everywhere. Aunties screaming.

After twenty minutes Uncle is covered in mac salad and the fly is sitting on his forehead, rubbing its little hands together. He swings one last time and smacks himself. The fly is gone. Nobody ever sees it again.

words.say_it: Blow an invisible whistle. "Now-NOW!"
words.picture: Ant sergeant stealing spam musubi
story_paragraphs: You drop one grain of rice on the kitchen counter. Just one.

Four seconds later a single ant marches out of the crack by the sink. He wears a tiny sergeant hat and has a whistle. He looks at the grain. Then he looks at your whole spam musubi sitting on the plate. He blows the whistle and screams "NOW! NOW! NOW!"

Out of every crack in the house pour 4,000 ants in perfect lines. They lift the musubi over their heads like a float in a parade and carry it across the counter, down the cabinet, across the floor and under the door. "Now! Now! Now!" You can hear the sergeant the whole way.
Nine seconds. The plate is empty. The grain of rice is still there. They left it for you.

words.say_it: Point at your arm and yell for Mom. "Mah-KEE-kah!"
words.bonus: Mosquitoes were not in Hawaiʻi until a ship brought them to Lahaina in 1826.
words.picture: Mom spin kicking a giant mosquito
story_paragraphs: Backyard party at dusk. The sun goes down and here it comes. A mosquito the size of a hummingbird, with a nose like a drinking straw and a tiny napkin tucked under its chin.
It lands on your arm and starts slurping like it is finishing a smoothie. You freeze. You can't slap it. It's too big. You scream across the yard "MA! KICK-ah! KICK-AH!"

Your mom puts down her paper plate. She runs across the grass in her muʻumuʻu, jumps off the cooler, and does a flying spin kick. The mosquito sails over the fence, over the neighbor's roof and lands somewhere near Pearl City.
Everyone claps. Ma picks up her plate and goes back for more teriyaki. You have a bump on your arm the size of a malasada.

words.say_it: Flap your arms slowly, then fast. "Poo-leh-leh-HOO-ah."
words.bonus: The Kamehameha butterfly, a pulelehua found only in Hawaiʻi, is the state insect. Lele, to fly, is hiding in the middle of the word.
words.picture: Giant butterfly sunbathing by hotel pool
story_paragraphs: At the hotel pool, a butterfly with wings as big as beach towels is lying on a lounge chair. Orange and black wings, spread out flat, catching sun. It has on tiny sunglasses.
The lifeguard walks over. "Excuse me, is this your chair?" The butterfly points one leg at the water and says "Pool." Then it points at the chair. "Lay. Lay." It lies back down.

It lays there all morning. It lays there all afternoon. Kids float by and stare. Then at exactly 3 o'clock it sits up, flaps once, blows every umbrella into the pool, and yells "HOO-AH!" It flies off over Waikīkī with a pink noodle float stuck on one leg.
Pool, lay, lay, HOO-ah. That is the whole butterfly routine, every single day.

words.say_it: Wiggle your fingers like spider legs and tease. "Nah-nah-NAH-nah."
words.bonus: Another word for spider is lanalana.
words.picture: Spider taunting you from its web
story_paragraphs: You walk into the garage with a broom. In the corner, in a web as big as a garage door, sits a spider. Eight legs. A tiny slippah on every one.

You swing the broom. The spider hops left. You swing again. It hops right. Then it sticks out its tongue, wiggles all eight legs at you and sings "Nah-nah-NAH-nah! Nah-nah-NAH-nah!" Two legs wiggle for every nah. It keeps perfect count.
You swing for ten minutes. You knock down the fishing poles, the Christmas box and Dad's old surfboard. The spider never stops singing.
When you finally give up and sit on a bucket, it drops down on a thread, pats you on the head with one leg and climbs back up. "Nah-nah-NAH-nah." It still lives there. It pays no rent.

words.say_it: Point up in terror and hold the last sound. "Kah-nah-PEEEE!"
words.bonus: Kanapī bites really hurt, so locals shake out their shoes and slippahs before putting them on.
words.picture: Six foot centipede in beach canopy
story_paragraphs: You are camping at the beach under a blue canopy tent. Uncle Keoni is asleep in his chair with his mouth open.
Something moves in the fold of the canopy right over his head. It is a centipede. Not a normal one. This one is six feet long, dark red, with dozens of legs clicking like tiny typewriters.
You try to warn him but you are so scared you can't say the word right. You point up and squeak "Can-a... PEEEEEEE!" The last part comes out long and high like a tea kettle.

Uncle opens one eye. Looks up. The centipede looks down. Uncle goes straight up out of the chair, leaves his slippahs on the sand, and lands in the ocean forty feet away. He stays out there until sunrise.

words.say_it: Grab your knee and hop. "ʻOooo-HEE-nee!"
words.picture: Grasshopper kicking Uncle in the knee
story_paragraphs: Uncle Bert is walking through a field of tall grass to get to the beach, in short pants. From the grass, a grasshopper watches him. It is green, it is the size of a surfboard, and its back legs are folded up like two giant springs.
Uncle gets closer. Closer. He is humming. The grasshopper does not like humming.

It turns around and kicks with both back legs. BOOM. It gets Uncle square in the knee. He stops. He gulps. His face goes through six colors. Then he hops on one foot in a circle howling "ʻOoooooooo! HEE... KNEE! OOOOO, HEE-KNEE!"
The grasshopper springs off over the trees and lands three streets away on somebody's car. Uncle ices his knee for a week. Now he takes the long way to the beach.

words.say_it: Hold out your palm like a toll booth. "Oh-peh-ah-PEH-ah!"
words.bonus: The Hawaiian hoary bat is the only native land mammal in Hawaiʻi and the official state land mammal.
words.picture: Tiny bat collecting mosquito tolls
story_paragraphs: Late at night you drive over the old bridge in Hilo. There is a new toll booth that was not there this morning. Hanging upside down inside it is a tiny fuzzy bat, gray and brown with frosty tips like a coffee drink, wearing a little visor.
You roll down the window. The bat squeaks "Ohhhh! Pay-ʻah! PAY-ʻah!" You say you have no money. It points one tiny wing at the mosquito buzzing around your head.
Oh. It wants mosquitoes.

You catch one and hand it over. The bat gulps it, stamps your hand with a little bat stamp and flips the gate up. "Pay-ʻah!" it squeaks at the next car. By morning there is not one mosquito left in Hilo, and that bat is the richest thing on the island.

words.say_it: Point at an imaginary shiny shell. "HO-noo!"
words.bonus: Honu ʻea is the hawksbill turtle. Give resting honu at least 10 feet of space.
words.picture: Sea turtle with price tag on new shell
story_paragraphs: You are on the beach at sunset when a green sea turtle hauls itself out of the water. Big one, four feet long, older than your grandpa.
But something is different. Its shell is shiny. Too shiny. It still has the sticker on it. A price tag flapping in the wind, $49.99, and a little sign that says NEW.
The old lifeguard, who has been sitting in his tower since 1987, sits up and yells "HO! NEW!" The turtle turns its head slowly, blinks at him, and very slowly nods. It is proud.
Everyone comes to look, from a respectful distance. The turtle poses. It turns left. It turns right. Then it falls asleep on the warm sand, snoring, while the price tag flaps.

words.say_it: Throw your hands up and hold the last sound. "Mah-NOOOH!"
words.bonus: Some Hawaiian families honor the manō as an ʻaumakua, a family guardian.
words.picture: Shark with bib circling pizza float
story_paragraphs: You are floating off Waikīkī on an inflatable pizza slice. Sun is out. Life is good. You have a juice box.
Then a gray fin cuts past. It circles once. It circles twice. Then a shark pokes its head up next to your pizza. It is wearing a bib. It has a fork in one fin and a knife in the other.
It looks at the pizza. It looks at you. It licks its lips.

You yell "Man... NOOOOOOOOO!" and you hold that no so long that you paddle all the way back to shore with your hands and it is still going. The lifeguard hears it. The hotels hear it. Ships in the harbor hear it.
The shark shrugs, takes one bite out of the pepperoni corner and swims away happy.

words.say_it: Put your hand on your chest like an opera singer. "Ko-ho-LAAAH!"
words.bonus: Koholā come to Hawaiʻi every winter, from about December to April, to have their babies.
words.picture: Humpback singing opera beside kayak
story_paragraphs: You are kayaking off Maui in February. The water is flat and quiet. Then the kayak starts to shake.
Right next to you, a humpback whale rises up. It is 45 feet long. It has barnacles on its chin like a beard. It looks you in the eye, opens its huge mouth, and starts to sing.
"Ko... ho... LAAAAAAAAAAAAAH!"
It holds that last note for twenty minutes. Your kayak buzzes. Your teeth buzz. Fish float up to see what is going on. Somewhere on Lānaʻi a dog starts howling along.
When the whale finally runs out of air, it slaps its giant tail on the water, soaks you from head to toe, and dives. You sit there dripping, clapping, alone in the quiet.

words.sound_hook: NIGH-ʻah! (a teasing nyah with a hiccup)
words.say_it: Spin halfway around, then tease. "NAI-ʻah!"
words.bonus: Mahimahi is sometimes called dolphinfish, but it is a fish, not a naiʻa.
words.picture: Spinning dolphin teasing you from water
story_paragraphs: You are on a tour boat off the Waiʻanae coast. Somebody yells and a whole pod of spinner dolphins shows up. Two hundred of them.

One gray dolphin with a smile on its face shoots out of the water and spins in the air. Once, twice, seven times. It splashes down, pops up next to the boat, looks right at you and sticks out its tongue. "NIGH... ʻah!" A teasing little noise with a hiccup in the middle.
You try to spin on the deck. You make it halfway around and fall into the ice chest.

"NIGH-ʻah!" says the dolphin. It spins eleven times this time. The others join in. "NIGH-ʻah! NIGH-ʻah!" Two hundred dolphins laughing at you in perfect circles while you sit in the ice with a soda can stuck to your leg.

words.say_it: Say it in slow chunks, then fast. "Ee-lee-oh ho-lo-ee kah-oo-ah-OO-ah."
words.bonus: Built from ʻīlio (dog), holo (run), i ka (in the) and uaua (rough). Monk seals live only in Hawaiʻi and are endangered, so stay about 50 feet away.
words.picture: Monk seal plowing into rough wave
story_paragraphs: Early morning at the beach. From way up the sand you see a big gray dog asleep by the water. Seven feet long, whiskers, flippers, and it smells like a fish market. You whisper "Eee... LEO?" because it looks like a Leo.
It opens one black eye. Not a dog. A Hawaiian monk seal, and it is not interested in you.

It humps down the sand toward the sea like a giant rolling sleeping bag. Your little brother cheers it on like a cowboy. "HOLO-EE! HOLO-EE!" It hits the biggest, roughest wave of the morning. KAOW! The spray blasts all the way up the beach and soaks you both. "OW-ah! Cold!"
The seal pops up past the break, totally happy in the rough water, and looks back at you like a wet puppy.
Ee-Leo, holo-ee, KAOW, OW-ah. The dog that runs in rough seas.

words.say_it: Crunch your teeth together, then hoot. "OO-hoo!"
words.bonus: Uhu really do grind up coral and poop out sand. A lot of the white sand on Hawaiʻi beaches went through a parrotfish first.
words.picture: Parrotfish pooping white sand
story_paragraphs: You are snorkeling at the reef. A fish swims up, bright blue and green and pink, like somebody spilled a whole box of crayons. Its mouth looks like a parrot beak made of teeth.
It bites the coral. CRUNCH. It bites again. CRUNCH CRUNCH. It sounds like a kid chewing ice.
You think, ooh. Nice fish.

Then the fish stops, lifts its tail, and out the back end pours a long cloud of fine white sand. It just keeps coming. A whole bucket's worth. You yell through your snorkel "Ooh... HOO!" and bubbles go everywhere.
You look at the beach. You look at your towel lying on the white sand. You look at the fish. The fish winks.

words.say_it: Coo like a pigeon, then moo like a cow. "Koo-MOO!"
words.bonus: Other goatfish in Hawaiʻi include weke and moano.
words.picture: Red goatfish cooing and mooing on ice
story_paragraphs: You are at the fish market and a red goatfish on the ice is having a crisis. It has two long whiskers under its chin, like a little goat beard. Everybody keeps calling it a goat. It has had enough.
It sits up on the ice and tries to figure out what animal it really is. First it tries being a pigeon. "Kooooooo." No. It tries being a cow. "MOOOOOOO." Better.
It puts them together. "Kooooooo... MOOOOOOO!" Both sounds long, like it is holding them for a contest.

The fish guy drops his scale. An aunty buying ʻahi faints into the tako. And out in the parking lot, a real cow in the back of a truck lifts its head and moos back. The goatfish smiles. It has found its people.

words.say_it: Point at the fish twice. "Mah-hee-MAH-hee!"
words.bonus: Mahi means strong, and one popular explanation is that doubling it makes mahimahi extra strong. Just ask Kai.
words.picture: Glowing green fish landing on cousin
story_paragraphs: You are on a fishing boat with your little cousin Kai. Something hits the line so hard the pole bends into a U. Kai grabs the pole and gets yanked off his feet.
Out of the water jumps a fish, four feet long, glowing electric green and gold, with a big square forehead like a bulldozer. It flips once and lands right in the boat. Right on Kai.
Kai is pinned. He can barely breathe. He can only point at the fish and scream for his mom, one word at a time. "MA! HE! MA! HE!" Meaning, Ma, he is on me, he is huge, help.
Ma walks over, lifts the fish off Kai with one arm, and says "Dinner." Kai lies on the deck whispering "Ma... he... ma... he..." all the way back to the harbor.

words.say_it: Crank an invisible reel with both hands. "Oo-LOO-ah!"
words.bonus: A young ulua is called a pāpio.
words.picture: Uncle dragged across rocks by ulua
story_paragraphs: It is 2 in the morning on the lava rocks. Uncle Sonny has three fishing poles jammed into the cracks, each one with a little bell on the tip. He has been out here four nights in a row. He has one bag of chips left.
Then the middle bell goes crazy. DING DING DING DING.

Uncle grabs the pole. Something huge and silver takes off toward Molokaʻi. It is an ulua, 110 pounds, with a head like a cinder block and the attitude of a nightclub bouncer. It drags Uncle across the rocks, through a tide pool and halfway into his own cooler.
Uncle does not let go. He yells at the sea "OOOH! LURE-ah! You like my LURE-ah? Come get um!" After forty minutes he pulls it up onto the rocks. He sits down next to it and they both breathe hard.

words.say_it: Say it with a hiccup in the middle. "Oh-ʻOH-poo."
words.bonus: Some ʻoʻopu really do climb waterfalls hundreds of feet high, using a sucker made from their belly fins.
words.picture: Tiny fish climbing waterfall with bird poop
story_paragraphs: You are hiking in a valley on Kauaʻi and you stop at a waterfall 300 feet tall. On the wet black rock, halfway up, is a tiny fish. It is climbing. A fish. Climbing.
It sticks onto the rock with a little cup under its belly, wiggles up one inch, sticks on again. One inch. Another inch. It has been doing this for eleven days.
Then a bird flies over and drops a big white splat right on its head.
The fish stops. It says "Uh... ʻOH." A little catch in the throat. "Poo."

Then it keeps climbing. It doesn't wipe it off. It doesn't complain. Nothing in the world is going to stop this fish. You stand at the bottom clapping as it flops over the top of the waterfall like it just won a marathon.

words.say_it: Hold out an invisible twenty dollar bill. "Oh-PEH-loo!"
words.bonus: ʻŌpelu is a local favorite, fried whole or dried in the sun.
words.picture: Chanting fish covering your porch
story_paragraphs: Last month you borrowed twenty dollars from Uncle Lou, the fisherman down the road. You forgot. Uncle Lou did not forget.

Saturday morning you open your front door and the whole porch is moving. It is covered in ʻōpelu, thousands of them, silver and blue and slim as hot dogs, flipping and flopping all the way down the driveway and into the street.
They are chanting. Every single fish. "Ohhhhhhh... pay LOU! Ohhhhhhh... pay LOU!" The ohhh part is long and spooky, like ghosts. The pay Lou part is sharp.

The neighbors come out in their pajamas. The mailman won't come up the walk. You find a twenty in the couch cushions and throw it out the window. The fish cheer and flop back to the ocean. That night Uncle Lou fries six of them for your dinner anyway.

words.say_it: Grab your toe and hiccup. "Ah-ʻAH-mah!"
words.bonus: Don't mix it up with ʻaʻā, the rough, jagged lava these crabs run across.
words.picture: Black crab pinching Mom's toe
story_paragraphs: Low tide at the lava rocks. You and your mom are looking in tide pools. The rocks are covered in black crabs, hundreds of them, flat and shiny, with little eyes on stalks. The second you move they all run sideways at once, like a black carpet sliding off the rock.
Your mom leans over to look closer. One crab does not run. It is the biggest one. It walks right up to her toe, looks up, and pinches.
"AH!" she yells. Then she hiccups from the shock. "ʻAH!" Then she screams for her own mother. "MAAAAA!"
Ah, ʻah, Maaa. The crab lets go, runs sideways at about forty miles an hour and disappears into a crack. Then all the other crabs come back out to see if she is okay.

words.say_it: Hold your arms out for a hug, then pull back fast. "VAH-nah?"
words.bonus: People eat the orange insides of some wana raw, like uni.
words.picture: Spiky purple urchin chasing for hugs
story_paragraphs: You are wading on the reef in reef shoes. Down between two rocks sits a sea urchin, a round purple ball covered in 300 long black spines. Each spine is as sharp as a sewing needle.
It sees you. It slowly spreads out all its spines like a hundred little arms and says in a sweet voice "Wanna? Wanna hug?"
You say no. You step back. It rolls closer. "Wanna? Wanna hug?"

You run. It rolls after you across the reef, bouncing off rocks like a spiky soccer ball, still asking "WANNA? WANNA?" You jump onto your big brother's shoulders. It sits at his feet, spines out, waiting. He does not want a hug either. You both stand there until the tide comes in and floats it away, still asking.

words.say_it: Pretend to lick a lollipop, then make a face. "LO-lee."
words.bonus: Loli also means to change. Hoʻololi means to change something.
words.picture: Sea cucumber spraying cousin's face
story_paragraphs: Your five year old cousin is poking around the tide pools and finds a sea cucumber. It is brown, squishy, about as long as a loaf of bread, and lying there doing absolutely nothing.
She thinks it is candy. "LOLLY!" she screams. "A giant LOLLY!"
She picks it up with both hands. It feels like a warm water balloon. She opens her mouth wide for a big lick.

The sea cucumber does not want to be a lolly. It squeezes itself and shoots a spray of sticky white strings right in her face. Her hair, her eyebrows, her sunglasses. She looks like a spider web with legs.
She gently puts it back in the water. She stands there dripping. Then she says, very quietly, "Worst lolly ever."

words.say_it: Knock on the table like it is a hollow log. "Ho-lo-ho-LO-nah."
words.bonus: You can hear holo, to run or go, inside it. Holoholo, a word you hear all the time here, means to go out for fun.
words.picture: Animals pouring out of a hollow log
story_paragraphs: At the end of the park there is a giant hollow log with a sign nailed on it. HOLLOW HOLLOW LOANER. Animals for borrow. Bring back by 5.
You knock. An aunty with reading glasses pops her head out of the log like a librarian. "Hollow, hollow... LOAN-ah?" You nod.

She stamps your card and starts pulling animals out of the log one by one. A goat. A pig. Twelve chickens. A horse, somehow. A mongoose. A donkey that has to back out slowly. They keep coming. The log is only nine feet long.
You walk home with 27 animals following you in a line down the street. At one minute to 5 you bring them all back. Aunty counts them. "Twenty-six." You look down. The mongoose is in your backpack.

words.say_it: Sing a long note, then rub your head. "Laaah-ʻOW."
words.bonus: Lāʻau lapaʻau is traditional Hawaiian plant medicine.
words.picture: Stick bonks singer, Tūtū heals bump
story_paragraphs: You are lying under the big tree in Tūtū's yard, singing to yourself. "Laaaaaaaaaa..." A long, lazy note.
The tree does not like your singing. Crack. A stick drops forty feet and bonks you right on top of the head. Your song stops with a hiccup. "Laaaaaaa... ʻOW!"

Tūtū walks out. She looks at the tree. She looks at the stick. She looks at the bump rising on your head like a baking bun. She pulls a few leaves off a plant by the steps, crushes them in her hand, and presses them on the bump. It stops hurting right away.
So in one minute you met all three. The tree. The stick. The medicine. Laaaa... ʻow.

words.say_it: Sniff the air, then smile. "POO-ah."
words.bonus: Pua also means to bloom or come out, and it can mean children or descendants, the flowers of a family.
words.picture: Baby with plumeria in her headband
story_paragraphs: Your aunty hands you her new baby for five minutes and runs to the store. The baby is chubby, smiling, and the pride of the whole family. Everybody calls her a pua.
Four minutes in you smell something. You sniff the air. You sniff the baby. You make a face and say "Poo?"
You lift her up to check. But the smell is not bad. It is sweet. Tucked in her little headband is a fresh white plumeria. You sniff it and your whole body relaxes. "Ahhhh."
Poo? Ahhh. A flower, and a baby. The two nicest things you can smell in one house.
Except when the baby smell actually is the other thing. Which it is, eleven minutes later. Aunty is still at the store.

words.say_it: Duck low and cover your head. "LOW!"
words.bonus: Laulau is food wrapped in leaves, so lau is right there in the name. Lau is also the number 400.
words.picture: Giant ti leaf wraps you like laulau
story_paragraphs: It is windy at the lūʻau. Up on the hill, a single ti leaf breaks loose and starts floating down. But it is not a normal leaf. It is the size of a king-size mattress, green and shiny, and it is heading straight for you.
Uncle sees it first. "DUCK! LOW! LOOOW!" You duck low. Too late. The leaf lands on you with a soft flap and wraps around you like a burrito.
