The aunties rush over. They tie the ends with string. They pick you up and carry you toward the imu. You yell from inside the leaf. One aunty taps on it and says "Ho, this one one good laulau."
They unwrap you just in time. You smell like kālua pig for three days.

words.say_it: Pat your ear in panic, with a catch each time. "ʻAh-no-ʻAH-no!"
words.bonus: Kanu means to plant, so kanu i ka ʻanoʻano means plant the seed.
words.picture: Watermelon vine growing out of your nose
story_paragraphs: You are six years old at a family picnic, eating watermelon as fast as you can. Your older cousin says "Careful, if you swallow one seed, one tree going grow inside you."
Gulp. You swallowed one.

That night you feel a tickle. In the morning a little green sprout is poking out of your left ear. "ʻAh... no." At lunch a vine is curling out your nose. "ʻAH, NO!" By dinner there are leaves in your hair and a baby watermelon hanging off your elbow. "ʻAH, NO! ʻAH, NO!" A little hiccup of panic every time.
Your mom takes one look, picks the watermelon, cuts it and serves it for dessert. Then she plants the rest of you in the backyard and waters you twice a day. You grow 14 more watermelons.

words.say_it: Hold both sounds long, like the branch is growing. "Laaah-LAAAH."
words.picture: Singing kid on a stretching mango branch
story_paragraphs: You climb the mango tree in your backyard and crawl out on a branch. You sing to scare away the mynah birds. "LAAAA-LAAAA!"
The branch creaks. It grows. It stretches out one foot.
Interesting. You sing longer. "LAAAAAAAA-LAAAAAAAA!" The branch shoots out over the fence, over the neighbor's carport, over their dog. The longer you hold the note, the longer it grows.
You take a huge breath and hold it for thirty seconds. The branch reaches across the whole street and taps on Aunty Fay's kitchen window. She opens it and hands you a malasada.
Then you run out of air. The branch snaps back like a tape measure and you land in your own yard, still holding the malasada.

words.say_it: Raise your hand for roll call. "Oh-HEE-ʻah!"
words.bonus: ʻŌhiʻa is often the first tree to grow on new lava. A disease called Rapid ʻŌhiʻa Death is killing many of them, so clean your shoes before and after forest hikes.
words.picture: Tiny tree answering roll call on lava
story_paragraphs: You are standing on a brand new lava field on the Big Island. Everything is black and shiny and cracked for miles. No grass. No bugs. Nothing.
A park ranger with a clipboard is taking roll call for the plants. "Grass?" Silence. "Fern?" Silence. "Mango?" Definitely not.
"ʻŌhiʻa?"

From a tiny crack, a little tree about six inches tall pokes up through the rock. It has gray-green leaves and one bright red pom-pom flower on top. In a tiny proud voice it answers "Ohhhhhh... HERE-ʻah!" A long oh, then a hiccup of nerves.
The ranger smiles and checks the box. You clap. The little tree stands up straighter. It is going to be here for hundreds of years, and it was the first one to show up.

words.say_it: Reach for a flower, then jump back. "Leh-HOO-ah!"
words.bonus: Red lehua is the official flower of Hawaiʻi Island. The ʻapapane, a red native honeycreeper, loves its nectar.
words.picture: Red bird with pollen mustache in blossom
story_paragraphs: Up in the rainforest you find an ʻōhiʻa tree covered in lehua blossoms. Each one is a fluffy red pom-pom made of a hundred tiny threads, like a cheerleader's pom-pom that shrank in the wash.
You reach out to pick one for a lei. "Lay..."

Out of the blossom pops a tiny red bird with a curved black beak. It has had its whole face buried in the nectar, and it comes out wearing a yellow pollen mustache. It looks at you. You look at it. "Lay... WHOA!"

It chirps, dives back in, and drinks some more. You decide this one is not for you. You leave it for the bird. Good choice, because the old folks say if you pick lehua on the way up the mountain, it will rain on you.

words.say_it: Holler and point at the tree. "HAH-lah!"
words.bonus: The long leaves of the hala, lauhala, are woven into mats, hats and baskets. Hala also means to pass by or to miss.
words.picture: Hala fruit dents Uncle's new truck
story_paragraphs: Uncle parks his brand new truck under the hala tree at the beach. The hala tree has roots that stand up like stilts, long spiky leaves, and fruit that looks like a pineapple somebody built out of orange building blocks.
You say "Uncle, maybe no park there."
Uncle says "Ah, no worry."

THUNK. A hala fruit the size of a basketball drops right on the hood. Uncle hollers "HAH-LAH!" He points at you. "Your fault!" You point at your cousin. Your cousin points at the dog. The dog points at the tree with its nose.
The tree just stands there on its stilt legs, guilty. The hala was the hala all along.

words.say_it: Hug your chest like you are guarding a lei. "MAI-leh!"
words.bonus: Maile lei are usually worn open, hanging down on both sides, not tied, at weddings and graduations.
words.picture: Graduate guarding her maile lei
story_paragraphs: It is graduation night. Your cousin Kanoe walks off the stage with so many lei she can only see out of a small hole at the top. Candy lei, money lei, ribbon lei, a lei made of gummy bears.

But one lei is special. Uncle hiked six hours up into the mountains to find the maile vine. He carefully slipped out the woody centers and draped it open around her neck, long and green and smelling like sweet forest.
At the party a little kid grabs the end of it. Kanoe does a karate move she did not know she had and yells "MY LEI!" The whole tent goes quiet. The kid lets go. Kanoe pats the maile softly. "MY lei."
She wears it all night. She sleeps with it next to her pillow.

words.say_it: Hold up one tiny flower. "ʻEe-LEE-mah!"
words.bonus: ʻIlima is the official flower of Oʻahu.
words.picture: Kid holding up the 700th flower
story_paragraphs: Aunty Lima is making an ʻilima lei for a wedding. The ʻilima flower is small, orange-yellow and thin as tissue paper. One lei takes hundreds and hundreds of them. Aunty wants exactly 700.
You have been picking since sunrise. Your fingers are orange. There is orange in your hair. You walk in with a bucket and dump it on the table. Aunty Lima counts. And counts. "699."
She looks at you over her glasses. You run back out.

You search every bush. You search your pockets. At last you find one tiny flower stuck to the bottom of your slippah, a little flat but still orange. You gasp so hard you hiccup, then run in holding it up like a gold medal. "ʻEEE, LEE-MAH! Number 700!"
She strings it on. Perfect.

words.say_it: Pop up from behind your hands. "Peeee-KAH-keh!"
words.bonus: The word means both jasmine and peacock. A Hawaiian princess loved her peacocks and the flower so much that the flower got the bird's name.
words.picture: Peacock playing peekaboo behind jasmine cake
story_paragraphs: It is your birthday and the cake is huge. Three layers, white frosting, and tiny white jasmine flowers all over the top that make the whole room smell sweet.

You lean in to blow out the candles. Something moves behind the cake. A peacock pops up, all blue neck and shiny eyes, and screams "PEEEEEEK... a CAKE!" Then it throws open its tail. Two hundred green and gold eyes fan out and knock every plate off the table.
It does it again. Ducks down behind the cake. Pops up. "PEEEEEK-a-CAKE!" Long first sound every time, like a squeaky door.
Everyone is terrified, but the cake is fine. The peacock eats one jasmine flower off the top, very politely, and walks out the back door.

words.say_it: Yell for the twins from the porch. "Meh-LEE-ah!"
words.bonus: Melia probably comes from the English word plumeria.
words.picture: Twins waist deep in plumeria flowers
story_paragraphs: Grandma has twins, Mel and Leah, and a plumeria tree in the front yard the size of a house. The tree has one strange habit. Every time somebody yells, it drops flowers.
Mel and Leah are always in trouble. "MEL! LEE-AH!" Grandma yells from the porch. Fifty pink and white flowers rain down.
"MEL! LEE-AH! Get in here!" Two hundred more.

By the end of the day the twins are standing waist deep in plumeria. They smell amazing. The mailman is sneezing. Grandma cannot even see the driveway. She stops yelling and just waves them in with a broom. The tree drops one last flower, very gently, right behind Grandma's ear.

words.say_it: Hold an invisible flower to your ear. "Ah-lo-AH-lo?"
words.bonus: The native yellow hibiscus, maʻo hau hele, is the state flower of Hawaiʻi.
words.picture: Giant hibiscus answering phone calls
story_paragraphs: In Aunty's garden there is a red hibiscus the size of a satellite dish. Five big petals open wide, and the long yellow stick in the middle pokes out like an antenna.
It picks up phone calls.
You walk by and it rings. BRRRING. The flower turns toward you and a voice comes out of it. "Allo? AH-lo? Allo?" You lean in and answer. It is a bee in Kona asking for directions.

Now it rings all day. "Allo? Allo?" Bees, moths, a gecko who wants to order pizza. Aunty puts a sign in the yard that says FLOWER IS NOT A PHONE. Nobody listens. Somebody from Kauaʻi calls at 3 in the morning to ask what time it is.

words.say_it: Admire an invisible bowl. "KO-oo."
words.bonus: Kou also means your. ʻO wai kou inoa? means What is your name?
words.picture: Family oohing at a glowing wooden bowl
story_paragraphs: Uncle Ben is a woodcarver. For three months he has been carving one bowl out of a single chunk of kou wood, from a tree with orange flowers that grows near the beach.
Today he finishes. He rubs on the oil. The whole family is sitting in the garage waiting.
He lifts the cloth. The bowl glows. The wood has swirls of gold and dark brown like a sunset caught in a wave. Everybody leans in at once and makes the same sound.
"Kohhhhhh... OOOOOH."

The neighbors come over to see. "Kohhhh... OOOH." The mailman. "Kohhhh... OOOH." A dog. "Kohhhh... wooo." Uncle has to hide the bowl in his closet so people stop coming over. They still stand in his yard, saying it at the house.

words.say_it: Bend back like you are doing the limbo. "MEE-lo."
words.bonus: Milo wood is prized for bowls, just like kou. Milo also means to twist, like twisting cord.
words.picture: Limbo under a low milo branch
story_paragraphs: At the beach park there is a big milo tree with heart-shaped leaves and yellow flowers. Its branches hang so low over the sand that you have to bend to get under them.
Your cousins turn it into a limbo contest. First round is easy. Round two you bend back. By round five the only way through is under the lowest branch, one foot off the sand.

It is your turn. Everybody is chanting. You point at yourself. "ME? LOW?" You bend back. Your knees shake. Your sunglasses slide into your hair. "ME! LOW!" You shimmy under so low your back leaves a trench in the sand.
You win. The prize is you get to lie in the shade of the milo for the rest of the day while everybody else sets up the tent.

words.say_it: Pound your fist on the table, tok tok tok. "VOW-keh."
words.bonus: Wauke bark is beaten into kapa, Hawaiian bark cloth.
words.picture: Aunty beating bark into a giant sheet
story_paragraphs: Your friend Kay comes over and finds Aunty in the carport with a strip of bark and a wooden beater. The bark is from the wauke plant, soaked for days, and it is two inches wide.
Aunty beats it. Tok tok tok. Hours of tok tok tok. The strip gets thinner and wider. Four inches. A foot. Two feet. A sheet as soft as paper.
Kay watches all afternoon. When Aunty finally holds up the finished sheet, it is big enough to wrap Kay like a present. You turn to her and say "WOW. KAY." She says "Wow is right."
So Aunty wraps Kay in it, ties it with string, and stands her in the front yard. The neighbor thinks it is a present and leaves a card.

words.say_it: Hold your nose and back away. "NO-nee!"
words.bonus: Noni is a canoe plant, one of the plants early voyagers carried to Hawaiʻi.
words.picture: Toddler chasing you with stinky fruit
story_paragraphs: Your little sister Nee is two and she has found a noni fruit under the tree. It is lumpy, pale yellow, covered in little bumps like a toad, and it smells like stinky cheese left in a hot car for a week.
She thinks it is a ball.
She picks it up and waddles toward you with it held up high. The smell arrives three seconds before she does. Your eyes water. The dog runs under the house.
"NO, NEE! NO! NEE!" She thinks it is a game. She laughs and speeds up. You run. She runs. Around the house, twice.
Tūtū steps out, takes the noni from Nee, squeezes it into a cup and drinks it. The whole family stares. Tūtū says "What? Good for you."

words.say_it: Pat the air, then flinch at the fluff. "Haaah-POO-ʻoo."
words.bonus: Long ago, the golden fluff from hāpuʻu, called pulu, was used to stuff pillows and mattresses.
words.picture: Tree fern poofing golden fluff on you
story_paragraphs: You are hiking near the volcano on the Big Island in a forest of tree ferns. They are twenty feet tall, like giant green umbrellas. New fronds curl up at the top like huge fuzzy question marks.
The trunks are covered in soft golden fuzz. Your friend says "Pat it." You pat it.
"HAAAAAAA..." A long sigh comes out of the tree. Then POOF. A cloud of golden fluff blows out all over you, into your hair and up your nose. You sneeze, you hiccup, and you say "ʻOoh."
Haaaa, poof, ʻooh. Now you look like a baby chick. Your friend laughs so hard he falls into another tree fern. HAAAAAA... POOF. Now you are both chicks.

words.say_it: Hop on one foot. "Kee-AH-veh!"
words.bonus: Kiawe wood is a favorite for smoking and grilling meat, and kiawe honey comes from its flowers.
words.picture: Barefoot kid stepping on kiawe thorn
story_paragraphs: The beach on the west side is lined with kiawe trees. Twisty gray trunks, tiny leaves, and thorns an inch long that fall on the sand and wait for you.
You forget your slippahs. You step on one.
The pain comes in three stages. First a small squeak. "KEE!" Then the real scream. "AHHHHHH!" Then you run out of breath and it comes out like a sad goat. "Vehhhh."

Uncle pulls out the thorn with the tweezers he keeps in his tackle box for this exact reason. Then he picks up the dead branch that dropped it, breaks it up and throws it in the grill. The kiawe smoke makes the best teri beef you ever had. You eat it with your foot up on the cooler.

words.say_it: Push an invisible mower, then gasp. "MOW-ʻoo."
words.bonus: Mauʻu covers grasses, sedges and rushes in general.
words.picture: Kid lost in ten foot grass
story_paragraphs: You live in Mānoa, where it rains every day. The grass in your yard grows so fast you can hear it. Creak, creak, creak.

Dad hands you the mower. "MOW." You start at the front. By the time you reach the back, the front is up to your knees again. You mow faster. The grass grows faster. It is up to your waist. Then your chest.

Dad comes out to check. The grass is ten feet tall. There are wild pigs living in it. A family from the continent is lost in it with a map. You pop out the top, green from head to toe, and gasp with a catch in your throat. "MOW... ʻOOH."
Dad nods, goes back inside, and comes out with a goat.

words.say_it: Grip an invisible rope and relax. "Oh-lo-NAAAH."
words.bonus: Olonā makes one of the strongest plant fibers in the world. It was used for fishing line, nets and the backing of feather capes.
words.picture: Spaghetti cord holding piano and grandpa
story_paragraphs: You are dangling off the edge of a cliff, holding a cord no thicker than a spaghetti noodle. Below you is a 500 foot drop into the sea.
Your friend at the top panics. "HOLD ON!" Then he looks closer at the cord and waves his hand. "Naaaaah. Relax. Is olonā."

The cord is made from olonā fiber. You are holding it with one hand. Your friend ties a piano to your foot to prove it. Then a canoe. Then his grandpa, who is eating a plate lunch. The cord does not even stretch.

"HOLD ON... naaaaaaah," your friend says again, holding the nah long and lazy because he is not worried at all. He goes to get a snack. You hang there with the piano, the canoe and the grandpa, watching the sunset.

words.say_it: Hold perfectly still, then say it. "Pah-lah-pah-LAI."
words.bonus: Palapalai is a favorite fern for hula lei and is linked to Laka, the goddess of hula. Don't mix it up with palapala, which means a document.
words.picture: Tūtū spray painting fern pattern on Pa
story_paragraphs: Tūtū wants a new pattern for Pa's aloha shirt. She has an idea. She lays Pa on the lawn in his plain white shirt, then covers him with palapalai, the lacy fern that looks like green snowflakes.
Then she gets out a can of blue spray paint.
Pa wiggles. "PA!" Pa scratches his nose. She starts to yell "La..." for lay, then remembers she was an English teacher for forty years and fixes it. "PA, LIE STILL!"
Pa, la, Pa, lie. She sprays. She lifts off the ferns. Pa's shirt is covered in perfect white lace ferns on a blue background. He looks like the fanciest man in Kāneʻohe.
He wears it to church. Six aunties ask where he bought it.

words.say_it: Spot a berry bush and light up. "Ohhh-HEH-lo!"
words.bonus: ʻŌhelo berries are sacred to Pele. Traditionally, you offer some to her before eating any.
words.picture: Hiker spotting red berries at the volcano
story_paragraphs: Your friend Jake is visiting from the continent. You take him hiking at the volcano. It is cold and foggy and the ground is black lava and low shrubs.

Jake is hungry and complaining. Then he sees a bush covered in little red berries, shiny and round like tiny cherry tomatoes. His eyes go wide. He says it the way people do when they see a brand new sports car. "Ohhhhhhh... HELLO!"

He reaches for a handful. Your aunty grabs his wrist. "Wait." She picks a few berries and sets them aside first, as an offering to Pele, whose home this is. She nods at the crater. Then she nods at Jake.
Jake eats one berry. It is sweet and a little tart. "Ohhhh, hello," he whispers, much more politely.

words.say_it: Wave at a passing car. "Kah-OH-nah!"
words.bonus: Kaona meaning town comes from English. Kaona meaning hidden meaning is a treasured part of Hawaiian poetry and song, where the words say one thing and mean another.
words.picture: Car owner singing through tiny town
story_paragraphs: There is a tiny town on the island with one gas station, one store and exactly one car. It belongs to Uncle Pono, a 1972 station wagon. When he drives by, the kids run along beside it yelling "CAR OWNER! CAR OWNER!"
Every evening he drives slow down the one street with the windows down, singing songs he wrote himself. Tonight he sings "The sweet mango on the high branch is waiting for me after the rain."
Everybody in town knows what it means. It is not about a mango. It means Aunty Leilani better not buy the last mango in the store, because he wants it.
Aunty Leilani hears the song, walks to the store and eats that mango on the front steps. The car owner honks. The whole town laughs.

words.say_it: Point up at tall buildings like Lana. "Koo-lah-nah-kow-HAH-leh."
words.bonus: Kauhale is a group of houses, like an old Hawaiian homestead. A city is a whole lot of them.
words.picture: Two country cows gawking in Honolulu
story_paragraphs: Two country cows, Lana and Holly, ride into Honolulu in the back of a truck for their very first trip to the big city.
Lana cannot stop saying cool. Tall buildings. "Coooool." Traffic lights. "Coooool." Escalators. She rides one up and down eleven times. "Cooooooool."
Holly is too shocked to talk. She just stands in the middle of the crosswalk staring up at the skyscrapers while the light changes and a hundred cars honk.

The farmer runs back and forth trying to keep them together. "COOOOL, LANA! COW, HOLLY! Let's go!" Cool Lana. Cow Holly. People on the bus start chanting it. By the end of the day the whole city is chanting it. They only came to buy feed.

words.say_it: Wave a rake at a chicken. "Ah-lah-NOO-ee!"
words.bonus: Ala means path and nui means big, so an alanui is a big path.
words.picture: Road crew chasing chicken on new asphalt
story_paragraphs: The city just paved your street. It is jet black, smooth as a bowling ball, and still steaming. The road crew guy is so proud he is standing on the sidewalk with his hands on his hips.
Then a chicken walks onto it.

Tiny chicken footprints, right down the middle. The crew guy screams "AHHH!" He grabs his rake. "La! La! La!" he yells, waving at the chicken. He chases it up the street, stepping in the hot road himself, leaving huge boot prints. "My NEW-ee! My NEW-ee road!"
The chicken escapes into a hedge. The crew guy looks back. His brand new street is covered in chicken tracks, boot prints and one lost slippah. He sighs and orders another truck of asphalt.

words.say_it: Lean back in an imaginary office chair. "Keh-ʻEH-nah."
words.bonus: Keʻena can also mean a room or a department in a building.
words.picture: Office line while Kay says nah
story_paragraphs: There is an office downtown with 400 desks, 400 phones and one person who is actually in charge. Her name is Kay. She sits in the corner office with the window, the good stapler and the key to the supply closet.
All day long people stand in line at her door. "Kay, can I have a new chair?" "Kay, can I leave early?" "Kay, can I borrow the good pen?"
Kay looks up. She thinks. She makes a little catch in her throat. "Kay? ʻEh... NAH."

Every time. Forty times a day. The chair guy cries. The early guy stays till 9. By Friday the whole office just says it for her. They walk up, point at themselves, say "Kay? ʻEh, nah," and walk back to their desks. Kay has never been prouder of her office.

words.say_it: Tug an invisible sleeve. "Maaah-KEH-keh!"
words.bonus: Mākeke comes from the English word market.
words.picture: Mom and kid hauling a giant cake
story_paragraphs: Saturday morning at the farmers market. You and your mom walk past tables of papaya, apple bananas, big bunches of green onion and bags of boiled peanuts. Everybody is shouting prices.
Your mom is supposed to be buying vegetables. She is not buying vegetables. She has smelled something.

At the end of the last row an aunty is selling cake. Chocolate haupia cake. A whole one, as big as a truck tire. You grab Mom's arm and yell "MAAAAAAA! CAKE-eh!" holding the Ma as long as you can so she hears it over the crowd.
She hears it. She buys it. It takes the two of you, a hand truck and the guy from the papaya table to get it to the car. You forget the vegetables.

words.say_it: Surf an invisible sliding house. "Kah-HOO-ah!"
words.bonus: Kahua also means a field or site. Kahua mokulele is an airport, a field for airplanes.
words.picture: House sliding downhill with no foundation
story_paragraphs: Uncle Dennis builds a house on the hillside in one weekend. No foundation. He says foundations are for people who worry. He just sets the whole house down on the grass and moves in.

That night it rains. At 2 in the morning, the house starts to slide. Slowly at first. Then faster. Uncle wakes up in his bed going down the hill at twenty miles an hour. He yells out the window "Ka-WHOOOOOA!" all the way down, past three houses and a church, until he stops in somebody's taro patch.

The next weekend he tries again. This time he pours a foundation first. Forty trucks of concrete. He jumps on it. He drives on it. He has the whole family stomp on it. It does not move. Now Uncle Dennis worries a little, and sleeps great.

words.say_it: Point at a van on the grass. "PAAAH-kah!"
words.bonus: Pāka comes from the English word park.
words.picture: Pa's van parked beside the picnic table
story_paragraphs: Sunday picnic at the park by the beach. Thirty relatives, four tents, a rice cooker plugged into the pavilion, kids everywhere.
Pa is late. He drives up in his old van, sees the parking lot is full, and keeps going. Right off the pavement. Onto the grass. Past the swings.

The aunties see him first. "PAAAAAAAA! CAR!" They hold the Pa so long it turns into a siren. Pa does not hear. He drives across the lawn, around the banyan tree, between two tents and parks right next to the food table.
He gets out and grabs a plate. "What? Close to the food." The park ranger writes him a ticket. He eats with the ticket sticking out of his pocket, very happy.

words.say_it: Throw your arms up on move-in day. "Koo-lah-NOO-ee!"
words.bonus: Kula means school and nui means big, so a university is a big school. Kula kiʻekiʻe is high school.
words.picture: Freshman shouting on move-in day
story_paragraphs: Move-in day at the university. Your parents drive you across the island in a car so full your little brother is riding inside the laundry basket.

You step out. There are buildings everywhere, students on skateboards, a library as big as a mountain. You have a new haircut. New shoes. New backpack. You throw your arms up and yell "COOL! A NEW ME!"
Everybody on the lawn turns around.
For the first week you really are the new you. You go to every class. You eat salad. You join the chess club, the canoe club and a club for people who like clubs.
By week three the old you shows up with a bag of chips and moves in. The two of you share the dorm room.

words.say_it: Stop walking and whisper. "Hay-OW."
words.bonus: Heiau are Hawaiian places of worship, and many are still sacred today. Look, but do not climb on, move or take the stones.
words.picture: Loud cousin silent before stone walls
story_paragraphs: Your cousin Brandon is loud. He is loud in the car. He is loud eating chips. On the family drive around the island he is loud for three straight hours.
Then Tūtū has everybody stop and walk to a heiau. Brandon runs ahead with his bag of chips, talking the whole way.

He comes around the trees and stops. In front of him are stone walls taller than a man, built from thousands of rocks fitted together by hand without cement, standing for hundreds of years. The wind is the only sound.
Brandon's mouth opens. He whispers, very small, "Hey... wow."
He puts the chips in his pocket. He does not climb. He does not touch the stones. He just stands next to Tūtū and looks. It is the quietest he has been in his whole life.

words.english: land division from mountain to sea
words.say_it: Trace a line from high to low with your hand. "Ah-hoo-poo-ʻAH-ah."
words.bonus: The name comes from ahu (a stone pile) and puaʻa (pig). Boundaries were marked by a stone altar where a pig carving or pig offering was placed.
words.picture: Hoop rolling from mountain to sea
story_paragraphs: You stand at the very top of the mountain with a giant hoop and give it a push.

It rolls down through the cool forest where the birds live. Along the stream. Past the terraces of kalo and the sweet potato patches. Past the houses. Across the fishpond wall. Down to the beach and out onto the reef. It never leaves your valley.
You run after it yelling "A HOOP! A HOOP!" And everywhere it passes, somebody has what they need. Wood, water, food, fish, all in one slice of land from the mountain to the sea.
At the very bottom it plops into the ocean. You run in after it. The cold water hits your legs and you gasp. "Poo... ʻAH-ah!"
A hoop, poo-ʻah-ah. The whole slice, top to bottom, feeding everybody.

words.say_it: Lift an invisible giant stamp. "Ow-POO-nee!"
words.bonus: Aupuni can also mean nation or kingdom. The Hawaiian Kingdom had its own aupuni too.
words.picture: Puny clerk lifting a giant stamp
story_paragraphs: You go to the government office to get a permit for a doghouse. You take a number. You are number 4,812. They are on number 12.
Six hours later you reach the window. The clerk is a tiny man with tiny arms. He needs to stamp your form. The official stamp is the size of a surfboard and made of solid brass.
He tries to lift it. His arms shake. His face turns purple. He gets it two inches up and drops it on his own foot. "OW!" He looks at his arms in disgust. "PUNY!"
It takes him, two security guards and a lady from the next window to lift it. KA-THUNK. Approved. You go home and find your dog has already moved into your bed.

words.say_it: Coo like a dove, then let out a long ahh. "Mo-koo-AAAH-ee-nah."
words.bonus: Moku means island or district and ʻāina means land. Hawaiʻi became the 50th state in 1959.
words.picture: Kid wearing cardboard islands in school play
story_paragraphs: The school play is called Fifty States. Fifty kids, fifty costumes. Your little brother Mo is number 50, Hawaiʻi, the last one out, wearing eight cardboard islands on a string.
His one job is to make a soft cooing sound, like the doves in the backyard, when the lights hit him.

The lights hit him. He freezes. The teacher hisses from the side "Mo, COO!" He coos. The whole audience melts. "Aaaaaaaah." Next, your little sister Ina, dressed as the ocean in three blue bedsheets, is supposed to roll across the stage. She doesn't. The teacher hisses again. "EE-NAH!"
Ina rolls. She rolls right into Mo. The islands go flying into the audience. Standing ovation. Mo, coo, aaah, Ina. Best state in the show.

words.say_it: Turn an invisible key and hiccup. "KAH-ʻah!"
words.bonus: Kaʻa also means to roll or to turn, which is exactly what wheels do.
words.picture: Old car hiccuping down the street
story_paragraphs: Aunty Mae's car is forty years old. It is three colors, none of them original. The driver's seat is a beach chair. It has 600,000 miles on it, and it has the hiccups.
Every time she turns the key it goes "KA... ʻAH!" and jumps a foot in the air. Hiccup. She puts it in drive. "KA... ʻAH!" Hiccup. The car hops down the street like a kangaroo.
She tries everything. She pours water in it. She scares it with a horn. She tells it to hold its breath. Nothing works.
She drives it to the drive-in anyway. It hiccups so hard in the line that the lady has to hand Aunty Mae her plate lunch through the sunroof.

words.sound_hook: Kah... ʻah... AH... HEEE! (a fire sneeze)
words.say_it: Wind up a big sneeze. "Kah-ah-AH-hee!"
words.bonus: Kaʻa means car and ahi means fire. A train is a fire car, named for the old steam trains.
words.picture: Sugar train sneezing fire
story_paragraphs: The old sugar train on the plantation is tired. It is black and rusty, and it has a cold.

Every mile it slows down, wobbles, and wheezes like it is about to sneeze. "Kah... ʻah... AHHH..." All the passengers grab their seats. "...HEEEE!" It sneezes fire. A big orange blast out of the smokestack. It singes the tops of the cane, lights up the sky and scares every mynah bird for a mile.
Then it feels better and chugs on. Choo choo. Another mile. "Kah... ʻah... AHHH... HEEE!" Fire sneeze.
The conductor keeps a box of tissues the size of a refrigerator. The tissues catch fire. He gives up and hands out marshmallows to the passengers in the back car.

words.say_it: Lean hard to one side. "KAH-ʻah oh-HOO-ah!"
words.bonus: ʻŌhua means passengers, so a bus is a passenger car. Remember the hiccuping kaʻa?
words.picture: Packed bus with everyone sliding left
story_paragraphs: You get on the bus in the morning. It is full. You squeeze in anyway. Somebody's surfboard is in your ear. Somebody's aunty is standing on your foot. There is a guy with a tuba, a lady with nine chickens in a box and a kid holding a birthday cake over his head.
The bus pulls out. Then the driver takes the corner onto the highway way too fast.
Everybody slides to the left at the same time. Surfboard, aunty, tuba, chickens, cake. Fifty people say it together, long and loud. "Ohhhhhhh... WHOA!"
Next corner, they all slide right. "Ohhhhhhh... WHOA!"
When you finally get off at your stop, you have somebody else's slippah, a feather in your hair and frosting on your elbow.

words.say_it: Strum an invisible ʻukulele faster and faster. "Mo-koo-LEH-leh!"
words.bonus: Moku means ship and lele means to fly, so an airplane is a flying ship. ʻUkulele has lele in it too.
words.picture: Plane flying on ʻukulele strumming
story_paragraphs: The airplane to Maui is ready to take off. The pilot gets on the speaker. "Folks, we have a problem. The engines are not working. We need... mo' ʻukulele."
Every passenger pulls out an ʻukulele. Two hundred of them. The pilot counts. "Not enough. MO' UKULELE!"

The flight attendants pass out more from the overhead bins. An aunty in row 12 has four in her purse. Everybody starts strumming the same song, and the plane starts to rise. Faster strumming, higher plane. Somebody plays a wrong chord and the plane dips over Molokaʻi. Everybody screams and strums harder.
You land in Kahului to a standing ovation from the whole airport. Your fingers are numb. Nobody remembered the luggage.

words.say_it: Do a baby cry with a catch at the end. "VAH-ʻah!"
words.bonus: A waʻa kaulua is a double-hulled voyaging canoe.
words.picture: Crying baby powers racing canoe
story_paragraphs: The canoe club is racing tomorrow and they have a secret weapon. It is Aunty's baby.

The baby sits in the middle of the canoe in a tiny life jacket. When the baby is happy, the canoe just floats. But when the baby cries "WAAAAAH... ʻAH!", with that little hiccup at the end, all six paddlers panic and dig in at once, so hard the canoe jumps out of the water.
At the race, the horn goes. The baby is asleep. Nobody moves. The other canoes are gone.

Aunty takes away the pacifier. "WAAAAAH... ʻAH!" The canoe takes off like a rocket. It passes every boat, crosses the finish line, slides up the beach and ends up on a lawn at a birthday party. The baby gets the pacifier back and a trophy.

words.say_it: Rev an invisible engine. "Kah-LAH-kah!"
words.bonus: Kalaka comes from English truck. English words borrowed into Hawaiian often swap t for k and r for l.
words.picture: Monster truck shaking the neighborhood
story_paragraphs: Your big brother Kawika's truck is lifted so high you need a ladder to get in. The tires are taller than you. The exhaust pipe is the size of a trash can.
When he starts it in the morning the whole neighborhood hears it. "Ka-LAH-ka... ka-LAH-ka... ka-LAH-ka..." Windows rattle. Car alarms go off. A dog down the street packs a little bag and leaves.

He drives you to school in it. You climb down from the passenger door on a rope. Kids stare. The principal stares. The truck idles at the curb. "Ka-LAH-ka, ka-LAH-ka." The flag on the pole flaps from the exhaust.
At pickup you can hear it coming from three neighborhoods away. The whole class says it at the same time. "Ka-LAH-ka."

words.say_it: Pedal your hands in circles. "Pai-kee-KAH-lah!"
words.bonus: Paikikala comes from the English word bicycle.
words.picture: Carla, pie and key flying off a bike
story_paragraphs: Your big sister Carla is riding her bicycle to Grandma's house on the other side of the hill. In the basket is a warm apple pie. Around her neck is the key to Grandma's house.
She pushes off. Mom runs out of the house yelling after her. "PIE! KEY! CARLA!" She wants to make sure Carla has both.
Carla hears "pie" and checks the basket. She hears "key" and checks her neck. She hears "CARLA" and looks back, and that is exactly when she hits the bump.
The bicycle flies. The pie flies. The key flies. Carla flies. They all land in Grandma's yard in one neat little pile. Grandma looks down from the porch. Pie, key, Carla. "Right on time."

words.say_it: Tiptoe on an invisible creaky pier. "Oo-AH-po!"
words.bonus: Uapo comes from the English word wharf.
words.picture: Uncle on couch sliding off pier
story_paragraphs: Uncle Po goes fishing at the end of the old wooden pier every Saturday. He does not believe in packing light. He brings nine coolers, sixty fishing poles, a grill, a couch and a TV.
Every step he takes, the planks bend lower. Creeeeak. Creeeeak. The fish underneath look up nervously.

The kids on the pier point and scream "WHOA, PO! WHOA, PO!" He does not listen. He sets down the couch. The end of the pier sinks into the water like a slide. Uncle Po rides down it on his couch, into the harbor, still holding a pole.
He comes up with his hat still on, spits out water, and holds up a fish. Somehow he caught one. He climbs back up onto the wharf and nobody says another word.

words.say_it: Spin your finger next to your head. "LO-ko EE-ʻah!"
words.bonus: Loko means pond or inside, and iʻa means fish. Small fish swim in through the mākāhā gate, grow fat, and cannot swim back out.
words.picture: Fat mullet stuck behind fishpond gate
story_paragraphs: Along the shore there is a big fishpond with a rock wall around it. In the wall is a wooden gate with little slots, called a mākāhā. Baby mullet swim in through the slots from the ocean. The pond is full of food. They eat. And eat. And eat.
Three months later one fat mullet decides to swim back out to sea. He goes to the gate. Too fat. He tries sideways. Too fat. He tries backwards.
He goes loco. He spins in circles, slaps the water with his tail and screams "LOCO! EE-ʻah! I'm going LOCO!"
The other fat fish float by, chewing, not worried. A tiny new fish swims in through the slot, looks at him, and says "What? The food is good." The fat mullet sighs and eats another bite of algae.

words.say_it: Hold up a soggy paper. "Hah-ʻah-VEE-nah."
words.bonus: Haʻawina is related to hāʻawi, to give. A lesson is something given to you.
words.picture: Homework wrapped around Vienna sausage can
story_paragraphs: You walk into class. Your teacher holds out her hand for the homework. You say "My dog ate it."
She laughs. "HA!"

You dig in your backpack to prove it. You pull out your homework. It is soaked, greasy and wrapped around an open can of Vienna sausage. You forgot you packed your snack in there. There are little sausage bites all through the page.
She gasps with a little catch. "ʻAh..." She stares. "VIENNA?"

Ha. ʻAh. Vienna. The whole class leans in. The paper smells like lunch. She thinks about it for a long time. Then she gives you an A for honesty, and a lesson you will never forget. Do not pack meat with your homework.

words.say_it: Crack an invisible egg and greet what comes out. "Hoo-ah-ʻoh-LEH-lo!"
words.bonus: Hua means egg, fruit or seed, and ʻōlelo means speech or language. A word is a little egg of speech.
words.picture: Egg hatching the word HELLO
story_paragraphs: There is an egg on the kitchen table. Nobody knows who put it there. It starts to shake.
Your brother says "WHO?" The egg cracks. "AH!" says Mom.
Out climbs something small and wet and wobbly. It is not a chick. It is a word. Five little letters standing in a row, H, E, L, L, O, shaking off bits of shell.
It looks up at the family and says in a tiny voice "Ohhhh... HELLO!"

Remember the ʻōhelo berries? Same greeting, but this time it hatched. The word runs around the table, jumps in the rice, and hides under a napkin. By dinner there are twelve more eggs. Every one hatches a different word. By bedtime your kitchen is full of words.

words.say_it: Line up your fingers like a train. "Maaah-mah-lah-ʻoh-LEH-lo."
words.bonus: Māmala means a piece or fragment, so a sentence is a piece of speech.
words.picture: Mama llama leading a train of words
story_paragraphs: The words that hatched in your kitchen have a problem. They run around one at a time and nobody can understand them. "Rice!" "Tuesday!" "Slippah!" It makes no sense.

So you call in a mama llama. She is big and fluffy and very organized. She walks into the kitchen and the words fall in line behind her like ducklings. Then she hooks them together, nose to tail, into one long train.
"Grandma. Wants. The. Rice. On. Tuesday."
It finally makes sense. You start to say "Maaaaaama lla..." but the train of words turns around and cuts you off. "Oh, HELLO!"
That little train of words is a sentence. The llama bows, eats a slippah, and leaves.

words.say_it: Lean in like it is story time. "Mo-ʻoh-LEH-lo."
words.bonus: Moʻo means succession and ʻōlelo means speech, so a story or history is speech passed along a line.
words.picture: Lizards passing a story down the line
story_paragraphs: Remember the lizards from moʻo, lined up from the little gecko to the giant dragon? They are back, and tonight they are telling a story.

The tiny gecko on your wall starts it. "Mo... ʻoh, HELLO. Long time ago..." He tells the first part and passes it to the lizard next to him. That one tells the next part and passes it on. Down the line it goes, out the window and across the yard, bigger lizard, bigger voice, same story.
At the very end, the dragon, still lying on your crushed mango tree, finishes it in a voice like thunder. You have been listening for three hours.
Then the little gecko on the wall says "Mo... ʻoh, HELLO," and starts it all over again for your little brother.

words.say_it: Point to your chest. "Ee-NO-ah."
words.bonus: ʻO wai kou inoa? means What is your name? Answer with ʻO ... koʻu inoa, like ʻO Noah koʻu inoa.
words.picture: Thirty kids all named Noah
story_paragraphs: It is the first day of school. The new teacher has a class of thirty kids. She looks at her list. Something is wrong with the list.
She says "Okay, when I call your name, raise your hand. Noah?"
Thirty hands go up.

She squints at the list. Every single name is Noah. Noah K. Noah M. Noah with the curly hair. There are even two girls named Noah. She squeaks "Eeeeee... NOAH?" and all thirty kids stand up at once, knocking over their chairs.
Name tags do not help. Every name tag says Noah. By lunch she gives up and calls everyone by their shoe color. Blue Shoes Noah. Red Slippah Noah. It works great until everybody goes barefoot for PE.

words.say_it: Dab an invisible bingo card. "Hoo-ah-HEH-loo!"
words.bonus: Helu means to count. Helu kelepona is a phone number.
words.picture: Aunties screaming at bingo numbers
story_paragraphs: Remember Uncle Lou, the fisherman with the chanting ʻōpelu? On Friday nights he runs bingo at the community hall. Two hundred aunties, two hundred dauber pens, total silence.
Lou turns the cage. The balls tumble. He pulls one out and reads the number. "B... 7!" An aunty in the back jumps up. "WHOA! HEY, LOU!"
He pulls another. "G... 52!" "WHOA, HEY LOU!" Every time a number hits, somebody screams it.

By 9 o'clock twelve aunties are standing on their chairs shouting "WHOA, HEY LOU!" at every single number, even the ones not on their cards. Lou keeps calling. Numbers, numbers, numbers. He has to stand on the table to be heard. Somebody wins a rice cooker. Somebody else cries.

words.say_it: Wave a sheet of paper over your head. "Pah-lah-PAH-lah!"
words.bonus: Palapala hānau is a birth certificate. Don't mix it up with palapalai, the lace fern, which adds an i.
words.picture: Boss buried in an avalanche of paper
story_paragraphs: Paula works at the county office in charge of documents. Forms, letters, permits, receipts. She has not seen the floor of her office in eleven years.
Today the boss needs one document, one single sheet from 2004. He walks into her office and it is paper to the ceiling. Nine feet of stacks. He cannot see her. He yells "PAULA! PAULA!"
The stacks shift. From somewhere in the middle, a hand pops up holding exactly the right sheet.

Then the stacks start to fall. Documents avalanche out the door, down the hall and into the elevator. The whole fourth floor is buried in writing. From under the pile you hear the boss, very small. "Paula... Paula..." Paula climbs out on top, sits down and starts filing.

words.say_it: Slap an invisible puck. "Hah-ʻOO-kee!"
words.bonus: Haʻuki is sport in general. Pōpeku, football, is one haʻuki.
words.picture: Hockey game on a shave ice court
story_paragraphs: Coach Kalani decides Hawaiʻi needs ice hockey. There is no ice. He does not care.

He rents the biggest shave ice machine he can find and runs it for nine hours straight on the tennis court. Rainbow shave ice, two feet deep, from net to fence. Strawberry at one end. Lemon lime in the middle. Both teams in slippahs and helmets.

He drops the puck. It is a frozen spam musubi. Everybody goes for it. Everybody slips. A kid does a triple spin on the lemon lime and scores. The crowd screams "HA... ʻOO-KEE!" like hockey with a hiccup in the middle.
By the third period the court is one big syrup puddle and both teams are sticky and blue. The coach calls it the greatest sport ever invented.

words.say_it: Kick an invisible ball. "Pohhh-PEH-koo!"
words.bonus: Peku means to kick, so pōpeku is a kick ball.
words.picture: Rooster riding a football to the end zone
story_paragraphs: Big football game at the park. Last play. Your team is down by three. Your cousin lines up to kick a field goal. Everybody holds their breath.
He kicks. The ball flies high, spinning, perfect. And a wild rooster flies up out of the bushes and meets it in the air.

The rooster lands on top of the ball and rides it down like a surfboard. The whole crowd calls out what happens next. It pokes the ball with its foot. "POOOOOKE!" It pecks the laces. "PECK!" The ball starts hissing air. "OOOOOO!"

Poke, peck, ooo. The ball lands in the end zone, flat as a pancake, with the rooster standing on it. The ref thinks for a long time. Then he signals good. Three points. The rooster gets carried off the field on everybody's shoulders.

words.say_it: Wave both arms to get Hannah's attention. "ʻOy-HAH-nah!"
words.bonus: You can hear hana, the word for work, hiding inside ʻoihana.
words.picture: Hannah juggling fourteen jobs
story_paragraphs: Hannah has fourteen jobs. At 4 a.m. she fries malasadas. At 7 she drives the school bus. At 9 she is a lifeguard. At noon she cleans teeth. At 3 she teaches ʻukulele. At 6 she fixes cars. At 9 at night she is a DJ on the radio.
Everywhere she goes, somebody needs her. "OY! HANNAH! The malasadas are burning!" "OY! HANNAH! My tooth!" "OY! HANNAH! My car!"
She is so good at every job that people follow her from one to the next. The kid from the bus is at the dentist. The dentist is at ʻukulele class. The ʻukulele class is getting their cars fixed.
Her business card is the size of a pizza box. She never sleeps. She says she is fine.

words.say_it: Pick up a thing and shrug. "MEH-ah."
words.bonus: Mea ʻai means food, a thing to eat. Mea kōkua is a helper, a person who helps.
words.picture: Garage sale of three thousand things
story_paragraphs: Aunty is having a garage sale. Her garage holds 3,000 things. She has not thrown away one thing since 1979.

You pick up a thing. A lamp shaped like a pineapple. "Meh." You put it down. You pick up another thing. A box of rubber slippahs, all left feet. "Meh." A cassette tape. "Meh." A frozen turkey from 2011. "MEH."
Aunty is watching you like a hawk. Then you pick up a thing and your eyes go wide. It is an old ʻukulele, perfect and beautiful. "AH!"
Aunty snatches it back. "That one not for sale."
Meh, meh, meh, AH. Every thing in that garage is a mea. And Aunty is the mea who keeps them all.

words.say_it: Throw an invisible hat in the air. "VAH-hee!"
words.bonus: A wahi pana is a storied or legendary place.
words.picture: Cowboy yelling at the perfect spot
story_paragraphs: A paniolo rides across the ranch lands of Waimea looking for the perfect place to camp. He is picky.
He stops at a spot. Too windy. He stops at another. Too many cows. Another. A pig already lives there. Another. The view is only okay.

Six days. Three tired horses. Then he rides over a hill and sees it. Green grass, a little stream, a giant shade tree, and a view all the way down to the ocean. He stands up in the stirrups, throws his hat in the air and yells "WAAAAH-HEEEEE!"
He plants a flag. He builds a fire. He takes off his boots. This is the place. He sleeps under the tree like a baby. In the morning he finds out it is his cousin's backyard.

words.say_it: Suck your finger, then rub your head. "ʻOw-ʻOW!"
words.bonus: Ma ka ʻaoʻao ʻākau means on the right side.
words.picture: Paper cut from a ten foot page
story_paragraphs: In the library there is a book so big it takes up a whole wall. Every page is ten feet tall. You want to read it.
You grab the edge of the first page and pull. The paper slices across your finger. Paper cut. "OW!"
You back up, turn around and walk right into the side of the book. It is as hard as a wall. BONK. "OW!"
So now you know. One ow for the page. One ow for the side. You stand there sucking your finger and rubbing your forehead while the librarian tells you to shush.
You try again and get the same two ows, each with a little hiccup at the start. "ʻOw! ʻOw!" After forty pages you have the hang of it. After eighty you just say it for fun.

words.say_it: Point into a corner and giggle. "KEE-hee!"
words.bonus: Doubled, kihikihi is the name of the Moorish idol, a fish that is all points and corners.
words.picture: Kid finding the key in a corner
story_paragraphs: Grandpa hides the house key in a corner every night so burglars can't find it. The problem is Grandpa's house has 400 corners. He built it himself and he loves corners.

You get home from school. Locked. You start looking. Corner of the porch. Nothing. Corner of the carport. Nothing. Corner of the mailbox, the doghouse, the hose reel, the window. Nothing, nothing, nothing.
Three hours. 399 corners. Then you see it, in the very last corner, the tiny one where the fence meets the wall. You grab it and yell "KEY! Hee hee hee!"
Grandpa opens the front door from the inside. It was never locked. While you are hugging the key, he takes it and hides it again. Hee hee.

words.say_it: Throw your hands up at a garden in the road. "Vah-EH-nah?!"
words.bonus: Ma waena o means between, among, or in the middle of.
words.picture: Garden planted in the middle of the street
story_paragraphs: Your neighbor Ena loves gardening, but her yard is full. So one morning she walks out into the middle of the alanui with a shovel.
She digs. She plants kalo. She plants sweet potato. She plants tomatoes, a mango tree and a whole row of green onions. Right down the middle of the road, from one stop sign to the next.
The garbage truck stops. The driver leans out. "WHY, ENA? WHY?!" A lady in a minivan honks. "WHY, ENA?" The mailman walks around it holding his hat. "Why, Ena..."
She does not answer. She just waters. Three months later the whole street is eating her tomatoes, and the city puts up a sign. GARDEN IN THE MIDDLE. DRIVE AROUND.

words.say_it: Point down and drop your voice. "LAH-lo."
words.bonus: Lalo means below, and its opposite is luna, up above. I lalo means downward.
words.picture: Piano lowered from a tenth floor window
story_paragraphs: The movers have to get Grandma's piano down from a tenth floor apartment. It will not fit in the elevator. So they tie a rope around it and lower it out the window.
The boss mover down on the sidewalk is directing. He sings every order, like he is warming up for church. "Laaaa... LOW! Laaaa... LOW!" Lower. Lower.
The piano swings past the ninth floor. Somebody is eating breakfast. It goes past the fifth floor. A cat jumps on it. Past the third. The cat plays a song on the keys going down.
"La... LOW! La... LOW!" His voice gets lower and lower until he is singing so low only whales can hear him. The piano touches down on the sidewalk, soft as a pillow. The cat takes a bow.

words.say_it: Point at the door. "VAH-ho!"
words.bonus: I waho means outside. The opposite is i loko, inside, the same loko as in loko iʻa.
words.picture: Fourteen cousins blasting out the door
story_paragraphs: It is a perfect sunny Saturday. Fourteen cousins are inside the house playing video games in the dark with the curtains shut. Nobody has seen the sun since Thursday.
Aunty Lani walks in. She opens the curtains. Fourteen cousins hiss like vampires. She opens the front door, points one finger into the yard, and says one word. "Waho."
Nobody moves.

She unplugs the TV. That does it. The cousins explode out the door like a cannon, all fourteen at once, screaming "WAH-HOOOOO!" They fly across the porch, over the steps and land in the grass in one pile.
Then they discover outside. There is a tree. There is a hose. There is a ball. By dark, Aunty Lani has to drag them back in, and they all beg to stay waho.

words.say_it: Blow a big kiss to whoever is in front. "MOO-ah!"
words.bonus: Ma mua means before or in front. I mua! means forward! and is a common cheer.
words.picture: Grandma kissing the grandkid in front
story_paragraphs: Grandma has 23 grandkids and one rule. Whoever is in front gets the first kiss.
Sunday lunch. She walks in the door. All 23 grandkids charge. They shove. They elbow. One climbs over the couch. One comes down the stairs on a boogie board. One army crawls under the table.
Little Keala, age four, somehow ends up at the very front. Grandma bends down, grabs her cheeks and gives her the loudest kiss in the history of the family. "MWAAAAH!"

Everyone else groans. Then Grandma goes down the line. "Mwah. Mwah. Mwah." But none of them are like the first one. The one in front always gets the big one. From then on, the grandkids start lining up in the driveway at 6 a.m.

words.say_it: Cross your fingers at the back of a line. "HO-peh."
words.bonus: Ma hope means after or behind. It pairs with ma mua, before or in front.
words.picture: Last in line for the last malasada
story_paragraphs: The line for the malasada shop wraps around the block. You are at the very back. Person number 400.
Up at the front, people walk away with pink boxes. The smell drifts all the way to the back of the line and hits you in the face. Warm dough. Sugar. You are shaking.
The guy in front of you turns around. "You think they going have any left by the time we get there?" You grip your wallet. You say "HOPE, eh?"
Three hours pass. The line inches forward. Every so often you whisper "Hope, eh? Hope, eh?"
You finally reach the window. There is one malasada left, at the very back end of the tray, all alone. The lady hands it to you. It is the best one. The one at the end always is.

words.say_it: Groan like an old car going uphill. "OO-kah!"
words.bonus: Mauka, toward the mountains, comes from uka. Makai means toward the sea.
words.picture: Old car groaning up to the uplands
story_paragraphs: Grandma's car is older than your dad. It is a little blue sedan, and it hates hills.
Today she drives the whole family inland, up the mountain road into the uplands. The car climbs and groans. "OOOOOOO..." It coughs. "KAH!" It climbs a little more. "OOOOOOO... KAH!"

The higher you go, the cooler it gets. Fog rolls in. Ferns everywhere. The trees change from mango to tall forest. Grandma rolls down the window and the air smells like wet leaves. The car keeps going "OOOO-KAH, OOOO-KAH," like it is trying to say where you are.
At the top, it lets out one long tired "OOOOO," and parks itself. You get out. It is cold. You can see the ocean far, far below.

words.say_it: Pat an invisible cow on your right. "Aaah-KOW!"
words.bonus: ʻĀkau means both north and right. If you stand facing west, north is on your right hand and south, hema, is on your left.
words.picture: Farmer following a north-facing cow
story_paragraphs: Farmer Mitch is lost in the fog. He doesn't have a compass. He doesn't have a phone. What he has is Bessie.
Bessie is a cow who always, always faces north. You turn her around, she turns back. You spin her, she spins back. Nobody knows why.

He also taught her to walk on his right side. Always the right. So he walks north through the fog with Bessie beside him. When he loses track, he reaches out, finds her on his right, and says with a big sigh of relief "Ahhhhhh... COW."
Right side. North. Cow. After six hours in the fog he walks out at the north end of the ranch, exactly where he wanted to be. He gives Bessie a whole bale of hay and a kiss on the nose.

words.say_it: Pinch your left pant leg. "HEH-mah!"
words.bonus: Lima hema is the left hand, and lima ʻākau is the right hand.
words.picture: Aunty hemming only the left pant leg
story_paragraphs: Down at the south end of the Big Island lives Aunty Dot, the seamstress. She is the best in the islands, but she has one quirk. She only hems the left side.
You bring her your new pants. She pins. She sews. She hands them back. The right leg drags on the floor. The left leg stops at your knee.
"HEM-ah!" you complain. "Aunty, the other side!"
She smiles and points at the left leg. "Hema." Then she points at the map on her wall, at the bottom of the island. "Also hema."
You walk out with one short left leg. For the rest of the day you keep drifting left, south, south, south, until you end up at the very tip of the island, staring at the ocean.

words.say_it: Face where the sun comes up. "Hee-KEE-nah!"
words.bonus: Hikina comes from hiki, to arrive, because the east is where the sun arrives.
words.picture: Cousin racing east to catch sunrise
story_paragraphs: Your cousin Makoa wants to be the first person on the island to see the sun come up. Every day. First. Nobody else.

He sets eleven alarms. At 3 a.m. he is out the door in his pajamas, running east with a flashlight and a spam musubi. He runs past the sleeping neighbors, past the closed store, all the way to the lookout on the east side.
Grandpa, up early to go fishing, sees him fly by. He shakes his head and says "He KEEN, ah!"

Makoa sits on the rock facing east. The sky goes gray. Then pink. Then the first sliver of sun comes up out of the ocean and hits him right in the face. He throws his arms up. First! Behind him, the rest of the island is still snoring.

words.say_it: Point to where the sun goes down. "Ko-mo-HAH-nah."
words.bonus: Komo means to enter. The west is where the sun enters the sea. Hikina, east, and komohana, west, make a pair.
words.picture: Friends pulling Hannah to watch sunset
story_paragraphs: Remember Hannah with the fourteen jobs? Once a day, for exactly four minutes, she takes a break. Only for one thing. The sunset.
Her friends have to drag her. She is holding a wrench and a stack of dentist forms. They pull her out to the beach on the west side and point at the sky. "Come on, HANNAH! It's going down!"
She sits in the sand. The sun turns orange and slides down toward the water, then into the ocean, like it is going home for the night. Everybody watches. Nobody talks.
It goes under. Hannah stands up, brushes off the sand, and runs back to her fifth job. Her friends yell after her "Same time tomorrow! Come on, HANNAH!"

words.say_it: Tap your stomach like a light just turned on. "Nah-ʻow-AH-oh."
words.bonus: Naʻau means gut or heart, and ao means light or daytime. Wisdom is light in the gut.
words.picture: Old fisherman lighting up your gut
story_paragraphs: You have a problem you cannot figure out. Your canoe leaks, your boss is mad, and your cousin owes you money. So you go see the oldest fisherman in the harbor, Uncle Sol, 97 years old, sitting on an upside down bucket.
You tell him everything. It takes forty minutes. He does not say one word. He just mends his net.
Then he asks you one small question. Just one.
You stop. You think. And slowly, like a light bulb warming up in your stomach, you understand the whole thing. "Now..." you say. Then "WOW..." Then, very quietly, "...oh."
Uncle Sol goes back to his net. You walk away knowing exactly what to do. Later you cannot even remember his question. But the light in your stomach stays on.

words.say_it: Raise one calm hand. "MAH-nah."
words.bonus: Mana lives in people, places and things, and people can gain or lose it by how they act. Don't mix it up with manaʻo, which means thought or idea.
words.picture: Tiny great-grandma quiets the reunion
story_paragraphs: It is your family reunion. Two hundred people in one backyard. Kids running, uncles arguing about football, three radios playing three different songs. Total chaos.
Then your great-grandma, Ma, 94 years old, stands up from her chair. She is five feet tall. She does not raise her voice. She just lifts one hand and says one word. "Nah."
Everything stops. The radios go off. The kids freeze mid-run. An uncle stops with a rib halfway to his mouth. Even the dog sits.
Nobody told them to. Nobody had to. A quiet power fills the whole yard. You whisper to your cousin "Ma... nah," and he nods like he felt it too.
Ma sits back down. The party starts again, a little softer, and everybody brings her a plate.

words.say_it: Salute like Leanna. "Koo-leh-AH-nah!"
words.bonus: Kuleana also means a right, and the Kuleana Act of 1850 let commoners claim the land they lived on. Not my kuleana means not my business.
words.picture: Nine year old commanding 42 chickens
story_paragraphs: Leanna is nine. Today her dad gives her a kuleana. She is in charge of feeding the family's 42 chickens. Every morning. Before school.

She takes it more seriously than any nine year old in history. She makes a chart. She names every chicken. She wakes up at 4 a.m., puts on a hard hat and a whistle, and marches the chickens into lines. She measures the feed with a ruler.
Her dad peeks out the window in his pajamas. The chickens are lined up by height. One is saluting. He gives her a thumbs up. "COOL, LEANNA!"
She does not even look up. "Not now, Dad. I have kuleana." A month later the chickens are laying twice as many eggs, and the neighbor asks if Leanna can take care of his dog too.

words.say_it: Sing one low note, then one high note. "Lohhh-KAH-hee."
words.bonus: Lōkahi and laulima go together. Everyone as one, and many hands doing the work.
words.picture: Family band finally singing in harmony
story_paragraphs: Your family band has one problem. Nobody plays together. Uncle on bass plays a slow song. Aunty on ʻukulele plays a fast one. Your little sister just screams. The dog howls along. It sounds like a truck full of pots rolling down a hill.
At the party, right before they play, Grandpa stands up. He points at Uncle. "You. Sing low." Uncle sings "LOOOOOOW." He points at your sister. "You. Sing high." She squeaks "ka-HEEEE!"
He waves his arms and they do it together. "LOOOOOOW... ka-HEEEE!" The low note and the high note fit together like rice and shoyu. Then Aunty joins. Then everybody.
For the first time ever, the whole family sounds like one voice. People stop eating to listen. Even the dog howls in tune.

words.say_it: Hold up both hands with everybody. "Lau-LEE-mah!"
words.bonus: Lau means many (it is also the number 400) and lima means hand. Laulima is many hands working together.
words.picture: Four hundred hands stringing a giant lei
story_paragraphs: Remember Aunty Lima and her ʻilima lei? Now she has a bigger job. The school wants a lei long enough to go all the way around the football field for graduation.
She cannot do it alone. So she gets on a bullhorn. Her voice is so loud people in the next town hear it. That is why everybody calls her Loud Lima. "EVERYBODY! BRING YOUR HANDS!"
Two hundred people show up. Kids, aunties, uncles, the mailman, the whole football team. Four hundred hands. Everyone picks, strings, ties and passes, in one long line around the field.
It takes four hours. When it is done, two hundred people stand up and cheer, "LOUD LIMA! LOUD LIMA!" and she cries into the bullhorn, which is also very loud.

words.say_it: Put your hand on your heart. "ʻOo-HAH-neh."
words.bonus: ʻUhane can mean the soul of a living person or the spirit of someone who has passed.
words.picture: Aunty's hand over your heart
story_paragraphs: You are sitting on your aunty's porch at night with your ʻukulele. You are playing an old song Grandpa used to sing. Grandpa passed away last year.
You don't know all the words. Your voice cracks. You keep going anyway.

Aunty comes out and sits next to you. She doesn't say anything at first. When you finish, she puts her hand on your chest, right over your heart. Her eyes are wet. There is a little catch in her voice. "ʻOoh, honey." Then, softly, "That came from your ʻuhane."
A soft breeze comes through and the wind chimes ring once, even though there was no wind a second ago. You both just sit there, smiling.
Ooh, honey. ʻUhane. The part of you that sings.

words.say_it: Spread your arms wide at something huge. "Ah-KOO-ah."
words.bonus: The four great akua of old Hawaiʻi are Kū, Kāne, Lono and Kanaloa, and Kanaloa is tied to the ocean. In church today, Ke Akua is used for God.
words.picture: Kid trying to scoop the ocean into a bucket
story_paragraphs: Your little nephew Keoni is five and has never seen the ocean at sunrise. Grandpa drives him to Makapuʻu at 5 in the morning. The wind is pushing, the waves are booming, the sky turns orange, and the water goes a blue so bright it looks fake.

Keoni stands there with his tiny plastic bucket. He opens his mouth and all that comes out is "Ah... AQUA!" Then he runs down and tries to scoop the whole ocean into the bucket. He fills it, runs back, dumps it on the sand, runs back again. Forty trips.
Grandpa laughs and sits him down. "Too big for your bucket," he says softly. "Our kūpuna looked at power this big, the sea, the sky, the rain, the growing forest, and they saw akua there."
Keoni looks at the ocean again, very quiet now. Ah... kua. Akua.

words.say_it: Grab your toe, tiny catch, then look up softly. "Ow-mah-KOO-ah."
words.bonus: The plural is ʻaumākua. Family guardians can take forms like the pueo (owl), manō (shark) or honu (turtle), and families treat their ʻaumakua with deep respect.
words.picture: Owl guiding a kid down a dark trail
story_paragraphs: You are eleven, on your first night hike with your mom at the back of the valley. It is darker than the inside of a rice pot. Your flashlight dies. You take one step, catch your toe on a root and yell "OW!" You freeze. Hiccup. "MA!"
From the tree right above you comes a soft, low call. "Koo... ah."

Two big yellow eyes. A pueo, a Hawaiian owl, wings spread as wide as your arms, looking right at you like it has been waiting. It drops off the branch and glides slowly down the trail, landing every twenty feet and turning to look back. You follow it all the way to the car.
Your mom is not surprised at all. She hugs you and says that in some families the ancestors watch over you in a form like this. Ow. Ma. Koo-ah. ʻAumakua.

words.say_it: Bounce backward off an invisible wall. "KAH-poo."
words.bonus: Kapu can also describe something, meaning forbidden or sacred. Kapu aloha is a code of respectful, peaceful behavior, even when people strongly disagree.
words.picture: Cousin bouncing off an invisible wall by a mango tree
story_paragraphs: Aunty Rose has one mango tree, and this year it grew exactly one perfect mango, gold and red, the size of a football. She ties a sign to the trunk. KAPU. That means keep off.

Your cousin Junior does not read signs. At midnight he tiptoes across the yard with a fruit picker pole 30 feet long. The second his foot crosses the rope around the tree, BOING. An invisible wall, soft like a bouncy castle, flings him backward into the bird bath. "KAH... POOF!"
He tries again with a running start. "KAH... POOF!" Into the hibiscus bush. Seventeen tries. Seventeen poofs.
In the morning Aunty finds him asleep in the hedge and laughs. In old Hawaiʻi a kapu was a sacred rule that everyone respected. Today a KAPU sign on a gate still means the same thing. Do not cross.

words.say_it: Stack your fists one on top of the other as you say it. "Mo-oh-koo-ow-HOW."
words.bonus: Moʻo means a succession or series, one after another. The same word is also used for a lizard.
words.picture: Family human tower on the beach
story_paragraphs: It is the family reunion at the beach park. 212 relatives, 9 pop up tents. The kids decide to build a human family tree.

Aunty Moana gets down on her hands and knees at the bottom and moos like a cow. "MOO... oh!" Her son climbs onto her back and coos like a pigeon, a long one. "Koooooo." His daughter climbs up next and bonks her head on the tent pole. "OW!" At the very top, the smallest baby wobbles, looks down at the whole shaky tower and asks, "HOW?" As in, how are all of us connected?
Moo. Oh. Koo. Ow. How.

The tower collapses into the sand, laughing. Then Tūtū stands up and answers the baby. She recites names, parent to child, back twenty generations, without looking at one piece of paper. Every tent goes quiet to listen. That long line of names is your moʻokūʻauhau.

words.say_it: Shake your head at a bottle. "AH-no."
words.bonus: Put ʻano in front of a describing word and it means kind of, somewhat. ʻAno maikaʻi means kind of good.
words.picture: Uncle pouring 400 syrups on one shave ice
story_paragraphs: You walk up to a shave ice truck parked at the beach. It has 400 bottles of syrup lined up on the counter like an army. Behind them stands Uncle Sonny with a scoop the size of a canoe paddle.
"What ʻano you like?" he asks.

"Strawberry?" He holds up the bottle and squints. "Ah, no. Not your kind." "Lilikoʻi?" "Ah, no." "Li hing mango?" "Ah, no." He goes through every single kind. Coconut, lychee, pickle, spam flavor, tuna flavor. "Ah, no. Ah, no. Ah, no."

Forty minutes later the line behind you is 90 people long. Uncle Sonny finally gets tired, grabs all 400 bottles and pours every kind at once. Your shave ice turns into a rainbow tower six feet tall. "There," he says. "Every ʻano."

words.say_it: Point at the leak and panic. "Pee-lee-KEE-ah!"
words.bonus: "No pilikia" is a common local way to say no problem, no trouble.
words.picture: Leaking whale pool shorting out the karaoke
story_paragraphs: It is Uncle Kimo's birthday and he has filled a giant inflatable whale pool on the lānai. It is 20 feet long and holds 3,000 gallons of water. Everybody is in swim shorts. The karaoke machine is plugged in right next to it.
Then your little cousin points and screams. "PEE! LEAKY! AHHH!"

There is a hole in the whale's tail. A thin stream of water is shooting sideways, straight into Uncle Kimo's plate lunch. Then into the karaoke machine, which sparks and starts singing by itself. Then the whale starts to sag, the tail slaps the table, and 40 musubi go flying into the yard where the dogs are waiting.
Water, sparks, dogs, flying rice. Pee, leaky, ah. Now that is pilikia.

words.say_it: Shake your fist and charge. "KOW-ah!"
words.bonus: Don't mix it up with kāua, with a long ā, which means "you and I, we two." One long vowel turns a war into a friendship.
words.picture: Cows in a mango war on a hill
story_paragraphs: On a ranch in upcountry Maui, two herds of cows have been arguing for years about who gets the good grass by the water trough. Today it becomes a full war.

The black cows line up on the left hill. The brown cows line up on the right hill. Each side has a pile of rotten mangoes as tall as a house. A goat hops up on the fence post and blows a conch shell. The black cows charge first and scream their war cry. "COW! AH!" The brown cows scream it right back. "COW! AAAH!"

Mangoes fly like cannonballs. SPLAT. SPLAT. A cow gets hit so hard its spots slide off. The fence breaks. The water trough tips over. By sunset the whole hill is yellow and sticky, and nobody got any grass.
Cow, ah. Kaua. War is messy.

words.say_it: Sink into an invisible bathtub and sigh. "Mah-loo-HEE-ah."
words.bonus: Maluhia is the calm, quiet kind of peace, like a still morning or a sleeping baby.
words.picture: Ma in a bubble bath, chaos outside the door
story_paragraphs: It is 6 pm and your house is chaos. Six kids are fighting over one TV remote. Two dogs are chasing the cat. The neighbor's pig got in again and is standing on the rice cooker. Somebody is practicing the trumpet.
Ma walks in the front door from work. She does not say one word. She walks straight to the bathroom, the loo, as fancy British people call it, and locks the door.

"MA?" the kids yell. From inside you hear the bathtub filling. The click of the radio. Slow ʻukulele music. A candle smell drifts under the door. Then comes the happiest sound in the world. Ma sinking into hot water and letting out a long "Hee... ahhhhh."
Ma. Loo. Hee. Ahh. Even the pig lies down. For twenty whole minutes, the house has maluhia.

words.say_it: Scoop water in cupped hands like it is gold. "Vai-VAI."
words.bonus: One popular explanation says waiwai is wai, fresh water, said twice, because water meant wealth. Pukui-Elbert thinks it more likely comes from a different wai that means to keep or retain.
words.picture: Pirate yelling at a treasure chest of water
story_paragraphs: You are on a treasure hunt with a pirate who is 80 years old and missing one slippah. The map leads to a spot under a hala tree. You dig for six hours. Finally your shovel hits wood. A chest! It weighs 500 pounds. You drag it out, bust the lock and throw open the lid.
It is full of water. Fresh, cold, clear water. That's it.
The pirate grabs his head and screams at the sky. "WHY? WHY?"

Then an old farmer walks by with a bucket, looks into the chest and smiles. "Brah, that's the real treasure." In old Hawaiʻi, fresh water fed the taro patches, and the taro fed everybody. A popular saying goes that water was wealth, so wai said twice became waiwai.
Why, why. Wai, wai. Waiwai.

words.say_it: Peek through your fingers, then cheer. "Poh-mai-KAH-ee!"
words.bonus: Pōmaikaʻi can also mean to be lucky or blessed.
words.picture: Fallen tree circling an untouched car
story_paragraphs: A storm hits your street at 2 in the morning. The neighbor's giant mango tree, 60 feet tall and a hundred years old, cracks and falls. It crushes the fence. It crushes the mailbox. It flattens the chicken coop, but the chickens are fine, sitting on the roof.
Your neighbor Po runs out in his pajamas to check his old rusty car, his kah, as they say around here. He can't look. He covers his eyes and moans, "Pooo... my KAH..."
Then he peeks. The whole tree fell in a perfect circle AROUND the car. Not one scratch. And on the hood, right in the middle, sits one perfect ripe mango.
He screams with joy. "POOO! MY KAH! EEEE!" He eats the mango in his pajamas at 2 am. The whole street calls it the luckiest night ever. Pōmaikaʻi.

words.say_it: Point up at a balloon over your head. "Mah-nah-oh-LAH-nah."
words.bonus: Manaʻo means thought and lana means floating, and lana ka manaʻo, the mind floats, is another way to say hopeful. Pukui-Elbert treats the -lana in manaʻolana as a noun ending, so the floating thought is a memory picture more than a proven word history.
words.picture: Thought balloon lifting a canoe
story_paragraphs: Your little canoe drifts for three days after the paddle breaks. No land in sight. No food except one soggy rice ball. The sun is cooking you like a laulau.

So you hold on to one thought. Mom's beef stew waiting at home, the big pot, the rice, the chili pepper water. You think about it so hard that the thought puffs out of your head as a bubble. A real one. It keeps growing. As big as a car. As big as a house. It turns into a giant balloon, the canoe lifts off the water, and you float over the sea toward home.

You look up at it and yell "MAN, OH... LANA!" Manaʻo is a thought. Lana means floating. A floating thought that carries you when nothing else can. That is manaʻolana. And the stew is still hot when you land.

words.say_it: Hand on your heart, then flap your arms. "Oy-ah-EE-oh!"
words.bonus: ʻOiaʻiʻo can also be said on its own, like "Really! Truly!" Its opposite is wahaheʻe, a lie, which comes next.
words.picture: Parrot dancing when you finally tell the truth
story_paragraphs: Mom comes home and the last malasada is gone. The box is on the counter, empty except for sugar. There are three kids in the house. Everyone says it wasn't them.
So Mom brings out the family parrot, Kolohe, who is 60 years old and has one job. He sits on your shoulder while you talk. When you lie, he does nothing. He just stares.
Your brother says a dog ate it. Stare. Your sister says a ghost ate it. Stare. You say you were asleep. Stare. The parrot leans closer. There is sugar all over your shirt.
Finally you blurt it out. "I ate it."
The parrot explodes. Wings flapping, feathers everywhere, dancing in a circle on your shoulder. "OY! AH! EE-OH! OY! AH! EE-OH!" That is the truth alarm. ʻOiaʻiʻo.

words.say_it: Laugh nervously and wiggle your lips. "Vah-hah-HEH-eh."
words.bonus: The opposite is ʻoiaʻiʻo, the truth.
words.picture: Octopus lips sliding under the fridge
story_paragraphs: Your cousin Kainoa has chocolate cake all over his face. Frosting on his nose. Crumbs in his eyebrows. A candle stuck in his hair. The birthday cake is gone. Kolohe the parrot from ʻoiaʻiʻo is on top of the fridge, staring.
"Did you eat the cake?" Aunty asks.
Kainoa laughs nervously. "Wa... ha ha... heh... eh? No."

The second the lie comes out, his mouth turns slippery. His lips go loose and wiggly like an octopus. They slide off his face, down his neck, across the floor, and try to escape under the fridge, still giggling "wa ha ha heh eh" all by themselves.

Aunty just crosses her arms and waits. Kainoa has to crawl under the fridge and bring his mouth back. Waha is mouth. Heʻe means to slide, and it is also the word for octopus. A lie is a slippery mouth.

words.say_it: Stretch the first two and pop the last. "Kaaah-naaah-VAI."
words.bonus: Some say kānāwai comes from wai, water, because early laws dealt with water rights. Pukui-Elbert doubts this, since many ancient kānāwai had nothing to do with water.
words.picture: Four year old questioning a giant law book
story_paragraphs: The neighborhood board passes a new book of laws. It is 900 pages long and weighs as much as a pig. They chain it to the telephone pole in front of your house.
Your little sister is four. She can't read yet, so she makes you read every law out loud, and after each one she asks the same thing.
"Caaaan I ride my bike on the sidewalk?" You check. "Naaaah." "WHY?"
"Caaaan I keep a goat in the bathtub?" "Naaaah." "WHY?"
"Caaaan I yell at the ice cream truck after 9 pm?" "Naaaah." "WHY?"
Long can, long nah, loud why. For six hours. Page 900 is a law that says no asking why after dark. She thinks about it for a second and says "Caaaan... naaaah... WHY?" Kānāwai. Law.

words.say_it: Come up from an invisible dive and gasp. "EH-ah!"
words.bonus: The Hawaiʻi state motto, Ua mau ke ea o ka ʻāina i ka pono, means the life (or sovereignty) of the land is perpetuated in righteousness. July 31 is celebrated as Lā Hoʻihoʻi Ea, Sovereignty Restoration Day.
words.picture: Diver bursting up for air beside a turtle
story_paragraphs: You are free diving at a calm reef off the Waiʻanae coast. You go down 25 feet and hold your breath while a turtle drifts past and a school of yellow fish swirls around you. Your chest starts to burn. Time to go up.

You kick hard toward the silver light. Twenty feet. Ten. Five. You break the surface and the first thing out of your mouth is "EH... AHHHHH!" Air rushes into your lungs. Your whole body comes back to life. The turtle pops up next to you and breathes out too. Pfff.

That first breath is ea. Life. Breath. And the same word means sovereignty, a people living free on their own land, breathing on their own. When you hear ea in a song or a speech, that is the meaning. The life of a nation.

words.say_it: Stand up straight on a step. "Koooo-LAH-nah."
words.bonus: Kū means to stand and noho means to sit. Your kūlana is your standing, whether on a team, at work or in a community.
words.picture: Girl on the top step with a bus-size pumpkin
story_paragraphs: It is the Giant Pumpkin Contest at the county fair. Three farmers have pumpkins so big they came on flatbed trucks. There is a podium with three steps. First place on top, second on the left, third on the right.

The judge is a tiny old man with a clipboard. He walks around each pumpkin, knocks on it, sniffs it. Then he points at the top step and calls out the winner, a nine year old girl named Lana with a pumpkin as big as a school bus.
"Koooooool, LANA!"
