Lana climbs to the top step and stands tall. The second place farmer stands one step lower and pouts. The third place farmer stands on the lowest step and pretends he doesn't care. Everybody knows exactly where they stand.
Kū means to stand. Your kūlana is where you stand.

words.say_it: Throw your arms up like Nana just stepped out. "Hah-NAH-nah!"
words.bonus: Don't mix it up with the fruit. Banana in Hawaiian is maiʻa.
words.picture: Nana stepping out of a giant banana
story_paragraphs: Nana is turning 90, and the family decides this has to be the biggest event in the history of the neighborhood. They rent the park. They hire a band. They build a paper mache banana as long as a city bus and park it in the middle of the lawn.
At exactly 7 pm the lights go down and the drummers start. 300 people hold their breath. The giant banana starts to peel itself. One side. Two sides. Three sides. Smoke. Fireworks.
Out steps Nana in a sparkly gold muʻumuʻu, holding a microphone.
The whole crowd jumps up and screams "HA! NANA!" She sings three songs, dances a hula, and then eats a slice of cake the size of a door.
Ha, Nana. Hanana. People will talk about that event for 40 years.

words.say_it: Look at a scary ride and shake your head. "Pah-pah-HAH-nah."
words.bonus: You can hear hana, work, at the end. A papahana is a planned piece of work, like a school program or a big project.
words.picture: Papa's backyard roller coaster into a pool
story_paragraphs: Papa gets a new drill for Christmas and decides his big weekend project will be a roller coaster. In the backyard. Made from old water pipes, two surfboards and a shopping cart.

He works Friday, Saturday and Sunday. Plans taped to the fridge. Nails everywhere. The coaster climbs over the roof, loops around the mango tree and ends in the neighbor's pool. He names it Program Number One.
He puts on a helmet and waves at the family. "Who wants the first ride?"
Everybody looks at the shopping cart. Everybody looks at the loop. Your sister shakes her head and says it for all of you. "Papa... ha... NAH."
So Papa rides it himself and lands in the neighbor's pool with a huge splash. The neighbor hands him a towel and says it's the best project on the street.

words.say_it: Open an invisible oven door and wince. "Ho-PEH-nah."
words.bonus: Don't confuse it with manaʻolana, which is hope itself. Hopena is what actually happened in the end.
words.picture: Nine layer cake collapsing into a pancake
story_paragraphs: You decide to bake your best friend a nine layer cake for her birthday. You follow the recipe for six hours. Nine bowls, 27 eggs, flour on the ceiling, the dog white like a ghost.

The cake goes into the oven as tall as a fire hydrant. You sit on the floor in front of the oven window with your hands pressed together. You HOPE. The timer dings. This is it. The ending. The big result.
You open the door. PFFFFFT. The cake sighs and collapses into a pancake one inch thick.
Your brother looks over your shoulder. "Hope, eh?" He shakes his head. "Nah."
You serve it anyway. Your friend eats three slices and says the result is the best cake she ever had, because nobody ever baked her one before. Hope, eh, nah. Hopena.

words.say_it: Tap an invisible board. "Koo-moo-HAH-nah."
words.bonus: Kumu means teacher, and also source or foundation. You'll see it again in kumu hula.
words.picture: Teacher's giant pointer drilling through the board
story_paragraphs: It is speech day in 7th grade. The topic is written on the board in giant letters. THE OCEAN. The kumu, the teacher, is a tall lady with a pointer stick 12 feet long.

The first kid gets up. "My speech is about my chicken." The kumu taps the board. "Ha. Nah." Next kid. "My speech is about video games." Tap. "Ha. Nah." Next kid. "My speech is about why we should have no homework." TAP. "HA! NAH!"
By the tenth kid, the pointer is circling THE OCEAN so hard it drills a hole right through the whiteboard, and you can see the actual ocean through the wall.
Finally a small girl stands up and says her speech is about sharks. The kumu smiles and puts down the stick. Kumu, ha, nah. Kumuhana. Stick to the topic.

words.say_it: Shoot an invisible hoop. "Pah-hoo-HO-poo!"
words.bonus: Pahu can mean a post or a box, and hopu means to catch. In sports it is the goal you score in, and in life it is the goal you aim for.
words.picture: Grandpa shooting hoops from a tree
story_paragraphs: The family basketball game is at the park. Pa is 72 years old, wearing black socks pulled up to his knees and slippahs. He announces his goal for the day. He will make a basket from the top of the monkeypod tree.
Everyone laughs. He climbs anyway. 40 feet up, leaves in his hair, a mynah bird yelling at him. He takes aim at the hoop across the court.

The whole family stares up. "PA? WHO...?" Nobody can finish the sentence. He throws. The ball flies over the court, over a car, bounces off a picnic table, rolls up a slide, flies off the top and drops straight through the hoop. Swish.
Everyone screams. "PA! WHO! HOOP! OOO!" Pa climbs down, bows, and asks for his plate lunch. Goal reached. Pahuhopu.

words.say_it: Snap your fingers and gasp. "AH-hah!"
words.bonus: ʻAha also means a cord braided from coconut fiber. You'll see ʻaha in ʻahahui (association) and in the phrase ʻaha mele (concert).
words.picture: 200 people shouting AHA at a rooster meeting
story_paragraphs: The neighborhood meeting at the community center has been going for four hours. 200 people on folding chairs. The only topic is roosters. There are 600 wild roosters on the street and they crow at 3 am.
One man wants a fence. One aunty wants to start a rooster choir. Somebody brought a rooster to the meeting and it is standing on the podium.
Then a six year old in the back raises her hand. "Just give everybody earmuffs."

Silence. Then all 200 people say it at once, with the same little catch in their throats. "...AHA!" It is so loud the roof lifts off for a second and lands back down. The rooster faints. The meeting ends. Everybody goes home in earmuffs.
That gathering of people is an ʻaha. Short and sharp, with a catch at the start.

words.say_it: Bang an invisible rice paddle. "Ah-hah-HOO-ee!"
words.bonus: A hui is a club or group, and "Hui!" is also what you shout to get a friend's attention. An ʻahahui is the more formal kind, like a society or association.
words.picture: Sixty aunties banging rice paddles
story_paragraphs: Every Thursday night, 60 aunties meet at the church hall for the Society of Very Serious Spam Musubi. They have rules. They have dues, $2 a month. They have matching purple muʻumuʻu, a president, a treasurer, and a secret handshake that takes 45 seconds.

The meeting opens the same way every week. The president bangs a rice paddle on the table like a judge. All 60 aunties stand up and shout the society chant. "AHA! HUI!" Then they sit down and argue for two hours about furikake.
When one member sees another across the grocery store parking lot, she yells "HUI!" and waves her rice paddle in the air.
Aha plus hui. A real group with rules, officers and members. That is an ʻahahui.

words.say_it: Catch invisible breadfruit falling from the sky. "Kai-aah-OO-loo!"
words.bonus: The hook borrows ʻulu, breadfruit, which is a great Hawaiian word to know too. But kaiāulu itself means the neighborhood and the people in it.
words.picture: Whole street sharing a breadfruit avalanche
story_paragraphs: Your neighbor Kai has a breadfruit tree that has gone crazy. This year it drops 300 ʻulu in one afternoon. They thump on the roof, roll down the driveway and chase the mailman down the hill.
Kai stands in the street and screams. "KAI... AAAH... ʻULU!" Kai, aah, oo, loo.

Doors open up and down the block. The aunty from the corner shows up with a laundry basket. The boys from the end of the street bring a wheelbarrow. The retired fireman sets up a folding table. Somebody starts a fire in a drum and roasts them. Someone else makes ʻulu chips. The family who just moved in last week goes home with 40 and a recipe.
By dark every house has breadfruit, and people who never talked before are sitting in the same driveway laughing. That is a kaiāulu. The people around you.

words.say_it: Mime peeling an orange and hand half over. "Pee-LEE-nah."
words.bonus: Pili means to cling or stick close, so pilina is what sticks people together.
words.picture: Old friend peeling an orange for 80 years
story_paragraphs: Two old ladies sit on a bench at the senior center. Lina is 88. You are 88 too. You have been friends since third grade.

Every single day for 80 years, Lina has peeled you an orange. At recess in third grade. At lunch in high school. At your wedding. In the hospital the day your first baby was born. Today her fingers are slow, but she still peels, one long curl of skin, and hands you half.
Somebody once counted. 29,000 oranges.
A young nurse walks by and asks what the secret is to a friendship that lasts that long. You smile and point. "Peel, Lina." And she does.
Peel, Lina. Pilina. The thing that sticks two people together, one small act at a time.

words.say_it: Hold something gross at arm's length, then hug it. "Ho-oh-ee-LEE-nah."
words.bonus: A hoʻoilina can be money or land, but also songs, stories, skills and names.
words.picture: Oily tackle box with a secret map inside
story_paragraphs: Grandpa passes away at 96 and leaves you just one thing. His old metal tackle box.

You open it. It is filthy. Every lure, every hook, every reel is coated in 60 years of fish oil. It smells like a tuna ran a marathon. You hold it away from your face. "Ho... oily... NAH." You almost put it out with the rubbish.

Then you notice a folded paper taped inside the lid. It is a map, drawn by hand, of every secret fishing spot on the whole coast. Next to each spot, a name. Grandpa's name. His father's name. His grandfather's name. 100 years of your family finding fish in the same places.
You close the box and hold it tight, oil and all. Ho, oily, nah. Hoʻoilina. The thing that gets handed down.

words.say_it: Grab your head at a rainbow dog. "Vai-ho-oh-LOO-oo!"
words.bonus: Wai is liquid and hoʻoluʻu means to dye, so color is literally dye water.
words.picture: Rainbow poodle shaking dye everywhere
story_paragraphs: Uncle Boy decides to tie dye 100 T-shirts for the family reunion. He fills a kiddie pool in the backyard with dye. Red on one end, blue on the other, yellow and purple and green in the middle.
Lulu, the family poodle, is pure white. She has been told to stay inside.
She does not stay inside.

She sprints across the yard and cannonballs into the kiddie pool. SPLOOSH. She comes out every color at once. Red ears, green legs, a blue tail, a purple face. She shakes, and every T-shirt on the line, the car and the neighbor's cat all turn rainbow too.
Uncle Boy grabs his head. "WHY? HO! OH... LULU!" Why, ho, oh, Lu-u. Waihoʻoluʻu. She stays colors for three weeks, and everybody at the reunion wants a picture with her.

words.say_it: Wave, shake your head, then rub your forehead. "Oh-LEH-lo no-eh-OW."
words.bonus: A famous one is ʻAʻohe pau ka ʻike i ka hālau hoʻokahi, which means not all knowledge is learned in one school.
words.picture: Texting kid walking into a pole
story_paragraphs: A wise old man sits on the same bench at the shopping center every day. White beard to his belly, lauhala hat, a cane made from a guava branch. When you walk past he says "Ohhh, hello!"
Then he gives you a wise saying. "Watch where you walk, not where you want to go."
You are texting. You don't even look up. "No, eh."
Three steps later, BONK. You walk straight into a pole. "OW!"
He does not laugh. He just says "Ohhh, hello" to the next person and gives them the same saying.
Oh, hello. No, eh. OW. That is how most people learn an ʻōlelo noʻeau. The first time you hear a wise saying, you ignore it. The second time, you remember the pole.

words.say_it: Shrug, look again, then point. "MEH-ah KAH-noo!"
words.bonus: Mea means thing and kanu means to plant, so a plant is a planted thing.
words.picture: Old racing canoe turned into a garden
story_paragraphs: Aunty Pua has an old wooden canoe in her front yard, 40 feet long, retired after 30 years of racing. She did not throw it away. She filled it with dirt.

Now it is the most famous garden on the street. Tomatoes as big as softballs. A banana tree growing out of the back seat. Taro in the middle. Chili peppers along the sides. Sweet potato vines hanging over the edge like the canoe is still in the water.
The first time you see it, you are not impressed. You glance and say "Meh." Then you look again. "Ah..." Then you see the whole thing. "CANOE!"
A papaya drops off the tree right into your arms. Meh, ah, canoe. Mea kanu. A plant. Aunty Pua has a canoe full of them.

words.say_it: Stretch your arms out wide and flinch. "Kah-OW!"
words.bonus: Moʻolelo is the general word for a story or history. A kaʻao leans toward the fanciful kind, full of wonders.
words.picture: Uncle's giant fish story smacking everyone
story_paragraphs: Uncle Joe tells the same fishing story at every lūʻau, and every year the fish gets bigger.
This year he stands up by the imu. "Was THIS big," he says, and stretches his arms out. His right hand smacks Aunty in the face. "Ka... OW!"
"No, no, was THIS big." He stretches wider. His left hand knocks over the poi. "Ka... OW!"

By the end of the story the fish is as long as a school bus, it had wings, it sang karaoke, and it pulled his boat to Tahiti and back before breakfast. Everybody sitting near him has a bruise. Nobody believes a single word, and everybody wants to hear it again next year.
That is a kaʻao. A fanciful tale. Ka, catch, OW.

words.say_it: Stand still at the edge and speak softly. "LAY-nah."
words.bonus: Kaʻena Point on Oʻahu is a famous leina. The full phrase is leina a ka ʻuhane, the leaping place of the soul.
words.picture: Grandma and kid at land's end at sunset
story_paragraphs: Tūtū takes you on a long walk to the far western tip of Oʻahu at sunset. The road ends. The trail keeps going over rocks and sand. Albatross sit on their nests and watch you pass. A monk seal sleeps on the beach and does not even open one eye. Your slippah breaks, so you walk the last mile barefoot.
Finally the land runs out, like a lane at the end of the world. The rocks point straight out into the sea. Tūtū stops and holds your hand.
"The lane, ah..." you say, looking at the end of it.

She nods. In the old way of thinking, this is a leina, a place where the spirits of the dead leap from the land into the sea to go on to the next world. You don't talk for a while. You just watch the sun go down into the water together.

words.say_it: Point out at the water. "PEE-ah!"
words.bonus: You can hear pia at the end of haupia. Before cornstarch, arrowroot starch is what made haupia set.
words.picture: Haupia pier stretching into the ocean
story_paragraphs: Aunty Lehua makes haupia the old way, with pia, arrowroot starch, and she makes it strong. Her haupia is so firm you can stand on it.

For the beach party she makes 400 pans. The kids start stacking the squares at the water's edge. Then they lay more squares out over the water, one after another, like planks. White coconut squares, wobbling but holding.

By noon it stretches 30 feet into the ocean. A real pier. The kids run to the end and cannonball off. A fisherman walks out with his pole and a folding chair. A white egret stands at the very end like it owns the place.
Everyone points and shouts "THE PIER!" Pier. Pia. And at the end of the day the kids eat the whole pier, one square at a time.

words.say_it: Hold your nose, then squeeze an invisible cone over your head. "Ah-vah-POO-hee."
words.bonus: The shampoo kind is ʻawapuhi kuahiwi, wild mountain ginger. Its red cones hold the slippery juice.
words.picture: Hiker's hair foaming with ginger juice
story_paragraphs: You have been hiking in the rain forest for nine hours. Mud on your legs, sweat in your hair, a spider living on your hat. Your hiking buddy walks upwind and holds his nose. "Ah... WAH... POO-EE! You stink!"

He grabs a red, pine cone looking thing from a ginger plant by the trail and squeezes it over your head like a sponge. SQUISH. Clear, slippery juice runs down your hair. He rubs it in. Suds! Bubbles! It smells clean and fresh, like a fancy hotel lobby.
He squeezes six more. By the time you reach the waterfall you are foaming like a washing machine and you smell like a flower.
Ah, wah, poo-ee. ʻAwapuhi. Ginger. Nature's shampoo, growing right there on the trail.

words.say_it: Push off on an invisible sled. "Laaah... EEEE!"
words.bonus: Lāʻī is short for lau kī, the leaf of the kī (ti) plant.
words.picture: Kid sledding down a hill on ti leaves
story_paragraphs: It is a rainy Saturday, and the grass hill behind the school is slick, green and 200 feet long. Your cousins show up with armfuls of ti leaves, long, green and shiny.
You sit on a bundle of ti leaves at the top, grab the stems like handlebars and push off.
"LAAAAAAA..."

You pick up speed. 20 miles an hour. 30. The wind flattens your cheeks. You pass a jogger. You pass a dog. You pass a car on the road below. At the bottom you hit a bump and catch air, and your throat catches too.
"...EEEEEEE!"
You slide 40 more feet into a pile of leaves. Everyone is cheering. Laaaa, catch, EEEE. Lāʻī. Ti leaf. The same leaf wraps your laulau, but today it is a sled.

words.english: pounded taro, not yet thinned into poi
words.say_it: Chew something sticky, then pop your jaw free. "PAH-ee AI!"
words.bonus: Also written paʻiʻai. The board is a papa kuʻi ʻai and the stone is a pōhaku kuʻi ʻai. Paʻi ʻai plus water makes poi.
words.picture: Kid's jaw glued shut with pounded taro
story_paragraphs: Uncle Kalani pounds cooked taro on a long wooden board with a heavy stone pounder. Thump. Fold. Thump. Fold. After an hour it becomes a thick, sticky, purple gray lump. Not poi yet. Too thick to pour. It is paʻi ʻai.

He wraps a chunk in ti leaves, the same ones from the sledding hill, and sets it on the table. Your little brother sees it and thinks it's dessert. "PIE?" He grabs a handful and stuffs it in his mouth.
He tries to chew. His jaw will not open. It is glued shut. He tries to talk. "Mmmf! Mmmf!" Finally it pops free. "AY!"
Pie? Ay! Paʻi ʻai. Uncle laughs and shows him the trick. Add water, a little at a time, and mix it with your hand. Now it becomes poi.

words.say_it: Hold on to a runaway fishing pole. "Oh-EE-oh!"
words.bonus: ʻŌʻio is so bony that people often scrape out the flesh and make it into fish cake.
words.picture: Bonefish dragging you across the flats
story_paragraphs: You are wading on the shallow sand flats with a thin fishing pole when something grabs your line and takes off. The reel screams. The line zips out 200 yards. The fish is so fast and strong it pulls you off your feet, and now you are water skiing on your belly across the flats.
"OHHH! EEE! OH!" you scream like a siren, all the way to the reef.
It turns out to be a bonefish. Silver, sleek, not even two feet long.

You bring it home to Aunty. She cooks it and you take one big bite. It is like chewing a bag of toothpicks. "OHHH! EE! OH!" again. Aunty laughs and takes the plate away. She scrapes the meat off the bones with a spoon and makes the best fish cake you have ever had.

words.say_it: Point at the fish and yell for help. "Ah-KOO-leh!"
words.bonus: Young akule are called hahalalū. Akule are often fried or dried.
words.picture: Net full of big-eyed silver fish
story_paragraphs: One summer morning the bay turns black. Not from a storm. From fish. A school of akule so big it looks like an oil spill, millions of silver fish with giant eyes, all swimming in one slow circle.

The uncles on the beach go crazy. They grab a long net, jump in the boat and surround the whole school. When they haul it in, the net is so full it takes 30 people to drag it up the sand. Silver fish everywhere, big eyes staring at you.
Uncle turns around and yells. "A COOLER!"
You bring a cooler. Full. "A COOLER!" Another one. Full. Every cooler in the neighborhood. Then bathtubs. Then the back of a truck.
A cooler. Akule. Enough for the whole town, fried with shoyu for a week.

words.say_it: Stuff something big into an invisible bag. "Oh-pah-kah-PAH-kah!"
words.bonus: ʻŌpakapaka is one of the Deep 7, the prized bottomfish caught in deep water around Hawaiʻi. Pukui-Elbert calls it blue snapper, but in Hawaiʻi markets it is sold as pink snapper.
words.picture: Giant pink snapper packed into a stroller
story_paragraphs: Aunty Mele enters a deep sea fishing contest. Everyone else brings fancy boats and sonar. She brings a hand line, a bucket and a thermos of coffee.

She drops her line 600 feet down into the deep blue. She waits four hours. Then the line goes tight, and she hauls up a pink snapper so big it glows like a sunrise. Pink scales, big dark eyes, longer than she is tall.
The problem is getting it home. Her boat is small. The fish won't fit. At the dock she points at every cousin she has. "Oh, pack-a! PACK-a! Pack-a!"

They pack it into three coolers, two surfboard bags and a baby stroller. They pack it into the back seat of a car with its tail sticking out the window. It wins first place and becomes the fanciest dinner in town.
Oh, pack-a, pack-a. ʻŌpakapaka.

words.say_it: Talk through an invisible snorkel. "Hee-naah-LEH-ah."
words.bonus: Hīnālea is the name for many kinds of wrasses. Some kinds work as cleaners, picking tiny pests off bigger fish.
words.picture: Henna-painted fish staring into your mask
story_paragraphs: You are snorkeling at the reef, and a tiny fish swims right up to your mask. It is only six inches long, but it is painted like the fanciest henna art you have ever seen. Neon green swirls. Purple stripes. An orange face. A blue line down the side. Layer on top of layer on top of layer.
You try to say "Henna layer" through your snorkel. It comes out "HEEEE... NAAAH... LAYER!"

The fish is a show off. It spins around so you can see the other side. It swims to a bigger fish and starts picking tiny bits off it like a barber. Then it comes back and pecks at its own reflection in your mask.
Heee, naaah, layer. Hīnālea. Every snorkeler meets one.

words.say_it: Point at your own knees. "Mah-NEE-nee!"
words.bonus: In local slang, manini also means small or stingy. "That's one manini slice of cake."
words.picture: Striped fish nibbling Ma's knees
story_paragraphs: Ma is wading at the beach, water up to her knees, eating a spam musubi. She holds it up high to keep it dry. Rice falls in the water. Big mistake.

A school of manini shows up. Two hundred little fish, pale yellow with black stripes, like tiny prisoners in striped jail uniforms. They eat the rice. Then they start nibbling Ma's knees. Nibble nibble nibble.
"MA! KNEE! KNEE!" you yell from the sand.

Ma looks down. Her knees are covered in striped fish like a pair of zebra kneepads. She tries to walk out, and they follow her like a marching band, all 200, stripes lined up. She drops the rest of the musubi. They don't care. They like her knees better.
Ma, knee, knee. Manini.

words.say_it: Point at the thief. "Ah-LAI!"
words.bonus: In an old story the ʻalae knew the secret of fire, and its forehead turned red when Māui rubbed it with a fire stick. Today the ʻalae ʻula is endangered and lives in wetlands and taro patches.
words.picture: Red-foreheaded mudhen caught with musubi
story_paragraphs: Someone has stolen your spam musubi from the edge of the taro patch where you left it. You walk down the muddy bank looking for the thief.
Standing in the water is a black bird with a bright red forehead and big green feet. It has rice on its beak. Nori on its face. Spam grease on its feathers.
"Did you eat my musubi?"
The bird shakes its head. No.
"A LIE!" you yell, pointing. The bird freezes. It gulps, a big catch in its throat, and a tiny piece of spam pops out. Its red forehead flashes even brighter, like a stop light.
It runs across the taro leaves on its giant feet, wings flapping, to the other side of the patch. A lie. ʻAlae. The Hawaiian mudhen. Watch your lunch.

words.say_it: Shoo a bird off your lunch. "Eh-leh-PAI-oh!"
words.bonus: Canoe builders watched the ʻelepaio. If it pecked at a koa tree, the wood was full of insects and no good for a canoe. Many people say its name imitates its call.
words.picture: Tiny bird sitting in uncle's pie
story_paragraphs: Uncle Kawika, a canoe builder, finds the biggest koa tree he has ever seen, deep in the upland forest. Enough wood for a six person canoe. He sets down his lunch, a whole apple pie, and raises his adze.
A tiny brown bird with a cocked up tail lands on the trunk. It hops. It pecks. Peck peck peck. Bugs pour out of the tree like pie filling. The whole inside is rotten.
Then the bird hops over and lands right in Uncle's pie.
"Eh! Leh... my PIE! Oh!"
He looks at the bird. He looks at the bugs. He puts down the adze. That little bird just saved him three months of work on a bad tree. So he lets it finish the pie.
Eh, leh, pie, oh. ʻElepaio.

words.say_it: Turn your head away from an invisible spoon. "Ah-pah-PAH-neh."
words.bonus: The ʻapapane is one of the most common native forest birds, and it sips nectar from red ʻōhiʻa lehua blossoms.
words.picture: Red baby bird refusing a caterpillar
story_paragraphs: High in the ʻōhiʻa forest at Volcano, a baby ʻapapane sits in its nest. Bright red feathers, black wings, a curved beak made for flowers.
Its papa flies in with breakfast. A green caterpillar. Very healthy. Wiggling.
The baby turns its head away. "Ah, Papa... NAY."
Papa flies off and comes back with a beetle. "Ah, Papa, NAY!" A spider. "Ah, Papa, NAAAY!"

The baby points its beak at the tree next to the nest, covered in fluffy red lehua blossoms dripping with sweet nectar. Papa lets out a tiny bird sigh, flies over, and brings back a beak full of nectar. The baby drinks it and sings so loud the whole forest can hear.
Ah, Papa, nay. ʻApapane. The red bird that lives on lehua.

words.say_it: Pat your pocket for your keys. "HO-kee!"
words.bonus: A mule is half horse and half donkey. Horse is lio, and donkey is kēkake, the next word.
words.picture: Mule jingling with swallowed truck keys
story_paragraphs: You are visiting a ranch way upcountry. The rancher, Uncle Ikaika, drops the keys to his truck in the grass by the barn. His mule, Pōhaku, sniffs them. Then eats them. GULP.
"HO! KEY!" Uncle yells. He shakes the mule. Jingle jingle. The keys are definitely inside.

The truck is not going anywhere. The only way down the mountain is the mule. Uncle climbs on, you climb on behind him, and the mule starts down a steep trail with a hundred switchbacks, slow and steady, never slipping once. With every step you hear the keys jingling in its belly.
Four hours later you reach the bottom. The mule burps. The keys fall out onto the grass, shiny and clean. Uncle picks them up and says the mule was the better ride anyway.
Ho, key. Hoki.

words.say_it: Bray like a donkey with a mouth full of cake. "Keh-KAH-keh!"
words.bonus: The word comes from the English word jackass. The donkeys that hauled coffee in Kona were nicknamed Kona nightingales because of their loud braying.
words.picture: Donkey covered in frosting braying "Cake!"
story_paragraphs: There is a birthday party on a coffee farm in Kona. On the table sits a three layer chocolate cake with 12 candles. Behind the fence stands the farm donkey, Keala, staring at the cake like it is the love of his life.
Nobody sees him open the gate with his nose.
When you turn around, the cake is gone, and the donkey has frosting on his ears, his nose and his eyelashes. A candle sticks out of his mouth, still lit.
He lifts his head, opens his mouth and brays. "KEEEH! KAAAH! KEH!" It sounds exactly like "A CAKE! A CAKE!" Crumbs spray across the yard.
The kids try to be mad but they are laughing too hard. Keh, kah, keh. Kēkake. The donkey who loves cake.

words.say_it: Zip up an invisible tiny parka. "Laah-PAH-kee."
words.bonus: Lāpaki comes from the English word rabbit, said Hawaiian style. Hawaiian has no r or b, so the r became l and the b became p.
words.picture: Forty rabbits in parkas on the snow
story_paragraphs: Your class has 40 pet rabbits, and the teacher decides they should see snow. So in winter the whole class drives them up Mauna Kea, 13,000 feet high, in a van that smells like carrots.
The rabbits hop out into the snow and start shivering. Their ears shake. Their noses turn pink. One tries to hide inside your sock.

Your little sister opens her backpack. For three months she has been secretly knitting. Out come 40 tiny rabbit parkas, each one a different color, each with a hood that has two holes for the ears. She calls them parkies.
She holds up the first one and sings, "Laaaa... PARKIES!" One by one, 40 rabbits in 40 parkas. They hop across the snow in a line like a tiny ski team.
Laaa, parky. Lāpaki. Rabbit.

words.say_it: Yodel in terror. "Eh-leh-LOOOO!"
words.bonus: Lele means to fly. When an ʻelelū starts to lele, everybody screams.
words.picture: Football player on top of a door fleeing a roach
story_paragraphs: It is a hot night, and your cousin Keola, who is 6 foot 4 and plays football, is brushing his teeth. A cockroach three inches long crawls out of the drain. It looks at him. It opens its wings.
Everybody who lives in Hawaiʻi knows what happens next. It flies.

It flies straight at his face. Keola screams in a voice higher than a whistle, a yodel that echoes through the whole house. "EH! LEH! LOOOOOOO!" He jumps onto the toilet, then onto the towel rack, then somehow onto the top of the door.
The roach lands on his toothbrush and cleans its antennae. The whole family comes running. Grandma walks in with one slippah, SMACK, and walks out.
Keola stays on top of the door for another hour. Eh, leh, looo. ʻElelū.

words.say_it: Scratch behind your ear like a dog. "OO-koo."
words.bonus: Uku without the ʻokina is a different word. It is a gray snapper fish, and it also means pay or wages.
words.picture: Fleas playing a band on a dog's belly
story_paragraphs: Your dog Poki won't stop scratching. His back leg is going like a motor. You part his fur and look closer. Tiny black dots are jumping everywhere. "OOKY! OOKY!" you scream, and you drop the dog.

Then you lean in with a magnifying glass. The fleas are not just jumping. They are jumping in rhythm. Four of them are hopping across Poki's belly like fingers on strings. One is bouncing on his ear like a drum. It sounds like a tiny band playing an old song right there on your dog.
Ooky. ʻUku. Flea. And here is the fun part. One popular explanation says the ʻukulele got its name from ʻuku plus lele, jumping flea, because a player's fingers jump across the strings like fleas.
Poki gets a flea bath. The band breaks up.

words.say_it: Throw a punch, pause, then look confused. "KO... eh?"
words.picture: Worm in a headband knocking out a mynah
story_paragraphs: Every summer the backyard hosts the great boxing match. In one corner, a mynah bird, loud and cocky, 18 wins and zero losses. In the other corner, a skinny earthworm named Wiggles, wearing a tiny headband.
The bell rings. The mynah hops in looking for a snack. The worm ducks, stretches out to twice its length, winds up like a spring and SNAPS back. POW. Right on the beak.
The mynah spins three times and lies flat on the dirt, snoring. The referee, a gecko, counts to ten and yells "K.O.!"
The worm, dizzy and confused, looks around at the cheering crowd of ants. "...Eh?"
K.O. Eh. Koʻe. The worm is the new champion. That little pause between KO and eh is the ʻokina, the worm catching its breath.

words.say_it: Throw invisible coins in the air. "Kah-MAH-nee!"
words.bonus: Kamani wood was prized for carving bowls, and the oil from its nuts is still used on skin today.
words.picture: Kid paying for ice cream with tree nuts
story_paragraphs: There is a giant kamani tree at the beach park, 60 feet tall, with a trunk as wide as a car and big shiny leaves. Its round green nuts fall to the ground like coins, hundreds of them.
Your cousin Nohea, age five, thinks they ARE coins. She runs around filling her bucket, screaming "KA-MONEY! KA-MONEY!" She fills two buckets. She fills a wagon.
Then she drags the wagon to the ice cream truck and dumps 900 kamani nuts on the counter. "One rainbow cone, please."
The ice cream man stares at the nuts. He stares at her. He gives her a free cone for being the richest person on the beach.
Ka-money. Kamani. The tree that rains coins on the beach park, and gives you shade while you count them.

words.say_it: Swing a giant fan, then do the wave. "LO-oo-loo!"
words.bonus: Loulu palms are the only palms native to Hawaiʻi. Their leaves were used for thatching and weaving.
words.picture: Aunty's giant palm fan starting the wave
story_paragraphs: It is 94 degrees at the high school baseball game. No wind. The bleachers are metal and your legs are sticking to them. People are melting.

Then Aunty Ipo walks in carrying a single loulu palm leaf. It is shaped like a giant folding fan, bigger than a satellite dish. She sits at the end of the bleachers, grips it with both hands and gives it one enormous swing.
A wave of cool air rolls down the whole row. Everyone it hits stands up and throws their arms in the air like a stadium wave. "LOW... OOOOO... LOOOO!"
She swings again. Another wave. "Low, oooo, loo!" By the seventh inning the whole stadium is doing the wave to her fan. Hats are flying. Even the umpire is doing it.
Low, ooo, loo. Loulu. The native fan palm.

words.say_it: Throw boxes into an invisible truck. "Now-PAH-kah!"
words.bonus: There is a beach naupaka (naupaka kahakai) and a mountain naupaka (naupaka kuahiwi). Put the two half flowers together and they make one whole.
words.picture: Half flower between two moving trucks
story_paragraphs: Moving day. Your family is splitting up for a year. Half is going to live with Grandma up in Volcano, cold and misty. Half is staying down by the beach in Kona. Two trucks sit in the driveway. Uncle Lopaka stands between them with a clipboard, yelling.
"NOW! PACK-A! NOW! PACK-A!"
Pillows fly. Somebody packs the cat. Somebody packs the rice cooker in the wrong truck and has to run it over. Uncle keeps yelling. "NOW PACK-A!"

When the trucks are loaded, your aunty picks a little white flower from the bush by the beach and hands it to you. It looks torn in half, all its petals on one side. She says the other half blooms up in the mountains. In the old story, two lovers were split apart, one sent to the mountains and one to the sea, and the flower has grown in halves ever since.
Now pack-a. Naupaka.

words.say_it: Whistle like a screaming kettle. "Maaah-MAH-kee!"
words.bonus: Māmaki is related to nettles but has no sting, and people have made tea from its leaves for generations. Long ago its bark was also beaten into kapa.
words.picture: Giant kettle screaming on the stove
story_paragraphs: You wake up sick. Sore throat, stuffy nose, head like a bowling ball. Aunty Nani marches in with a bag of dried leaves from her backyard and a kettle the size of a trash can.

She stuffs a whole armful of leaves inside, fills it up and puts it on the stove. You wait. The kettle rumbles. Then it starts to whistle, and it is not a normal whistle. It is a long, loud scream that sounds like it is calling for its mother.
"MAAAAA... MAAAH... KEEEE!"

The windows shake. The dog hides. The neighbors call to check on you. Aunty pours you a giant mug of tea that tastes earthy and mild. You drink three cups. By dinner you feel good enough to eat two plates of stew.
Maaa, mah, kee. Māmaki. The native tea plant.

words.say_it: Bend low, sniff deep, then look up. "Lau-AH-eh."
words.bonus: Crushed lauaʻe smells a lot like maile, so it is a favorite for lei. Flip a frond over and you'll see neat rows of round orange-brown spots.
words.picture: Kid lying in ferns, sniffing
story_paragraphs: Aunty Pualani is making a lei for her son's graduation. She sends you to the side of the house, where a fern grows all over the ground, with long shiny fronds and bumpy edges.

You bend way down LOW to pick some. You crush one frond in your fingers by accident, and the smell hits you. Sweet and green, like the forest after rain. "AHHHH." You forget where you are. You lie down in the ferns and sniff for ten minutes.
Aunty sticks her head out the window. "You picking or sleeping?" You hold up one sad frond. "Eh?"
Low, ahh, eh. Lauaʻe. She comes out, picks an armful and braids them into a lei so fragrant that at graduation the whole row of parents behind her son turns around to sniff him.

words.say_it: Swing on an invisible vine and yell. "EE-eh-EE-eh!"
words.bonus: The long aerial roots of ʻieʻie were woven into baskets and fish traps.
words.picture: Cousin swinging vine to vine, yelling
story_paragraphs: Deep in the wet upland forest, a skinny vine with long leaves and roots like ropes is climbing up every tree. It loops from branch to branch, from trunk to trunk.
Your cousin Makoa grabs a thick rope of it, backs up and runs. He swings off the ridge, out over the stream, beats on his chest with one fist and lets out a jungle yell. "EE-EH-EE-EH!"

At the top of the swing he lets go, grabs the next vine and keeps going. "EE-EH-EE-EH!" Tree to tree, 200 feet through the forest, knocking off leaves, scattering birds, until the last vine drops him into the stream with a splash.
He comes up with a crown of orange red ʻieʻie blossoms stuck on his head. Ee-eh-ee-eh. ʻIeʻie. The vine that climbs the whole forest.

words.say_it: Wave at a passing plane. "OH-heh!"
words.bonus: The ʻohe hano ihu is a bamboo nose flute, played with breath from the nose.
words.picture: Kid waving from shooting-up bamboo
story_paragraphs: You plant a little bamboo shoot in the backyard. It is the size of a pencil. You lean on it to fix your slippah.
It starts growing. With you on it.
You grab on. By 9 am you are as high as the fence. By 10 you are passing the neighbor's second floor window. She is eating cereal. You wave. "Oh... HEY!"
By noon you are over the roof, passing a flock of birds. "Oh, hey!" By 2 pm you are next to a small plane. The pilot waves. "Oh, hey!"

At sunset you are 90 feet up, hugging a green bamboo pole that sways in the wind, saying "oh, hey" to everything that goes by. Oh, hey. ʻOhe. Bamboo. Some kinds really can grow almost three feet in one day.

words.say_it: Lift an invisible log with your pinky. "Vee-lee-VEE-lee!"
words.bonus: Wili by itself means to twist or wind, like the wili style of lei making.
words.picture: Skinny guy lifting a log with his pinky
story_paragraphs: Your friend Willy is not a big guy. He weighs about 110 pounds with his slippahs on. But on the dry side of the island, he walks up to a fallen wiliwili log as long as a canoe, slides his pinky under it and lifts it over his head.
You stare. "Willy... WILLY!"
He tosses it to you. You catch it with one hand. It is so light it's like catching a pillow. You throw it in the ocean and it floats so high you can stand on it and surf.

Willy, Willy. Wiliwili. The native tree with some of the lightest wood around. Old surfboards were made from it, and outrigger floats, and fishing net floats too. In summer it drops bright red and orange seeds, and Willy's grandma strings them into a lei.

words.say_it: Crank an invisible wrench, then flinch. "PAI-poo!"
words.bonus: Paipu comes from the English word pipe, and it is also used for a faucet. Don't mix it up with Poʻipū, a beach area on Kauaʻi.
words.picture: Burst pipe blasting uncle out the back door
story_paragraphs: The kitchen faucet has been dripping for a month. Uncle Nalu finally gets under the sink with a wrench as long as his arm. He says it will take five minutes.
He twists the pipe. It groans. He twists harder. It shakes. He gives it one more big crank.

KA-BOOM. The pipe bursts. A column of water blasts up through the sink, hits the ceiling and shoots Uncle out from under the cabinet like a cannonball. He slides across the kitchen floor, out the back door and lands in the hibiscus.
The whole family stands in the doorway, soaking wet, staring at the fountain in the kitchen. Uncle sits up, spits out a flower and says just two words. "PIPE... OOOH."
Pipe, ooh. Paipu. Nobody lets him fix anything anymore.

words.say_it: Look around an empty room, then fill it with your arms. "LAH-ko."
words.bonus: Lako also works as a describing word, meaning well supplied or prosperous. Lako hale means house furniture.
words.picture: Family unloading furniture into an empty dorm
story_paragraphs: It is your first day in the college dorm. The room is empty. No bed. No lamp. No pots. No rice. You sit on the floor and send a sad text to your family. "Total LACK. Oh."
Twenty minutes later there is honking outside. Your whole family pulls up in two trucks and a borrowed van.

Out comes the lako. A mattress. A futon. Three rice cookers. 40 pounds of rice. A mini fridge full of frozen stew. A folding table, eight chairs, a lamp, a fan, a whole case of spam, an ironing board and a karaoke machine. Aunty is carrying a rocking chair on her head.
By dinner your room is so full of supplies that 12 other students come by to borrow stuff. Lack, oh? Not anymore. Lako. Supplies and gear, everything you need. The opposite of lack.

words.say_it: Hold up an invisible camera and grin. "KEE-ee PAH-ee!"
words.bonus: Kiʻi means picture or image, and paʻi means to print, so a photo is a printed picture.
words.picture: Pie hitting uncle in the family photo
story_paragraphs: It is the big family photo. 64 relatives packed onto the lawn, tall ones in the back, babies in front, three dogs, one chicken. The photographer is on a ladder, and he wants everyone smiling at the same time.
"Okay, everybody say... KEY! EE! PIE!"
"KEY! EE! PIE!" all 64 yell together. At that exact moment a coconut cream pie flies in from the left, thrown by a six year old cousin, and hits Uncle Boy square in the face.
FLASH.
The photo is perfect. 63 people smiling. One uncle covered in cream, eyes wide, mouth open. It gets framed and hung in every house in the family. It is on the Christmas card for ten years.
Key, ee, pie. Kiʻi paʻi. A photograph. Every family has a favorite, and it's never the one where everybody behaved.

words.say_it: Press an invisible shutter button. "Pah-hoo-pah-ee-KEE-ee!"
words.picture: Talking photo booth serving pie
story_paragraphs: At the county fair there is an old wooden photo booth the size of a refrigerator. You put in a dollar. The box starts to shake and talk.
First the lid pops up. "PAH!"
A voice from inside asks, "WHO?" You say your name.
A little door opens and a pie slides out on a tray. "PIE?" You eat it.
Then comes a huge, bright flash. The box screams "KEY-EEEE!" and slides out a photo of you with cream all over your face.

Pah, who, pie, key, ee. Pahupaʻikiʻi. Camera. Remember kiʻi paʻi, the photo with the pie? Here the pieces come back in a new order. Pahu means box. Paʻi means print. Kiʻi means picture. A camera is a box that prints pictures, even if this one also serves pie.

words.say_it: Juggle something, then catch it. "EE-poo HEH-keh!"
words.bonus: An ipu is a single gourd drum. The heke is the top gourd, and joining it on makes the double gourd ipu heke.
words.picture: Kid juggling a double gourd drum
story_paragraphs: Before hula class, Uncle Kapono, who drums for the hālau, asks you to carry the ipu heke to the front of the room. It is two big dried gourds joined together, one on top of the other, like a gourd snowman with a hole on top.

You pick it up. It is lighter than you think. It jumps right out of your hands. "EEP!" You juggle it. It bounces off your knee. "Pooh..." you breathe as you almost catch it. It slips again. "HECK, EH!"
Just before it hits the floor, Uncle Kapono catches it with one hand without even looking.
He sets it on a soft pad, lifts it and drops it. DOOOM. A deep sound that shakes the floor. Then he slaps the side. PAH. DOOM, pa, pa. Every dancer in the room starts moving to the beat.
Eep, pooh, heck, eh. Ipu heke.

words.say_it: Shake an invisible rattle beside your head. "Oo-lee-oo-LEE!"
words.bonus: ʻUlīʻulī are filled with seeds or pebbles, and the feathers on top flash as the dancer moves.
words.picture: Feather rattle spinning a tiny tornado
story_paragraphs: Your cousin Lee is learning to dance with the ʻulīʻulī, a gourd rattle full of seeds with a round cap of red and yellow feathers on top. He practices in the backyard every day after school.

At first he shakes it like a salt shaker. Tsk tsk. Then he gets better. Faster. By week three his hand moves so fast the feathers turn into a blur. By week five he spins it, and the feathers whip up a little red and yellow tornado that lifts the neighbor's newspaper, three leaves and a very surprised gecko into the air.
At the big show he steps up with one in each hand. Shake, shake, spin. The crowd can't help it. "OOH, LEE! OOH, LEEE!"
Ooh, Lee, ooh, Leee. ʻUlīʻulī.

words.say_it: Tap your shoulder with invisible bamboo. "Poo-EE-lee!"
words.bonus: Pūʻili are played in pairs, struck on the body, on the floor or against each other. Don't mix them up with the feathered gourd ʻulīʻulī.
words.picture: Brother buzzing his own forehead with bamboo
story_paragraphs: Lee from the ʻulīʻulī is back, and now his sister Mahina is learning the pūʻili. Two sticks of bamboo, split into thin strips at one end, so they buzz and rattle when you hit them.
She taps them on her shoulder. BZZZT. It tickles. She taps them on her knee. BZZZT. She taps them together. CLACK BZZZT. She is doing great.
Then Lee wants a turn. He grabs them, spins them like drumsticks and smacks himself right in the forehead. BZZZT. His eyebrows are buzzing.
Mahina takes them back and wrinkles her nose at him. "POOEY, LEE!"
He tries again. Hits his nose. "Pooey, Lee!" His chin. "POOOOEY, LEE!"
Pooey, Lee. Pūʻili. Leave the bamboo rattles to the sister.

words.say_it: Click two invisible stones in each hand. "Ee-lee-EE-lee."
words.bonus: ʻIliʻili also just means pebbles. ʻIli by itself means skin.
words.picture: Kid slipping in a stream, grabbing hula stones
story_paragraphs: You are at a cold mountain stream looking for the perfect hula stones. They have to be smooth, flat and about the size of your palm. Four of them, two for each hand.
The stream bed is covered with round, wet stones. They are so slippery they wiggle under your feet like eels. You take one step and your legs go in two directions. "EELY! EELY!"
You slip. You land on your butt in the icy water. You come up holding four perfect stones, black and smooth as glass.
That night at practice you hold two in each hand. Click click. Click click. It sounds like tiny castanets, or rain on a tin roof. The whole line of dancers clicks at the same time.
Eely, eely. ʻIliʻili. Small stones, big sound.

words.say_it: Bend your knees deep and hold. "Haaah-LOW."
words.bonus: Hālau first meant a long house, like the ones built to shelter canoes. Hula schools carry the name.
words.picture: Uncle sinking to the floor in hula stance
story_paragraphs: Forty dancers stand in lines on the wooden floor of the hālau. The kumu sits at the front with her drum. She says one word, long and low.
"HAAAAA... LOW!"
Everyone bends their knees. Lower. "HAAAA... LOW!" Lower. Legs start shaking. Someone's slippah slides away. "HAAAA... LOW!"

In the back row, a big uncle who joined last week is trying his best. He goes lower. And lower. And lower, until he is sitting on an invisible chair, then on the floor, then lying flat on his back with his feet in the air, still doing the hand motions perfectly.
The kumu looks at him for a long second. Then she smiles. "Maybe not that low." The whole room laughs. Haaa, low. Hālau. The school, the family and the long house where hula lives.

words.say_it: Point two fingers at your eyes, then out at the yard. "Laah-NAI."
words.bonus: Don't mix up lānai, the porch, with Lānaʻi, the island, which has an ʻokina.
words.picture: Uncle guarding his lawn from a goat
story_paragraphs: Uncle Moku has not been inside his house in six years. He lives on the lānai. It has 14 chairs, a fridge, a TV, a hammock, a rice cooker on an extension cord, a fan, a karaoke machine and a sleeping cat.
He has one job out there. Keeping an eye on his lawn. The neighbor's goat keeps sneaking over to eat his grass, so Uncle sits on the lānai all day with a slippah ready.
The goat creeps through the fence. Uncle squints. "LAAAAWN... EYE!" He points two fingers at his eyes, then at the goat. The goat backs up. He never has to throw the slippah.
Laaawn, eye. Lānai. Every house in Hawaiʻi has one, and every family has one uncle who lives on it.

words.english: island of old land surrounded by lava
words.say_it: Peek through an invisible keyhole. "Kee-POO-kah."
words.bonus: Kīpuka Puaulu at Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park is a well known one you can walk through.
words.picture: Green forest keyhole in black lava
story_paragraphs: You are hiking across a lava field at Volcano. Black rock for miles. Crunchy, sharp, hot. No trees, no birds, no shade. Your water is gone. Your shoes are melting a little.

Then up ahead you see green. A round patch of old forest, like an island in a black sea. Long ago the lava flowed all around it but never touched it. Tall ʻōhiʻa trees, ferns, red birds singing. It looks like a keyhole in a giant black door.
You push into the shade and fall on your back in the ferns. "KEEE... PUKA!" A key puka, a keyhole. You can hear birds. Everything smells wet and alive.
Keee, puka. Kīpuka. An island of old land that the lava went around.

words.say_it: Point down a row of invisible pies. "PAI AAH-ee-nah."
words.bonus: Pae means a row or cluster, and ʻāina means land. Ka pae ʻāina o Hawaiʻi means the Hawaiian Islands.
words.picture: Row of pies shaped like the islands
story_paragraphs: Tūtū Lani is throwing a party, and she has baked pies. Many pies. She lines them up on a long table in a crooked row.
A tiny pie at the far left. A small one. A medium one. Then a cluster of four in the middle. And at the far right end, one gigantic pie the size of a truck tire.

You stand back and look at the row. "Pie... AAAAH... I, nah..." You were about to say you can't eat that many. Then you see it. It's the Hawaiian Islands. Niʻihau, Kauaʻi, Oʻahu, the four Maui County pies, and the big one at the end.
Tūtū nods. "Pae ʻāina." Pie, aaah, I, nah. A chain of islands. Everyone gets a slice of their home island, and the Big Island feeds the whole party.

words.say_it: Run your finger down your own spine. "Koo-ah-MO-oh."
words.bonus: Kua means back, and moʻo is a lizard, so picture the bumpy back of a lizard.
words.picture: Mowed ridge path shaped like a spine
story_paragraphs: Uncle Palani gets a riding lawn mower and decides to mow a path along the whole mountain ridge behind the house. Three miles. Up and down every bump.

He starts at dawn. Vroom. Up the first hump. Down the dip. Up the next hump. The ridge is so narrow the mower wheels hang over the edges. You follow on foot, yelling encouragement. "COOL! AH! MOW! OH!"

By sunset he is done. A drone flies over and takes a picture. From the sky, the mowed path looks exactly like a giant backbone. Bump, dip, bump, dip, all the way to the top, like the spine of a sleeping lizard.
Cool, ah, mow, oh. Kuamoʻo. A backbone. And also a path or trail, because the ridge is the backbone the trail runs along.

words.say_it: Point up the trail and call the rooster. "AH-lah HEH-leh!"
words.bonus: Ala means path or road, like in Ala Moana, the road by the ocean. Hele means to go.
words.picture: Rooster leading a line of hikers
story_paragraphs: The best trail guide in the valley is a rooster named Leh. Nobody trained him. He just showed up at the trailhead one day, and hikers started following him.

He knows every path. He struts up the trail, turns left at the big rock, hops over the roots and waits at the stream crossing. When anyone wanders off the path, he stops, turns around and glares until they come back.

When he stops to peck at a bug, the hikers call to get him going again. "Ah, la... HEY, LEH!" And off he goes, tail feathers bouncing, up the trail. If you ever get lost, you yell "Ah, la, hey, Leh!" and somewhere up the path you hear him crow.
Ala is a path. Hele is to go. Ah, la, hey, Leh. Ala hele. The path you go on.

words.say_it: Push an invisible, very heavy cart. "Hoh-KEH-leh!"
words.bonus: Hōkele comes from the English word hotel, said Hawaiian style, with the t turning into a k.
words.picture: Tiny bellhop pushing a tower of luggage
story_paragraphs: A fancy hotel on the beach in Waikīkī has one bellhop. Her name is Kelly and she is five feet tall.

A tour bus pulls up. 52 guests get off. Each one has three suitcases, a golf bag and a boogie board. Kelly stacks them all on one brass cart. The stack is 40 feet high, taller than the palm trees. She pushes it through the lobby with one hand while holding a guest's baby in the other.
The guests stare. The manager stares. The doorman drops his hat. "HOOOO, KELLY!"
She rides the elevator up with the whole stack, delivers every bag to every room and is back in the lobby in four minutes. Hooo, Kelly. Hōkele. The whole hotel runs on Kelly.

words.say_it: Coo like a pigeon at a counter. "HAH-leh koo-AI."
words.bonus: Hale means house and kūʻai means to buy or sell, so a store is a buying house.
words.picture: Pigeon buying rice at a corner store
story_paragraphs: Holly runs the tiny corner store at the end of your street. It is the size of a garage and sells everything. Rice, bait, slippahs, dried aku, birthday cards, fishing line, crack seed and one lawn mower.

Her first customer every morning is a pigeon. It walks in at 7 am, stands on the counter and coos. "COOOOO." Holly nods. "AYE." She hands it one grain of rice. It pays with a shiny bottle cap. This has been going on for eleven years.
Everyone who walks into the shop greets them the same way. Her name, the pigeon noise, her answer. "Holly! COOOO! AYE!"
Holly, coo, aye. Hale kūʻai. A store. The little shop where everybody, even the birds, comes to buy stuff.

words.say_it: Put your hand on your heart, then on the ground. "Ah-LO-hah AAH-ee-nah."
words.bonus: Aloha ʻāina also means love of country. In 1897 a group called Hui Aloha ʻĀina gathered more than 20,000 signatures from Hawaiians against annexation.
words.picture: Kid in the taro patch who won't leave
story_paragraphs: It is a Saturday workday at the family taro patch. You are nine, standing in mud up to your knees. You pulled weeds all morning. You planted 60 huli, the taro tops, one by one, the way your grandpa showed you. You slipped and sat in the mud twice and laughed both times.
At sunset your mom calls from the car. "Time to go!"

You look at the patch. The water shining. The little green leaves. The mountain behind it turning pink. You don't want to leave. You open your mouth to say okay, and what comes out is "Aloha... ah... I... nah."
Mom walks back down, rolls up her pants and stands in the mud next to you until it's dark.
Aloha, aaah, I, nah. Aloha ʻāina. The love of the land that makes you want to stay.

words.say_it: Freeze with an invisible pen in your hand. "Hoh-ai-LO-nah."
words.bonus: Hōʻailona also means a symbol or emblem.
words.picture: Gecko landing on uncle's checkbook
story_paragraphs: Uncle Sonny is about to loan his cousin $500 for a boat that the cousin swears will make them both rich. He sits at the kitchen table, pen over the checkbook.
"Ho... I loan-a..." he starts to say.
A mynah bird flies through the window and steals the pen.
He gets another pen. "Ho, I loan-a..." Thunder, out of a clear blue sky. The lights go out.
He lights a candle. "Ho, I loan-a..." The rooster crows three times. A gecko drops from the ceiling right onto the check. The candle blows out by itself.
Uncle looks at the gecko. The gecko looks at him. He closes the checkbook. "Okay. That's a sign."
Ho, I loan-a. Hōʻailona. A sign. An omen. Sometimes it is a gecko on your checkbook.

words.say_it: Let invisible wind flap your cheeks. "Hee-oh-hee-OH-nah!"
words.bonus: Nani ka hiʻohiʻona means the view is beautiful.
words.picture: Wind flapping faces at a cliff lookout
story_paragraphs: You drive up to the Pali Lookout for the famous view. Green cliffs, the whole windward coast, clouds racing past. The wind is blowing 60 miles an hour.
You open your mouth to say "wow," and the wind grabs your cheeks. They flap like a flag. Your lips blow out. What comes out is "HEE... OH... HEE... OH... NAH!"

Your friend turns to look at you and cracks up. Your hair is straight up. Your ears are folded back. Your face looks like a dog with its head out a car window. She takes a picture. Then the wind gets her too. "HEE OH HEE OH NAH!"
Two faces with a brand new appearance, and behind them, the most beautiful scenery on the island. Hee oh hee oh nah. Hiʻohiʻona.

words.say_it: Raise your arms like a conductor. "AH-hah MEH-leh!"
words.bonus: Mele is a song or chant, and it can also mean to sing.
words.picture: Park full of ʻukuleles, aunty conducting on a table
story_paragraphs: Remember the ʻaha, the neighborhood meeting about the roosters? This time the same 200 people meet in the park, but nobody argues. Everybody brought an instrument.

Aunty Melly runs it. She stands on a picnic table in a muʻumuʻu covered in music notes. In front of her are 300 ʻukuleles, 12 guitars, a washtub bass and a kid with a pot and a spoon. Even the roosters are wearing earmuffs.

She raises her arms. "AHA!" Everybody gets ready. She points at the crowd and they shout back, "MELLY!" Then the whole park starts to play at once. The music is so loud the leaves shake off the trees and the waves at the beach start rolling in time.
Aha, Melly. ʻAha mele. A concert. ʻAha is a gathering and mele is a song, so a concert is a gathering for songs.

words.say_it: Lean in to look, then jump back. "Hoh-ee-keh-EE-keh!"
words.bonus: ʻIke means to see, hōʻike means to show, and hōʻikeʻike is a big showing, an exhibit.
words.picture: Moldy lunch exhibit at the science fair
story_paragraphs: The 5th grade science fair is in the school cafeteria. Most tables have volcanoes and solar system models. Then there is table 17.

Table 17 belongs to a boy named Kekoa, and his exhibit is called 100 Days of Lunch. It is every lunch he did not eat since August, sealed in plastic bags and labeled. The moldy musubi. The green hot dog. The fuzzy banana, which now has a fuzzy family. A carton of milk that is somehow moving.
People walk up, lean in and jump back. "HO! ICKY! ICKY!"
The line to see it goes out the door. Parents take pictures. The principal takes pictures. The judges hold their noses and give him first place.
Ho, icky, icky. Hōʻikeʻike. An exhibit. A show where people come to look, even when they really shouldn't.

words.say_it: Whisper like it is a bedtime story. "Mo-oh-kah-lah-LEH-oh."
words.bonus: Leo means voice, so you can hear a voice right at the end of the word.
words.picture: Lion in reading glasses putting kids to sleep
story_paragraphs: It is bedtime at your sleepover, and the six kids will not go to sleep. Pillow fights. Jumping on the bed. One kid is riding the ceiling fan.
Mom sticks her head in. "Moe?" she asks, which means sleep. They laugh at her.
She sighs. "Oh... call-a LEO."

Leo is the family lion. He is 400 pounds and wears reading glasses. He pads in carrying a thick book of old legends, chants and great stories under one paw. He lies down across the doorway and starts to read in the softest, deepest roar you have ever heard. Heroes, voyages, volcanoes, love, all written down long ago.
In ten minutes all six kids are asleep on his mane. Moe, oh, call-a Leo. Moʻokalaleo. Literature. The great written stories of a people, read in the best voice in the house.

words.say_it: Throw your arms wide and sing. "MAAAH-lah!"
words.bonus: A māla ʻai is a food garden, and a māla pua is a flower garden.
words.picture: Mom singing opera to giant tomatoes
story_paragraphs: Your mom has a garden in the backyard, and she believes plants grow better when you sing to them. Not just sing. Opera.
Every morning at 6 am she stands in the middle of the tomatoes in her bathrobe, spreads her arms and belts out one long note. "MAAAAAAAH... LAAAAAA!"

The plants love it. The tomatoes swell up as big as beach balls. The green onions grow as tall as street lights. The sweet potatoes push up out of the dirt to listen. One cabbage gets so big that a family of mongooses moves in.
The neighbors used to complain. Now they come over every morning with baskets and sing along. Maaah, laaa. Ma sings la. Māla. The garden where the food grows.

words.say_it: Fold your hands, then mime a dive. "Laah-POO-leh."
words.bonus: Pule also means week, so Lāpule is the prayer day of the week.
words.picture: Kid whispering about the pool in church
story_paragraphs: Sunday morning. You are eight, sitting in the front row at church in your stiff aloha shirt. The fans spin slowly. The choir sings. Everyone bows their head for the prayer.
You bow too, but your mind is somewhere else. All you can think about is the afternoon, when the whole family goes to the pool at the park. Grandma promised.
During the quiet prayer, a little too loud, you whisper, "Laaa... POOL, eh?"
Forty heads turn. Grandma gives your ear a very gentle tug, but she is smiling. After church she takes you to the pool anyway, and she jumps in first, church dress and all.
Laaa, pool, eh. Lāpule. Sunday. Lā means day and pule means prayer. Prayer in the morning, pool in the afternoon.

words.say_it: Hold out an invisible mug and moan. "Poh-ah-KAH-hee."
words.bonus: The weekdays count up. ʻAkahi is one, ʻalua two, ʻakolu three, ʻahā four, ʻalima five and ʻaono six, so Monday through Saturday are Pōʻakahi to Pōʻaono.
words.picture: Zombie line at a giant coffee pot
story_paragraphs: Monday morning at the office. Everyone walks in like a zombie. Eyes half closed, hair sticking up, one guy wearing two different slippahs.
In the break room there is a coffee pot the size of a water tank. Every person who shuffles in grabs a mug, holds it out and moans the same thing. "Pour... a... COFFEE!"
The pot pours. And pours. The line wraps around the building. A police officer stops by and gets in line. So does the mailman, and a stray cat.
By 9 am the whole city has had one cup and everyone is awake. Pour a coffee. Pōʻakahi. Monday. It means day one, and nobody can do day one without coffee.

words.say_it: Look at empty tables and sigh. "Poh-ah-LOO-ah."
words.bonus: Lua means two. You'll also hear lua used for a hole or pit, and for the bathroom.
words.picture: Two guests at a huge empty lūʻau
story_paragraphs: Your family decides to throw a big lūʻau on a Tuesday night. Nobody knows why. It's just a Tuesday.
They dig the imu. They roast two whole pigs. They set up 40 tables, a stage, a band and a slide show. They make 300 pounds of poke.
Then 6 pm comes. Everyone is at work, at school, at soccer practice. Only two guests show up. Your mailman, and a lost tourist looking for the bus stop.
Uncle looks at the 40 empty tables. He looks at the two guests. He shakes his head. "Poor... a... LŪʻAU."
The two guests eat like kings for four hours. Two pigs, two guests. Pōʻalua. Tuesday. Day two, because lua means two, and that is why Tuesday is the worst day for a party.

words.say_it: Pour three invisible cups. "Poh-ah-KO-loo."
words.bonus: Kolu means three, so Pōʻakolu is day three of the week.
words.picture: Three camels drinking cola at school
story_paragraphs: Wednesday is hump day. The middle of the week. And on this Wednesday, three camels show up at your school.
Nobody knows where they came from. They are standing in the parking lot, humps in the air, looking thirsty. One is chewing on the principal's car antenna.

The principal runs out with three cups and a giant bottle of soda. The lunch lady yells, "POUR A COLA!" He pours one. Camel one slurps it and burps. "POUR A COLA!" Camel two. "POUR A COLA!" Camel three.
Three camels, three colas, three humps. They burp in harmony, lie down in the shade and nap until Thursday.
Pour a cola. Pōʻakolu. Wednesday. Day three. Kolu means three.

words.say_it: Laugh long and loud. "Poh-ah-HAAAH!"
words.bonus: Hā means four, and the same word also means breath.
words.picture: Four uncles, one whoopee cushion, big laugh
story_paragraphs: It's Thursday. The weekend is almost here, so Thursday night is comedy night at your house. Four uncles sit on the couch. Each one tells one joke.
The first uncle tells a joke about a chicken. Everybody laughs one short laugh. "Ha."
The second uncle's joke is about a fisherman. "Ha ha."
The third uncle's joke is about Aunty's cooking. Aunty throws a slippah. "Ha ha HA."
The fourth uncle stands up, says nothing and slowly sits down on a whoopee cushion. PFFFFFT. The whole room explodes into one long, huge laugh that lasts four minutes. "POHHH... AHHH... HAAAAAAH!"
Four uncles, four jokes, one big long HAAAH. Pōʻahā. Thursday. Hā means four, and you stretch it out like the best laugh of the week.

words.say_it: Give an invisible high five. "Poh-ah-LEE-mah!"
words.bonus: Lima means both five and hand, which makes sense because a hand has five fingers.
words.picture: Fifty workers high fiving at 5 pm
story_paragraphs: It is 5 pm on Friday. The whistle blows at the construction site, and 50 workers drop their tools at the exact same second.

Then they start the Friday tradition. Everyone high fives everyone. Five fingers smacking five fingers. POW! POW! POW! 50 workers means over 1,200 high fives. Hands turn red. Birds fly away from the noise.
The foreman stands in the middle holding up one giant hand. "POW! Ah... LEE-MAH!" He wiggles his five fingers. Lima means hand, and lima also means five.
The workers chant with him. "POW! Ah, LEE-MAH!" Then they all run to the parking lot and go straight to the beach.
Pow, ah, lima. Pōʻalima. Friday. Day five. High five.

words.say_it: Read an invisible list and grab your head. "Poh-ah-OH-no!"
words.bonus: Ono means six. Don't mix it up with ʻono, with an ʻokina, which means delicious. Ono without it is also the name of a tasty fish, the wahoo.
words.picture: Chore list taped to a sleeping kid's forehead
story_paragraphs: It is Saturday. You sleep till 11. You wake up stretching and happy, thinking about the beach, a plate lunch and a nap in the hammock.
Then you notice something stuck to your forehead. A list, taped there while you were sleeping. Mom's handwriting. Six chores.
Clean the bathroom. Wash the car. Mow the lawn. Fold 18 loads of laundry. Bathe the dog. Paint the house.
"Po... ah... OH NO!"
You try to hide under the blanket. Mom is standing in the doorway holding a mop like a sword. The dog has already heard the word bath and is hiding under the house.
Po, ah, oh no. Pōʻaono. Saturday. Day six, one chore for each.

words.say_it: Hold on to an invisible tent in the wind. "EE-no!"
words.bonus: ʻIno also means bad or wicked, and hana ʻino means to treat someone badly.
words.picture: Beach picnic blowing away in a storm
story_paragraphs: You set up the perfect beach picnic at Kailua. Tent, cooler, plate lunches, a cake, a kite and a little inflatable pool for the baby.
Then the sky turns black in 30 seconds. The wind hits 80 miles an hour. Rain comes sideways, like somebody is spraying a hose at your face.

The tent lifts off like a rocket. "EEE! NO!" The plate lunches fly out of the cooler like frisbees. "EEE! NO!" The cake lands in a tree. The kite takes Uncle for a ride down the beach. The baby's pool, with the rubber duck still in it, sails out to sea.
Five minutes later the sun comes out. The beach is calm. The only thing left is you, holding one chopstick. Eee, no. ʻIno. Storm.

words.say_it: Pat your own back pocket. "Oh-KO-leh."
words.bonus: ʻŌkole is a casual, not very polite word. The more polite word is lemu. The toast ʻōkole maluna, bottoms up, is common today, but many older Hawaiians consider it vulgar, so use it with care.
words.picture: Uncle stuck in a giant bowl of coleslaw
story_paragraphs: It's the graduation party in the garage. Eight long tables of food. Uncle Keoki has been dancing for three hours, and finally he is tired. He backs up to sit on a folding chair without looking.
The chair is not there. What is there is a bowl of coleslaw as big as a washtub, sitting on a low stool.
SQUISH.
He sits right in it. Cabbage up to his waist. Mayo everywhere. He stands up, and the whole bowl comes with him, stuck to his rear end like a big white skirt.
He looks back over his shoulder and yells "OHHH! COLE..." He can't even finish the word slaw. The kids start chanting it. "Oh, cole! Oh, cole! Oh, cole!"
Oh, cole. ʻŌkole. Your rear end. Uncle Keoki wears that bowl for the rest of the party.

words.say_it: Rub your eyes and wail. "Vai-MAH-kah!"
words.bonus: Maka by itself means eye.
words.picture: Kid in goggles chopping onions in a flood of tears
story_paragraphs: It's the day before the big family lūʻau, and Ma hands you the job nobody wants. Fifty pounds of onions to chop for the lomi salmon. You start at 7 am.

By onion number three your eyes are watering. By onion twenty you are crying so hard the tears fill a bowl. By onion forty, a bucket. By noon the tears have filled the kitchen sink and spilled onto the floor, and your little brother is floating past on a boogie board.
You turn to Ma, sobbing. "WHY, MA? KAAAH!"
She hands you swim goggles. You finish the onions in goggles, standing in a lake of your own tears, while a few little fish swim around your feet.
Why, Ma, kah. Waimaka. Tears. Wai is water and maka is eye. Tears are eye water.

words.say_it: Take a deep breath and let it out long. "Haaaah."
words.bonus: Hā also means four, like in Pōʻahā, Thursday.
words.picture: Sixty kids blowing out 100 candles
story_paragraphs: Great Grandma Luana is turning 100. The cake has 100 candles and is so bright the neighbors think the house is on fire. She is too small to blow them all out by herself.
So all 60 grandkids and great grandkids gather around the table. Everyone leans in. Everyone takes the biggest breath of their lives. And together they let out one long breath.
"HAAAAAAAAAH!"
Every candle goes out at once. The napkins fly. A little cousin's hat blows off. The curtains flutter. Grandma's hair lifts up, and she laughs.
Then she does it the old way. She pulls you close, presses her nose and forehead to yours and breathes in. A honi. Sharing breath. Haaah. Hā. The breath of life, passed down and shared.

words.say_it: Wave your whole arm like a flag in the wind. "HAI!"
words.bonus: Ka Hae Hawaiʻi, the Hawaiian flag, has eight stripes for the eight main islands. Hae can also mean to bark, like a dog.
words.picture: Giant flag waving hi at everyone
story_paragraphs: Field day at school. The principal raises the biggest flag you have ever seen up the tall pole. It is 60 feet long, and the trade winds are blowing hard.
The flag flaps out over the field. It flaps so hard it looks like it's waving at people. Everyone waves back. "HI!"

It dips lower and knocks a kid's hat off. "HI!" It sweeps across the bleachers and gives every parent a gentle pat on the cheek. "HI! HI! HI!" It swings over the parking lot and wraps around the ice cream truck like a hug.
By the end of the day every person at school has been personally greeted by the flag. Hi. Hae. The flag that says hi to everybody.

words.say_it: Poke an invisible friend in the ribs. "Mah-kah-MAH-kah!"
words.bonus: A makamaka is the kind of friend you give to and take from freely, with no counting.
words.picture: Two old fishermen teasing each other on a boat
story_paragraphs: Uncle Kona and Uncle Bert have fished from the same little boat every Saturday for 40 years. And for 40 years they have not stopped teasing each other.
"Nice hat. Did a bird make it?" "Nice cast. Were you trying to catch the moon?"
The whole harbor calls them the Mock-a Mock-a Brothers, even though they are not related. When Bert pulls up in his truck at 4 am, Kona yells from the dock, "MOCK-A, MOCK-A!" and they both cackle.
But when Kona's truck broke down, Bert drove him to work for three months. When Bert's roof leaked, Kona showed up with shingles before breakfast. Neither one has ever kept score.
Mock-a, mock-a. Makamaka. A close friend. The one you can tease forever and give anything to.

words.say_it: Tap your foot twice and start dancing. "KOO-moo HOO-lah."
words.bonus: Kumu hula trace their knowledge through their own teachers, a line going back many generations.
words.picture: Kumu seeing the back row without turning around
story_paragraphs: You are in the back row of hula class, the very last line. You figure the kumu hula can't possibly see you back here. So you stop moving. You check your nails. You fix your slippah strap. You sneak a bite of a granola bar.
The kumu is at the front with her back to everybody, beating the drum. She doesn't turn around. She just says, calm and clear, "Come. Move. Hula."
You freeze. How? You start dancing again. Five minutes later you slow down. Without turning, "Come. Move. Hula."

After class she tells you she has been teaching for 40 years. She learned from her kumu, who learned from theirs, all the way back. She sees everything. Come, move, hula. Kumu hula. The teacher who holds the dances and passes them on.

words.say_it: Wag your finger at an invisible kid. "Hah-NOW-nah."
words.bonus: Hanauna is related to hānau, to be born, but hanauna itself has no kahakō. Hauʻoli lā hānau means happy birthday.
words.picture: Five generations wagging fingers down the line
story_paragraphs: Five generations of your family line up for a photo. Great great grandma, 101. Great grandma, 82. Grandma, 60. Mom, 38. And you, 15, holding your phone.
Great great grandma starts. "In my day we walked five miles to school with no shoes. HA! Now? NAH." She points at great grandma.
Great grandma turns to grandma. "In my day there was one phone for the whole street. HA! Now? NAH."
Grandma turns to Mom. "In my day we had to get up to change the TV channel. HA! Now? NAH."
Mom turns to you. "In my day we waited a whole week for the next show. HA! Now? NAH."
You turn to the family dog and open your mouth. Everyone cracks up. Ha, now, nah. Hanauna. A generation. Every one thinks the next one has it easy.

words.say_it: Ride an invisible tiny pony with your knees bent. "Pah-nee-OH-lo!"
words.bonus: The word comes from español. Cowboys from Mexico came in the 1800s to teach cattle work, and the paniolo tradition grew from there.
words.picture: Cowboy on a tiny pony, boots dragging
story_paragraphs: A cowboy rides into the Waimea rodeo. Big hat with a lei around it. Leather chaps, spurs, a rope coiled at his side. Very serious face.
He is riding a pony. A very, very small pony. So small that the cowboy's boots drag in the dirt on both sides, leaving two long lines behind him.
The whole crowd stands up and shouts. "PONY! OH... LOW!"

He doesn't care. He enters every event. He ropes a calf with his boots still dragging. He wins the race because the pony is so low it runs right under the fence. He tips his hat, the lei falls onto the pony's head, and the pony looks very proud.
Pony, oh, low. Paniolo. The Hawaiian cowboy.

words.say_it: Slice an invisible pan into tiny pieces. "Aah-PAH-nah."
words.bonus: ʻĀpana is also used for a section of land or a district.
words.picture: Aunty handing out mochi with tweezers
story_paragraphs: Aunty Wehi brings a pan of butter mochi to the park. Sixty kids line up. She has one pan.

She cuts it into 12 pieces. Not enough. She cuts each piece in half. Not enough. In half again. And again. By the time she's done, each piece is the size of a grain of rice, and she is handing them out with tweezers.
A kid holds his tiny piece up to the sun and squints at it. "Aaah... PAN, ah?" He looks at the empty pan, then back at his crumb.
Aunty shrugs and pulls a second pan from behind her back. Everyone screams.
Aaah, pan, ah. ʻĀpana. A piece. A section. Big or tiny, everyone gets one.

words.say_it: Break an invisible musubi in two. "HAH-pah."
words.bonus: Hapa comes from the English word half. Hapa haole music mixes Hawaiian style with English lyrics, and hapa is also used, warmly, for a person of mixed background.
words.picture: Uncle with a bag full of half foods
story_paragraphs: Uncle Keahi is on a diet, so he only eats half of everything. Half a musubi. Half a donut. Half a malasada. Half a plate lunch. He walks around with a bag full of the other halves, saving them for later.
At the drive in he orders "Half-a hamburger, half-a fries, half-a shake." The worker squints. "Half-a?" "HALF-A!" Say it fast and it sounds like hah-pah.

Then he looks up at the menu and sees the mixed plate. Chicken, beef, fish, rice and mac salad. A little part of everything, all together on one plate. His eyes light up. "That one! Little bit of this, little bit of that. Hapa everything."
Half-a. Hapa. A part, a portion. And also mixed, like a mixed plate.

words.say_it: Look at a price tag and grab your chest. "Koo-moo-koo-AI!"
words.bonus: Kumu means base or source, and kūʻai means to buy or sell. You saw kūʻai in hale kūʻai, the store.
words.picture: Broken cuckoo clock screaming at price tags
story_paragraphs: You walk into a fancy new store at Ala Moana. Everything is white and shiny. You pick up one mango. The price tag says $400.
On the wall, a cuckoo clock pops open and the little bird shoots out. But the prices here are so crazy they broke it. Instead of cuckoo it screams "KOO-MOO! KOO-AYE!"
You pick up a pair of slippahs. $900. "KOO-MOO! KOO-AYE!" A bag of rice. $2,000. The bird is shooting in and out so fast it gets dizzy.

Every time anyone looks at a price, the cuckoo goes cuckoo. You put everything down and walk back to Holly's corner store from hale kūʻai, where a mango costs 50 cents and the pigeon still pays in bottle caps.
Koo-moo, koo-aye. Kumukūʻai. The price.

words.say_it: Guard your plate and flinch. "Ow-HOW!"
words.bonus: In old Hawaiʻi, goods like food, kapa and feathers were brought as tribute to the chiefs during the Makahiki season.
words.picture: Goose with a clipboard taxing your lunch
story_paragraphs: You buy a plate lunch. Two scoops rice, mac salad, chicken katsu. You sit down at the picnic table, lift your chopsticks, and a big gray goose in a green visor lands on the table holding a clipboard.
It looks at your plate. It checks the clipboard. Then it leans in and bites off a piece of katsu, and a little of your finger too. "OW!" You stare at it. "HOW?!"

It pecks a scoop of rice. "OW! HOW?!" It takes a spoon of mac salad. "OW! HOW?!" By the time it's done, a fifth of your lunch is gone. The goose writes something on the clipboard, hands you a tiny receipt and waddles to the next table.
Ow, how. ʻAuhau. Tax. The piece of what you have that somebody always comes around to collect.
